_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences describing the TEXT itself: its contents, structure, and interest, with author and date kept brief. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: Justin composed this Latin epitome in the later Roman imperial period, abridging Pompeius Trogus's forty-four books of universal history. The preface states that the compiler excerpted material from Trogus while staying in Rome, omitting details that were neither pleasant to learn nor useful as examples. This choice aimed to remind readers who knew Greek and instruct those who did not. The text surveys world history from the Assyrian and Median monarchies of Ninus, Semiramis, and Sardanapalus, covering the rise of Persia under Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius. It includes the wars of the Athenians and Spartans from Marathon to the Sicilian expedition, detailing the reigns of Philip and Alexander, followed by the struggles of his successors, including the Ptolemies, Seleucids, and Antigonids. The work features digressions on Scythia, Carthage, Mithridates, Armenia, and Parthia, closing with the early history of Rome, including the Greek foundations of Massilia, and addresses Spain, from the story of Geryon to Augustus's reduction of the province.
la.hyginus.fabulae: The Fabulae of Hyginus is an early Imperial Latin collection of mythological summaries written in plain prose, where the title Fabulae means tales or stories. This selection presents individual entries from a handbook of roughly three hundred short summaries compiled under the name of Hyginus, perhaps in the second century AD. It opens with Prometheus, who fashioned humankind from clay and carried fire to them, before moving through compressed versions of the principal Greek myths arranged roughly by heroic generation. These include the loves of the gods, the Argonautic expedition, and the labours of Hercules, while the narrative continues with Theseus, the house of Oedipus, and the Trojan War. It concludes with the calamitous returns of the Greek leaders, including the wanderings of Ulixes, and shorter closing items offer the allegory of Cura and tales of famous friendships.
la.hyginus.astronomica: The Astronomica ('Astronomical Treatise') is an early imperial Latin prose work attributed to Hyginus. It draws on the Greek catasterism tradition to explain the placement of figures in the sky. A dedicatory preface to a learned correspondent defends the project and surveys the topics. The text begins with definitions of the world, the sphere, and the earth's habitability. It then recounts the mythological histories of the constellations and their placement among the stars. Later sections detail star arrangements, celestial circles, and the courses of the sun, moon, and planets.
la.isidore.etymologiae: Isidore's Etymologiae is a Latin prose encyclopedia of early medieval date. The title means 'Origins' and reflects the work's method of explaining terms through their word history. It is arranged in twenty successive books by subject. The first book on grammar defines discipline and art, lists the seven liberal arts, and treats letters, syllables, accents, metrical feet, and the parts of speech. Rhetoric, dialectic, and philosophical definitions follow, after which the text passes through the human body, its ages, portents, and monstrous peoples. Later books survey nations, kingdoms, military and civic institutions, kinship, marriage, war, games, ships, buildings, clothing, food, drink, vessels, and many other instruments and practices.
la.petrarch.africa: Africa is a Latin epic in hexameters by the Renaissance poet Petrarch, which recounts the Second Punic War in nine books. Modeled on Virgil and drawing its history from Livy, the work opens with an invocation to the Muses and an appeal to King Robert. The poem follows Scipio's campaigns in Spain and the invasion of Africa, incorporating Massinissa's love for the captive Sophonisba. A celestial vision shows Scipio's dead father foretelling victory, while the narrative covers the battle before Zama and Hannibal's flight. It closes with Scipio's triumphal return to Rome, and a dream features Homer prophesying the poem and its author's fame. The poet laments that King Robert died before the work was finished.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: Pomponius Mela's De Chorographia ('Description of the Earth') is the earliest surviving geography in Latin. Written around AD 43, this prose work opens by noting the difficulty of describing the world. It first outlines the earth's zones and its threefold division into Europe, Asia, and Africa. The text then surveys the Mediterranean coasts from Mauretania to Spain, recording cities and customs. From the Pillars of Hercules, it follows the outer ocean to India and the Red Sea. The account blends topography with ethnography and marvels before returning to the African shore.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: De Lingua Latina is a prose treatise by Varro on language and usage, written during the era of the Roman Republic. The work opens with a preface addressed to Septumius, where Varro outlines a six book plan for explaining how words were imposed on things. He distinguishes objections to etymology from arguments in its favour, using popular usage and the poets as the two main sources of vocabulary. The exposition ranges over the origins and corruption of words through age and change, setting out four graded levels of etymological explanation. These levels range from popular understanding to the most recondite, while the text treats the vocabulary of places and of times in turn. Abundant examples are drawn from early drama and everyday speech, and the work closes with a systematic account of analogy involving the like inflection of like words. Varro gives formal definitions of the word, likeness, and inflection, marking the classes of words in which analogy does or does not apply.
la.varro.res_rusticae: Varro's Res Rusticae ('On Agriculture') is a three-book prose treatise on farming from the Roman Republic. The octogenarian author opens with a preface to his wife Fundania, noting the need for practical guidance for her new farm. Book 1 is cast as a conversation at the temple of Tellus during the Sementivae festival. It covers land, soil, buildings, labor, and the seasonal round of ploughing, sowing, and harvesting. Book 2 turns to animal husbandry, treating the purchase, breeding, and care of sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle. Book 3, addressed to Pinnius, expounds villatica pastio, the rearing of birds, hares, bees, and fish near the villa.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: Velleius Paterculus composed this Latin prose universal history for the consul Marcus Vinicius, compressing it into two books, though only the second and greater part survives. It opens with the aftermath of the Trojan War and the movements of Greek peoples, then traces the succession of empires and the founding of colonies. The text gives particular weight to the Punic wars and the conquests of Greece, Africa, and Asia, highlighting the careers of commanders such as the Scipios, Marius, Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar. From the Gracchi onward, the author follows the civil wars in detail, describing the rise of Augustus and the military achievements of Tiberius. Velleius served in the German and Pannonian campaigns under Tiberius, and the history ends with a panegyric of the reigning emperor and a prayer for stability.
la.frontinus.strategemata: Frontinus's Strategemata is a Latin prose work of military science from the early imperial period that distinguishes the broad art of generalship from cleverly contrived deeds. The text presents a collection of examples arranged in three books, with Book 1 gathering stratagems used before battle, such as concealing plans and evading difficult positions. Book 2 covers battle and its aftermath, including feigned retreats and surprise attacks, while Book 3 turns to siegecraft, treating sudden assaults and the steadfastness of the besieged. A closing supplement collects exempla of generalship, discipline, and justice, which are drawn chiefly from Greek and Roman military history.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: De Aquis ('On the Waters') is a Latin prose treatise by Frontinus on the aqueducts of Rome. He wrote it after becoming curator aquarum under Nerva, with a closing note on improvements begun under Trajan. The preface explains his resolve to learn the office at first hand rather than rely on assistants. The text surveys the nine aqueducts, giving each builder, date, source, and delivery capacity. It then details pipe measures, water distribution, and the frauds practiced by workers and landowners. Later sections quote statutes, set out the staff and revenues, and list Frontinus's predecessors.
la.sidonius.carmina: Sidonius Apollinaris composed these poems in fifth-century Gaul before becoming bishop of Clermont, creating a Late Antique set of Latin verse in mixed meters. Its center of gravity is panegyric, which opens with a mythological prologue where gods, heroes, and demi-gods vie in celebrating Jupiter before the poet praises Anthemius. Later pieces extend this mode to Majorian and Avitus, while the range includes mythological narrative, epithalamia for Polemius and Ruricius, and invocations. It also features consolatory poems and short occasional verse, closing with lighter fare, including a valediction. This sends the little book on a circuit of friends' country houses in Gaul.
la.sidonius.epistulae: Sidonius' Epistulae comprise a prose collection in nine books by the Late Antique author, and a preface to Constantius explains that these polished letters were gathered into a single volume. The author professes to follow the roundness of Symmachus and the discipline of Pliny, while the addressees include aristocrats, holders of imperial office, and bishops in Gaul. The correspondence ranges from short notes of recommendation to extended set pieces, including a portrait of Theodoric, king of the Goths, which details his physical appearance and daily routine. A narrative describes a journey from Gaul to Rome, taking in the wedding of the patrician Ricimer, and an account covers the trial and condemnation of the ex-prefect Arvandus. A detailed tour of a villa includes its baths, porticoes, and lake, while playful exchanges about the author's own verses embed panegyric, epigrams, and metrical experiments in the prose. A concluding book is addressed largely to bishops, praising their conduct and pleading for captives, and it treats ecclesiastical affairs amid the disruptions of Gothic and Burgundian power.
la.fronto.epistulae: This correspondence of the orator Marcus Cornelius Fronto with his imperial pupils, chiefly Marcus Aurelius as Caesar and later as Augustus, was recovered from a palimpsest in 1815. It opens with affectionate exchanges in which Fronto and the young prince debate whether love needs a reason and trade playful literary exercises over sleep. The collection ranges across the Later Imperial epistolary world, taking in greetings, health reports, household news, and condolences. Their chief concern is eloquence, with criticism of word choice, comparisons of Cato, Sallust, and Cicero, and advice on composing and delivering speeches. Many letters pass between Latin and Greek, and the correspondence extends beyond the imperial house to Antoninus Pius, Lucius Verus, Herodes Atticus, and other friends. It closes with Greek letters and a miscellany of detached pieces, including a debate with a pupil over the value of rhetoric versus philosophy.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: Nemesianus of Carthage composed these four pastoral poems in the later third century AD, following the tradition established by Virgil and Calpurnius Siculus. The first eclogue invites the old shepherd Tityrus to sing, quickly becoming a lament for the recently deceased Meliboeus, who was a venerable arbiter of rural quarrels and a patron of song. The second poem features a serenade where Idas and Alcon vie for the love of Donace, while the third recounts how two boys steal the pipe of the sleeping god Pan. Pan consoles them with a hymn to Bacchus on his birth and nurture, and the fourth eclogue presents shepherds Lycidas and Mopsus exchanging songs of thwarted love. They use the refrain that each should sing what he loves to relieve cares.
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: The Cynegetica, a didactic poem in Latin hexameters on the chase, is attributed to Nemesianus, a poet of the later imperial period who wrote around AD 283. Its proem calls on Calliope and Diana while setting aside familiar mythological subjects, promising future verse on the victories of the sons of the deified emperor Carus. The instruction covers the choice of hounds from Laconian, Molossian, and British stocks, detailing their mating, rearing, and treatment of ailments like mange and rabies. Precepts on hunting horses of Greek and Cappadocian breeds follow, and the poem closes with hunters riding out at dawn across dew-laden meadows.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: The De aucupio, a brief Latin didactic poem in hexameters, is of later imperial date and attributed to Nemesianus, though its authorship is uncertain. The work survives only as a short fragment, opening in the midst of a survey of birds, declaring the tetrax the most foolish of them all. This bird, which at Rome they have begun to call 'taracem', runs heedlessly into snares, and the poem then follows the fowler's craft across particular species. It describes a bird that nests near Peltinum at the foot of the Apennines, and it also mentions the small-bodied guardian of the Tarpeian citadel, with a passing reference to Palamedes. A second section, set when the grove is stripped of its green, instructs the hunter on taking the woodcock, which feeds on worms along the water's edge and locates its prey by sharp scent rather than by sight.
la.symmachus.epistulae: The Epistulae preserve the correspondence of Symmachus, a late antique Roman senator and urban prefect, whose collection opens with letters to his father. These early texts mix news of life in the Campanian resorts with an exchange of epigrams and remarks on literary style. The middle section runs through letters to literary friends such as Ausonius and Agorius Praetextatus, containing a large body of letters of recommendation, congratulation, condolence, and friendly reproach addressed to relatives and unnamed correspondents. The closing portion consists of official reports to emperors including Theodosius and Honorius, covering judicial appeals, fiscal disputes, and the provisioning of Rome. These reports include the plea for the restoration of the Altar of Victory and the traditional rites, and the collection ends with prefectural correspondence on the contested episcopal election of Boniface and Eulalius.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: The Historia Calamitatum, a medieval Latin prose epistle by Peter Abelard, opens with the claim that examples console better than words. The writer sets down his trials so an absent friend may judge them slight, framing the correspondence with Heloise that follows. Abelard traces his Breton origins and renunciation of inheritance for study, detailing his rise as a controversial master of dialectic. His quarrels with William of Champeaux and Anselm of Laon are noted, continuing with his love for Heloise and their secret marriage. The brutal punishment of that union is described, leading to his monastic life at Saint-Denis and the condemnation of his treatise on the Trinity at Soissons. He fled the abbey after a dispute over its patron saint, closing the text with the founding of the oratory of the Paraclete, which he gifted to Heloise and her nuns. His unhappy tenure as abbot of Saint-Gildas in Brittany is recounted, marked by violence from rebellious monks and a local tyrant, ending with a concluding exhortation to patience drawn from scriptural authorities.
la.abelard.epistolae: This medieval Latin collection, attributed to Abelard, gathers the surviving correspondence between him and Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete. The exchange followed the Historia calamitatum ('The History of My Calamities'), the letter in which Abelard recounted his misfortunes to a friend. Heloise's opening letter salutes Abelard as her lord, father, husband, and brother, replying to that letter and complaining that he has sent her no consolation since their entry into religion. Abelard's responses offer spiritual counsel and forms of prayer for the sisters of the Paraclete, and answer her objections to his remarks on death and the manner of their conversion. The final and longest letter, written at Heloise's request, traces the authority and dignity of the monastic profession of women from its scriptural origins. It presents a complete rule for the Paraclete community, ordering its officers and divine office, and regulating solitude, food, dress, and discipline.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: This Latin prose dialogue, ascribed to Gregory the Great and composed in the late sixth century, is framed as conversations between Gregory and his deacon Peter. The work opens with Gregory lamenting the burdens of his pastoral office, recalling the contemplative peace of monastic life at this point. Peter then urges him to recount the holy men of Italy, and the first three books present lives and miracles of Italian saints and ascetics. These include Honoratus and Libertinus of Fundi, Equitius, and Germanus of Capua, while Benedict of Nursia is treated in extensive detail within this section. The text also covers Paulinus of Nola and martyrs under the Lombards, with doctrinal digressions on miracles, compunction, and prophecy interwoven throughout. The fourth book turns to the fate of souls after death, offering visions and exempla concerning judgment and purgatorial fire, and discussing the efficacy of masses for the dead before concluding with the eternal punishment of the damned.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: Gregory the Great's Regula Pastoralis, an early medieval Latin prose treatise on the pastoral office, opens as a letter of dedication to a fellow bishop named John, in which the author answers criticism that he had fled the burdens of rule and announces the book's fourfold plan. The first part weighs who should and should not undertake spiritual rule, the second sets out how a ruler should live, pure in thought, eminent in action, discreet in silence and in speech, and combining contemplation with care for his subjects, humility with the exercise of authority. The third and longest part teaches how the pastor should admonish, in a long series of paired admonitions matched to opposite dispositions among his hearers, from the proud and the diffident to the gluttonous and the abstinent, while the fourth treats how a pastor who has taught well should remember his own infirmity lest success breed elation. The argument advances by continuous scriptural exposition, with Old Testament persons, priestly vestments, and ritual objects read allegorically as images of the pastoral life.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: Lactantius Placidus's late-antique Latin prose gloss presents itself as a line-by-line explication of Statius's Thebaid, beginning with the opening invocation. It details the fraternal contest for the Theban throne, including the war between Eteocles and Polynices and the catalogue of Argive champions. The text covers Adrastus's double wedding, the fatal peregrinations of Oedipus's sons, and Amphiaraus's descent through the earth. Later passages gloss the deeds of Capaneus, Hippomedon, and Parthenopaeus, along with Menoeceus's self-sacrifice and the battle scenes where champions meet their ends. The commentary concludes with the mutual slaughter of the brothers, Creon's burial prohibition, and the arrival of Theseus's forces. Throughout, the author pauses on mythological allusions, Homeric and Vergilian echoes, and grammatical points, while marginal line markers allow the reader to follow the exposition verse by verse.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The Prima Pars, or First Part, of the Summa Theologiae is a Latin summa of theology by Thomas Aquinas. Written around 1265 to 1268, it contains 119 questions on God, creation, angels, and human nature. Each question is divided into articles that argue objections, an answer, and replies. The text opens with ten questions on the nature and necessity of sacred doctrine. It then argues for God's existence by five ways before treating the divine essence and attributes. The work covers the Trinity, the procession of creatures, and the hierarchy of angels. It concludes with questions on divine government, providence, and the propagation of man.
la.aquinas.hymni: This collection gathers five medieval Latin hymns attributed to Thomas Aquinas, which were composed for the feast of Corpus Christi in 1264. The work devotes itself entirely to the Eucharist and the presence of Christ under the forms of bread and wine. The volume opens with Pange lingua gloriosi corporis mysterium, which recounts the institution of the sacrament at the Last Supper. It ends with the famous stanza Tantum ergo, and the remainder includes Lauda Sion, a long sequence in praise of the eucharistic bread. It also contains Sacris solemniis, which features the Panis angelicus, and the collection further presents Verbum supernum prodiens, closing with the O salutaris hostia. Finally, it offers Adoro te devote, a devotional address to the deity veiled in the consecrated host.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: Moriae Encomium, meaning The Praise of Folly, is a Latin prose satire by Desiderius Erasmus that takes the form of a mock encomium delivered by the personified Folly. The work opens with a letter to Thomas More, who hosted the author in 1509, before Folly addresses an assembly of gods and mortals to praise her benefits. She lists youth, pleasure, friendship, and the happiness of simpletons, then turns to mock grammarians, poets, and scholastic theologians. The speech widens to criticize monks, bishops, and kings, and the text closes by arguing that Christian piety is a blessed folly.
la.erasmus.colloquia: Colloquia familiaria ('Familiar Dialogues') is a collection of Latin prose dialogues by Erasmus, who wrote and revised these texts during the early decades of the sixteenth century. The work presents an imagined series of conversations among schoolboys, travellers, merchants, and monks, and it also features soldiers, pilgrims, women, and personified figures such as Charon and a letter-writing Virgin. The collection opens with a narrative spoken by a shipwrecked traveller, who recounts a violent storm at sea and the superstitious vows of his fellow passengers, while the desperate swim that saved a handful of them concludes this opening scene. Across its many colloquies, the collection moves through satirical accounts of religious pilgrimages and relic-vending shrines, and it also covers the quarrels of mendicant orders at a deathbed and a pious household meal. The text includes an exposure of fraudulent exorcism and alchemy, as well as soldiering and mercenary life, and further topics include courtship and unequal marriage, and a dispute between wives on the dignity of women. A prostitute reclaimed by Evangelical reading and catechetical examinations of the Creed also appear, and the work closes with a defence of the true Epicurean pleasure of a pious conscience.
la.alan_de_insulis.anticlaudianus: The Anticlaudianus, a Latin allegorical epic by Alan of Lille, mocks Claudian's invective against Rufinus by proposing an opposite. Its prose prologue submits the text to the reader's correction, announcing that literal, moral, and allegorical levels suit different grades of understanding. Nature gathers the personified virtues to forge a perfect new man, while Prudence rides a chariot built by the arts of the trivium and quadrivium. She travels through the planetary spheres and fixed stars to the empyrean, where she obtains from God the soul that the fashioned body requires. The completed hero receives gifts from Fortune and Nobility, then routs the army of vices in a final battle. The closing epilogue turns from the created universe to its Creator.
la.alan_de_insulis.de_planctu_naturae: De Planctu Naturae ('The Lament of Nature') is a medieval Latin prosimetrum attributed to Alan of Lille. It alternates elegiac verse with ornate prose in a dialogue written around 1160 to 1170. The speaker laments that laughter has turned to tears as mankind perverts the laws of Venus. Nature appears in a vision to discourse on her office as God's deputy in generation. She condemns sexual deviance, gluttony, avarice, and pride among other vices. The priest Genius finally pronounces excommunication upon the offenders.
la.bernard_silvestris.cosmographia: Bernard Silvestris's Cosmographia, also known as De mundi universitate, is a medieval philosophical allegory in mixed prose and verse. Written around 1147, the work draws on Plato's Timaeus by way of Chalcidius to explain the creation of the world. It opens with a dedicatory letter to Thierry of Chartres, where the author hesitantly submits his difficult treatise for correction. The first book, the Megacosmus, describes how divine providence orders the greater world from prime matter. Natura's complaint moves Noys to separate the elements, establish angelic hierarchies, and fix the stars and planetary orbits. The second book, the Microcosmus, turns to the lesser world and the making of man, where Natura and Urania descend to gather the soul's celestial endowment, while Physis fashions the human body from the remaining elements. The text closes with an account of the head, senses, heart, liver, and organs of generation.
la.cassiodorus.institutiones: A didactic prose treatise in two books by Cassiodorus, written in Late Antiquity for the monks of the Vivarium monastery. The opening preface recounts the author's grief that public teachers of Scripture were lacking, recalls his failed plan, with Pope Agapitus, to endow a Christian school in Rome, and offers these introductory books in its place. Book 1 organises the study of Scripture around nine codices, surveying for each the Latin and Greek commentators and translators, giving rules for correcting, punctuating and copying manuscripts, and cataloguing the fathers, historians and other writers the monastic library should contain. Book 2 turns to secular learning, presenting compressed accounts of grammar, rhetoric and dialectic and of the four mathematical disciplines of arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy, so that worldly letters may serve divine reading.
la.cassiodorus.variae: The Variae ('Miscellanies') is a Latin epistolary collection in twelve books by Cassiodorus, a Roman official of late antiquity who drafted state papers for the Ostrogothic rulers of Italy. A preface relates how friends persuaded the reluctant author to gather into one place the dictations pronounced in his successive high offices, and the collection took shape around 537. Its books assemble royal edicts and letters of appointment couched in praise and moral exhortation, alongside instructions on justice, taxation, the grain supply and public building. There is also diplomatic correspondence with the Eastern emperors and neighbouring peoples, while the later books contain letters issued from the author's own praetorian prefecture. Books six and seven preserve formulas for the palatine offices, included, as the author explains, to assist successors pressed for time.
la.venantius_fortunatus.carmina: Carmina, a late-antique Latin collection of occasional verse in mixed meters, was written by Venantius Fortunatus, an Italian who settled in Merovingian Gaul. The work opens with a panegyric for Bishop Vitalis of Bordeaux, then ranges widely through verse letters and encomia for bishops like Gregory of Tours. It also includes praise and petition poems for Merovingian kings and queens, featuring a notable epithalamium celebrating the marriage of Sigibert and Brunhild. The volume features a long lament for the dead queen Gelesuintha, while prose supplements the verse with expositions of the Lord's Prayer and the Creed. Four books detail the life and miracles of St Martin of Tours, and a light first-person travel poem on a journey up the Moselle closes the work.
la.venantius_fortunatus.vita_martini: Venantius Fortunatus composed this late antique epic in Latin hexameters across four books, titled Vita Martini, which means the life of Martin, the bishop of Tours. The work closely follows the prose accounts written by Sulpicius Severus, casting a saint's biography in the meter and diction of Virgilian epic. The poem opens with Christ's triumphal return to heaven after despoiling hell, and a survey of earlier Christian poets precedes the author's self-deprecating prologue. The narrative traces Martin from his birth in Pannonia to his renunciation of military service under Julian, detailing his gift of a cloak to a beggar at Amiens. His association with Hilary of Poitiers and his episcopate at Tours follow, marked by the destruction of rural temples and various miracles. These include resurrections, healings, exorcisms, and visions of angels, while Martin also confronts emperors such as Maximus and Valentinian. The poem closes with Brictio's rebellion and subsequent reconciliation, and further miracles show the saint's advocacy for prisoners. A closing itinerary leads to his shrine, where prayers ask for Martin's intercession, including the restoration of the poet's eyesight.
la.walter_de_chatillon.alexandreis: The Alexandreis is a medieval Latin epic in hexameters by Walter of Châtillon, which recounts the career of Alexander the Great in ten books. Completed around 1180, the work closely follows the ancient historian Quintus Curtius Rufus, and a prose preface explains why the author had long withheld the poem from the public. This introduction leads into an invocation that calls on the Muse to sing the deeds of the Macedonian king, and the narrative follows Alexander from his boyhood and the moral instruction he receives from Aristotle. It covers his accession, the subjugation of Greece, and his crossing into Asia, where victories over Darius at Granicus, Issus, and Arbela are followed by the fall of Tyre, Gaza, Persepolis, and Babylon. Set speeches and reflections on the mutability of Fortune punctuate the later books, which relate Darius's murder by the traitor Bessus and the Scythian war. The poem also describes the defeat of Porus in India and Alexander's death by poison at Babylon, and an epilogue commends the finished work to its episcopal patron.
la.nigel_wireker.speculum_stultorum: A Latin verse satire of medieval date, attributed to Nigel Wireker and written in elegiac couplets, opening with a prologue addressed to one Willelme in which the author defends the use of humble and apparently inept matter to convey serious moral teaching. The work follows the talking ass Burnellus, who first seeks to lengthen his short tail against the advice of the physician Galienus, a counsel framed by the tale of the cows Brunetta and Bicornis and the losses that follow Bicornis's impatience. Setting out for Salerno for remedies, Burnellus is cheated of his goods, attacked by Cistercian dogs, and dispatches their prior Fromundus in the Rhone before turning to study at Paris, where he learns nothing in seven years, adopts the name Parisius, and after various mishaps resolves to found a new religious order combining whatever he likes from each of the existing orders. On his way to Rome for confirmation he encounters Galienus again, and their ensuing exchange unfolds into a long satirical survey of the vices of the age, attacking the greed of the Roman curia, the failings of kings, unworthy bishops and pastors, monastic orders, secular canons, and nuns, with embedded beast fables of the crow, cock, and other birds on ingratitude and the dangers of a loquacious tongue. A final exemplum of the rustico Bernardus, who rescues Dryanus and his animal companions from a pit and is rewarded while his ungrateful lord is punished, closes the poem, which the author ends by directing the reader to seek the moral sense beneath the surface of the tale.
la.johannes_hanville.architrenius: The Architrenius, a medieval Latin satire in hexameter verse attributed to Johannes Hanville, was written around 1184. The poem follows a young man who seeks out Mother Nature to complain of human vices. After a prologue addressing a patron, the hero journeys through a world of personified temptations. He encounters the golden house of Venus, gluttonous banquets, and the poverty of Parisian scholars. The narrative also features the mountain of ambition, court flatteries, and the tyranny of avarice. Ancient philosophers deliver long moralising speeches against anger, envy, luxury, lust, and hypocrisy. Nature eventually appears to arrange the hero's marriage to a modest and virtuous bride. The work concludes with a farewell address to the book and its author.
la.carmina_burana.carmina_burana: The Carmina Burana is a medieval Latin collection of goliardic verse of uncertain authorship, drawn principally from clerical and student circles of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The poems are preserved in a manuscript associated with the Bavarian abbey of Benediktbeuern, and this corpus transcribes the complete sequence of poems CB 1 to 228 together with the supplement. The opening poem is a satire on the power of money, depicting how coin perverts courts and church offices, while the collection continues through moral and satirical verse against avarice, simony, and corruption among prelates. The poems then turn to laments on Fortune and the wheel of fate, with its famous meditations on mutable prosperity, followed by love songs in springtime settings, drinking songs of the tavern, and pieces on gambling. The later portion includes liturgical plays on the Nativity, the Passion, and the Resurrection of Christ, and it also features laments of the Virgin at the Cross and miracle material such as the story of Mary Magdalene. The collection closes with devotional poems to saints and Easter and Passion-tide offices.
la.tiberianus.carmina: The Carmina ('Poems'), a small collection of Late Antique lyric poems in mixed meters, are attributed to Tiberianus, a fourth-century Roman senator and praetorian prefect of Gaul under Constantine. It opens with an ornate description of a springtime landscape, its clear stream winding between flowering banks amid birdsong and fragrant groves, the rose reigning as queen of colors. The remaining pieces are shorter and varied in theme, among them an invective against gold unfolded through mythological episodes that show its power to corrupt. A fable tells of a bird weighted down by rain-soaked plumage that falls from the sky, with a moral against those who soar on prosperous winds. Another poem is a hymn invoking a single omnipotent deity as the cause, soul, and sustaining order of the universe. The collection closes with a few epigrammatic lines, including one on Pegasus and another defining nature as a stream that mirrors what it receives.
la.pentadius.carmina: Pentadius was a Late Antique Latin poet of the third or fourth century, known only from Riese's Anthologia Latina, which preserves six short elegiac epigrams by him. The collection opens with a series of couplets built on a repeated phrase whose sense is reversed or darkened between hexameter and pentameter. These draw moralising turns from mythological exempla such as Procne, Medea, Orpheus and Eurydice, and Daedalus and Icarus. A longer poem, De adventu veris ('The Coming of Spring'), describes the season's swallows, flowers, echoing streams and the shade of the plane tree. It passes into couplets on the youth Narcissus, who wastes away gazing at his reflection in his father's river. The closing epigrams on adultery and women's supposed faithlessness end in the verdict that no woman is good, and that even a good one is made so by some strange fate.
la.prudentius.cathemerinon: Prudentius composed the Cathemerinon, a title meaning the book of the hours, as a cycle of twelve Latin hymns. These poems follow the daily rhythm of Christian devotion, moving from dawn to night. The opening hymn uses the cock's crow as an allegory for Christ calling the soul to wake from sin. Subsequent verses address sunrise, meals, lamp lighting, and sleep in a similar devotional key. The collection also treats biblical narratives, including the crossing of the Red Sea and Jonah at Nineveh. It concludes with hymns praising Christ as king and covering Christmas themes.
la.matthew_of_vendome.ars_versificatoria: The Ars Versificatoria is a medieval Latin art of versification attributed to Matthew of Vendôme, composed largely in prose and illustrated throughout by Latin verse examples. It opens with a polemical prologue in which the author, defending his novelties against a detractor named Rufinus, presents the work as an introduction for the less advanced. The instruction then covers ways of beginning a composition (zeugma, hypozeusis, the general proverb), epithets, the eleven attributes of persons and the circumstances of a deed, and the threefold elegance of verse residing in meaning, verbal ornament, and manner of speaking. Later sections on figures of speech, tropes such as metaphor and antithesis, the execution and paraphrastic variation of material, and the correction of verses are punctuated by sustained original descriptions in praise and blame, of a pope, Caesar, Ulysses, the slavish Davus, Marcia, a beautiful girl, and a hideous old woman, before the treatise ends with a doxology and a mention of the author's Summula for teaching boys.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.poetria_nova: Geoffrey of Vinsauf's Poetria Nova ('The New Art of Poetry'), a medieval Latin treatise on the art of composition, cast in hexameter verse, was written around 1208 to 1213. Organized around the stages of invention, arrangement and style, it opens with a dedicatory address to Pope Innocent III, whose name the poet divides to satisfy the metre. The bulk of the poem is a systematic course in rhetorical craft, covering mental design before writing, the choice between natural and artificial order, and techniques of amplification and abbreviation. A long succession of 'colours' of diction follows, among them apostrophe, prosopopoeia, description and emphasis. These are illustrated by examples ranging from a lament for King Richard and the complaint of the Holy Cross to descriptions of beauty and banquets. Advice on memory and on delivery in recitation, followed by a closing dedication to a William, brings the work to its end.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.documentum: Geoffrey of Vinsauf wrote this Latin treatise as a prose companion to his Poetria Nova. The title Documentum means a manual or instruction, fitting its schoolroom purpose. It covers the art of letter writing and verse composition in a systematic way. The text begins by cataloguing natural and artificial ways to start a piece. It then explains how to expand or contract material using various rhetorical devices. Later sections address elegant style, delivery, and methods for concluding a work.
la.eberhard_the_german.laborintus: The Laborintus, a medieval Latin didactic poem in mixed metres, is attributed to Eberhard the German, who was active in the early thirteenth century. Framed as a complaint about contemporary education, the poet receives a commission from his Muse to write on the schoolmaster's burden. He must address governing himself and his pupils, followed by an allegory of a boy born under baleful stars and doomed to poverty. Philosophy presents her seven daughters, the liberal arts, to this student, while Grammar nurses him on Donatus, Cato, and elementary schoolbooks. The central portion expounds metres, tropes, schemes, and composition, surveying authors from Cato and Ovid to Virgil and Prudentius. The text displays unusual verse forms, and the work closes with the mother of elegies lamenting the teacher's miseries.
la.petrus_riga.de_ornatu_mundi: De Ornatu Mundi, a short medieval Latin religious poem in elegiac couplets, is attributed to Peter Riga, a twelfth-century canon of Reims. The work is distinct from his much longer verse Bible paraphrase, the Aurora, though a printed source transmits it under the name of Hildebert of Lavardin. The poem opens with an invocation to Clio to sharpen the poet's style, then offers an elaborate encomium of paradise, describing its trees, fruits, and springs. The text also details the birds, beasts, and a great cedar harbouring bees, alongside an encircling wall, river, and bridge. A towering gate, wrought by Vulcan with the aid of the Cyclopes, gleams with silver, gold, gems, and ivory. The closing lines concede that this ornament must wither, urging the pursuit of the unfading rose, the flower of the field.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_africo: De Bello Africo ('On the African War') is a Latin prose account of Caesar's campaign in 47 to 46 BC. It continues the Civil War commentaries in a plainer style, written by an officer who served in the conflict. The text narrates the landing at Hadrumetum and the struggle against Scipio, Labienus, Cato, and Juba. It details operations around Ruspina and Uzitta, including supply issues and naval skirmishes. The narrative culminates in the battle of Thapsus, Cato's suicide, and the deaths of Juba and Scipio. The work also features speeches and close attention to tactics, logistics, and the use of elephants.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_alexandrino: The Bellum Alexandrinum, a Latin prose narrative of uncertain authorship, continues the account of the civil wars after Pompey's defeat. Likely written soon after the events by an author in Caesar's circle, it opens with Caesar summoning fleets and auxiliaries from Rhodes, Syria, and Cilicia. The narrative follows the urban and naval fighting around the city, detailing the intrigues of Arsinoe and her minister Ganymedes. A relief force led by Mithridates of Pergamum arrives, and King Ptolemy is defeated and killed, so Caesar settles Egypt under Cleopatra. Later chapters recount Domitius Calvinus's defeat by Pharnaces near Nicopolis, while Vatinius wins a naval victory over Marcus Octavius in Illyricum. Quintus Cassius Longinus faces extortion, mutiny, and death in Further Spain, and the work closes with Caesar's rapid march through Syria, Cilicia, and Asia. He achieves a decisive victory over Pharnaces near Zela, reorganizes the eastern provinces and client kings, and then makes a hurried return to Italy.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_hispaniensi: De Bello Hispaniensi, a Latin prose account of uncertain authorship, narrates the final campaign against the younger Gnaeus Pompeius in 45 BC. The text opens after Caesar's victories over Pharnaces and in Africa, while Pompeius ravages Further Spain. The narrative follows Caesar's rapid arrival and the siege of Ategua, continuing along the river Salsum and at Ulia and Corduba. These encounters feature frequent skirmishes, sieges, and defections, culminating in the decisive battle of Munda. Labienus and Attius Varus fall during this engagement, and the work closes with the younger Pompeius's flight and death. It also covers the reduction of remaining towns and his fleet, ending with Caesar's address to the provincials at Hispalis.
la.vegetius.epitoma_rei_militaris: Vegetius's Epitoma Rei Militaris ('Epitome of Military Science') is a late-antique Latin technical treatise on warfare, addressed to an unnamed emperor. Written about AD 390 and compiled from earlier writers rather than from experience, it abridges their military doctrine in four books. A preface outlines the scope of each book and argues that victory derives from training and discipline rather than from mere numbers. Book one treats the selection and training of recruits, and book two the organisation, ranks, and administration of the legion. Generalship and the tactics of land battle are the subject of book three, which closes with a set of general maxims on war. Book four turns to siegecraft, covering the fortification and defence of cities, the machinery of assault, and the conduct of naval warfare.
la.grattius.cynegetica: The Cynegetica, an Augustan didactic poem in hexameters by Grattius, opens with an invocation to Diana that frames hunting as a divine gift and a stage in human progress. The bulk of the work surveys the hunter's equipment, including nets, lines, snares, and spears, while noting materials drawn from various regions. It invokes the legendary Arcadian huntsmen Dercylus and Hagnon, who serve as exemplars of the tracking dogs known as metagones. The poem then catalogues dog breeds and their temperaments, offering instruction on breeding, rearing, and training puppies. It covers the choice of a trainer and his arms, as well as the diseases of dogs and their cures, ranging from practical treatments to a healing ritual at the volcanic spring of Vulcan. The work ends with an account of the horses suited to the chase, where the surviving text breaks off.
la.germanicus.aratea: The Aratea is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters by Germanicus, nephew and adopted son of Tiberius. It adapts Aratus's Phaenomena into verse during the Early Imperial period. The work opens with a dedication to the emperor, recalling Aratus's beginning from Jove. It credits the imperial peace with leaving mortals free to study the heavens. The body surveys the constellations of both hemispheres and recounts their attached myths. It also treats of stars scattered through the sky that form no figure. The poem closes with the risings of the signs, which serve as markers of the hours of the night, of winds, and of weather.
la.solinus.collectanea_rerum_memorabilium: Solinus, a Latin author of uncertain date, wrote this prose compendium in later imperial times, and the title means a collection of memorable things. The work opens with a preface explaining its method and sources, and it begins with Rome, covering its legendary origins and kings. The text then surveys Italy, Sicily, Greece, and Macedonia, and it proceeds through Thrace and the northern regions of Europe. The greater part tours the inhabited world by region, including Germania, Gaul, Hispania, and Africa, while Egypt, Arabia, Asia, and India are also described. Each region lists notable rivers, mountains, and cities, and stones, plants, animals, and exotic customs are recorded. The work closes with distant islands like the Fortunatae, and it ends with an account of the ocean surrounding the oikoumene.
la.censorinus.de_die_natali: De Die Natali is a Latin treatise by Censorinus from the later imperial period, serving as a birthday offering to Quintus Caerellius. The work opens with a preface explaining that Censorinus chose learned questions over moral precepts, and it explores the genius honoured on birthdays. It covers ancient views on human origins, Chaldaean planetary doctrines, and Pythagorean numerology, while discussing the ages of man and their climacteric years. The treatise examines natural and civil saecula, including Etruscan and Roman examples, and details the great years assigned by various peoples. The Roman year and Julius Caesar's calendar reform receive attention, and the names of the months are listed. The work concludes with definitions of day and hour, though the transmitted text breaks off before the epilogue.
la.obsequens.liber_de_prodigiis: The Liber de Prodigiis, meaning Book of Prodigies, is a late antique Latin work by Obsequens that assembles reports of portents drawn from Roman republican history. The text is arranged year by year under consular dates, running from the early second century BC into the age of Augustus. Entries catalogue rains of blood, milk, and stone, along with monstrous births, and they also record speaking oxen, sweating statues, and celestial fires. Most marvels are followed by expiations prescribed by the haruspices, and interwoven with these are notices of wars, pestilences, and political crises. These range from struggles with the Celtiberi to the campaigns of Drusus.
la.adamnan.de_locis_santis: De Locis Sanctis is an early medieval Latin prose treatise by Adamnan, which records the topography of Jerusalem and surrounding sites as reported by the pilgrim Arculf. The text supplements these accounts with excerpts from earlier authorities such as Jerome, and it opens with the situation of Jerusalem, its walls, towers, and gates. The round church of the Anastasis over the Holy Sepulchre is described next, with its form detailed from a plan Arculf drew on a wax tablet. The narrative then proceeds through Golgotha and Constantine's basilica, covering relics preserved in the city, the Mount of Olives, and Bethlehem. Hebron and the tombs of the patriarchs are also discussed, and the tour continues to Jericho, the Jordan, and the Dead Sea. The lake of Tiberias, Sichem, Nazareth, and Tabor follow in sequence, while Damascus and Tyre are described before later chapters turn to Alexandria. The Nile and Constantinople are treated, including the veneration of the True Cross, and several miracle stories appear in the section on Constantinople. The work concludes with a volcanic island east of Sicily, and it closes with an appeal for the reader's prayers.
la.aethelwulf.carmen_de_abbatibus: Carmen de Abbatibus ('Song of the Abbots') is a medieval Latin poem of the Carolingian era by Aethelwulf, its title announcing a verse account of abbots. It opens with a humble dedication to a bishop preeminent among the English, offering rustic verses and asking indulgence for the poet's untutored song. From there the poem turns to Northumbrian history, recounting the fall of King Ecgfrith to the Picts and the accession of his brother Aldfrith. Under Aldfrith a monastery was founded, and the poem recounts the community's noble first abbot, Eanmund, who abandoned a military life for monastic service. The deeds and piety of the abbots who succeeded him form the work's principal subject.
la.agius_of_corvey.epicedium_hathumodae: The Epicedium Hathumodae ('Funeral Lament for Hathumoda') is a Carolingian Latin funeral lament composed by Agius of Corvey for Hathumoda, an abbess who died in the flower of her youth. The poem opens with the poet explaining that the consolations he had spoken amid weeping to Hathumoda's sisters at her death he now casts into verse at their request, adding further material. The greater part is a dialogue of mourning with her community. The speaker urges moderation of grief, catalogues biblical deaths from patriarchs and prophets to apostles and Christ himself to show mortality's universality, and argues that the spirit rather than the flesh is to be loved. He also assures the nuns that God and Hathumoda herself will continue to protect them. A closing exchange with Gerberga, Hathumoda's successor as abbess, recalls and interprets dream visions of a tottering wall and a tall tree that concern her family and confirm her worthy succession.
la.agius_of_corvey.versus_computistici: The Versus Computistici is a Carolingian Latin didactic poem on the computus, the reckoning of calendar days and movable feasts. It is attributed to Agius of Corvey and addressed to a certain Rimbert. The prologue asserts that God is the source of all arts and that number excels other disciplines. The author explains that he compiled the work at Rimbert's request and puns that his name means clear in number. The main body expounds tables constructed by means of letters and numerals, including pages for finding the weekday of each kalends throughout the year. These tables also cover solar and lunar cycles, epacts, and concurrents, while paired tables of thirty and twenty-nine days follow the moon through its nineteen-year cycle. Later sections describe the paschal cycle, which is complete after 532 years, and a great cycle of the same length marks common years in black ink and embolismic ones in red. Leap years are marked by the letter B, and the poem closes with instructions for reckoning the date of Easter and of three feasts in any year, backward or forward.
la.agnellus_ravennatis.liber_pontificalis: The Liber pontificalis ('Book of the Pontiffs') is a Latin ecclesiastical history composed in the Carolingian period by Agnellus of Ravenna, a priest of the city. Though largely prose, it carries a verse preface and verse inscriptions. In the metrical opening Agnellus recounts how local priests urged him to write down the lives of the city's pontiffs, long left unrecorded. The body of the work consists of numbered biographies of Ravenna's bishops and archbishops, running through late antiquity to the author's own contemporaries. The series opens with Apollinaris, the disciple of Peter sent to preach at Ravenna. Alongside the lives it preserves miracle narratives, accounts of church foundations and restorations with their dedicatory verses, and the epitaphs of several Ravennate bishops.
la.aimoin_of_saint_germain.carmen_de_transl: Carmen de Translatione Vincentii, a short medieval Latin poem from the Carolingian era, is attributed to Aimoin of Saint Germain and follows relic translation conventions. The narrative opens with a chronological formula, introducing Audaldus, a monk and priest of Castrum, who sets out with a single companion for Valencia in Spain. They aim to recover the relics of Vincent, a Spanish deacon and martyr, and they bribe Zacharias, the Muslim custodian, to uncover the tomb after reading its inscription. The pair carry the sacred body home beneath the stars to the cell of Saint Benedict, where the poem recounts the arrival of the relics. A woman who doubted their origin is healed, and the text describes many subsequent miracles, including the body's placement behind the altar, where it shines with signs of virtue.
la.alcuin.carmina: This Latin verse collection, attributed to Alcuin, a prominent Carolingian scholar, contains long narrative, epistolary, and epigraphic poems. It opens with an invocation to Christ and the saints, followed by a substantial poem on the church of York. This narrative traces the city from its Roman foundation through the arrival of the Saxons and the conversion of the Northumbrians under Edwin and Paulinus. It details the reigns and miracles associated with Oswald and Oswiu, while also honoring the saints Cuthbert, Bede, and Wilfrid. The poem concludes with the poet's own masters, pupils, and library, and the remainder gathers occasional and devotional verse. Court poems and precepts are addressed to Charlemagne, who is styled Karolus and David in these texts.
la.amalarius.versus_marini: The Versus Marini is a short medieval Latin narrative poem from the Carolingian period, whose title means the verse of the sea. Attributed to Amalarius, the work follows a party of monks on a voyage by sea, opening with a questioning address to an abba. The narrative carries the travelers to Constantinople, where they pass a long sojourn before being summoned to the royal palaces by the emperor Leo. The homeward leg brings fierce winds and a prophetic warning against Moors and Slavs, closing with a tearful welcome from the brethren in green Italy.
la.ambrose.exameron: Ambrose's Exameron is a late antique work of Latin theology in prose, comprising nine sermons that expound the six days of creation in the opening chapter of Genesis. It opens with a survey of the opinions of Plato, Aristotle, and other Greek philosophers on the origin, matter, and eternity of the world, against which Moses' words 'In the beginning God created heaven and earth' are set. The sermons then follow the creation week day by day, treating the first light, the firmament and the waters above it, the gathering of the seas and the appearance of dry land with its vegetation, the sun, moon, and stars, the fish and birds of the waters and air, and finally the land animals and humankind, interweaving discussion of the elements and the heavens with refutations of philosophical, astrological, and heretical teaching and with moral exhortation drawn from the behaviour of animals. The work closes with an account of the human being made in God's image and likeness, a survey of the human body as a microcosm of the universe, and God's rest after the completion of the works.
la.ambrose.explanatio_psalmorum_xii: A Latin prose commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, explaining twelve Psalms. Opening with a discussion of how delectation, or pleasure, figures both in the divine call to virtue and in the devil's promptings toward error, the work proceeds psalm by psalm, beginning with the first Psalm's 'Beatus vir' and passing through Psalms 30-50, including the penitential Psalms 38, 39 and 50, and Psalm 47. Each psalm is expounded verse by verse, with sustained attention to its title and inscription, and the exposition alternates between moral exhortation on virtue, silence, patience and poverty and christological and mystical readings that see the passion, priesthood and resurrection of Christ foreshadowed in the text. Ambrose draws extensively on the Old Testament narratives and on the Apostle Paul, quotes alternative Greek and Latin renderings of difficult verses, and closes discussions with doxological conclusions, while the opening book offers a broader encomium on the psalter as a school of doctrine, medicine for the soul and a discipline uniting the whole people in song.
la.ambrosiaster.pseudo_augustini_quaestione: This Late Antique Latin collection contains 127 questions on scriptural and theological difficulties. It is attributed to Ambrosiaster but was long transmitted under Augustine's name. The work opens with a treatise on the divine nature and the nature of evil. It then addresses problems raised by Genesis and the Mosaic law. These topics include creation, the fall, and the giving of the law. The collection later turns to the Psalms, Gospels, and Pauline epistles. It also discusses the Trinity and refutes contemporary opponents.
la.ammianus.rerum_gestarum: Ammianus Marcellinus composed this Late Antique Latin prose history, known as the Res Gestae, or 'deeds done.' The surviving later books open with the savage rule of the Caesar Gallus in the East. The narrative then follows Constantius's reign, the court purges, and Julian's rise to sole rule. It covers Julian's Persian expedition and death, along with the reigns of Valentinian and Valens. The story closes with the Gothic crossing of the Danube and the defeat at Hadrianople. Valens perished in that battle, ending the account of Roman affairs from Nerva to his death.
la.angilbert_carmina: This short collection of Latin occasional verse is by Angilbert, a poet of Charlemagne's court who styles himself Homerus. The opening poem addresses Pippin returning from Italy and dwells on the joy of his father Charles. It also describes the longing of his brother Chlodowih and the royal sisters. A long central cycle praises the palace circle under the biblical king David. This section includes Charlemagne, his consecrated sister Gisla, and the princesses Rothrude and Bertha. The remainder of the work contains religious and epigraphic material. It features prayers for Saints Richarius and Eligius and tituli for buildings at Centula. The collection concludes with epitaphs, including a verse monument for the priest Chaidocus.
la.angilbert_versus: This short Carolingian poem, ascribed to the abbot Angilbert, opens by praising the sound doctrine that Augustine set forth in his work De doctrina christiana. The body of the text runs through the contents of that work's four books, with the first teaching Christ's precepts and distinguishing right use from enjoyment. The second shows how signs are to be recognized, while the third treats what signs and words signify. The fourth gathers the sayings of the earlier books and sets forth the three manners of speech. The closing lines name the lowly abbot Angilbert as the one who had the little book made. He offered it to the pious King Louis, ending with praise of the Trinity.
la.angilbertus_miles.versus_de_fontaneto: The Versus de Fontaneto is a short Carolingian Latin poem about a battle at Fontaneto, where the title refers to the village. It is attributed to Angilbertus, who presents himself as a soldier and eyewitness to the events. The poem opens with dawn breaking on the day of battle, depicting a scene of fratricidal strife. God's right hand shields Lothar as the victor, while the fields on the side of Charles and Louis grow white with the garments of the dead. Corpses are abandoned unburied to vultures, crows, and wolves, and the speaker, sole survivor of his part of the front line, curses the day of battle. He also curses the grass where the brave men fell, and the poem ends with a prayer to the Lord for the souls of the slain.
la.anonymi.planctus_de_obitu_Karoli: The Planctus de Obitu Karoli, an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, belongs to the planctus tradition marking a ruler's death. It opens with grief stretching from the rising to the setting sun, as all peoples beat their breasts at the news of the emperor's death. The poem enumerates mourners, including Franks, Romans, infants, and elders, while portraying Charles as the common father of orphans, pilgrims, widows, and virgins. Woes are uttered against Rome, Italy, and Francia over his burial at Aachen, and the work closes with prayers to Christ and an address to the scribe Columbanus. Each stanza ends with the refrain 'Heu mihi misero!'
la.anonymous.breviarius_de_hierosolyma: The Breviarius de Hierosolyma is a brief anonymous Latin prose guide to the holy places of Jerusalem, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens with the city set upon its mountain, where the basilica of Constantine is described first. The relic of the True Cross was kept there, and the author notes the silver and marble columns. The itinerary then leads through Golgotha and the round church of the Holy Sepulchre, visiting the sanctuaries of the Passion. The route continues to the basilica on Sion and the houses of Caiaphas and Pilate, marking the pinnacle of the Temple. The Mount of Olives, the valley of Josaphat, and Galilee complete the tour, commemorating biblical events and relics.
la.anonymous_pilgrim_of_piacenza.itinerariu: This late antique Latin prose itinerary, attributed to an anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza, is known as the Itinerarium, a term meaning a journey or travel account. The author opens by recording his purpose under the protection of the martyr Antoninus, and the journey runs from Constantinople by way of Cyprus and the Phoenician coast into Galilee. It continues through Samaria and Judaea, with careful accounts of the Jordan and its Epiphany rites, covering Jericho, as well as the churches, relics, and miracles of Jerusalem and Bethlehem. The pilgrim then crosses the desert to the monasteries of Sinai and descends into Egypt, passing through Clysma, Memphis, and Alexandria before returning to Jerusalem. His homeward way leads through Syria and Mesopotamia to the shrine of St Sergius at Tetrapyrgium, while the text notes distances and local customs of Jews, Samaritans, and Saracens. It also records liturgical observances and natural marvels such as the Dead Sea and the petrified host of Pharaoh.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_ludovicum_pium: The Carmen ad Ludovicum Pium is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date that stands in the tradition of admonitory verse addressed to rulers. The opening dedication asks Louis the Pious to accept a book composed in dactylic verses, where the king is likened to the wisdom of Solomon. The work then unfolds as a sustained mirror for a ruler, urging faith, love of God, hope, and the reading of scripture. It also commands mercy, patience, humility, and the confession of sins, while warning against deceit, false witness, envy, and pride. The closing section arms the king with the four cardinal virtues, providing celestial armour including the breastplate of justice and the helmet of hope. This equipment prepares him for the ceaseless battle against the enemy, aiming to prevail and receive the crown of justice at the day of judgement.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_compoti_ratione: The Carmen de compoti ratione ('On the Calculation of the Calendar') is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date. It teaches the elements of computus in verse. The text opens with the lengths of the months and the placement of their kalends, nones, and ides. It also provides the regular numbers needed to find the day of the week. The poem then explains how to reckon the moon's age from the epacts of the nineteen-year cycle. It describes a method of reckoning on the joints of the hand and shows how to locate movable feasts like Easter and Pentecost, including adjustments for bissextile years.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_conversione_saxonum: The Carmen de Conversione Saxonum is a short anonymous Latin poem of the medieval period, which places its own composition in the ninth year of Charlemagne's reign. It opens with an account of the six ages of the world, mankind's fall into death, and the Father's sending of Christ, who vanquished death and returned in triumph to heaven. The greater part describes the pagan Saxons, given to sacrificing cattle and venerating demons, and Charlemagne's conquest of them by arms, figured as the transformation of wolves into lambs, ravens into doves, and other fierce creatures into gentle ones. The poem closes with the Saxons' baptism in the name of the Trinity and a prayer that Charlemagne, while the wicked are consigned to punishment, may gain the rewards of the starry kingdom when God weighs all merits at the Last Judgment.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_nynia_episcopo: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Nynia Episcopo versifies the life of Saint Ninian (Nynia), the apostle and bishop of the Picts. It opens with an account of Christ's incarnation and the spreading of divine light through the world before introducing Ninian, who travels to Rome, receives episcopal rank, and returns to convert the Picts and to found the church of Candida Casa dedicated to Martin. The narrative then recounts his miracles, including the restoration of the blinded King Tudvael, the speaking infant that vindicates an accused priest, the instantaneous growth of garden herbs, and the punishment and revival of cattle thieves, before describing his death and ascent to heaven. Its closing section treats the wonders worked at his tomb, notably the healing of the boy Pethgils, of a leper, and of a blind woman, the vision granted to the priest Plecgils of Christ as an infant on the altar during mass, and a final encomium on the saint's virtues and heavenly reward.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_pippino: A short medieval Latin poem of anonymous authorship and uncertain date, the Carmen de Pippino celebrates the victory of the Frankish king Pippin over the Avars. It opens with an address to Christ, creator of all peoples, before turning to the Avars' destruction of shrines, monasteries and consecrated vessels in earlier times. God then sends Saint Peter to aid Pippin, son of a great king, who encamps with the Frankish army on the Danube; the terrified Avar khagan, urged on by his consort Catuna, comes with gifts to pay homage and surrenders his realm with its forests, mountains and children to the Christian ruler. The closing lines give thanks that God confirmed the king's rule over the Avar kingdom, acclaim Pippin with wishes for long life and heirs, and end with a doxology.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_temporum_ratione: The Carmen de Temporum Ratione is an anonymous medieval Latin didactic poem of uncertain date that opens by distinguishing three bases for reckoning time. It details the divisions of the day and proceeds through the Hebrew, Egyptian, Greek, and Roman calendars, including their month names and key dates. The signs of the zodiac are described month by month, alongside an extensive body of lunar doctrine covering the moon's phases, distance, and influence on the tides. Later portions treat the solar year, equinoxes, climates, and varying day lengths, while the zones of the earth and seasons are discussed with their correspondence to the humours and ages of man. The planets and their cycles are examined, as are leap years and the nineteen-year cycle, before the poem concludes with the computus of Easter. It provides the dating of Easter Sunday and the Lenten fast, including rules for the paschal moon and epacts.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_timone_comite: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Timone Comite opens with an address to a king, presenting Count Timo as his envoy who restores neglected law in the land of the Norici, punishing thieves and robbers and upholding justice. The poem supports its praise of the count with scriptural examples of just and merciful rule, recounting the deeds of David, Job, Moses, Joshua and Joseph. A later section describes a spring flowing on a mountain beside a hall, attributed to the gift of Christ through Bishop Corbinian, and the work closes with the tale of the count's dog, which died after tasting poisoned food at the mountain's summit.
la.anonymus.carmina_cenomanensia: Carmina Cenomanensia is an anonymous medieval Latin collection of poems of uncertain date, and the title refers to Le Mans, the city known in Latin as Cenomanum. The opening verses praise Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the relics of the martyrs Gervasius, Prothasius, and Stephen, which are honoured in the cathedral where Aldric served as bishop. The poems then trace Aldric's upbringing at Metz and his rise through the ecclesiastical orders, recording his elevation to the see of Le Mans under King Louis. Later verses detail his benefactions to the church, including vestments and a golden chalice from Queen Judith, and the collection also notes altar dedications. The transfer of the monastery of Carilephus occurred under a charter issued by the emperor Louis, and the work closes with epitaphs and petitions for eternal rest. These prayers are offered for Aldric himself and for a priest named Franco.
la.anonymus.corneli_translationes: Corneli Translationes is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date celebrating the translation of the relics of Pope Cornelius into a church founded by a king named Charles. It opens by hailing the blessed place where the martyr rests after his agonies, contrasting the Rome that once flourished through his deeds with the Francia that now glories in his triumph. The poem then narrates the solemn procession by which king, clergy, and people receive the relics into the royal palace church, records Charles's lavish endowment of gold, silver, vestments, and gems, and catalogues the miracles of healing and exorcism worked at the shrine, together with the repulse of barbarian raiders who sought to burn the temple. It closes with prayers asking Cornelius to intercede for the king, the Franks, and the monastery, from which his body had earlier been driven toward Senlis, and with a summons to the papal shepherd to return to his own flock.
la.anonymus.hymnus_nynie_episcopi: The Hymnus Nynie Episcopi is an anonymous medieval Latin hymn of uncertain date that honors Bishop Nynia through an alphabetical structure of fifty-four lines. Each couplet repeats its opening words at the close of the second line, and the poem begins by invoking God as the sole creator and source of light. It then traces the penalty of ancient sin and the healing advent of Christ, while the greater part celebrates Nynia's radiance among the citizens of heaven. The text details his many miracles on earth, including the cleansing of leprosy from his tomb, and describes his burial beneath the temple roof and his spirit borne to the stars. The closing lines depict the serpent groaning before the dominion of Christ, and they also show the good at rest, singing mystical words to the king day and night.
la.anonymus.karolus_magnus_et_leo_papa: Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa is an anonymous medieval Latin epic poem of uncertain date that identifies Charlemagne and Pope Leo III. The work opens with a nautical figure as the poet spreads sail on shifting winds and launches into praise of the king. He likens the king to the sun and to David while describing Charlemagne building a second Rome with a forum. The poem also details a hunting expedition joined by his queen Liutgard and his son Pippin before a dream shows the Roman pontiff weeping. The narrative recounts the assault on Leo by a murderous Roman faction and follows his healing and flight to Charlemagne's court. The king crosses the Rhine with his army to meet the pope, and they reunite amid mutual homage, a solemn mass, and a banquet. The exchange of gifts ends with Leo honorably received as a refugee.
la.anonymus.laudes_mediolanensis_civitatis: The Laudes Mediolanensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin encomium of uncertain date, belonging to the urban encomium tradition that promotes a see city through its sacred dead. It opens with a depiction of the lofty and spacious city long known as Mediolanum, then surveys the thickness of its walls, its nine iron-bound gates, and its paved streets. The text extols Milan as queen of cities, a metropolis to which all Italy's bishops come, praising the piety of its people and cataloguing the saints whose relics rest there, including Ambrose, Protasius, Gervasius, and Nazarius. The closing lines mention the Lombard ruler Liutprand and the bishop Theodore, who adorned the city, while a final hymn and prayer to the Trinity asks for the city's protection.
la.anonymus.laudes_veronensis_civitatis: The Laudes Veronensis Civitatis ('Praises of the City of Verona') is an anonymous medieval Latin poem. It belongs to the genre of civic praise descended from classical laudes urbis. The text extols Verona's square walls, forty-eight towers, and paved forum. It also mentions the city's labyrinth, pagan temples, and bridges over the Adige. The poem then traces the Incarnation and Resurrection of Christ. It lists Veronese bishops, martyrs, and the gilded shrine prepared by Bishop Anno. The work closes with King Pippin residing in the city and a doxology to God.
la.anonymus.tituli_metrici_saeculi_viii: This anonymous collection of Latin metrical tituli, or inscriptions, is assigned to the eighth century by its title. The opening poem is an epitaph spoken by Peter, bishop of Pavia, who recounts his exile and restoration under King Charles. He addresses the reader from his tomb, asking for prayers and praising his own episcopal virtues. The remaining verses commemorate a broad range of the dead, including popes, bishops, abbots, and kings. Many of these individuals are remembered at Italian sites, with some poems voiced by the deceased and others by mourners. Throughout the collection, the dead are praised for their lineage, virtue, and benefactions. Passers-by are consistently urged to pray for the souls of those interred.
la.anonymus.versus_ad_ebonem_remensem: This anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date is addressed to Ebbo, archbishop of Reims. It opens by hailing him as the glory of Reims, shepherd, and friend of Christ. The body recounts how the abbot Peter, at Ebbo's command, crafted a Gospel book. This volume was adorned with gold within and ivory without, and dedicated to the apostle Peter. The poem celebrates the book as the fourfold chariot of Christ, a vehicle for the Gospels. It also describes the text as a medicine that heals the sick and restores the feeble. The closing lines invite sinners to seek these remedies and pray for eternal peace.
la.anonymus.versus_de_eversione_monasterii_: The Versus de Eversione Monasterii Glonnensis is an anonymous medieval Latin poem recounting the burning and restoration of the monastery of Glonna. It opens by summoning the Thracian lyre, Orpheus's mountains, rivers, and woods to join a lament for the basilica of Saint Florentius. The narrative follows the basilica from its pious foundation by King Charles, whose son Louis enriched the house before his death divided the kingdom. Nemenoius, a poor farmer enriched by a buried treasure, rebels against Charles and crosses the Loire with men from Rennes and Nantes to burn the monastery. Saint Florentius appears from heaven to weaken the ravager, who then begs pardon, and Abbot Dido obtains the grant of other abbeys and the rebuilding of the ruined house. The poem closes with a prayer to the saint.
la.apuleius.de_deo_socratis: The De deo Socratis, a Latin philosophical oration attributed to Apuleius, belongs to the later imperial period and expounds Plato's doctrine of the daimonion. The text opens with a tripartite division of nature into gods, daemons, and men, cataloguing celestial gods visible as stars or grasped only by the intellect. The argument then establishes daemons as intermediate beings dwelling in the air, whose subtle bodies and mediating offices account for divination, omens, and the varied rites of cult. The work turns to the human soul as a kind of daimon, discussing the Genius and the Lemures, Lares, Larvae, and Manes. A higher guardian spirit is assigned to each person as an unseen witness, while the closing portion treats Socrates' familiar daimon as a perceived sign rather than an audible voice. This spirit forbade but never urged, and the oration ends by exhorting hearers to cultivate the soul, illustrated by Socrates' indifference to wealth and Odysseus' prudent passage.
la.apuleius.metamorphoses: The Metamorphoses, also known as The Golden Ass, is an eleven book Latin prose fiction from the later imperial period. The title refers to the narrator Lucius, who is transformed into an ass. He introduces himself as a Greek educated traveller promising a Milesian tale of human figures changed into other shapes. His curiosity about witchcraft in Thessaly leads to his metamorphosis. In that form he passes through robbers caves and the households of successive owners. The narrative includes the embedded story of Cupid and Psyche amid many comic and perilous misadventures. The closing books recount his return to human form through the intervention of Isis. He then undergoes initiations into the mysteries of Isis and Osiris. Finally, he resumes a career as a pleader at Rome.
la.audradus_modicus.carmina: Carmina is a Carolingian Latin collection of poems by Audradus Modicus, and the title simply means poems in Latin. It opens with a visionary colloquy in which Hincmar urges the poet to seek a wondrous fountain. A guardian voice declares that its waters are denied to mortals who come without a vessel. The collection proceeds through the poet's disappointed vigil at the spring, and it then turns to a versified martyrdom of Saint Julian. Before a tyrannical prefect, Julian steadies his weeping followers by likening his ordeal to gold refined in the furnace. Later poems recount the miracles that attend churches dedicated in Julian's name, and the collection closes with a doxology praising the Trinity and invoking the intercession of the martyrs for the forgiveness of sins.
la.audradus_modicus.de_sancta_trinitate: De Sancta Trinitate is a verse treatise by the Carolingian author Audradus Modicus, which opens with a prayer for mercy and a survey of his other writings.
