These include books dedicated to the apostle Peter, to Martin of Tours, and to ten-year truces. The poem then defends the full equality of the Son with the Father, while affirming the equal substance and procession of the Holy Spirit. It recounts the creation of angels and the fall of the tenth of their number, describing the making and deception of man. This is followed by Christ's incarnation from the Virgin, whose victory over hell restores the place the fallen angel had lost. The work ends with the risen Christ instructing the disciples in his eternal generation from the Father.
la.augustine.confessiones: The Confessions is a Latin prose work of theology by the Late Antique author Augustine, taking the form of an extended first-person prayer addressed directly to God. The text interweaves autobiographical narrative with philosophical and scriptural meditation, opening with praise of the Creator and a plea from a restless heart. The narrative recounts the author's life from infancy through youthful sin and Manichaeism, detailing his movement toward Christianity under Ambrose at Milan. The story culminates in conversion, baptism, and the death of his mother Monica at Ostia, after which the later books turn from memoir to sustained reflection on memory, time, and evil. They also offer a running commentary on the opening of Genesis and the account of creation.
la.augustine.contra_adimantum: Contra Adimantum, a Latin prose treatise by Augustine, answers Adimantus, a disciple of Mani, who claimed Old Testament passages contradicted the New. The work opens with Genesis, which Manichaeans opposed to the Gospel, and Augustine refutes this charge in three ways before addressing other paired passages. He draws on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets, treating the sabbath, marriage, circumcision, and dietary laws. He also discusses the love of enemies and the severity of God, arguing that both Testaments come from one God. He shows they agree when their figures are spiritually interpreted, and the text closes with Isaiah's vision of the Lord. It describes three kinds of vision, corporeal, imaginative, and intellectual, showing the prophet's seeing does not conflict with God's invisibility.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelegian: Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum ('Against Two Letters of the Pelagians') is a four book treatise by Augustine. He addresses Pope Boniface to refute two hostile letters from Pelagian leaders. One letter came from Julian of Eclanum to Rome. The other was sent by eighteen bishops to Thessalonica. Augustine defends original sin, infant baptism, and divine grace against their claims. He also contrasts Pelagian errors with Manichaean ones to show both oppose the faith. The final book cites Cyprian and Ambrose to prove these doctrines are ancient.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_fundamenti: Contra Epistulam Fundamenti is a Late Antique Latin treatise by Augustine that addresses Manichaeans to refute their core text, the Letter of the Foundation. The work opens with a prayer for a tranquil mind and a plea for humility, then dissects the salutation to argue that Mani is not Christ's apostle. Augustine insists that belief must rest on Catholic authority rather than unverifiable promises, and the greater part of the text examines the cosmogony recounted in the letter. He criticizes the account of the realm of light bordered by the land of darkness, arguing that every nature is good insofar as it exists. Augustine maintains that evil is corruption contrary to nature rather than a substance, and the treatise concludes by reserving remaining doctrines for refutation in subsequent books.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_parmeniani: Contra Epistulam Parmeniani is a Late Antique Latin treatise by Augustine, which serves as a reply to a letter in which the Donatist bishop Parmenian rebuked Tychonius. Augustine explains that he answers this letter at the request of the brothers, and the text rebuts charges that churches in Gaul, Spain, and Italy were founded by traditores. It recounts the hearings of Caecilian before African councils and before Miltiades of Rome, while Augustine argues that wicked clergy do not defile sacraments or justify rebaptism. He presses the Donatists with their own divisions, notably the Maximianist schism, and the work closes by denying that punishment for schism counts as martyrdom.
la.augustine.contra_felicem: Contra Felicem is a stenographic record of a public disputation held in the church at Hippo in December 404, during the sixth consulship of Honorius. The debate took place between Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and Felix, a Manichaean layman, who was challenged to defend Mani's claim as the promised Paraclete. The first day featured readings from the Gospels, Acts, and Pauline epistles regarding the promise of the Holy Spirit. Augustine then tested the cosmology of Mani's Fundamental Epistle through sustained questioning of its core tenets. The second book records the adjourned session, where Augustine attacked the Manichaean doctrine of two natures. He defended free will and the incorruptibility of God against claims of divine pollution, and the proceedings concluded with both disputants subscribing a written anathema of Mani and his teaching.
la.augustine.contra_litteras_petiliani: Contra Litteras Petiliani ('Against the Letters of Petilian') is a late-antique Latin polemical treatise in which Augustine, then bishop of Hippo, writes against Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta. It opens with his reply to an intercepted letter in which Petilian attacked Catholic baptism, arguing that its validity rests not on the minister's moral worth but on Christ himself. When the remainder of the letter came to light, Augustine produced a longer second book that answers it clause by clause, quoting Petilian's words and setting his responses beneath them. Here he defends the unity of the Church spread through all nations and cites the case of the Maximianists, whom the Donatists had condemned while accepting their baptism. He also rebuts Petilian's charges about the betrayal of the scriptures, persecution and rebaptism. The treatise closes with further argument on scripture, the exercise of imperial power against schism, and the insistence that no one be compelled into the faith unwillingly.
la.augustine.contra_partem_donati_post_gest: Contra Partem Donati post Gesta, a short Latin prose treatise by Augustine, addresses the rank and file of the Donatist party after their bishops lost a public disputation at Carthage. The work opens by taunting the Donatists with the gap between their recorded statements and their refusal to return to Catholic unity. Augustine then uses gospel parables to show that good and bad remain mixed in the church until the final judgment. He defends Caecilian's acquittal before Constantine against the charge of a bribed judge, while exposing Donatist inconsistencies over the Maximianist schism and their claim to be the suffering church. Biblical cases, such as Haggai's two peoples under one temple, refute their demand for bodily separation. The treatise closes with an exhortation to abandon error, embrace peace, and acknowledge their Catholic opponents as brothers.
la.augustine.de_beata_vita: De Beata Vita ('On the Happy Life') is a short Latin prose dialogue by Augustine. This work of Late Antique philosophical theology is dedicated to Manlius Theodorus. It opens with a preface that figures the approach to philosophy as a voyage toward a harbour. The main body recounts conversations held over three days, beginning at a birthday banquet. The company includes Augustine's mother, his brother Navigius, his son Adeodatus, and the young Licentius and Trygetius. Through successive arguments, the speakers conclude that the happy life consists in the possession of wisdom and truth, that is, of a propitious God.
la.augustine.de_bono_coniugali: De Bono Coniugali ('On the Good of Marriage') is a Latin prose treatise by Augustine. He argues that marriage is a genuine good rooted in the creation of the first couple. The union forms the first bond of human society through friendship, kinship, and offspring. Augustine examines the three goods of marriage, which are offspring, fidelity, and the sacrament. He also addresses issues like adultery, divorce, and the marital debt. The work ranks marriage below widowhood and virginity while defending the patriarchs' plural marriages.
la.augustine.de_civitate_dei: Augustine's De ciuitate Dei, a Latin theological prose work from the Late Antique era, was written in response to the recent sack of Rome and addressed to Marcellinus. The text defends the city of God, which lives by faith as a pilgrim among the impious, while the early books answer pagan charges by surveying disasters that befell Rome before Christ. These early sections also attack theatrical rites and obscene legends attributed to the pagan gods, whereas the later books trace the origins of earthly and heavenly societies among angels and first humans. Their history is followed from Cain and Abel to their mingling in the present age, and the final books defend the resurrection of the body against philosophical objection. They record contemporary miracles at the shrines of the martyrs, and the work ends with the last judgment and the eternal blessedness of the City of God. This state is figured as an unending sabbath.
la.augustine.de_continentia: De Continentia ('On Continence') is a Latin prose treatise by Augustine of Late Antiquity. It argues that this virtue is a divine gift rather than a human achievement. The work addresses the struggle between flesh and spirit under grace. It defends the goodness of the body against Manichaean dualism. The text closes with the hope of a future peace.
la.augustine.de_doctrina_christiana: De Doctrina Christiana ('On Christian Doctrine') is a late-antique Latin treatise by Augustine. It offers rules for interpreting and expounding the Christian Scriptures. The work divides its instruction between discovering meaning and communicating it. Book one treats things, ordering love through the distinction between enjoying and using. Books two and three address signs, covering the canon, languages, and the seven rules of Tychonius. Book four discusses eloquence, aiming to teach, delight, and persuade the audience.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_symbolo: De Fide et Symbolo is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine that expounds the creed entrusted to newly baptised Christians, article by article. The work opens by arguing that faith demands confession with the mouth as well as belief in the heart, and the creed's few words were fixed as a defence against the subtleties of heretics. The exposition proceeds through the articles on God the omnipotent Father and creation from nothing, covering the eternal generation of the Word, his incarnation, passion, burial, resurrection, and ascension. The text also addresses the Holy Spirit as consubstantial with Father and Son, and it closes with the church, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh. Sustained polemic against heretical misreadings runs throughout the work, and a final notice from Augustine's Retractationes qualifies his account of the transformation of the risen body.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram: De Genesi ad Litteram, a twelve book prose commentary by Augustine, interprets Genesis' opening chapters according to the letter of the text. It distinguishes scriptural narration from figurative discourse, asking whether creation occurred in time or through God's coeternal Word. Augustine argues that God created all things at once in their causal reasons, whose temporal unfolding continues in his unceasing operation. The text treats Adam's body formation from earth and his soul's creation by divine breathing, denying the soul is part of divine substance. He rejects the idea that souls transmigrate through animals, while later books consider Paradise, its rivers, the commandment, and the first transgression. The serpent and the devil's fall are discussed, followed by the punishment of the first parents and an analysis of vision occasioned by Paul's rapture.
la.augustine.de_gratia_christi: This late antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine addresses the question of grace in the controversy with Pelagius, cast as a letter to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania. The work opens with greetings and an announcement that their specific inquiries will now be treated, quoting and examining Pelagius's own words. Augustine attacks his division of possibility, will, and action, arguing that God works in humans both the willing and the doing of good. He contrasts law and grace through Pauline texts and reviews Pelagius's letter to Innocent, also considering his letter to the virgin Demetrias. Ambrose's testimony that God calls and makes religious whom he wills is adduced, affirming that human nature is healed only by grace. The work closes by announcing a further treatment of original sin.
la.augustine.de_nuptiis_et_concupiscentia: De Nuptiis et Concupiscentia ('On Marriage and Concupiscence') is a two-book Latin prose treatise by Augustine. He composed it for the distinguished count Valerius during the late-antique controversy over original sin. The work opens with a dedicatory letter praising Valerius's faith and conjugal chastity. The first book maintains that marriage remains good in its three goods of offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. It distinguishes these from the concupiscence of the flesh, a penal disorder that transmits original sin. The second book answers objections from Pelagian opponents point by point. Augustine defends the view that all born of Adam lie under the devil's power unless reborn in Christ.
la.augustine.de_peccato_originali: The De peccato originali is a short Late Antique Latin treatise by Augustine, which argues that Adam's transgression passes to all his descendants. Consequently, infants are baptized for the remission of that sin, and the work opens by warning its addressees to listen cautiously to Pelagius and Caelestius. These men concede infant baptism while denying that any sin is transmitted from Adam, so Augustine reviews the ecclesiastical proceedings against the two men. He quotes at length from the acts of the councils of Carthage and Diospolis, and he also cites the letters of Popes Innocent I and Zosimus. The text includes the writings and professions of Pelagius himself, whom Augustine accuses of evasive and self-contradictory answers. The treatise closes by insisting that the question touches the core of the Christian faith, not a matter of indifferent debate, and Augustine adduces passages from Ambrose as orthodox testimony against the Pelagian position.
la.augustine.de_peccatorum_meritis_et_remis: De peccatorum meritis et remissione et de baptismo parvulorum is a Latin prose treatise by the late antique theologian Augustine, who wrote it in answer to questions from his correspondent Marcellinus. The work opens with a brief exordium that excuses the delay caused by the author's cares, then addresses the view that Adam would have died even without sinning. Augustine argues that death and concupiscence entered the human race through Adam's disobedience, maintaining that infants are baptized for the remission of original sin rather than their own faults. The text asserts that no one in this life is wholly without sin except Christ, and each point is supported by a dense chain of testimonia from the Pauline epistles, gospels, Psalms, and Job. A concluding section quotes and answers arguments advanced by Pelagius in his expositions on Paul.
la.augustine.de_perfectione_iustitiae_homin: This short late antique treatise by Augustine is addressed to his fellow bishops Eutropius and Paul, and it is traditionally titled On the Perfection of Human Righteousness. The work answers brief definitions circulating under the name of Caelestius, which concern whether a human being can live without sin. Augustine takes up each definition in turn to argue his case, maintaining that nature, vitiated by the first man's fall, can be healed only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ. The author then reviews scriptural testimonies advanced for human perfection, expounding the Lord's Prayer and the claim that divine commandments are not grievous. He also examines the case of Job and passages from the apostles, arguing that only the one mediator lived wholly without sin. The work closes by declaring that no one in this mortal life, apart from Christ, is free from the need for the remission of sins, and whoever denies this contradicts both the gospel and the apostle John.
la.augustine.de_trinitate: De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise by Augustine, a major doctrinal work of Late Antiquity on the nature of the triune God. The text opens with a dedicatory letter to Aurelius, where Augustine recounts that he began the books in youth and published them in old age. He explains that he was compelled to finish a work taken from him before he could revise it. The opening argument warns against three kinds of error in thinking about God, which arise from reasoning about bodily things, the soul, or false suppositions. Scriptural language accommodates human weakness through bodily and spiritual figures, and Augustine then proceeds to the purification of the mind. This mind is nourished by faith as the path toward understanding the divine substance.
la.augustine.epistula_ad_catholicos_de_sect: This late-antique Latin epistolary treatise by Augustine, bishop of Hippo, addresses the Catholics entrusted to his pastoral care. It opens by announcing a reply to a letter from Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Constantine. The central question concerns where the Church is truly found, whether with the Catholics or the Donatists. Augustine argues that the one Church, diffused through the whole world as the body of Christ, cannot be confined to the African party of Donatus. He marshals testimonies from Genesis, Isaiah, the Psalms, and the Gospels to show the Church's spread to all nations. The letter also treats the mixture of wheat and chaff, the reception of heretics, and the violence of the circumcellions.
la.augustine.liber_qui_appellatur_speculum: The Liber qui appellatur Speculum is a late antique Latin prose collection of moral precepts attributed to Augustine, drawing material from canonical scripture. It opens by distinguishing passages meant to be known from commandments still binding in the New Testament era, announcing a plan to gather these rules into a single book. This book serves as a mirror for the believer, allowing the reader to inspect his progress in good conduct and see what he lacks. The compilation proceeds book by book through the Old Testament, citing precepts from Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy at length. It continues with selections from Joshua, the Psalms, Proverbs, and other sapiential books, together with Tobit. The remaining material is taken from the New Testament, beginning with the Gospel of Matthew and continuing through the Pauline letters and other apostolic epistles, closing with precepts from the Apocalypse.
la.augustine.locutiones_in_heptateuchum: Locutiones in Heptateuchum ('Expressions in the Heptateuch') is a prose work by the late antique writer Augustine. It opens with a programmatic statement announcing its subject: the turns of phrase in scripture that appear to be governed by the properties of the Hebrew or Greek language. The entries run in order through the seven books of the Heptateuch from Genesis to Judges. Each entry quotes a verse in the Latin of the Septuagint and adds a short note on some unusual wording. The notes explain doubled words, singulars for plurals, shifts of gender, number and case, ellipses, hyperbaton, and part-for-whole expressions as Hebrew or Greek idiom rather than error. Augustine often sets the Greek reading against the Latin codices and distinguishes genuine locutions from questions of sense.
la.augustine.psalmus_contra_partem_donati: Augustine's Psalmus contra Partem Donati is a Late Antique polemical work shaped as a psalm that addresses the Donatists and urges their return to Catholic unity. The text opens with the parable of the net cast into the sea, where good and bad fish are mixed together until the shore. The refrain 'Omnes qui gaudetis de pace, modo uerum iudicate' recurs throughout the work, which traces the origins of the schism in the charge against Caecilian of Carthage. It details the hearings before Roman and imperial judges, Donatus's appeal, his introduction of rebaptism, and the violence of the circumcellions. Scriptural figures such as Judas at the supper and the threshing floor are drawn upon, and the see of Peter is also invoked. The argument holds that the righteous must tolerate sinners within the one church until the final separation, and a speech by Mother Church closes the piece. She reproaches her departing children, contrasts their refusal of imperial peace with her own endurance, and the text ends with the announcement of the coming judge.
la.augustine.quaestiones_in_heptateuchum: Augustine's Quaestiones in Heptateuchum ('Questions on the Seven Books') is a late-antique Latin work of biblical theology. It collects and answers questions arising from the first seven books of the Old Testament. The prologue explains that these queries were noted briefly during the author's reading of the scriptures. The longest portion treats Genesis, addressing issues like Cain's city and Methuselah's lifespan. It also covers the angels who consorted with the daughters of men and the construction of Noah's ark. Questions then follow on Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and the judges down to Samson.
la.augustine.retractationum: Augustine's Retractationes, a late-antique Latin prose work of theology, was written in the author's old age to review and criticize his entire body of writings. The preface announces a resolve to examine his books with judicial severity, aiming to forestall the reproach of others. The two books proceed by numbered entries in the order of composition, covering ninety-three works in two hundred thirty-two books. The survey begins with early dialogues such as Contra Academicos and De beata vita, moving through anti-Manichaean, anti-Donatist, and anti-Pelagian polemics. It also includes commentaries on Genesis and the Pauline epistles, with major treatises like De doctrina Christiana and the Confessiones appearing later. Each entry records the occasion and summarizes the contents, noting passages the author would now correct in wording or doctrine, and the whole closes with a tally of what has been reviewed.
la.ausonius.cupido_cruciatus: Cupido Cruciatus, a short late antique Latin poem by Ausonius, opens in the plains of air where heroines who died for love gather in a shadowy myrtle grove. They re-enact the circumstances of their deaths while bearing the tokens of their fates, and figures such as Semele, Procris, Sappho, Ariadne, Phaedra, and Dido pass in review. Their rites are interrupted when Cupid blunders into their midst, and the women seize him to bind him to a myrtle tree. They take turns scourging him with the instruments of their own deaths, and Venus arrives to join the punishment. The heroines eventually relent and intercede for the boy, who slips his captors and escapes through the ivory gate. The whole episode presents itself as the phantasm of a troubled dream.
la.ausonius.de_bissula: De Bissula is a short lyric collection by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, whose title refers to Bissula, a Suebian girl captured beyond the Rhine. She was raised in Ausonius's household after being taken in war, and the work opens with a prose letter to his friend Paulus. Ausonius yields to Paulus's insistence to share these private verses, which include a preliminary poem urging readers to drink. The collection features epigrams on Bissula's charm and mixed origins, contrasting her natural beauty with painted cosmetics. These pieces conclude with instructions for a painter to depict her.
la.ausonius.de_herediolo: De Herediolo is a short Latin lyric poem by the late antique poet Ausonius, who explains in a prose note that he returned to his father's small villa after many years as a consul. He composed these verses in a Lucilian manner to address the estate itself, greeting the property cultivated by his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father. The poem reflects on inheritance, the piety of succession, and the limits of desire, while including exempla of Croesus, Diogenes, Aristippus, and Midas. The closing section inventories two hundred iugera of field and a hundred-iugerum vineyard, along with meadows, woodland, a spring, a well, and a navigable stream. Produce stored for two years completes the inventory, and the estate lies neither far from the city nor at it, allowing the owner to alternate life in country and town.
la.ausonius.eclogarum_liber: The Eclogarum Liber is a book of short lyric pieces by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, opening with a dedication to his friend Pacatus, whom he asks to be its only judge. What follows is a miscellany of gnomic and didactic verse: the miseries of every age and condition of life, the sage who weighs each day's deeds, and a dispute between the monosyllables 'Est' and 'Non'. A larger group treats the reckoning of time, from the planets that name the weekdays and the Roman months with their kalends, nones and ides to the seasons, the signs of the zodiac and the sun's yearly course. Catalogue poems on the four great Greek games, the Roman festivals, the twelve labours of Hercules and the bodily attributes of the gods follow, and a set of one-line maxims closes the book.
la.ausonius.ephemeris_id_est_totius_diei_ne: The Ephemeris id est totius diei negotium is a lyric poem by the late-antique poet Ausonius, which traces the round of a single day in the life of a man of affairs. The text alternates between Sapphic stanzas and limping iambic metres, opening at dawn with the speaker's exasperated efforts to rouse his sluggish servant Parmeno. The day proceeds through washing, a long Christian prayer, dressing, and morning greetings, while the speaker orders luncheon with the steward Sosia and addresses a comic shorthand notary. Further engagements carry the hours toward dusk, and the poem ends at night with dreams of triumph and shame. Nightmares are dismissed to the moon's realm, where a green elm grove is dedicated to their harmless keeping.
la.ausonius.epicedion_in_patrem: The Epicedion in Patrem is a short late antique Latin poem by Ausonius, whose prose preface explains the Greek title as a funerary term. The verses are cast in the dead father's own voice as a self-composed obituary, where he names himself Ausonius and recalls his medical practice at Vasates and Bordeaux. He mentions his membership of the curia and senate, along with his frugal and unblemished conduct, while recording his avoidance of factions, lawsuits, and false friendship. The father describes a harmonious marriage of forty-five years that produced four children, noting the honours attained by a son who became prefect of Gaul, Libya, and Latium. It also mentions a daughter of distinguished marriages and the father's own prefecture of Illyricum, before closing with his account of ending a ninety-year life unimpaired by prayer to the divine. He leaves hope, vows, and fear behind among sorrowing friends, with a parting address to the reader.
la.ausonius.epigrammata_ausonii_de_diversis: The Epigrammata de Diversis Rebus is a collection of short poems by the late antique poet Ausonius, which opens with a joke addressed to the poet's own little book. This book would rather be eaten by moths than cost him sleep and lamp oil, and the poems that follow range widely in subject and tone. They include satirical pieces on rhetors and grammarians, as well as riddling verses on names and letters, while mythological vignettes feature Narcissus, Hermaphroditus, Leda, and Myron's bronze heifer. Other epigrams target doctors, haruspices, and various professions, alongside some openly obscene pieces, and the collection also celebrates the contemporary emperors Valens and Gratian. It closes with a running series of attacks on a Briton named Silvius Bonus.
la.ausonius.epistularum: This collection of letters by the late antique poet Ausonius is addressed to friends, kinsmen, and fellow writers, including Paulus, Symmachus, Theon, Proba, and Ursulus. The work opens with prose letters in which Ausonius praises a correspondent's writings, weighing the man's eloquence against his character and urging him to keep composing. The collection then proceeds through epistles in prose and a wide range of metres, including elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, iambics, Sapphics, and bilingual Greek Latin verses. These letters trade compliments, invitations to visit, jokes, and gifts of books, oysters, thrushes, and fish. A substantial sequence is devoted to Ausonius's attempts to draw the younger Paulus back from his withdrawal into Christian devotion and abandonment of poetry, to which Paulus replies to defend his new life.
la.ausonius.epitaphia_heroum_qui_bello_troi: This Latin poem of 185 lines by the late-antique poet Ausonius presents imagined epitaphs for the heroes of the Trojan War. A prose preface explains that the author found these ancient sepulchral inscriptions in the keeping of a philologist. He rendered them into Latin and arranged them freely rather than by strict order. The verses then speak largely in the voices of the dead, including Agamemnon, Menelaus, Ajax, and Achilles. Other figures such as Ulysses, Diomedes, Nestor, and Hector also lament from beyond the grave. A closing series moves beyond the Trojan matter to include Diogenes the Cynic and a circus charioteer.
la.ausonius.griphus_ternarii_numeri: The Griphus ternarii numeri, or Riddle of the Number Three, is a short Latin lyric poem by the late antique poet Ausonius. It devotes its entire scope to the occurrences and powers of the number three, opening with the drinking injunction 'Ter bibe', which proclaims a mystical law. The work then proceeds as a dense catalogue of triads from mythology, history, and law, including Cerberus, Hecate, the Fates, and the three Punic Wars. It also covers philosophical and arithmetical concepts alongside the divisions of Rome, closing by returning to its opening toast to assert the supremacy of three. The final lines playfully reckon the poem's own length in nines and tens.
la.ausonius.ludus_septem_sapientum: The Ludus Septem Sapientum is a short dramatic poem by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, whose title means the game of the seven sages. The work opens with a preface addressed to Pacatus Drepanius, who is asked to judge the verses with severity or indulgence. The play then stages the seven sages of Greece appearing in the theatre, where a Roman speaker explains their Greek dress and the role of the theatre. Each sage delivers a maxim in Greek and expounds it in Latin, with Solon giving the longest speech by narrating the story of Croesus. The sages depart one by one amid applause.
la.ausonius.mosella: The Mosella is a Latin poem in hexameters of Late Antique date that belongs to the tradition of Latin river praise. Ausonius, a native of Burdigala, celebrates the river Moselle and names himself at the close of the work. The speaker crosses the mist covered Nava and follows lonely woodland tracks to the Belgic borderland. From Noiomagus, the vine clad slopes come into view, which recalls his homeland. The poem catalogues the river's translucent waters and lists many kinds of fish. It describes the terraced vineyards and the vintage, accompanied by a playful mythological excursus. Boatmen and fishermen are mirrored in the stream, while villas and bathhouses line the banks. The text ends with a survey of tributaries and claims the river might rival the Tiber. The Rhine is summoned to share in triumphs, and the poet promises further works.
la.ausonius.oratio_consulis_ausonii_versibu: This late antique Latin prayer by Ausonius bears a title that styles its author as consul. The composition uses rhopalic verses, a form in which each line lengthens by one syllable at every step. It opens with an appeal to God as the reconciler of eternal rest, begging Christ the Trinity for pardon and grace. From there the prayer ranges over night, fasting, and the cleansing font of baptism, recalling the redemption wrought by Christ's suffering on the cross. The witnesses it invokes are Stephen, Paul, and the penitent thief, and the closing petition of the aged servant asks to be numbered among the glorified in heaven. Its final verse repeats the poem's own first line, so that the prayer ends where it began.
la.ausonius.ordo_urbium_nobilium: The Ordo urbium nobilium is a short late antique Latin poem by Ausonius that ranks famous cities in lyric verse. Rome stands first, while Constantinople and Carthage contend for precedence, and the survey then moves to Antioch and Alexandria. Later passages celebrate Trier, Milan, Capua, Aquileia, Arles, Hispalis, Athens, Catania, Syracuse, Toulouse, and Narbo. Each city is praised for its origins, wealth, site, or monuments, and the poem ends at Burdigala. The poet's native city is extolled for its climate, walls, and the spring Divona. The closing antithesis notes he is citizen of Burdigala and consul in both cities, with his cradle in one and his curule chair in the other.
la.ausonius.parentalia: The Parentalia is a cycle of short poems by the late-antique poet Ausonius, which mourns members of the poet's own family in elegiac couplets. A prose preface links the title to the ancient festival of offerings to departed kin, and the collection opens with a programmatic elegy announcing the names of the departed. It then proceeds through epitaphs for parents, the teacher Arborius, and other relatives, where each poem records lineage, character, offices, and the manner of death. Longer laments follow for the poet's wife Sabina and an infant son, and the sequence closes with commemorative pieces for further relatives and their kin.
la.ausonius.praefatiunculae: The Praefatiunculae, meaning Little Prefaces, is a short collection of introductory pieces by the late antique poet Ausonius of Bordeaux. These texts, written mostly in lyric verse with one prose item, were attached to individual books of his works. The collection opens with an autobiographical preface recording the poet's family origins in Aquitaine. It traces his career from teaching grammar and rhetoric at Bordeaux to life at the imperial court and the consulship. A preface addressed to his friend Syagrius follows, along with a prose letter from the emperor Theodosius. The emperor addresses Ausonius affectionately and asks for the poet's writings. The collection closes with a verse preface declaring that the emperor commanded the poems to be composed. It notes that refusal of such a command is unsafe.
la.ausonius.technopaegnion: The Technopaegnion is a late antique Latin poem by Ausonius, whose title means a technical game of words. Addressed to the proconsul Pacatus, the work features verses that begin and end with a monosyllable. The closing word of each line opens the next, and two prefatory epistles explain the game and its difficulty. The verses discuss Fors, Spes, and Mors, while also covering parts of the human body. Later sections catalogue gods, foods, and plants, and they pose riddles answered in single monosyllables. The poem treats Latin and Greek letters, addresses disputed words and grammar, and ends with a final address asking Pacatus for indulgence.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_consolatoria_laude_c: De consolatoria laude castitatis ('On the Consolatory Praise of Chastity') is a Late Antique Latin poem by Avitus of Vienne. It serves as a consolatory exhortation addressed to his sister Fuscina, a consecrated virgin. The poet styles himself Alcimus and commends her vow of chastity in the opening apostrophe. The main body argues for virginity over marriage by detailing the perils of wedlock and childbirth. It supports this case with biblical and hagiographic examples, including Deborah, Susanna, Joseph, and the Virgin Mary. The work closes with praise for Fuscina's kindred and a call for her to lead by example.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_spiritalis_historiae: De Spiritalis Historiae Gestis, a late antique biblical epic by Avitus of Vienne, consists of five books of dactylic hexameter verse. It retells sacred history from creation to the Exodus, opening with an address to Adam and God's creation. The poem describes the fashioning of Adam from clay and the formation of Eve, then follows the serpent's temptation and the Fall. It details the penalties pronounced on the serpent, woman, and man, and covers the miseries of post-lapsarian life. The narrative moves on to Noah and the Flood, the Tower of Babel, and the plagues of Egypt. The final books narrate the Israelites' departure, their travel under the pillar of fire and cloud, and their passage through the Red Sea. Pharaoh's host drowns in the waters, and the poem closes with a song of triumph and a meditation on baptism as the fulfillment of the sea crossing.
la.bede.historiam_ecclesiasticam_gentis_ang: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum opens with a dedicatory letter to King Ceolwulf, in which the author names his informants and asks the king to approve the work before it is copied. The five books that follow trace the church among the English from the Roman invasions of Britain, covering the Anglo-Saxon settlement and Augustine of Canterbury's mission despatched by Pope Gregory. The narrative details the conversion of the several kingdoms and the settlement of the Easter and tonsure disputes at the Synod of Whitby, while weaving through this political and ecclesiastical history the deeds of kings, bishops, and abbots. The text also includes the lives of saints such as Aidan, Oswald, and Cuthbert, along with numerous miracle stories and visions of the afterlife. The history runs down to Bede's own day, closing with a survey of the state of Britain about 731, and ends with a chronological recapitulation of the whole work and the author's autobiographical account of his writings.
la.bernowinus.carmina: This collection of Latin verses by the Carolingian poet Bernowinus was composed during the reign of Charlemagne, whose rule is invoked throughout the devotional and epigraphic content. The work opens with a sequence passing through the annunciation, nativity, passion, and resurrection of Christ, where each scene closes with a prayer for mercy. The remaining pieces include verses on the house of prayer that Bernowinus founded and presented to the priest Illidius, along with long acrostic prayer sequences addressed to Christ. A lament in the voice of a once wealthy dead man warns against riches, while an acrostic intercession for Angilbert and praise of a priest who built a church are included. Epitaphs for Hebrarius, a youth, and Dida, wife of Ardoinus, conclude the set, urging visitors to pray for the souls of the founder and the departed.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto is a Latin verse legend by Bertharius of Monte Cassino, belonging to the Carolingian period and setting the Benedictine hagiographic tradition in verse. The poem opens with an apostrophe to the saint as father, way, and pastor, praising the divine protection that attended him from childhood. The text proceeds through episodes, where a broken vessel is restored and a poisoned meal is turned aside. The drowning Placidus is rescued, and a Goth's iron is drawn back from the waters, while boys are entrusted to the saint's threshold. Further miracles follow, including the cleansing of a possessed monk, empty granaries filled through a vision, and slanderous sisters' words returned to their tombs. A crushed boy's body cannot be held by the sepulchre, and a serpent vomits itself out before a brother fleeing to Benedict's shelter. The legend closes with the healing of a crippled Welsh youth, styled a second David, and a prayer to Benedict and Christ asks for the safekeeping of the faithful. The poet names himself as the humble composer Bertharius.
la.boethius.commentaria_in_porphyrium_a_se_: Boethius wrote this Latin prose commentary on Porphyry's Isagoge, an introductory treatise to Aristotle's Categories. The work takes the form of a dialogue between Boethius and his student Fabius. They meet during a winter retreat in the Aurelian mountains to discuss the text. The conversation addresses six standard preliminary questions about the purpose and order of the work. It also identifies the five predicables, which are genus, species, difference, property, and accident. The dialogue references a Latin version by the orator Victorinus and divides philosophy into theoretical and practical parts.
la.boethius.liber_de_persona_et_duabus_natu: This late antique Latin treatise by Boethius, cast as a letter to the deacon John, responds to a council debate over the Eutychian formula regarding Christ's natures. The author distinguishes several senses of natura and defines persona as an individual substance of a rational nature, while sorting out the Greek terms ousia, hypostasis, and prosopon. He argues against Nestorius that Christ cannot be two persons, and rejects Eutyches by stating that the two natures were neither converted nor confused. The text closes by affirming that Christ consists in and from two natures within one person, and it also weighs the state of human nature in his assumed flesh.
la.boethius.utrum_pater: Utrum Pater ('Whether the Father') is a short late-antique Latin prose treatise by Boethius. It is addressed to John the Deacon and explores the grammar of divine naming. The work asks whether the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated of the divinity substantially. It argues that attributes like deity, truth, and goodness belong to the one simple substance. These qualities are therefore predicated substantially of the indivisible divine essence. In contrast, personal names hold only relatively and arise from the plurality of persons. The treatise concludes by asking John to accept the argument or examine the points more closely.
la.caesar.de_bello_gallico: The De Bello Gallico is a Latin prose account of Julius Caesar's campaigns in Gaul, written during the Roman Republican era as year by year commentaries. It opens with a survey of Gaul and the Helvetian migration, then traces campaigns against the Helvetii and Ariovistus, the subjugation of the Belgae, and operations against coastal and Aquitanian peoples. Two crossings of the Rhine and two expeditions to Britain follow these early conflicts, while the narrative culminates in the great revolt of Vercingetorix and the siege of Alesia. Ethnographic digressions on Gallic institutions, druids, and Germanic customs are interspersed with the military record throughout the text. A concluding book, introduced by an address to Balbus, covers the suppression of the last revolts and notes the growing political tensions in Italy and Rome on the eve of the civil war.
la.calpurnius_siculus.eclogae: The Eclogae, a collection of seven Latin hexameter poems from the early Imperial period, is attributed to Calpurnius Siculus and follows the Virgilian model of pastoral dialogue. The first eclogue features verses carved on a beech tree by the god Faunus, which foretell a golden age of peace under a young Caesar. The remaining poems stage singing contests and conversations among shepherds, including a jealous lover's complaint against the fickle Phyllis. An old goatherd also instructs his pupil in the seasonal care of goats, while the collection concludes with prayers for the reigning emperor's welfare. The final eclogue describes a countryman's visit to Rome, where he witnesses the spectacle games, beasts, and wonders of the amphitheatre.
la.candidus_of_fulda.epitaphia_aegili: These two short Latin epitaphs honor Eigil, abbot of Fulda, during the Carolingian period, and they are transmitted under the name of Candidus of Fulda. The first text addresses a reader entering the small cave of the tomb, recounting Eigil's happy rule and his translation of a martyr's bones with the bishop. It also notes his dedication of two churches and his death, while naming his successor, Hrabanus, as the composer of this titulus. The second epitaph speaks in Eigil's own voice from the modest tomb he built, expressing confidence that the Lord will raise him up when death is loosed.
la.candidus_of_fulda.vita_aegili: The Vita Aegili is a Latin verse life of the Carolingian abbot Aegil, ascribed to the Fulda monk Candidus, who addresses his brother Modestus. The poet follows Aegil from his boyhood journey to Fulda, where Sturmi receives the young man, who later serves under Baugolf. The text recounts the discord among the brethren after Baugolf departs, and Louis intervenes, and Aegil is elected abbot. He consults with Archbishop Haistolf of Mainz, and the work describes the consecration of the church and its crypts. It details the translation of the relics of the martyr Boniface, and liturgical hymns sung at the ceremony are included. The poem narrates Aegil's final illness and burial, and an epitaph by Hrabanus accompanies the account, closing with reflections on mortality and virtue.
la.cato_the_elder.de_agricultura: De Agricultura, a Latin prose manual of estate management by Cato the Elder, was composed during the Roman Republic. Its preface praises agriculture over trade and moneylending as the source of strong citizens. The text offers practical instruction on buying and siting a farm, detailing equipment inventories for olive groves and vineyards. It clearly defines the duties of the bailiff and his wife, while seasonal operations include ploughing, planting, grafting, manuring, and harvesting. The work covers the care and doctoring of livestock, with recipes for breads, cakes, wines, and salted pork appearing alongside religious rites. These rites include prayers, sacrifices, and purifications for field and household, and contracts for hiring harvesters and selling oil, wine, and pasture close the main body. An extended account of the cabbage as food and medicine follows, and the text ends with a charm for setting dislocated limbs.
la.catullus.carmina: Carmina, a collection of lyric and epigrammatic verse in mixed metres from the late Roman Republic, opens with a dedication to the historian Cornelius Nepos. The short poems that follow range over hendecasyllabic and choliambic pieces on the poet's passion for Lesbia, addressing companions such as Veranius, Fabullus, and Calvus, as well as targets of invective like Mamurra and Egnatius. A group of longer compositions then presents the epithalamia for the wedding of Manlius and Vibia, followed by the Galliambic lament of Attis and the mythological epyllion on the marriage of Peleus and Thetis. This epyllion includes an extended tableau of Ariadne on Naxos, and a star-myth poem on the lock of Berenice and an elegy to Allius complete this section. The collection closes with a run of epigrams that continue the satirical attacks and the alternating despair and devotion of the Lesbia cycle, ending in the epitaphic farewell to the dead brother.
la.celsus.de_medicina: Celsus composed De Medicina, a Latin prose treatise on the art of medicine, during the early Imperial period. The work spans eight books and opens with a prologue tracing medical history from Aesculapius and Hippocrates to the author's own day. It weighs the claims of the rationalist, empiricist, and Methodist schools before sketching the plan for the entire text. Books one and two address regimen, covering the maintenance of health and general therapeutic measures like bleeding and diet. The middle sections detail the signs and treatment of specific diseases, followed by a pharmacology of simple drugs and compound recipes. The final books are devoted to surgery, including operative procedures and the treatment of fractures and dislocations.
la.cicero.de_divinatione: Cicero's De Divinatione ('On Divination') is a philosophical dialogue written during the Roman Republic. It was composed as a companion to his work on the nature of the gods. The text frames a conversation between Cicero and his brother Quintus at the Tusculan villa. The first book defends divination through artificial and natural forms. The second book refutes these claims using Academic scepticism. It closes with a distinction between religion and superstition.
la.cicero.de_domo_sua: The De Domo Sua, an oration by Cicero from the late Roman Republic, addresses the college of pontiffs to support his claim to the Palatine house. Publius Clodius had demolished this home and consecrated it as a shrine of Libertas while Cicero was in exile. The speech opens with an appeal to the pontiffs to balance state welfare with religious claims. Its body combines sustained invective against Clodius with legal argument, defending Cicero's recall and conduct as consul. He denies the validity of Clodius's tribunate, challenging the adoption, legislation, and consecration itself. The text discusses broader questions of extraordinary commands and the inviolability of a citizen's house, closing with a prayer to Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Vesta, and the household gods for his restoration.
la.cicero.de_haruspicum_responso: The De Haruspicum Responso is a prose oration by Cicero that opens with his clash with Publius Clodius in the senate. Cicero resolves to answer Clodius' exploitation of a fresh response from the haruspices, taking their pronouncements item by item. He argues that his Palatine house was lawfully freed of religious scruple following the verdicts of the pontiffs, the senate, and the Roman people. He denounces the riot that polluted the Megalesian games of the Great Mother, which served as an omen of servile violence. He catalogues Clodius' sacrileges, including the profanation of the rites of the Bona Dea, the destruction of shrines, and the sale of the sanctuary at Pessinus. The speech reviews the scandalous career by which a patrician reached the tribunate, dwelling on the haruspices' warnings of discord among the optimates. It mentions murder threatening the leading citizens and the state falling under one man's power, ending with an exhortation to concord and to expiation of the portents.
la.cicero.de_imperio_cn_pompei: Cicero delivered this oration before the Roman people during the Republic, supporting the tribune Manilius' proposal to grant supreme command of the war against Mithridates and Tigranes to Gnaeus Pompeius. Also known as the Pro Lege Manilia, the speech explains why he had previously avoided popular addresses from the Rostra, having devoted his early career to the defense of private clients. The text assesses the necessity and magnitude of the war, detailing the devastation of Asia and Bithynia and the peril to allies and revenues, while noting the collapse of credit at Rome. Cicero argues for Pompey's fitness under four heads, namely military knowledge, courage, authority, and good fortune, and he refutes the objections of Q. Catulus and Q. Hortensius. The speech defends Gabinius' role in the command and closes with an appeal to Manilius to stand firm against threats.
la.cicero.de_natura_deorum: De Natura Deorum ('On the Nature of the Gods') is a three-book philosophical dialogue by Cicero, composed during the Roman Republic, staging a debate on the nature of the gods. It opens with a preface addressed to Brutus on the obscurity of the question of the nature of the gods and on the Academic practice of suspending judgement. Set at the house of C. Cotta during the Latin holidays, the conversation presents the theology of three schools. The Epicurean Velleius speaks first, expounding gods that are blessed, idle, and human in form, and Cotta rebuts him. The second book gives the Stoic Balbus's argument that the world and its celestial order are divine, governed by providence and arranged for the benefit of gods and humans. In the third book Cotta subjects Balbus's Stoic case to a sustained critique, and the dialogue ends with the disagreement unresolved.
la.cicero.de_oratore: De Oratore is a three-book rhetorical dialogue by Cicero, written in Latin during the late Roman Republic, and it opens with a dedication to his brother Quintus, who laments the troubled state of public life. The work then shifts to a remembered conversation held at the Tusculan villa of Lucius Crassus shortly before his death, where participants include Crassus, Marcus Antonius, Q. Mucius Scaevola, Catulus, and Caesar. They debate the education and character of the ideal orator, asking whether eloquence can be reduced to a specific art, while also examining the need for wide learning in law, philosophy, and history. Later books treat invention, arrangement, memory, style, humour, and delivery, and the frame closes with an account of Crassus's death soon after the conversation.
la.cicero.de_republica: Cicero's De Republica, meaning 'On the Commonwealth', is a philosophical dialogue on the best constitution that survives in fragments, with substantial portions preserved through quotation in later authors. The opening argues for active political life against the philosophers' case for retreat, citing Roman exemplars such as Cato, Marcellus, and Scipio Africanus. The dialogue then ranges over the classification of simple and mixed constitutions, offering a long account of Rome's constitutional history from Romulus through the kings. The text also examines the qualities required of the ruler who governs the state, closing with the Dream of Scipio, in which Africanus appears to Scipio in a vision. He expounds the harmony of the spheres and the smallness of the inhabited earth, while the vision also addresses the vanity of earthly glory and the celestial reward for public service.
la.cicero.de_senectute: A Latin prose philosophical dialogue of the Roman Republic by Cicero, De Senectute opens with a metrical address to Atticus and a preface explaining that the argument on old age is placed in the mouth of the elder Cato, with Laelius and Scipio Aemilianus as his admiring young interlocutors. In the main dialogue Cato answers the four standard complaints against old age, that it withdraws men from active affairs, weakens the body, cuts off pleasures, and brings death near, countering each with exempla from Roman history and his own career, including Fabius Maximus, Appius Claudius, and the old farmers Cincinnatus and Curius. The speech goes on to praise the studies and rural delights befitting age, dwells on the authority that an honorably lived old age confers, and closes with Platonic and Pythagorean arguments for the immortality of the soul and a serene acceptance of death as nature's maturity.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_q_caecilium: The Divinatio in Q. Caecilium ('Investigation against Quintus Caecilius') is a forensic speech by Cicero from the Roman Republic. It was delivered at the divinatio, a preliminary hearing where the court selected the prosecutor for the extortion trial of Gaius Verres. Cicero opens by addressing the judges to explain why a man who has spent his career defending clients now steps forward as an accuser. He maintains that the Sicilian communities, plundered during Verres' three-year praetorship, have themselves chosen him as their advocate. His rival Quintus Caecilius, who served as quaestor under Verres, is disqualified by partiality and lack of forensic ability. The argument ranges over Verres' depredations and closes by urging the judges to appoint the accuser best able to sustain so great a cause.
la.cicero.in_catilinam: Cicero's In Catilinam gathers four consular speeches from the late Roman Republic, addressing the conspiracy of L. Sergius Catilina. The first, delivered in the senate, opens with the challenge 'quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?' and confronts Catiline with evidence of his plots until the consul bids him leave the city. The second, spoken to the Roman people, announces his departure and reviews the classes of indebted and desperate men who remain in Rome. The third reports the interception of the Allobrogian envoys and the letters that incriminated Lentulus, Cethegus and their fellow conspirators. The fourth, before the senate, sets Caesar's proposal of perpetual imprisonment against the call for execution and closes with an exhortation to judge decisively for the safety of the state.
la.cicero.in_vatinium: In Vatinium is a section of Cicero's defence of Publius Sestius, recording the cross-examination of the prosecution witness Publius Vatinius. Cicero claims he would have dismissed the man out of contempt, but he interrogates him instead to crush his ferocity and entangle his loquacity. The questioning covers his disreputable youth and his quaestorship at Puteoli, and it also probes his irregular journeys as legate in Spain and Africa. His tribunate is attacked for trampling the auspices and the Aelian and Fufian laws, with the consul Bibulus mentioned in this context. Further questions address the Vettius conspiracy and his professed Pythagoreanism, and his servility toward Caesar is also examined. The speech closes with his private disgraces, including a banquet attended in mourning dress, his obstruction of his own trial, and a self-granted legation, while Cicero presses contradictions between Vatinius's earlier statements and his testimony against Sestius and Titus Annius.
la.cicero.letters_to_atticus: The Letters to Atticus (Epistulae ad Atticum) comprise the correspondence between Cicero and his close friend Titus Pomponius Atticus. This collection is arranged in sixteen books and opens with reports from Cicero's canvass for the consulship. The letters mix running commentary on public affairs with intimate news of family and finances. Topics range from elections and trials to the rivalry of Pompey and Caesar. They also cover property purchases, legal business, and literary projects. Written in conversational prose studded with Greek phrases, the text traces Roman politics and private concerns across the closing decades of the Republic.
la.cicero.pro_a_caecina: Pro Caecina is a forensic oration by Cicero from the Roman Republic, which defends Aulus Caecina in a suit arising from the interdict de vi armata. The speech opens by contrasting Aebutius' armed audacity in the fields with his impudence in court, while the narrative recounts the tangled history of the Fulcinian estate and the armed ambush at the ravine. It details the widow Caesennia's purchase of the land and her subsequent marriage to Caecina, and the bulk of the text argues against the advocate Piso on legal points. The oration weighs whether Caecina was expelled within the meaning of the interdict, and it also examines intimidation without bloodshed and the relation of verbal formulae to equity. It addresses Caecina's citizenship despite Sulla's settlement of Volaterrae, and the speech closes with an appeal to the panel's sense of justice.
la.cicero.pro_a_cluentio: The Pro Cluentio is a forensic oration by Cicero from the Roman Republic, which defends Aulus Cluentius Habitus of Larinum against a charge of poisoning. The speech opens by announcing that the defense will address two main issues, namely the prejudice from the earlier Junian trial and the formal charge before the court. The body of the speech refutes the claim that Cluentius bought the conviction of Statius Albius, while exposing the crimes of the dead Oppianicus and the agitation of the tribune Quinctius. The oration also answers the censors' notations of the jurors, and it then dismantles the poisoning accusation itself. Cicero attributes the charge to the schemes of Cluentius' mother Sassia and the prosecutor Titus Attius, and a peroration invokes the support of Larinum and neighboring municipalities. It entreats the judges to save the defendant from his mother.
la.cicero.pro_archia: Pro Archia ('In Defense of Archias') is a judicial oration by Cicero from the Roman Republic. It was spoken to defend the Greek poet A. Licinius Archias against a challenge to his citizenship. Cicero begins by acknowledging Archias as his first guide in rhetorical studies. He then argues the case using Archias's career and the testimony of Lucullus. The speech turns into a sustained praise of literary studies as moral formation. It closes with an appeal to preserve a poet who witnesses Roman deeds.
la.cicero.pro_balbo: This forensic oration by Cicero defends Lucius Cornelius Balbus of Gades against charges of unlawful citizenship, acknowledging that Pompey and other distinguished figures have already defended the cause. He then takes up the task of finishing the argument for his client, who was prosecuted over the Roman citizenship that Pompey had conferred on him. This grant was made by the verdict of Pompey's council under the lex Gellia Cornelia, and Cicero argues that Pompey acted lawfully. He denies that the treaty with Gades barred the grant, disputing the prosecution's doctrine of municipal peoples and the supposed sacrosanctity of the Gaditanian treaty. The speech marshals precedents from Marius, Pompey's father, Crassus, Sulla, and Metellus, while also citing Rome's long standing practice of admitting new citizens from Romulus onward. The latter part rebuts oblique charges over Balbus's wealth, luxury, and tribal enrolment, and it also addresses his adoption by Theophanes and his closeness to Caesar. The speech closes on the claim that the judges are really passing on Pompey's benefaction, and they are not judging any crime committed by Balbus.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_perduellionis_reo: This forensic speech by Cicero defends Gaius Rabirius, an elderly senator prosecuted for perduellio, or high treason, by the tribune Titus Labienus. The case was tried by the archaic duumviral procedure, which allowed an appeal to the Roman people. Cicero argues that his client's acquittal is bound up with the survival of senatorial authority and consular imperium. He answers the specific charges raised by Labienus and then turns to the death of the tribune Saturninus. The oration defends the senatus consultum by which the consuls Marius and Valerius called citizens to arms. Cicero denounces the threatened penalty of scourging and crucifixion as alien to the liberty of Roman citizens. The speech closes with an appeal that the defendant be allowed to die a natural death at home.
la.cicero.pro_fonteio: Pro Fonteio, a Latin forensic oration by Cicero, defends Marcus Fonteius, a former governor of Transalpine Gaul, against extortion charges before a Roman court during the Republic. The surviving text begins abruptly in the middle of the argument, where Cicero defends Fonteius's handling of public money during his earlier quaestorship. He dismantles accusations of illegal exactions and profiteering from road building, contrasting hostile Gallic envoys with Roman colonists and Massiliote allies. The orator urges the judges to weigh testimony carefully rather than accept it blindly, while also dwelling on the Gauls' earlier wars and their barbarous rites. Cicero invokes the support of Fonteius's family, including a Vestal virgin sister, and the speech closes by calling for the acquittal of a loyal citizen.
la.cicero.pro_ligario: Pro Ligario ('In Defense of Ligarius') is a forensic oration by Cicero from the Republican era. It was spoken before Julius Caesar to defend Quintus Ligarius against charges of bearing arms in Africa. The speech opens by conceding the charge and shifting the focus to an appeal for mercy. Cicero argues that Ligarius served only as a legate in peacetime and avoided Varus's command. He also notes that the accuser, Quintus Tubero, had fought at Pharsalus. The oration closes with a plea for clemency, citing the grief of Ligarius's brothers and Roman knights.
la.cicero.pro_milone: Pro Milone is a prose forensic oration by Cicero from the Roman Republic, serving as a defence of Titus Annius Milo against the charge of murdering Publius Clodius on the Appian Way. The speech opens with the advocate confessing that the sight of a court ringed with soldiers unnerves him, while arguing that killing in self-defence is permitted by nature and sanctioned by Roman precedent. The text defends the senatorial decree and Pompey's special statute from the charge that they condemned the deed, reconstructing the meeting on the Appian Way to show that Clodius, not Milo, had laid an ambush. An extended invective against Clodius's life and designs gives way to a peroration, in which Milo's imagined stoic speeches and Cicero's own tears plead for acquittal.
la.cicero.pro_plancio: The Pro Plancio ('In Defense of Plancius') is a forensic oration by Cicero from the Roman Republic. It defends Gnaeus Plancius, who was prosecuted for electoral corruption by Marcus Laterensis. The speech argues that the people's verdict in the election should not be overturned in court. Cicero also attacks the prosecution's selection of tribes and rebuts the witnesses' charges of bribery. He recounts how Plancius protected him during his exile through Brundisium and Macedonia. The oration closes with emotional appeals to the judges' mercy.
la.cicero.pro_publio_quinctio: Pro Publio Quinctio ('In Defense of Publius Quinctius') is a forensic speech by Cicero, a Roman orator of the Republican era. It was delivered in a civil action on behalf of Publius Quinctius against Sextus Naevius before the judge Gaius Aquilius. The opening laments that the influence of Naevius and the eloquence of Hortensius are arrayed against the defense. The body reconstructs the partnership between Quinctius' brother and Naevius in Gaul, the brother's death, and the inheritance by Quinctius. It details the disputed debt, the alleged abandonment of the vadimonium, and the seizure of Quinctius' goods under the praetor's edict. The speech argues that nothing was owed and that the goods were never lawfully possessed. It concludes with an appeal to the judge's equity, presenting the case as a struggle for Quinctius' reputation and fortune.
la.claudian.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora, meaning the lesser poems, gathers the shorter works of Claudian. This late antique poet wrote in hexameters, mostly in a panegyric mode. The collection opens by addressing Stilicho, who served as both son-in-law and father-in-law to the emperor. Other poems praise the imperial circle and describe marvels like the phoenix and crystal. The sequence also includes invectives against rivals and mythological narratives. It closes with Christian poems on the birth of Christ and redemption.
la.claudian.de_bello_gothico: De Bello Gothico is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, which praises the general Stilicho for his campaigns against the Goths. The opening proem sees the poet roused after a long silence to invoke the Muse, comparing Stilicho's deliverance of Italy to Tiphys steering the Argo past the Clashing Rocks. This introduction leads into the narrative of the Gothic invasion under Alaric, where the text records omens that terrify Rome, including the prodigy of two slain wolves. An elder Goth pleads for retreat, but Alaric proudly rejects the advice, and Stilicho then crosses the Alps to Rhaetia during the winter. Troops gather there from Britain, Germany, and the Rhine frontier, and rallying his forces, he brings the invaders to battle. The poem ends with the Roman victory at Pollentia, noting the recovery of captives and spoils, and finally compares Stilicho to Marius, who defeated the Cimbri on the same plain.
la.claudian.de_consulatu_stilichonis: The De Consulatu Stilichonis is a Latin panegyric in hexameter verse, consisting of three books by the late antique poet Claudian. It celebrates the consulship of Stilicho, a general of the Western Roman empire, opening in heaven where the gods prolong their rejoicing over the imperial wedding. They also celebrate the triumph over the defeated Gildo, while the poet weighs how any single song could encompass the mass of Stilicho's deeds. The poem then traces his career from boyhood, highlighting his justice, courage, and achievements in peace as in war. Personified provinces, including Gaul, Britannia, and Africa, testify to his defense against Franks, Picts, Scots, and Saxons, and attest to the recovery of Africa. The closing section turns to triumphal spectacle, culminating in a fantastic maritime procession where elephants, sea monsters, and a Bacchic fleet of Silenus and the Satyrs attend the victor.
la.claudian.de_raptu_proserpinae: De Raptu Proserpinae is a Latin epic in three hexameter books by the late antique poet Claudian, narrating the abduction of Proserpina by Pluto. After a prelude on the first mariner to dare the deep, the poet invokes Phoebus and the gods below. The first book shows Pluto chafing at his unwedded state while Ceres conceals the girl in Sicily before she departs for Cybele's rites on Ida. The second book brings Venus, Minerva, and Diana to lure Proserpina from her half-woven tapestry, but Pluto bursts from a fissure and carries her off. The underworld keeps festive wedding rites, and Proserpina is consoled by a vision of her future throne, while the third book follows Ceres. She wanders land and sea for her lost daughter, warned by omens and a dream, as Jupiter forbids any god to reveal the abductor.
la.claudian.epithalamium_de_nuptiis_honorii: This Latin hexameter epithalamium ('a marriage song') by the Late Antique poet Claudian celebrates the marriage of the emperor Honorius to Maria, daughter of Stilicho. The poem opens with the mythological wedding of Peleus and Thetis, at which Apollo's song foretells Achilles, before turning to Honorius pining in secret love for his bride. The greater part follows Venus and Amor, as Amor carries news of the union to Cyprus and Venus sails to Italy with sea deities bearing bridal gifts. Venus prepares the wedding chamber and adorns Maria, whose beauty she praises at length. It closes with the nuptial procession and a wedding song extolling Stilicho's virtues and blessing his children and hoped-for descendants.
la.claudian.in_consulatum_olybrii_et_probin: Claudian composed this late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters to honor the joint consulship of Olybrius and Probinus, who were sons of the noble Probus and members of the Anician house. The poem opens with an invocation to the Sun and an encomium of that lineage, then recounts an allegorical episode in which Rome, personified as a warrior goddess, journeys to the war god. She pleads for the brothers after his victory over Alpine foes, and his assent leads to a vision of the consuls entering the forum attended by the senate. A festive banquet among the river gods follows this scene, and the work closes with a prayer that the seasons and the fasti favor their year of office.
la.claudian.in_eutropium: Claudian's In Eutropium ('Against Eutropius') is a late antique Latin invective in hexameter verse. The poem spans two books and targets the eunuch Eutropius, who rose from slavery to the consulship. It opens with a catalogue of cosmic portents that yield to the greater prodigy of a eunuch consul. The text recounts Eutropius' castration, his careers as slave, pimp, and courtier, and his traffic in offices. The first book dwells on his dishonorable rise and military pretensions, bringing personified Roma to plead with Stilicho. The second follows the Gothic revolt of Tribigild through the cities of Phrygia. It details the rout of the court's forces and Eutropius' fall into condemnation and exile.
la.claudian.in_rufinum: Claudian's In Rufinum ('Against Rufinus') is a late antique Latin panegyric in two books of hexameters, pairing invective against the eastern minister Rufinus with praise of the general Stilicho. The poem opens with Apollo's slaughter of Python and asks whether the world is governed by providence or chance, a doubt the poet says Rufinus's punishment finally dispels. The narrative then follows the Fury Megaera's rearing of Rufinus and his rise to power at the court of Arcadius. His avarice, cruelty, and collusion with barbarian peoples meet the resistance of Stilicho, whose eastern campaign against him is halted by an imperial command. The second book carries the story through Rufinus's killing by the soldiers at an imperial muster and his dismemberment by the populace of Constantinople. It ends with his trial before Minos, who consigns his shade to the deepest pit of Tartarus.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_quarto_consulatu: Claudian composed this Latin hexameter panegyric to celebrate the fourth consulship of Honorius, depicting the returning fasces and the army reassuming civilian dress. Bellona herself is shown bearing the consular trabea in this ritual display, while the poem traces the dynasty's rise through the conquests of Theodosius the Great. These campaigns extended from Britain to Ethiopia and included the suppression of two western tyrants, followed by a long paternal address from the dying emperor. He counsels self-mastery, piety, justice, and the conduct of war, with exempla from early Roman history supporting these moral lessons. The text next describes Stilicho's pacification of the Rhine peoples and his repulse of the barbarians who had overrun Greece. Praise of his justice and moderation in peacetime completes this section, returning to Honorius and his training in arms. His journey to Rome and consular procession are detailed, noting the defeat of the Greuthungi under Odothaeus. The poem ends with the prospect of marriage and shared triumphs with Arcadius.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_sexto_consulatu_: The Panegyricus de Sexto Consulatu Honorii Augusti is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, celebrating the emperor Honorius' entry upon his sixth consulship. It opens with a dream-vision in which the poet recites verses before Jupiter in the heavens, an omen confirmed by news of the emperor's approach to Rome. The body of the poem traces Honorius' upbringing and rooted devotion to the city, his cession of the eastern court to his brother, the suppression of the rebel Gildo in Africa and of Alaric through Stilicho, the Gothic defeat at Pollentia and the fighting at Verona, and Alaric's despairing retreat over the Alps, with speeches assigned to the river god Eridanus and to Alaric himself. Roma then pleads in person for the emperor's presence, recalling Stilicho's night rescue of the young Honorius across the Addua, and travels to Rome to adorn the adventus, after which the poem closes with the civic spectacles of the games and the inauguration of the consulship, prized as a victory over a foreign foe rather than, as in earlier imperial visits, over fellow citizens.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_tertio_consulatu: Claudian's Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius is a Latin poem in 229 hexameters by a late antique court poet, celebrating the young Western emperor's assumption of the consulship. It opens with an eagle exposing its fledglings to the sun's fire, an allegory of imperial upbringing and testing. The poem traces Honorius's birth amid the camps of his father Theodosius, his harsh martial training, and the tales of his grandfather's campaigns. There follow the overthrow of the usurper who had seized the Western throne, the victory at the Frigidus river, and Honorius's triumphal progress through Italy to his father's embrace. In the closing scene Theodosius, ascending to the heavens, entrusts his sons to Stilicho and prophesies that the brothers will together subdue the peoples of the East.
la.claudius_mamertinus.panegyricus: This Latin prose panegyric was delivered by Claudius Mamertinus to thank the emperor Julian for a consulship. The title identifies the work as a formal speech of praise. The speaker begins by apologizing for his delayed gratitude and reviewing Julian's earlier gifts. He then details the emperor's recovery of Gaul and his frugal, just rule. The text also highlights Julian's rapid Danube voyage and his restoration of Greek cities. It contrasts these virtues with the corruption of earlier courts. The speech closes with the consular procession and a pledge of lifelong devotion.
la.columella.de_re_rustica: De Re Rustica ('On Agriculture') is a Latin prose treatise by Columella from the Early Imperial period. It opens with an address to Publius Silvinus that rejects the claim that the earth has grown old and barren. The preface laments the neglect of husbandry and surveys earlier Greek and Roman writers on the subject. Successive books then take up the choice of land and the siting and arrangement of the villa. They also cover the management of coloni, slaves, and overseers, along with soils, ploughing, and sowing. Later books pass to farm animals, birds kept for the table, fishponds, and bees, closing with a promise of a verse treatment of gardens.
la.commodian.carmen_apologeticum: The Carmen Apologeticum ('Apologetic Poem') is a Latin work of apologetic theology by Commodian, an author of the later imperial period. It opens with the speaker's recollection of his own wandering in error and the illumination he found in the book of the law. This personal testimony establishes his resolve to turn others from deception. The body of the poem argues from the law and the prophets that the one God foretold to Israel came in the flesh as Christ. It rehearses prophetic testimonies, Christ's miracles, and the promise of resurrection while rebuking Jewish unbelief and idolatry. The final movement is apocalyptic, foretelling a last persecution, the return of Nero as Antichrist, and the burning of Rome.
la.commodian.instructiones: The Instructiones is a two-book Christian didactic work by Commodian, a writer of the later Roman Empire, whose opening preface recalls his conversion. He announces his intention to instruct the ignorant and show the errant the way to eternal life, mounting a sustained polemic against paganism and Jewish unbelief. The text ridicules the gods and their myths, including Saturn, Jupiter, and Apollo, while denouncing idols, diviners, and venal priests. Arguments are drawn from the law and the prophets, with figures like Adam read as types of Christ, before the second book turns to believers. It reproves worldliness and laxity in the face of persecution, prescribing conduct for catechumens, women, the wealthy, and pastors. Precepts cover baptism, penance, charity, martyrdom, and funerary display, closing with a full scheme of last things, including a revived Nero and the Antichrist. It also describes the return of Elijah, a thousand-year reign, and the final judgment by fire.
la.corippus.johannis: The Johannis, meaning the poem of John, is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameters attributed to Corippus. It spans roughly 4,700 lines across eight books and celebrates the campaigns of the Byzantine general John against Moorish peoples in North Africa under the reign of the emperor Justinian. The poem opens with an invocation and panegyric to Justinian, then describes the devastation of Africa before following John's voyage from Constantinople to Carthage. The narrative covers his battles with Antalas and the Laguatan, details his discipline of the troops, and recounts the death of Stutias in civil strife.
