The story continues with the usurpation of Guntarith, followed by successive campaigns against Carcasan and the Nasamones. Set-piece battle scenes alternate with speeches and divine interventions, while episodes of famine and mutiny are interspersed with reflections on divine providence that govern the theme of Roman victory throughout the text.
la.cyprian.ad_donatum: Ad Donatum is a short Latin prose treatise of late antique Christian theology where Cyprian addresses his friend Donatus in a work that opens with a promised conversation in a garden. The author gives a first-person account of his conversion and baptism, recalling how implausible moral rebirth once seemed to him before baptism and the Holy Spirit made possible what he had thought impossible. He ascribes this change to the free gift of divine grace, and a long central survey frames a vision of the world seen from a mountain height. It catalogues the corruptions of secular life, including warfare, gladiatorial games, and theatrical spectacles, while also listing sexual vice, law courts, political honours, wealth, and power. The text concludes that peace and security are found only in withdrawal to God, and the work closes with exhortations to purity, constant prayer, and reading. It ends with a day concluded in sober psalmody.
la.cyprian.de_lapsis: De Lapsis, a Latin prose treatise by Cyprian on church discipline, addresses a community rejoicing at peace restored after a recent persecution. The work praises confessors who endured prison and torture for their faith, while Cyprian laments those who sacrificed to idols or obtained certificates of compliance. He attributes this collapse to greed, luxury, and slackened observance, condemning hasty reconciliation without prior penance. The author argues that the power to forgive sins belongs to God alone, urging full confession, satisfaction, and tears. The treatise closes by holding out hope that true penitents may be restored to grace.
la.cyprian.de_mortalitate: Cyprian's Latin treatise De Mortalitate ('On Mortality') addresses Christians facing a lethal pestilence. It argues that the present crisis is a test of faith rather than a common ruin. The text cites Simeon, Job, Tobias, Abraham, and Paul to show that adversity proves the just. It contends that death for the faithful is a liberation from the devil's warfare. The author urges readers to receive the departed with joy as they move toward their true homeland. The work closes by likening the collapsing world to a tottering house and a storm-tossed ship.
la.cyprian.epistulae: The Epistulae, meaning letters, are a collection of correspondence by Cyprian, written in Late Antique Latin. They address church order and clerical conduct, discussing ecclesiastical discipline and specific cases of misconduct. One ruling forbids clergy from serving as guardians in wills, while another excludes a stage performer from communion for continuing his trade. A third reproves a deacon who insulted his bishop, and biblical precedent supports these decisions throughout the text. Each letter ends with a formulaic wish for the recipient's health.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_senatorem_ex_christian: This short Latin admonition, attributed to Cyprian and dating from the later imperial period, addresses a senator who abandoned Christianity for the worship of old gods, especially Isis. The speaker opens by declaring that he hastened to answer in song because the senator loves poetry, then proceeds as a sustained rebuke of the addressee's return to vain rites. The text ridicules the effeminate dress and conduct of Isiac priests, mocking a former consul ministering with the sistrum, while arguing that excess destroys what it feeds. Citing Maro's line on the eternally seated Theseus, the author warns that knowingly abandoning known truth is a grave offence, urging the senator to amend before old age arrives. Since remorse excuses only a first lapse, the work closes by emphasizing the urgency of this final chance for redemption.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_pascha: De Pascha is a brief Latin poem transmitted under the name of Cyprian, whose date remains uncertain though it belongs to the later imperial period. The work presents an allegorical vision of Easter centred on Golgotha, where a tree cut from barren stock bears wholesome fruit. It grows to heaven and spreads twelve branches over the whole earth, and fifty days later a heavenly breath pours divine nectar upon them. Beneath their shade, a clear spring draws peoples of every age, sex, and rank, though some reject the unfamiliar flavour while others fall back into the mire. The faithful bathe fasting in the waters on the seventh day, and they are purified for the journey to heaven. The poem closes by identifying the tree as the wood of life for all who believe.
la.cyprianus_cordubensis.cypriani_et_samson: This short Latin collection of epigrams and sepulchral verses comes from medieval Cordoba, transmitted under the names of Cyprian of Cordoba and Abbot Samson. It opens with poems praising Count Adulfus, who renewed a book-case at his own expense to hold the Old and New Testament as nourishment for the soul. The text includes an admonition to his son Fredenand and a piece on a gilded fan inscribed with the name Guifredus. The greater part consists of epitaphs and memorial inscriptions for various figures, including Abbot Samson, Hermildis, John, a priestly virgin, the abbot Athanagild, and Valentinian. One of these inscriptions bears the year 918.
la.cyprianus_gallus.heptateuchos: The Heptateuchos, a late antique Latin epic in hexameters, is attributed to the poet Cyprianus Gallus. It versifies the first seven books of the Bible, from Genesis to Judges, opening with the six days of creation and the story of Adam and Eve. The narrative follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, then turns to Moses and the Exodus, treating the plagues and the crossing of the Red Sea. Extended passages cover legal and ritual prescriptions from Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, while the closing books carry the story through the conquest of Canaan under Joshua. The poem ends within the period of the judges, from Othniel through Gideon and Samson.
la.descartes.meditations: René Descartes wrote this philosophical treatise in Latin prose, cast as a sequence of meditations conducted over successive days. The work opens with a resolve to demolish all former beliefs, entertaining systematic doubt concerning the senses and the difference between dreaming and waking. The author also considers the hypothesis of a deceiving God or malignant genius, from which the text derives the certainty of the thinker's own existence as a thinking thing. It examines the nature of mind through the example of a piece of wax, moving from the idea of an infinitely perfect being to the existence of God. The text also establishes the truth of whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived, explaining error as the will's assent extending beyond what the intellect apprehends. Later meditations demonstrate the real distinction between mind and body, re-establishing the existence of material things and showing the senses to be reliable in their proper office of signalling what benefits or harms the composite of mind and body.
la.dhuoda.rhythmy_ex_manuali_dhuodanae: The Rhythmy ex Manuali Dhuodanae gathers Latin verses from a Carolingian text that Dhuoda wrote for her young son William. It opens with an invocation to God as maker of light and eternal king, asking the boy to know, love, and praise his creator. Prayers follow for William's welfare of body and soul, while exhortations urge humility, chastity, and reverence for the clergy. Dhuoda also calls for just judgement and generosity to the poor, noting the haste and illness that constrained her writing. The collection closes with an epitaph and burial prayer for Dhuoda, and shorter pieces then address creation, the fall, and peace.
la.dicuil.versus: This short Latin poem by the Carolingian author Dicuil places the work in the circle of the Carolingian court. It opens by declaring an intention to please Charles in speech and song. The poet presents playful arguments and asks the hearer to mark which month it is, reckoning from April. The text then salutes Louis as Charles's successor and states that it was completed in May. It notes the date as eight hundred and fourteen years from the conception of the Lord. The poem ends by likening the poet's humble offering to the widow's two mites.
la.dracontius.de_laudibus_dei: De Laudibus Dei ('On the Praises of God') is a Late Antique Latin Christian epic in three books of hexameters by the poet Dracontius. The opening invites readers to know God in wrath and mercy, noting that all goods and calamities descend from his throne. The first book celebrates creation across the six days, the ordering of sky, sea, plants and animals, and the fate of Adam and Eve. The second and third books set God's justice and forbearance against human sin through biblical punishments and pardons. They contrast pagan feats of rash valour with acts of faith. The poem ends in a first-person penitential prayer where a captive speaker confesses his offences and begs for release, health and restoration.
la.dracontius.romulea: The Romulea of Dracontius is a Late Antique Latin collection of eleven short lyric poems. The title refers to the poet's own name, which is derived from the Latin word for wolf. The work opens with a preface that evokes Orpheus and addresses a revered master of letters. It then turns to a narrative of Hylas, the beloved companion of Hercules, among the nymphs. The remaining poems range across mythological narrative and occasional verse, including festive scenes of personified virtues. The collection ends with the image of a gleaming serpent trailing through the clouds.
la.engelmodus.carmina: This small collection of Latin verse by the Carolingian poet Engelmodus consists of a personal epistle and a long panegyric to the same addressee. The opening poem is a complaint addressed to a beloved friend named Agi, reproaching him for neglect and changed affections. It pleads for the renewal of their bond despite the gulf of wealth and rank between them. The remainder of the work is an extended encomium and prayer to Agi, now addressed as pope. It praises his noble upbringing, eloquence, learning, and manifold virtues, along with his care for the poor and defence of his flock. The text concludes with visions of the last judgement in which the poet begs the pontiff's protection and intercession.
la.ennius.annales: The Annales of Ennius is an epic poem written in hexameter verse during the Roman Republic, surviving only as scattered fragments. It opens with an invocation of the Muses and a dream featuring Homer, while also including famous passages on the soul and its transmigration. The poem traces Roman history from the fall of Troy to Ennius's own day, covering Aeneas's wanderings and arrival in Latinus's land. The narrative continues through early kings and Republic wars, concluding with military campaigns and embassies from the poet's contemporary period. Much space is given to battles fought on both land and sea, among which are set pieces like a widowed heroine's tearful dream. Another fragment depicts Sisyphus straining at his heavy rock, and a final passage uses the phrase lateralis dolor to announce approaching death.
la.ennodius.carmina: The Carmina ('Poems') of the late antique poet Ennodius is a varied collection of Latin verse. It opens with an itinerary poem describing a journey through wintry Alpine country. The speaker travels to the shrines of martyrs such as Saturninus, Crispinus, and Daria. The rest of the collection ranges across praise poems addressed to friends and patrons. It also includes pieces on nature, love, and mythological subjects such as Phaethon and Venus. A substantial devotional sequence on Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the saints closes the work.
la.ermenricus_elwagensis.epistola_ad_grimal: The Epistola ad Grimaldum ('Letter to Grimald') is a Carolingian Latin verse letter by Ermenricus Elwagensis, dedicated to one Grimald and devoted to Saint Gall. It opens with prayers to the Trinity and to Gall himself for the gift of worthy song, weaving Greek words into the Latin verses. A geographic prologue then surveys the Alps, the Danube, the Rhine and Lake Constance, pausing on the island monastery of Augia and its abbot Folcwinus. Then comes a jesting apostrophe to Homer, renouncing epic matter in favour of the saint's story. The remainder recounts where Gall was born, whence he came to these lands, where he dwelt beside the Rhine, and the deeds he performed there, told in humble verse. Its hymnic opening, professions of authorial inadequacy, and direct address to the reader place it among Carolingian verse prefaces.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_honorem_Ludo: This Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters by Ermoldus Nigellus is addressed to the emperor Louis the Pious, adapting the classicizing heroic epic to the panegyric of a Christian emperor. The poem opens with a prayer to Christ in which the poet rejects the Muses, asking for aid during his exile before turning to praise of Louis. The narrative recounts Louis's Aquitanian campaigns and the capture of Barcelona from the Moors, while also covering Charlemagne's partition of the realm and the coronation of his son. It describes the visit of Pope Stephen and war against the Breton ruler Murman, including the conversion of the Danish king Herold and the painted halls at Ingelheim. Miracle tales connected with a Strasbourg church of the Virgin are also told, and the work closes with the exiled poet's direct appeal to Louis and Judith for pardon.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_laudem_pippi: A Latin panegyric in hexameter verse by the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus, addressed to King Pippin and written throughout from the standpoint of an exile seeking the ruler's favour. The poem opens with an invocation to Thalia, who is sent to the royal palace to herald the exiled poet's arrival and convey his greetings to the court. Its course then takes in a dispute between the personified Rhine and the Vosges region over their respective gifts, a portrait of Strasbourg and its learned bishop Bernold, exempla of celebrated exiles and of biblical and Frankish rulers, and the humorous episode of the cat whose presence hinders a monk's vision of Christ; counsel on kingship and praise of Louis the Pious lead to a closing prayer for Pippin and his wife and a passage spelling out the author's own name.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carminum_appendix: The Carminum Appendix is a short Carolingian Latin poem in hexameters attributed to Ermoldus Nigellus, opening as a song for King Pippin. It addresses a boy performer and a pipe, urging the child to learn wisdom, read Cato, and sing psalms. These counsels alternate with refrain-like lines and catalogues of ivory, incense, agates, and gold, while recalling Louis becoming emperor through the coronation by Pope Stephen. The text also notes Bishop Ebbo renewing the foundations of his see before shifting to the epitaph of Himiltrudis, Ebbo's mother. She recounts her upbringing on the German Rhine and later life by the Loire and Seine, describing her son's elevation as bishop and their ten years of labor. The poem closes with her death at the Kalends of September, offering a warning to travellers against excess and a prayer for pardon.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.formulae_spiritalis_in: The Formulae spiritalis intellegentiae, or formulas of spiritual understanding, is a late antique Latin manual by Eucherius of Lyon. It addresses the author's son Veranus to explain how scripture must be read figuratively. The preface sketches the historical, tropological, allegorical, and anagogical senses of the text. The body follows ten headings covering bodily members, creatures, animals, and other categories. Each entry defines a biblical term's spiritual meaning and cites a supporting text. The work closes with a catalogue of numbers from one to one hundred.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.instructiones: Instructions is a two-book Latin work of scriptural explanation by Eucherius of Lyon, composed in the late antique period and dedicated to his son Salonius. The first book proceeds in questions and answers that resolve difficulties in biblical passages, ranging from Genesis through the historical books, Job, Psalms, and the Prophets. These also cover the Gospels, the Pauline epistles, and Acts, where the author favors allegorical and moral senses alongside the literal. The second book is a compact glossary giving the meanings of Hebrew and Greek proper names, and it also defines obscure biblical terms for objects, animals, vestments, weights, and measures. This glossary includes the names of peoples, places, months, and festivals, and it further lists the chief vocabulary of ecclesiastical usage. Eucherius presents his explanations as drawn from the judgments of earlier doctors, closing by describing the collection as a seed-bed of understanding spread over nearly the whole body of Scripture.
la.eutropius.breviarium: Eutropius, a magister memoriae, dedicated this Latin prose epitome to the emperor Valens. The work is titled Breviarium, which means a summary or abridgment. It gathers the outstanding events of Roman history in a brief narrative ordered by time. The account begins with Romulus and the seven kings, then covers the early Republic. It details the Samnite wars and the Punic wars against Carthage, including Hannibal's invasion. The text follows the late Republic, the emperors from Augustus to the Severans, and the third-century crises. It concludes with the tetrarchy, Constantine, and the death of Jovian.
la.fardulfus.carmina: Carmina, meaning songs, is a short Carolingian Latin poem by Fardulf, who identifies himself as an abbot in the closing lines. The work opens with an address to the reader, where Fardulf states that he made these verses for his Charles. He recounts how adverse fortune drove him from the sceptre of his own people into exile, and the narrative follows his loyal service to Charlemagne. It details the king's abundant gifts in reward for his fidelity, and Fardulf was appointed head of the church of Saint-Denis. He constructed a richly adorned basilica there, fulfilling vows first made amid the hardships of banishment, and the poem closes with Charlemagne's approval of the work. It includes prayers that the king's friendship and days may long increase, and a description follows of the abbey as a house of grace and salvation. God dwells there among the bodies of the saints, and a final notice states that Abbot Fardulf made its ciborium.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_gratia_libri_duo: The De gratia ('On Grace') is a two-book prose treatise by Faustus of Riez. It addresses Leontius, who convened a council to condemn the error of predestination. The author aims to refute both Pelagian excess and the opposite extreme of total grace. Book one combats Pelagian views on infant baptism, free choice, and divine prescience. Book two argues that the will remains free even before Christ and the law. It cites gentiles like Nebuchadnezzar and the Ninevites as examples of natural reason. The work closes with an imagined divine deliberation on creating a man free to sin.
la.faustus_of_riez.sermones: Faustus of Riez, a Late Antique author, composed these Latin prose sermons for mixed lay and monastic audiences. The collection spans the liturgical year, beginning with an urgent call to purify conscience and body. This opening piece prepares hearers to celebrate the Lord's nativity and receive the Eucharist worthily. The cycle then moves through the Epiphany and the martyrdoms of Stephen, Vincent, and the Holy Innocents. It also includes commemorations of Honoratus and Augustine. Moral discourses on penitence, almsgiving, fasting, and the last judgment alternate with typological readings of Abraham, Isaac, and Joseph. Doctrinal sermons on the Trinity and the Holy Spirit culminate in instruction for Pentecost.
la.florus.epitome_bellorum_omnium_annorum: The Epitome bellorum omnium annorum, a Latin prose history by Florus, compresses Roman military history from the city's founding to the reign of Augustus. The preface divides this span into the ages of a human life, describing infancy under the kings and adolescence in the conquest of Italy. Robust manhood appears in the overseas wars, with old age briefly renewed under Trajan, while the narrative follows this scheme through the seven kings and the early Republic. It covers the Samnite and Punic wars, along with the conquests of Macedonia and Syria, and details the wars in Spain and Gaul, the northern invasions, and the suppression of pirates. The text closes with the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Caesar, and Pompey, before describing Octavian's victory at Actium and the pacification of the frontiers. Augustus then establishes peace and closes the gates of Janus.
la.gerwardus.versus: This six-line Latin epigram is of Carolingian date and attributed to Gerwardus. It opens with the poet offering these verses to a prince to secure his praise and eternal memory. The speaker styles himself a suppliant servant who raises his patron's distinguished name to the stars. The closing couplet addresses the reader directly and bids that the deed concerning Einhard be set down in writing. Einhard is identified as the glorifier of great Charles. The poem evidently served as a dedicatory preface to a copy of Einhard's account of Charlemagne's life and deeds.
la.giovanni_aurelio_augurelli.chrysopoeia: Chrysopoeia ('The Making of Gold') is a Renaissance Latin didactic poem in four books by Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli. It explores the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into gold. The proem asks a pope for protection and invokes Apollo, Vulcan, and other powers. The text treats the origin of metals, mining, and the theory of metallic generation. It details the preparation of the elixir, describing apparatus and color changes. Digressions on gems and pigments lead to warnings against fraud and a lament for war.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carminum_appendix: Carminum Appendix, a short Latin collection of two poems, is attributed to Godescalcus Saxus and assigned to the Carolingian period. The work pairs penitential supplication with a creation hymn, where the opening poem hails Christ as the light of darkness. It begs deliverance from the pit of sin and pardon for lapses, while asking for a heart that loves God. The longer closing poem addresses Christ as maker and governor of all things, recounting the creation of the heavens, stars, seas, and fields. It describes his birth from the mouth of the omnipotent Father and his enclosure in the womb of the Virgin Mary. The text mentions his conquest of death, after which the speaker blesses a dear friend, celebrating the friend's keen understanding and ready eloquence. The friend is hailed as a shining star and a teacher, and the speaker prays that Christ grant him prosperity.
la.hegesippus_pseudo.de_excidio_hierosolymi: The De Excidio Hierosolymitano ('On the Destruction of Jerusalem') is a late antique Latin prose history attributed to Pseudo-Hegesippus. Its preface announces a continuation of Jewish history in historiographical style, while faulting Josephus for neglecting religious truth. The narrative traces Jewish fortunes from the Maccabean revolt under Mattathias and Judas Maccabaeus to the Roman campaigns of Vespasian and Titus. It details the sieges of Jotapata, Jopa, and Jerusalem, along with Josephus's capture and his debate over suicide. Long speeches, such as Titus's address to the besieged and Eleazar's final exhortation, punctuate the account. The work closes with the mass suicide at Masada, where a single woman survives to reveal the event.
la.hibernicus_exul.carmina: These Latin poems are attributed to Hibernicus Exul, a Carolingian court poet whose title means the Irish exile. The collection opens with a prayer for the emperor Charles, then covers court panegyric and a debate with the Muse. A long allegory shows the serpent breaking peace between Charles and Dasilo, while later pieces include petitions for the royal family and an exhortation to study. Epitaphs honor priests, monks, and kings, and an elegy records Charles's death at seventy. A tour of a house visits seven rooms of learning, and the book ends with a verse letter from Dungal to Baldo.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_historica: The Fragmenta historica ('Historical Fragments') is a Late Antique Latin prose work transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers. It preserves fragmentary documents from the ecclesiastical conflicts surrounding the councils of Nicaea and Ariminum. The contents are chiefly episcopal correspondence and conciliar material. It opens with a synodal letter from Gallican bishops to their Eastern counterparts. This letter upholds the confession of homoousios and denounces the silencing of the term ousia at Ariminum. It also excommunicates Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, and Gaius.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_mysteriorum: The Tractatus mysteriorum ('Treatise on Mysteries') is a work of Late Antique Latin prose theology by Hilary of Poitiers. It opens with a declaration that sacred books announce the advent of Christ through words, deeds, and examples. The author promises to treat in order all that prefigured Christ's preaching, passion, and resurrection. The treatise proceeds sequentially through Genesis, interpreting figures like Adam, Noah, and Abraham as types of Christ. It continues with Moses' rescue, the burning bush, and the manna, linking each event to the Church. A closing reflection argues that these histories were written for posterity's instruction. In all of them, God the Father, the Son, and Christ as God and man are recognized.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_evangelico: De evangelico, a short later imperial Latin poem in hexameter verse, is attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and consists of one hundred and fourteen lines. The opening presents a lyrical account of the Nativity, depicting Christ as a flower and light born of the virgin. A rejoicing earth and the terror of the serpent accompany the Magi bearing gold, incense, and myrrh. The central portion addresses Christ as the true Son of God, at once divine and human, described as a lion and lamb. He is the judge of the living and the dead, and the poem interprets the four winged creatures about the heavenly throne as figures of Christ. These include the man, lion, calf, and eagle, along with the twenty-four elders and the Trisagion, representing universal worship amid the groping blindness of the nations. The work closes with Gospel episodes of healing, such as the paralytic rising to carry his bed, and the man born blind is also granted new eyes toward heaven.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.hymni: This short Latin collection of two hymnic pieces is transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, though the attribution is doubtful and the work is placed in the later imperial period. It opens with a hymn greeting the returning day and addressing Christ as the giver of light, who is called the true morning star outshining the lesser star of night. The prayer asks for inward illumination, freedom from the deceiver's frauds, and chastity of body and mind, while the remainder is a much longer alphabetical penitential hymn whose quatrains run from A to Z. The speaker confesses being crushed under the weight of sins beyond counting and catalogues personified vices that wound him, including pride, envy, discord, vainglory, and gluttony. He calls on stars, beasts, the sea, and mountains to weep with him, appealing to Christ the sole redeemer for mercy, cleansing, and restoration. The hymn professes an orthodox faith that rejects the dogmas of Arius and Sabellius, and a doxology to the undivided Trinity closes the collection.
la.hilary_saint_archbishop_of_arles.epistul: This brief Latin letter was written by Hilary, archbishop of Arles, to Eucherius, explaining that he has returned the books as promised in an earlier letter. He could not resist the messenger's insistence and feared the heavy rains would harm the uncopied works. The writer records his admiration at reading the entire collection in a single sitting. He hopes to study the texts again with Eucherius's own pages as a guide. Hilary asks to be counted among the young men formed by Eucherius's teaching, making this request earnestly because the weakness of age now presses upon him. The letter closes with a prayer that the Lord preserve Eucherius, whom he addresses as most blessed pope.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.collecta: This Late Antique Latin dossier, compiled by Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, gathers conciliar acts, episcopal letters, creeds, and synodal documents. The material addresses the mid-fourth-century Arian controversy, opening with a confession of faith set out by Gallic bishops. They condemn those who returned from the Council of Ariminum having accepted silence over the term ousia. The text proceeds through the correspondence and decrees of the Eastern bishops at the Council of Sardica. It includes their accusations against Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, along with parallel Greek and Latin versions of the synodal letter to Emperor Constantius. Later items include the exchanges between Liberius of Rome, Ossius of Corduba, and the Eastern hierarchy, as well as professions of faith composed at Ariminum and Sirmium. The dossier concludes with Hilary's own defense of the Nicene doctrine of the Son's consubstantiality with the Father.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmen_in_libros_r: Carmen in Libros Regum ('Song on the Books of Kings') is a medieval Latin verse retelling of the four Books of Kings. The work is attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin and spans 1,350 lines. It opens with Elkanah offering sacrifice at Shiloh and proceeds through the biblical narrative. The poem covers Samuel's birth, Saul's reign, and David's rise to power. It also details Solomon's Temple, the division of the kingdom, and the ministries of Elijah and Elisha. The story concludes with the capture of Jerusalem and the removal of its treasures to Babylon.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora ('Minor Poems') is a medieval Latin collection of shorter poems ascribed to Hildebert of Lavardin. Each piece is introduced by a heading that names its addressee or subject. The book opens with verses addressed to a Bishop William on how Nature created him free of vice. It then ranges widely over epistolary poems to bishops, queens, countesses, and abbots. The collection also includes epitaphs, moral meditations, satirical pieces, and religious verse on the Trinity and the Incarnation. Among the longer items are two laments on fallen Rome and a prophetic poem on England's coming peace.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carminum_supplemen: Carminum Supplementum ('Supplement to the Poems') preserves medieval Latin verse attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It opens with an allegory where water, sun, crystal, and fire figure the Trinity. These elements revive the dead and restore order to the fallen. The bulk of the work expounds the twenty-four hours of day and night. Each hour is tied to a biblical event, such as the deluge or the Passion. A longer elegy denounces a wealthy rival who won the speaker's beloved. The collection closes with short satirical epigrams on the effects of heavy drinking.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_machabaeis: De Machabaeis is a medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin that recasts biblical material in the manner of classical epic. The 479-line verse narrative covers Maccabean history, opening with the Macedonian conquest of Persia and Alexander's death. The partition of his empire among successors leads to the rise of Antiochus, a persecutor depicted as a sword of heaven's wrath. The poem recounts Heliodorus's attempt on the Temple treasury and details the Hellenizing pontificates of Jason and Menelaus. Antiochus sacks Jerusalem, abolishes the Law, and desecrates the sanctuary in a series of acts. The work closes with Mattathias's uprising at Modin, his deathbed exhortation, and Judas Maccabeus's first victories over Apollonius and Seron.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_mysterio_missae: De Mysterio Missae, a medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin, expounds the rite of the Mass as a system of figures fulfilled in Christ. The opening couplets name the author and announce the aim of showing what the mystic rites represent, while the poet begs the reader's pardon for the work's faults. The poem then follows the liturgy in sequence, from the introit to the canon, assigning each element an Old Testament counterpart, such as the ministry of Aaron. Later sections treat the Lord's Prayer and the conversion of bread into Christ's flesh, before the work closes with the claim that the types of the old law ceased at the cross.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_ordine_mundi: De Ordine Mundi ('On the Order of the World') is a medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It retells the sweep of sacred history in verse, opening with a prayer for Christ's return. The poet aims to retrace redemption from the Virgin birth through Adam's fall and Cain's crime. The narrative covers the flood, Babel, the patriarchs, and the plagues of Egypt. It celebrates David, Judas Maccabaeus, and Judith before turning to the incarnation and passion. The poem closes with a Trinity exposition and Peter's preaching in Rome.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_querimonia_et_c: This medieval Latin poem, De Querimonia et Conflictu Carnis et Spiritus, is attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It stages a dialogue where the Spirit laments its captivity in the crumbling house of the body. The speaker recalls a former betrothal to Christ and grieves that a seducer has robbed it of chastity. A consoling reply promises a lasting dwelling beyond the prison and offers moral instruction. This includes a denunciation of worldly care and an exemplum of Peter accepting Paul's correction. The text also details the soul's seven acts, from vegetative growth up to union with God. In the closing exchange, the weary Flesh protests against dying daily and longs for a single death. The poet explains that the will becomes sinful only when the Spirit, figured as a wife, consents to the Flesh as husband.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.in_primum_caput_ec: In Primum Caput Ecclesiastes is a medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin, which serves as a verse exposition of the first chapter of Ecclesiastes. The work opens with the famous words 'Vanitas vanitatum' and a portrayal of King Solomon, who surveys a created order in which everything is mutable and vain. The body of the poem follows the Vulgate chapter lemma by lemma, quoting each scriptural verse and glossing it in turn. The sun's rising and setting temper cold and heat, while rivers flow into the sea without filling it. Generations succeed one another like waves, and the hidden causes of things remain grasped only through enigmas. Later passages explain that nothing under the sun is new, and every thing returns through its seed. Oblivion has swallowed the titles and pomp of the world's tetrarchs, praetors, and monarchs. The poem closes in Solomon's voice, recalling the wisdom and wealth with which he surpassed all crowned kings. It ends with the admonition that God's judgments come by measure, number, and weight, and those who strive to fathom them will be held detestable.
la.hincmar.carmina: The Carmina ('Poems') gathered under the name of Hincmar collect occasional and devotional Latin verse by a Carolingian author who speaks in them as bishop of Reims. The collection runs to 378 lines and is largely dedicatory and epigraphic in character. It opens with a poem on an altar of the Virgin Mary adorned by the bishop, followed by epitaphs for his predecessors Tilpinus and Remigius. Among the later pieces are a long poem addressed to Mary on the incarnation and the Eucharist, and memorial verses for Remigius with chronological notices. A gift-poem accompanied by verses to King Charles and a pointed exchange between two clerics named Hincmar over the right of free appeal to the apostolic see also appear. A closing epitaph bids the reader remember Hincmar and pray for his soul.
la.horace.ars_poetica: The Ars Poetica, a didactic hexameter poem by the Augustan poet Horace, is addressed to the Pisones and opens with a grotesque image of a painter joining a human head to a horse's neck. This image argues that a work of art must be single and unified, and the poem then ranges across the whole craft of poetry, covering choice of subject and diction. It also examines the metres and conventions of the several genres, and later sections review the history of drama from Thespis and Aeschylus to Roman tragedy and comedy. The text insists on patient revision and honest criticism, weighing natural talent against trained art. The poem ends with warnings against the poet's vanity and the flattery of admiring friends.
la.horace.carmen_saeculare: Horace's Carmen Saeculare is a short Augustan choral lyric that serves as a public hymn to Apollo and Diana. Taking its name from the centennial cycle of games it celebrates, the poem opens with an invocation of the deities of the seven hills. It asks them to grant the prayer prescribed by Sibylline verses for chosen maidens and chaste boys, while calling on Ilithyia, the Parcae, Ceres, and the bright sun. The text seeks fruitful marriage, safe childbirth, and abundance of corn and cattle, recalling Aeneas' escape from burning Troy and his settlement in Latium. The poet petitions the gods for good morals in the young and gentle rest for the old, declaring that Rome's power is now feared by the Mede, the Scythian, and the Indian alike. It closes with the return of Fides, Pax, Honos, Pudor, and long-neglected Virtus, as the trained chorus reports good hope to Jupiter and all the gods.
la.horace.epistles: The Epistles of Horace are moral verse letters written in hexameter during the Augustan age. They belong to the satiric tradition and consist of two books totaling 1,513 lines. The opening letter to Maecenas announces the poet's withdrawal from public striving. He resolves to weigh what is true and fitting while professing allegiance to no single philosophical master. The speaker counsels friends on avarice, envy, moderation, and friendship, often through anecdote and fable. The second book turns toward literary matters, addressing poetic talent, audience judgment, and patronage.
la.horace.epodes: The Epodes are seventeen iambic poems by the Augustan poet Horace, each using couplets of a longer line followed by a shorter one of varying metre. The opening poem addresses Maecenas, promising the poet's company through every danger of Caesar's campaigns, while the collection ranges over praise of country life undercut by a moneylender's backsliding. It includes comic invective on garlic and unattractive lovers, as well as attacks on an upstart ex-slave and the poetaster Mevius, with scenes of sorcery dominated by the witch Canidia appearing alongside laments over Roman civil bloodshed. The work also celebrates Caesar's naval victory at Actium and calls for the virtuous to abandon a doomed city, closing with the speaker's unsuccessful appeal for release from Canidia's incurable curse.
la.horace.odes: The Carmina, meaning songs, are four books of lyric poetry by the Augustan poet Horace. They open with an ode to Maecenas that surveys human ambitions and claims a place for the poet among lyric singers. The collection alternates between private and public registers throughout its four books. Private themes include love poems to Pyrrha and Chloe, drinking songs, and hymns to Venus and Mercury. Public odes address Roman virtue and the achievements of Augustus, from Cleopatra's defeat to the campaigns of Drusus. The famous monument ode stands out, while the collection closes with a renunciation of war themes to sing of Troy and Anchises.
la.horace.satires: Horace's Satires (Sermones) are two books of hexameter verse satire composed in the Augustan age. The work opens with an address to Maecenas asking why no one is content with the lot that fate or reason has assigned him. The first book ranges over discontent, greed, ambition, and the failings to be pardoned in friends, includes an autobiographical account of the poet's upbringing by his freedman father, follows the poet on a satirical journey from Rome to Brundisium, and discusses the satiric art in dialogue with Lucilius's practice. The second book proceeds largely through dialogue, presenting Ofellus's praise of frugal living, Damasippe's lecture on universal madness, Catius's precepts on gastronomy, Ulysses's consultation of Tiresias on legacy-hunting, the fable of the town mouse and the country mouse, the slave Davus's reproach of his master, and the disastrous banquet of Nasidienus, before closing on Horace's contentment with his modest Sabine estate.
la.hrabanus.carmen_evangeliorum: This short medieval Latin poem, attributed to Hrabanus, dates from the Carolingian period and belongs to the tradition of patristic allegorical exegesis concerning the four evangelists. Matthew is introduced as the foremost maker of the evangelical art, while Mark is described as Peter's disciple who carried the teaching from Italy to Egypt. Luke is linked with Achaia, and John is honoured by Asia as the Lord's beloved table-companion. A central passage has all four bear common witness to Christ, who humbly became man, and the latter half expounds the symbolic creatures of man, calf, lion, and eagle. These figures first represent the evangelists and then serve as tropological emblems, signifying reason, bodily discipline, victory in struggle, and contemplation of heaven. The poem closes with the Church's celebration of Christ's name in prayers and chants.
la.hrabanus.carmina: This Carolingian collection of Latin poems is attributed to Hrabanus, a humble servant and later abbot of Fulda. The opening dedicatory poem presents a book on the passion of Christ, composed with figured numbers and tropological figures. The rest is chiefly occasional verse, including dedications to popes, bishops, and Queen Judith, as well as letter-poems of friendship and spiritual counsel addressed to fellow clerics. Didactic pieces explore the virtues and the transience of worldly things, while a long poem narrates salvation history from Creation through Christ to the Last Judgement. A substantial group describes the altars, relics, and tombs of Fulda, and the collection closes with epitaphs for monks, bishops, and lay notables, ending with one for Hrabanus himself.
la.hrabanus.carminum_appendix: Carminum Appendix ('Appendix of Poems') is a Carolingian collection of Latin verse attributed to Hrabanus. It consists of short hymnic and devotional poems, many in four-line stanzas with refrains. The work opens with a praise of charity, tracing its role from creation to the church. Subsequent poems treat the chief feasts of the liturgical year, including the nativity and resurrection. They also cover the apostles Peter and Paul, a confessor's feast, and a lament for Hatto.
la.hrabanus.laudes_crucis: Laudes Crucis, a Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Hrabanus, opens with an invocation to the muse to sing of the supreme Father. The speaker presents himself as a poor servant offering a slight tribute before unfolding a sustained encomium of the cross as the instrument of redemption. It celebrates the cross's victory over the serpent, death, and hell, while gathering Old Testament prefigurations of the Passion alongside the symbols of the four evangelists. Much of the poem is devoted to number symbolism, including fives, tens, twelves, eights, and sixes, which are expounded as mysteries of the cross. These figures appear alongside catalogues of virtues and angelic orders, as well as prophetic testimonies and the ranks of saints and virgins. The text closes with a personal prayer in which the author names himself Hrabanus, offering his song to Christ as a sacrifice upon the altar.
la.iulius_firmicus_maternus.liber_de_errore: The Liber de errore profanarum religionum ('Book on the Error of Pagan Religions') is a Latin Christian polemic by Iulius Firmicus Maternus. This later-imperial prose treatise addresses the emperors Constantius and Constans. It argues that divination was invented by the devil. The author surveys cults of the four elements and specific deities. He contrasts these rites with Christian sacraments. The work closes by urging the emperors to abolish idolatry.
la.jerome.epistulae: The Epistulae, meaning letters, form a large corpus of Latin prose by Jerome, a late antique Christian writer who addressed bishops, priests, monks, and noble women. Paula and Eustochium appear among his many correspondents, and the collection opens with a preface using an extended nautical metaphor. Jerome protests his inadequacy while recounting the ordeal of a woman at Vercellae, who withstands repeated torture while refusing to condemn herself. The letters alternate among personal news, moral counsel, and scriptural exposition, with biographical narrative and doctrinal polemic also featuring prominently. Sustained attacks target Origenist teaching and later Pelagians, while the final pieces were composed in evident old age and frailty. They urge firmness against heretical teaching and record the deaths of friends.
la.jerome.in_hieremiam_prophetam: Jerome's In Hieremiam Prophetam, a late fourth century Latin commentary on the Book of Jeremiah, is addressed to his friend Eusebius. It forms the final part of his series on the prophets, and the preface explains his plan to follow the Hebrew text rather than the Septuagint. He also notes that he will skip Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah, while the six books proceed verse by verse through the prophet's oracles. They offer philological discussion and compare the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, with interpretation moving between literal history, moral exhortation, and Christological readings. The work extends from the call of Jeremiah to the promises of restoration.
la.jerome.vulgate: The Vulgate ('the common version') is Jerome's late antique Latin translation of the Bible, presenting the whole of Christian scripture in prose. In time it became the authoritative biblical text of the western Latin tradition. The text opens at the head of Genesis with the creation of heaven and earth and the six days of God's work. From there it runs through the patriarchal narratives of the Pentateuch and the histories of Israel. The Psalms, the wisdom of Proverbs and the prophetic books follow, with apocryphal writings such as the visions of Esdras, before the text reaches the books of the New Testament.
la.johannes_hymonides.versiculi_de_cena_cyp: Johannes Hymonides composed this Carolingian Latin poem to recast the Cena Cypriani in verse, invoking Cyprian as the rhetor and pope of Libyan Carthage. It playfully imagines performance at the banquets of Emperor Charles, assembling a vast company of biblical figures, patriarchs, kings, and prophets. The work also includes notorious sinners as guests at a wedding feast, where each guest receives a fitting seat, dish, and garment from scriptural incident. The narrative proceeds from arrivals and seating to the serving of the meal, concluding with the king distributing vestments to his guests.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carmina: The Carmina of John Scotus Eriugena gather the Latin poems of a Carolingian author. The opening poem is programmatic, setting pagan epic tradition against Christian hymnody on Christ's Passion. It addresses King Charles, weaving Greek terms into its Latin text. The collection offers verse on Easter, a panegyric on Queen Irmintrud, and Greek acrostics. It also includes prayers for Charles and a description of his royal church. Other pieces touch on Dionysius the Areopagite and Maximus the Confessor. The work ends with a short satirical epitaph on Hincmar.
la.juvenal.satires: Juvenal's Satires comprises sixteen poems in dactylic hexameter by the Roman poet of the early imperial period. The opening piece announces that indignation itself compels verse, setting the tone for the collection. The remaining poems range across Roman society, from the hypocrisy of ostentatious moralists to the perils of city streets. They also address the humiliation of clients at their patrons' tables and a sweeping attack on women and marriage. Further targets include the dependence of letters on patronage and the hollowness of aristocratic pedigree. The final poem breaks off unfinished while discussing the legal privileges of soldiers.
la.juvencus.historia_evangelica: Juvencus's Historia Evangelica ('Gospel History') recasts the gospel narrative in four books of Latin hexameters. This Christian epic belongs to the later imperial age and follows the whole gospel course. It opens under the bloody king Herod with the angel's annunciation to the priest Zacharias. The poem then details the nativity, the Magi, and John's preaching and baptism of Christ. It continues with the temptation in the wilderness and Christ's Galilean ministry of sermons and healings. The work closes with the journey to Jerusalem for the Passion and a dedication praising Constantine.
la.lactantius.carmen_de_passione_domini: The Carmen de Passione Domini ('Song of the Passion of the Lord') is a short late-antique Latin poem attributed to Lactantius. It is cast as a first-person speech by Christ, who greets a passer-by at the doors of a temple. He bids the listener contemplate the Passion and recounts his incarnation and humble birth in Judaea. The speaker describes the flight from Herod into Egypt and the return, followed by a ministry of teaching and miracles. He then turns to the betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the scourging, and the crucifixion. The closing lines urge veneration of the cross and detachment from fleeting worldly goods.
la.lactantius.de_ave_phoenice: The De Ave Phoenice, a late antique Latin poem attributed to Lactantius, opens with a description of a blissful eastern land untouched by disease, old age, death, and vice. The solitary phoenix dwells in the sun's grove within this idyllic paradise, and the work traces the bird's thousand-year life and its flight to Syria. It builds a nest of aromatic spices that serves as both tomb and cradle, where the bird dies in flames and is reborn from the ashes as a worm. This young phoenix gradually recovers its former shape and journeys to the temple of the Sun, depositing the remains of its predecessor amid the homage of Egypt and the assembled birds. The poem closes with reflections on the creature's self-generation and abstinence from sexual union, and it also considers the eternal life the phoenix attains through death.
la.lactantius.epitome_divinarum_institution: The Epitome of the Divine Institutes is a Late Antique Latin Christian apology in prose, where Lactantius explains to his brother Pentadius that he has condensed his seven book work into a shorter form. The text argues for providence and the unity of God using pagan poets and philosophers, while maintaining that Greco Roman deities were mortal men and that daemons are fallen angels. The author rejects philosophy as false wisdom by surveying the conflicting doctrines of various sects, and the second half presents true religion and wisdom as united in Christ. It covers his divine generation, birth, passion, and resurrection, and the work also addresses the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. Closing chapters prescribe Christian conduct, justice, mercy, and penitence, and it concludes with proofs of the soul's immortality and an account of the last things.
la.lios_monocus.libellus_sacerdotalis: The Libellus Sacerdotalis, or little book on the priestly art, is a Carolingian Latin verse treatise attributed to Lios Monocus. It opens with a prayer to Christ for the gift of eloquent speech, and it addresses ministers and clergy through moral exhortation. The poem dramatizes the devil luring churchmen into complacency about sin, while the text dwells at length on the torments of hell. It sets out the seven virtues that cleanse the seven deadly sins, and it also lists the seven causes of the remission of sins. Much of the work is cast as quoted teaching, which includes a versified rendering of the beatitudes and denunciations of worldly riches. The author urges almsgiving and forgiveness of one's neighbour, and the work closes with a vision of the heavenly city. It describes the never-failing light and rivers of that place, highlighting the everlasting rewards prepared for the humble and the merciful.
la.livy.ab_urbe_condita: Livy's Ab Urbe Condita ('From the Founding of the City') is an Augustan prose history narrating the fortunes of the Roman people from the city's origins onward. Its preface weighs the difficulties of the undertaking and presents Roman history as a record of conduct to be imitated or avoided. The narrative then opens with the Trojan settlement of Latium under Aeneas, the founding of the city, and the reigns of the early kings. Composed in annalistic Latin prose, the work proceeds year by year, recounting wars, domestic politics, and the leading figures and institutions of the Republic.
la.lucan.bellum_civile: Lucan's Bellum Civile ('The Civil War'), also called the Pharsalia, is a Latin epic in ten books of hexameter from the early Imperial period. It treats the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey, opening with a proem that deplores wars 'more than civil' and addresses the emperor Nero. After Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and the flight of the Senate from Rome, the poem recounts the earlier massacres of Marius and Sulla. Its course then takes in Caesar's Italian campaign, the siege of Massilia, Pompey's crossing to Greece, and the battle of Pharsalus. It continues with Pompey's murder in Egypt and Cato's march through the African desert and Syrtes, including a long catalogue of serpents. The narrative breaks off, apparently incomplete, during Caesar's struggle in Alexandria, and throughout it is marked by speeches, storm scenes, portents, and necromantic episodes in a heavily rhetorical style.
la.lucretius.de_rerum_natura: De Rerum Natura ('On the Nature of Things') is a didactic epic of the Roman Republic, composed in six books of hexameters and addressed to Memmius. It opens with a hymn to Venus and a celebration of Epicurus before turning to Epicurean physics. In this system nothing arises from nothing, and all things consist of atoms moving through the void of an infinite universe. Later books extend the system to the mortality of the soul and to the formation and eventual destruction of the world. The poem then traces the natural origins of life, language, religion, and civilization. It closes with meteorological phenomena and an account of the plague of Athens, arguing throughout that knowledge of natural causes dispels the fear of gods and of death.
la.lupus_servatus.versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Lupus Servatus, cast as a dedicatory address to a patron named Evrardus. It opens by inviting whoever wishes to know the causes of all the laws to seek out the book that Evrardus has had compiled. The body of the poem enumerates the law codes gathered in that collection, the Salic law of the Franks, then the Ripuarian, Lombard, Alamannic and Bavarian laws, each paired with the depicted figures of the people whose law it is, and it exclaims over the shining countenances of Charles, Pippin, Louis and Lothar and the far-resounding force of their laws. It closes with the poet signing himself Lupus, the least of men, promising worthier song should God grant him further years, and calling on Father, Son and Holy Spirit to protect, exalt and honour Evrardus.
la.macrobius.fragment: This short Latin prose fragment is attributed to Macrobius, a late antique author, and it opens with idle men dicing, drenched in perfume and surrounded by courtesans. The sketch follows them through their day as they send a boy to the comitium, where they learn what has been done in the forum and how the tribes voted. On the way, they drain every wine jar in the alley, and in court, the judge demands witnesses while stepping out to relieve himself. He then examines documents with eyelids heavy from wine, and the closing speech dismisses involvement with such triflers. It favors drinking honeyed Greek wine and eating fattened thrush, and it also mentions fine fish caught between two bridges.
la.macrobius.in_somnium_Scipionis_commentar: Macrobius wrote this late antique Latin prose commentary on the Dream of Scipionis, the concluding portion of Cicero's De re publica, which he addressed to his son Eustathius. A long prefatory essay sets Cicero's dream alongside Plato's myth of Er, defending the philosopher's use of figurative narrative against its critics. The text classifies the five kinds of dreams, fixing the dream's purpose as the teaching that souls of the just return to heaven after death. The commentary then follows Cicero's words through the numerological significance of seven and eight in gestation and the ages of life, exploring the soul's immortality and its descent through the planetary spheres. The author details the order, zones, and measurements of the heavens and earth, also discussing the harmony of the spheres. He argues for the self-moved nature of the soul against Aristotle's objections, closing with exhortations to public virtue and contempt for fame, while observing that moral, natural, and rational philosophy are all comprised within the dream.
la.macrobius.saturnalia: The Saturnalia ('The Saturnalia') is a learned Latin dialogue in seven books composed by Macrobius in late antiquity. It is framed as gatherings of Roman aristocrats and men of letters at the house of Vettius Praetextatus during the festival. An opening preface addressed to the author's son Eustachius presents the work as a digest of varied reading. The dialogue ranges over the origins and rituals of Roman religious festivals and cults. It also covers linguistic and antiquarian questions, along with an extended appreciation of Virgil as orator and poet. The final book poses questions on physiology, medicine, astronomy, and other natural phenomena.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.benedictio_cerei_i: The Benedictio Cerei I ('Blessing of the Candle') is a late antique Latin prose prayer attributed to Magnus Felix Ennodius. It opens with the declaration that humanity owes God vocal thanks for the gifts it has received. The text praises the Creator who fixed the earth, joined the seasons, and divided light from darkness. It then turns to the night that freed mankind from servitude, at whose ministry the candle is offered. The symbolism treats the wax, wick, and flame as engendered without union, like the offspring of the Virgin. The slain Lamb replaces animal victims, while the burning column recalls the pillar that led Israel through the sea. The prayer closes with petitions for protection against storms and for the fruitfulness of the times.

The Benedictio Cerei II ('Blessing of the Candle') is a Latin prose liturgical prayer by Magnus Felix Ennodius. It serves as a blessing for the paschal candle during the Easter vigil of late antiquity. The text opens with the preface formula 'Dignum et iustum est' to unlock the offices of the blessed night. It then praises the creator who formed man from dust and recounts the fall into voluntary error. The prayer celebrates regeneration in baptism, where water and flame are reconciled beyond natural order. The candle, fed by rivers and wax from bees whose virginity suffers no loss, recalls Christ in the burning bush. It closes by asking that the consecrated light withstand every storm and that the priest receive abundance and innocence.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_1_praefati: Two prose prefaces introduce the first book of the Carmina, or poems, of Magnus Felix Ennodius, a late antique author who wrote these introductions to frame his poetic work. The first preface opens by noting that gladness attends a man's return to his native soil, arguing that such joy needs a clear voice to avoid resembling mourning. It then defends eloquence against envious detractors and cites prophets who set prayers into verse, closing by commending a gifted young addressee whose talents restore the writer's flagging powers. The second preface is much shorter and thanks an unnamed correspondent for past support, lamenting the postponement of further favour and admitting that verses were appended to the poem. Finally, it bids the reader take pleasure in the poetry that follows.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.petitorium_quo_abs: The Petitorium ('petition') of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a short late Antique prose text. It seeks the formal manumission of his slave Gerontius before Roman ecclesiastical authorities. The work opens with a meditation on God as the arbiter of human affairs. Ennodius praises Gerontius for his good faith, integrity, and free bearing. He explains that he acquired the slave by exchange but now prefers a solemn judgement. The petition asks that Gerontius be admitted to perpetual fellowship in the Roman college. It also requests that his whole peculium be conceded to him without diminution.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.vita_epiphanii: The Vita Epiphanii is a late antique Latin prose saint's life that chronicles the career of Epiphanius, the bishop of Pavia. A prologue weighs the perils of praising eminent persons and invokes the Holy Spirit as a witness to the narrative. The text traces his birth and early clerical service under Bishop Crispinus, where he advanced through the ranks of lector, subdeacon, and deacon. The body follows his consecration to the episcopate and ascetic discipline, during which he served as an envoy to the emperor Anthemius and the Visigothic king Eurich. He protected captives during Odoacer's sack of Pavia, rebuilt ruined churches, and performed exorcisms, while a mission to the Burgundian king Gundobad won the release of prisoners. Petitions for tax relief were directed to Odoacer and then Theoderic, and a final journey to Ravenna preceded his death in his fifty-eighth year. The closing chapters narrate his funeral and the grief of the people, with the narrator claiming eyewitness standing in these events.
la.manilius.astronomica: The Astronomica of Manilius is a didactic poem in five books of Latin hexameters, written during the Augustan era, that expounds the principles and practice of astrology. It opens with an invocation to Caesar and a claim that the poet is the first to sing in Latin of the stars' governance of human fate. The opening books describe the fabric of the heavens and the earth, survey the constellations and the celestial circles, and classify the signs of the zodiac by their natures, subdivisions, aspects, and tutelary deities. The later books set out the reckoning of the horoscope and the rising times of the signs, the character and callings that each sign, degree, and decan bestows on the newborn, the distribution of the world's peoples and regions among the signs, and the influence of the constellations that rise in company with the zodiac.
la.marbodus_redonensis.certamina_septem_fra: A medieval Latin poem by Marbod of Rennes on the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother. The poem compresses the biblical Maccabean narrative into a sequence of set-piece disputations and torments. It opens with a royal edict that would force the Israelites to eat forbidden food, which seven brothers, steadfast with their mother, refuse on pain of death. Each brother in turn confronts the tyrant Antiochus with a speech of defiance before dying under torment, including flaying, mutilation, fire, and the frying pan. The king's attempt to win over the youngest with promises collapses when the mother exhorts her son to stand firm. The work closes with the youngest brother's tortured death and that of the mother, who shines last among her sons, crowned with seven crowns as victor of the contest.
la.martial.epigrams: Marcus Valerius Martialis, a poet from the Spanish town of Bilbilis, wrote these short satirical poems during the early Imperial period. The collection is arranged in successive books and opens by presenting the author as famous throughout the world. He asks the reader's indulgence for wanton pages written in an honest life. The range includes scathing portraits of Roman social types such as legacy-hunters, sponging dinner guests, and needy patrons. It also features erotic verses, epitaphs for children and freedmen, and flattering addresses to the emperor. The closing books contain two-line verses attached to Saturnalia gifts.
la.martialis.de_spectaculis: De Spectaculis ('On the Spectacles') is a cycle of short hexameter poems by Martial. The work celebrates the games staged in the newly built Flavian Amphitheatre. It opens by ranking the arena above the ancient wonders and Nero's works. The collection then surveys the diverse events held within the structure. Spectators from every province watched criminals executed in scenes drawn from myth. Exotic beasts fought in hunts and naval battles were staged in a flooded arena. The poems close with epigrams on gladiators and the fortunes of the Flavian house.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.opus_prosodiacum: This very short Latin poem is attributed to Micon of Saint-Riquier, a Carolingian author. It is transmitted under the title Opus Prosodiacum, a designation pointing to a prosodiacal verse form. The work is an occasional epigram composed around a gift of soap. The opening lines invoke one who washes the pious with fire and living water. The speaker then prays that the soap dissolve heaps of sin and guard virginal adornment. The final line breaks off incomplete in the source record.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.prologus_in_tract: Micon of Saint Riquier composed this verse prologue to the grammatical treatise De primis syllabis, explaining that no established art exists for recognizing which initial syllable is long or short. The author therefore sets the matter out briefly so young learners can find it without labour, outlining the treatise's plan beginning with an account of the courses of the sun and moon. It then treats initial syllables of fixed quantity across six parts of speech, deliberately setting aside the interjection because the Greeks do not number it as a category. Further discussion covers the particle pro, verbs in the present and perfect, and defective impersonal verbs, while the text also examines the gerund, vowel letters, mute letters, and liquid letters. The prologue closes by announcing that the metrical portion ends there, and the remaining teaching, framed for boys at their studies, will proceed in prose.
la.minucius_felix.octavius: The Octavius is a late antique Latin apologetic dialogue of uncertain date, attributed to Minucius Felix and framed as a fond recollection. The narrator remembers a debate where his friend Octavius converted the pagan Caecilius during a walk along the shore from Rome to Ostia. Caecilius first defends traditional religion and philosophical doubt against the Christian cause, also rehearsing the stock accusations made against believers. Octavius then replies with a long oration arguing for a single provident creator, exposing pagan myth, idolatry, and imperial conquest. The speaker ascribes oracles and portents to demons, refutes slanders of infanticide and incest, and further defends the resurrection and Christian conduct. The dialogue closes with Caecilius submitting to the argument, and the narrator expresses joy that his friend has both believed and triumphed.
la.moduin.carminum_appendix: This brief Carolingian Latin poem by Moduin is preserved as a short self-contained piece. The aging speaker urges a young brother to turn his muse away from Virgil toward Arator. Virgil sings of pastoral causes and Aeneas' wars, keeping company with Jove. He is seized by Cerberus and praised an incestuous Venus. Arator recounts apostolic virtues and the Lord's sweet words. He sings how Paul overcame the world and shares Peter's heavenly kingdom with the mother of God. The closing lines exhort the young man to follow the better writings. These works drive sordidness from the heart and fix the mind on God.
la.moduin.eclogae: This Carolingian Latin eclogue, attributed to the poet Moduin, is titled Eclogae, which means pastoral poems. The work opens with a dedication to Charles and a defense of rustic verse, cast as a dialogue between shepherds named David and Meliboeus. The younger speaker praises the renewed golden Rome of the Carolingian court, listing rewards won by poets from Ovid to contemporaries. He summons his companion to sing amid bees and grazing flocks, while a closing vision proclaims universal peace under Charles's rule. War is chained and buried, wild beasts rest with the herds, rivers rejoice, and the untilled earth yields its harvest. The final lines ask the pious king to read and correct the songs.
la.nithardus.historiae: Nithard's Historiae is a prose history in four books of Carolingian Latin, and the title means histories, a term that signals the work's focus on recorded events. The author explains his royal commission in a preface before turning to Charlemagne, and the narrative follows the division of the empire among Louis's sons. It details the wars between Charles, Louis, and their brother Lothar, while campaigns and embassies are punctuated by storms, eclipses, and comets. The text includes the mutual oaths sworn at Strasbourg in Romance and Teutonic, and it also covers the Saxon Stellinga rising and Norse raids on the coasts. A fourth book carries the story into renewed negotiations for a tripartite division, and this section is interrupted by a digression on the author's own kindred.
la.optatian.epistula: This Latin prose epistle, or letter, is a panegyric addressed to the emperor Constantine. It belongs to the tradition of imperial praise from the later period. The poet presents his verse for the emperor's acceptance and thanks him for his gracious reception. He contrasts his own slender talent with that of Virgil, the Mantuan priest of the Roman Muses. The writer notes that his work gains weight from the emperor's judgement. He closes by asking Constantine to admit the verses he has dared to bind.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.s_optati_: This seven book Latin prose treatise by Optatus, bishop of Mileve in Numidia, belongs to the late antique controversy between the catholic church of Africa and the Donatist schism. The work opens by appealing to the one faith of all Christians and to the peace that Christ left them, a peace the author says has been broken by the authors of schism. Addressed over its course to the Donatist bishop Parmenianus and written against his treatises, it argues for the unity of the one catholic church throughout the world. It defends the catholic clergy against charges concerning the armed soldiers sent under Macarius, rejecting Donatist rebaptism and their treatment of penance and consecrated virgins. The text also condemns their violation of altars and chalices, discussing the traditores and whether children inherit their fathers' guilt. Finally, it urges the schismatics' return to the see of Peter and communion with the universal church.
la.ovid.ars_amatoria: The Ars Amatoria ('The Art of Love') is a didactic poem in elegiac couplets by Ovid of the Augustan period. It casts the poet as a self-styled teacher of love who claims that affection must be governed by skill. The work proceeds by witty mock-technical precept, parodically claiming the authority of didactic poetry. Books 1 and 2 address men, moving from finding women in Rome to sustaining desire through tactful service. Book 3 turns to women, treating dress, cosmetics, and the conduct of the bedchamber. It ends by asking pupils to inscribe the words 'Naso magister erat' upon their spoils.
la.ovid.ex_ponto: Ex Ponto, meaning From the Black Sea, is a collection of elegiac epistles in Latin that Ovid wrote during his exile at Tomis. The four books comprise roughly fifty verse letters addressed to named friends and relatives, and they also reach members of the imperial house in a continuing plea for recall. The poet pleads for a mitigation or recall of his banishment while describing the harsh climate and warfare of the Pontic frontier. The text reflects on friendship, fame, and the poet's craft, and it commemorates events such as the triumphs of Tiberius and Germanicus. The opening poem presents the new book itself to Brutus, explaining that these letters differ from the Tristia only in being openly addressed. The collection runs through petitions, consolations, and descriptions of Tomis and the Getae, including poems of thanksgiving and friendship, and it closes with an invective against an envious detractor of the poet's verse.
la.ovid.fasti: The Fasti of Ovid is an Augustan poem in elegiac couplets that follows the Roman calendar month by month. Its six books run from the first rites of January to the close of June. The opening address to Germanicus sets out the poet's programme to sing of times and their causes. It also covers the risings and settings of the stars, beginning with Janus, god of the year's origin. Each month unfolds as a sequence of festival days and commemorations, such as the Lupercalia and Parilia. These are explained through etymologies, aetiological myths, and dialogues with deities like Mars and Vesta. Astronomical entries punctuate the flow, fixing legends and events to their specific dates. This includes the exposure of Romulus and Remus and the rape of Lucretia.
la.ovid.heroides: Ovid's Heroides ('Heroines') is an Augustan collection of fictional letters in elegiac couplets, written in the voices of mythological women to absent lovers or husbands. Penelope addresses Ulysses, Phaedra writes to Hippolytus, Dido to Aeneas, down to Sappho's epistle to Phaon. Each letter compresses an entire epic or tragic storyline into the voice of female complaint, rewriting Homer and the tragic tradition from the perspective of the women left behind. The collection opens with Penelope's letter from Ithaca, in which she reproaches Ulysses for his long delay and reports the suitors consuming his household. The remaining letters vary this situation of separation and betrayal, each heroine blending complaint, reminiscence, entreaty and occasional threats of self-destruction. The work closes with three paired exchanges, between Paris and Helen, Hero and Leander, and Acontius and Cydippe, in which both parties of each love affair write in turn.
la.ovid.ibis: Ovid's Ibis, an Augustan curse poem written in elegiac couplets, targets an enemy whom the speaker pointedly declines to name. Belonging to the invective tradition associated with Callimachus, the work complains that a hostile figure harasses him in northern exile. This compels the poet to take up weapons and devote his foe under a veil. The bulk of the text is a vast catalogue of imprecations that draws on figures from myth and legend. These range from bodily torments to unending punishment among the damned, and the poem closes with a warning about a fiercer future attack. This later work will use iambics and name its target outright.
la.ovid.medicamina_faciei_femineae: The Medicamina Faciei Femineae, meaning the cosmetics for a woman's face, is a short didactic elegy by the Augustan poet Ovid. It is composed in elegiac couplets and addressed to women on the care and adornment of the face. The work belongs with the Ars amatoria and Remedia amoris in Ovid's erotic-didactic project. It opens by bidding girls learn what care commends beauty, arguing from fields, fruit, wool and ivory that cultivation improves whatever nature supplies. The poem then urges that character is the surest and most enduring basis of charm. It sets out recipes for facial preparations, including barley moistened with eggs and ground, blended with narcissus bulbs, gum and honey.
la.ovid.metamorphoses: Ovid's Metamorphoses is a Latin epic in dactylic hexameter, written in the Augustan age, and its title refers to the transformations that form the work's unifying thread. Divided into fifteen books, it traces the world's history from creation to the poet's own day, opening with an invocation to the gods and an account of the world's formation from chaos. The poem then describes the decline of mankind through the golden, silver, bronze, and iron ages, ranging in roughly chronological order through Greek and Roman legend. It includes the flood of Deucalion and the stories of Phaethon, Narcissus, Daedalus, Pygmalion, and Orpheus, while the Calydonian boar hunt and the Trojan War also feature prominently. Turning to the early legends of Rome, the narrative closes with the apotheoses of Romulus and Julius Caesar, ending with praise of Augustus and the poet's claim to enduring fame.
la.ovid.remedia_amoris: Remedia Amoris, an Augustan didactic elegy by Ovid, serves as the therapeutic counterpart to his earlier work on acquiring love. The poem opens with an apology to Cupid and an appeal to suffering lovers, where Ovid promises that the hand which taught love will also teach its cure. He urges resistance at love's onset and an active life in courts, war, and travel, while prescribing dwelling on the beloved's faults and avoiding places that feed desire where passion is established. Mythological exempla of ruined lovers such as Phyllis, Dido, Medea, and Circe punctuate the instruction, and the poem closes with the healed summoned to pay votive garlands to the poet.
la.ovid.tristia: The Tristia, a five-book collection of elegiac couplets by Ovid, was written during his banishment from Rome under Augustus. Composed from Tomis on the Black Sea coast, the work opens with the exiled poet addressing his book as it travels to Rome. The remaining poems are cast as letters to the emperor, his wife, and friends, lamenting his fall and recounting the perilous sea voyage to the Pontic shore. These texts also defend the erotic poetry that led to his punishment, while an autobiographical elegy in the fourth book surveys his upbringing and career.
la.paschasius_radbertus.carmina: This short Carolingian Latin poem, attributed to Paschasius Radbertus, remains undated and is cast as a funerary lament with allegorical dialogue. It opens with a summons to men of every age to weep for a departed spiritual father, asking them to lay him to rest at Corbie amid flowers, tears, and song. The lament then unfolds through alternating speeches by a grieving daughter figure, a mother, and a maiden named Galathea, who bewail death's indiscriminate power. These voices console themselves with the soul's ascent to the heavenly bridechamber, invoking the sister virtues Faith, Hope, and Charity as the means by which the soul reaches the royal banquet of Christ. The closing section addresses the virgin Sophia, bidding her go before King Charles to present an offering on behalf of one who styles himself abbot Radbertus. This offering reveals the mysteries of the body and blood of Christ.
la.paul_the_apostle_saint.epigramma: This brief Latin item, attributed to Paul the Apostle under the title Epigramma, functions as prefatory prose rather than verse.
