It consists of a note on transmission and an argumentum, reporting that the piece survives in Parisinus 7558. Appended to Claudius Marius Victor's Alethia under the inscription S. Paulini epigramma, it was first printed by Gagneius as Victor's work. Wernsdorf judged it a sermon rather than an epistle, so its authorship remains disputed. The summary relates how Salmon, a priest, revisits his birthplace and discusses the vices of the city's men with the aged monk Thesbo. He criticizes the women even more severely despite the blow of barbarian ravages, dating the item to the Early Imperial era. Classed as theology, it serves readers of intertexts as evidence for attribution history and illustrates themes of civic corruption in Christian Latin poetry.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.carmina: Paulinus of Aquileia's Carmina is a Carolingian collection of religious verse, and the title means poems, a term that fits this body of work well. It opens with a first person confession of Trinitarian faith, which includes anathemas against ancient heretics from Cerinthus to Sabellius. Occasional pieces follow, such as a request for prayers from the Irish priest Zacharias, and a lament for the warrior Heric also appears in this section. The rivers and cities of the Aquileian countryside mourn his death in battle, and longer biblical narratives come next in the collection. One retells the raising of Lazarus in typological, allegorical, and moral senses, while another versifies the life of Joseph, from his dreams to his reunion with Jacob in Egypt. A penitential abecedary features personified vices assailing the sinner, and liturgical poems on the nativity, charity, and the resurrection round out the collection, concluding with a prayer for God's command over the winds.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.versus_de_destructi: The Versus de Destructione Aquilegiae ('Verses on the Destruction of Aquileia') is a Carolingian Latin lament by Paulinus of Aquileia. It addresses the ruined city directly to mourn its fall. The poem unfolds across twenty-three four-line stanzas, each beginning with a successive letter of the alphabet. It contrasts the city's former glory as the metropolitan seat of Venetia with the pride that drew divine wrath. Attila's devastating siege brought massacre, enslavement, and the burning of sacred books and vessels. The work closes with Attila tormented in hell and prayers to Christ to protect the faithful.
la.paulinus_of_nola.carmina: The Carmina gathers the Latin Christian poetry of Paulinus of Nola, opening with a prose preface and verses on ficedulae sent to Ausonius. The collection ranges across verse epistles defending the poet's turn to Christ, including a narrative poem on the birth of John the Baptist. Metrical renderings of psalms and annual natalicia for St. Felix of Nola follow, recounting the saint's life, miracles, and the growing basilica at Nola. Further poems commemorate the return of the priest Niceta, while others console friends over the death of the child Celsus. The volume also polemicizes against pagan cult and records inscriptions for Paulinus's churches.
la.paulinus_of_nola.epistulae: The Epistulae ('Letters') of Paulinus of Nola preserve the prose correspondence of a late antique aristocrat who renounced wealth for clerical service. This collection addresses a recipient in the language of honeyed sweetness, praising scriptural words and the correspondent's renunciation of wealth for Christ. Paulinus then turns to questions of how the faithful should answer those who demand a reckoning for their conduct. Over the course of the correspondence, he consoles a bereaved husband and urges a widow to perseverance. He also exhorts a young soldier to leave Caesar's service for Christ's and recounts marvels attending a shipwrecked sailor. The collection closes with letters of pastoral instruction and scriptural interpretation addressed to figures such as Severus, Augustine, and Alypius.
la.paulinus_of_pella.eucharisticus: Paulinus of Pella composed the Eucharisticus, a Late Antique Latin autobiography that serves as an act of gratitude to God for the course of his life. An aged writer explains in a prose preface that divine mercy moved him to record his story, as he was worn down by long exile and troubled idleness before beginning this task. The narrative follows his birth at Pella in Macedonia and his upbringing at Bordeaux, detailing his schooling, marriage, and management of family estates before the Gothic invasions. He recounts his father's death, the burning of Bordeaux, and the siege of Bazas, while the text also covers his dealings with the usurper Attalus and the Goths of Ataulf. The poem closes with his impoverished resettlement at Marseilles and his embrace of a religious life.
la.paulus_albarus.carmina: The Carmina attributed to Paulus Albarus is a collection of medieval Latin devotional verse from the Carolingian era, and the title simply means songs. This term fits the assembly of religious poetry, which recasts the classic nightingale topos in a Christian key, setting bird song against hymnic praise. The work opens with an invocation urging the nightingale to let her song surpass all instruments and the Muses, and the remainder assembles several longer pieces. These include a poem where the cock and other creatures laud the Creator, followed by a versified survey of Scripture expounding the books from Genesis through the prophets to the Apocalypse. Another poem describes the cross shining in the full moon and extols Jerome as the authoritative interpreter, while the collection closes with a hymn on the martyrdom of Eulogius and an epitaph. In this final piece, Albarus names himself, confesses his sins, and asks the reader for tears and prayer.
la.paulus_diaconus.carmina: The Carmina, meaning poems, were written by Paul the Deacon, a scholar of the Carolingian age, whose work is rooted in Lombard Italy and the circle of Charlemagne. The collection opens with a chronological poem that reckons the years of the world, tracing history from creation through the patriarchs and the giving of the law. This narrative continues through the Babylonian captivity down to the poet's own day, while the remainder of the collection ranges widely in subject and form. It includes verses on the miracles of St Benedict and a praise poem on Lake Como, and a riddle exchange with Charlemagne also appears in the text. The collection features a verse catalogue of the bishops of Metz, listing figures from Clement to Angilramn, and epitaphs and laments honor Carolingian queens and princesses. They also mourn the Beneventan prince Arichis, and a fable of the sick lion and the flattering fox is included, while hymns and devotional pieces close the collection. Among them is the Baptist hymn beginning 'Ut queant laxis resonare fibris', and a metrical life of St Paulinus of Aquileia also concludes the work.
la.persius.saturae: The Saturae, meaning satires, are a collection of poems by the Early Imperial poet Persius. The work opens with a prologue where the poet addresses a skeptical imagined reader. The subsequent verses deliver a severe moral critique of contemporary Roman life. They attack literary affectation, fawning audiences, and empty prayers for riches. The poems also condemn neglected study and the vices hidden behind respectable exteriors. A later piece urges a young heir to live plainly rather than indulge in luxury. The book closes with a dialogue in which a legacy hunter named Chrysippus counts his gains.
la.petronius.satyricon: This volume gathers the verse fragments surviving from the Satyricon, a sprawling satirical prose work of the early Imperial period attributed to Petronius. The text opens with a trochaic prologue urging an aspiring poet to temper his art with frugal morals. It then directs him to drink deep of the Homeric spring before proceeding to the narrative poems. These include moralising epigrams on money, fortune, friendship, and theatrical pretence. A long account of the Trojan horse and the death of Laocoon follows these shorter pieces. The collection also features a declamatory passage on civil war and verses on baldness and gluttony. A prayer to Priapus and the god's boastful reply appear alongside a witch's catalogue of her power.
la.petrus_riga.aurora: The Aurora is a medieval Latin verse work by Petrus Riga that paraphrases the books of the Bible in hexameter-style verse while folding in spiritual exposition. It opens with prefatory matter, including verses by a certain canon praising the book through a catalogue of scriptural figures, comparing it to the manna sent from heaven, to Ezekiel's scroll written within and without, and to Moses' veiled face unveiled by the light of Christ. The body of the work follows the order of Scripture, versifying the narrative of each book and interlacing allegorical and moral interpretation, as when the stone rejected from the building of the temple is read as Christ the Mediator joining synagogue and Church. Its closing books expound the Song of Songs as the discourse of Christ the Bridegroom with his bride, the faithful soul, whose answer to the perverse ends the poem.
la.phaedrus.fabulae_aesopiae: The Fabulae Aesopiae is a Latin verse collection from the Early Imperial period where Phaedrus recasts Aesop's material into senarii. The opening prologue claims a twofold dowry, promising to move laughter and counsel a prudent life before leading into the quarrel between a wolf and a lamb. Across its several books, the text offers brief animal fables rounded off with a moral, and it also includes anecdotes in which Aesop appears among Athenians, masters, and patrons. Episodes from Greek and Roman history appear alongside prologues and epilogues that defend fable as veiled speech under servitude. These sections also deliver satirical jabs at busybodies, flatterers, and the rich, while the collection closes with mythological exempla of fruitless punishment. It ends with precepts voiced by the Delphic oracle, including Tantalus, Sisyphus, and the Danaids.
la.philastrius.diversarum_hereseon_liber: The Diversarum Hereseon Liber, a late antique Latin prose work by Philastrius, opens with a programme to enumerate errors from the world's beginning, first among Jews and then after Christ's coming. The devil is likened to the partridge in Jeremiah's prophecy, and the text then catalogues Old Testament groups such as Ophites, Cainites, Sadducees, and Pharisees. It continues with Christian heresiarchs from Simon Magus through Marcion, Arians, and Donatians, where each entry names a founder and summarizes his doctrine with scriptural refutations. A final section treats further heresies defined by misreadings of the Bible, including creation, the soul, angels, and the origin of languages. The work also addresses the Greek versions of the Old Testament and Christian fasts, while standing polemic against Judaism and paganism is interlaced throughout this closing stretch.
la.plautus.amphitruo: Plautus' Amphitruo is a Latin comedy from the Roman Republic, and the title names the Theban general who is impersonated by Jupiter. Mercury opens the play by asking the audience for silence, and he declares the work a tragicomoedia because kings and gods appear alongside a slave. Jupiter impersonates Amphitruo to court his wife Alcmena during a marvellously long night, while Mercury takes the shape of the slave Sosia to keep the household at bay. The real Amphitruo arrives home with Sosia fresh from victory against the Teloboans, and each man finds himself doubled, so mutual charges of madness and adultery follow. Alcmena swears her chastity while Amphitruo seeks a witness from the fleet, and the entanglement dissolves when the slave girl Bromia reports the birth of twin boys. The infant Hercules strangles two serpents, and Jupiter reveals himself, so he restores Amphitruo to his wife's favour and promises the hero immortality.
la.plautus.bacchides: The Bacchides is a Latin comedy in dramatic meter by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic. The title refers to the two courtesan sisters who bear the same name, Bacchis. The play begins abruptly in mid-scene without a prologue, as the young Pistoclerus is berated by his tutor Lydus. The plot centers on the resourceful slave Chrysalus, who repeatedly cheats the elderly fathers Nicobulus and Philoxenus out of gold. He triumphantly likens each deception to episodes from the Trojan War. After the claims of the soldier Cleomachus are bought off, the fathers arrive to reclaim their sons. They are charmed by the sisters into joining the banquet, and the play closes with an appeal for applause.
la.plautus.cistellaria: The Cistellaria ('The Casket') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period by Titus Maccius Plautus, composed in dramatic metres within the tradition of plays adapted from Greek models. The work survives only in part, and the 680 lines preserved in Leo's 1895 edition centre on the world of the courtesans. Its opening scene follows Selenium and her companions as they weigh friendship, freedwoman status, and the raising of daughters against the hazards of their trade. The plot as a whole turns on recognition and on a young woman's recovered parentage, as the title suggests. The play offers parallels with Greek New Comedy and with other Plautine and Roman comic treatments of recognition tokens, stock lovers, and courtesan diction.
la.plautus.curculio: Curculio is a Latin comedy by Plautus from the Roman Republic. The title refers to the parasite who sets the plot in motion. The story follows Phaedromus, who loves the slave girl Planesium. She is held by the pimp Cappadox, and trickery secures the money for her ransom. The play ends with a recognition scene that restores the heroine to free birth. It includes a famous fourth-act monologue about the Roman Forum.
la.plautus.epidicus: Epidicus is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a fabula palliata of the Roman Republic set in Athens, where the title refers to the quick-witted slave who drives the plot. The play opens without a prologue, mid-conversation, as Epidicus is stopped by the soldier Thesprio, who informs him that his young master Stratippocles has bought a captive girl with borrowed money. Epidicus tries to raise the debt behind his master's father Periphanes, duping him into paying for a hired piper-girl, thinking she is his long-lost daughter. A wealthy soldier arrives to purchase the captive, but the imposture collapses, and a recognition reveals that the girl Telestis is actually Periphanes' daughter. She is therefore Stratippocles' half-sister, leaving the two old men comically outwitted, while Epidicus wins his freedom as a reward for his roguish services.
la.plautus.menaechmi: The Menaechmi is a Roman comedy of the Republic by Plautus, written in dramatic meter, and its title refers to the twin brothers who drive the plot. A prologue addressed to the spectators announces the poet and recounts the backstory of twin sons of a Syracusan merchant separated as boys. One was carried off at Tarentum and brought up in Epidamnus, and both were afterwards given the name Menaechmus. The action follows the Syracusan brother's arrival in Epidamnus with his slave Messenio, who searches for the lost twin, and a tangle of mistaken identity ensues. The resident Menaechmus's wife, his mistress Erotium, and the parasite Peniculus mistake first one brother and then the other, and scenes of feigned madness before the wife's father and a physician follow. Messenio rescues the brother he takes for his own master and is subsequently manumitted, and the twins are recognized through their shared name, parentage, and childhood memories. The play closes with an announcement of an auction of the Epidamnian's household, slaves, land, and wife, and it ends with a farewell to the audience.
la.plautus.miles_gloriosus: Miles Gloriosus ('The Braggart Warrior'), Plautus's Latin comedy of the Roman Republic, is composed in dramatic meter and refashions the manner of Greek New Comedy for the Roman stage. Set in Ephesus, it opens with the braggart soldier Pyrgopolynices and his parasite Artotrogus inflating one another with extravagant tales of martial prowess. The cunning slave Palaestrio schemes to reunite the Athenian Pleusicles with Philocomasium, whom the soldier abducted from Athens and keeps as his concubine. With the help of the neighbour Periplectomenus, Palaestrio has Philocomasium pass as her own twin sister, slipping through a hole in the party wall to fool the watchman Sceledrus. He then stages a courtesan in the role of Periplectomenus's wife to entice the soldier into giving up the girl, and Philocomasium departs by sea with her lover. The comedy closes with the duped soldier, caught as an adulterer in the neighbour's house, beaten and bound to silence.
la.plautus.stichus: Stichus is a Latin comedy by the Republican playwright Plautus, whose title names the slave who hosts the final banquet. Two sisters lament the three year absence of their husbands, fearing their father Antiphon intends to remarry them. He questions their wifely conduct and urges them to leave, while the parasite Gelasimus stages a mock auction of his slender goods. He seeks a dinner invitation from the household, and the slave Pinacium reports that the husbands have returned from Asia. The brothers Epignomus and Pamphilippus are now enriched, greeting their wives and reconciling with their father in banter. They grant their slaves a day of freedom, and the play closes with a drinking party hosted by Stichus. His rival Sangarinus also attends the celebration, as they are both lovers of the courtesan Stephanium. Songs and dancing mark the farewell to the spectators.
la.plautus.truculentus: Truculentus is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a dramatist of the Roman Republic, whose title refers to the rough country servant who gives the play its name. Its prologue asks the audience for a small piece of their city so the scene may be set at Athens, where the courtesan Phronesium and her maid Astaphium exploit the men who love them. The action turns on Phronesium's feigned childbirth to extract gifts from two suitors, as she passes off a supposititious infant, in fact the child Diniarchus fathered on the daughter of Callicles. Diniarchus had once been betrothed to this woman, while the servant Truculentus is tamed by Astaphium, and the young Strabax squanders his father's money at the same door. When Callicles uncovers the deception, Diniarchus admits his fault and marries Callicles' daughter, and the child is restored to its family, and the rival suitors are left still outbidding one another for the courtesan's favor.
la.pliny_the_younger.letters: Pliny the Younger composed this collection of Latin prose letters during the early Imperial period. The opening letter to Septicius Clarus explains that the author gathered his writings with unusual care. He arranged them not chronologically but as each had come to hand. The nine private books address friends on matters ranging from villa life to senatorial trials. They also cover recollections of Domitianic tyranny and the eruption of Vesuvius that killed the author's uncle. A tenth book preserves official correspondence with the emperor Trajan from Pliny's governorship of Bithynia and Pontus.
la.poeta_saxo.annales_de_gestis_karoli_magn: The Annales de Gestis Karoli Magni ('Annals of the Deeds of Charlemagne') is a Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters. It was written by the poet known as Poeta Saxo and preserved in five books. The work narrates the reign of Charlemagne, opening with Christ's birth and Charles's accession to sole rule. It proceeds year by year through his wars against the Saxons, Lombards, and other enemies. The text also covers embassies, church synods, and his imperial coronation in Rome. It closes with a lament for the emperor's death and a detailed account of his life.
la.polignac.antilucretius: The Antilucretius is a Modern Latin philosophical poem in hexameters, and its title signals a direct rebuttal to Lucretius and the Epicurean school. Addressed to a friend named Quinti, the work opens by invoking divine Wisdom to guide the argument. The speaker warns against the seductions of pleasure, then launches a systematic refutation of atomism, attacking the theory of atoms and the void. He challenges the motion of matter and the origin of mind, while critiquing the Epicurean gods and the denial of providence. The author also disputes claims from Gassendi, Descartes, and Newton, and similarly rejects the Hobbesian account of justice. Throughout, the poem argues for a provident Creator, defending the immortality of the soul and free will, and it closes with an appeal to divine religion, promising rewards and punishments after death.
la.pontius_diaconus.acta_proconsularia: The Acta Proconsularia ('Proconsular Acts') is a brief Latin prose record ascribed to Pontius the Deacon. It recounts the judicial examinations and martyrdom of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, under Valerian and Gallienus. The text opens with Cyprian's interrogation by the proconsul Aspasius Paternus at Carthage. There, the bishop confesses his faith and is banished to Curubis. The remainder follows his recall and second hearing before Galerius Maximus. It concludes with his execution, burial near the Mappalian road, and the proconsul's death.
la.priscian.perihegesis: The Perihegesis is a Latin geographical work of Late Antique date attributed to Priscian, whose title means a description of the world. It opens with a prayer to the creator asking leave to sing of the lands, seas, rivers, cities, and peoples. The earth is presented as an island girdled by Ocean and divided among Libya, Europe, and Asia. The body of the work tours each continent in turn, covering Africa with Egypt and the Nile. It describes Europe from Spain and Italy through Greece to its islands, and Asia from the Black Sea and Caucasus across Syria, Arabia, Persia, and India. Sustained attention is given to mountains, rivers, seas, cities, and peoples, while accounts of natural marvels, above all stones and gems credited with remarkable properties, are woven through the geographic description.
la.propertius.elegies: Sextus Propertius composed this four book collection of Latin love elegy during the Augustan age, and the title refers to the poet's name. The work is written in elegiac couplets, opening with the poet declaring that Cynthia first ensnared him with her eyes. This account of amorous servitude includes warnings to his friend Tullus against the miseries of love. Books two and three continue the turbulent relationship through jealousy, quarrels, and reconciliations, featuring reflections on wealth, faithlessness, and the poet's own art and calling. The fourth book widens to Roman themes, presenting poems on the god Vertumnus and the wife Arethusa. It also covers the treachery of Tarpeia, Hercules and Cacus, and the temple of Apollo, concluding with a nocturnal visit from Cynthia's ghost and the farewell speech of Cornelia.
la.prudentius.apotheosis: The Apotheosis is a didactic Latin poem by the Late Antique Christian poet Prudentius, whose title means the exaltation of Christ to divine status. It serves as a polemical treatise on the divinity of Christ and the unity of the Trinity, aiming to confute a series of heresies through sustained argument. The work opens with a confession of the threefold God, one in substance, followed by a prayer for sure guidance through the false paths of erring teachers. The poem then takes up successive errors in turn, including the Sabellian confusion of Father and Son and doctrines that deny the Word's full deity. It confronts Jewish rejection of Christ and lingering paganism, while an episode shows a Christian page disrupting a sacrificial rite at the imperial court. The Manichaean denial of Christ's real body is refuted, and the claim that the human soul is divine or a part of God is rejected. The poem closes with an affirmation of the resurrection of the flesh, as the poet addresses his own members and bids them rise with Christ, wholly restored to their former state.
la.prudentius.contra_symmachum: Contra Symmachum is a two-book Latin poem by the late antique Christian poet Prudentius, which responds to the plea of the pagan senator Symmachus for the restoration of the Altar of Victory. The first book opens with an allegory of the apostle Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, shaking off a venomous serpent, which represents resurgent paganism striking at the church. The text then surveys the births, loves, and disgraces of the traditional gods, and it also covers the deification of emperors and Constantine's victory under the sign of the cross. The second book stages a debate between a learned orator and personified Faith, where the orator defends the ancestral cult of Victory, while Faith argues for the one Creator. She presents Roman conquest as providential preparation for Christian unity, and the poem closes with a defense of Christian virginity against the Vestals. It ends with an appeal to end gladiatorial slaughter.
la.prudentius.dittochaeon: The Dittochaeon is a short Late Antique Latin Christian poem by Prudentius, a cycle of four-line verses each devoted to a single biblical scene. Each quatrain condenses its episode into a few densely allusive lines, so that the sequence works as a chain of compact verse glosses, like captions for biblical pictures. The opening quatrains treat Eve and the Fall, Cain and Abel, Noah's dove, and the patriarchs Abraham and Joseph, before the sequence follows Moses and the Exodus. The poem then turns to the Gospel narrative, with quatrains on the Annunciation, the Nativity, and the adoration of the Magi and shepherds. Later Gospel scenes include the massacre of the Innocents and figures such as John the Baptist. It closes with episodes from Acts and the Apocalypse, among them the martyrdom of Stephen, Peter's vision, the conversion of Saul, and the elders who praise the Lamb.
la.prudentius.epilogus: The Epilogus, meaning the closing section, is a brief Latin poem by the late antique Christian poet Prudentius, serving as the final piece in his collected verse. It offers a statement of humble devotion, where the speaker contrasts the pious donor who feeds the poor with a poet who can only consecrate his swift iambics. He admits his verses are poor in holiness and powerless to relieve the needy, yet he trusts in divine approval. The poem then pictures a rich man's house stocked with vessels of every sort, from golden cups to earthenware pots. It develops the Pauline image of the household vessel, asking Christ to find use for a worn earthenware pot, which the poet likens to himself. He concludes that even the least service to God has its profit and brings joy.
la.prudentius.hamartigenia: The Hamartigenia, meaning the origin of sin, is a late antique Latin didactic poem by Prudentius that attacks the Marcionite doctrine of two gods. It argues that the one God is not the author of evil, opening with the offerings of Cain and Abel. The poem reads the fratricide as a figure of the heretic, then refutes the dualist position at length. It attributes evil to the pride of a fallen angel and the free choice of human beings. A catalog of vices and a defense of free will support the argument, surveying the soul's fate after death. The text closes with a prayer to Christ for pardon and mitigation of punishment.
la.prudentius.peristephanon: Prudentius's Peristephanon, meaning on the martyrs' crowns, is a Late Antique collection of Christian poems. It comprises fourteen hymns in varied metres that celebrate individual martyrs and groups of martyrs. The cycle includes Lawrence, Eulalia, Vincent, and Agnes among its subjects. The poems narrate the saints' trials, tortures, and deaths. They also describe shrines, relics, and the author's pilgrimages to tombs in Spain and Rome.
la.prudentius.psychomachia: The Psychomachia, a late antique Latin allegorical poem by Prudentius, stages the struggle for the human soul as an armed combat between personified Virtues and Vices. The work opens by presenting the patriarch Abraham as the first exemplar of faith, whose rescue of Lot prefigures the believer's warfare against profane gentibus. A prayer to Christ then arms the mind against sin, leading into a main narrative where Faith, Chastity, and Patience defeat their opposing Vices. Biblical exempla such as Judith and David are woven into the victors' speeches, while the disguised Discordia infiltrates the camp and wounds Concordia. She is destroyed before the Virtues build a jeweled temple for the enthroned Wisdom, and the poem closes with a final prayer of thanks to Christ.
la.pseudo_cyprian.adversus_judaeos: Adversus Judaeos, a Latin theological treatise from the later Roman Empire, is transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage, though its authorship remains uncertain. The work defends the Christian claim to the scriptural inheritance through a polemical prose argument, opening by urging readers to perceive the divine sacrament of Christ with the eyes of faith. It then surveys salvation history from Adam through Noah, Abraham, and Moses, casting Israel's persecution of the prophets and the killing of Christ as a breach of the paternal testament. This breach justifies God's transfer of the covenant to the Gentiles, who are summoned to baptism and the new testament without distinction of rank, age, or condition. The treatise closes with Israel depicted as an exile stripped of temple, kingdom, and homeland, yet it offers pardon on repentance and envisions the humble and unlearned now teaching the scriptures to their former instructors.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_duplici_martyrio: This Latin prose treatise is attributed to Cyprian, though its author and date remain uncertain. It presents itself as a second book on the twofold kind of martyrdom. The work opens as a letter of thanks to a correspondent named Fortunatus. It surveys the open martyrdom of blood and the meaning of witness. The text then turns to the hidden, unbloody martyrdom of daily life. It condemns avarice, lust, drunkenness, and idolatry as covert apostasy. The treatise closes by urging believers to bear loss and temptation with patience.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_singularitate_clericor: This Latin prose treatise on clerical discipline is transmitted under Cyprian's name, though its author and date remain uncertain. It belongs to the later imperial period and argues that clergy must live apart from women. The text opens as an address to dearest sons, where the author recalls promising a general letter on clerical conduct. He reports being compelled by a divine warning and community scandals to write against cohabitation instead. The argument proceeds chiefly through authorities such as Solomon and Paul to portray female proximity as a snare. It rebuts objectors who cite examples of Elijah, the apostles, Christ, angels, and martyrs in defence of such households. Only liturgical gatherings and works of charity are conceded as legitimate occasions for contact with women. The work closes with a sustained encomium of singularitas, the single chaste life, and practical directions on households. A final exhortation drawn from Paul gathers these practical instructions together.
la.quintilian_pseudo.major_declamations: The Major Declamations are extended fictional courtroom speeches in Latin prose from the early imperial period, transmitted under the name of Quintilian, though this attribution is not secure. The corpus opens with a case where a blind son and his stepmother accuse each other of murder, and the pleadings turn on evidence such as a sword left in the wound and bloodied palm-prints on a wall. Each subsequent speech is prefaced by a brief statement of a hypothetical case and then argued at length before the judges, ranging over disputed inheritances, alleged poisoning, and an astrologer's prediction that a brave soldier will kill his father. It also features a doctor who dissects one twin to cure the other, and a poor man's son who dies in the arena to ransom his rich friend. Further themes include ghosts bound by magic, suspected incest, and conflicts of parental severity, fate, suicide, and vengeance. These cases are sustained by dense moral and psychological argument in the manner of the declamation schools.
la.rufinus_of_aquileia.interpretatio_oratio: Rufinus of Aquileia rendered nine orations by Gregory of Nazianzus into Latin at the request of his friend Apronianus. The collection opens with a dedicatory preface that recounts Gregory's life, chastity, and eloquence. It then presents the Apologeticus, a defense of Gregory's withdrawal from priestly office after ordination. This section offers an extended meditation on the care of souls and the discipline required of teachers. It also warns against the danger of disputing about God unseasonably. The remaining books translate further discourses, including sermons on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord. They also contain orations against the Arians and those who contend indecently over the law. These texts move through biblical exempla of prophets and apostles to reflect on speech, silence, and the duties of shepherds.
la.rusticus_presbyter.epistula_ad_eucherium: This Late Antique prose letter, written by presbyter Rusticus to Eucherius of Lyon, carries theological content. Rusticus confirms the return of requested copies of Eucherius's writings, which open great questions of both Testaments. He confesses that the recipient's doctrine cannot be worthily praised, as it pours light into the eyes of the heart. Recalling an epigram beneath Virgil's portrait, Rusticus notes that the poet is best praised by his own songs. He applies this idea to Eucherius's work, which needs no external panegyric, and foretells that Eucherius will be celebrated by all Christians as a teacher of posterity. The letter closes by asking Eucherius to pray for his correspondent.
la.rutilius.de_reditu: De Reditu ('On the Return') is a Late Antique Latin elegy by Rutilius, composed in elegiac couplets. The opening lines pair an address to the reader with a hymn to Rome as mother of men and gods. The hymn praises her for making a city of what had been the world, before the poem turns to the speaker's reluctant departure from the city. It then recounts a sea voyage from Rome toward the speaker's native Gallic estates, a route chosen because Getic devastation has wrecked the Tuscan countryside and the Via Aurelia. Its contents combine first-person travel narrative, topographical description, patriotic panegyric, and lament for a war-torn Italy.
la.sallust.catilina: Sallust's Catilina, a prose monograph on the Roman Republic, recounts the plot of Lucius Sergius Catiline against the state and its suppression. The work opens with a preface on the pursuit of lasting glory, then sketches Catiline's character and digresses on Rome's moral decline. The narrative follows the growth of the plot among indebted nobles and veterans, detailing the betrayal of the conspirators through Q. Curius and Fulvia. Opposing senate speeches feature Caesar arguing for imprisonment and Cato for execution, after which the condemned are put to death in the Tullianum prison. Catiline marches into Etruria and exhorts his troops, but he is defeated and killed in battle against the army of Antonius. The text ends with a picture of mingled grief and joy in the camp.
la.sallust.jugurtha: Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum, a Latin prose monograph on Roman Republican history, opens with a preface on the superiority of mental virtue to bodily goods. The author also describes his withdrawal from politics into writing, and the narrative follows Rome's war against Jugurtha, king of Numidia. It begins with his murder of his adoptive brother Hiempsal, and Adherbal is expelled, and the siege of Cirta ends in massacre. Roman embassies fail, and senators and commanders accept bribes, and the Mamilian inquiry and the campaigns of Metellus follow. Marius, a new man, rises to the consulship, and Capsa and a mountain fortress by the Muluccha are captured. Sulla negotiates with King Bocchus of Mauretania, and Jugurtha is betrayed into Roman hands, and he is led in chains to Rome, and Marius celebrates a triumph as consul.
la.salvianus.ad_ecclesiam: Ad Ecclesiam, a Latin prose treatise on almsgiving, is addressed to the catholic church in the voice of a humble servant. Its authorship is assigned to the presbyter Salvian of Massilia, who opens by lamenting that many believers hoard wealth rather than use it for mercy. The work argues that wealth is held from God only in usufruct, describing avarice as a form of idolatry. It contends that failure to dispense riches brands even the religious as unbelievers, while rebutting objections regarding inheritances and exemptions for specific groups. The text appeals to scriptural precepts and the parable of Lazarus and the rich man, closing with exhortations to repent and give alms before the final judgement.
la.scriptores_historiae_augustae.historia_a: A late-antique Latin prose collection of imperial biographies of uncertain authorship and date, transmitted under the names of various scriptores such as Spartianus, Capitolinus, Lampridius, Gallicanus and Vulcacius, and traditionally entitled the Historia Augusta. Its file opens with the life of Hadrian narrated from his Spanish origins and upbringing through his reign, travels, building projects and troubled succession, and the work proceeds through the lives of emperors and claimants from Hadrian's adopted heirs and the Antonines down through the Severan dynasty, the rival usurpations of Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus, the reigns of Caracalla, Geta, Macrinus and Elagabalus, the virtuous Alexander Severus and the brutal Maximinus Thrax, ending with the Gordians and the brief joint rule of Maximus and Balbinus. The biographies mix genealogy, omens and portents, military campaigns, administrative and legal measures, personal habits and physical descriptions, and frequently quote letters, speeches and verses attributed to their subjects, while naming earlier writers such as Marius Maximus, Herodian and Dexippus as sources.
la.secundinus.epistula_secundini_ad_augusti: The Epistula Secundini ad Augustinum is a late antique prose letter in which Secundinus writes to Augustine from a Manichaean perspective. He responds to Augustine's earlier writings against Manichaeus, opening with a salutation that praises Augustine's holiness and prays for protection against an evil spirit. The author denies that Augustine was ever a true Manichaean, while rebuking Augustine's attacks on the Old Testament. The letter portrays the devil's long campaign of deception, which spans the fall of the apostles to the rise of heresies. Doctrinal passages defend the two natures and describe the primal battle between light and darkness. Secundinus offers to settle remaining points in a peaceful colloquy, closing with repeated pleas for Augustine to return to the truth.
la.sedulius.a_solis_ortus_cardine: A Solis Ortus Cardine, meaning from the rising of the sun, is a late antique Latin hymn by Sedulius. It consists of twenty-three quatrains whose opening letters run alphabetically from A to Z. The poem opens with a call to sing of Christ, born of the Virgin Mary. It then proceeds through the nativity narrative, the annunciation, and the birth in the manger. The text continues with the angels, shepherds, Herod, and the Magi. It surveys Christ's miracles, including the water changed to wine and the healing of the centurion's servant. The poem closes with the betrayal, scourging, and crucifixion. It ends with the resurrection and an invitation to sing his victory.
la.sedulius.carmen_paschale: The Carmen Paschale is a Christian epic in six books of Latin hexameters by the Late Antique poet Sedulius. Its prologue sets the fictions of pagan poetry against the saving miracles of Christ, whom the poet invokes as his theme and guide. The poem first surveys Old Testament wonders, from Enoch, Sarah, and the crossing of the Red Sea to Jonah, the fiery furnace, and Daniel, presented as anticipations of Christ, and then proceeds through his life: the virgin birth and the adoration of the magi, the miracles and teaching of his ministry, and at length the Passion, with the two thieves, the earthquake and opened tombs, and the resurrection, appearances to the disciples, and ascension. A short elegiac epilogue offers the finished work as a modest dish of greens from a poor garden, set against the rich banquets of learned writers.
la.sedulius.carmina_ad_sedulium_spectantia: Carmina ad Sedulium spectantia is a small late antique collection of Latin poems associated with the Christian poet Sedulius, though he did not certainly compose them. The volume opens with an elegiac epigram by Turcius Rufus Asterius, which praises Sedulius' truthful verse and urges him to remember Asterius. Two acrostic poems by the scholastic Bellesabius follow, their initial letters spelling the poet's name in a distinctive visual pattern. The first acrostic commends Sedulius' verses on Christ's miracles, contrasting a modest banquet with noble luxury and recalling the feeding of the five thousand. The second acrostic pictures Sedulius in a flowering field, where he hears David's song and takes up the plectrum of Christian poetry. The collection closes with an anonymous poem on the Incarnation, narrating the Father's resolve to send the Son, the annunciation to the Virgin, and the birth marked by a guiding star, ending with a promise of peace and eternal reward.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium: The Epistola ad Macedonium is a prose dedicatory letter by the late-antique Christian poet Sedulius, serving as the preface to his Paschale carmen, a verse work on the paschal mystery. Sedulius addresses the letter to a priest named Macedonius, apologizing for venturing into this vast subject without training in ancient learning. The author recounts his conversion from fruitless secular studies to sacred verse, defending his choice of meter, arguing that readers retain sweetened lines more readily than rhetorical prose. Sedulius answers an imagined objection that worthier figures might better have received the work, naming Ursinus, Laurentius, Gallianus, and Felix among these potential recipients. He also mentions Jerome, the virgin Syncletica, and her sister Perpetua, commending his four books of Christ's miracles to Macedonius. These books gather material from the four gospels up to the Ascension, and Sedulius explains that he named the poem Paschale carmen because Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.
la.sedulius.hymnus_i: This Latin hymn by the late-antique poet Sedulius uses short paired verses to map salvation history. Each longer line is followed by a shorter one that recasts an Old Testament event. The pattern typically turns a statement about a biblical figure towards its fulfilment in Christ. The opening line invites companions to sing praise to the Lord and sound forth Christ's love. The poem then runs through Adam's fall, the flood, the patriarchs, and the Exodus. It concludes with the virgin birth, the passion, and a doxology to the Trinity.
la.sedulius_scotus.carmen_pastorale: The Carmen pastorale, meaning the pastoral song, is a short Carolingian Latin didactic poem attributed to Sedulius Scotus. It is addressed throughout to a priest and arranged in brief rubricated sections. The work opens by urging the shepherd to guard his flock against the wolf, and any loss through negligence must be answered for before its creator. The poem then proceeds through the honour and burdens of the priestly office, covering zeal for reading, the sevenfold daily hours of praise, and proper conduct at synods. Later sections take up fraternal charity, baptism, and the reverent celebration of the mass, while the closing parts address diligence in church service and the right use of gifts. They also cover the prohibition on clergy bearing arms and the priest's relation to wife and bride, finally discussing the administration of penance and the prayers owed to a priest at his death.
la.seneca.agamemnon: Agamemnon, a Latin tragedy on a Greek mythological subject by Seneca of the Early Imperial period, dramatizes the victor's homecoming from Troy and his murder at Mycenae. The play reworks the material of Aeschylus' Oresteia and belongs to the wider epic and tragic traditions of the house of Atreus. It opens with the ghost of Thyestes, who surveys the crimes of the house of Pelops and foresees fresh bloodshed in the palace above. Clytemnestra and Aegisthus debate and harden their resolve against the returning king, whose fleet a long messenger speech reports scattered by a storm on the voyage home. Cassandra, possessed by Apollo, prophesies the deed before it is done, and the murder is consummated at a banquet through the trap of the fatal robe. The closing scenes bring Electra's concealment and flight of the boy Orestes, the leading away of Cassandra to die, and threats of further vengeance to come.
la.seneca.apocolocyntosis: The Apocolocyntosis, or gourdification, is a short Latin verse satire from the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca, which mocks the death of the emperor Claudius. The work also ridicules his abortive reception among the gods, and the title twists the word apotheosis into a gourdification of the deified ruler. The poem opens with the Fates spinning a golden thread for the young Nero, while Apollo sings of the golden age to come in this opening scene. The narrative then carries Claudius up to heaven for a divine judgment, where the gods, persuaded by Augustus, refuse him divine honours and send him down. The scene shifts finally to earth with a mock dirge over the dead emperor, whose dependants lament his loss, chief among them lawyers and dice players.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_helviam: De Consolatione ad Helviam is a Latin prose work from the early imperial period, in which Seneca writes to his mother Helvia from exile. He explains why he hesitated to console her before resolving to prove his equanimity, arguing that banishment is merely a change of place. He maintains that poverty and loss of standing cannot injure a mind schooled in virtue, and suggests that Helvia's grief should be tempered by the example of steadfast Roman women such as Cornelia and Rutilia. The text closes by directing her attention to her surviving sons, grandchildren, and kinswomen, while Seneca also describes his own contented devotion to study and the contemplation of nature.
la.seneca.medea: Seneca's Latin tragedy Medea is a drama from the early imperial period written in dramatic meter. It opens with Medea summoning infernal deities and invoking Jason's wedding oaths to call down ruin on him. The plot follows Creon's banishment order and Medea's debates with the Nurse over revenge and flight. She prepares a poisoned robe and crown for the bride, delivered through her own children. Choral odes reflect on the first voyage of the Argo and the fury of love. A messenger recounts the bride's death by unquenchable fire and the burning of the palace. Medea then slaughters her two sons, torn between maternal feeling and vengeance. The play closes with Jason confronting the corpses while Medea escapes in a chariot drawn by winged serpents.
la.seneca.octavia: The Octavia is a Latin drama from the early imperial period. It is transmitted among the tragedies of Seneca, though scholars generally regard it as the work of a later imitator. The play is the sole surviving fabula praetexta, a tragedy drawn from recent Roman history rather than myth. It dramatizes Nero's repudiation of his wife Octavia in favor of Poppaea and her subsequent banishment to death. The action opens with Octavia lamenting the ruined house of Claudius and the deaths of Agrippina and Britannicus. She speaks with her nurse before the plot proceeds through dialogue and a lyric chorus. The drama depicts Nero's fury, the counsel of the philosopher Seneca, and the princess's final condemnation.
la.seneca.oedipus: Seneca's Oedipus is a Latin tragedy from the Early Imperial period that dramatizes the Theban king's discovery of his own crimes. The play opens with Oedipus lamenting the plague destroying Thebes, and he recalls the Delphic oracle that drove him from Corinth. Creon brings back the god's demand that the murderer of Laius be banished, and when sacrifice proves equivocal, Tiresias raises the ghost of Laius by necromancy. The shepherd Phorbas then confirms that Oedipus is Laius's son and his mother's husband, leading to Oedipus putting out his own eyes. Jocasta kills herself over his body, and choral songs on the plague, the cult of Bacchus, and fate punctuate the action.
la.seneca.phoenissae: The Phoenissae is a Latin tragedy of Early Imperial date by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, preserved in roughly 672 lines of dramatic verse. Bearing the traditional title of dramas on the Theban legend, the play opens with the blind Oedipus, guided by his daughter Antigone toward Cithaeron, and belongs to the cycle of stories surrounding Oedipus' cursed house and the strife of his sons. Even its opening speech displays the compressed mythological texture typical of Senecan tragedy, piling up exempla of Actaeon, Pentheus, and Ino in rapid rhetorical succession. For readers of intertexts, the play stands as a major Latin reworking of Greek tragic material on Thebes and a rich source of verbal and thematic echoes for later European drama.
la.seneca.quaestiones_naturales: Quaestiones Naturales ('Natural Questions') is a Latin prose treatise on natural philosophy by Seneca of the Early Imperial period. The work is addressed to Lucilius and arranged in seven books. It opens with a preface contrasting the part of philosophy that concerns human conduct with the higher part that contemplates the gods and the heavens. Seneca surveys the physical world, treating celestial fires, thunder and lightning, the annual flooding of the Nile, and other phenomena. He closes with an extended discussion of comets. Throughout, he sets out and tests explanations proposed by earlier Greek thinkers such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, Posidonius, and Diogenes of Apollonia, frequently rejecting them in favor of his own physical arguments. Moralizing prefaces and digressions on the smallness of human affairs beside the cosmos, on luxury, and on contemporary neglect of philosophy frame the scientific inquiry.
la.seneca.thyestes: Thyestes is a Latin tragedy by Seneca from the Early Imperial period. The ghost of Tantalus opens the play by summoning renewed fury upon the house of Pelops. Atreus feigns reconciliation to lure his exiled brother back to Argos with a promise of a shared throne. Choral odes on kingship and fortune alternate with scenes of escalating violence. Atreus slaughters Thyestes' three sons and serves them to him at a banquet. A messenger reports the crime, and the sun reverses its course in horror. Atreus reveals the truth, and Thyestes curses him while prophesying future vengeance.
la.seneca.troades: The Troades is a Latin tragedy from the Early Imperial period attributed to Seneca, whose title refers to the Trojan women forming the central chorus. It opens with Hecuba and the captives lamenting in the ruins of Troy while Greek leaders quarrel over the fate of Polyxena and the infant Astyanax. Calchas demands their sacrifice at the tomb of Achilles, and Andromache tries to hide her son within Hector's sepulchre. Ulysses defeats this attempt through a clever stratagem, leading to the double killing and the division of spoils. Hecuba is allotted to Ulysses among the prizes, and the captive women depart from the coast of Troy in a final chorus.
la.seneca_the_elder.controversiae: Seneca the Elder's Controversiae is a Latin prose work from the early Imperial period that preserves excerpts of declamations by Roman orators and rhetors. The text opens with a preface addressed to the author's three sons, in which the aged writer draws on his memory for the sayings of an earlier generation. He also laments the decline of eloquence since the time of Cicero, and the remainder is arranged in five books around successive imaginary legal cases. These cases involve matters such as parricide, disputed wills, captives, and the crimes of tyrants, under which Seneca records the striking sententiae of individual named speakers. He adds divisiones and colores that show how they ordered their arguments, while also interweaving anecdotes and critical remarks about the declaimers. Sayings delivered in Greek stand alongside the Latin text.
la.seneca_the_elder.fragmenta: This small collection gathers fragments attributed to Seneca the Elder, an early Imperial rhetor. The pieces survive only as quotations in later writers, chiefly Quintilian and Donatus. The volume opens with a report on a youthful debate about tragic diction. A striking exchange from a controversia follows, involving a father who kills his son and stepmother. A dry remark notes that oath-taking belongs to witnesses rather than advocates. The final anecdote features the poet Julius Montanus praising Virgil's delivery.
la.sigloardus_remensis.rhytmi: Rhytmi is a short collection of medieval Latin poems from Carolingian Reims, and the title means rhymed verses, a form used for this monk's work. The author is the monk Sigoard, whose name appears in a closing prayer, and the opening piece laments Fulco, bishop of Reims, and praises his noble character. It then curses Guinemarus, who attacked and killed the bishop with armed followers, and subsequent poems commemorate the translation of the relics of St Remigius in 901. They narrate the sudden healing of a lame man during the procession, and the body was enshrined in the church of the martyr Timothy. The collection closes with epitaphic verses on Fulco's tomb, and these lines record the length of his episcopate and his violent death. Final prayers commend the souls of Sigoard and Adeloldus to St Remigius.
la.smaragdus.carmen_in_psalterio: This brief Latin poem, attributed to the Carolingian author Smaragdus, serves as a prologue to a treatment of the Psalter. The text opens with the image of a golden casket enclosing a small book that holds the holy teachings of the church fathers. The poem contrasts the book's plain outward appearance with its deep mystical meaning, as David's songs lie veiled under a literal covering. Newer expositors later clarified the sacred proclamation of the old prophets, and Smaragdus concludes by declaring his wish to pluck gems from the book. He hopes this effort will make its pages illustrious.
la.smaragdus.carmina: The Carmina of Smaragdus is a Carolingian Latin verse collection of roughly 500 lines, opening with an elegiac prologue that invites the reader into a little book. This section joins scriptural material to grammatical instruction, while the greater part of the work is an allegorical grammatical poem. It treats the parts of speech in turn, including nouns, pronouns, verbs, and adverbs, presented under images of money, seafaring, roads, and royal rule. A substantial passage praises the Rule of St Benedict as the narrow path to the heavenly kingdom. The collection closes with a trochaic poem addressing Christ as the fount of light and life, describing the eternal joys of the heavenly Jerusalem.
la.smaragdus.epitaphium: This short Carolingian Latin epitaph is attributed to Smaragdus. It commemorates an abbot who flourished during the reign of the pious emperor Louis. The text notes that he moved his seat because the original site was ill suited to human uses. Upon his call to the heavenly kingdom, his body was returned to the old place for burial. The poem closes by fixing his death at the hour when the sun stood in Scorpio. At that moment, the heavens lay open to him as a theologian.
la.smaragdus.versus_ad_filium_ludovici_pii: Smaragdus, a Carolingian author, composed this didactic poem in Latin verse, which is addressed to a son of the emperor Louis the Pious. The work belongs to the tradition of advice literature for princes, opening with a prayer that the Lord's love fill the young king's heart. The poet then summons the ruler to keep God's commandments, ranging through the duties of a Christian sovereign. The poem urges wisdom, prudence, and simplicity of heart, while also calling for patience and justice in judgement. Care for the poor, widows, and orphans is emphasized, and the text advises payment of tithes and generosity against avarice. It further promotes peace, clemency, and trust in divine protection, closing with a prayer against rulers who refuse Christ, which expands into praise of the creator of all things.
la.statius.achilleid: The Achilleid is an unfinished Latin epic in hexameters by the early imperial poet Statius, surviving in two books with the second breaking off in mid-sentence. The proem invokes the Muse to sing Achilles' life from his concealment on Scyros onward, extending beyond the Homeric story of Troy to cover his earlier years. The first book follows Thetis as she removes her son from the centaur Chiron's care on Pelion, hiding him disguised among the daughters of Lycomedes on Scyros. There he seduces Deidamia and fathers Pyrrhus before Ulysses and Diomedes unmask him, presenting arms among the princesses to speed his departure for the war. The fragmentary second book contains Deidamia's parting lament and the subsequent voyage, including Ulysses' account of Paris and Helen. The poem stops during Achilles' autobiographical recital of his upbringing and training under Chiron.
la.statius.silvae: The Silvae of Statius, a work of the Early Imperial period, are a collection of occasional poems in hexameters. The title means woods, a metaphor for the varied and natural growth of these verses. The collection is arranged in five books and opens with a welcome for a colossal equestrian statue of Domitian. That statue stands in the Roman Forum and marks the beginning of the series. The following books gather pieces on a wide range of occasions, including panegyrics and descriptions of villas. They also contain birthday poems, wedding verses, and consolations for the bereaved. The final book closes with a grieving father's remembrance of a young child. This last poem recalls the child's first words and earliest sleep.
la.statius.thebaid: Statius's Thebaid is a Latin epic in twelve books of hexameter verse, recounting the war of the Seven against Thebes and the destruction of the house of Oedipus. The proem invokes the Muses and announces the theme of fraternal strife, deferring celebration of the reigning emperor's deeds to a future poem. The narrative begins with Oedipus's malediction and the collapse of the brothers' alternate rule, following the exile of Polynices to Argos and the muster of the champions. The failed embassy of Tydeus precedes the fighting before the walls, where the gods remain divided among the combatants during these battles. Menoeceus offers his self-sacrifice to save the city, while the seer Amphiaraus dies and Capaneus falls beneath Jupiter's bolt. Funeral games are held for Archemorus, and Eteocles and Polynices kill one another in single combat. Creon refuses burial to the dead, prompting the widows to appeal to Theseus at Athens and at the altar of Clementia. Antigone and Argia die on the contending pyres, and the poem closes with an envoi bidding itself farewell.
la.sulpicius_severus.chronica: The Chronica, meaning the chronicles, is a prose work of sacred history by Sulpicius Severus, which compresses biblical and ecclesiastical narrative from the creation of the world into two books. The author interweaves scriptural events with secular chronology to fix the succession of times, and a preface announces his design of brevity and his decision to continue beyond the passion of Christ. The work runs through the patriarchs, Moses, the judges, and the kings down to the birth of Christ, while the second part carries the narrative into Roman history, treating Nero's persecution and the fall of Jerusalem. It covers Constantine's conversion, Helena's finding of the cross, and the Arian controversy, and the text closes amid the discords that trouble the episcopate of the author's own day.
la.sulpicius_severus.vita_martini: The Vita Martini, a Latin prose saint's life by Sulpicius Severus, recounts the career of Martin, a monk and bishop of Tours. Its prologue contrasts the futile pursuit of fame in pagan biographies with the author's purpose to record a holy man's life as a moral exemplar. The narrative follows Martin from his Pannonian birth and military service under Constantius and Julian, detailing his baptism, his gift of half his cloak to a beggar, and his renunciation of arms. Martin later associates with Hilary of Poitiers and lives as a monk before becoming bishop, and later chapters record his destruction of rural pagan shrines and his healings. They also describe his exorcisms, visions of angels, and confrontations with the devil, while the text closes with a portrait of his humility and unceasing prayer.
la.tacitus.agricola: The Agricola is a Latin prose biography of Gnaeus Iulius Agricola, who conquered much of Britain, and it was composed in the Early Imperial period after Trajan's accession. The author was the subject's son-in-law, and the preface contrasts the Republic's commemoration of great men with the silence forced on writers by Domitian. The narrative traces Agricola's ancestry, education, and early posts, and it follows his magistracies and command in Aquitania. The text details his governorship of Britain, and it surveys the island's geography, inhabitants, and Roman conquest. The account includes his campaigns and the speech of Calgacus before Mons Graupius, and the work ends with his recall, retirement, and death. A closing lament marks the turn from public history to personal mourning.
la.tacitus.annales: The Annales is a Latin prose history by Tacitus covering the Roman principate, beginning with Augustus's death in AD 14 and following Tiberius. It includes the later reigns of Gaius, Claudius, and Nero, detailing Rhine and Pannonia mutinies, Germanicus's wars, and Sejanus's fall. Tiberius withdraws to Capri, where delations and executions follow, while later sections treat Agrippina and Octavia's murders. The Pisonian conspiracy, Rome's great fire, and Nero's artistic pretensions appear, along with Corbulo's Armenian war. Trials and deaths of Seneca, Thrasea Paetus, and Petronius are recorded, closing with Nero's unended reign. The incomplete work features a preface promising history written sine ira et studio, free from flattery and fear.
la.tacitus.de_origine_et_situ_germanorum_li: Tacitus wrote this early Imperial Latin treatise on the Germanic peoples, titled De Origine et Situ Germanorum, which means 'On the Origin and Location of the Germans'. It opens by setting the boundaries of Germany between the Rhine, the Danube, and the Ocean, and the author then weighs what may be said of the origins and purity of its inhabitants. The longer first half describes the land and its peoples in general terms, covering their cults, assemblies, military organisation, and domestic life. The second half proceeds people by people through the nations east of the Rhine, moving from the Batavi and Chatti to the Suebian tribes. The work closes with the obscure races of the far northeast, where the author reports rumours of these groups while leaving the truth undecided.
la.tacitus.dialogus_de_oratoribus: The Dialogus de Oratoribus is a prose work attributed to Tacitus from the early Imperial period, answering Fabius Iustus's question about why the eloquence of earlier ages has withered. The narrator recalls a debate witnessed in the sixth year of Vespasian at the house of Curiatius Maternus, where Marcus Aper, Julius Secundus, and Vipstanus Messalla join the discussion on the condition of oratory. Aper argues for the practical rewards of speaking against the fleeting fame of poetry, while also defending modern eloquence against Messalla's admiration for Cicero and the Republican masters. Messalla blames the decline on faults of upbringing and the artificial exercises of rhetorical schools, identifying changed political conditions as the primary cause of this loss. Settled peace and concentrated power leave no room for the great oratory bred of civic discord, and the participants part amicably, each jesting that the others will accuse him of favouring poets, antiquarians, or rhetoricians.
la.tacitus.historiae: The Historiae is a Latin prose history by Tacitus that covers the civil wars following the death of Nero, and the title means histories, a term that signals the work's focus on recent events. It opens with a preface that sets the start at the consulship of Galba and Titus Vinius, where the author laments the distortion of truth under one man rule. The narrative traces the rise of Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian in turn, following the Flavian commanders through the battle and sack of Cremona. Later books address senatorial trials, the rebuilding of the Capitol, and the Jewish war, while the text also details the revolt of Civilis and the Gallic conspirators on the Rhine.
la.terence.adelphi: The Adelphi, a Latin comedy by Terence of the Roman Republic, is written in dramatic verse and opens with a prologue. The poet asks the audience to judge the controversy and announces that the two old men will disclose the plot. The work turns on the opposed methods of two brothers in bringing up their sons, Micio and Demea. Micio is the indulgent city dweller and adoptive father of Aeschinus, while Demea is the harsh countryman father of Ctesipho. Aeschinus carries off a music girl from the procurer Sannio, ostensibly to further his brother's love affair. His seduction of the citizen maiden Pamphila comes to light in the tenth month of her pregnancy. The resulting entanglements end in marriage for Aeschinus and a wife forced upon Micio. The slave Syrus is manumitted, and Demea demonstrates a sudden conversion to liberality.
la.terence.andria: Andria ('The Woman from Andros') is a Latin comedy by the Roman playwright Terence. It adapts Menander's Greek work of the same name along with his Perinthia. The prologue defends the poet's practice of combining Greek plots against a rival's attacks. Simo arranges mock wedding preparations to probe his son Pamphilus's attachment to Glycerium. The slave Davus schemes to expose a newborn at Simo's door, driving the plot toward crisis. Crito reveals that Glycerium is an Athenian and the daughter of Chremes' brother Phania. Recognition follows, the marriage is settled, and Davus is released from the threat of the mill.
la.terence.heautontimorumenos: The Heautontimorumenos, or The Self-Tormentor, is a Latin stage comedy by Terence, composed during the Roman Republic and adapted from a Greek original. The prologue announces that a second plot has been joined to the main story, and an actor speaks on the poet's behalf to defend this practice. He asks the audience for a fair hearing against a malicious rival, while the action turns on two neighbouring fathers, Menedemus and Chremes. Menedemus torments himself with remorse after driving his son Clinia away, and Chremes has a son, Clitipho, who is secretly infatuated with the courtesan Bacchis. The slave Syrus schemes to pass Bacchis off as Clinia's mistress, and Chremes feigns the grant of his estate as her dowry to recall Clitipho. The recognition of Antiphila as Chremes' long-lost daughter clears the way for marriage, so she marries Clinia, and Clitipho is reconciled and betrothed elsewhere.
la.tertullian.adversus_hermogenem: Adversus Hermogenem ('Against Hermogenes') is a Late Antique Latin theological polemic in which Tertullian attacks the teacher Hermogenes, who held that God fashioned the world out of pre-existing, eternal matter. The treatise opens with the conventional argument that heresy is a latecomer to truth and with invective against Hermogenes, a painter who turned from the church to Stoic philosophy. The refutation that follows seeks to establish that God made all things out of nothing, rebutting Hermogenes' proofs that matter is unbegotten and coeternal with God. Tertullian distinguishes the divine names of God and Lord and identifies the Wisdom and the Word of God, rather than any material substrate, as the medium of creation. He then takes apart claims about matter's corporeality, moral quality, location, and motion, while also addressing whether God can be the author of evil. A closing section argues that what was made from nothing will pass back into nothing, appealing to scriptural promises of the world's end.
la.tertullian.adversus_marcionem: Tertullian's Adversus Marcionem, a Latin prose polemic from the late second or early third century, targets the Marcionite doctrine that the god proclaimed by Christ is other than and superior to the creator. The opening preface recounts the loss and reworking of earlier versions of the treatise, after which the author paints a vitriolic portrait of Marcion as a Pontic barbarian and heretic. The work proceeds systematically to refute the possibility of a second or unequal god, defending the creator's goodness, justice, foreknowledge, and patience. Tertullian also vindicates Christ and Paul as belonging to the creator, adducing the law, the prophets, the Gospels, and Paul's letters to support this claim. The treatise includes sustained discussion of the resurrection of the flesh, judgment, and marriage, moving book by book through the whole Marcionite system. Each claim is tested against the Old and New Testament writings, which Tertullian takes as the one God's own revelation.
la.tertullian.de_anima: De Anima is a Latin prose treatise by Tertullian that belongs to the tradition of late antique Christian theology. The work opens by turning from a dispute with Hermogenes to a broader critique of philosophy, using Socrates' composed death in prison as a test case for pagan wisdom. The argument asserts that God created the soul through his breath rather than from matter, describing it as corporeal, simple, and propagated with the flesh through procreation. Tertullian rejects Platonic pre-existence, recollection, and the transmigration of souls into beasts, while later chapters examine the senses, the intellect, sleep, and dreams. These sections also cover the timing of death and the condition of the soul in the underworld, closing with the soul's expectation of judgment and resurrection.
la.tertullian.de_idololatria: De Idololatria ('On Idolatry') is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Tertullian. It argues that idolatry is the principal crime of humankind and encompasses every other sin. The work condemns artisans who fashion images and the trades that supply temples. It also rejects the plea that earning a living excuses such activity. Further chapters examine participation in pagan festivals and household customs. The text closes with the figure of faith as a ship sailing safely through danger.
la.tertullian.de_pudicitia: De Pudicitia is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Tertullian that argues against psychici who admitted the lapsed to reconciliation for sexual sins. The work opens with an exalted encomium of chastity and a denunciation of an episcopal edict that remitted the sins of adultery and fornication to those who had done penance. The argument then ranks these offenses with idolatry and murder among capital and irremissible sins, rereading the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son as concerning gentiles rather than fallen believers. The text works through the Pauline letters, including the case of the incestuous Corinthian, in support of a stricter rule, and it also cites 1 John, Revelation, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the leprosy laws of Leviticus. The treatise ends by denying that bishops or martyrs possess any authority to grant ecclesiastical peace to fornicators and adulterers, reserving judgment on such sins to God alone.
la.tertullian.scorpiace: The Scorpiace, a prose treatise by Tertullian, a Carthaginian Christian author of the late second and early third century, argues that martyrdom is willed by God. It opposes Christians, especially Gnostics and Valentinians, who discouraged confession of the faith under persecution, opening with the scorpion figure. The sting at the tail figures the venomous pressure of persecution and heretical teaching, to which the treatise offers itself as an antidote. From the Old Testament, the argument establishes that God ordained martyrdom, adducing the prohibition of idolatry and repeated punishments of apostates. It cites the vindication of the faithful, such as the three youths and Daniel, while answering the charge that such a God is cruel. Christ's sayings on confession and persecution complete the case, and the sufferings of the apostles, as witnessed by Peter, John, Paul, and Acts, are also cited. A closing refutation addresses the claim that confession is due in the heavens rather than on earth before human powers.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.carmina: This collection of Latin verse is attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a Carolingian bishop and courtier, whose Carmina comprise some seventy-two book files and about five thousand lines of poetry. The work spans didactic, devotional, occasional, and satirical genres, opening with a long poem on vices and virtues that treats sorrow and anger as a moral physician. The collection also includes exhortations on pastoral duty addressed to bishops, while verses on monastic rules and ecclesiastical arts appear alongside an allegory of the liberal arts. Greetings to Charlemagne and Louis the Pious are mixed with hymns and prayers, and epigrams on altars and letters in verse round out the devotional material. Lines of exile include appeals to charitable readers from prison, and one extended poem narrates marvels of rivers and birds. Other pieces record visions, dreams, and courtly anecdotes.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.epitaphia: This Latin verse epitaph was composed by Theodulf of Orléans, a Carolingian bishop, and serves as a memorial over his grave, cast in the poet's own voice. The speaker records that the ashes of one who was both bishop and abbot lie preserved in stone, and he recounts his birth in Hesperia and upbringing in Gaul. He held the see of Orléans above the Loire and served under Charlemagne, whose virtues he celebrates, before losing his position when Louis succeeded by paternal right. Louis gave credit to slanderous accusations, leading to Theodulf's confinement and death in exile, and he was buried in a foreign land, far from the shores where he wished to rest. The closing lines profess trust in the judge who knows the weight of his cause and express hope of rising from the dust at the divine command. The poet asks readers to pray for Theodulf the servant and seek Christ's mercy.
la.valerius_flaccus.argonautica: The Argonautica, an early Imperial Latin epic in eight books of hexameters, recounts Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece and his voyage to Colchis. The poem opens with a proem on the first ship to traverse the seas, including a prayer for poetic inspiration before the action begins. Pelias, alarmed by prophecy, sends Jason from Iolcus at the head of the Argonauts, and the narrative follows the Argo's voyage with its storms, rites, and episodic labours. It details the arrival in Colchis and Medea's overpowering passion for Jason, whose aid helps him subdue the fire-breathing bulls, earthborn warriors, and sleepless dragon. The story ends abruptly during Jason and Medea's flight from Colchis with the prize.
la.vergil.aeneid: The Aeneid is a Latin epic in twelve books of hexameters that Vergil wrote during the Augustan period. It tells of Aeneas' flight from Troy and his arrival in Italy, where the hero fights a war to secure a home for his followers, who are the forebears of the Roman people. The poem opens with an invocation to the Muse of arms and ascribes the hero's trials to the wrath of Juno. The first six books recount the fall of Troy at Carthage, covering Aeneas' love for Dido and his descent to the underworld. The remaining six books shift the setting to Latium, where Allecto's intervention embroils Trojans and Italians in war against Turnus. The poem closes in single combat between the two men, as Aeneas sees the spoils of young Pallas on Turnus' shoulders and plunges his sword into his enemy, causing the life of Turnus to flee indignant beneath the shades.
la.vergil.eclogues: The Eclogues, also known as the Bucolics, are ten pastoral poems in hexameter by Vergil, composed during the Augustan age. They stage conversations among herdsmen, with the first poem featuring a dialogue between Tityrus and Meliboeus. Tityrus has been freed and restored to his land by a divine benefactor, while Meliboeus must abandon his confiscated farm. The remaining eclogues offer a varied cycle of shepherd scenes, including the hopeless love of Corydon for the boy Alexis. A bitter contest of abuse and song also appears, alongside a prophecy of a new golden age at the birth of a wondrous child. The work features a lament for the dead Daphnis and Silenus's cosmological song, with paired singing matches woven into the narrative. Refrained song exchanges surround themes of love-magic, and the poems address the dispossession of farmers by land confiscation. They conclude with the lovesick lament of Gallus, blending rustic idyll with political upheaval throughout.
la.vergil.georgics: The Georgics is a didactic poem in four books of hexameter verse, composed by the Roman poet Vergil during the Augustan age. It is addressed to Maecenas, who is invoked alongside the tutelary gods of agriculture. The first book treats the cultivation of arable fields and the weather signs that govern the farmer's year. The second book covers the planting of trees, vines, and olives, interspersed with an encomium of Italy. The third book details the breeding of horses, cattle, and goats, closing with a devastating plague of livestock. The final book focuses on the keeping of bees and contains the tale of Aristaeus, which brings forth the story of Orpheus and Eurydice, ending with the poet's recollection of his earlier pastoral verse.
la.vergil_pseudo.aetna: The Aetna is a Latin poem in hexameters transmitted under Virgil's name, though its authorship and date remain uncertain. The title refers to Mount Etna, the volcano whose fires form the central subject of the work. Opening with an invocation to Apollo, the poet announces his intent to explain the causes of eruptions. He rejects the mythological explanations of earlier singers, from Vulcan's forges to the Giants' revolt. The bulk of the poem offers a physical account of volcanic activity, describing the hollow interior of the earth and the winds compressed in its caverns. It also details the combustible stones that feed the flames and the behaviour of molten rock as it hardens. A digression defends the study of nature against the pursuit of mineral wealth. The poem closes with the story of two brothers who bore their aged parents unharmed through an eruption. The fire yielded before their piety, earning them the name of the Pious.
la.vergil_pseudo.ciris: The Ciris, a Latin mythological epic in hexameters of Augustan date, is attributed to Vergil though its authorship remains uncertain.
