The opening prologue addresses Messalla and renounces a loftier philosophical theme, dedicating the work as the first fruits of early years. A digression distinguishes its Scylla from the Homeric monster and surveys rival versions before the narrative recounts how Minos besieged Megara. King Nisus's life depended on a purple lock, which Scylla cut after being inflamed with love for the enemy king and encouraged by her nurse Carme. She betrayed both father and city, only for Minos to reject her and tow her behind his ship. As she dies over the waves, the sea god transforms her into the ciris bird, while Nisus becomes a sea eagle, and the two are fated to pursue one another endlessly.
la.vergil_pseudo.dirae: The Dirae, a short Latin poem in dactylic hexameters from the Augustan era, is ascribed to Pseudo-Vergil, though its authorship remains uncertain. The speaker, a farmer exiled from land confiscated after civil war, calls down curses upon the divided estates and the soldier who seized them. The poem opens with an urging for his companion Battarus to join in song, then lists sterile fields, drought-stricken meadows, and a grove consumed by fire. The sea is let loose upon the land, and rivers are turned back, while refrains recall Battarus' counter-songs and laments for the soldier. The exile bids farewell from a distant hilltop to his fields and Lydia, vowing that his love will outlast every reversal of nature.
la.vergil_pseudo.moretum: The Moretum, a short Latin poem of the Augustan era, is attributed to Pseudo-Vergil. The title refers to the savoury paste that gives the work its name. The narrative follows the smallholder Simylus through a winter morning. He rises before dawn and coaxes a fire from dying embers. With the help of his African slave Scybale, he grinds grain and bakes a loaf. He then gathers herbs, garlic, and cheese to pound in a mortar. Finally, he yokes his oxen and drives his plough into the fields.
la.vergil_pseudo.priapea: The Priapea is a short Latin poem from the Augustan era, attributed to Pseudo-Vergil, and spoken largely in the voice of Priapus, the god who guards gardens. The work opens with the god lamenting that winter is his pest, fearing his wooden body will serve only as firewood for idle farmers. The bulk of the poem describes his rustic image watching over a poor man's plot, cataloguing seasonal offerings such as garlands, corn, grapes, and olives. He also lists milk, a kid, and a lamb among these gifts, while threatening would-be thieves with obscene punishment. This includes a club fashioned from the wrenched-off arm of a farm bailiff, and the poem closes with advice to two boys to spare his garden. They are told to plunder the nearby estate of a rich and negligent neighbour instead.
la.victor_vitensis.historia_persecutionis_a: The Historia persecutionis Africanae provinciae is a five book Latin history composed by Victor Vitensis, bishop of Vita, in Late Antiquity. The opening prologue addresses bishop Diadocus, stating the author's purpose in obedience to a command to record events in Africa. Book one traces the Vandal crossing from Spain under Geiseric, detailing the devastation of cities, churches, and clergy. The remaining books follow the persecution under Huniric, covering the elevation of Eugenius to the see of Carthage. Nearly five thousand clergy were banished toward the desert among the Moors, and the text includes a public disputation with Arian bishops. It quotes the king's anti Catholic edict at length, describing tortures and mutilations of noble confessors, while presenting famine and pestilence as divine judgment before closing with Huniric's death.
la.victorinus_saint_bishop_of_poetovio.comm: This Latin commentary on the Apocalypse is attributed to Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, and belongs to the later imperial era. It was transmitted with a preface and proceeds through the Book of Revelation section by section. The letters to the seven churches are interpreted as addresses to classes of believers. The visions of the throne, seals, trumpets, and bowls are read as figures of the church's preaching. These images also represent tribulation and the final judgement, while the beasts, Babylon, and the millennial reign are surveyed within the last times. The work closes with an account of the two resurrections and the defeat of Antichrist, expounding the heavenly Jerusalem in both allegorical and literal senses.
la.vitruvius.de_architectura: De Architectura, a Latin prose treatise in ten books, was written during the Augustan period and dedicated to the emperor Caesar. The work promises a complete account of the architect's discipline, beginning with the education and proper qualifications of the architect. It also covers the siting and planning of cities, followed by building materials, timber, and methods of walling. Books 3 and 4 set out the proportions of temples, detailing the Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Tuscan orders. Later books treat public buildings such as fora, basilicas, theatres, and baths, as well as private houses in both Roman and Greek styles. Wall plaster, pavements, and pigments are discussed, while the final books deal with the finding, testing, and conducting of water, sundials, water clocks, and various machines.
la.vulfinus_diensis.vita_marcelli_metrica: The Vita Marcelli metrica is a Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Vulfinus of Die, who identifies himself as the local bishop near the end. It opens by praising Marcellus, the bishop of that see, as he sits on the episcopal throne. The text traces his austere youth and renunciation of family wealth, noting his service as a deacon to his elder brother Petronius, the bishop of the city formerly called Essa. After Marcellus's deathbed exhortation, he fled from election to a cave on a neighbouring mountain, where a searching crowd eventually discovered him. The poem describes miracles, including the cure of a possessed queen and the rescue of a tottering column in a church he founded, which is described in a lengthy account of its painted and gilded decoration. It ends with wonders at his tomb, listing healings of a paralyzed mother, a blind girl, and a girl with a crippled hand, the final cure worked at the intercession of the poet-bishop Vulfinus himself.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_cultu_hortorum_carmen: De cultu hortorum, a Carolingian didactic poem by Walafrid Strabo, describes the cultivation of a small kitchen and herb garden. The work opens with a defence of gardening as a worthy pursuit, and it recounts clearing a neglected plot beside the speaker's door as spring arrives. The body surveys many plants, including sage, rue, gourds, and melons, while combining instructions for sowing and watering with remarks on appearance and medicinal virtues. The poem closes allegorically on the rose and the lily as emblems of martyrdom and faith. A dedicatory epilogue offers the finished work to Strabo's revered master Grimald.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_vita_et_fine_mammae: De Vita et Fine Mammae, a Latin hagiographic poem attributed to Walafrid Strabo, recounts the life and martyrdom of Saint Mammes of Caesarea in Cappadocia. The work deliberately transfers classical epic conventions to hagiography by contrasting pagan invocations with Christian prayer, and the poet begins by confessing his sins and asking friends for prayers before invoking his subject. Mammes grows from a pious child into a shepherd who tames wild beasts on a mountain, and he receives a heavenly staff and gospel book, then supplies the poor with milk and cheese. Under Aurelian's persecution, the governor Alexander tortures him with the rack, hooks, and a furnace, while Mammes feeds fellow prisoners through a dove and is spared by a bear and a lion. The lion speaks with a human voice and slaughters the spectators, and after emerging unharmed from a stoning, Mammes dies and is received into paradise. The epilogue lists biblical figures whose virtues Mammes combines in himself.
la.walafrid_strabo.in_natalem_s_mammetis_hy: This short Latin hymn, attributed to Walafrid Strabo, dates from the Carolingian period and was composed for the feast day of the martyr Saint Mammes. The opening lines call on humble suppliants to praise the blessed martyr, offering this praise to the glory of the Trinity, who crowns his witnesses. The central stanzas recount Mammes' contempt for worldly wealth and his abounding charity, while also describing his life among beasts and his victory over princes and a dragon. Faith, hope, and charity are said to dwell within him during these trials, and the poem then bids the assembly to rejoice and seek his intercession. It addresses Mammes directly with pleas for favour, protection, and deliverance from evil, and the text closes with a doxology to the Trinity.
la.walafrid_strabo.visio_wettini: The Visio Wettini ('The Vision of Wettin') is a Carolingian Latin afterlife vision composed in hexameter verse by Walafrid Strabo. It opens with a prayer for grace in the poetic undertaking and a survey of the island monastery of Augia (Reichenau), its abbots, and Wettin, a learned monk there. The bulk of the poem recounts the vision Wettin received during an illness, in which an angel led him through the places of punishment. There clerics, monks, and laypeople suffer for avarice, lust, and other vices, while Wettin hears detailed moral admonitions to proclaim what he has seen. He then passes through the dwellings of saints, martyrs, and virgins before returning to dictate his experiences, dying the next day as foretold. The work closes with the narrator's lament for his dead master, whose vision he has set down in verse.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carmina: Carmina is a collection of Latin verse by the Carolingian poet Walahfrid Strabo, whose opening poem addresses a bishop as the sublime head of the clergy. It urges him to strengthen the church through sound teaching and example, citing Paul's warning against giving scandal to Jew, gentile, or the church. The collection then ranges over devotional and epistolary pieces, including a vow of perpetual service to a revered spiritual father. The work closes with mnemonic verses that attach numbers to the Kalends, Nones, and Ides, drawing on biblical and liturgical matters.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carminum_appendix: This short Carolingian Latin appendix is attributed to Walahfrid Strabo. It opens with an epitaph lamenting his death while crossing the Loire. The poem records his burial at Auua through the care of the scribe Reginbert. The collection then turns to dedicatory pieces for a church rebuilt by Abbot Haito. These verses praise the silver altar wrought by Geroltus and list gifts from donors. Later poems address travellers and communicants, urging repentance and unity under Benedict's rule. The sequence closes with eucharistic imagery drawn from the marriage feast at Cana.
la.walahfrid_strabo.versus_de_Blaithmaic: The Versus de Blaithmaic is a Latin hagiographic poem by Walahfrid Strabo, whose title refers to the Irish saint Blaithmaic. The work recounts the life and martyrdom of this Carolingian period figure, whose fair birth is signaled by his name. The poet, born of Alamannian soil, writes at the urging of a father named Felix. He follows the saint from royal stock to a life of monastic humility, eventually moving to the island of the Picts to join Columba. Blaithmaic refuses to reveal the hiding place of the relics to Danish raiders, and he is slain and buried on the spot where miracles occur. The poem closes with a prayer for the author's pardon.
la.wandalbert.de_creatione_mundi: De Creatione Mundi, a Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, offers a versified account of the six days of creation. The opening invokes the eternal, triune God, who fashions the world through the Word, and follows the Genesis narrative through light, the firmament, and the seas. It continues with dry land, plants, the sun, moon, and stars, and also covers fish, birds, land animals, and the forming of woman from man's rib. The Creator rests on the seventh day, and the latter part turns to man as a second world endowed with the light of mind. He is called to govern the lower senses and cultivate virtue like seed brought to fruit, urging readers to distinguish deeds of light from darkness and look toward the eternal paradise promised to a worthy heir.
la.wandalbert.horarium: The Horarium is a short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, a didactic piece on the changing length of a sundial's shadow through the day's hours and across the year. It offers practical instruction in telling the time from a shadow, precise numerical rules for timekeeping cast in verse. The poem opens with December and January, giving in feet the shadow measured at each of six successive hours. The remaining months follow in pairs of equal daylight, beginning with February paired with November and March with October. April with September, May with August, and June with July complete the scheme, each pair set out with the same hour-by-hour figures. A closing precept directs the reader to observe this method of reckoning everywhere.
la.wandalbert.horologium: The Horologium, a short didactic Latin poem attributed to the Carolingian author Wandalbert, serves as a versified lesson in reckoning the seasonal hours. It opens with an address to the reader, promising to teach how the sun's course joins the months. The text pairs January with December, February with November, and the remaining months by equal daylight. It then sets out which hours correspond in every month, noting that shadow lengths vary with latitude. The instructions are anchored in a region stretching from the Danube westward, marked by Lyon and the Rhône. This area faces the Britons surrounded by the Ocean, and the work ends by warning that shadow measurements should not be fixed at the kalends. Shadows grow and diminish gradually from mid-month to mid-month as the rising of the signs turns.
la.wandalbertus.martyrologium: A Latin martyrology in verse from the Carolingian period, the poem is the work of Wandalbert. It opens with an invocation to God, an exhortation to imitate the saints, a commendation of earlier Christian writers, and a dedication to a Carolingian ruler. In nearly 1,200 lines the poet begs his creator for aid in singing the battles and deaths of the saints across the recurring days of the annual cycle. A following section explains how the year is divided into months, weeks, seasons, and feast-keeping. The main body proceeds month by month through the calendar, recording the feast days of martyrs, confessors, popes, and virgins, often noting where each suffered or was venerated. A concluding prayer in the author's own voice and a hymn to Christ close the work.
la.william_of_tyre.historia_rerum_in_partib: William of Tyre, minister of the church of Tyre and chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem, composed this Latin prose chronicle in the late twelfth century at the command of King Amalric. The work consists of twenty-three books, and a prologue on the hazards and duties of writing history precedes the main account. The narrative runs from the departure of the Western princes who won the promised land and nearly all Syria, covering the successive rulers of the Latin kingdom from Godfrey to Baldwin IV. The text details campaigns against the rulers of Damascus and Egypt, and it also records the captivity and deliverance of King Baldwin II. The Venetian fleet and the siege of Tyre are described, while the Council of Nablus and the charters and privileges of the realm are included. The chronicle closes with the quarrel between Baldwin IV and the count of Joppa, ending with the entrusting of the kingdom's administration to the count of Tripoli.
la.ambrose.apologia_altera_prophetae_david: The Apologia altera prophetae David is a late-antique Latin prose homiletic treatise by Ambrose that defends the prophet David against the scandal of his adultery with Bathsheba and his contrivance of Uriah's death. The work opens by acknowledging the offense taken at the title of the fiftieth psalm and the gospel reading of the adulteress. The defense unfolds in three divisions, addressing pagans, Jews, and Christians, while pagans reproach Christianity with the crimes of its forefathers. Jews object that such a man cannot be the ancestor of God's son, a point that broadens into a refutation of Photinian, Sabellian, Arian, and Manichean errors about Christ's person and incarnation. Among Christians, the biblical history is read allegorically, with Bathsheba figuring the human condition or the church, and Uriah representing the law. David's name, interpreted as the humble one, signifies the humbled Lord, and Nathan's parable of the rich man and the poor man's ewe is expounded as synagogue against church. The treatise concludes with a running exposition of the Miserere psalm on confession of sin, the magnitude of divine mercy, and the unity of God against heretical division.
la.ambrose.apologia_prophetae_david_ad_theo: Ambrose wrote this Latin apology for the prophet King David, which is addressed to the emperor Theodosius as its title states. The work opens with the author's declaration that he takes up the defence, arguing that David, who flourished with such merits and virtues, does not need it. Many readers, following the bare sequence of his deeds, wonder how so great a prophet failed to avoid the contagions first of adultery and then of homicide. The text recounts the sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, arguing that David was justified by God and redeemed his fault through immediate confession and immense sorrow. The author holds that the lapses of the saints were permitted so that later generations might take from their lives a lesson in penitence as well as innocence. The work reads figures of the Old Testament, from the brazen serpent, Joseph, and Judah to Solomon and Bathsheba, as types pointing to Christ and the church, while surveying David's virtues and acts of forbearance. The text closes with a long exposition of the fiftieth psalm, the Miserere, as David's own testimony to confession, baptism, and the forgiveness of sins.
la.ambrose.de_benedictionibus_patriarcharum: De Benedictionibus Patriarcharum is a single-book exegetical treatise by Ambrose, the late fourth-century bishop of Milan, which expounds the deathbed blessings that Jacob pronounces over his twelve sons in Genesis. The work opens by dwelling on the dignity of a father's final blessing, and it also notes Joseph's presentation of his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, whom Jacob adopts. The body proceeds tribe by tribe through the blessings of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, continuing with Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, and Benjamin. Ambrose reads each blessing as a prophecy fulfilled in Christ and the Church, incorporating Moses' later blessings from Deuteronomy into this analysis. Along the way, he sets his allegorical and christological interpretations against the explanations of the Jews, identifying Judah's lion with Christ and the serpent of Dan with the future Antichrist. The rapacious wolf of Benjamin is identified with the apostle Paul.
la.ambrose.de_cain_et_abel: De Cain et Abel is a late antique Latin theological treatise by Ambrose, which opens by recalling an earlier treatment of Paradise and the fall of Adam and Eve. The text follows the scriptural narrative of the two brothers, who serve as figures of opposing tendencies within the soul. One brother refers all good to God, while the other arrogates it to itself, and they also type the synagogue and the church. The exposition ranges widely over the meaning of the brothers' offerings, drawing on the rival figures of Pleasure and Virtue from Proverbs. It addresses Christ's three temptations and the secrecy and discipline of prayer, further exploring the spiritual births of virtue in the soul. The Levites appear as a figure of redemption, and the closing episodes include Abel's blood crying from the ground, Cain's mark and punishment, along with the story of Lamech.
la.ambrose.de_fuga_saeculi: This short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose addresses the spiritual duty of fleeing the world, noting how often such escape is urged yet rarely accomplished. The author observes that earthly desires and the senses continually recapture the mind, while the main body allegorizes the six Levitical cities of refuge as refuges in God and in Christ. Christ is described as the eternal high priest whose death releases the fugitive, and the text gathers scriptural exemplars of holy flight to urge escape from sin and vice. These figures include Jacob, Moses, David, Jonah, Lot, Susanna, and Paul, who illustrate the necessity of fleeing the world in spirit while detained in the body. The work closes with counsel to die to the age with Christ, taking refuge in penitence and grace.
la.ambrose.de_helia_et_ieiunio: De Helia et Ieiunio is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose that opens with a biblical trumpet call recast as a summons to the approaching solemn fast. Christ's forty day fast in the wilderness and his victory on the cross set the pattern for the Christian contest. The work then praises abstinence, citing Elijah's heaven closing fast and examples from Elisha, John the Baptist, Moses, Daniel, and the three youths in the furnace. It traces the discipline of fasting back to the six days of creation and the command laid upon Adam in paradise. The transgression by eating brought sin and death into the world, while a long closing movement denounces drunkenness and luxurious banqueting. It uses the stories of Noah, Lot, the rich man and Lazarus, Judith, and Esther, along with satirical pictures of gluttons, drinking contests, and merchant ventures. The text ends with prophecies against Tyre and exhortations to conversion, baptism, and readiness for the day of judgement.
la.ambrose.de_iacob: De Iacob, a Latin prose treatise on theology by Ambrose, belongs to the period of late antiquity. It opens with a discussion of good discourse and the rule of reason over the passions. The work argues that concupiscence can be tempered but not eradicated, illustrated from the lives of David, Jacob, and Joseph. The argument proceeds through free will and servitude to sin, examining the relation of law and grace after Paul's letter to the Romans. The patriarch Jacob's career serves as the principal exemplar, with his exile and reconciliation with Esau detailed. His marriages to Lia and Rachel figure law and grace, while his wrestling with God is analyzed. His deathbed prophecies and blessings are read morally and christologically. A concluding section presents the Maccabean martyrs, naming Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother. They exemplify beatitude maintained under persecution and torment.
la.ambrose.de_joseph: This Late Antique Latin prose sermon by Ambrose proposes the lives of saints as a pattern for living. It announces the history of Joseph the patriarch as its subject, above all as a mirror of chastity. The work follows the Genesis narrative of Joseph throughout, from Jacob's partiality to his dreams and betrayal. It details his sale into Egypt, service in an Egyptian household, and rejection of his master's wife. The text also covers his imprisonment, dream interpretation, rise to power, and reconciliation with his family. The story is read allegorically as a figure of Christ, with the sale prefiguring the passion. Benjamin foreshadows Paul, and the famine prefigures the hunger for divine teaching. Moral exhortation addresses chastity, patience toward enemies, and freedom within servitude. A closing section treats Jacob's descent into Egypt and his prophetic blessing of his sons.
la.ambrose.de_mysteriis: De Mysteriis is a Late Antique prose treatise by Ambrose, offering a catechetical exposition addressed to the newly baptized. It opens by recalling earlier moral sermons on the patriarchs and Proverbs, explaining why the mysteries were withheld from those not yet initiated. The text follows the neophytes' experience, beginning with the renunciation of the devil and a turn toward the east. Baptismal water is prefigured by the Spirit moving over primeval waters, the flood, the crossing of the Red Sea, and the sweetening of Marah. Further examples include Naaman's washing in the Jordan and the pool of Bethesda, while the threefold witness of water, blood, and Spirit accompanies a confession of the Trinity. Rites following the font include anointing, footwashing, and the donning of white garments, interwoven with nuptial allegories of the Church as Christ's bride. The final part treats the Eucharist, arguing its superiority over synagogue rites, supported by Melchizedek's offering and the manna in the desert. The words of consecration change bread and wine into the true body and blood of Christ, a change supported by biblical transformations of nature and the Virgin Birth. The treatise closes with exhortations to guard the mysteries inviolate.
la.ambrose.de_nabuthae: De Nabuthae, a late antique Latin prose work attributed to Ambrose, treats the biblical story of Naboth's vineyard as a sustained sermon against avarice. The text opens by declaring the story ancient in time yet daily in experience, noting that Ahab's covetousness is reborn in every age. The argument follows the narrative in which Ahab and Jezebel procure false witness to secure Naboth's death, expanding this into an indictment of the rich. This covers luxury, hoarded granaries, and a father driven to sell his children in famine, while also treating almsgiving as a loan made to God. Allegorical treatments include the rich fool's barns, Lazarus, and the horses of the psalmist, before the closing sections weigh Ahab's remorse and its limits. They also consider his wars with the king of Syria and his bloody death.
la.ambrose.de_noe: De Noe ('On Noah') is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology in which Ambrose expounds the biblical flood narrative. He opens by announcing his intent to detail the life and character of holy Noah, and the text moves through the Genesis account from God's threat to destroy humankind. It covers the building of the ark, the deluge, and the sending of the raven and dove, while the narrative continues with the disembarkation, Noah's viniculture, and the sin of Cham. Literal and allegorical exegesis alternate throughout the treatise, where the ark is read as a figure of the human body. The flood represents the inundation of the passions, and details such as the birds and the rainbow serve as signs of vice and virtue.
la.ambrose.de_paradiso: De Paradiso is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose that opens by citing Genesis on God's planting of a garden in Eden. The author acknowledges the difficulty of determining what and where Paradise is, invoking Paul's rapture to the third heaven to frame this inquiry. The work then follows Genesis 2–3 in continuous commentary, discussing the site and nature of Paradise while allegorizing it as the fruitful soul. The four rivers are interpreted as the cardinal virtues of prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice, which are further mapped onto successive ages of sacred history. The latter part takes up the two trees and the command laid on Adam, also covering the making of Eve from his rib. The text answers a series of objections about divine foreknowledge of the fall, some of which are drawn from heretics such as Apelles, and it also addresses the threat of death. The author expounds the serpent's deception and Eve's transgression, finally detailing the sentences pronounced on serpent, woman and man.
la.ambrose.epistula_ad_sororem: This Latin prose letter, attributed to Ambrose and addressed to his sister, dates from the late antique period. Responding to her repeated inquiries about the state of the church, he promises a full account of recent events. The text narrates a standoff with the emperor Valentinian over the surrender of the city's basilicas. He refuses on the grounds that divine things are not subject to imperial power. He recounts the occupation of a basilica by soldiers, where fines were imposed on merchants and threats were made against his own life. Amid the crisis, he preached sermons on Job and Jonah, and the account closes with the withdrawal of the troops. Restitution followed for what had been exacted, though the author tempers this with foreboding of graver disturbances to come.
la.ambrose.epistulae_variae: Epistulae Variae is a Latin prose collection by Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the Late Antique period, where most letters address emperors Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, and Eugenius. The volume opens with a letter to Gratian praising his piety and defending the full divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit. Remaining letters follow Ambrose's episcopate, reporting on the Council of Aquileia and its judgments against Arian and Photinian bishops. They also detail disputes with Valentinian over the restoration of the altar of Victory and the surrender of Milanese basilicas to Arians. Correspondence with Theodosius covers the burning of a synagogue at Callinicum, the massacre at Thessalonica, and the burial of Valentinian II. Throughout, Ambrose asserts that matters of faith belong to episcopal judgment, urging clemency and penance on Christian rulers while treating the emperor as subject to God.
la.ambrose.expositio_evangelii_secundum_luc: The Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam is a Late Antique theological work by Ambrose that presents a continuous prose commentary on the third Gospel. The text opens with a prologue on Luke 1:1, where Ambrose argues that the evangelist wrote diligently under divine inspiration. Unlike many others, he completed the task of narration, and the exposition follows Luke's narrative from the annunciations to Zacharias and Mary. It moves through the birth and preaching of John the Baptist, covering the parables and miracles of Jesus's ministry. The commentary also addresses his discourses, the Passion, and the resurrection appearances, drawing moral and mystical meanings from each episode. Ambrose discusses disputed points such as the agreement of the evangelists' genealogies and examines the resurrection accounts throughout the work. He defends the full divinity of Christ, upholds the perpetual virginity of Mary, and maintains the unity of the Trinity.
la.ambrose.expositio_psalmi_cxviii: Ambrose, a late-antique Latin author, offers a prose exposition of Psalm 118, which celebrates the law of the Lord. This alphabetical psalm moves through the twenty-two Hebrew letters, assigning eight verses to each. Ambrose ranks the psalm as the summit of David's moral teaching, comparing its brilliance to the sun at midday. The bulk of the work expounds the verses as moral instruction, covering amendment of conduct and custody of God's commandments. The author also addresses resistance to temptation and readiness for martyrdom, while the commentary continually shifts from the moral to the mystical sense. It relies on the Song of Songs figures of the bride and bridegroom, with recurring topics including baptismal purification and the relation of law and gospel. The text also examines the discipline of speech and silence, tracing the passage of divine truth from synagogue to church. The final letter, Tau, closes with a confession of straying, where the author pleads for the Lord to seek out his servant.
la.anonymous.laudes_domini: Laudes Domini, meaning The Praises of the Lord, is an anonymous Latin poem of uncertain date, whose closing prayer for the victory of a Constantine is the only fixed point in its chronology. The text opens with rhetorical questions about the apparent slowness of divine rewards, which are answered by the story of a devoted couple among the Aedui on the Arar. Their vow of a shared tomb is confirmed when the dead wife's outstretched hand invites her husband to join her. The greater part of the poem addresses Christ directly, praising his ordering of sea, land, vines, and trees, as well as his care for animals, seasons, and nightly rest. The poem then recounts the virgin conception, his teaching, miracles, and raising of the dead, concluding with his ascent to heaven and the opening of hell's gates to release all but the wicked. The final lines describe his apportioning of places of punishment and the prayer for Constantine's victory and joy.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_agobardum: This anonymous medieval Latin poem, composed of four-line stanzas addressed to Agobard, spells his name in the initial letters. The text opens with an invocation to the creator who holds the earth in his fist, begging the omnipresent judge to be appeased. The bulk of the work is a penitential lament from a man facing death, who contemplates the punishment awaiting the proud. He sees his life draining away and awaits the moment his spirit leaves its fleshly seat, asking friends, kinsmen, and a survivor to help bear his cold body. Christ is called upon to strengthen him for life and death, and the poem ends by offering the verses to the addressee as father. The speaker bids him read his own name in the initial letters, closing with petitions for the addressee's welfare and a trinitarian doxology.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_exordio_francorum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de exordiis Francorum addresses a Frankish ruler named Charles and undertakes a versified account of the origins of the Frankish people. It opens with a declaration that a prose narrative of the nation will now be supplemented in verse. The poem then traces a line of descent from the decline of Rome through Ansbertus, who marries Blithild, daughter of the Frankish king Hlotharius, and their children, among them the martyred bishop Feriolus, the confessor Modericus, and the miracle-working virgin Tharsicia, before continuing through the line of Arnulf, Ansgise, and Pippin to the deeds of Charles himself, praised for subduing the Saxons and checking the Northmen. A closing section celebrates the pious reign of Louis, exhorts the young Charles to temper the valour of David with the wisdom of Solomon as his successor, and promises a further verse account of Christ's miracles and deeds under the figures of man, lion, calf, and eagle.
la.anonymus.carmina_augiensia: The Carmina Augiensia is a medieval Latin collection of anonymous verse, whose title points to the monastery of Reichenau, known in Latin as Augia. The text survives in a fragmentary state with many lacunae, opening with a greeting to St Valentine, whom Christ admits to the apostolic choirs above the stars. The collection consists mainly of inscriptional verses for altars, images, and the cross, following the manner of tituli, which are short inscriptions on sacred objects. One piece honours an altar of St Mary offered by a priest-monk, invoking Peter, Paul, John the Baptist, Sebastian, and Valentine. Another poem describes a cross dedicated to the Virgin, naming Egino, while further verses address the signs of the cross. A series names the four evangelists and includes short pieces on Gospel miracles, covering the raising of Lazarus and the widow's son, an exorcism, the stilling of wind and wave, and cures by touch and spittle.
la.anonymus.carmina_bibliothecarum_et_psalt: This anonymous medieval Latin collection gathers dedicatory and descriptive verses composed for a royal Bible and for psalters. The opening lines name the four companions of David, Asaph, Eman, Ethan, and Idithun, before praising a King Charles likened to Josiah and Theodosius. Jerome is credited with transcribing David's psalms, and the completion of the book is ascribed to the scribe Liuthard. Further poems enumerate the uses of the two Testaments gathered in the book's library and count the years since Christ's birth and of Charles's reign. They also expound the evangelist symbols depicted in the manuscript, including the calf and the eagle. The closing verses retell episodes from Paul's conversion, his baptism by Ananias, and his flight in a basket, before Christ the Lamb unseals the seven seals of the Apocalypse.
la.anonymus.carmina_de_ludovico_ii: This anonymous medieval Latin poem laments the death of the emperor Louis II, opening with a summons to the ends of the earth to hear of a crime at Benevento. There, Adelpherius and the citizens seize the pious emperor, fearing for their kingdom, and lead him from his palace as though to martyrdom. Louis protests in words that recall the passion of Christ, while the narrative describes the imperial crown being placed on the head of a scheming tempter. This man is vexed by a demon and falls to the ground before wondering crowds, after which the Lord's judgment brings a Saracen invasion into Calabria and up to Salerno. An oath is sworn on holy relics to defend the kingdom and seek another ruler, closing with an elegiac epitaph on Louis Caesar. It recalls the sceptres of Italy handed on by his grandfather and the imperial name conferred by Rome, noting his strong and peaceful rule and endurance of frequent Saracen attacks. Finally, it mentions the mourning of Rome, Latium, and Gaul at his death, while his spirit rejoices in heaven.
la.anonymus.carmina_libris_saec_viii_adiect: This collection of anonymous Latin verses, transmitted as additions to eighth century books, opens with an invocation asking Christ to preserve a man named Ragnard. A note also names the young scribe Hieronimus, who was of noble stock, while the remainder assembles dedicatory prefaces and praise poems from the circle of Charlemagne. These include a verse epistle to Pope Hadrian celebrating the overthrow of the Lombard king Desiderius, and other pieces feature prefaces to a golden psalter naming the scribe Dagulf and his pupil Deodatus. A dedication by Adam son of Haynhard was written at Worms, and verses record how the deacon Godesscalc completed a gospel book after a journey to Rome. They also note the baptism of Carloman under the name Pippin, and Wigbod wrote a preface to a compilation of Mosaic verses made at the king's command. Closing lines accompany a herbal, and throughout, the poems dwell on golden letters on purple parchment, highlighting royal piety toward the apostolic see and the humility of servile scribes.
la.anonymus.translatio_sancti_mercurii: An anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date, narrating the translation of the relics of Saint Mercurius; it opens by announcing that the saint's passio has been told in the verses preceding it. The poem recounts how the emperor Constans, campaigning to subdue Apulia, took charge of the martyr's body with three monks and sacked the wealthy city of Quintodecimum near Benevento before meeting a violent death in Sicily on his homeward way, while the monks buried the body beneath a basilica threshold marked by a stone, where it lay forgotten for some ninety-five years. Prince Arechis, having built a basilica of Holy Wisdom at Benevento and entombed the twelve martyr brothers there, resolved to join Mercurius' bones to theirs; with the bishop he excavated the half-ruined shrine, and after the martyr appeared urging the work's completion, the body was carried toward Benevento, the bier halting miraculously outside the walls. The people's lamentations and Arechis' prostrate vows, including the donation of Quintodecimum itself, together with the heaven-sent lightness of the bier, lead to the saint's honourable entombment in the basilica, an event the closing lines date to the seventh of August in the 738th year from the Incarnation.
la.anonymus.translatio_xii_martyrum: Translatio XII Martyrum is a medieval Latin poem, anonymous and of uncertain date, that gives a versified account of the removal of the relics of twelve martyrs to Benevento under the prince Arechis. It opens by observing that the bodies of many saints long lay hidden in obscure graves until divine grace brought them to light. The narrative then follows Arechis's petition for relics from Apulia, the joyous procession of the whole populace into the city, the gifts of land and treasure offered by citizens and prince alike, the construction of a marble church beside the princely palace where the martyrs are buried together in a single altar, the enclosure of dedicated virgins in a cloister there, and the prince's night vision in which the martyrs promise that his devotion will be rewarded. The closing lines state that Abbot Matthew ordered the book to be made and commend the work to Christ.
la.apuleius.apologia: Apuleius' Apologia, or Pro se de magia ('In his own defense against magic'), is a prose speech delivered before the proconsul Claudius Maximus. The author faces a capital charge of magic pressed by Sicinius Aemilianus and other kinsmen of his wife, the wealthy widow Pudentilla. The text opens by portraying the accuser as a reckless calumniator and claims the trial as an occasion to vindicate philosophy itself. The argument then works through the alleged evidence in turn, including amatory verses, a mirror, and the purchase of fish. It also addresses an incantation that supposedly felled a boy, an inscribed wooden image, and excerpts torn from Pudentilla's letters. The speaker interleaves digressions on Plato, Aristotle, natural history, and medicine while defending the motives and domestic concord of the marriage. The work closes with a summary rebuttal of each accusation and a declaration that he fears the proconsul's disapproval more than his judgment.
la.apuleius.florida: The Florida is a Latin prose miscellany of excerpts from the public display speeches delivered at Carthage by Apuleius, a philosopher and orator of the later imperial period. It opens with a comparison between the reverent pauses travellers make at sacred spots along the road and the ceremonial pause a speaker owes on entering so venerable a city. The excerpts then range over anecdote, encomium and moral reflection: Socrates's manner of judging men, the piping contest of Marsyas with Apollo, the gymnosophists of India, Alexander's edict confining his portraiture to three artists, Hippias of Elis with his self-made implements, the talking parrot, the Cynic Crates, Pythagoras's schooling and rule of silence, the comic poet Philemon dying over an unfinished play, Asclepiades reviving a man already prepared for burial, and Protagoras's paradoxical bargain with his pupil Euathlus. Many of the pieces praise the learning of Carthage, thank its magistrates and proconsuls, and speak of a statue decreed to the author by the city.
la.arnobius.adversus_nationes: Arnobius composed Adversus Nationes, a seven book Latin prose defense of Christianity in the late antique period, which opens by answering the charge that the world has suffered calamity after calamity since the Christian religion first appeared on earth. Across the seven books, the author contends that pestilence, drought, and war long antedate the Christians, while he also derides the births, loves, and crimes that poets and theologians ascribe to the gods. The text condemns temples, cult statues, sacrifice, and divination as unworthy treatments of deity, and it further rejects the Platonic doctrines of the soul's divine origin and natural immortality. A sustained defense of Christ's miracles and messianic mission binds the treatise together, and the claim that the one supreme God is the only object of worship completes this argument.
la.augustine.adnotationes_in_iob: Adnotationes in Iob, a late-antique Latin exegetical work by Augustine, consists of short interpretive notes on the Book of Job. The author expounds the biblical verses chiefly in a spiritual or allegorical sense, opening with the sacrifices Job offers for his children. These acts are read as figures of confession and charity, and the text then follows the whole course of the poem. It covers Job's laments and the speeches of his three friends, as well as the intervention of Elihu and the Lord's answer. The work concludes with Job's final reply and submission, reading Job and his trials as bearing on Christ. They also relate to the Church and the penitent sinner throughout the entire commentary.
la.augustine.breviculus_collationis_cum_don: The Breviculus Collationis cum Donatistis, a Latin prose work by Augustine, summarizes the official acts of a conference between Catholic and Donatist bishops. Held at Carthage by imperial command before the tribune Marcellinus, the meeting involved three days of disputation in chronological order. Augustine compiled this breviary with numbered headings because the full transcript was too long to read easily. The text covers imperial edicts, written petitions, procedural conflicts, and disputes over the number of bishops present. It also records scriptural arguments about evil men within the church and recounts earlier councils concerning Caecilianus of Carthage and Felix of Aptunga. The summary ends with the cognitor's final sentence pronouncing the Donatist position confuted after noting their efforts to obstruct unfavorable documents.
la.augustine.contra_academicos: Contra Academicos, a Late Antique Latin prose dialogue by Augustine, opens with an exhortation to his friend Romanianus toward the philosophical life. The text records discussions held at a country villa where Augustine, Alypius, Licentius, and Trygetius debate whether a happy life is possible for one who seeks truth without finding it. They then turn to Augustine's promised attack on the Academics, expounding their doctrines that nothing can be perceived and that the wise must suspend assent. Augustine argues that many truths, mathematical, moral, and sensible, are known with certainty, maintaining that wisdom itself can be attained. The dialogue distinguishes the old from the new Academy, tracing the school from Arcesilas and Carneades through Antiochus to Plotinus. It closes with Augustine's declaration that he will hold fast to the authority of Christ, pursuing truth by reason chiefly among the Platonists.
la.augustine.contra_cresconium_grammaticum_: This Latin prose polemic by Augustine targets Cresconius, a Donatist grammarian, and responds to a letter Cresconius sent after Augustine wrote to Petilian. The opening addresses Cresconius directly to explain the correspondence, while Augustine defends eloquence and dialectic against accusations that they serve falsehood. The work then covers the full range of the Donatist controversy, arguing that baptism remains valid regardless of the minister's moral state. Augustine defends the Catholic practice of not rebaptizing converts from schism and also contests the appeal to Cyprian's authority. A long section examines the case of the Maximianists, whom the Donatists had condemned but later received back without rebaptism. Augustine argues this concession refutes their own principles, treats accusations of traditor and the violence of the circumcellions, and closes with a summary recapitulation of the argument. Augustine urges Cresconius and his party to return to Catholic unity.
la.augustine.contra_faustum: Contra Faustum is a Late Antique Latin prose polemic targeting the eloquent African Manichaean Faustus, whose anti-Christian volume had been read in Augustine's community. The work opens with an account of Faustus and the brothers' request for a reply, then quotes his words section by section and answers them in turn. Augustine defends the Old Testament against Manichaean rejection, arguing that the Gospel fulfils rather than abolishes the law of Moses. The text refutes Manichaean teaching on the two principles, the sun and moon, and marriage, while also addressing food prohibitions and the Paraclete. Later books take up the Christian feasts and the authority of the apostolic scriptures, examining the fate of the patriarchs and comparing Manichaeans with pagans. The work closes with an exhortation to abandon the sect's error.
la.augustine.contra_gaudentium_donatistarum: This late antique prose polemic sees Augustine refute two letters from Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, which were addressed to Dulcitius, an imperial tribune and notary tasked with enforcing Christian unity. These letters followed Gaudentius's threat to burn himself and his followers in a church, prompting Augustine to explain his plan to quote and reply to each passage in turn. He adopts this method instead of the disputed Petilianus dixit arrangement used in his earlier rejoinder, while the main body defends imperial coercion and rejects the Donatist claim to persecution. The text also denounces the violence of the circumcelliones and discusses the hearing of Emeritus of Caesarea, further including the exemplum of Razias in Maccabees, rebaptism, and charges against Secundus of Tigisis. The work closes with an appeal to Cyprian's witness that the catholic church spreads through the whole world, which stands against the Donatist claim to be the one true church.
la.augustine.contra_mendacium: Contra Mendacium, a late antique Latin prose treatise, takes the form of a letter addressed to Consentius. Augustine argues that lying is never lawful, even for pious ends, while apologizing for a year's delay in replying. He praises Consentius's zeal against the Priscillianists but rejects their view that falsehood could hunt hidden heretics. The main body refutes this claim by stating that sin cannot fight sin, and Augustine examines scriptural passages. These include the Hebrew midwives, Rahab, Jacob, Lot, David, and Christ, which he shows to be truthful or sins. He closes by urging Consentius to overturn the Libra of Dictinius, insisting no cause justifies lying.
la.augustine.contra_secundinum: Contra Secundinum is a short anti-Manichaean treatise by Augustine of the Late Antique period, composed as a reply to a letter from Secundinus, a Manichaean who questioned Augustine's motives for leaving the sect. The work opens with an acknowledgment of the correspondent's goodwill and a refusal to trade suspicions, as Augustine insists that only his conscience before God matters in this regard. The argument then turns to doctrine, attacking the Manichaean cosmogony of two opposed natures, while defending creation from nothing, the immutability of God, and the nature of evil as a voluntary defect. The text also distinguishes between Christ as unigenitus and as primogenitus of all creation, and it closes by answering objections to episodes of the Old Testament. Augustine upholds the reality of Christ's flesh, death, and resurrection against Manichaean teaching, urging the correspondent to return to the catholic faith.
la.augustine.de_agone_christiano: This late-antique Latin treatise by Augustine explores the Christian combat against the devil, arguing that Christ conquered the enemy by taking on human nature. Victory is promised only to those who actively fight the adversary, while the devil reigns through cupidity but is cast out when the heart renounces the world. Augustine explains that the invisible enemy is defeated within through submission to God, and the Incarnation serves as medicine that heals human vices such as pride and avarice. The latter part rehearses a rule of faith in the one unchangeable Trinity, answering heretical denials concerning Manichaean teaching and the Son's divinity. The text also addresses the reality of Christ's body and his resurrection, affirming the worldwide catholic church against Donatists and Luciferians. The treatise closes with an exhortation to grow in charity and merit the crown.
la.augustine.de_baptismo: This late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine addresses the Donatist controversy, arguing that baptism administered by heretics remains Christ's own sacrament. Such rites are valid, though unprofitable outside the Catholic Church, so converts should not be rebaptized. The work opens by recalling a promise made in earlier books against Parmenian, aiming to refute Donatist objections and answer their appeal to Cyprian. Augustine maintains that the sacrament keeps its integrity wherever gospel words are used, distinguishing between holding baptism and holding it usefully. The text treats remission of sins, John's baptism, and infant baptism, while also considering the effect of unworthy ministers and recipients. Later, Augustine turns to Cyprian and cites his letters to Jubaianus, Quintus, and Pompey, noting the opinions of African bishops gathered at Carthage. Augustine contends that Cyprian, though in error on rebaptism, remained in communion with colleagues, thus offering no warrant for schism.
la.augustine.de_bono_viduitatis: This Late Antique prose treatise takes the form of a letter from Augustine to Juliana, a devout Christian widow who had pressed him to write on holy widowhood. The work opens with an apology for the delay and a note on its wider utility, then expounds Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 to order the goods of marriage, widowhood, and virginity. It maintains that widowhood excels wedlock without condemning it, while rebutting those who denounce second marriages and weighing the merits of widows against the scriptural examples of Anna and Ruth. The text also asks whether third or later marriages can be condemned, and the longer second half urges perseverance in the widowed vow. It defends the necessity of prayer and divine grace against those who rely on free will alone, and the letter closes with practical counsels on prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and reputation.
la.augustine.de_conjugiis_adulterinis: De coniugiis adulterinis is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a reply to his correspondent Pollentius. Pollentius asks if Paul's injunction that a departed wife remain unmarried applies only to a woman who has left an adulterous husband. Augustine contends that the marital bond endures as long as both spouses live, arguing that neither divorce for fornication nor separation from an unbelieving partner frees anyone to remarry. The author defends the reconciliation of penitent adulterers against objections drawn from human law, while also addressing the weakness of the flesh and the double standard that judges male and female incontinence differently. The text closes with a discussion of the baptism of catechumens, and it also considers persons living in adulterous unions who, near death, can no longer answer for themselves.
la.augustine.de_consensu_evangelistarum: This Late Antique treatise by Augustine defends the harmony of the four canonical Gospels, addressing pagans and others who allege contradictions among the evangelists. The work opens by ranking the gospel above all other scriptures, and Augustine assigns each evangelist a distinct role in the narrative. Matthew and Luke emphasize the human Christ, while John soars in his account of divinity, and Mark serves as an abridging follower of the others. The author then rebuts objections that Christ wrote nothing or taught magic, and the greater part of the text proceeds through the gospel narratives. It moves from the genealogies and infancy of Jesus through his ministry, and the Passion, resurrection, and post-Easter appearances follow in sequence. Augustine compares the four accounts episode by episode, showing that omissions and variations of wording do not entail real disagreement.
la.augustine.de_cura_pro_mortuis_gerenda: Augustine's De Cura pro Mortuis Gerenda is a brief Latin prose treatise cast as a letter addressed to the bishop Paulinus. The work opens with an answer to a widow's question about burial beside a saint's memorial. Augustine argues that funerary care and the choice of a grave at martyrs' shrines provide solace for the living. He maintains that such acts do not aid the dead, while prayer and almsgiving profit only those whose lives merited help. The treatise then examines scriptural passages on burial and reports of the dead appearing in dreams. It most fully considers the case of Curma and his vision of paradise. Augustine also addresses whether martyrs assist petitioners in person or through angels, a point he declines to settle. He closes by restating that burial is an office of humanity and a testimony to the resurrection. He notes that commendation of the dead at martyrs' memorials serves chiefly to quicken the supplications of the living.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_operibus: Augustine's De fide et operibus is a late-antique prose treatise on theology that opens by setting out the position of certain opponents, namely that all who present themselves should be admitted to the baptismal washing without exception, even those who openly profess their resolve to persist in sins such as adultery. In reply, Augustine argues that those seeking baptism must first be instructed both in the rule of faith and in the conduct proper to Christian life, since faith without works is dead, drawing on the rich young man of the Gospel, John the Baptist's preaching to publicans and soldiers, and Peter's call for repentance before the three thousand were baptized at Pentecost. The argument then answers a series of scriptural objections, including the baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch, Paul's claim to have known nothing among his hearers but Christ crucified, the two precepts of charity, and Israel's passage through the Red Sea before the giving of the Law, and takes up the parables of the wheat and the tares, the net, and the wedding feast to show that the presence of the wicked in the church requires patient tolerance without any relaxation of ecclesiastical discipline, a discussion that touches the Donatist schism. A long concluding section treats the saying in 1 Corinthians 3 about building on the foundation with wood, hay, and stubble and being saved as through fire, which Augustine, together with the Epistle of James, reads as excluding any promise of salvation to those who remain in manifest sins on the strength of faith alone.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram_imperfec: This unfinished Latin prose treatise by Augustine addresses the literal interpretation of the Genesis creation account. The work opens with a preface urging that obscure natural questions be treated by inquiry rather than rash assertion. It briefly names four recognised modes of scriptural exposition, including historical and allegorical approaches. Augustine then states the Catholic faith in summary, affirming the consubstantial Trinity and the renewal of humanity through Christ. The main body works through the opening verses of Genesis, asking what the phrase in the beginning signifies. It weighs rival readings on time, angels, light, and the firmament before breaking off within the first chapter.
la.augustine.de_mendacio: De Mendacio is a Late Antique prose treatise on lying by Augustine, opening with the observation that the question of falsehood disturbs ordinary daily conduct and announcing an inquiry pursued with little care for verbal elegance. The work first defines lying, distinguishing the speaker who declares what he takes to be true from the liar who has one thing in his heart and another in his words, and then asks whether any lie can be useful, weighing the scriptural cases that defenders of lying adduce, such as Sarah's denial, Jacob's deception of Isaac, and the Egyptian midwives. Augustine goes on to test the divine prohibitions of falsehood and disputed passages about oaths and false witness, considers whether bodily chastity may ever be shielded by a lie, and arranges eight kinds of lies in descending order of gravity, from falsehood in religious teaching down to lies that harm no one. He concludes that lying is never permitted under any of these heads, rejects the claim that the apostle Paul lied in the episode involving Peter and Barnabas, and closes with a prayer for strength against temptation.
la.augustine.de_natura_boni: De Natura Boni is a compact Latin theological treatise by Augustine, written in late antiquity and directed against the Manichaeans. The work opens by identifying God as the supreme, immutable, and eternal good, from which every other good, great or small, derives. All created things were made from nothing and are therefore mutable, so Augustine argues that evil is not a nature or substance. Instead, it is the corruption of the measure, form, and order proper to each creature, treating sin, pain, and punishment as privations within goods. The author reinforces this case with a series of biblical testimonies, while the closing section assails the Manichaean mythology in detail. It critiques the war between the kingdom of light and the race of darkness, addressing the mixture and purification of the divine substance. The text further examines the practices of Mani's elect, ending with a prayer for the conversion of those ensnared in error.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_gratia: On Nature and Grace is a Latin prose treatise by Augustine, who composed it in Late Antiquity and addressed it to Timasius and Jacobus. The work opens with his report of reading their book closely, which excuses sins by blaming human nature rather than the will. Augustine offers a sustained rejoinder to their claim that free choice prevents sin, arguing that nature, injured by Adam, requires Christ's grace for forgiveness and aid. He cites Pauline passages on original sin and infant baptism, while also weighing texts from Ambrose, Hilary, Jerome, and his own De libero arbitrio. He excepts the Virgin Mary from the universality of sin, and the treatise ends by expounding the charity that makes divine commandments light.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_origine_animae: De Natura et Origine Animae is a Late Antique theological treatise by Augustine that responds to Vincentius Victor's doctrines. The work opens as a letter to Renatus, who forwarded two books by the young writer Victor, a recent convert from Rogatist Donatist circles. The remainder comprises further letters addressed to the presbyter Peter and to Victor himself, where Augustine refutes claims that the soul emanates from God's breath. He rejects the idea that the soul is a body rather than a spirit, denying that it merited guilt before its bodily existence. Augustine also argues against the view that unbaptised infants dying young may reach paradise, while maintaining a suspended judgment on whether souls are propagated from parents or newly infused by God. He insists that the soul is a mutable creature made from nothing and not of the substance of God.
la.augustine.de_opere_monachorum: De Opere Monachorum is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, written as a letter at the request of his fellow bishop Aurelius. It opens by acknowledging that commission and posing its central question about monks who refuse manual labour. The text asks whether such monks may rightly appeal to Paul's precept that whoever will not work shall not eat. The main body argues from Paul's letters that the apostle's admonition concerns bodily labour, reviewing his own practice of supporting himself by handwork. It also discusses Paul's refusal of support owed to evangelists and the alms supplied to needy servants of God. The author rebukes idle wandering monks who trade on relics and feigned sanctity, while censuring long-haired brethren who claim self-castration made them neither male nor female. The letter closes with instructions for its circulation among Augustine's monks.
la.augustine.de_ordine: De Ordine ('On Order') is a Late Antique Latin prose dialogue by Augustine. It opens with a preface to Zenobius on the rarity of perceiving the world's governing order. The main text stages conversations at a country villa among Augustine, Licentius, Trygetius, Alypius, and his mother. A night dispute over water sounds prompts a definition of order and the place of evil in providence. The group also reads a cockfight as evidence of natural law and discusses educational authority. The work closes with a survey of liberal disciplines, showing how number purifies the soul for contemplation of God.
la.augustine.de_patientia: Augustine's late antique treatise De Patientia opens by asking how patience can be predicated of a God who cannot suffer, concluding that divine patience is real though ineffable. The work defines human patience as the equanimous endurance of evils for the sake of higher goods, distinguishing it from the endurance of the greedy, the ambitious, and the criminal. Such endurance springs from cupidity rather than virtue and merits no praise, while Job figures as the exemplar of endurance and the argument rejects self-inflicted death. True patience is not the fruit of unaided free will but a gift of God, poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit by charity. The closing pages answer objections concerning grace and election, weighing whether endurance shown in schism counts as this gift. The text ends with the assurance that the patience of the poor of Christ will not perish but yield eternal fruit.
la.augustine.de_sancta_virginitate: Augustine's Latin treatise De Sancta Virginitate ('On Holy Virginity') is a work of Late Antique prose theology. It opens by recalling his recently published De Bono Coniugali ('On the Good of Marriage'). The author urges consecrated virgins not to despise the married faithful. He argues that holy virginity stands above wedlock and widowhood without condemning marriage. The text treats Mary's motherhood, Paul's counsel, and the parable of the denarius. It closes with a long exhortation on humility and a warning against pride.
la.augustine.de_spiritu_et_littera: This Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine opens as a letter to Marcellinus, where he answers the objection that nothing is possible without a prior example. He addresses the specific case of a human living without sin through divine aid, opposing the view that the will can attain righteousness alone. Augustine expounds Paul's saying that the letter kills but the spirit gives life, maintaining that even human justice is God's work accomplished through grace. The text proceeds through sustained exegesis of the book of Romans, contrasting the law of works with the law of faith. The Decalogue written on stone is set against the law written in the heart, while the old and new testaments are also compared. The work closes by defending free will as established by grace, asking whether the will to believe is itself a gift from God.
la.augustine.de_utilitate_credendi: This Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine is addressed to his friend Honoratus. It defends the Catholic practice of believing before understanding against the Manichaean promise of pure reason. The work opens by distinguishing the heretic, who follows false opinions for gain, from the honest man deceived into crediting them. Augustine recalls his own nine years among the Manichaeans and sets out a fourfold reading of the Old Testament. He answers Manichaean attacks on the Old Law and separates blameless belief from culpable credulity. The text argues that authority, confirmed by miracles, must precede reason for minds not yet capable of grasping truth directly. It closes by urging Honoratus to commit himself to the teachers of the Catholic church and to prayer.
la.augustine.epistulae: The Epistulae of Augustine form a Latin prose collection of Late Antique correspondence that addresses friends, fellow clergy, and lay men and women. The collection opens with a defense of the author's treatment of the Academics, arguing that he imitated rather than attacked their veiling of Platonic truth. The text then moves through exchanges with Nebridius and Alypius on beatitude and the soul, covering a lengthy inquiry into how God may be seen. Further topics include the spiritual body of the resurrection and instruction on baptism, which are set against Novatianist views on penance. Shorter letters handle practical and pastoral business, including a debt of seventeen solidi and appeals for alms. The correspondence also notes the dedication of a basilica and offers encouragement to correspondents in faith and charity.
la.augustine.gesta_cum_emerito_donatistarum: The Gesta cum Emerito records a disputation at Caesarea's greater church, held under Honorius's twelfth and Theodosius's eighth consulships. Augustine of Hippo debated Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, while attended by Catholic bishops including Alypius and Possidius. The text opens with Augustine describing how Emeritus entered the city and consented to come into the church. The proceedings then turn on Augustine's demand that Emeritus state why he has come, and on the Donatist's persistent refusal to speak. Augustine has Alypius read aloud a letter addressed to the tribune and notary Marcellinus, in which the Catholics undertook to surrender their sees if defeated at the Conference of Carthage. He then expounds at length the Donatists' own condemnation of the Maximianist schism, arguing that their reception of bishops once excommunicated exposes their inconsistency over rebaptism and schism. The record closes with an appeal to the congregation to pray for Emeritus rather than despair of him.
la.augustine.liber_de_divinis_scripturis_si: The Liber de divinis scripturis sive Speculum is a late antique Latin florilegium transmitted under Augustine's name, gathering proof texts from Scripture under a long sequence of doctrinal and moral headings. The work opens with a table of more than a hundred chapter titles, which run from the one God and the distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These titles also cover precepts on almsgiving, oaths, idolatry, virginity, and widowhood, while the table explains figurative names in Scripture such as the vine, the mountains, the stars, and the dogs. The body then supplies the corresponding passages, which are introduced by formulae such as 'In genesi' and 'Item apostolus ad romanos'. The texts are drawn from the Pentateuch, the Psalms, the wisdom books, and the prophets, and they also come from the Gospels, the apostolic epistles, and the Apocalypse. The chapters move from Trinitarian doctrine through conversion, fear of the Lord, peace, and charity, addressing just judgment and the care of the poor, widows, and orphans. The text then turns to penitence, prayer, resurrection, and the tribulations of the just, including warnings against idolatry, fornication, drunkenness, usury, and false prophets. The work concludes with the sanctity of Samuel and Paul, the washing of feet, and the Lord as the fountain of life.
la.augustine.liber_de_unico_baptismo: The Liber de unico baptismo is a late antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, which serves as a polemical reply to a Donatist composition. That work claimed baptism outside their communion was invalid and required repetition, so Augustine opens by addressing Constantine and explaining his need to answer those who err from truth. He responds to a Donatist sermon on the one baptism that reached him via a presbyter, and the main argument holds that God's truth may persist even in iniquity. This applies to Jews, idolaters, and demons who confessed Christ, therefore baptism given by heretics and schismatics must be acknowledged rather than destroyed. Rebaptism is condemned as a diabolical presumption, and Augustine also reviews the old dispute over rebaptism between Cyprian of Carthage and Stephen of Rome. He defends bishops such as Caecilian, Miltiades, and Marcellinus against Donatist accusations, and the text closes by reaffirming that the church corrects iniquity without violating the divine sacrament.
la.augustine.sermo_ad_caesariensis_ecclesia: This Latin prose sermon by Augustine addresses the church at Caesarea, and it is preserved among his writings against the Donatists. The text opens with the preacher's joy that Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, has shown willingness toward unity, while the congregation acclaims the phrase aut hic aut nusquam. Augustine argues that schismatics may be received because their baptism belongs to Christ rather than to Donatus, and he distinguishes the sacramental sign from salvation. He urges the wanderer to return so the sign may then profit rather than condemn him, and an extended exposition of charity from 1 Corinthians follows. The inheritance of peace is discussed under the figure of Sara and her rivals, and the sermon closes by rehearsing the origins of the Donatist party. It mentions the persecution of Caecilian and the colloquy at Carthage, and Augustine defends the Catholic pursuit of the stray brother. He prays that Emeritus may communicate in peace, unity, and love.
la.aurelius_victor.de_caesaribus: Aurelius Victor's De Caesaribus ('On the Caesars') is a short Latin prose history of the Roman emperors. This work of Late Antique historiography arranges its material as a succession of biographical notices. It opens with the collapse of republican institutions and the rise of Octavian, who became Augustus. The narrative then covers the Julio-Claudian house, the civil wars of 69, and the Flavians. It continues through the adoptive and Severan emperors to the military turbulence of the third century. The text closes with Diocletian's tetrarchy, the rise of Constantine, and the reign of Constantius II. Portraits of individual rulers alternate with sketches of their deeds and moralizing judgments on character.
la.aurelius_victor.epitome_de_caesaribus: The Epitome de Caesaribus ('Summary of the Caesars') is a Latin prose work of imperial historiography from the Late Antique era. It is attributed to Aurelius Victor and consists of short biographies of the Roman emperors. The text opens by recording how, in the 722nd year from the founding of the city, obedience to a single ruler was revived. Octavian, renamed Augustus for his victory, then assumed supreme power. The narrative proceeds reign by reign, covering the Julio-Claudians, the Flavians, and the adoptive emperors. It continues through the soldier-emperors, the tetrarchy of Diocletian, and Constantine, ending with the death of Theodosius at Milan.
la.pseudo_aurelius_victor.de_viris_illustri: The De Viris Illustribus ('On Famous Men') transmitted with the Aurelius Victor corpus is a short Latin prose history of eighty six Roman figures from the founding generation of Rome to the age of Augustus. Its authorship is unknown, and it is traditionally printed alongside Aurelius Victor's own De Caesaribus, though modern scholarship treats it as the work of a different, anonymous writer. Each chapter is a brief biographical notice in the manner of Suetonius' lives, opening with the kings of Alba Longa and the birth of Romulus and Remus. The narrative continues through the early kings, the fall of the monarchy, and the wars of the early Republic. It follows generals and statesmen through the Punic Wars and the conquest of Greece and Asia Minor, down to the civil wars of the late Republic. The text closes with the deaths of Marcus Antonius and Cleopatra after the battle of Actium.
la.pseudo_aurelius_victor.origo_gentis_roma: The Origo Gentis Romanae ('Origin of the Roman People') is a short Latin prose history transmitted with the Aurelius Victor corpus, though its authorship is unknown and unrelated to Aurelius Victor himself. It survives in a single defective manuscript and traces the legendary prehistory of Rome from the arrival of Saturn and Janus in Italy through the Trojan migration led by Aeneas. The twenty three short chapters cite named sources throughout, among them Cassius Hemina, Fabius Pictor, Licinius Macer, Varro, Cato, and Vergil, often weighing variant versions of the same episode against one another. The narrative follows Aeneas to Latium, the reigns of Latinus and the Alban kings, and the birth of Romulus and Remus. It closes with their dispute over the auspices taken before the founding of the city and the conflicting ancient accounts of how that dispute ended.
la.ausonius.de_xii_caesaribus: De XII Caesaribus is a Late Antique Latin work by Ausonius, consisting of short epigrammatic notices on the Roman emperors. The proem promises a single monostich for each of the twelve Caesars, whereas Suetonius had previously set out their names, deeds, lives, and deaths at length. The opening is followed by verse tallies of the length and manner of death for each reign. The work then extends to rulers beyond the original dozen, proceeding from Julius Caesar and Augustus through Tiberius, Gaius, Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius. It continues to the Flavians, Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Pertinax, Didius Julianus, Septimius Severus, Caracalla, and Macrinus. The text closes with a denunciation of the emperor who falsely bore the Antonine name, described as the foulest monster ever seated in Roman power.
la.ausonius.gratiarum_actio: This Late Antique Latin prose oration by Ausonius is a formal speech of thanks addressed to the emperor Gratian on behalf of the speaker. The author served as the emperor's tutor before his elevation to the consulship, and the opening declares that the emperor's benefactions match his majesty in scale. They require no repayment and can be answered only by deep gratitude, while the body of the speech dwells chiefly on the consulship itself. It highlights the divine sanction of the appointment and its official precedence, and the text also notes the consular robes sent from Illyricum. Ausonius extolls Gratian's piety toward his deified father Constantius, and he praises the emperor's victories on the Danube and the Rhine. The speech also mentions the remission of tribute and care for sick soldiers, anticipating objections to a schoolmaster's elevation by comparing his case with earlier tutors. He cites Seneca, Quintilian, and Fronto as precedents, and the oration closes with a prayer to God.
la.ausonius.libri_de_fastis_conclusio: The Conclusio, meaning the conclusion, is a short closing poem by the late antique poet Ausonius, which gathers the final verses of his Fasti, a verse reckoning of Roman time. This work spans from the city's foundation to the poet's own consulship, presenting the completed calendar as the fruit of sleepless nights. It offers an ordered account of Rome's eternal years and early names, while later sections provide arithmetical rules for summing the total span of years. Readers are told to add further entries if fate grants the poet no more, and the poem directs curious readers to a title where they may find the author's name. It closes with an address to Proculus, who will receive the yearly series running from king Quirinus down to Ausonius's consulship. Proculus is expected to mark the finished count of Olympiads, completing the final tally of the ancient Roman calendar.
la.ausonius.precationes: This short sequence of lyric prayers by the late antique poet Ausonius opens with the repeated invocation 'Iane, veni'. The speaker addresses Janus and the sun as the January fasces are taken up for a new consular year. The prayers ask for seasonable weather month by month and the favourable course of the planets. They also seek peace throughout the world. Further stanzas call for victories over the Franks, Suebi, Sarmatians, and Huns. The sequence closes with a renewed petition to the two-faced Janus to renew the year and guide the sun and moon.
la.ausonius.versus_paschales_pro_augusto_di: This short late antique Latin poem by Ausonius is written in lyric metre for Easter, speaking in honour of the emperor. It opens with the return of Christ's saving feast, then addresses God as the father of all things whom the earth, sea, and heavens obey.
