The hymn credits God with granting eternal life and delivering law and prophets to humankind, noting his pity for Adam and the sending of his son, true from true. The poem closes by finding an earthly counterpart in the elder Augustus, sire of two co-emperors, who embraces his brother and son to share an undivided rule. It ends in prayer that Christ present these mild governors before the eternal father.
la.bede_the_venerable.de_locis_santis: This short Latin prose treatise by Bede the Venerable describes the holy sites of Palestine and the wider eastern Mediterranean. It opens with the walls and gates of Jerusalem, then moves through the church of the Holy Sepulchre and Mount Sion. The text continues to Bethlehem, Hebron, Jericho, the Jordan, the Dead Sea, and Galilee. It then turns to Damascus, Alexandria, and Constantinople. Throughout, Bede records churches, tombs, relics, and measurements alongside local marvels and legends. The concluding chapter states that the account follows the report of Arculf, a bishop of the Gauls, as set down by Adamnan, together with older written sources.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto Interpolatum is a Carolingian Latin verse life of St Benedict of Nursia, whose title marks the version as interpolated. The poet ascribes the work to Bertharius of Monte Cassino, whose name appears in the closing prayer. The poem opens by addressing Benedict as the confessor chosen by God from boyhood to guide seekers of the heavenly kingdom. The body then recounts a long sequence of episodes from the saint's career, including the broken sieve restored, exorcisms, the spring, and the recovered billhook on Monte Cassino. Further scenes cover Maurus's rescue of Placidus, the poisoned loaf carried away, the conversion of pagan temples, and prophecies to Totila and concerning Rome. The narrative also details the Lombard sack of the monastery, the shared tomb of Benedict and his sister, and visions witnessed by Servandus. The text ends with healing miracles at Benedict's shrine, including the cure of the lame Andreas, and a final prayer begs Christ to guard the flock and to protect Bertharius himself.
la.boethius.consolatio_philosophiae: Boethius' Consolatio Philosophiae, a late antique Latin work, opens with a poem where the fallen statesman laments his disgrace. Personified Philosophy appears at the prisoner's bedside and banishes the Muses, leading him through a dialogue that moves from complaint to an account of true happiness. This happiness is defined as the possession of the supreme good, which is God, while the text argues the powerlessness of the wicked and the rule of divine providence. The final book reconciles God's timeless foreknowledge with human free will, and short lyric metres punctuate the prose argument across the five books.
la.boethius.de_fide_catholica: This brief late-antique prose treatise attributed to Boethius sets out the essentials of the Christian faith, proclaiming that the authority of the Old and New Testaments reveals the religion. The faith rests on the eternity of the one divine substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while the author notes the errors of Arius, the Sabellians, and the Manichaeans along the way. The tract recounts salvation history, beginning with the creation of the world, the fall of the angels and of Adam, and the patriarchs from Abraham through Jacob. It details the deliverance from Egypt and the law given through Moses, continuing with the kings from David onward until the birth of Christ from the Virgin of Davidic stock. The teachings of Pelagius, Nestorius, and Eutyches are rejected in passing, and the closing pages follow Christ's baptism, passion, resurrection, and ascension. They describe the sacraments and the spread of the church, distinguishing the sources of doctrinal authority before ending with the expectation of the world's end, the resurrection and last judgment, and the eternal contemplation of the creator.
la.boethius.quomodo_substantiae_in_eo_quod_: Boethius wrote this short late-antique Latin prose treatise as a letter to the same recipient as a companion work, opening with a promise to clarify a question drawn from his Hebdomads. The core issue asks how substances are good in virtue of their existence without being substantial goods, and the body sets out nine axioms, including the distinction between being and that which is. It then states the puzzle that if all things are good only by participation, they cannot tend to the good, whereas if they are good by substance, everything that exists would turn out to be God. The solution proceeds by a mental separation of the first good in thought, showing that things are good in their being because their existence flows from the will of the first good. They are not good because they resemble or participate in it, and a closing passage contrasts goodness, which belongs to essence, with justice, an act that does not extend to all things.
la.boethius.quomodo_trinitas: Boethius wrote this short Late Antique Latin treatise to explain how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, dedicating it to his father-in-law, Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus. The work begins by explaining why the question is difficult and why the argument uses veiled philosophical vocabulary, while rejecting Arian attempts to rank the divine persons by degrees. It distinguishes the senses of same and different by genus, species, and number, and separates speculative disciplines into the natural, mathematical, and theological. Applying Aristotle's categories, the treatise argues that terms like deus signify what is beyond substance and accident, claiming that repeated predication creates enumeration rather than plurality. Relational predicates such as pater and filius alter nothing in the divine essence, so unity resides in substance while relation alone multiplies the trinity into persons. The argument closes by submitting the question to Symmachus's judgment.
la.caesar.de_bello_civili: This prose historiographical account in Latin covers Caesar's civil war in three books of uneven length. It is conventionally attributed to Caesar himself, though scholars debate its date and authorship. The narrative opens with the tribunes Antony and Cassius fleeing to Caesar at Ravenna. It then follows the surrender of Corfinium and the campaign in Spain against Afranius and Petreius. The story continues through the siege of Massilia and Curio's African expedition. It concludes with the battle of Pharsalus and Caesar's arrival in Egypt.
la.caesar_augustus.res_gestae_divi_augusti: The Res Gestae Divi Augusti is a first-person Latin prose account where Augustus summarises his achievements and expenditures. Presented as a copy of an inscription on two bronze pillars at Rome, the work opens with a preamble naming its subject. It claims that at nineteen, Augustus raised a private army at his own expense to free the republic from a dominating faction. The text proceeds thematically through his career, covering civil and foreign wars, as well as the offices and priesthoods he held or declined. It also details his censorial lustra and counts of citizens, listing gifts of land, money, and grain to soldiers and the plebs. The account describes the temples, aqueducts, and public buildings he built or restored, mentioning the games and spectacles he gave. It notes the pacification of the seas and the extension of the empire's frontiers, which included Gaul, Spain, Germany, Egypt, Armenia, Pannonia, and Arabia. The text closes with the submissions and embassies of foreign kings, recording the restoration of the state to the senate and people. It also notes the honours of the name Augustus and the title pater patriae, concluding with a summary of his total outlay.
la.cicero.brutus: The Brutus is a Latin prose dialogue by Cicero set in the Roman Republic, framing a history of Roman eloquence as a conversation among Cicero, Atticus, and Brutus. The text opens with Cicero grieving the death of the orator Quintus Hortensius, news that reaches him on his return from Cilicia before the men begin to talk. The dialogue surveys oratory at Rome from its earliest practitioners down to Cicero's contemporaries, sketching the careers and styles of successive generations of speakers. It weighs questions such as popular versus expert judgment and the Attic and Asiatic manners of speaking, while also considering the parts and training of the orator. An autobiographical account of Cicero's rhetorical education and forensic career is woven through the survey, including his rivalry with Hortensius. The work closes with an address to Brutus, encouraging him to pursue eloquence amid the disorders of the state.
la.cicero.cum_populo_gratias_egit: A prose oration of the Republican era, delivered by Cicero to the Roman people in formal thanks for his recall from exile. It opens with the vow he had once made to Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the other immortal gods, devoting himself and his fortunes to the safety of the citizens, and with his joy that the judgment of the gods, the testimony of the senate, the consent of Italy, and the confession of his enemies have vindicated that devotion. The speech goes on to recount how absence taught him the worth of his brother, his children, his property, his friendships, and his fatherland, contrasts his restoration, effected through the senate, the consul P. Lentulus, and above all Cn. Pompeius, with those of Popilius, Metellus, and Marius, and closes with promises of perpetual gratitude and unwavering service to the res publica.
la.cicero.de_fato: A philosophical dialogue of the late Republic by Cicero, set at his Puteolan villa after Caesar's death, De Fato opens with a preface on the Academic practice of arguing on both sides and a conversation in which the consul-designate Hirtius asks for a disputation on fate. The discussion then examines whether all events occur from antecedent causes, whether divination implies necessity, and how the logical puzzles of Chrysippus and Diodorus over the truth and possibility of future-tense statements bear on the question. Along the way it treats Posidonius's appeals to the influence of place and the stars, the Epicurean doctrine of the swerving atom, Carneades' defense of voluntary motion without external causes, Chrysippus's distinction between principal and auxiliary causes together with the analogy of the pushed cylinder, and the refutation of the 'lazy argument' and of objections drawn from 'co-fated' events such as the birth of Oedipus. The work breaks off unfinished in the midst of the argument against Epicurus.
la.cicero.de_finibus_bonorum_et_malorum: Cicero's De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum is a five book philosophical dialogue composed in prose during the Roman Republic to examine the highest good and evil. The work opens with a preface to Brutus where Cicero defends writing philosophy in Latin. The first two books stage an Epicurean defence of pleasure as the supreme good, which Cicero then refutes in the same section. Books three and four present Cato's Stoic exposition of virtue as the only good, to which Cicero offers a counter argument. The fifth book gives Piso's Old Academy account of goods according to nature, which Cicero answers in conversation with Quintus and Pomponius. The work closes as the disputants set off together into town.
la.cicero.de_inventione: A Latin treatise on rhetoric in two books by Cicero, composed in the Republican era, De Inventione opens with a prolonged meditation on whether the power of speech has brought men and states more good or more harm. The first book defines the art, its office, end and subject-matter, enumerates the parts of rhetoric, and concentrates on invention: the four constitutions or issue-types of a cause, the six parts of the oration from exordium to conclusion, and argumentation by induction and ratiocination, together with the commonplaces. The second book supplies hypothetical cases and precepts for accuser and defender under each constitution, treats controversies arising from written instruments, including ambiguity, letter versus intent, conflicting laws, inference and definition, and closes with instruction on deliberative and demonstrative oratory, covering the honourable, the useful, necessity and the topics of praise and blame. The work ends by announcing that the remaining subjects, notably style, are reserved for later books.
la.cicero.de_officiis: Cicero composed this philosophical treatise in the final years of the Roman Republic, addressing it as a letter of instruction to his son Marcus, who was studying in Athens. The work opens with paternal counsel on uniting Greek and Latin learning, then sets out a theory of moral duty in the Stoic tradition. Cicero follows Panaetius's scheme while supplying parts that Panaetius left unfinished, and the first book treats the morally honourable, tracing it to wisdom, justice, and propriety. The second examines the expedient, covering goodwill, glory, and the management of wealth, while the third addresses apparent conflicts between honour and advantage. It argues that nothing can be truly useful which is not honourable, and historical examples from Regulus to Caesar support this final argument.
la.cicero.de_optimo_genere_oratorum: A short Latin rhetorical treatise by Cicero of the Republican era, De Optimo Genere Oratorum opens by rejecting any division of oratory into genera on the analogy of poetic genres, arguing instead that there is one perfect kind of orator, who teaches, delights and moves his hearers. The work goes on to enumerate the qualities of words, thoughts and arrangement required for that ideal, distinguishes the Attic manner from the abundance characteristic of Asia, and holds up the orators of Athens, and Demosthenes above all, as the standard of excellence. It closes by presenting itself as the preface to Cicero's Latin versions of the opposing speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes in the case arising from Ctesiphon's decree honouring Demosthenes with a golden crown, summarising the laws, accusations and history of that trial and defending a method of translation that preserves the force and figures of the original rather than rendering word for word.
la.cicero.de_provinciis_consularibus: In this prose oration of the Roman Republic, Cicero speaks in the senate as a senator to give his formal opinion on the assignment of the consular provinces. He opens by remarking that the senators can work out for themselves whose removal from their provinces he will propose, since his known grievances make his view plain. The greater part of the speech denounces Piso and Gabinius for the extortion, violence, and military ruin that have overtaken Macedonia and Syria under their command. Cicero argues that both men must be recalled, while contending that Caesar should stay in Gaul until the conquest there is complete. The close is a long justification of his political reconciliation with Caesar, weighing their earlier dealings, his own exile and restoration, and the public advantage of finishing the Gallic war.
la.cicero.epistulae_ad_familiares: The Epistulae ad Familiares ('Letters to Friends') is a Latin prose collection of Cicero's correspondence. It comprises sixteen books that group the letters largely by addressee. The opening letter, sent during Cicero's consulship to Lentulus Spinther in Cilicia, reports on the senate's handling of the Alexandrian king. From there the collection ranges across the final decades of the Republic. It covers the political struggles over Caesar's command and the civil war between Caesar and Pompey. The volume also includes letters of bereavement for Tullia and humorous exchanges with Papirius Paetus.
la.cicero.letters_to_brutus: Letters to Brutus is a Latin prose collection of Cicero's correspondence from the closing phase of the Roman Republic. It was written during the civil war against Mark Antony in the aftermath of Caesar's assassination. The opening letter offers reassurance about the loyalty of the tribune-designate Clodius and reports on Antony's standing. Cicero then details senatorial debates, honours decreed to Caesarian leaders, and the deaths of consuls Hirtius and Pansa. He also describes operations against Dolabella in Asia. Brutus replies with a severe rebuke for appealing to the young Caesar, while shorter letters address troops, money, and strategy. The correspondence breaks off abruptly without a formal close.
la.cicero.letters_to_quintus: Letters to Quintus is a collection of epistolary prose by Marcus Tullius Cicero, which addresses his brother during the final decades of the Roman Republic. The opening piece is a long fraternal admonition urging Quintus, then governing the province of Asia, to integrity and self-command. The remaining letters range across Cicero's own fortunes, including his exile at Thessalonica, and report on senatorial debates, trials, and the manoeuvres of Pompey, Caesar, and Clodius. Family news, building work on the brothers' estates, and remarks on literary projects fill the rest of the correspondence. This collection blends political commentary, private business, and fraternal affection in a conversational Latin style.
la.cicero.lucullus: The Lucullus is a Latin prose dialogue on Academic skepticism, composed during the Republic and transmitted as part of the Academica. It opens with a eulogy of Lucius Licinius Lucullus, celebrating his campaigns against Mithridates and his devotion to Greek letters. This section also notes his attachment to the philosopher Antiochus of Ascalon, whose position Lucullus defends in a long speech. He argues that truth can be grasped and known, marshaling evidence from the senses, memory, the arts, and virtue. This stands against the views of Arcesilas and Carneades, while Cicero replies at length on behalf of the New Academy. He expounds the Carneadean doctrine of the probable, turning the Stoics' dialectic and the sorites against them. He surveys the schools' irreconcilable disagreements over nature, the gods, and the supreme good, and Catulus and Hortensius close the conversation with brief pronouncements.
la.cicero.orator: Cicero wrote this Latin treatise on rhetoric in the late Roman Republic, addressing Marcus Brutus directly and claiming that Brutus's urging overcame his hesitation. The work defines the perfect orator as an ideal form grasped by the mind, grounding eloquence in philosophy and answering the narrow standard of the Atticists. The author distinguishes three styles of oratory, the plain, the temperate, and the grand, considering what befits each style in subject, person, and occasion. The text also covers the orator's need for dialectic, civil law, history, and philosophy, while a long closing portion examines the arrangement of words and prose rhythm. It illustrates these points from Greek and Roman orators and poets, concluding by submitting the whole discussion to Brutus's judgment.
la.cicero.paradoxa_stoicorum_ad_m_brutum: Cicero wrote this short prose treatise in the late Republic for Marcus Brutus, defending six counter-intuitive Stoic doctrines that the author found difficult to accept. A preface explains that admiration for Cato of Utica prompted this inquiry, and Cicero sought to make these severe ideas acceptable to a Roman audience. He used oratorical polish to present the paradoxes in turn, arguing that moral rectitude alone is a good and that virtue suffices for the happy life. The author maintains that all offences are equal, and a section on the madness of fools survives only in part. Cicero asserts that only the wise man is free, and he also argues that only the wise man is rich. Each point is argued with examples from early Roman history, and the work includes pointed attacks on figures like Clodius and Crassus.
la.cicero.post_reditum_in_senatu: This Latin prose oration by Cicero is addressed to the Roman senate upon his return from exile during the late Republic. It offers thanks for the body's role in his recall, opening with the claim that no abundance of eloquence could repay the senate's benefits. These benefits had restored to him his brother, his children, his fortunes, and his fatherland. The speech proceeds to recount the senate's steadfast support during his absence, while Cicero hurls sustained invective against the consuls of his exile year, Piso and Gabinius. He praises a long series of benefactors, above all the consul Lentulus, Pompey, the tribunes Annius and Sestius, and his brother Quintus. The text closes with Cicero's account of his own decision to withdraw rather than fight, expressing his sense that he returned together with the republic itself and stating his resolve to defend it with undiminished freedom.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_postumo: This forensic oration by Cicero dates to the Republic, where it defends Gaius Rabirius Postumus, a Roman eques charged under the Julian extortion law. The charge held that money taken by the condemned governor Gabinius had reached Rabirius, whom Cicero opens by conceding acted rashly in entrusting his fortune to King Ptolemy of Alexandria. He begs the judges not to add ruin to a man already crushed by fortune, arguing that the charge rests on a novel and inapplicable clause of the statute. Rabirius was neither named nor called as a witness in Gabinius's trial, and Cicero warns that a conviction would set a dangerous precedent against the whole equestrian order. He refutes accusations that Rabirius served as the king's financial minister, while also denying that Rabirius wore Greek dress or skimmed a tithe from the monies collected. Cicero praises Caesar's generosity in sustaining the bankrupt defendant, and the oration closes with an appeal to pity, recalling Rabirius's support of Cicero and his family during the exile.
la.cicero.pro_m_caelio: Cicero composed this forensic defence for Marcus Caelius Rufus, who faced prosecution under the law on public violence. The opening notes the odd timing of the trial during public festivals, highlighting the gap between the grave statute and the youthful defendant. Cicero neutralises moral slanders regarding Caelius's indulgent youth and debts, while addressing his former association with Catiline and his move to the Palatine. The argument confronts formal charges that Caelius took gold from Clodia and plotted poison, dismantling these claims by ridiculing Clodia through imagined speeches. He dissects the implausible account of the poison's handover at the baths of Senias, appealing to the sworn testimony of L. Lucceius. The peroration pleads for acquittal based on Caelius's ability and ambition, citing his father's dependence on him and a pledge of future loyalty.
la.cicero.pro_marcello: This short oration from the Roman Republic addresses the senate and Julius Caesar after his civil war victory. Cicero gives thanks for the pardon and recall of Marcus Marcellus, an adversary the senators had begged Caesar to spare. The speech opens by explaining that the day's proceedings break a long silence kept out of grief and shame. It then turns to gratitude for Marcellus's restoration and ranks Caesar's clemency above his military exploits. Cicero defends his own record as a consistent advocate of peace during the war. He confronts Caesar's suspicion of plots, arguing that the safety of the commonwealth now depends on him. The text closes by urging Caesar to complete the state's settlement through restored courts, credit, and laws. It ends with renewed thanks on behalf of the senate, Marcellus's brother Gaius, and Cicero himself.
la.cicero.pro_murena: Pro Murena is a forensic oration delivered by Cicero as consul, who defends Lucius Murena, a consul elect, against charges of electoral bribery. The accusers include M. Cato, Servius Sulpicius, and C. Postumus, and the speech opens with a prayer Cicero offered when he announced Murena's election. He also answers critics who argued that a consul who passed anti bribery laws should not defend such a case. The body of the text addresses slurs regarding Murena's conduct in Asia, covering his service as legate under Lucullus and rebuts Cato's taunt that the soldier was a dancer. Cicero argues that military distinction outweighs Servius's legal expertise in the race for the consulship, extending this point with a mockery of the jurists' art. Later sections examine evidence concerning canvassers, shows, and dinners, while the oration weighs Cato's Stoic severity and dwells on the Catilinarian conspiracy. It highlights the danger of leaving the state with only a single consul, and the speech closes with an appeal to the judges' pity for the defendant and his family.
la.cicero.pro_rege_deiotaro: Cicero's Pro Rege Deiotaro is a forensic oration from the late Roman Republic, spoken before Julius Caesar to defend Deiotarus, king and tetrarch of Galatia. The king faced charges from his grandson Castor of plotting Caesar's assassination, which Cicero begins by noting his unease at pleading a capital case in a private house. He then works to discredit the accusers, highlighting the oddity of a grandson suing his grandfather, while the speech also reviews Deiotarus's long record of service to Rome. This includes his alliance with Pompey down to the battle of Pharsalus, and Cicero later details the king's subsequent cooperation with Caesar. He dismantles each alleged proof in turn, such as the supposed ambush at Blucium, and the orator also addresses the reported remarks of Blesamius. Cicero praises the king's gravity, temperance, and loyalty, closing with an appeal to Caesar's clemency to preserve the accused's life and reputation.
la.cicero.pro_s_roscio: This forensic oration from the Roman Republic features Cicero defending Sextus Roscius of Ameria, presenting himself as a young advocate who has never before spoken a public case. The prosecutor in this charge of parricide is Erucius, and Cicero explains why he alone has risen while orators of the highest rank sit silent. He states that the murdered man's estates were bought for a trifling sum by the powerful freedman Chrysogonus, and the narrative reconstructs the killing near the baths of Pallacine and the flight of news to Ameria. It also details the seizure of property by Titus Roscius Magnus and Capito, while the accused found refuge with Caecilia at Rome. The refutation dismantles alleged motives of paternal hatred and intended disinheritance, and digressions praise rural life and describe the Roman penalty of the sack for parricides. The later part turns to counter-accusation against the two Roscii, who profited from the death and refused the interrogation of the slaves, and Cicero arraigns Capito's betrayal of the legation sent to Sulla. He exposes Chrysogonus' luxury and the irregularity of his purchase under the proscription laws, and the speech closes with an appeal that the judges prevent a fresh proscription of the victims' children.
la.cicero.pro_sestio: Pro Sestio is a forensic oration in which Cicero defends Publius Sestius against charges of public violence, beginning by asking why so few courageous citizens now come forward to defend the state. The speech traces the political crisis of the preceding years, including the gang warfare of P. Clodius, and details the complicity of the consuls Piso and Gabinius in those events. Cicero recounts his own exile and recall, as well as Sestius's tireless work as tribune on his behalf, which exposed Sestius to prosecution and forms the core of the legal argument. A lengthy digression defines the optimates as men who pursue otium cum dignitate, contrasting them with popular agitators and praising Milo's resistance to Clodius. The orator exhorts the young nobility to imitate the great defenders of the commonwealth, closing by appealing to the jurors to acquit Sestius, Milo, and Lentulus. Their ruin would dishonour his own restoration to public life.
la.cicero.pro_sulla: This defense oration by Cicero was composed in the late Roman Republic, where it pleads the case of Publius Sulla against the charge of complicity in the Catilinarian conspiracy. The speech opens with Cicero lamenting Sulla's fallen fortunes, explaining that he must defend his client while answering the prosecutor Lucius Torquatus. Torquatus had attacked Cicero for testifying against alleged conspirators while defending Sulla, prompting the text to work through the prosecution's evidence, including the testimony of the Allobroges. It also addresses the purchase of gladiators through Faustus Sulla and an alleged alteration of the public record, while Cicero repeatedly vindicates his own consulship and suppression of the conspiracy. The speech closes with an appeal to the judges' mercy based on the defendant's life and character.
la.cicero.pro_tullio: The Pro Tullio is a fragmentary forensic speech by Cicero from the Republican period, delivered in defence of Marcus Tullius, a landowner of Thurii, against Publius Fabius. The opening explains that the task has shifted from proving the deed to arguing its legal character, a change following the opponent's household confessing to the killing. The surviving portions recount a night raid in which Fabius' armed servants killed Tullius' slaves, and they also describe the wrecking of a farm building during the attack. The text then argues at length over the force of specific legal terms in the formula, covering the origin of the action under Lucullus and the jurisdiction of the recuperatores. It also addresses interdicts on forcible dispossession and the Twelve Tables' rules on self-defence.
la.cicero.timaeus: A Latin philosophical prose work of the Republic by Cicero, being a version of Plato's Timaeus that breaks off before the dialogue's end. It opens with a preface in which Cicero recalls his disputations on natural philosophy with P. Nigidius, a reviver of Pythagorean teaching, and a meeting with the Peripatetic Cratippus, before turning to Timaeus' distinction between what always is and what is generated. The rendering then follows the cosmology of that speech: a benevolent craftsman god brings order out of disorderly matter, fashions the world as a single, spherical, rational living being, builds the world-soul from blended indivisible and divisible substance in harmonic numerical proportions, sets the orbits of the fixed stars, sun, moon and planets to measure time, and creates the celestial gods and the daemones or Lares. The creator then charges the younger gods to fashion mortal beings; souls are allotted to the stars and sown into bodies, the fortunes and transmigrations of human souls into women and beasts are set out, and an account of the formation of bodies and of the eyes and their divine gift of philosophy carries the work to its abrupt close.
la.cicero.tusculanae_disputationes: Cicero's Tusculan Disputations is a philosophical treatise in five books, written during the Roman Republic and addressed to Brutus. The work recounts the disputations Cicero held over five days at his villa at Tusculum. The opening preface explains that, freed from forensic and senatorial labours, Cicero has undertaken to set forth Greek philosophy in Latin. It also describes the Socratic method whereby a thesis is proposed and Cicero argues against it. The five books argue in turn that death is no evil, that pain can be borne through fortitude, and that grief does not befall the wise. They further contend that the remaining disturbances of the soul arise from judgement and opinion rather than nature, and that virtue alone suffices for a happy life. Throughout, the discussions are presented as they were conducted, with Cicero weighing the doctrines of the several philosophical schools in an Academic, probabilistic manner.
la.cicero_pseudo.in_sallustium: This Latin prose invective is preserved among the works ascribed to Cicero, though its authorship and date remain uncertain. It is cast as a speech delivered in the senate in answer to a denunciation by C. Sallustius. The speaker asserts that a man's words should accord with his life and that his task is to answer a slanderer whose own record will not bear examination. The speech alternates between self-defence and attack, recalling the speaker's consulship, his verses on civic harmony, his exile and recall, and his public friendships. It then catalogues Sallust's alleged youthful vices, a publicly confessed adultery, a corrupt quaestorship, and extortion as governor of Africa. The text ends with the observation that open denunciation of others' disgraces usually offends an audience more than the offences themselves.
la.cicero_pseudo.pridie_quam_in_exilium_ire: This Latin oration, transmitted under Cicero's name, is preserved as a pseudo-Ciceronian piece whose actual date of composition remains uncertain. Framed as the address he delivered to the Roman people the day before his departure into exile, the speaker urges citizens to defend the man who risked his own head so they might not be consumed. He recounts his suppression of the Catilinarian conspiracy and protests that he is banished without witness, accuser, or trial, attributing this banishment to tribunician fury and the envy of the wicked. He appeals to the Roman knights and to Jupiter and the other gods of the Capitol for aid, invoking the precedents of Marius, Scipio, and Pompey. Finally, he resolves to withdraw into exile rather than let civil bloodshed follow, asking the people to protect his children, his household, and the reputation won by his virtue.
la.claudian.de_bello_gildonico: Claudian composed this late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters to celebrate the war against Gildo, the Moorish count who seized Africa's grain supply, bringing famine to Rome under the western emperor Honorius. The poem opens with the startling swiftness of Gildo's overthrow, and personified Roma then pleads before Jupiter against the starvation his rebellion has caused. The bulk of the work consists of formal speeches, where Roma laments her lost greatness, while Africa complains against the tyrant's outrages. The ghost of Theodosius reproaches his son Honorius and vindicates Stilicho, and a proposal follows that Mascezel, Gildo's wronged brother, lead the expedition. A satirical portrait of Gildo's cruelty and luxury appears as the forces muster, and the narrative ends with the fleet assembled at Pisa. It lies in the harbour of Caralis in Sardinia, waiting for a favourable wind, and no battle is yet narrated.
la.claudian.panegyricus_dictus_manlio_theod: Claudian composed this hexameter panegyric to honor the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, opening with the Muse hesitating before such an august audience. Winged envoys from East and West then meet to survey the world, while the body traces Theodorus from early eloquence to judicial posts in Libya and Macedonia. He later serves as palatine judge for Spain, Germany, and Britain, followed by a catalogue of Greek schools after his withdrawal into philosophy. Personified Justice descends to summon him back to public life, and after a dialogue, he assumes governance of Italy, Africa, and Illyricum. The closing movement describes consular games with lavish detail, ending with a prayer for the Manlian line.
la.claudianus_mamertus.de_statu_animae: De Statu Animae is a three book prose treatise by Claudianus Mamertus, which opens as a reply to a priest on how to answer Arian claims about the Son. The author argues that divine names signify persons rather than natures, while the bulk of the work addresses an anonymous opponent who held the soul to be a body. Mamertus defends the soul's incorporeality, immortality, and local independence through reasoned argument, citing Plato, the Pythagoreans, Varro, Cicero, and Christian authorities like Augustine. The text also treats measure, number, and weight as marks of bodies and souls, and it closes with syllogistic proofs, an admonition, and a diagram summarizing the argument.
la.claudianus_mamertus.epistolae: Claudianus Mamertus, a Late Antique writer, composed these Latin prose letters for a learned and eloquent correspondent. The opening letter protests rare visits and rebukes the addressee for his long silence. It threatens to avenge that silence with a persistent stream of writing. The remaining letters dwell in lavish praise of the recipient. They extol his treatise on the state of the soul and celebrate one of his hymns. The author sets the addressee's eloquence beside a roll call of Greek and Latin orators. One letter laments the neglect of liberal studies in the author's own day. It urges the addressee, as citizen and teacher of Vienne, to shun modern novelties. The writer advises him to model his style on Naevius, Plautus, Cato, Varro, and Cicero.
la.commodianus.instructiones: The Instructiones is a two-book Latin collection of Christian instructional pieces by the Later Imperial writer Commodianus, whose dates are uncertain. The work opens with a preface before the first book attacks pagan religion, targeting individual gods such as Saturn, Jupiter, Apollo, and Mercury. It also covers idols, gentiles, Jews, and the time of Antichrist, while the second book addresses Christians, including catechumens, the faithful, penitents, and apostates. This section further treats soldiers of Christ, matrons, and clerics, covering topics like the first resurrection, the day of judgement, penance, and martyrdom. The final sections discuss funeral customs and the duties of readers, ministers, and pastors.
la.couplet_et_alii.confucius_sinarum_philos: This Latin prose treatise by Couplet and collaborators presents the Chinese sage Confucius to a European royal audience. It opens with a dedication to Louis XIV, imagining Confucius transported to France to admire the king's triumph over heresy. The body examines the doctrines of the Chinese literati and rival sects. It also disputes whether the ancient classics attest knowledge of a supreme deity. The text recounts Matteo Ricci's deliberations and labours in establishing the Jesuit mission at Peking. A concluding life of Confucius narrates his birth, career, disciples, teachings, death, and posthumous honours. It argues that the rites observed at his academies are civil rather than religious in character.
la.cyprian.ad_quirinum_aut_testimoniorum_li: Cyprian addresses this treatise to Quirinus, explaining in the preface that he compiled a compact anthology of scriptural passages at the recipient's request. The text is arranged under numbered chapter headings for easy reference, and Book I assembles Old and New Testament citations to argue that the Jews forfeited God's favor by rejecting the prophets and Christ. It further contends that the old law, circumcision, sacrifice, and priesthood gave way to new ones, while Book II gathers testimonies on the person and work of Christ. This section covers his pre-existence as the wisdom, word, and arm of God, along with his virgin birth at Bethlehem, and details his humble advent, passion, crucifixion, descent to the underworld, and resurrection on the third day. It concludes with his future coming as judge and everlasting king, and Book III is likewise introduced by a preface and a list of 120 chapters. It collects scriptural precepts for Christian conduct and church discipline, ranging from almsgiving, humility, and patience under persecution to baptism and virginity, and addresses the duties of masters and slaves, as well as separation from idolaters, heretics, and schismatics.
la.cyprian.de_bono_patientiae: Cyprian's late-antique treatise De bono patientiae opens by addressing his audience as beloved brothers, noting that patience is required even to hear a discourse on the subject. The work presents patience as the foremost of the heavenly disciplines, which originates in God the Father and is distinguished from the false patience professed by the philosophers. It traces the divine patience that grants sun and rain alike to just and unjust, while Christ's incarnation, temptation, teaching, and passion supply the central exemplar. This is reinforced by the endurance of Abel, Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph, and Moses, David, Job, Tobias, and Stephen also provide examples of steadfastness. Impatience, beginning with Adam's transgression, is shown to be the devil's work, and it is the source of idolatry and heresy. The treatise closes with an account of the many operations of patience, which governs anger, tongue, and mind, and sustains bodily affliction and persecution, while the author exhorts readers to await the day of divine vengeance rather than seek vindication.
la.cyprian.de_dominica_oratione: A Latin treatise of Late Antique date, the De dominica oratione sets out Cyprian's teaching on the prayer Christ gave his followers. It opens by presenting the evangelical precepts as divine instruction and by arguing that Christ, who both prayed and taught, himself supplied the form of prayer the faithful should use. The body of the work first considers how to pray, urging quietness, modesty, and humility before God with examples drawn from scripture, and then expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, from the invocation 'our Father' through the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, the doing of God's will in heaven and on earth, daily bread, the forgiveness of debts, and deliverance from temptation and from the evil one. A closing section points to Christ's own practice of prayer as an example and urges vigilance of heart, fasting, almsgiving, and prayer at the traditional hours, in the morning, the evening, and through the night.
la.cyprian.de_habitu_virginum: De Habitu Virginum, a Latin Christian treatise attributed to Cyprian, opens by praising discipline as the guardian of hope and the foundation of religious life. The work then narrows its focus to consecrated virgins, described as the flower of the church, whose calling is defined as the devotion of both body and spirit to Christ alone. The bulk of the text exhorts virgins against outward adornment, jewellery, and costly dress, while also warning against the misuse of wealth and attendance at mixed baths. The treatise closes by ranking the reward of virginity second only to that of the martyrs, likening virgins to angels and urging them to persevere in purity.
la.cyprian.de_opere_et_eleemosynis: De Opere et Eleemosynis ('On Work and Almsgiving') is a brief Latin prose treatise on almsgiving by the Christian writer Cyprian of the late-antique period. It opens by enumerating the divine benefits bestowed on humanity through Christ and presents alms as the appointed remedy for sins committed after baptism. The body of the work gathers scriptural precepts and examples, among them Isaiah's summons to feed the hungry, Raphael's counsel in Tobit, and Peter's raising of Tabitha. The widow's mites, the widow sustained by Elijah, and Job's sacrifices for his children likewise urge the faithful to exchange earthly wealth for treasure in heaven. Cyprian answers the objection that generosity toward the poor will impoverish donors and their families, and contrasts the spectacle of almsgiving before God and Christ with pagan public games. In closing, the treatise turns to the Last Judgment scene of Matthew 25 and calls for continued works of mercy on the model of the earliest Christian community.
la.cyprian.de_unitate_ecclesiae_catholicae: Cyprian wrote this Latin treatise to defend the unity of the Catholic Church against heretics and schismatics. It opens by urging vigilance against the devil, who threatens believers through secret deception as well as open persecution. The central argument rests on scriptural grounds, presenting Peter as the starting point of the church's oneness. Cyprian insists that the episcopate is one and that each bishop holds its power entire. He illustrates this indivisible unity through images such as the sun's rays, the streams of one fountain, and Christ's seamless tunic. The work closes by warning that martyrdom avails nothing outside the church and urging its audience to hold fast to peace and watchfulness.
la.cyprian.de_zelo_et_livore: This late antique Latin prose treatise by Cyprian examines the nature of zeal and envy, opening by describing envy as a deceptively light sin that allows the devil to enter the soul unnoticed. The author urges constant vigilance against these hidden spiritual attacks, and the argument then surveys the history of the vice, from the devil's fall to Cain's murder of Abel. It also covers Esau's hatred of Jacob and the selling of Joseph, continuing with Saul's persecution of David and the Jews' blindness to Christ. Within the church, envy breeds hatred, avarice, ambition, and discord, while also fostering schism and heresy. Citing the Psalms and apostolic letters, the work exhorts believers to humility, charity, and peace, ranking victories over such passions among the crowns won in daily spiritual struggle. The treatise closes with an address to the once envious, urging them to love those they had hated and to set their minds on paradise.
la.cyprian.quod_idola_dii_non_sint: Quod idola dii non sint ('That idols are not gods') is a short late-antique Latin apologetic treatise attributed to Cyprian. It argues that the deities worshiped by the nations are not gods at all. The work opens by observing that common deities were originally kings honored after death. It surveys mythological and Roman examples to expose the mortals behind these divinities. The text then ascribes oracles and religious deception to deceiving demons. It proclaims the one invisible God, whose temple is the whole world. The treatise closes with an account of Christ, his miracles, and his resurrection.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_iona: De Iona ('On Jonah') is a later imperial Latin work on the prophet Jonah, transmitted under the name of Cyprian. It opens by recalling God's punishments of Sodom and Gomorrah and his practice of warning sinners through prophets before sending Jonah to preach Nineveh's destruction. The narrative then follows Jonah's flight by ship from Joppa and the storm raised against the fugitive. He confesses to the sailors and is cast into the sea, where a great fish swallows him alive. Preserved within the creature's belly, Jonah is presented not as one destroyed but as a witness to death overcome and a future sign of the Lord.
la.cyprian_pseudo.orationes: This short Latin collection of prose prayers, spuriously attributed to Cyprian, dates from the later Roman imperial period. It comprises three orations followed by a brief preface, with the first opening with the trisagion. The first prayer invokes God as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, asking for integrity of heart. It seeks deliverance from the devil's snares, appealing to Sara, the three youths in the furnace, Daniel, and the apostles. The second and third orations commend the soul to God, petitioning the Father and the Son for mercy. They marshal scriptural precedents, including Jonah, the Ninevites, David, Tobias, and Sara, while rehearsing Christ's miracles at Cana, his healings, death, and resurrection as grounds for aid. A concluding preface on the twelve abuses of the world enumerates moral failures, listing the wise without works, the old without religion, the negligent bishop, and the people without law. Through these failures, justice is suffocated, and the wheel of the world turns toward the darkness of hell.
la.cyprian_saint.de_exhortatione_martyrii: A Latin prose treatise of the later Roman imperial period transmitted under the name of Cyprian, addressed to a correspondent named Fortunatus who had asked for scriptural exhortations with which to steel fellow Christians for the persecutions weighing upon them and the approaching time of antichrist. The work proceeds as a compendium of biblical testimonia arranged under numbered headings rather than as a continuous argument, opening with proofs that idols are not gods and that God alone is to be worshipped, together with the divine threats against idolaters. Its central and longest portions assemble passages on steadfastness under trial: the foretold hatred of the world, God's protection and aid in persecution, perseverance rewarded with the martyr's palm, and the contrast between the water baptism that remits sins and the baptism of blood that wins the crown. The closing sections retell the Maccabean martyrs, the seven brothers, their mother, and Eleazar, as models of confession and gather the biblical promises of the rewards awaiting the just, whether they actually suffer or hold fast in faith.
la.dracontius.orestes: Orestes is a Latin tragedy in dramatic metre by the late-antique poet Dracontius, which retells the fortunes of the house of Atreus from Agamemnon's homecoming to his son's formal acquittal. The poem opens with a prologue invoking Melpomene and announcing the lamentable triumphs of a hero who was pious in his very impiety. The narrative follows Agamemnon's return from Troy and his discovery that Iphigenia still lives as a priestess of Diana, before he is murdered by Aegisthus and Clytaemestra. Electra rescues the child Orestes, who is raised in Athens beside Pylades until their father's ghost rouses both men to revenge. After the slaying of Aegisthus and Clytaemestra, the poem traces Orestes' torment by his mother's ghost and his madness, leading to his recognition by Iphigenia among the Taurians. He later stands trial at Athens, where a court evenly divided between life and death yields to the verdict of the gods, and the acquitted hero returns in triumph to Mycenae.
la.ennodius.epigrammata: The Epigrammata is a late-antique Latin collection of short poems by Ennodius, opening with an epitaph on a young man of noble house. This piece mourns his sudden death and affirms that merit outlives the tomb, while the collection ranges widely across funerary and consolatory pieces. It includes poems praising bishops and clergy, such as Ambrose and Simplician, and inscriptions describe churches dedicated to Lawrence, Sixtus, and other saints. Riddling verses address animal mimes, pictures, gems, and works of art, while satirical invective targets gluttons, drunkards, a eunuch, and a man falsely styling himself Virgil. Epigrams on gifts, books, horses, and dining close the book, and the first-person epitaph of a woman named Melissa also ends the collection.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.de_laude_heremi: Eucherius of Lyon wrote this short Late Antique Latin prose treatise as a letter to his friend Hilarius. The work celebrates the desert as God's chosen dwelling and the nursery of the spiritual life. Eucherius commends Hilarius's withdrawal from family and wealth into solitude, surpassing even the bond with a brother. The body assembles scriptural exempla, including Moses, the Israelites, Elijah, Elisha, John the Baptist, and Christ. It then turns to the desert monks John and Macarius and closes with praise of the island community of Lérins. Throughout, the barren wilderness is figured as paradise, temple, and battlefield over the devil.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.unknown: The Passio Agaunensium martyrum, a late-antique Latin prose account by Eucherius of Lyon, opens by announcing its purpose of setting down in writing the passion of the martyrs who illumined Agaunum with their glorious blood. The narrative tells how the Theban legion, six thousand six hundred strong and summoned from the East to serve under Maximian, refused the order to persecute Christians, endured successive decimation, and, urged on by Maurice, Exuperius and Candidus, submitted to the sword in the narrow Alpine valley of Agaunum rather than deny their faith. It continues with the soldier Victor, killed on the spot after refusing a banquet held over the martyrs' spoils, the martyrdoms of Ursus and Victor at Solothurn, Maximian's own death by strangling after his plot against Constantine, the revelation of the bodies to bishop Theodore, and two miracles worked at the basilica raised in the martyrs' honour. The account closes in epistolary form, presenting the written passion to its addressee and tracing the tradition through Isaac of Geneva back to Theodore himself.
la.eugippius.epistula_ad_probam_virginem: This short Latin prose epistle by Eugippius is addressed to the virgin Proba. The compiler defends his undertaking, which was prompted by his abbot Marinus and other holy brethren. He assembled excerpts from the works of Augustine to avoid a charge of presumption. The letter praises Augustine's erudition and authority while admitting the compiler's limited skill. It notes that each chapter indicates the specific work from which it is drawn. The collection begins with Augustine's letter to Jerome on the soul and is framed by titles on charity and the divine law.
la.eugippius.exerpta_ex_operibus_augustini: Eugippius compiled this late-antique Latin anthology to present Augustine's thought through selected passages, opening with a letter to Jerome asking how individual souls arise. It also asks how infants come under the bond of sin that baptism dissolves, while excerpts range across treatises, letters, and sermons. These address the figurative interpretation of Gospel sayings and parables, and the text classifies kinds of lying and discusses the discipline owed to sinners. Further topics include the origin of souls and the nature of the resurrection body, closing with an extended praise of caritas. This virtue is set forth as the fulfillment of the law and the heart of the divine Scriptures.
la.eugippius.vita_sancti_severini: Eugippius composed this late antique prose saint's life, known as the Vita Sancti Severini, which opens with the death of Attila. The narrative introduces Severinus, a holy man from the eastern provinces, who settles at Asturis in Noricum Ripense. He warns the local people of an impending barbarian raid, and the body of the work follows him through fortified towns. It recounts his relief of famine, redemption of captives, and various prophecies, while also detailing his healings and exorcisms. He founded monasteries and dealt with the Rugian kings Flaccitheus and Feletheus, as well as the queen Giso and the young Odoacer. The work closes with his prophecy that the Roman population must migrate to Italy, and his uncorrupted body was translated to Italy.
la.evagrius_monachus.altercatio_legis_inter: The Altercatio legis inter Simonem Iudaeum et Theophilum Christianum is a late-antique Latin theological dialogue in prose. Its title means the dispute of the law between Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian. The work is ascribed to Evagrius Monachus, who reports a recent disputation to his correspondent Valerius. The bulk of the text consists of Theophilus's replies to Simon's successive challenges. He marshals testimonies from the Pentateuch, Psalms, and prophets to establish Christ's divinity and sonship. He also argues for his two advents, virginal birth, and the passion foretold despite the curse of Deuteronomy. The dialogue closes with Simon's anointing and prayer of thanksgiving to Christ.
la.evodius.de_fide_contra_manicheos: This late-antique Latin treatise, attributed to Evodius, serves as a polemic against the Manichaean religion, opening with a compact confession of one invisible God. It immediately addresses the Manichaean claim of a rival prince of darkness, maintaining that evil is a sin of the will rather than a nature. The argument cites Mani's Thesaurus and Epistula Fundamenti, along with the apocryphal Acts of Leucius, to show that souls sin by their own volition. The work defends the reality of Christ's passion against Manichaean teaching, affirming the virgin birth and the resurrection of the flesh. It upholds the harmony of the two testaments while ridiculing the myth of divine substance held captive in plants. Finally, the author urges Manichaean readers to return to the church.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_ratione_fidei: Faustus of Riez composed this late-antique treatise in a question and answer format. The title, De Ratione Fidei, translates as On the Rule of Faith. It addresses readers who claim the Son is inferior based on gospel texts. The author explains Christ's two natures to clarify his dual speech. A second section defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit. The work concludes by affirming one shared nature among the three persons.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_spiritu_sancto_libri_: Faustus of Riez composed this two book Latin treatise in the Late Antique period, defending the full divinity and distinct personhood of the Holy Spirit. It argues against the Macedonian claim that the Spirit is a creature, opening with chapter headings and an exposition of the creedal confession. The text distinguishes between believing that God exists and believing in him, asserting that faith is owed to the Spirit rather than to the church. The author assembles testimonia from prophets, evangelists, and apostles, showing that the Spirit is creator and not creature. The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and shares one substance with the Father and Son, while the treatise treats the Spirit's titles, work in baptism, and role in forgiveness. It also answers objections drawn from passages naming only the Father and Son, pressing the argument that only God can know the human heart. The text ends with an exhortation to make oneself a worthy temple.
la.faustus_of_riez.epistulae: The Epistulae of Faustus of Riez is a late-antique collection of Latin prose letters that treats doctrine and pastoral discipline. The opening letter urges a wavering brother to hold together divine grace and the obedience of the baptized servant. It ends with anathemas against Pelagian positions and subscriptions from a college of bishops. Later letters refute Arian arguments for the Son's subordination, arguing that only God is truly incorporeal, while souls and angels are corporeal substances. The text also takes up whether faith suffices without works, considering the fate of sinners after death and the discipline of fasting and abstinence. The collection closes with letters of spiritual direction and recommendation, which mingle counsel on humility, almsgiving, and the ransoming of captives, while an appended note addresses clerics who return to their wives.
la.favonius.disputatio_de_somnio_scipionis: Favonius Eulogius, a writer of the later Roman empire, composed this Latin prose treatise expounding the arithmetic, numerology, and music theory embedded in Cicero's Dream of Scipio. The work opens with a preface arguing that Cicero wrote the dream as rational philosophy rather than fable, promising to show that Scipio's death at fifty-six was fixed by number. The body proceeds from the monad through the octonarius, treating each number's role in the world's structure, and links the pentad to the five planets and the septenarius to the heavens and the soul. The author also discusses the perfect number twenty-eight, noting that two such numbers sum to fifty-six, while a closing section expounds the harmony of the spheres, defining sound, interval, and symphony. It details the four numerical ratios and the Pythagorean tuning of the eight celestial circles.
la.flavius_josephus.de_iudaeorum_vetustate_: A Latin translation of Josephus's two-book apologetic treatise against those who denied the antiquity of the Jewish people, addressed to Epaphroditus and presented as a sequel to the Jewish Antiquities. The work opens with an argument that the Jews are an ancient nation ignored by Greek historians, whose own records are late and mutually contradictory, and then marshals testimony from Egyptian, Phoenician, and Chaldean writers such as Manetho, Menander, and Berosus, along with Greek authors from Pythagoras's circle to Hecataeus, to establish Jewish antiquity. Book 1 proceeds to refute the Egyptian accounts of Manetho, Chaeremon, and Lysimachus that portray the Jewish ancestors as expelled lepers; Book 2 answers the grammaticus Apion on Moses, the sabbath, the status of Alexandrian Jews, and slanders about the Temple, and closes with a substantial defence of the Mosaic legislation, its divine monotheism, and the endurance with which the Jews have kept their laws.
la.fulcher_of_chartres.historia_hierosolymi: Fulcher of Chartres, a chaplain to Baldwin of Boulogne, wrote this Latin prose chronicle of the First Crusade, which covers the years 1095 to 1127 and details the early Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem. It opens with a prologue on the profit of recording the deeds of God's warriors, and the narrative then describes the Council of Clermont and Pope Urban II's preaching of the journey. Fulcher traces the march through Asia Minor, the sieges of Nicaea and Antioch, and the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, while also recording the consolidation of settlements in Edessa and Palestine. He details the campaigns of Baldwin I and II, and the taking of Tyre in 1124, and the chronicle includes digressions on the geography, marvels, animals, and customs of the eastern Mediterranean. It closes with events of the year 1127.
la.gellius.attic_nights: A Latin prose miscellany in twenty books by Gellius, composed in the later imperial period and titled from the author's claim to have gathered his notes during winter nights in the Attic countryside. The opening preface explains this origin and contrasts the work's plain name with the more ornate titles other compilers of miscellanies have chosen. Thereafter the books proceed in no fixed order, presenting short chapters on grammar and etymology, literary criticism of Greek and Roman authors, points of law, augury, and pontifical practice, philosophical disputes such as Chrysippus and Diodorus on ambiguity, and anecdotes about figures from Romulus to Gaius Gracchus. The final chapters return to the preface's themes, catalogue the varied titles such works have borne, and promise further volumes as leisure allows.
la.giraldus_floriacensis.carmina: This medieval Latin collection of poems is attributed to Giraldus Floriacensis. The opening piece recounts the Lombard devastation of Italy and Monte Cassino. It then follows Aigulf on the journey that brought the relics of Benedict and his sister Scholastica to Fleury on the Loire. The text details the miracles attending their remains and the founding of a convent there. The rest of the collection turns to shorter celebratory pieces. These include verses on Benedict's feast, virtues, and miracles, some composed in mirrored parallel lines. The volume also contains poems on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary and a Nativity poem in heroic verse addressed to a noble matron.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carmina: This collection of Carolingian Latin religious verse by Godescalcus Saxus is preserved in two books, opening with a long rhythmic prayer to Christ that begs pardon for a fallen sinner. The poems that follow are chiefly penitential in nature, including laments built on refrains and a complaint of exile likening the poet to Israel in Babylon. A paraphrase of the prodigal son and a plea for resurrection modelled on the raising of Lazarus also appear in the text. A verse epistle to the teacher Rathramnus accompanies questions on a saying of Augustine, while a cycle of hymns for the hours of the day closes the work. These hymns run from evening through cockcrow, matins, prime, terce, sext and none, ending with renewed praise of the Trinity and prayers for forgiveness.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_minora: This short Latin collection gathers excerpts attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, a Gallic bishop, whose anthology's date and compiler remain uncertain. It opens with a citation from Hilary's writing to the emperor Constantius, which affirms that the Son of God, made man, is truly God. The remaining passages address the exaltation of Christ's assumed human form and discuss the devil's war against humankind as taught in the book of Job. Divine mercy is said to turn that malice to our purgation, while another excerpt treats the petition for daily bread as Christ dwelling in the faithful. Further items come from the prologue of Hilary's exposition of the Gospel of Matthew, and the collection also includes his exposition of the epistle to Timothy on the two natures in Christ. A closing notice hails Hilary as a vehement defender of the Catholic Church, quoting his treatment of Christ sent in the likeness of sinful flesh.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.hymni: This short collection of Latin hymns is transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, a bishop of the late antique period. A prefatory note presents the prophet David as the first to announce Christ to the world in song. The opening hymn meditates on the Son's eternal generation from the unbegotten Father, considering the fullness of the godhead communicated in that begetting and the unity of the two divine persons. A second hymn, whose successive lines run through the alphabet, is spoken in the voice of Christ, recounting the incarnation, the scourging and crucifixion, the descent into the underworld, the defeat of death, and the resurrection. A third hymn on the glorious battles of Adam moves through Satan's despair before the nativity, covering the angelic message to the shepherds, John the Baptist's preaching, and Christ's baptism in the Jordan.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.oratio_synodi_sardice: This Latin prose oration from late antiquity, addressed to the emperor Constantius, is attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and presents itself as a petition from the council of Sardica. The text opens with praise for the emperor's benign nature and a plea for the Catholic church, while the bishops ask that judges avoid ecclesiastical causes and that exiled bishops be restored to their sees. They name the two Eusebii, Narcissus, Theodore, and Stephen as inventors of Arian corruption, and the work also defends the acquittal of Athanasius as duly settled by synodal judgment. The closing section recounts recent events at Milan involving Eusebius of Vercelli and Dionysius of Milan, who resisted demands to subscribe to a condemnation of Athanasius by appealing to the faith expounded at Nicaea.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_super_psalm: This Latin prose commentary on selected Psalms is attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, a fourth-century bishop of Gaul. A lengthy prologue opens the work, discussing the unity and authorship of the Psalter and the Septuagint translation. It also considers the significance of superscriptions and musical terminology, together with the numerical arrangement of the psalms into three fifties. The commentary then turns to verse-by-verse exegesis, proceeding through psalms that include the first two, several penitential psalms, and portions of Psalm 118. Each psalm is read throughout as prophecy of Christ's incarnation, passion, resurrection, and eternal kingdom. In support of this reading the work appeals to texts from both the Old and the New Testament.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.libri_tr: This Latin theological compilation by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, targets Valens and Ursacius, and it was assembled in three stages dated 356, the winter of 359/360, and 367. The text opens with a preface and a lost section on the council of Arles, then presents the letter of the Eastern bishops at Sardica with their creed. The remainder gathers the acts and correspondence of the Western Sardican council, including the address to Constantius and the letters of Valens and Ursacius. Documents from Bishop Liberius of Rome and Emperor Constantius are also included, followed by records of the councils of Milan, Ariminum, and Seleucia. From 367, the text adds the letter of the synod of Paris, and it also contains two letters on reconciling lapsed bishops. The creed and letters of Germinius of Sirmium conclude the collection, which arranges conciliar letters, creeds, and imperial letters in chronological sequence to set out the course of the mid-fourth-century doctrinal controversy.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.spuria: These short Latin pieces are transmitted among the spuria of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, whose date and authorship remain uncertain. The collection opens with a prose letter titled Accepi litteras tuas, in which a father on a long journey writes to his daughter. He describes seeking a garment and pearl of inestimable worth from a beautiful youth, who promised these gifts on condition that she renounce silk and dyed clothing. The youth also required her to give up gilded garments and other jewels, and the letter closes with a plea that she await these gifts. It includes an enclosure of morning and evening hymns, followed by a morning hymn titled Lucis largitor splendide, which hails Christ as the true light of the world. The alphabetical Versus de paenitentia concludes the set, where a penitent recounts his subjection to personified lust, pride, envy, and discord, while also listing vainglory and gluttony among his sins. The speaker calls on the whole creation to weep with him, professes right faith while rejecting the teachings of Arius, Sabellius, and Simon, and finally implores the redeeming Trinity for mercy.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.vita_mariae_aegypt: The Vita Mariae Aegyptiacae is a medieval Latin verse life of the penitent Mary of Egypt, composed by Hildebert of Lavardin around the figure of the monk Zosimas. The poem opens with Zosimas as a boy spurning wealth for monastic life, and he outstrips his teachers in virtue until a warning against pride sends him to the desert. There he encounters a naked fugitive who proves to be Mary, and the center of the poem is her long confession of a corrupt youth in Alexandria. She describes passing to Jerusalem bought with her body and exclusion from the church, and her repentance before an icon of the Virgin leads to decades of desert penance. Zosimas returns at her bidding with the Eucharist a year later, and he finds her dead and incorrupt after she has crossed the Jordan unaided. A lion helps him dig her grave, and he carries her story back to his monastery.
la.italicus.ilias_latina: This early Imperial Latin epic in hexameters is attributed to Italicus, who condenses the entire Iliad into a compact verse narrative. The poem opens with an invocation to a goddess to unfold the wrath of Peleus' proud son, echoing Homer's proem. The text runs through the plague sent by Apollo and the quarrel of Agamemnon and Achilles, covering the duel of Menelaus and Paris. It includes the catalogue of the Greek fleet and the exploits of Diomede and Hector, continuing with the night exploit against Rhesus. The narrative features Patroclus' death in Achilles' borrowed arms, concluding with Achilles' vengeance, the slaying and dragging of Hector, and Priam's ransom. The poem closes with a valediction addressing Calliope and Phoebus, declaring that his ship has reached the port and goal of mighty Homer.
la.john_cassian.conlationes: John Cassian's Conlationes ('Conferences') is a Late Antique Latin work of monastic theology. It is cast in prose as a series of recorded conferences with the Egyptian desert fathers. The text opens with a preface dedicating the teaching of the anachorets of Scetis to Pope Leontius and the monk Helladius. The body comprises twenty-four conversations in which Cassian and his companion Germanus put questions to successive elders. Abba Moses, Chaeremon, Theonas and Abraham are among those consulted on the goal of the monastic profession. They also discuss purity of heart, discretion, grace, free will, mortification, chastity and charity. The final conference gathers up and concludes the traditions and statutes of all the elders.
la.john_cassian.de_incarnatione_domini_cont: De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium ('On the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius') is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date by John Cassian. It was composed at the entreaty of Leo, a deacon of the Roman church whose praise and importunity fill the preface. The work is a polemic against the recently arisen Nestorian heresy, which the author introduces under an extended image of heresy as a hydra whose severed heads regrow. An opening survey catalogues earlier Christological errors, among them those of the Ebionites, Sabellians, Arians and Apollinarians. The treatise then turns to the contemporary error, of uncertain name but sprung from the old Ebionite stock, that the title identifies with Nestorius.
la.john_cassian.institutiones: John Cassian wrote this Late Antique Latin treatise for Bishop Castor, who asked him to record monastic customs for a new foundation in Gaul. The opening preface compares the task to building God's true temple, which is made of sanctified souls rather than lifeless stones. The work then details the outward institutions of coenobitic observance, covering the monk's dress and the canonical hours of psalmody. It also describes the testing and obedience required of new entrants, while later books examine the eight principal vices and their remedies. These include gluttony, lust, avarice, and anger, and the text also addresses dejection, acedia, vainglory, and pride. Each vice is explored through the deeds of desert elders, and scriptural exposition sustains the discussion of these spiritual dangers.
la.lactantius.de_ira_dei: Lactantius wrote this Latin prose treatise for a reader named Donatus. It challenges the philosophical view that a beneficent deity cannot be angry. The author surveys the positions of the Epicureans, Stoics, and atomists. He then argues for a single divine creator and the unity of God. The work explains that good and evil were set before humanity to allow wisdom to exist. It distinguishes just anger from furious passion and defends divine patience. An epilogue in Ciceronian style closes the text with pagan testimonies.
la.lactantius.de_mortibus_persecutorum: Lactantius's De Mortibus Persecutorum is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise belonging to the Christian apologetic tradition. Framed as an address to Donatus, it opens with thanksgiving for the end of a recent persecution. The text surveys emperors who assailed Christians, listing Nero, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, and Diocletian. It continues with Maximian Herculius, Galerius, Maxentius, and Maximinus Daia, recounting their crimes and agonizing deaths. Woven into this scheme is a political narrative covering Diocletian's abdication and Constantine's rise. The account includes the victory at the Mulvian Bridge, Licinius's defeat of Maximinus, and the edict granting freedom of worship. The treatise closes by cataloguing the extinction of the persecutors' houses, ending in praise of God's triumph and a prayer for the church's lasting peace.
la.lactantius.de_opificio_dei: De Opificio Dei is a Latin prose treatise by the late-antique author Lactantius, framed as a letter of moral admonition to a young correspondent named Demetrianus. The work demonstrates divine providence through a detailed account of the human body, which Lactantius presents as a fuller treatment of a theme he finds only summarily handled in Cicero. He argues that man's nakedness and weakness are marks of rational dignity rather than defects, while the text surveys the body part by part, from the frame and senses to the internal viscera. It also covers the process of generation, punctuated by polemic against Epicurean atomism and the doctrines of Lucretius. The closing portion turns to the mind and soul, treating their seat and nature, and examines the mechanism of sleep and dreams, the soul's divine origin and immortality, and the gift of wisdom. The treatise ends with a promise of further writings in defense of truth.
la.lactantius.divinarum_institutionum: The Divinae institutiones is a seven book Latin apologetic treatise by the Late Antique author Lactantius, which opens by contrasting ancient philosophers who sought truth without finding it with divine revelation. The work announces a plan to join true wisdom to true religion across its volumes, and the first three books refute pagan religion, arguing that the gods were mortals deified after death. They claim these cults stem from demons, poets' fictions, and human credulity, while the text then turns against philosophy itself as a human wisdom that can expose error but never attain truth. Book four expounds the Christian faith, treating the unity of God and the two births of Christ, and it also covers his miracles, passion, resurrection, and ascension. The remaining books set out justice and its precepts, along with the worship owed to God in place of sacrifice, and they provide an account of the last things, including the second coming and the final judgement. The text describes the thousand year reign, the resurrection of the dead, and the renewal of the world, closing with an exhortation to embrace wisdom and religion together.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_conven: De non conveniendo cum haereticis is a late antique Latin prose treatise of anti-Arian polemic attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, and framed as a direct address to the emperor Constantius. The author opens by replying to the charge that he and his fellow bishops are enemies of peace, defending their withdrawal from the Arians by citing the example of Moses pitching the tabernacle outside the camp. The body of the work assembles a long chain of biblical exempla to prove that Christians must refuse communion with heretics, including Moses, Jericho, the man of God of Bethel, and the apostolic epistles. Lucifer brands the heretics as spiritual adulterers, serpents, and servants of the devil, while denouncing Constantius as a persecutor and naming his court bishops. The author recalls his own exile and imprisonment, and ranks Arianism among the sects excised from the church.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_parcen: This late antique Latin prose treatise, written by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, defends his rebuke of the emperor Constantius for introducing Arian idolatry into the church. Lucifer opens by answering the emperor's complaint that God's servants treated him with contumely, insisting that he has spoken only the truth. The work assembles a long chain of scriptural exempla, including Moses, Phinehas, Samuel, Saul, Achan, Uzziah, Josiah, and the Maccabean martyrs. The apostles before the council and Daniel's fourth beast also appear, showing that rebuking persecutors has always been a duty. This duty belongs to prophets, priests, and apostles, while Constantius is likened to Judas, the tyrant Antiochus, and the forerunners of Antichrist. The text repeatedly exhorts readers to abandon the Arian heresy and urges a return to the faith described at Nicaea.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.epistulae: This late-antique Latin collection of prose epistles is attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, and is bound up with the Arian controversy. It opens with a letter from Lucifer to Bishop Eusebius urging him to hasten the overthrow of Arian doctrine, which he compares to the downfall of Simon Magus. The remaining letters include greetings from Liberius of Rome and Athanasius, who commend Lucifer's confession amid exile and persecution. Other exchanges involve the official Florentius concerning a codex offered to the emperor, and an embassy is also described. In this embassy, Lucifer and his companions plead with Constantius Augustus for a council on the faith. The collection closes with an exhortation warning the faithful and monks against communion with those of Arian sympathies.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.moriendum_ess: This Late Antique Latin prose treatise was written by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, and takes the form of an invective addressed to the emperor Constantius.
