The work opens by rebuking Constantius for altering the divine scriptures, accusing him of falling into the Arian heresy and persecuting Christians. The bulk of the text argues that believers must die for the Son of God, exhorting them to endure torments, exile, and execution rather than deny his divinity. The author catalogues the emperor's cruelties against martyrs in Alexandria, defending the Son's equality and coeternity with the Father against Arian teaching. Extensive quotations from the Psalms, the Gospels, and the apostle Paul support this case, while the treatise closes by contrasting the eternal glory promised to those who confess Christ with the unending punishment awaiting the unrepentant emperor and his adherents.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.ennodius_ambrosio_: Magnus Felix Ennodius composed this late-antique Latin prose work as a didactic exhortation at the repeated request of a youth named Ambrosius. The author opens by explaining that he deliberated whether to use verse or a letter format before personified virtues and liberal arts address the pupil in turn. These figures include Verecundia, Pudicitia, Fides, Grammatica, and Rhetorica, with verse passages interspersed among the prose sections. The text closes by naming contemporary aristocrats and Christian matrons as living models, specifically citing Symmachus, Boethius, Barbara, and Stephania for their eloquence and conduct. A short verse appeal ends the work.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.libellus_adversus_: Magnus Felix Ennodius wrote this Latin treatise to defend Pope Symmachus, and the work also supports the synod convened to hear charges against the pope. Its prologue justifies the author's decision to speak after a period of silence, and he dedicates his oratory to the priesthood, which detractors had attacked. The body of the text refutes specific arguments from an adversarial document, addressing claims that not all bishops were summoned to the council. The author also counters the idea that the pope should have called the synod himself, and he rejects the notion that Christ and Peter submitted to judgment. The text further argues that the assembly acted before any crime was established, and each point is answered with scriptural citations and sustained invective. The author defends the pope's retreat from his accusers, and he also justifies the general conduct of the gathering. The work closes with imagined addresses from the Apostle Peter, who rebukes the schismatics in this final section. The personified city of Rome also speaks in the conclusion, lamenting the discord and summoning the parties back to concord.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.panegyricus_theodo: This Latin prose panegyric by Magnus Felix Ennodius addresses Theodoric, the ruler of Italy, and reflects on the duties of praise. The speaker recounts Theodoric's victories over the Bulgar leader and the Gepids, detailing the defeat of Odoacer at Verona and on the Athesis. It further describes the campaigns of generals Pitzia and Herduic at Sirmium, presenting these conquests as the restoration of Roman order. The speech closes with praise for Theodoric's rebuilding of Rome and his patronage of learning, highlighting his clemency and personal magnificence. The work ends with a prayer that an heir be born to the king.
la.maximianus.elegiae: Maximianus composed this cycle of late antique Latin elegies in elegiac couplets, where the opening poem gives voice to an old man's plea for death as release from bodily decay. He recalls the fame he once won as orator and poet, along with his youthful athletic and military prowess, while the remaining elegies follow the same first-person speaker through the amours of old age. These include an aged former mistress and a courtship of a young woman conducted on sufferance, and a final liaison sees his young beloved console him before departing as if from his funeral. The close finds the poet reckoning himself in part already dead, hurrying along the road that boys, old men, rich and poor alike must take towards a common death.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carminum_appendix: This Carolingian Latin collection of occasional verse is preserved as the Carminum Appendix of Milo of Saint-Amand, opening with couplets honouring the scribe Lotharius, who copied the book. Verses on the shrine enclosing the relics of Saint Amandus follow, and the collection then gathers epitaphs for abbots, sacristans, teachers, and other figures buried at the monastery. A hymn and further versified lauds celebrate Amandus as shepherd, healer, and intercessor, while a courteous verse address to a patron named Haimin also appears. The work closes with a long sequence of short, often numerical and figured verses, which are repeatedly addressed to a Charles. These verses play on motifs of gold, theft, concord, and discord among brothers.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.appendix_: This late-antique Latin collection contains ten documents concerning the Donatist schism in Roman Africa, transmitted as an appendix to the seven books of Optatus, bishop of Mileve. The text opens with a numbered index of its ten items, then presents proceedings before the consular governor Zenophilus, where witnesses from Cirta testify about the bishop Silvanus. They address the charge of surrendering scriptures during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, while subsequent acts show how Felix, bishop of the Autumnitani, was purged of the same accusation. A series of letters follows, in which Constantine labours to settle the dispute between Caecilian of Carthage and his opponents, arranging a hearing at the council of Arles. He receives that council's synodal letter to Pope Silvester, rejects the appeal of the Donatist bishops, and instructs officials such as the vicar Celsus and the prefect Petronius. The collection closes with an appeal for patience addressed to the African episcopate and people, ending with a letter restoring to the Catholics the basilica at Constantina that their rivals had seized.
la.ovid.amores: The Amores is a three book collection of love elegies written in elegiac couplets during the Augustan period. The opening poem explains that five booklets were reduced to three and recounts how Cupid stole a foot from the poet's attempted epic. This theft conscripted the author into the service of love verse, and the books then follow the first person lover's affair with Corinna through various dramatic episodes. These include dinner parties under her husband's eye, midnight pleas at locked doors, and the machinations of the bawd Dipsas. Further scenes cover disputes over gifts, a circus meeting, a prophetic dream, and a flooded river. The narrative also features an episode of impotence, the death of Corinna's parrot, and her perilous abortion. The collection concludes with the funeral of Tibullus and a farewell to elegy in favor of loftier work. Throughout, love is cast as military service and poetry as the poet's immortality.
la.paulus_orosius.historiae_adversum_pagano: Paulus Orosius wrote this seven book Latin history in the late antique period, titled Historiae Adversum Paganos, which means Histories Against the Pagans. Orosius opens with a preface answering Augustine's charge to compile past misfortunes, aiming to rebut the claim that the Christian era suffers more than earlier times. The work gathers accounts of wars, famines, plagues, and other calamities from creation onward, beginning with the geography of the three continents. It proceeds through the Assyrian, Persian, Greek, and Carthaginian powers, then covers Roman history in detail from the founding of the city. This section addresses the kings, republican wars, civil wars, and emperors, concluding with the Christian emperors and the Gothic sack of Rome. Orosius argues that earlier ages endured miseries no lighter than the present.
la.petronius.fragmenta: Petronius, an early Imperial satirist, left behind scattered Latin verse fragments transmitted without book division and in a mixture of meters. The opening poem claims that genuine poetry springs from inner torment rather than levity. The remaining works chiefly use elegiac couplets alongside hendecasyllabic and choliambic meters. They explore the origin of religion in fear, the flight of rumor, and Midas's hidden ears. Other themes include the deceptions of the senses, the turns of fortune, and a series of amorous poems. These love pieces feature an epigram on golden apples sent by Marcia and verses on Julia's snow-cooled touch. The collection closes with a poem on the anchoring of Delos and a letter begging for an embrace.
la.plautus.aulularia: The Aulularia, a Latin comedy by Plautus from the Republican period, is written in dramatic metres and centers on a buried treasure. The household guardian spirit opens the play to explain the plot, revealing that an ancestor hid the gold for Euclio's daughter. He allows Euclio to find it so he can dower her, who has been secretly seduced by a man of high rank. Euclio obsessively guards the hoard while a wealthy neighbor, the uncle of the girl's seducer, proposes marriage. Wedding preparations fill the miser with alarm, and the pot is stolen from the house. Euclio confronts the slave who took it, and the theft comes fully to light in sharp exchanges.
la.plautus.captivi: Captivi ('The Captives') is a comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, the Latin playwright of the Roman Republican period. Its prologue lays out the plot involving Hegio of Aetolia, whose younger son was kidnapped and sold into slavery in Elis. Hegio's elder son has been taken prisoner in the war between the Aetolians and the Eleians. He buys captives in the hope of arranging an exchange. The Eleian prisoner Philocrates and his slave Tyndarus swap names and clothing to serve each other's hidden designs. The prologue also notes that the play departs from comic convention by omitting stock figures and keeping its battles offstage.
la.plautus.casina: Casina is a Latin comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic, whose prologue addresses spectators directly and extols old plays over new. It identifies the Greek original as Diphilus's Kleroumenoi, or Sortientes in Latin, while the plot centers on an old husband and his son, both enamoured of Casina. She is a foundling raised as a slave in their house, and the father arranges her marriage to his bailiff, Olympio, to secure access. His wife, Cleostrata, backs the absent son's claim through the armour-bearer Chalinus, after lots are drawn in Olympio's favour. The women substitute Chalinus dressed as the bride, and the bailiff and then the old man are each humiliated at the rustic wedding. The play closes with a spoken summary of the resolution, revealing Casina as the freeborn daughter of a neighbouring household promised to Euthynicus, the son.
la.plautus.mercator: Mercator ('The Merchant') is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic era, a stage work in dramatic verse built around a trading voyage. It opens with the young Charinus, sent by his father Demipho to trade at Rhodes, recounting how he fell in love with a beautiful slave woman and bought her. He brings her home hoping to keep her hidden from his father, but Demipho, seeing the girl, conceals his own desire and maneuvers her sale to his friend Lysimachus. Lysimachus's wife returns unexpectedly from the country, finds the young woman installed in her house, and protests both her husband and the laws that let offending husbands go unpunished. Charinus, believing his beloved lost to an unknown buyer, despairs and contemplates exile until the girl is restored to him and the wives appeased. The comedy closes with a jesting proposal that old men who keep mistresses be judged by the same standard as their wives.
la.plautus.persa: The Persa ('The Persian') is a comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic. The story opens with the lover Toxilus declaring the labours of love worse than those of Hercules. He then undertakes to raise six hundred nummi to free his beloved Lemniselenis from the pimp Dordalus. With the slave Sagaristio and the parasite Saturio, he passes off Saturio's daughter as a captive Persian girl. They use a forged letter and a Persian disguise to extract the price from the credulous pimp. A second imposture as the girl's twin brother robs Dordalus again. The play ends with the ruined pimp beaten and mocked, while Toxilus holds a banquet to celebrate Lemniselenis' liberty.
la.plautus.poenulus: Poenulus ('The Little Carthaginian') is a comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic that opens with a mock edict delivered by a stage herald. This 'commander of actors' bids the audience keep silence and comically regulates who may watch, from hungry and well-fed spectators to slaves and nurses. The action centers on the young Agorastocles' love for a girl kept by the pimp Lycus at Calydon and on the schemes of his slave Milphio. These schemes are overtaken by the arrival of Hanno, a Carthaginian merchant who speaks partly in Punic as he searches for two daughters kidnapped from Carthage years before. Hanno proves to be the girl's father and a kinsman of the young man, while the pimp, trapped into accepting stolen gold, is forced to surrender her. After submitting to threats of prosecution and imprisonment, the pimp is punished and then pardoned, the rival soldier is mollified, and Hanno prepares for his journey home to Carthage.
la.plautus.pseudolus: Pseudolus ('Little Liar') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by the playwright Plautus, named for the cunning slave who drives its plot. It opens with the lovesick young Athenian Calidorus showing Pseudolus a letter from the courtesan Phoenicium, whom the pimp Ballio has sold to a Macedonian soldier. Ballio will surrender her next day unless twenty minae are paid, and Pseudolus promises to outwit him and wring the money from Calidorus' father Simo, staking it on a wager. With a forged letter, a stolen seal, the help of a garrulous cook and the crafty slave Simia, he deceives soldier, pimp, and old men alike. The girl is delivered to her lover, and a drunken scene follows in which the defeated Simo sues for mercy. The play closes with Pseudolus declining to summon applause until the morrow.
la.plautus.rudens: The Rudens, a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, is set on the coast of Cyrene, where the star Arcturus explains that Jupiter has stirred a storm. This tempest wrecks the ship of the leno Labrax as he carries off the Athenian girl Palaestra, whose companion Ampelisca is also aboard. The young Plesidippus had contracted to buy Ampelisca, and the girls are sheltered by the priestess of Venus near the villa of Daemones. The slave Trachalio defends them at the goddess's altar against the leno's violence, while Daemones' slave Gripus dredges up a chest containing gold and childhood tokens. These items lead to the recognition of Palaestra as Daemones' long-lost daughter, and the play closes with Labrax compelled to pay the talent he has sworn. He must also free Gripus, and the girls are restored to freedom, with betrothals arranged between Palaestra and Plesidippus, and between Ampelisca and Trachalio.
la.plautus.trinummus: The Trinummus is a Roman comedy adapted by Plautus from the Greek original Thensaurus by Philemon. The prologue identifies the source and opens with allegorical figures and a sketch of the plot. The elderly Charmides has sailed away, leaving his family and a hidden treasure that his dissolute son Lesbonicus has already sold. The story follows the debates of Callicles and Megaronides on friendship, and it also tracks the negotiations between Philto and his reformed son Lysiteles. Lysiteles seeks Lesbonicus's sister without a dowry, but Lesbonicus refuses, so an impostor is hired to pose as a messenger bringing gold. This ruse aims to keep the lost treasure a secret, but the scheme collapses when the real Charmides returns and confronts the deceiver, ending with a double betrothal and the father's reconciliation.
la.pliny_the_elder.naturalis_historia: Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia ('Natural History') is a Latin prose encyclopaedia from the Early Imperial period. It opens with a dedicatory epistle to the emperor that outlines the author's method and sources. The work then proceeds systematically through the natural world in thirty-seven books. These cover cosmology, the geography of Europe, Asia and Africa, and the animal kingdom. Later sections address medicine, metals, stones, pigments, and the visual arts. Each book includes an index and lists of the Greek and Roman authorities excerpted.
la.pontius_diaconus.vita_caecilii_cypriani: This later-imperial Latin prose life of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was composed by a deacon, Pontius, who presents himself in the narrative as an exile accompanying his subject. An opening prologue defends the recording of the deeds of a man already celebrated for his writings. The narrative follows his conversion under the presbyter Caecilian, his rapid elevation to the episcopate despite his reluctance, and his almsgiving and leadership of the church during a devastating plague. His banishment to Curubis is attended by visions foretelling his death, and the work goes on to recount his trial and execution before the proconsul at Carthage. Cyprian is identified in a concluding passage as the first African bishop to win the martyr's crown. The life ends with the author's mingled exultation in his master's victory and grief at having survived him.
la.priscian.carmen_in_laudem_Anastasii_impe: This Late Antique Latin panegyric by Priscian praises the emperor Anastasius, opening by asking the ruler to accept a song of thanksgiving for restored peace and justice. The main body catalogues the emperor's virtues, including justice, wisdom, clemency, and piety, which are compared with those of Nerva, Titus, Trajan, Antoninus, and Marcus. A long account follows of the suppression of Isaurian rebels near the Lycian coast, where heaven is said to have defeated them with storms, floods, and lightning. Later sections praise his mercy toward the vanquished and his rebuilding of cities, harbours, and farmland, while also noting his reform of taxation and the grain supply. The poem highlights his protection of plaintiffs and soldiers, as well as the rout of raiders near the Euphrates, before closing with commendation of the Augusta and of Hypatius. It ends with a promise to speak only truth, rejecting mythological flattery.
la.priscillian.tractatus_undecim: The Tractatus Undecim ('The Eleven Treatises') is a collection of Late Antique Latin prose works attributed to Priscillian. The first tractate takes the form of a confession of faith addressed to the most blessed priests. In it, the author professes the creed and answers accusations raised against him and his followers. He also pronounces anathemas against a long catalogue of named heresies. The remaining tractates continue this defensive and instructional course through various theological discussions. The series closes with a doxology addressed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
la.priscillian_bishop_of_avila.canones_in_p: Priscillian, bishop of Avila, composed this Latin theological work in the late antique period. He wrote it to answer a request for a compact scriptural defence against heretics. The author divided the fourteen Pauline epistles into numbered testimonia. From these, he distilled ninety short doctrinal canons, each annotated with references. The body of the work consists of these canons, each beginning with the word Quia. Their subjects range from the veracity of God to the resurrection of the body.
la.proba_active_4th_century.cento: The Cento is a Late Antique Latin biblical epic by the fourth-century poet Proba, which recasts verses of Vergil to retell the narrative of scripture. The opening dedication urges the emperor to acknowledge Maro transformed into the better, commending the poem to Arcadius and renouncing the pagan Muses. The poet announces her design to sing Christ's gifts in Vergil's words, and the narrative proceeds from creation and the fall through the flood and the patriarchs. It covers the deliverance from Egypt and the prophets' foretelling of Christ, while the later movement recounts the annunciation, baptism, and temptation in the wilderness. The poem details the teaching, miracles, passion, and resurrection, closing with the risen Christ's appearance and the charge to continue his work.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_novatianum: This Latin prose treatise of uncertain date and authorship is preserved among the works of Cyprian, arguing against the rigorist Novatian over the reception of Christians who lapsed during the Decian persecution. The text opens with the speaker's anguished deliberation over wounded brethren, while Novatian appears as a new adversary who denies the fallen the Father's mercy and the grace of penance. The argument then ranges widely through scripture, reading Noah's ark, the raven, and the twice-released dove as figures of the church and of two persecutions. In the first of these, the lapsed fell, while in the second they stood victorious, and Novatian is assailed as a new Cain who usurps a judgment that Christ reserves to himself. Prophetic, gospel, and apocalyptic passages on divine clemency, repentance, and the day of judgment are amassed in support, urging confession and full satisfaction while the way of forgiveness stands open.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_vigilium_de_iudaica_in: This Latin epistolary treatise, of uncertain date and transmitted among the works attributed to Cyprian, is addressed to one Vigilius and concerned with the unbelief of the Jewish people. It opens with a lament over the inherited obstinacy of Israel, who persist in refusing to turn to God even though Christ has proclaimed himself the light of the world. The body assembles scriptural proofs of Christ's manifestation, drawing on the psalmists and prophets, the evangelists' narratives of the magi and Simeon, and Malachi's promised sun of righteousness. The faith of Abraham is upheld as the model by which believers become his sons, while unbelieving Israel has forfeited that name. The author also gives an account of his Latin rendering of the disputation between Jason the Christian and Papiscus the Jew. It closes with personal words to Vigilius, presented as a bishop unexpectedly chosen by God and destined for martyrdom, and with a request for his prayers on the author's behalf.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_disciplina_et_bono_pud: De disciplina et bono pudicitiae is a Latin prose treatise of uncertain date transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage. The text takes the form of a bishop's written address to his congregation, opening with an apology for time spent on daily gospel exposition. The author resolves to exhort the faithful by letter, praising chastity as the honor of bodies and ornament of morals. This virtue is ranked first among virgins, then the continent, and finally the married, with precepts grounded in apostolic teaching on marriage and divorce. The text denounces adultery and unnatural lust, celebrating Joseph and Susanna as examples of victorious chastity while criticizing elaborate female adornment. The treatise closes with counsel on governing the body through the soul, ending with a farewell to the brothers.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_laude_martyrii: De Laude Martyrii, a Latin prose sermon on the glory of martyrdom, is attributed to Cyprian and transmitted among the Pseudo-Cyprianic works. Dating from the later imperial period, the text opens by pleading the inadequacy of the speaker's powers before such a grand subject. The argument proceeds through three heads, defining what martyrdom is, how great it is, and to whom it brings profit. It expounds martyrdom as the end of sin and the foundation of salvation, using scriptural exempla like Daniel and Abraham. The text ranks the martyrs' crown above virginity, denounces love for the world, and offers a vision of hell for deniers. A seasonless paradise awaits the faithful, who are called to imitate Christ's passion, closing with a glimpse of the shining host of martyrs.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_rebaptismate: The De Rebaptismate, a short Latin theological treatise of uncertain authorship, is transmitted in the corpus of Cyprian of Carthage and generally counted among the pseudo-Cyprianic works. Dating from the later imperial period, the text opens with a question circulating among the brethren about those baptized in heresy yet in the name of Christ. The author argues that rebaptism is unnecessary for such penitents returning to the church, assembling scriptural testimony from John the Baptist, Acts, and the Gospels to support this view. A baptism invoking the name of Jesus is perfected rather than annulled when the Spirit is supplied, and the author treats baptism by water, by blood in martyrdom, and by the Spirit as one baptism. The work closes by defending the church's venerable custom against innovators, while also denouncing the fraudulent fire-tricks of heretical baptizers and the apocryphal Praedicatio Pauli.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_spectaculis_liber: De Spectaculis Liber, a Latin prose treatise from the later imperial period, is transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage, though likely by a different author. Opening as an address to fellow believers, it welcomes the chance to write while lamenting that flattering patrons twist scripture to justify the pleasures of the shows. The body argues that idolatry lies behind every kind of pagan spectacle, condemning circus races, theatrical plays, and the gladiatorial arena for their cruelty and vanity. The author claims that scripture's silence on these entertainments forbids rather than permits them, contrasting pagan shows with the beauty of the created world. It highlights the wonders wrought by God, above all the devil defeated beneath Christ's feet, and ends with a doxology and a farewell to the brethren.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_xii_abusionibus_saecul: De duodecim abusivis saeculi ('The Twelve Abuses of the World') is a late-antique Latin theological treatise ascribed to Cyprian, though its date and authorship remain uncertain. Its subject is the twelve abuses that corrupt the world, and it opens by cataloguing them in summary fashion. Among those named are the wise man without good works, the unjust king, the negligent bishop, and the people without law. Each abuse is then taken up in turn and expounded with moral argument and copious quotation from scripture. The chapters on kingship and episcopal office set out at length the duties of rulers and bishops, while those on the laity treat humility, discipline and observance of God's law. The treatise closes by warning that a people without law is a people without Christ, since Christ is the end of the law.
la.pseudo_cyprian.epistulae: These Latin letters, attributed to Cyprian of Carthage though their authorship remains uncertain, are composed in the theological idiom of the later imperial church. The collection opens with an exhortation to hold fast to a single, unified reading of divine scripture, while the remaining pieces address the controversies of a divided Christian community. One letter rebukes a bishop for writings against the catholic faith concerning baptism and demands their retraction, and another transmits conciliar rulings that bar traditores from clerical and liturgical standing. A long consolatory epistle urges a father grieving his daughter's death to accept it as a passage to God rather than a loss. Throughout, the letters combine pastoral exhortation with scriptural argument on faith, martyrdom, resurrection, and ecclesiastical discipline.
la.pseudo_cyprian.liber_de_aleatoribus: The Liber de Aleatoribus is a Latin theological treatise against dice-playing, transmitted under Cyprian's name and attributed to a pseudo-Cyprianic author of the later imperial period. It opens with a bishop's account of his pastoral office and his alarm at the audacity of gamblers among the faithful. The work then expounds the bishop's duty as shepherd and steward of the gospel to correct sinners rather than pardon them laxly, before passing into a long denunciation of the gaming table as the devil's snare, ruinous of wealth and reputation and fertile in perjury, quarrels, blasphemy, and secret vice, together with a legend of the game's inventor, who demanded sacrifice to himself from all who played. It closes by declaring gamblers estranged from Christ and unworthy of his sacraments, and urges them to abandon the dice, distribute their goods to the poor and the church, and lay up treasure in heaven.
la.pseudo_eucherius.de_situ_hierusolimitana: De situ Hierusolimitanae urbis atque ipsius Iudaeae is a short late antique Latin prose treatise handed down under the name of Eucherius and addressed to Faustus, a presbyter of the island. The brief preface promises a treatment as compact as the work itself, which surveys the hilltop site, walls, and gates of Jerusalem. It describes Mount Sion with its clerics and monks, along with the Constantinian sanctuaries of the Martyrium, Golgotha, and the Anastasis. The text then moves outward to the ruined Temple, the pool of Bethsaida, Siloa, and the valley of Jehoshaphat. It covers the Mount of Olives and neighbouring places from Bethlehem, Jericho, and the Jordan to the Dead Sea, Hebron, and Joppa. Distances are reckoned in miles, and a closing section sets out the length and breadth of Judaea from Dan to Beersheba. It incorporates long excerpts from Jerome's letter to Dardanus and from Josephus on the bounds, cities, and fertility of Galilee, Samaria, and Judaea. The Jewish historian is cited as a witness to the truth of the account.
la.pseudo_severus_sulpicius.epistolae_septe: Seven prose letters of Christian exhortation are handed down under the name of Sulpicius Severus, whose attribution remains doubtful. The first letter addresses a devout woman, thanking her for her progress in faith and urging perseverance against the devil and the world. The remaining letters turn to moral and ascetic instruction, including a long admonition to a consecrated virgin arguing that virginity profits nothing without observance of all commandments. This text enjoins purity of soul and body, modesty in speech, dress, and conduct, and contempt for worldly nobility and glory. Further letters praise the conversion of a stage performer and playfully send a monastery a rustic cook, who is ignorant of pepper but skilled in beans and porridge. Other texts commend a youth guilty of boyish error and argue over tenant farmers, closing with a reflection on how letters sustain affection between absent friends.
la.pseudo_tertullian.adversus_omnes_haerese: This short Latin treatise, transmitted under Tertullian's name, surveys various sects during the later Roman imperial period. Its author declares that only a selection of heresies will be sketched in this work. The text passes swiftly over Jewish groups such as the followers of Dositheus and the Sadducees. It then turns to those who erred from the gospel, proceeding heresiarch by heresiarch. The body of the work outlines doctrines concerning the origin of the world and the nature of Christ. Denial of Christ's real flesh and rejection of the resurrection of the body recur throughout as marks of error.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.passio_septem_mon: This short Latin martyr narrative, doubtfully attributed to Victor of Vita, recounts the sufferings of seven monks during the persecution of African Catholics under the Vandal king Huneric. The work opens with a prologue begging divine aid for the task of narrating the martyrs' triumphs. It then describes Huneric's edicts of exile, the closing of churches, and the confiscation of monasteries. The seven brothers, Bonifatius, Servus, Rusticus, Liberatus, Rogatus, Septimus, and Maximus, are arrested and brought to Carthage. They refuse promises of wealth and the rebaptism urged by an Arian bishop. Condemned to be burned on a ship at sea, they are slain with oar-stocks when the fire repeatedly fails. Their bodies are miraculously returned to the shore and buried with hymns beside the basilica of Celerina. The account ends with a doxology to the Trinity, under whose confession the martyrs completed their course.
la.q_cicero.on_running_for_consul: This Latin epistolary treatise from the Roman Republic is attributed to Quintus Cicero, who writes a letter of advice to a candidate for the consulship. The writer explains that he arranges scattered thoughts into one ordered view for the reader, detailing how to build support among publicani, equestrians, and municipal towns. It also prescribes daily attention to callers, escorts, and companions, illustrating these methods with the practice of C. Cotta. The text classes potential enemies under three heads and urges the cultivation of popular favour, advising reliance on Pompey's goodwill. It supplies invective against Antonius and Catiline, while the closing pages address preserving the esteem of the senate, equites, and plebs. They discuss countering electoral bribery through vigilance and the restraint of divisores, ending by inviting corrections to this little handbook on electioneering.
la.quintilian.institutio_oratoria: Quintilian composed the Institutio Oratoria, or 'Institution of Oratory', as a twelve book Latin prose treatise after twenty years of teaching in early imperial Rome, addressing it to Marcellus Victorius. The opening preface defines the orator as a good man skilled in speaking, while the first book covers a child's education from infancy through schools and the study of letters. The second book turns to the teacher's duties and the first exercises of rhetoric, and five books follow on invention and disposition. Four books address elocution, memory, and delivery, while the eleventh book ends with prescriptions on voice and gesture. The twelfth and longest book forms the orator himself by insisting on character and wisdom, examining which causes he may undertake and offering practical advice on pleading. The work closes with an exhortation to pursue virtue and eloquence together.
la.remigius_of_auxerre.expositione_in_pasch: This early medieval Latin prose commentary on Sedulius's Paschale Carmen is transmitted under the name of Remigius of Auxerre. It opens with an accessus that draws on Jerome's catalogue of illustrious men, recounting Sedulius's life, his earlier prose treatment, and his dedication to the priest Macedonius. The body proceeds lemma by lemma through the dedicatory epistle and the poem itself, glossing difficult vocabulary with etymologies and notes on grammar and rhetoric. The commentary also offers allegorical and moral readings of the narrative, which runs from the fall of Adam through Old Testament figures to Christ's birth, miracles, passion, resurrection, and closing prayer.
la.rufius_festus.breviarium: The Breviarium is a late-antique Latin prose epitome of Roman history, presented to the reigning emperor with the promise that its compressed record may be counted rather than read. The work opens by reckoning 1,117 years from the founding of the city, dividing this span into the ages of the kings, the consuls, and the emperors. The body then recounts how Sicily, Africa, Spain, and Gaul were acquired, and it also describes how these provinces are governed in the author's own day. A long final section narrates the wars between Rome and Parthia and Persia, running from the defeat of Crassus to the peace concluded under Jovian.
la.ruricius_i_bishop_of_limoges.epistulae: The Epistulae is a Late Antique Latin letter collection by Ruricius, Bishop of Limoges, which opens with a highly wrought letter to a revered priest. In this opening piece, the bishop praises his correspondent's sanctity while pleading for the priest's prayers and correction. The remaining letters are addressed chiefly to fellow bishops and clergy, but they also reach monastic friends and members of Ruricius's own family. These texts are composed in ornate, rhythmical prose, studded with biblical quotation, and cover a wide range of business. The correspondence includes requests for books and letters of commendation, as well as exchanges of gifts such as horses, pears, and game. The letters offer consolations on the deaths of children and kinsmen, contain appeals for leniency toward offenders, and include exhortations to penance and notes on synods.
la.sallust.histories: The Histories, a Latin prose historical work of the late Republic by Sallust, survive in fragments consisting principally of speeches and letters. The work opens with a public speech exhorting the Quirites to throw off the tyranny of Sulla and his partisans. The surviving material follows the discord of the decades after Sulla's dictatorship, from senatorial speeches urging and resisting war against Lepidus to a consul's ritual self-dedication for the state. Among them are a commander's letter from the Spanish war protesting the neglect of his army, and an oration on the restoration of tribunician power. In another letter Mithridates calls on Arsaces of Parthia to join him against Rome, reviewing Roman aggression from Philip of Macedon onward.
la.salutati.de_laboribus_herculis: De Laboribus Herculis is a Renaissance Latin prose treatise by Salutati, which opens with a defense of poetry against detractors who despise the art despite Aristotle's reliance on poets. The work then unfolds a systematic account of poetry, defining it as praise and blame cast in figured, metrical speech, and traces its origin alongside religion and idolatry. It argues that poetry is composed of all the liberal arts, a claim illustrated at length through musical proportion and the harmonies of the heroic hexameter. The greater part of the treatise expounds the myth of Hercules, running through the labors and further deeds, including the Hesperides, Cacus, Cerberus, and the descent to the underworld. These sections include digressions on Orpheus, Theseus, and Pirithous, where each fable is read as both history and moral, physical, or theological allegory in which Hercules figures the virtuous man. The closing portions follow Eneas's descent among the shades, expounding the golden bough, Charon, and the death of Misenus in the same allegorical vein.
la.salutati.de_tyranno: This Renaissance Latin treatise by Coluccio Salutati, chancellor of Florence, takes the form of a letter written in answer to Antonio di Aquila, a student of arts at Padua. The text opens with a salutation and a protest against the correspondent's extravagant praise, then announces five questions for treatment. Salutati addresses the definition of the tyrant, the lawfulness of killing one, the character of Caesar's principate, and the justice of his assassination. The argument draws on etymology, authorities such as Gregory, and Roman legal and historical exempla, permitting force against an invader of a people's liberty but insisting on lawful title. On this basis, the work acquits Julius Caesar of tyranny and condemns his assassins as murderers, while a closing section vindicates Dante's condemnation of Brutus and Cassius in the lowest hell. The work ends with a briefer, deliberately undecided survey of ancient testimony on whether Antenor and Aeneas betrayed Troy.
la.salvianus.de_gubernatione_dei: De Gubernatione Dei is a Late Antique prose treatise by Salvian, a presbyter of Massilia, who defends divine providence against the charge that God is careless of human affairs. The work opens by contrasting the author's aim of writing remedies rather than verbal displays, then frames the objection that the good suffer while the wicked prosper. The bulk of the work argues by reason and biblical examples that God governs the world, citing figures from Adam and Cain through Abraham, Moses, and David. The author also uses scriptural testimonies to show that God continually sees and judges, asserting that the calamities befalling the Roman Empire are deserved punishment. Later portions list the vices of Roman Christians, including greed, oppressive taxation, and sexual impurity, while noting a fondness for the circus and theater, and casual swearing by Christ. These faults are contrasted with the chastity and piety of barbarian peoples such as the Goths and Vandals, and the treatise ends by denouncing as blasphemy the claim that God neglects mankind.
la.saxo_grammaticus.gesta_danorum: The Gesta Danorum ('Deeds of the Danes') is a Latin history of the Danes composed by Saxo Grammaticus at the urging of Archbishop Absalon, its date uncertain. Its prologue, addressed to Absalon, to the canon Andrew, and to King Valdemar, announces an account of Danish deeds that begins with a description of the homeland. The account extends from legendary antiquity to the author's own day, tracing the deeds of Danish kings across their whole recorded past. Among his sources are old Danish songs, whose matter is rendered in Latin metres, and the reports of Icelandic informants versed in antiquity. The work also draws on Absalon's own testimony of deeds he performed or learned of, and is written in elaborate prose interspersed with verse.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium_altera: This late-antique Latin dedicatory letter by the Christian poet Sedulius is addressed to the priest Macedonius and prefixed to his prose Paschale Opus ('Easter Work'). It opens with a greeting and an acknowledgment of Macedonius's command to render the earlier Paschale Carmen ('Easter Song') from verse into prose. The body of the letter defends the new edition against anticipated critics, appealing to Hermogenianus and Origen as precedents for reissuing and expanding one's own work. Sedulius also distinguishes between altering what is complete and supplying what was left unfinished. The letter closes by naming the verse work Paschale Carmen and the prose rendition Paschale Opus, both offered in prayer to Christ.
la.sedulius.hymnus_ii_a_solis_ortus_cardine: Sedulius composed this Late Antique Latin Christian hymn to praise Christ the prince, whose title, A solis ortus cardine, means from the rising of the sun. It calls for song from the east to the limits of the earth, and the work is an alphabetic hymn whose quatrains begin with successive letters. Its stanzas trace the course of Christ's life from the annunciation, covering the nativity, the magi, and Herod's fear. The text also describes the slaughter of the innocents, and later stanzas move to the baptism and a sequence of miracles. These include the water made wine and the healing of the centurion's servant, while Peter walking on the sea and the raising of Lazarus are also noted. The narrative then turns to Judas's betrayal and the passion, where Christ is crucified between thieves, and women bear myrrh after the sabbath. The hymn ends with Christ trampling the envious dragon, and he also defeats the mouth of the lion before returning to the heavens.
la.sedulius.opus_paschale: The Opus Paschale is a Late Antique Latin prose treatment of the life of Christ, opening with a preface that contrasts pagan poetry unfavourably with Christian truth. The author invokes God's aid before surveying Old Testament miracles, where figures such as Enoch, Abraham, Lot's wife, Moses, and Jonah appear as types fulfilled in the Gospel. The narrative then follows Christ's life from the Virgin birth through his ministry, detailing the miracles, teachings, and the Lord's Prayer. The Passion receives extensive allegorical interpretation, followed by the Harrowing of Hell, and the work concludes with the Resurrection, Ascension, and allusions to the evangelists. Sustained rhetorical commentary throughout directs its arguments against pagan idolatry and heresy, notably targeting Arianism by this exegetical mode.
la.seneca.ad_lucilium_epistulae_morales: Seneca's Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales, a Latin prose collection of moral-philosophical letters, was composed in the early Imperial period and addressed to his friend Lucilius. The opening letter urges him to reclaim time, which Seneca argues is the only possession truly his own. The sequence forms a continuous course of moral instruction, with each letter opening with the same salutation and closing with a pithy saying. These sayings often quote Epicurus and serve as the payment for the day, while subjects range across friendship, reading, solitude, and the fear of death. They also cover gladiatorial spectacles, poverty, wealth, and the passions, interweaving these topics with anecdotes from Roman life. The text includes notices of Seneca's own health and travels, along with occasional digressions into physics and dialectic.
la.seneca.carminum_fragmenta: This brief collection of lyric fragments in mixed metres is attributed to Seneca and belongs to the Early Imperial period. The text opens with an address to a parent and lord of the lofty heaven, allowing no delay in obedience. The speaker concedes that the fates lead the willing while dragging the unwilling, and the remaining excerpts dwell on wealth and virtue. Many of these are single-line sententiae asking whether men seek riches rather than goodness, expressing the wish to be called the worst so long as one is called rich. Another line states the resolve to live rich or die poor, and a passage styles money a great good of humankind. It places this value beyond a mother's delight in her children, and gnomic sayings such as 'the speech of truth is simple' close the assemblage. A fragment on a thick woollen gausapa garment also ends the collection.
la.seneca.de_beneficiis: Seneca composed this seven book Latin treatise in the early imperial period, addressing it to Aebutius Liberalis. The work opens with a complaint about human ingratitude, arguing that a benefit resides in the giver's willing mind. He then considers how recipients should be chosen, examining how benefits are given, received, and repaid. The text also explores the many causes of ingratitude, asking whether benefits can be taken away or outweighed by later injury. Seneca discusses what is owed to parents, children, slaves, and the gods, using examples from Roman history and legend to illustrate these arguments. A closing book urges forbearance toward the ungrateful, ending with the Cynic Demetrius and the question of giving to the sage.
la.seneca.de_clementia: Seneca's De Clementia is a Latin prose treatise from the Early Imperial period, addressed to the young emperor Nero, whom the preface promises to confront with his own clemency. The work argues that clemency is the virtue most proper to rulers, and a prince's safety rests on the love of his subjects rather than on fear. The author illustrates this with Augustus sparing the conspirator Cinna, while cautionary examples of cruelty include Sulla and Vedius Pollio. A later section defines clementia in Stoic terms, distinguishing this virtue from pity and from formal pardon. The text also considers when punishment is owed and how far it should be tempered, but the main argument breaks off in the discussion of reforming offenders. The surviving copy then appends aphoristic chapters on clemency for princes, which are introduced as from an epistle attributed to Hildebert of Le Mans.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_marciam: This prose consolatio by the early Imperial philosopher Seneca is addressed to Marcia, daughter of the historian Cremutius Cordus, who has spent three years in unrelenting mourning for a son. The text opens with praise of her fortitude and her restoration of her father's suppressed writings, contrasting the endless grief of Octavia over Marcellus with Livia's self-command after losing Drusus. Seneca argues that sorrow is a matter of opinion rather than nature, noting that all life's goods are held on loan from fortune. Death can be a release and even a gain, with examples ranging from Sulla, Paulus, Caesar, and Cornelia to Lucretia and Cloelia. The work closes with an imagined speech from Cordus in the heavens, setting human loss within the vast scale of cosmic time and the world's eventual conflagration. He urges her to accept her son's early death as a return to blessed company and lasting peace.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_polybium: This Latin prose consolation by Seneca addresses Polybius, a powerful figure close to the emperor, on the death of his brother. The work opens by contrasting the fragility of human life with the seeming firmness of stone monuments. It argues that grief benefits neither the mourner nor the dead, a point illustrated by Roman nobles who endured similar losses. Seneca suggests that the bereaved should honor the deceased through studies and writings that outlast marble. An extended encomium of the emperor's clemency incorporates the author's own account of exile and plea for recall. The text ends with counsel to temper tears and an apology for the author's limited Latin vocabulary.
la.seneca.de_constantia: De Constantia ('On Constancy') is a Latin prose dialogue in which Seneca, writing in the early Imperial period, addresses Serenus. He opens by ranking the Stoics above all other professors of wisdom and asserting that the sage, exemplified by Cato, stands beyond the reach of injury. The body of the work argues that injury cannot befall a man whose only true good is virtue. Seneca illustrates the thesis with Stilbo's reply to Demetrius Poliorcetes after the fall of Megara, with Socrates' equanimity under abuse, and with the insults of Gaius Caesar. A second part distinguishes insult from injury, treating the slights of slaves, women, and kings alike as the behaviour of children. The dialogue closes with counsel on despising insults and on the liberty of a mind set above fortune.
la.seneca.de_ira: Seneca's De Ira ('On Anger'), a three-book prose treatise addressed to his brother Novatus, examines anger as the most destructive of the passions. The first book defines anger, denies that it is natural or useful, and refutes the Aristotelian view that it can serve courage. The second analyses how anger arises in the mind and sets out preventive remedies, among them the education of children and the restraint of first impressions. The third turns to the management of one's own anger and the pacification of others, illustrated with anecdotes of rulers such as Cambyses, Alexander and Augustus. Throughout, Seneca argues that anger must be eradicated rather than moderated, and the work closes with reflections on mortality and the brevity of life as arguments for calm.
la.seneca.de_providentia: This short Latin prose treatise by Seneca, written in the Early Imperial period, is addressed to Lucilius and opens with a question about the misfortunes of good men. The work asks why such suffering occurs if the world is governed by providence, and Seneca answers in Stoic terms that adversity is assigned by the gods to test the virtuous. He illustrates this point with examples such as Cato, Socrates, Regulus, and Mucius Scaevola, who are contrasted with the softness of Maecenas and Sulla. Later chapters treat fate and the ordered course of the universe, while also discussing the wise man's willing assent to divine will. The text notes the readily available escape of death and closes with an exhortation to despise poverty, pain, fortune, and mortality.
la.seneca.de_tranquillitate_animi: De Tranquillitate Animi, a philosophical prose dialogue from the Early Imperial period, opens with Annaeus Serenus confessing a restless malaise of spirit to Seneca. The speaker feels caught between frugality and luxury, as well as public ambition and withdrawal, prompting Seneca to name the goal the euthymia of Democritus, which he calls tranquillitas. He surveys causes of self-discontent, including inconstant desire, wandering restlessness, and envy of others, while also noting hidden shame over one's own failings. The author then offers remedies in turn, starting with public service or useful private study, and advises honest self-assessment, choice of friends, and moderation in wealth and expenditure. Further counsel includes acceptance of fortune and readiness for death, as well as avoiding aimless busyness and alternating solitude with society. The work ends with counsel to regard human folly with laughter rather than tears, following the manner of Democritus rather than Heraclitus, and concludes with the warning that only constant vigilance can preserve the wavering mind.
la.seneca.de_vita_beata: Seneca, a philosopher of the early imperial period, wrote this Latin prose treatise on the happy life for his brother Gallio. The work opens by noting that all men wish to live happily but go astray because they do not first determine what the happy life is. The swifter their course, the further they stray from the true path, and the argument then sets out a Stoic account of beatitude as a life in accord with nature. It grounds this view in virtue as the sole good and attacks the doctrine that pleasure can be joined with virtue. Seneca defends Epicurus against those who use his name as a cover for luxury, and later sections take up the wise man's relation to wealth, which may be possessed and given away with profit though it is not a good. The text answers critics who charge philosophers with failing to live by their own precepts, and it closes with the sage's rebuke of those who malign virtue and with the example of Socrates.
la.seneca.hercules_furens: A Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Seneca, on the madness of Hercules. It opens with Juno's prologue, in which the goddess, displaced in Jupiter's favour by Alcmene and her son, summons the Furies to madden Hercules at the height of his success. The plot follows the Theban usurper Lycus, who has slain Creon and seized the throne and now threatens Megara, her children, and Amphitryon while Hercules descends to the underworld for Cerberus; Hercules returns in time to kill Lycus, but Juno's frenzy overtakes him and he slaughters his wife and children in the belief that they are enemies. Waking, he learns of the massacre from Amphitryon and Theseus, whose account of the lower world and of the capture of Cerberus fills much of the later action, contemplates suicide, and is persuaded by his father and his friend to live on, withdrawing from Thebes to expiate his crime.
la.seneca.hercules_oetaeus: Hercules Oetaeus is a Latin tragedy from the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca and transmitted with his other plays. The title refers to the hero's death on Mount Oeta, where the drama opens with Hercules petitioning Jupiter for a place in heaven. He sends Lichas ahead with the spoils of Oechalia, while the action turns on Deianira's jealousy of the captive Iole. She trusts the supposed love charm of the dying Nessus, sending her husband a robe whose poison consumes his flesh. The poison drives him to slay Lichas and build a pyre, after which Deianira commits suicide in remorse. Alcmene laments while Philoctetes reports the burning, and the deified Hercules appears to console his mother, promising vengeance on Eurystheus as closing choruses celebrate virtue's ascent to the stars.
la.seneca.phaedra: Seneca's Latin tragedy Phaedra, a drama of the Early Imperial period, opens with Hippolytus mustering his companions and hounds for the hunt through the hills of Attica and invoking the goddess Diana. The action follows Phaedra's consuming passion for her stepson: rebuffed after confessing her love, and fearing exposure, she falsely accuses Hippolytus of assault before his father Theseus. Theseus, who has just returned from the underworld, answers by calling down a curse through his father Neptune. A messenger then narrates how a sea monster destroys Hippolytus as he drives his chariot along the shore, after which Phaedra takes her life with a confession of the truth. Theseus is left to lament over the dismembered remains of the youth. Choral odes interspersed among the acts meditate on the dominion of love, the inconstancy of Fortune, the merits of the simple country life, and the transience of beauty.
la.seneca_the_elder.excerpta_controversiae: A Latin prose work of the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca the Elder, collects rhetorical material from the declamation schools. Its excerpted Controversiae ('Controversies') preserve imaginary legal cases together with sample sayings, divisions and colours drawn from the declaimers who argued them. The surviving portion opens with themes such as the disinherited son who supported his uncle and the captive priestess who killed her abductor. Each case is followed by opposing arguments delivered in the voices of various rhetoricians. The work then runs through a long sequence of such cases on themes of family conflict, piracy, tyranny and inheritance, interspersed with anecdotal asides about individual declaimers. It concludes with the prefaces addressed to Seneca's sons, in which he discusses famous orators such as Cassius Severus, Asinius Pollio and Haterius.
la.seneca_the_elder.suasoriae: The Suasoriae is a Latin prose compilation assembled by Seneca the Elder in the early Imperial period, preserving deliberative declamation exercises along with memorable sayings and stylistic treatments from celebrated orators. The collection opens with a debate on whether Alexander should sail beyond the Ocean, while subsequent themes include the Spartans at Thermopylae and the Athenians debating the trophies of Xerxes. Agamemnon also deliberates the sacrifice of Iphigenia in these pages, and Cicero weighs whether to burn his speeches against Antonius or plead for his life. The compiler interlaces judgments on individual declaimers with anecdotes of their lives and rivalries, while extended descriptive passages from performances and verse excerpts from poets like Cornelius Severus appear throughout. Historical narratives, including several accounts of Cicero's death, are also included in this comprehensive work.
la.servius_honoratus.in_virgilii_georgicon_: Servius Honoratus composed this late antique prose commentary on Virgil's Georgics, which is transmitted in four books mirroring the poem's structure. The opening preface situates the Georgics among Virgil's other works, arguing that he followed Homer in the Aeneid and Theocritus in the Bucolics. The author claims Virgil expanded a single Hesiodic book on farming into four, addressed to Maecenas just as Hesiod addressed Perses. The notes gloss Virgil's wording with grammatical and stylistic analysis, providing etymologies of names and terms while introducing alternative explanations by the phrase et aliter. Mythological narratives of Achelous, Orpheus, and Eurydice appear throughout, alongside seasonal and astronomical lore and Stoic allegorization of the gods invoked in the poem. The work closes with the sign of the bees from the oxen, ending with verses where Virgil reviews his Bucolics and Caesar's wars.
la.silius_italicus.punica: Silius Italicus composed the Punica, an epic in hexameters from the early Imperial period. The title refers to the Punic Wars, specifically the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage. The poem spans seventeen books and opens with Hannibal's oath against Rome. It then details the siege of Saguntum and the Roman disasters at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae. The narrative continues with the long resistance under Fabius Cunctator and the campaigns of Scipio in Spain and Africa. It concludes with the deaths of Hasdrubal and other commanders, Hannibal's defeat and exile, and the final triumph.
la.suetonius.de_vita_caesarum: The work opens with the life of Julius Caesar, tracing his youth from the loss of his father to his defiance of Sulla. It then follows a sequence of biographies covering the rulers from Caesar to Domitian. This includes the brief reigns of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius, which round out the period of civil war. Rather than proceeding as continuous annals, each life is arranged topically under specific headings. These sections cover ancestry, omens, military campaigns, public offices, and the manner of death. Suetonius cites letters, memoirs, and senatorial records to preserve a mass of anecdote and documentary detail.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_Bassulae_p: Sulpicius Severus wrote this short late-antique prose letter to his mother, Bassula, opening with mock-legal banter about her stealing his private correspondence. He promises the account of Martin of Tours' death, granting it only on the condition that she shows it to no one. The narrative details Martin's journey to Candes to reconcile discordant clerics, and it also describes his expulsion of a flock of birds with a single word. The saint's sudden failing strength and his refusal to choose between life and death in prayer follow, and his passing is marked by a vision of the devil rebuked and Abraham's bosom. The letter closes with the luminous appearance of the saint's body, and a vast funeral gathering of monks, virgins, and crowds from city and countryside attends. Sulpicius compares these exequies to a worldly triumph.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_aurelium: Sulpicius Severus addresses a correspondent named Aurelius in this Late Antique prose letter. The writer describes a sleep in which he sees Martin, bishop of Tours, radiant in white. Martin blesses him and ascends to heaven, followed by the presbyter Clarus. The writer wakes to the news of Martin's death and urges Aurelius to join him in mourning. He argues that Martin achieved a bloodless martyrdom through fasting, vigils, and hardship. The letter closes with a hope that Martin's intercession will atone for the writer's sins.
la.terence.eunuchus: A Latin comedy in verse by Terence of the Republican period, adapted from a Greek original by Menander. Its opening prologue has the poet answer a charge that he took the parasite and the boasting soldier from an earlier Latin play, and invites the audience to judge the case for themselves. The action turns on the young Phaedria's rivalry with the braggart soldier Thraso for the courtesan Thais, and on Phaedria's brother Chaerea, who slips into Thais's house disguised as a eunuch sent among the gifts, where he rapes a young woman who proves to be Thais's long-lost Athenian sister. Recognition, a threatened lawsuit before the archon, the soldier's abortive assault on the door, and the servant Parmeno's punishment carry the plot to a resolution in which Chaerea marries the girl, Thais is taken under the family's patronage, and Thraso is brought into the household as an obliging rival.
la.terence.phormio: Phormio is a Latin comedy in dramatic verse by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic. In the opening prologue a poet answers the attacks of an older rival before announcing the play, a Greek comedy rendered in Latin and named after its title character. The plot follows two young Athenians, Antipho and Phaedria, whose guardians are away. Antipho, advised by the bold parasite Phormio, marries Phanium under a law allowing next of kin to wed an heiress. Phaedria meanwhile seeks money to ransom his beloved from a procurer, and deception, fabricated kinship, and a promised dowry pile confusion upon the returning fathers Demipho and Chremes. The discovery that Chremes fathered Phanium long ago in Lemnos untangles the marriages, and the resourceful Phormio is welcomed into the family.
la.tertullian.ad_martyres: This short Latin prose exhortation by Tertullian addresses designated martyrs held in prison, urging them to nourish the spirit while the church supplies their bodily needs. The author warns against discord, which he calls the devil's weapon within the cell, and reverses the usual comparison by calling the world the true dungeon. The imprisonment is likened to the desert retreat of prophets and the training of soldiers, setting the flesh subject to the spirit in anticipation of various deaths. It closes by marshalling pagan exempla of endured and self-inflicted suffering, ranging from Lucretia and Mucius Scaevola to Regulus and Cleopatra. The argument is that endurance for a heavenly reward should come more readily than endurance for earthly glory.
la.tertullian.adversus_valentinianos: Tertullian wrote this late-antique Latin prose polemic against the Valentinian heresy, opening by likening the sect's secrecy to the Eleusinian mysteries. He pleads for Christian simplicity against their professed wisdom, recounting the school's origins in Valentinus, who was disappointed of a bishopric. The text traces development under Ptolemy, Heracleon, Secundus, and Marcus, before expounding the Valentinian mythology with sustained irony. This includes the thirty Aeons of the Pleroma and the fall of Sophia, describing the generation of Achamoth and the Demiurge's creation of the world. It details the threefold division of humankind into material, animal, and spiritual natures, covering the sect's eschatology of spiritual marriages in the Pleroma. The work closes with a survey of variant versions taught by Ptolemy and Secundus, showing how the doctrine branches into wilder Gnostic growth.
la.tertullian.de_carnis_resurrectione: Tertullian's De Carnis Resurrectione is a Latin prose treatise that defends the bodily resurrection against pagan ridicule and heretical groups. It targets Marcionites, Valentinians, and followers of Basilides and Apelles, who admitted only a spiritual resurrection. Tertullian opens by calling the resurrection the chief confidence of Christians, noting that the crowd mocks this belief while still practising funeral rites. The text then proceeds with a systematic argument that defends the dignity and divine origin of the flesh from Genesis. The author marshals the authority of scripture and the power of God in nature, citing the phoenix and the necessity of divine judgement. The treatise refutes allegorising and spiritual readings that explain away promises made to the flesh, closing by addressing objections about the condition and functions of the risen body. Tertullian concludes that all flesh, the same flesh, and the whole of it shall rise, preserved with Christ as a pledge in heaven.
la.tertullian.de_ieiunio_adversus_psychicos: Tertullian wrote this Latin prose polemic to defend the strict dietary discipline of the New Prophecy, supporting the teachings of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla against their critics. It opens with scorn for the psychics, whom the author accuses of pairing frequent marriage with a hatred of fasts, framing the dispute as a choice between fasting and marrying more often. The body of the text assembles biblical exempla from Adam's fall through eating to Israel's craving in the wilderness, citing Moses, Elijah, Daniel, Nineveh, and Ahab to support its arguments. These examples show that fasting expiates sin, averts divine anger, and wins revelation, while the author treats xerophagies, which are abstinences from meat, wine, and moist foods. He also defends the station days as ancient observances rather than novelties, denouncing the gluttony and banquet customs of his opponents along the way. The discipline of hunger is tied to the endurance of prison and martyrdom, closing with the taunt that lean flesh is better fitted for the narrow gate of salvation.
la.tertullian.de_patientia: De Patientia is a Latin prose treatise by Tertullian, a Christian writer of Late Antiquity, who opens by confessing his unfitness. He admits to being afflicted with the very impatience he would prescribe against, then surveys divine patience in God's forbearance. This virtue is seen supremely in Christ's incarnation and passion, while impatience is traced to the devil and first sins. The text covers precepts for loss, insult, grief, revenge, forgiveness, penance, charity, and bodily discipline. Job serves as the great exemplar, and the work closes with Patience enthroned beside the Spirit of God. This image is set against the false patience of the pagans.
la.tertullian.de_spectaculis: Tertullian's De Spectaculis, a Latin treatise on Christian moral theology, argues that believers must renounce all public games and spectacles. The work opens by addressing new converts on the rule of faith, explaining how baptismal renunciation bars the pleasures of the circus and theatre. The argument then surveys the origins, titles, and equipment of each entertainment, tracing chariot racing, the stage, and gladiatorial combat to idolatry. The author also answers pagan objections to these prohibitions, while the text closes by opposing fleeting worldly shows to the Christian's true spectacle. This final vision is the coming Last Judgment before Christ's tribunal.
la.tertullian.de_testimonio_animae: This brief Late Antique treatise of Latin theology, attributed to Tertullian, is titled De Testimonio Animae, which aims to prove Christian truth from the human soul itself. It dismisses pagan philosophers and poets as sources of testimony, instead summoning the soul as it exists in ordinary people, unformed by schools. The argument shows that common speech and instinctive belief reveal knowledge implanted by God, which outweighs the divergent doctrines of Plato, Pythagoras, and Epicurus. The work concludes that the soul is guilty of error yet a witness to truth, destined to stand before the courts of God on the day of judgement.
la.thedulf_of_orleans.carmina_appendix: This short appendix gathers Latin poems attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a writer of the Carolingian period. It opens with a sequence of riddling pieces in which objects, creatures and natural things speak in the first person. Through paradox, enumeration and wordplay, each speaker defines itself while leaving its solution unspoken. This enigmatic manner continues through verses on speech, harmony and healing, before the closing lines turn to Christian admonition. The collection ends with a prayer in gardening imagery, asking that the root of the heart be transplanted to the fields of heaven and bear fruit.
la.theodosius.de_situ_terrae_sanctae: The De Situ Terrae Sanctae ('On the Situation of the Holy Land') is a late antique prose guide to the holy places of Palestine. Its date remains uncertain. The text opens with the gates of Jerusalem and the distances to Jericho and the Jordan. It then proceeds through measured itineraries across Judaea, Samaria, Galilee, and the coastal plain. These sections record mileages and identify churches, martyria, and the biblical events attached to each site. Later passages extend farther afield to describe saints' cults and holy places in Arabia, Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Cilicia, Egypt, and the Black Sea region. The guide also includes notes on provinces, rivers, monasteries, and local marvels such as the field at Galgala and the salt statue of Lot's wife.
la.valerius_maximus.facta_et_dicta_memorabi: Valerius Maximus's Facta et Dicta Memorabilia, a Latin prose compilation of memorable deeds and sayings composed in the early imperial period and addressed to the ruling Caesar, opens with a preface in which the author explains that worthy acts and words of Rome and of foreign peoples have been gathered from distinguished writers so that those seeking examples may be spared long research. The nine books are arranged by theme rather than chronology: the first treats religion, auspices, omens, prodigies, dreams, and miracles, and the remainder pass in turn through Roman and foreign institutions and customs, military discipline and the law of triumphs, and long sequences of virtues and vices, from fortitude, continence, clemency, gratitude, piety, chastity, liberty, justice, friendship, and liberality to luxury, cruelty, anger, avarice, pride, perfidy, sedition, and rashness. Each chapter assembles brief anecdotes drawn largely from Roman history, with foreign examples appended for variety, and the final book closes with notable kinds of death and accounts of bodily resemblance.
la.vergil_pseudo.catalepton: The Catalepton is a small collection of short lyric poems attributed to Vergil and of Augustan date, and the title means a collection of short poems. It opens with epigrams on a mistress who hides from the speaker's friend Tucca, and another early piece mocks a rhetorician who mangles his Greek while devoted to Thucydides. The collection then ranges over a meditation on Fortune's sudden overthrow of a mighty man, and a poem of friendship follows along with the speaker's renunciation of rhetoric and the Muse. He sets sail for the blessed harbors of Siro's teaching, and lighter and later pieces include jests on a quarrelsome father and son in law. There is also a farewell to the little farm once Siro's, and the text praises a triumphing general and offers a comic dedication to a renowned mule driver named Sabinus. A lament for the young Octavius appears, as do coarse wedding jests at the expense of Noctuinus, and an invective against Licinius is included in the set. The collection closes with a vow to honor Venus with sacrifice, and this vow is made if the poet's Latin song of Trojan Aeneas proves worthy.
la.ambrose.de_interpellatione_iob_et_david: A Latin prose theological treatise of late antiquity by Ambrose, De interpellatione Iob et David examines how the righteous may question God in the midst of adversity. It opens from the scriptural commonplace that life is full of disturbances yet supplied with consolations that outweigh them, citing Paul on the present sufferings and coming glory. The greater part of the work follows Job's pleas to God, his losses, his ulcers, his replies to the friends who charge him with sin, and draws from his speeches discussions of human frailty, the vanity of riches, the inaccessibility of divine wisdom, and the promise of resurrection, before turning to David's laments in the Psalms, above all the soul's longing for God like a deer for the waters in the forty-first psalm and Asaph's puzzlement at the prosperity of the wicked in the seventy-second. Throughout, a moral and allegorical exposition insists that God's justice, though hidden, and his consolations surpass every present affliction.
la.ambrose.de_tobia: De Tobia is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose that begins with a reading of the biblical Book of Tobit. The author praises the hero's virtues of justice, mercy, and patience before launching a sustained invective against usury. This section depicts the seductions and exactions of moneylenders, causing debtors to pledge and lose property, freedom, and even their children. The text includes digressions on despair and the devil as creditor, while marshalling scriptural prohibitions of interest from Exodus, Deuteronomy, and the Gospels. The latter part recasts lending in a positive key, urging alms to the poor as a loan to God, illustrated from Peter's healing and the parable of the two debtors. The work closes with Tobit's counsels on almsgiving and sobriety.
la.anonymous.s_silviae_peregrinatio: This anonymous Latin prose account, transmitted under the name of Silvia, reports an extended journey to the holy places of the Near East. Its date remains uncertain, though the text opens mid-journey in the mountains of Sinai. Guided by local monks and clergy, the narrator visits sites associated with Moses and the Israelites. The itinerary then carries the pilgrim through Goshen, Mount Nebo, and the Jordan valley. The journey continues to Edessa, where the story of King Abgar and the letter of Christ is retold. The narrative concludes with a detailed report on the life of the Jerusalem churches, addressed to a community of women far away.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_aquilegia: This anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date is an alphabetical composition, its lines beginning one after another with successive letters of the alphabet. It opens with praise of Aquileia as a glorious and warlike city, chief city of the Venetians, until laid waste long ago by the savage Attila. The poem recounts the city's evangelization through the apostle Mark and the martyr-bishop Hermagoras, before turning to the sins that provoked its destruction by the pagan Avars. The faith passed to the Venetians, and the Lombard-era patriarch John is condemned for the heresy by which he divided the church as Jeroboam had divided Israel. It closes with God's delivery of Italy to the Franks and the deposition of the deceitful patriarch Maxentius under Louis and his son Lothar. A final prayer to the undivided Trinity asks for victory over the false Aquileians.
la.aristotle.economics_book_3: The third book of the Economics attributed to Aristotle outlines the reciprocal duties of spouses in governing a household, where a good wife must rule the interior under written law and admit no one without her husband's knowledge. She is also required to keep modest dress and expenditure while leaving public business to him, and the husband must instruct his wife gently rather than with servile fear and honour her above all others. He should keep faithful to her and beget children from a worthy union, much as a farmer commits seed to well-tilled ground, while Homer's Penelope, Odysseus, Agamemnon, and Nausicaa are cited as instances of conjugal fidelity and its failures. The book closes by urging concord of will between husband and wife in prosperity and adversity alike, so they should govern children, parents, friends, and goods in common to reap an honourable old age.
la.augustine.commonitorium: The Commonitorium, a short Latin prose document attributed to Augustine, dates from the late antique period and addresses the reception of Manichaean converts. It prescribes steps for those who confess their error to rejoin the catholic church, requiring them to anathematise the heresy in a set form and submit a written confession. Converts then obtain a dated letter from a bishop that protects them from further penalty, allowing them to remain catechumens or penitents until their conversion is proved over time. The greater part of the work consists of anathemas against specific Manichaean doctrines, including the two opposed principles and the captivity of divine substance in plants and humanity. The text also condemns the fabulous generation of Adam and the transfiguration of divine virtues, while rejecting the eternal globe of damnation and the denial of the Mosaic law. The anathemas further deny Christ's true flesh and the true Holy Spirit, and a final curse is pronounced upon Manes himself. The document closes with the prescribed form of the bishop's letter to converts, which also includes rules confining former Manichaean elect to monasteries or hostels. Their movements are restricted until the sincerity of their conversion is evident.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelagian: This late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine is cast as a letter to Boniface, bishop of Rome. It was written against two Pelagian epistles, one sent by Julian to Rome and another by eighteen bishops to Thessalonica. The work opens with an amicable dedication explaining why Augustine must answer writings that entice the unwary away from catholic teaching. The three books then take up the Pelagian positions point by point, defending the priority of grace to all human merit. They affirm original sin washed away in baptism, though human infirmity remains, and treat of the law, marriage, and free will. The final book supports the argument with extensive quotations from Cyprian and Ambrose, presented as witnesses that the doctrine is the faith handed down from antiquity.
