la.augustine.contra_fortunatum: This stenographic record captures a public disputation between Augustine and Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter, which took place in the baths of Sossius at Hippo before a gathered crowd. Its opening heading dates the occasion by the consulship of Arcadius and Rufinus, and the discussion centers on the nature of God and the origin of evil. Augustine argues that Manichaean claims about divine substance mingling with the world are incompatible with an incorruptible God, while Fortunatus counters that the soul is of divine origin but sins under the constraint of a contrary nature. Augustine replies by appealing to creation from nothing, the free choice of the first man, and the binding force of habit, supporting each step with citations from the apostle Paul. After a second day's session before the notary, the disputation breaks off without agreement, and Fortunatus defers his answer until he has consulted his seniors. The record closes with Augustine's thanksgiving.
la.augustine.de_divinatione_daemonum: De Divinatione Daemonum is a Latin prose theological treatise by Augustine of the late antique period, which opens with a recollected conversation with Christian laymen during the octave of holy days. They discuss pagan pretensions to knowledge and a demon's foretelling of the temple of Serapis in Alexandria being overthrown, while the dialogue works through successive objections about what God permits and why sacrifices are now suppressed. Augustine ascribes demonic forecasts to their keen sense, speed, and long experience in aerial bodies, noting that demons often predict what they themselves will bring about or read natural signs inaccessible to humans. They sometimes report what they have heard from angelic and prophetic oracles, yet such knowledge is not divine, and the treatise concludes by setting the prophesied destruction of temples against the dwindling remnant of pagans who mock Christian simplicity.
la.augustine.de_duabus_animabus: This late-antique Latin treatise by Augustine opens with the author, delivered from Manichaean error, resolving to deplore the doctrine of two kinds of souls. He argues that every soul, grasped by intellect rather than bodily sense, surpasses visible light. Even souls the Manichaeans call evil must, insofar as they live, come from the same creator as sun and moon. The text defines the will and sin, locating wrongdoing in the will alone. It explains the fluctuation of deliberation without positing two souls and argues that repentance presupposes a single created nature. Gospel sayings seemingly denying that sinners are of God are reconciled with the affirmation that all things are from him. The work ends with a prayer for friends still attached to the sect.
la.augustine.de_gestis_pelagii: De gestis Pelagii is a Late Antique Latin theological treatise addressed to Bishop Aurelius, which Augustine wrote after fourteen bishops in Palestine had pronounced Pelagius catholic. The arrival of the official acts ended his hesitation and prompted a fuller response to an earlier note. The bulk of the work weighs each objection and reply in the synodal record point by point, examining topics such as the law, free will, eternal punishment, and the possibility of living without sin. Augustine argues that the bishops acquitted the man while condemning his doctrines and those of Caelestius. The closing chapters recapitulate anathematized propositions and cite letters from Timasius and Jacobus, also examining a disputed letter that treats the acquittal as a triumph. The text concludes that the heresy remains condemned even though Pelagius was absolved.
la.augustine.sermo_de_rusticiano_subdiacono: This short Latin sermon by Augustine, preserved among his writings against the Donatists, opens with the bishop standing before his congregation in tears. He had tried three times to preach but failed through grief, and the occasion involved the loss of a venerable pastor. Rusticianus, a deacon of Mutigena, neglected his charge and fled to the Donatists, where he was received, rebaptized, and ordained by their bishop Macrobius. Augustine recounts his interventions and reads aloud the letter he sent to Macrobius, allowing the people to see how peaceably the matter was handled. The sermon then widens into an argument against rebaptism, defending the sanctity of the Catholic font against Donatist charges of defilement. The text closes with a plea for one baptism, one faith, and one profession of charity.
la.ausonius.cento_nuptialis: The Cento Nuptialis ('Wedding Patchwork') of Ausonius is a late-antique Latin wedding poem in hexameters, pieced together almost wholly from lines and half-lines of Virgil. It opens with a prose preface to Paulus defining the patchwork form, apologising for the triviality of the undertaking, and attributing the commission to the emperor Valentinian. The poem then follows a wedding from the banquet and the arrival of bride and groom, through the gifts and songs of the guests, to the wedding night. The night is first wrapped in periphrasis and then set out in a closing sequence of patched verses of remarkable frankness. An epilogue, mingling verse and prose and appealing to Juvenal, Martial, Pliny, and other classical writers, pleads that the wanton page accompanies a chaste life. It sets a limit to reading and leaves the remainder to the curious.
la.cicero.de_lege_agraria_contra_rullum: De Lege Agraria contra Rullum is a series of prose speeches by Cicero, who delivered them to the Roman people while serving as consul in the Republic. The target was the agrarian bill proposed by the tribune P. Servilius Rullus, and the opening imagines young colonists occupying Capua and holding other towns with garrisons. The argument then follows the proposed law clause by clause, attacking the sweeping powers given to the land commissioners to sell public lands and revenues. The text also dwells on the law's intrusion into the eastern conquests of Cn. Pompeius, while the closing sections take up the law's dealings with Sulla's land assignments. Cicero rebuts the charge that he protects Sulla's beneficiaries, and he ends with a defiant appeal to the people to stand by their consul.
la.cicero.de_partitione_oratoria: De Partitione Oratoria is a Latin prose treatise on rhetoric from the Roman Republic, taking the form of a dialogue where the younger Cicero asks his father to explain the art of speaking in Latin. The father, who had previously taught him these principles in Greek, proceeds in strict question and answer form through the whole of rhetorical theory. The text divides the art into the power of the orator, the speech, and the question, covering the discovery and arrangement of arguments from their loci. It also addresses style, word choice, delivery, and memory, expounding the four parts of the oration, namely introduction, narration, confirmation, and peroration. The work further treats amplification and the kinds of questions and causes, distinguishing praise and blame, deliberation, and judicial pleading. The closing portions address the statuses of conjecture, definition, and quality, covering disputes over written documents and ambiguous wording, while grounding oratory in Academic dialectic and ending with the father urging his son to pursue these studies further.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_c_verrem: The Divinatio in C. Verres is a forensic speech by Cicero, delivered as an accusation in the Roman courts of the late Republic. Cicero claims the trial offers judges a chance to restore their order's reputation, while warning against the bribery and delay tactics Verres is attempting. The speech surveys Verres' career, including his quaestorship under Carbo, his legateship in Asia under Dolabella, and his praetorship in Sicily. Cicero marshals charges of extortionate grain levies and theft of temple treasures, citing the bribery surrounding a fleet commanded by Cleomenes. The oration closes with a defence of the Roman franchise, ending with a prayer that the gods will favour the verdict.
la.cicero.in_l_pisonem: In L. Pisonem is a prose invective delivered in the senate by Cicero against Lucius Calpurnius Piso, opening with an apostrophe to the immortal gods for granting the speaker the spectacle of the 'monster of the city'. It then ranges over Piso's lowly Gallic origins and debased character, contrasting his discreditable consulship with Cicero's own preservation of the state from the Catilinarian conspiracy. Cicero holds Piso and his colleague Gabinius responsible for his exile and the humiliation of the senate, while ridiculing Piso's Epicurean doctrines, drunken revels, and obscure return from Macedonia. The text closes with an indictment of his provincial misgovernment and a declaration that Cicero seeks his disgrace rather than his blood.
la.cicero.philippicae: The Philippicae is a set of fourteen prose speeches Cicero delivered in the Senate and before the Roman people, targeting Marcus Antonius during the crisis that followed Caesar's assassination. The first oration explains Cicero's recent departure from and return to Italy, praising Antony's early conduct before warning against his subsequent laws and acts. The speeches grow steadily harsher as they survey Antony's whole career and consulship, pressing the Senate to declare him a public enemy and reject any negotiated peace. They also urge honor for Decimus Brutus, the young Caesar, Lepidus, and the legions at Mutina, while the final orations welcome news of victory over Antony and decree thanksgivings for the commanders. They further order monuments and rewards for the fallen soldiers and denounce Dolabella as a public enemy.
la.cicero.pro_q_roscio_comoedo: This prose forensic speech by Cicero defends the comic actor Quintus Roscius, who faces a claim from Gaius Fannius Chaerea over their partnership in the slave performer Panurgus. The opening attacks the plaintiff's accounts, contrasting the official codex accepti et expensi with his informal adversaria, while Cicero presses Fannius to explain why a large sum lay unrecorded for years. The argument establishes that the money was neither given, entered as paid, nor secured by stipulation, and it contrasts the rigour of a judicium with the moderation of arbitrium. Fannius's earlier resort to arbitration proves the debt was fictitious, and later sections weigh the parties' characters against each other. They argue that Panurgus's value lay chiefly in Roscius's training, and the speech defends Roscius's settlement with Quintus Flavius as made for his own share alone. The case rests on Cluvius's testimony, reported on oath by the senators Manilius and Luscus.
la.curtius_rufus.historiae_alexandri_magni: Curtius Rufus's Historiae Alexandri Magni is an early Imperial Latin prose history narrating the campaigns of Alexander the Great. The work opens with Alexander's operations in Asia Minor, taking in the capture of Celaenae and the episode at Gordium, where he cuts the knot of the royal chariot. From there the history follows Alexander to his victories over Darius at Issus and Arbela, the sieges of Tyre and Gaza, the conquest of Egypt with its consultation of Ammon's oracle, the foundation of Alexandria, and the pursuit that ends with Darius's murder. The later portions carry the war through Bactria and Sogdiana amid purges of the king's own officers, then on to India and the hard-won victory over Porus at the Hydaspes, the army's mutinies, the expedition to the Ocean, Alexander's death at Babylon, and the succession struggles that close with the division of his empire among his generals.
la.cyprian.ad_demetrianum: Ad Demetrianum is a Late Antique prose treatise in Latin by Cyprian, which serves as an apology addressed to a pagan named Demetrianus. Cyprian explains that he had long scorned to answer Demetrianus's railings against the one true God, but he can no longer keep silent now that Christians are blamed for wars, famine, and plague. The author argues that the world is undergoing the natural decline of old age, and such calamities were foretold in Scripture as signs of the approaching day of judgement. They fall upon humankind for its sins and neglect of God rather than for abandoning the old deities, while Cyprian catalogues the moral corruptions of pagan society and protests the persecution of Christians. He contrasts their patient endurance and hope with pagan despair, and the work closes with a warning of eternal punishment. It also includes an appeal to Demetrianus to seek God's forgiveness, which remains open even at the end of life.
la.cyprian.sententiae_episcoporum: The Sententiae Episcoporum records the opinions of bishops gathered at Carthage on 1 September. They came from Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania to decide on the baptism of converts. The text belongs to the controversy over heretical baptism involving Cyprian of Carthage. It opens with Cyprian's correspondence with Jubaianus on the unlawful baptism of heretics. The greater part of the work is a sequence of short verdicts delivered by participants. They hold that only the church possesses true baptism and that converts must be baptized.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_flavium_felicem_de_res: Ad Flavium Felicem de Resurrectione Mortuorum, a Latin poem from the later Roman Empire, is transmitted under the name of Cyprian and addressed to a Flavius Felix. The speaker sets aside earlier rustic songs to address loftier themes, beginning with creation, the true God, and the fall of Adam and Eve. This fall is presented as the cause of death entering the world, while the body of the work argues that God can reassemble dissolved bodies. It cites seeds, the daily return of light, and the phoenix as evidence, then depicts the last judgment, where angels gather all humanity from their graves. The just are welcomed into an eternally flowering paradise rich in streams, gems, and fruit, while the wicked, their manifold crimes rehearsed, are driven into everlasting fire. A closing exhortation urges amendment of life and repentance while the day of grace yet endures.
la.dante.divina_comedia: This medieval Latin hexameter version adapts Dante's Divine Comedy, which recounts the poet's imagined journey through the Christian afterlife. It opens with the pilgrim astray in a dark wood at the midpoint of life, where Virgil appears to lead him down through the circles of Hell. The second book follows their toilsome ascent of Mount Purgatory, whose terraces purge souls of the seven deadly sins. Virgil withdraws as Beatrice assumes the role of guide, and the third book carries Dante upward through the celestial spheres of Paradise. Beatrice directs him toward a final vision of divine light and love.
la.dracontius.satisfactio: The Satisfactio is a Late Antique Latin poem by Dracontius, taking the form of a penitential apology where a captive poet begs pardon from an offended ruler. The work opens with a hymnic invocation of God, and the poet confesses to praising another lord while staying silent about his own. The greater part of the text sustains the plea with examples, including figures from Scripture and Roman history. The poet argues that clemency is godlike and guilt is universal, so punishment should correct rather than destroy. Meditations on creation and time lead to a closing petition, where the poet asks for the captives' lives and his own restoration. The plea is sealed with the image of a horse checked by the spur.
la.ennodius.epistulae: Epistulae is a collection of prose letters by Ennodius, a Latin author of the late antique period, whose title means letters. The collection opens with an ornate literary epistle in which the writer praises the eloquence of a young friend, comparing his speech to the restless sea. The remaining letters are addressed to aristocrats, clerics, and friends in Italy and beyond, forming a body of highly rhetorical epistolary prose. Many pieces chide a correspondent's silence and exhort him to renewed exchange, while others carry recommendations and petitions for patronage. Some console the bereaved or report the writer's illnesses and recoveries, and the letters also conduct ecclesiastical and secular business. Occasional verse insertions include an epitaph and a poem on the hot springs of Aponus.
la.eobanus.iliad: Eobanus Hessus, a Renaissance German humanist, rendered the Iliad into neo-Latin hexameters. This verse translation spans twenty-four books and totals twenty-six thousand lines. The poem opens with an invocation to the Muse and the quarrel over Briseis. It then follows the Trojan war through the catalogue of ships and the duel of Paris. The narrative continues with the embassy to Achilles and the death of Patroclus. Achilles returns to battle, and the epic closes with Priam's ransom of Hector.
la.florus_of_lyon.carminum_appendix: This brief appendix gathers Latin poems linked to Florus of Lyon, a Carolingian poet and scholar. The opening verse summons joy on a day brightened by light, then dwells on sweet songs sent by a dear friend. The speaker praises a faithful love that outdoes hills, valleys, rivers, and winds, and prays that this implanted love endure untouched by wealth or glory. The text calls it a heavenly treasure beyond the reach of thief, rust, and moth, while the speaker begs the friend to accept the verses and keep sending his own in return. The appendix ends with short fragmentary pieces, including lines on a festival day for Florus and a broken invocation of Christ as witness.
la.glass.washingtonii_vita: Washingtonii Vita is a prose Latin life of George Washington by Francis Glass, an Ohio schoolmaster who composed the text for school use in 1824. He died before its publication in 1842, and the editor's lengthy English preface recounts finding Glass teaching classics in a log schoolhouse near Lebanon, Ohio. The Latin narrative traces Washington from his Virginia birth in 1732 and years as a surveyor, following his embassy to the French and Braddock's defeat through the Revolution. The account covers battles from Lexington and Bunker Hill to Trenton, Princeton, and Yorktown in 1781, closing with Washington's resignation, presidency, and death in 1799. It also includes sketches of other commanders, and an appendix on teaching ancient languages concludes the work.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.liber_ad_constantium_: The Liber ad Constantium Imperatorem is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Hilary of Poitiers, which serves as a theological defense addressed directly to the emperor Constantius. Hilary protests that his exile results from faction and false synodal reports rather than any crime, citing the emperor's Caesar, Julian, as a witness to his cause. The plea widens into an attack on creeds composed since the synod of Nicaea, arguing that these successive novelties have undermined the baptismal confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The author charges that Marcellus, Photinus, Sabellius, and Montanus speak the scriptures without their sense, and he also includes Manichaeus and Marcion in this list of misinterpreters. The work ends by asking to be heard before the synod now disputing over the faith, setting out a creed confessing one God the Father, from whom are all things. It also confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, the image and word of God, who was born before eternal times and incarnate of the Virgin.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.ad_leonem_papa: A Latin work of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and addressed to Pope Leo, retelling the biblical history of creation and early humankind. It opens with a dedication to the pontiff, announcing a song of thanks to God the omnipotent father, the origin and source of all things. The narrative moves from primordial chaos through the days of creation, the separation of sky, land and waters, the sun, moon and constellations with their guidance for farmers and sailors, the springing up of plants and the birth of animals, to the making of man in the divine image, endowed with reason, speech, memory of the past and foreknowledge, and given dominion over the world. After the transgression of the forbidden tree brings mortality and a race increasingly given to war, perjury and fraud, the work recounts the flood that washes away the world's crime and the preservation of Noah, prefiguring the church and the coming baptism, and closes with the renewed people, boys unharmed among flames and lions, and kings and prophets praising God, while the remnants of the ancient poison await cleansing by better waters from a better teacher.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_martyrio_ma: This late Latin poem, of uncertain date, is transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, and it recounts the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under Antiochus, king of Syria. The narrative opens with Antiochus failing to win the mother over through promises of gold and treasure, then turning to torments that leave her defiant. The greater part of the work is a sequence of martyrdoms in which each son refuses the king's commands, and encouraged by a speech from his mother, each dies unafraid in the flames. Her address invokes the patriarchs Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, and Jacob, and it also recalls God's wonders, from the crossing of the Red Sea to the water struck from the rock. The poem closes with the ordeal of the youngest and only remaining boy, and it ends with the mother's own collapse and death, and the reception of her and her sons among the saints.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.epistula_ad_ab: This late antique Latin prose letter, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, is addressed to his beloved daughter Abra, who receives an excuse for a long absence. The writer recounts a journey to seek a marvellous garment and pearl, prostrating himself before a beautiful young man after travelling many difficult roads. He weeps and prays until shown a garment finer than silk, snow, or gold, and a pearl surpassing heaven, sea, and earth. A bystander explains that the garment never wears out, while the pearl preserves its wearer from sickness, age, and death. The young man consents to grant both only to a daughter who renounces dyed, silken, and gilded clothing, and all other jewels. The father urges Abra to refuse such adornments, sends morning and evening hymns to keep him in her memory, and promises to reveal the youth's identity once she has written back.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_operibus_sex_di: Hildebert of Lavardin composed this medieval Latin poem, De Operibus Sex Dierum, to offer an allegorical reading of the six days of creation. The text begins with the Almighty making heaven and earth, then proceeds day by day, interpreting each Genesis event as a figure of spiritual reality. The first light represents the faith that follows baptism, while the firmament stands for Scripture, and dry land and sea symbolize the just and the wicked. Plants serve as teachers, the sun and moon figure Christ and the Church, respectively, and creatures of the fifth and sixth days reflect the motions of man's outer and inner life. Humanity, made in the divine image, receives the gift of reason, and the poem closes with the seventh day, explaining God's rest as the cessation of new creation. It ends by contrasting divine bounty with human labor undertaken for the sake of rest.
la.hrabanus.de_imagine_caesaris: This short Carolingian Latin poem, attributed to Hrabanus, is titled De imagine Caesaris, meaning 'On the Image of Caesar'. It opens with a prayer to Christ, the king of kings, who absolved human sins through the cross. The text then addresses a ruler styled Caesar and Augustus, whose image stands armed in faith before the work. This depiction shows his God-granted dominion over the whole world, including the homage and gifts of nations such as Greeks and Persians. The emperor also appears as protector of the flock under divine guardianship, and the author closes by offering his libellum to the emperor. This work is composed in both verse and prose.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carminum_appendix: The Carminum Appendix is a brief collection of Latin poems attributed to the Carolingian scholar John Scotus Eriugena. It opens with verses on the weaving of a sindon, a cloth wrought with gems and golden thread. The image of Christ's body on this fabric is promised to guard its beholder from blows, bonds, and hunger. The collection then turns to a lament on Rome, once built by noble patrons but now subjected to slaves. Its name and honour have passed to the Greeks, while Constantinople flourishes as the new Rome. The final lines charge Rome with pride, avarice, and trafficking in false relics.
la.lactantius.fragmenta: This volume gathers Latin fragments and testimonia for Lactantius, a late-antique Christian writer whom Jerome describes as a rhetoric teacher at Nicomedia under Diocletian. He later instructed Crispus in Latin letters, and the collection opens with Jerome quoting the third book of Lactantius's letters to Probus. This passage traces the Galatians to the milk-white Gauls named by the Sibyl and Vergil, while remaining excerpts from Jerome and Rufinus preserve remnants of letters to Probus, Demetrianus, and Severus. These treat comic metre and the Holy Spirit, and a fragment on the affections of the soul comes from an Ambrosian codex. A metrical remark reported by Victorinus and a Vergilian scholion citing Firmianus as a commentator are also included, and a Greek preface to the Sibylline oracles names Firmianus and quotes a Sibylline acrostic. Biographical and evaluative notices from Jerome, the chroniclers, Damasus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Sidonius, Gennadius, and papal decretals close the collection, covering his life, works, eloquence, and doctrine.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_regibus_ap: Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, wrote this Latin treatise to address the emperor Constantius. He regards the ruler as an apostate and an Arian. The work opens by announcing a comparison with ancient kings who were similarly cruel. Lucifer aims to refute the emperor's boast that his long reign proves divine favor. Biblical examples such as Gideon, Saul, Solomon, and Jeroboam show that wicked rulers often prospered for years. This pattern suggests that survival on the throne is no evidence of God's approval. The text closes with exhortations for Constantius to repent and return to the faith confessed at Nicaea.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_2: Carmina 2 is the second book of poems by the late antique writer Magnus Felix Ennodius, whose title simply means poems, a common label for such collections. It opens with an epitaph for a young man of good family who died in his twentieth year, and much of the book celebrates churches, their founders, and their ornament. The basilica of Saint Lawrence receives particular attention, as do inscriptions for various donors, while praise is offered to bishops and aristocrats such as Ambrose, Simplicianus, Senator, and Boethius. Satirical attacks on named enemies, including a man falsely calling himself Virgil, also appear, and epigrams on animals, gifts, and vices, along with occasional prose prefaces, complete the collection.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.eucharisticum_de_v: The Eucharisticum de vita sua, a Late Antique prose work by Magnus Felix Ennodius, frames an autobiographical account as a confession and thanksgiving to God. It opens with a meditation on weakness and contrition as paths to divine restoration, before Ennodius recounts his youthful absorption in secular rhetoric and poetry. A grave fever directed him toward the martyr Victor, prompting a vow to renounce worldly writing, while later episodes include his orphaning at sixteen during Theodoric's entry into Italy. He also describes an arranged marriage, his pride, and the ecclesiastical office that corrected him, closing with an appeal to Victor and praise of his wife's piety.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.praeceptum_quando_: This brief Latin prose decree by Magnus Felix Ennodius is cast as an instruction to all bishops, carrying the authority of the apostolic see in its opening address. The text begins with a disquisition on the man schooled in divine discipline, arguing that detraction cannot extinguish the brightness of an innocent life. The argument then turns to the duty of pastors to cut away occasions for scandal, a shift prompted by a recent violent uprising against the bishop of the apostolic see. The author also notes the danger that the careless and solitary may fall under false accusation, so the operative ruling forbids any bishop, priest, or lower cleric to dwell alone. It commands that all their dealings be open rather than clandestine, prohibiting them from keeping women in their households beyond those the canons allow. The decree threatens offenders with the loss of their honours, and those who give rise to suspicion are themselves censured as at fault.
la.nepos.vitae: Cornelius Nepos, a Roman writer of the Republican period, composed this Latin collection of prose biographies focusing on outstanding commanders in a brief and anecdotal style. An opening preface addressed to Atticus defends the author's attention to Greek customs, explaining that these practices might seem improper or humble to Roman readers. He then announces his design for writing about excellent generals, and the ensuing lives cover Greek commanders such as Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristides, and Cimon. Other figures include Lysander, Alcibiades, Thrasybulus, and Conon, along with Dion and Iphicrates, while the collection also features Chabrias, Timotheus, Epaminondas, and Pelopidas. Agesilaus and Eumenes are included, and Phocion and Timoleon are joined by the Persian Datames in this extensive roster. A compact survey of Persian and Macedonian kings follows, including the successors of Alexander, and fuller lives of Hamilcar and Hannibal then appear in the text. The work closes with the Romans M. Cato and T. Pomponius Atticus, ending with the reflection that character shapes fortune.
la.orientius_saint.carmina: The Carmina ('Songs') of Saint Orientius is a small late-antique collection of Latin Christian poems. It opens with a brief piece on the Nativity of the Lord, presenting the day of Christ's birth as outshining every other day of the year. There follows a catalogue of the Saviour's names and titles, door, lion, word and shepherd among many others. The greater part of the work elaborates these in a long poem on the Trinity, which moves through Christ's divinity, his passion and the triumph of the cross. The Trinity poem includes a symbolic reading of the Greek letters of the crucifix, and a verse-by-verse explanation then takes up each epithet in turn. The collection closes with a passage of praise that turns into direct prayer, as the poet calls himself unworthy and begs Christ for mercy on himself and his own.
la.orientius_saint.commonitorium: The Commonitorium is a Late Antique Christian didactic poem attributed to Orientius, which serves as moral instruction for those who seek eternal life. It opens by inviting the reader to learn the way to heaven, while a prayer to Christ asks for the eloquence needed to teach this path. The first book expounds the two lives granted to humankind, detailing the love of God and neighbour. The text warns at length against lust, envy, and avarice, drawing examples from biblical history. The second book turns to vainglory and restraint in speech, also addressing gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly ambition. The poem meditates on the brevity of life and the approach of death, closing with a vivid account of the Last Judgement. This section describes the punishments of the wicked and the blessedness of the righteous, ending with a plea for the reader to remember him in prayer.
la.paschasius_radbertus.epitaphium_arsenii: This Carolingian prose dialogue by Paschasius Radbertus opens with three speakers resolving to finish an epitaph for their deceased father, Arsenius. The text unfolds as a sustained lament and defence of his life, recounting his fearless remonstrances before the emperor, bishops, and senators against ecclesiastical corruption. It also details his denunciation of the adulterous tyranny that endangered Augustus and his sons, followed by a series of exiles, including a cavern in the Alps and a remote island. He later undertakes a hazardous journey to assist the pope in reconciling the imperial family, but after that mediation fails, he withdraws to the monastery of St. Columbanus in Italy. The dialogue closes with his burial beside the saint and meditations on the good of death, ending with a report to Queen Ermengard that nuns at Brescia heard angelic choirs bearing his soul to heaven.
la.paulinus_petricordiae.de_vita_sancti_mar: The De Vita Sancti Martini of Paulinus of Périgueux (Petricordiae) is a late-antique Latin epic in six books recounting the life, miracles, and afterlife of Martin of Tours. It opens with a prose epistle in which the poet, replying to the bishop who commissioned the work, excuses the presumption of versifying an account of the saint's merits and pledges obedience to the task. The verse narrative then traces Martin from his Pannonian birth and unwilling military service, through his conversion, the famous division of the cloak, his association with Hilary of Poitiers and his life as hermit and monk, to his episcopate at Tours, his confrontations with pagan cult, demons, and emperors, and his many miracles of healing, exorcism, and rescue, closing with the wonders worked at his tomb, from which the city of Tours rejoices in its bishop for ever.
la.paulus_orosius.commonitorium_de_errore_p: Paulus Orosius addresses a revered bishop in this brief Latin prose memorandum of theology, apologizing for his boldness in cataloging heresies. He asks that their malign plantings be uprooted, detailing doctrines attributed to Priscillian, including the descent of souls through circles. The work describes their imprisonment in bodies under a chirograph annulled by Christ, citing Priscillian's own letter and a book called Memoria apostolorum in support. Orosius then reports teachings linked to Origen, such as the eternal existence of creation in God's wisdom, which include a single substance shared by angels, souls, and demons. The text also notes a purgatorial and non literal eternal fire, and Orosius closes by assuring the bishop that he has recorded only what he could retain. He petitions the addressee to hasten the remedy for the plague of error.
la.petrus_of_pisa.carmina: This short collection of medieval Latin verses is attributed to Petrus of Pisa, a poet of the Carolingian court. Its opening lines form a hymn to Christ as creator and redeemer, born before the ages, who conquered hell and led the lost to paradise. The remainder addresses a Paul described as the most learned of poets and teachers, praising his command of Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters and thanking him for instruction in grammar. Later pieces exchange verses with him and set him three riddling questions to be answered by letter. A dawn vision follows in which a beautiful youth propounds a riddle about what a father gives the son, alongside gnomic maxims on restraint of tongue and peace between brothers. The sequence closes with a prayer that God preserve Charlemagne, whose prosperous sceptre the poems celebrate and whose daughter's journey overseas to a kingdom they record.
la.plautus.asinaria: The Asinaria ('The Comedy of Asses') is a Latin comedy by Plautus from the Roman Republic. It is written in dramatic verse and follows a specific plot structure. The prologue names the Greek model, the Onagos of Demophilus, and the translator Maccus. It also explains the title before the dialogue begins between Demaenetus and his slave Libanus. The story centers on Demaenetus helping his son Argyrippus secure the courtesan Philaenium. He and the slaves Libanus and Leonida raise money while hiding the scheme from his wife.
la.plautus.mostellaria: The Mostellaria, a Latin comedy by Plautus from the Roman Republic, opens with the slave Tranio driving the rustic Grumio from the kitchen. His young master Philolaches has squandered the estate during his father's three year absence, and the father Theopropides returns unexpectedly to find the household in disarray. Tranio fends him off with a fiction that the house is haunted by a ghost, sustaining this deception through trickery involving a moneylender and the neighbour Simo. When the truth emerges, Tranio takes sanctuary at an altar, and the friend Callidamates then wins reconciliation between the father and son. The father at last pardons the slave.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_montibus_sina_et_sion_: A pseudonymous Latin treatise on the two mountains Sinai and Sion, written against the Jews and transmitted under Cyprian's name, of later imperial date. It opens with a probatio capitulorum declaring that what was written figuratively in the Old Testament must be understood spiritually in the New, through its fulfilment in Christ. The main argument, carried forward in prose through paraphrase and quotation of scripture, opposes the earthly Sinai, whence the law was given to the carnal people of the Jews, to the heavenly Sion, which the author identifies with the wood of the cross, whence the law went forth to the Christians; along the way it offers etymologies of Hebrew names from Adam to Moses, reads Rebecca's twins as synagogue and church, interprets the two thieves as the two peoples, and expounds the Passion, Pilate's trilingual titulus, and the heavenly Jerusalem. A closing figurative comparison likens Christ, crucified on high, to a boy set on a scaffold in a vineyard with a mirror of reeds, guarding God's vine, the Christian people, against the marauding devil.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_pascha_computus: This short Latin prose treatise, transmitted among the works attributed to Cyprian, addresses the calculation of Easter in the later imperial period. The author begins by describing an anxious search of the divine scriptures to seek the first day of the new month for the Passover. The argument proceeds from the separation of light and darkness in Genesis, and it also draws on the institutions of Exodus to establish the true first day. A table fixes the dates of the fourteenth moon and both Easters, using a sixteen-year cycle extended through seven sedecennitates to 112 years. The work reckons the years from the Exodus to Christ, tracing this period through the judges and kings, and it also covers the seventy years of captivity. The rebuilding of the temple in the mystic number of Adam is included, and the seventy weeks of Daniel are expounded of the restoration.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.notitia_provincia: The Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae, a Late Antique Latin work, is preserved under the name of Victor of Vitensis. It opens by announcing the names of catholic bishops who came to Carthage by royal command. These leaders arrived in the sixth year of the Vandal king Huneric to render an account of their faith. The body of the work lists these bishops see by see and province by province. It covers Proconsular Africa, Mauretania Caesariensis, Mauretania Sitifensis, and Tripolitana, followed by exiles on Sardinia. Head counts are appended to each roll, with notes of sees left without bishops. A concluding tally sums the whole episcopate and distinguishes those who perished, were relegated to Corsica, remained in their sees, or fled.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae: The Epistulae of Salvian of Marseilles is a small collection of late-antique Latin prose letters that opens with a meditation on love, which is at once good and evil, sweet and harsh. This reflection leads into an appeal for a young kinsman taken captive at Agrippina, whom the author commends to the charity and material aid of the addressees. The remaining letters are largely short notes of recommendation, apology, and courtesy addressed to clerical and lay correspondents, including the bishops Eucherius and Agroecius. Other recipients include Ursicinus, Hypatius, Quieta, Palladia, Auspiciola, Cattura, Limenius, Apro, Verus, and Salonius, whose subjects cover breaches of epistolary etiquette and the spiritual profit of bodily sickness. They also discuss proper humility in exchanging letters with superiors and thanks for books received, while the collection closes with a long letter to Salonius. It defends the libelli addressed to the church that bear Timothy's name, explaining why he wrote for the whole church and concealed his own name out of humility. He chose Timothy's name as expressing the honour of God and thereby escaped the suspicion of apocrypha.
la.sedulius_scotus.carminum_appendix: This short Carolingian Latin poem, attributed to Sedulius Scotus, opens with lines on the two laws that war within a person. The bad law rules the body, while the good law resists in the mind. The text then unfolds as a dream vision on a dark night, where a radiant maiden of towering stature appears to the weary poet. She names herself Wisdom, which is Sophia among the Greeks, and she is also called sapientia among the Latins. The maiden bids the dreamer visit the house of Guntarius, reciting at length the praises of this venerable bishop. He is described as gentle, humble, and generous, serving as the chosen shepherd of his flock. The bishop mortifies the flesh and delights in the study of wisdom, enjoying the pages of scripture and songs to God. He provides for the poor, the blind, and the lame, and he is a man of noble Frankish descent. Near the close, the vision recalls the twin laws of human nature, and the verse breaks off in the midst of the bishop's encomium.
la.seneca.de_brevitate_vitae: A philosophical prose treatise of the early imperial period by Seneca, addressed to Paulinus, arguing that life is long enough for anyone who spends it well and short only for the 'occupied.' It opens with the common complaint that nature grants too brief a span and immediately rebuts it with the claim that people are prodigal, not poor, in time. The argument proceeds through portraits of wasted lives, Augustus craving leisure amid power, Cicero calling himself 'semifree,' busy officials, devotees of luxury and grooming, antiquarian pedants, and turns to praise of the sage, who by communing with past thinkers possesses all the ages. It closes with a direct exhortation to Paulinus to withdraw from administering the public grain supply to higher study, illustrated by the elderly S. Turannius, who feigned death rather than give up his duties.
la.seneca.de_otio: De Otio, a Latin prose treatise by the philosopher Seneca, survives in incomplete form and opens mid-sentence with a defense of withdrawal from public affairs. This retreat offers a path to moral consistency and release from popular judgment, asking whether the sage may rightly retire from civic duties. The text contrasts the Stoic view that the wise man engages in public life unless prevented with the Epicurean choice of withdrawal on principle. Seneca concludes that both sects lead to leisure by different roads, distinguishing the greater commonwealth that embraces gods and humans from the particular city of one's birth. Corruption in the local city may justify such retreat, as one serves humanity in leisure by investigating virtue, God, and the cosmos. Nature made humans for both action and contemplation, and closing passages argue that contemplation benefits posterity, citing Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes as men whose teaching served all humankind more than armies, offices, or laws.
la.severus_sulpicius.epistulae_tres: The three epistles of Sulpicius Severus, a Christian writer of Late Antiquity, are addressed to the venerable Bassula and centre throughout on Martin, bishop of Tours. Opening the collection is a reply to a detractor who mocked Martin for nearly perishing in a house fire. In answer, Sulpicius retells the episode in full and compares the bishop's trial with the Apostle Paul's shipwreck and serpent. The second letter recounts Martin's foreknowledge of his end, his last days during a visitation, his death, and his solemn funeral procession, attended by monks and crowds. After Martin's passing, the third records the author's grief and the dream vision in which the saint appears to console him with promises of his continuing presence.
la.sulpicius_severus.dialogi: The Dialogi, meaning 'Dialogues', is a Late Antique Latin prose work in dialogue form featuring conversations among the author, his friend Postumianus, and Gallus, a disciple of Martin of Tours. The text opens with Postumianus returning from three years in the East, and the three friends reunite joyfully at a secluded retreat. Postumianus then narrates his journey through Carthage, Alexandria, Bethlehem, and the Egyptian desert, describing the Origenist controversy, a stay with Jerome, and many miracles performed by monks, hermits, and even animals. Gallus answers with an extended account of the virtues and miracles of Martin of Tours, detailing Martin's clashes with imperial officials and doubting clergy, as well as his prophecies of the end times. This presentation casts Martin as a match for the ascetics of the East, and the work closes with Postumianus charged to carry Martin's fame to Paulinus and the churches of the East. He is also told to visit the grave of the dead Pomponius, and the friends part in tears.
la.terence.hecyra: The Hecyra, meaning The Mother-in-Law, is a Latin comedy written in dramatic metre by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic. He opens the work with a prologue in his own person, recalling how the play twice lost its audience to rope-dancers and gladiators. The poet pleads for a quiet hearing now that the stage is free, and the plot follows Pamphilus, who marries Philumena while still devoted to the courtesan Bacchis. He leaves for Imbros soon after the wedding, and his wife withdraws to her mother's house, claiming illness but actually concealing a pregnancy begun before her marriage. Quarrels between the two mothers-in-law, Sostrata and Myrrhina, embroil both households, and a ring torn from Philumena by her assailant in the dark is identified as one given by Pamphilus. This proves him the father of her child, and in an unusual turn, Bacchis brings reconciliation by swearing an oath that she has kept apart from Pamphilus since his marriage, reuniting the families around the newborn son.
la.tertullian.ad_nationes_libri_duo: Ad Nationes is a two-book Latin apologetic treatise by the late-antique theologian Tertullian, which addresses the pagan nations in defence of Christianity. The work argues that hatred of Christians stems from the accusers' own ignorance, and those who learn the name often cease to hate it and embrace the faith. Book one replies to charges of infanticide, incest, and ritual crime, turning these accusations back on Greek and Roman practice. The text also defends Christian steadfastness under torture, which is grounded in hope of resurrection and judgment. Book two attacks pagan religion directly, arguing that the gods were merely men deified after death. The author exposes contradictions in philosophical, poetic, and civic theology, ridiculing the Roman apparatus of cult from Saturn and Jupiter down to tutelary spirits, while denying that the empire's dominion was a reward for piety.
la.tertullian.adversus_praxean: Tertullian wrote this Latin polemic in late antiquity to refute the view that the Father suffered on the cross, defending a single divine monarchy ordered through a threefold economy of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It opens by denouncing Praxeas for expelling the new prophecy at Rome and thus crucifying the Father, then establishing the Word as a second person of one substance with the Father. He supports this claim with analogies of root and shoot, source and stream, and sun and ray, while reviewing Genesis, the Psalms, the prophets, and the Gospel of John for evidence of distinct yet inseparable persons. Closing chapters treat the appearances of God under the patriarchs and in the Gospel, examining the conjoined divine and human substances in Christ and the sense of the name Christ. The text distinguishes the suffering of the flesh from that of the divinity, identifying the Spirit as the third name and grade of divinity. These points mark the difference between Christian confession and Jewish monotheism.
la.tertullian.apologeticum: The Apologeticum is a Latin prose apology for Christianity by Tertullian, addressed to the magistrates of the Roman empire. It opens with a plea for a fair hearing rather than condemnation based solely on the name of the faith. Tertullian argues the case at length by exposing the injustice of punishing without inquiry, refuting charges of infanticide, incest, and disloyalty to the emperor. The work also contends that pagan gods were mortal men or deceiving demons, defending the antiquity and truth of the Hebrew and Christian scriptures. The author describes Christian worship, charity, and communal life, ending with an account of resurrection and judgement. It concludes with the steadfastness of martyrs, whose blood Tertullian calls the seed of Christians.
la.tertullian.de_baptismo: De Baptismo ('On Baptism') is a Latin prose treatise by Tertullian on the sacrament of baptism, composed in Late Antiquity. It opens by celebrating the 'happy sacrament' of water and denouncing a recent heretical teacher who had been drawing followers away by undermining the rite. The argument establishes the dignity of water from creation, the flood, and the crossing of the Red Sea, defending baptism's necessity against those who would rest salvation on faith alone. The treatise then takes up John's baptism, whether Christ and the apostles were baptized, the single administration of the sacrament, and the 'second' baptism of blood through martyrdom. The latter part turns to discipline and practice, weighing who may administer baptism and the advisability of delaying it for the young and the unmarried. It also covers the proper days for the rite and preparation through prayer and fasting, ending with an appeal for prayer on the author's own behalf.
la.tertullian.de_oratione: De Oratione is a late-antique Latin theological treatise by Tertullian that examines the form and discipline of Christian prayer. The author presents the prayer taught by Christ as a new form suited to the new covenant, grounded in the Word, Spirit, and Reason of God. This prayer comprises in brief the whole gospel, and the work expounds the petitions of the Lord's Prayer one by one. These include the hallowing of the divine name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, the remission of debts, and deliverance from temptation. The text takes up accessory questions of observance, including reconciliation, purity, posture, dress, the kiss of peace, stations, veiling, kneeling, fixed hours, and psalms. A closing encomium celebrates the power of Christian prayer, describing this practice as a spiritual sacrifice that prevails with God.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_iona_propheta: This later-imperial Latin theological work of uncertain authorship has been transmitted under Tertullian's name. It opens with the living deaths of Sodom and Gomorrah and asks how sinful Nineveh might escape a like punishment, before God commands Jonah to preach its destruction. Jonah flees by ship from Joppa toward Tarsos, and God raises a storm in pursuit. The sailors jettison their cargo and pray to their gods while Jonah confesses his guilt and, at his own urging, is cast into the sea. A great sea creature swallows him alive, yet the storm subsides and the sailors offer their sacrifices in gratitude. Jonah remains untouched by the waters within the creature's belly, kept there as a sign of the Lord and the glory of heaven.
la.tibullus.elegies: The Latin elegiac corpus transmitted under the name of Tibullus belongs to the Augustan age, comprising three books of erotic and occasional elegies. Book 1 opens with a prayer to the Lares contrasting rural poverty with wealth, then follows the poet's devotion to Delia and his servitude to the boy Marathus. The volume also celebrates his patron Messalla, including a song for the Egyptian festival of Osiris. Book 2 introduces Nemesis as a new and grasping mistress, adding festival hymns and a birthday poem for Cornutus. Verses on Messalla's son Messalinus and the omens of his day also appear here. The third book is the work of several hands besides Tibullus, containing six elegies under the name Lygdamus on his beloved Neaera. An anonymous hexameter panegyric of Messalla is also included, followed by a cycle concerning Sulpicia and her lover Cerinthus. Six short elegies in Sulpicia's own voice are present, and a closing epitaph for Tibullus pairs his death with Virgil's in the fields of Elysium.
la.vergil_pseudo.copa: The Copa, meaning the barmaid, is a brief Latin lyric poem from the Augustan period, handed down among works attributed to Vergil, though its authorship remains disputed. Scholars conventionally class it as the product of a pseudo-Vergilian imitator, and the poem opens with a Syrian barmaid dancing drunkenly in a smoky tavern. Her head is bound in a Greek headband as she sways to the castanets, then invites a weary traveller to enjoy the inn's pleasures. These include rough wine, running water, and various flowers and fruits, while the shade of the arbour and the sound of a shepherd's pipe also feature. The closing lines press the invitation with an admonition to drink and crown the head now, warning against hoarding garlands for ungrateful ashes. Death itself whispers that one should live, for it is coming.
la.vergil_pseudo.culex: The Culex, meaning the gnat, is a short Latin epic in hexameters attributed to Virgil and of Augustan date. It opens with a playful dedication to the young Octavius, acknowledging a lighter strain than warfare and giants demand. The narrative relates how a shepherd sleeping at noon among his grazing goats is roused by the sting of a gnat. Just as a huge serpent is about to seize him, he kills the serpent while unwittingly crushing his tiny rescuer. In a dream, the gnat's ghost appears, bewails its death, and rehearses the lower world at length. It describes punished giants, mythological transgressors, the tale of Orpheus and Eurydice, and the heroes of Troy. The ghost also recounts the noble dead of Roman history before departing. The shepherd then raises a burial mound, plants it with flowers, and sets an epitaph in the gnat's honor.
la.vergil_pseudo.lydia: Lydia is a short Latin lyric poem from the Augustan age, preserved under Vergil's name, though its authorship remains uncertain. The speaker begins by envying the meadows where his beloved now plays and sings, then laments his own wasting away in separation from her. He congratulates the bull and he-goat whose mates stay close to them, while upbraiding Nature, the moon, and Phoebus for denying him such companionship. He cites the liaisons of Jupiter, Mars, and Aurora as proof of a kinder age, closing with the lament that he was born too late into a harsher world.
la.victor_claudius_marius.alethia: The Alethia, a late antique Latin epic by Claudius Marius Victor, offers a versified retelling of Genesis in three books. It opens with an invocation to the triune God as the source of all being, and it includes a prayer for aid in teaching young souls the world's origin. The first book narrates the six days of creation and the formation of Adam and Eve, covering life in Paradise, the temptation, the Fall, and the judgment of the first parents. The second book follows their expulsion into a barren earth and their prayers for relief, detailing the discovery of metals, Cain's murder of Abel, and the spread of violence among giants. Noah's ark and the flood conclude this section, while the third book takes up Noah's sacrifice and covenant, along with the curse of Ham. It traces the origins of idolatry, magic, and divination, and the tower of Babel and the confusion of tongues follow these events. The narrative continues with the call and wanderings of Abraham, describing his meeting with Melchisedech after the war of the kings. The poem ends with the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, down to Lot's wife and the salt lake.
la.victor_claudius_marius.commentariorum_in: The Commentariorum in Genesim Libri Tres is a late antique Latin epic in three books that retells the early narrative of Genesis and is attributed to Claudius Marius Victor. This orator of Massilia, or Marseille, is named in the work's headings, and the text opens with a prefatory prayer to God that praises the Trinity. It invokes divine aid to set forth the origin of the world from Moses's writings, and Book 1 narrates the six days of creation and the fashioning of Adam and Eve. It also describes the delights of paradise and its four rivers, while the fall and expulsion of the first parents conclude this section. Book 2 follows their life after Eden through Cain's murder of Abel, covering the spread of wickedness and Noah's ark amid the flood. Book 3 treats Noah's covenant and the curse of Ham, including the tower of Babel and the confusion of tongues, and the work closes with Abraham's call, journeys, and covenant, detailing his circumcision and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.
la.victorinus.de_machabeis: The De Machabeis is a Latin poem from the Later Imperial period, attributed to Victorinus, which retells the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under the Syrian king Antiochus. The narrative opens with Antiochus using promises and then torments to force the family to abandon their law, while the sons are killed one by one in fire, each strengthened by their mother's exhortations. Her words recall creation, the patriarchs from Abraham through Jacob, and God's delivery of Israel from Egypt, as the king's fury and the hesitation of his ministers punctuate this sequence. After the youngest boy casts himself into the flames, the exhausted mother collapses and dies, and her soul is received with her sons among the saints.
la.walafrid_strabo.vita_sancti_galli_confes: Walafrid Strabo composed this Latin verse life of the Irish missionary saint Gall, whose prologue addressed to Gozbert announces the fulfilment of an old promise. It recasts Gall's earlier prose deeds into metrical form, recounting his journey from Ireland as a companion of Columbanus. The poem describes the mission to the Alamanni and their expulsion, which was forced by hostility from Brunihild and the king. The narrative then covers the stay at Arbona on Lake Constance, where illness kept Gall behind when Columbanus departed for Italy. He then led a solitary life of asceticism, exorcisms, and miracles, later telling of the healing and consecration of Gunzo's daughter. Gall refused the see of Constance and the abbacy of Luxeuil, and the text details the building of his church. It concludes with his death in old age and posthumous miracles, including a bier that only untamed horses could move. His hair shirt and bloodstained chain were also discovered.
la.wandalbert.de_mensium_nominibus: De Mensium Nominibus, a Carolingian didactic poem by Wandalbert, traces the origins of the twelve month names and their zodiac signs. The text details seasonal work that sustains land and livelihood, moving from January to December while linking each month to Roman figures. It describes tasks like ploughing, sowing, and the pruning of vines, with later sections covering harvest, the vintage, and the fattening of swine. The closing lines note that Gallic lands preserve these customs, and Wandalbert states he wrote at a friend's urging near Cologne.
la.alcuin.carmina_rhytmica: This Carolingian Latin collection of rhythmical verse is attributed to Alcuin, opening with a hymn to God the creator. It proceeds through an alphabetical series of couplets, each beginning with a successive letter from A to Z. The doctrinal couplets treat creation, the Trinity, and the incarnation, while also addressing the motherhood of the Virgin and the Passion. A middle group of penitential prayers confesses sin in detail, begging cleansing and protection from the devil. These prayers appeal to Christ as both saviour and judge, and the collection closes with polemical verses. These verses set orthodox teaching against several heresiarchs, including Arius, Sabellius, Manichaeus, Photinus, Nestorius, and Eutyches.
la.anonymous.itinerarium_hierosolymitanum: The Itinerarium Burdigalense ('Bordeaux Itinerary') is an anonymous Latin prose record of a journey from Bordeaux to Jerusalem and back. It lists road stations, distances in miles, and the changing points and overnight halts between them. The outward route runs through Gaul and northern Italy, crosses the Alps and the Balkan provinces to Constantinople, and then leads through Asia Minor and Syria into Palestine. At Jerusalem and its environs the text slows to fuller prose, describing the city's pools and the site of the former temple. It also details the places of the crucifixion and resurrection, the Mount of Olives, Bethlehem, Jericho, the Jordan, and Hebron, together with the biblical events attached to each. A consular notice dates the return journey to the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus in 333. The route then passes through Macedonia, crosses by sea from Aulona to Brindisi, and makes its way through Italy to Rome and finally Milan, with summary totals of stations and mileage closing each stretch.
la.augustine.de_dialectica: De dialectica ('On Dialectic') is a short Late Antique Latin prose treatise attributed to Augustine. It defines dialectic as the science of disputing well and the art of disputation. The text divides words into simple and conjoined forms, framing these as the matter and working of the discipline. It then distinguishes between word, thing, and sign, surveying the origin of words and Stoic claims about etymology. The main burden is classifying obscurity and ambiguity as impediments to judging truth. The surviving text breaks off while discussing ambiguity found only in writing.
la.augustine.libellus_adversus_fulgentium_d: This late-antique Latin treatise, attributed to Augustine, answers a libellus sent by the Donatist Fulgentius. The author resolves to reply using divine scripture, addressing claims about one baptism and one enclosed garden. The text also mentions one oil that dying flies corrupt, staging a point-by-point refutation as alternating speeches. Fulgentius's objections are answered under specific headings, where the author cites the Samaritan woman and the waters of Jericho. He also references the widow's vessel of oil and Haggai, arguing that baptism retains its force outside the Donatist communion. The text rehearses charges of traditio against named clerics, discussing the compulsion of schismatics and the rebaptizer as a pirate. The case of the Maximianists is also examined, and the work closes by appealing to Donatist decrees. It ends with the gospel saying on a divided kingdom.
la.cicero.academica: Academica ('Academic Questions') is a Latin philosophical dialogue by Cicero of the Roman Republic. It opens at Cumae, where Cicero, Atticus, and Varro meet and agree to discuss the history of the Academy in Latin. Varro speaks first, expounding the doctrine of the Old Academy as Antiochus taught it, presenting Plato, Aristotle, and the early Stoa as heirs of a single philosophy. He also sets out its teachings on the highest good, on nature, and on logical method. Cicero then answers on behalf of the sceptical New Academy, recounting Arcesilas's denial that anything can be known and Carneades's doctrine of the 'probable' as a sufficient guide for action. The dialogue breaks off unfinished, and the work survives only in fragmentary form.
la.cicero.pro_l_flacco: Cicero's defense speech for Lucius Flaccus is a Republican forensic oration in Latin prose, opening with an exordium pleading for a man who supported the consul during the Catilinarian crisis. Flaccus now faces extortion charges arising from his praetorship in Asia, and the body of the speech dismantles the prosecution's case in sequence. It attacks the reliability of Greek and Asiatic witnesses and their popular decrees, while the orator defends Flaccus's requisition of money for a fleet and his sequestration of Jewish gold. He also rebuts charges brought by Roman individuals such as Decianus, Lurco, and Falcidius, and the peroration widens the stakes to the condition of the republic. It presents the verdict as a judgment on all who suppressed the conspiracy, closing with an emotional appeal centered on Flaccus's young son.
la.cicero.pro_scauro: The Pro Scauro is a prose oration from the Roman Republic, where Cicero defended Marcus Aemilius Scaurus against charges regarding his provincial administration. Sardinian witnesses pressed accusations, most notably a grave charge concerning the grain levy, while the speech opens with Scaurus' wish to preserve his family's dignity without incurring hatred. It reviews his client's earlier prosecutions before addressing the deaths of Bostar of Nora and his wife, which the prosecution ascribed to poison and fear of violation. The core argument meets that charge by weighing conjecture and circumstance, considering the two explanations current in Sardinia for the woman's death. The orator digresses on voluntary death, citing Greek and Roman examples, and references Plato's teaching on the soul. Later portions discredit the Sardinian prosecutors as degenerate Phoenician stock, alleging their unanimous testimony was bought, while arraigning the haste and motives of the prosecutor Triarius and criticizing the presiding consul. The oration closes with an appeal to the temples and ancestral honours of the Scauri.
la.cyprian_pseudo.sodoma: This Latin poem of the later Roman Empire, transmitted under the name of Cyprian though its authorship is uncertain, retells the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah from Genesis. It opens with God's covenant after the Flood, the rainbow pledging that water would no longer destroy the world, before humankind's renewed wickedness calls instead for punishment by fire. The narrative follows Lot's hospitality to the two angelic visitors and the onslaught of the Sodomite mob. Lot's household is then urged to flee, and the poem traces his journey to Segor, the rain of sulphur and flame, and his wife's transformation into a pillar of salt. A final survey describes the ruined region's ash-covered fields and its bitumen-bearing waters, in which nothing floats and bodies cannot sink. The poem closes with the punishment as an enduring sign teaching unjust nations to fear God.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.de_vita_beati_anto: The De Vita Beati Antoni Monachi is a late-antique Latin prose biography written by Magnus Felix Ennodius for the abbot Leontius, who had commissioned it. The text opens with a preface where the author asks Leontius for prayer, arguing that written remembrance preserves the deeds of saints beyond their lifetimes. The narrative traces Antony's life from his birth at Valeria on the Danube in Pannonia, following his upbringing under Severinus and the bishop Constantius. Antony fled barbarian devastations to settle on a mountain above Lake Como, where he lived beside the shrine of the martyr Fidelis and exposed a hidden murderer. He also tamed a marauding bear before withdrawing to the island of Lérins, where Antony spent the final two years of his life.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carmina_figurata: Carmina Figurata ('Figured Songs') is a short sequence of Latin figure verses attributed to the Carolingian poet Milo of Saint Amand and addressed throughout to a King Charles. It opens with repeated petitions that Charles accept the poem with kindly favour, hailing him as one who holds his sceptre by God's eternal rule. This acclamation continues as the poems celebrate the king's justice, piety, and a dominion reaching to Thule. They describe their own verses as painted figures, including shapes of the cross, wrought in the poet's modest craft. The sequence also professes to record the blessed deeds of a beloved bishop's life and is composed in Amand's name. It closes with a farewell to the poet Milo and a prayer for mercy that names Haimo.
la.paulus_orosius.liber_apologeticus: The Liber Apologeticus, a late antique Latin prose treatise in theology by Paulus Orosius, opens with an address to the bishops excusing the author for speaking not from presumption but from the necessity of injury, as defender of his own faith and unmasker of another's error. The work is a polemic against Pelagius and Caelestius: it recounts the condemnation of Caelestius in Africa, Augustine's written reply to Pelagius, and Orosius's disputation in Jerusalem before Bishop John over the reported assertion that a man cannot be without sin even with God's help, a quarrel referred to the Roman see. Its bulk refutes the Pelagian claim that a person may live sinlessly in this life, marshalling scriptural figures such as Job, David, Solomon, Zechariah, Peter and Paul to argue that perfection is reserved for the resurrection, that God's aid operates continually in all times and among all peoples, and that human nature is weak rather than evil, with free will upheld. It closes with Orosius's confession that he hates heresy but not the heretic, and with an appeal for fraternal correction within the bond of the church.
la.petrus_diaconus.de_locis_santis: De locis sanctis is a medieval Latin prose treatise attributed to Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino, whose dedicatory prologue is addressed to Guibaldus, abbot of Monte Cassino and Stavelot. The author explains that the work was compiled from various books and the oral accounts of pilgrims who had visited the Holy Sepulchre, commending the little book to the abbot's approval. The body of the treatise surveys the sacred sites of Palestine and Egypt, beginning with the Holy Sepulchre, Golgotha, and the Temple precincts of Jerusalem. It then proceeds to Mount Sion, Bethlehem, Jericho, and the Jordan, continuing through the towns of Galilee and Samaria before concluding with Egypt. The final sections cover the route of the Exodus by the Red Sea and the mountains of Sinai and Horeb. Throughout, the author records the relics, churches, tombs, and monuments shown at each place, together with distances measured in miles.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae_selectio: This short Latin prose epistle by Salvian of Marseilles, a Christian writer of the late antique period, is addressed to an unnamed correspondent who has sent him books. Salvian opens by praising the volumes as brief in style yet abundant in teaching, composed above all for the instruction of his own sons. He has formed these young men, he says, as a temple to God crowned with doctrine. His prayer is that God will make them equal to the books and that their teaching may become the fruit of the churches. He asks as well that they bring credit both to the father who begot them and to those whom they have in turn instructed. The letter ends with a request that these former pupils stand as his daily intercessors, followed by an affectionate farewell.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_sodoma: De Sodoma, a short Latin hexameter poem, narrates the sin and punishment of Sodom. Transmitted under Tertullian's name, its authorship remains uncertain, and it belongs to the later imperial period. The poem opens with the flood that destroyed the first age of mankind, where God set a rainbow in the clouds as a pledge. It then turns to the renewed impiety of a second race of men, whose lusts against nature mark Sodom for destruction by fire rather than water. The narrative follows the arrival of two angelic youths at the gate, describing the hospitality of the righteous Lot. The Sodomite mob threatens an assault on the guests, and Lot offers his daughters in their stead. The divine decree of the city's annihilation follows, and his sons-in-law respond to this news with incredulous laughter.
la.vergil_pseudo.elegiae_in_maecenatem: The Elegiae in Maecenatem are two Latin laments for Maecenas, written as elegiac couplets and handed down under Vergil's name as pseudepigrapha of Augustan date. The first poem opens with the speaker declaring that he has lately bewailed a young man's fate in sad verse, and he now turns his songs to Maecenas, a deserving old man of Etruscan royal stock. The text praises Maecenas' loyalty to Caesar, his harmless candour, and his patronage of poets, while it recalls the battles of Philippi and Actium, along with the eastern war. Extended comparisons link Augustus to Bacchus and Hercules, and the speaker wishes for Medea's rejuvenating herb or the long days of Tithonus and Nestor. The poem ends with Maecenas' dying words of devotion to Augustus, and the second elegy is voiced in the person of Maecenas, who consoles Augustus with the promise of unending remembrance. The text closes with blessings on Augustus, Livia, and the Caesarian line.
la.ausonius.commemoratio_professorum_burdig: The Commemoratio Professorum Burdigalensium, a late antique Latin work by Ausonius, consists of memorial notices for deceased teachers of grammar and rhetoric in his native Bordeaux. The text opens with an invocation to men joined to the author by fame and a shared life of study. Ausonius undertakes to commemorate these figures after their deaths, and the body proceeds through individual encomia and laments for various teachers. These include celebrated rhetoricians, teachers of druidic lineage, and his uncle Arborius, while humble grammarians whose names might otherwise perish are also praised. Each notice highlights the subject's eloquence, character, and manner of death, and the work closes with a statement of the commemorative rule observed throughout. It offers a farewell to the spirits of the honoured dead, whose names should live on while their ashes rest.
la.cicero.de_amicitia: De Amicitia is a philosophical dialogue composed by Cicero during the Roman Republic, recording a discourse delivered by Gaius Laelius, a man renowned for his wisdom. The conversation takes place a few days after the death of his close friend Scipio Aemilianus, and Cicero opens with a prologue explaining his choice of Laelius as the speaker. Fannius and Scaevola, Laelius' sons-in-law, then visit him at home to draw him into conversation, and Laelius first addresses their concern over his grief for Scipio. He praises the dead man's life and death before discussing the nature of friendship, arguing that true bonds arise from affection rather than need or profit. Such ties exist only among good men and must never involve dishonourable acts, while private attachments remain subordinate to the welfare of the state. Laelius also considers the choice and testing of friends, noting the superiority of long-standing attachments and the menace of flattery, and he asserts that a failing friendship should be loosened rather than ruptured. The dialogue closes with Laelius' recollection of his enduring bond with Scipio.
la.cicero.topica: Cicero's Topica is a Republican prose treatise on rhetoric that opens with a preface to the jurist Gaius Trebatius. Trebatius found Aristotle's work obscure in Cicero's Tusculan library, so Cicero promised an account of its teaching. He wrote this text from memory during a sea voyage, defining a locus as the seat of an argument. The work surveys topics inherent in the subject, such as definition and partition, and covers extrinsic topics grounded in testimony and authority. Examples are drawn largely from Roman civil law, while the closing sections classify questions of cognition and action. They also address the three kinds of cause and legal disputes.
la.einhardus.rythmus_de_passione_marcellini: Einhard's Carolingian Latin poem, Rythmus de Passione Marcellini et Petri, recounts the passion of the Roman martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. The narrative opens with the exorcist Peter imprisoned in Rome, where his preaching and healings win over his jailer Artemius. Artemius' daughter is also freed from a demon, and the poem then narrates the saints' trial and torments before the judge Serenus. An angel offers consolations to the prisoners in their cell, while Artemius is martyred together with his wife Candida and daughter. Marcellinus and Peter are beheaded in a dark wood, where they clear the ground and die singing praise. The text closes with the burial of their remains near the tomb of Tiburtius, performed by the women Lucilla and Firmina, while the executioner Dorotheus is converted, and Pope Damasus is reported to have committed the story to writing.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.hymni: The Hymni attributed to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, gather Late Antique Latin hymns on Christian doctrine and the life of Christ. The collection opens with a hymn addressing Christ as existing before the ages, expounding the eternal generation of the Son from the Father and their unity. It also describes the creation of all things through him, while a second hymn, headed De resurrectione Christi, celebrates Christ's triumph over death and the underworld. This second piece also celebrates the believer's promised rising, and a third hymn, De tentationibus Christi, follows Satan's alarm at Christ's birth. It traces the beginning of the temptation before breaking off incomplete, and the collection closes with a hymn of doubtful attribution, Hymnum dicat turba fratrum. This final piece runs through the whole gospel narrative, moving from the virginal conception and nativity through the miracles, passion, and resurrection, ending with a summons to sing praise before dawn.
la.maffeo_veggio.aeneid: Maffeo Veggio composed this Renaissance Latin epic in hexameters, which takes up the story of Aeneas in Italy. It begins at the moment Turnus dies in single combat, and the Rutuli then submit to the Trojan victor. The narrative follows the aftermath of the war, detailing the funerals and laments for Turnus voiced by Latinus and his father Daunus. The text also describes the burning of Ardea, and an embassy led by Drances sues for peace. Latinus and Aeneas are eventually reconciled, and the marriage with Lavinia is celebrated with feasts. Songs of Trojan and Latin history are performed, and a flame shining over Lavinia's head is explained by Venus. She calls it an omen of future glory, and the poem closes with Latinus yielding the kingship. Venus washes away Aeneas's mortality in the Numicius, and he then ascends to the heavens as an Indiges.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.dictiones: The Dictiones of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a late-antique Latin prose collection of set speeches and rhetorical declamations. It opens with an elaborate congratulatory address to Bishop Laurentius of Milan on his consecration, praising his endurance through persecution, war, and the desolation of his city. The remaining pieces range over panegyrics and addresses for bishops, aristocrats, teachers, and pupils, including speeches of thanks and recommendation delivered at dedications, commencements, and other civic occasions. Alongside these stand purely fictitious school exercises on both sides of imaginary cases, such as the redemption of sons from pirates, the enslavement of captured priests and Vestal virgins, and accusations of parricide. Deliberative speeches are also cast in the voices of mythological figures like Medea, Dido, and Hercules.
