la.florus.vergilius_orator_an_poeta: Vergilius orator an poeta ('Vergil, Orator or Poet') is a short Latin prose dialogue attributed to Florus, an author of the early imperial period. The text opens with the narrator resting near a temple when a stranger, driven ashore while returning from Rome to Baetica, greets him. This visitor recognizes Florus as the winner of a poetic contest held under Domitian. The remainder of the work presents the narrator's account of his wanderings through Sicily, Crete, and Egypt. He also praises the provincial city where he has settled and defends teaching letters to boys. He argues that this office is as honourable as military command.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.de_sobrietate: De Sobrietate is a two-book Latin didactic poem by the Carolingian writer Milo of Saint Amand, which announces sobriety as the head and end of the work. The opening casts the poet as a captive weeping by the rivers of Babylon, resolving to lament the gluttony for which Adam lost paradise. The body stages the conflict between sobriety and the vice it calls gastrimargia, exploring this through a long allegorical survey of biblical history. The narrative moves from Noah's drunkenness and Esau's pottage to the murmuring Israelites, continuing with Judith and Holofernes, Jael, and Esther. The survey also covers the Maccabean martyrs and John the Baptist before Herod's banquet, concluding with Christ fasting against the devil's three temptations. Later sections turn to humility, charity, almsgiving, and the duties of teachers, closing with Milo's confession of his own sins and praise of the Virgin Mary.
la.catholic_church_pope.epistulae_imperator: This Late Antique Latin collection, compiled by an unknown hand, transmits letters and documents from emperors, popes, and bishops. It bears the title Epistulae imperatorum pontificum aliorum, which means letters of emperors, popes, and others. The volume opens with a narrative of persecution under the emperor Constantius, detailing the exile of Pope Liberius and the violent struggle for the Roman see between Damasus and Ursinus. Subsequent documents range from theological discussion of the resurrection of the body to records of councils, covering episcopal rivalries in Alexandria and Constantinople, along with the controversy surrounding Acacius. The collection closes with a formal profession of faith presented to Pope Hormisdas, which affirms the orthodoxy preserved in the apostolic see.
la.florus_of_lyon.carmina: The Carmina is a Carolingian collection of Latin poems by Florus of Lyon. The opening piece versifies the Gospel life of Christ as told by Matthew. It traces the narrative from the evangelist's call at the tollbooth to the nativity. The poem also covers the magi led by the star and the flight into Egypt. Later pieces turn to devotional subjects, including a first-person meditation on divine care. The collection ends with a liturgical poem for the Easter vigil.
la.erchempert.martyrologium: Erchempert, a monk of Monte Cassino writing in the late ninth century, is best known for his prose history of the Lombards of Benevento. This short verse martyrology, attributed to him, turns the calendar of saints into hexameters. Its first line names its model, the martyrology of the priest Bede, and the poem moves through the year's feasts with the saints celebrated on fixed days.
la.maffeo_veggio.supplementum: Maffeo Vegio wrote this thirteenth book of the Aeneid in 1428, carrying Vergil's poem past the death of Turnus to the surrender of the Rutulians, Aeneas' marriage to Lavinia, the founding of Lavinium and Aeneas' reception among the gods. This is a second copy of the Supplementum in the corpus, in a different edition from the text filed as Vegio's Aeneid, and the two can be compared line by line. It was filed under Polignac until October 2026.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: Genesis is the Greek prose rendering of the first book of the Hebrew scriptures. It was translated in Alexandria during the third century BC. This text forms the oldest portion of the Septuagint. The narrative opens with God creating the world in six days. It then recounts the stories of Adam, Noah, and the patriarchs. The final chapters follow Joseph from slavery to power in Egypt.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The Greek Exodus of the Septuagint is the second book of the Pentateuch, continuing the third century BC Alexandrian translation of the Torah. The text opens with the enumeration of Jacob's sons who went to Egypt, where a new king who did not know Joseph oppressed their multiplying descendants. Moses is rescued as an infant and raised at Pharaoh's court, later fleeing to Midian and receiving his commission at the burning bush. His contest with Pharaoh involves ten plagues and the institution of the Passover, leading to the Israelites departing Egypt and crossing the Red Sea. Moses and Miriam sing a canticle during this event, while wilderness marches are marked by manna, water from the rock, and battle with Amalek. The theophany at Sinai brings the Decalogue and covenant laws, followed by detailed prescriptions for the tabernacle, its furnishings, and priestly vestments. The apostasy of the golden calf and its aftermath are also described, concluding with the erection of the tent, where the cloud and glory of the Lord settle over it.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The Levitikon is the Greek translation of the biblical Book of Leviticus, serving as the third book of the Mosaic Torah. An anonymous translator rendered the Hebrew original into Greek during the Hellenistic period, forming part of the Septuagint collection. The text opens with the Lord calling Moses from the tent of meeting, prescribing burnt, grain, and peace offerings. Laws then cover sin and guilt offerings, detailing the consecration of Aaron and his sons. The narrative includes the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, followed by dietary rules and purity regulations. These address childbirth, skin disease, and bodily discharges, while the Day of Atonement is also described. A closing section of holiness legislation sets out sexual and moral prohibitions, including the festival calendar and sabbath and jubilee years. Rules for vows and dedications complete the code, all cast as continuous divine speech to Moses at Sinai.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: Arithmoi, meaning numbers, is the Hellenistic Greek Septuagint version of the fourth book of the Pentateuch, which is the work of an anonymous translator whose precise date remains uncertain. The title refers to the two censuses of the Israelite tribes that frame the narrative, opening with the Lord commanding Moses to muster men of twenty years and upwards in the wilderness of Sinai. This command is given in the second year after the exodus from Egypt, and the book combines narrative and legislation throughout its pages. It details the ordering of camp and march, along with the duties of Levites and priests, while including laws of purity, the ordeal for a suspected wife, and the Nazirite vow. The priestly blessing appears alongside the mission of the spies and the sentence of forty years' wandering, and the rebellions of Korah, Dathan, and Abiron are recounted in the narrative. Oracles of Balaam, summoned by Balak of Moab, feature prominently in the story, and the defeats of Sihon and Og mark further military encounters for the Israelites. The book closes with a second census on the plains of Moab, where laws of inheritance and festivals are presented near the end of the text. The settlement of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh beyond the Jordan is described, and finally, Joshua is designated as Moses' successor on the eve of the crossing into Canaan.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The Deuteronomion is the Greek rendering of Deuteronomy found in the Septuagint. It is the last book of the Pentateuch, presented as Moses's farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before his death. The text opens with Moses addressing all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness during the fortieth year. The book consists chiefly of retrospective discourses on the journey from Horeb and the events east of the Jordan. It repeats the Decalogue and the command to love God alone, followed by a long legal corpus regulating worship, tithes, and festivals. The work closes with blessings and curses, the Song of Moses, and an account of Moses' death on Mount Nebo.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: Basileion A, the Greek title for 1 Samuel, is the first of four volumes forming a continuous history of the Israelite monarchies. This Hellenistic prose rendering translates a Hebrew narrative of the shift from judges to kings, opening at Shiloh with Hannah's prayer and Samuel's birth. The story traces Samuel's career as judge and prophet alongside the corruption of Eli's sons, covering the Philistine capture of the ark and the people's demand for a king. Saul is anointed but eventually rejected for his repeated disobedience, while the latter part follows David's rise, his victory over Goliath, and his bond with Jonathan. David flees Saul's jealous pursuit until Saul consults a medium at Endor, and the narrative concludes with the deaths of Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: This Greek text is the second book of Kingdoms, corresponding to the second book of Samuel. It continues directly from the first book, a division made for length rather than content. The narrative opens with David's lament for Saul and Jonathan after the Amalekite messenger's report. David then consolidates his power, capturing Jerusalem and bringing the ark to the city. Nathan delivers the dynastic promise, and David campaigns against neighboring peoples. Later chapters detail the Bathsheba affair, Absalom's revolt, and the census that brings plague.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The Greek text of the Third Book of Basileion (1 Kings) from the Septuagint, the Old Testament as translated into Greek by Hellenistic-era Jewish translators; the precise dates and authors of that translation are not recorded, and the work survives here in an old Greek biblical form. It opens with the aged David, the succession intrigue of Adonijah, and Solomon's anointing as king, then follows Solomon's reign: his wisdom and judgment, the building of the temple with the help of King Hiram of Tyre, the visit of the queen of Sheba, and his eventual fall into idolatry. The narrative continues with the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam, the alternating accounts of the kings of Judah and Israel, and the prophetic activity of Ahijah, Elijah on Carmel, and the contest with the prophets of Baal, down through Ahab's wars with Ben-hadad of Syria, the episode of Naboth's vineyard, and Micaiah's prophecy at Ramoth-gilead. The book ends with the reign of Ahaziah, son of Ahab, who did evil in the sight of the Lord and worshipped Baal.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth book of the Reigns, or Basileion D, is the Greek version of 2 Kings, which presents the biblical history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah in prose. The narrative opens with Moab's rebellion and the prophet Elijah's denunciation of King Ahaziah, then follows Elijah's fiery ascent and the subsequent ministry of Elisha. Key episodes include the widow's oil, the Shunammite woman's son, and Naaman's healing, while the story moves to Jehu's overthrow of the house of Ahab and the alternating reigns of kings. It covers the Assyrian fall of Samaria and the deportation of its people, and later chapters detail Hezekiah's defense of Jerusalem against Sennacherib. The text also describes Manasseh's idolatry and Josiah's reform after finding the law, concluding with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of Judah.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Greek Anthology is a vast collection of epigrams spanning the Hellenistic period through late antiquity. It is preserved in sixteen books that cover an enormous range of subjects and meters. The work opens with Christian dedicatory epigrams on church buildings and sacred images. The corpus moves through books of amatory verse, funerary pieces, and satirical invective. It also includes epigrams on statues, athletes, and famous poets. Traditional collections by Meleager, Philip, and Agathias are woven into this larger arrangement. The text mixes pagan mythological themes with late antique Christian material.
grc.achilles_tatius.leucippe_et_clitophon: Leucippe and Clitophon is an ancient Greek prose romance by Achilles Tatius, whose title names the two central figures who drive the narrative. Clitophon of Tyre narrates the story in the first person, opening at Sidon with a detailed description of a painting of Europa. This scene leads into his account of love for the Byzantine maiden Leucippe, whose courtship takes place within her father's house before they elope by sea. The couple suffers shipwreck off Egypt and falls into bandit captivity, where Leucippe appears to be slain in a staged human sacrifice. They later face slavery and a series of trials at Ephesus, which includes several apparent deaths and improbable revivals. The story closes with their reunion and the vindication of her chastity, as their long deferred marriage finally takes place before the Ephesian assembly.
grc.acta_joannis.acta_joannis: The Acta Joannis is an anonymous Greek apocryphal act of the apostle John, of uncertain date, opening with a prologue on Vespasian's destruction of Jerusalem and Domitian's subsequent persecution. This conflict brings John from Ephesus to trial in Rome, where he drinks poison unharmed before the emperor and raises a condemned criminal to life. He is then banished to Patmos, returning to Ephesus under Nerva and Trajan to resume his ministry, which includes the raising of Lycomedes and Cleopatra. The Ephesian episodes also feature the commissioning of John's painted portrait, a sermon in the theatre, the collapse of the temple of Artemis, and a lesson commanded to bedbugs. Drusiana dies and is restored, along with her would-be lover Callimachus, before a final revelatory section where John teaches the believers about the polymorphic Christ and the cross of light. He also describes the circle dance hymn sung before the passion, and the text concludes with John lying down in a grave he has caused to be dug and giving up his spirit.
grc.aelian.de_natura_animalium: Aelian's De Natura Animalium ('On the Nature of Animals') is a Greek prose miscellany in seventeen books. It examines the natures and habits of various creatures. A preface defends the claim that irrational animals share in virtue by nature. The text then proceeds through short, self-contained notices on beasts, birds, fishes, and insects. Entries range from the fishing of the scarus to the mutual rescue behaviour of shoals. They also include marvellous tales such as the herons of Diomedes' island, said to be the hero's transformed companions.
grc.aelian.varia_historia: The Varia Historia of Aelian is a Greek miscellany of anecdotes and short notices covering natural history, human history, and moral exempla. It opens with chapters on animal behaviour, including the predatory polyp, the weaving of spiders, and the cunning of foxes. The work also notes the sagacity of Egyptian frogs, dogs, turtles, and mice before turning to human affairs. It gathers stories of lawgivers and tyrants such as Solon and Archelaus, as well as orators and philosophers like Demosthenes, Aeschines, Theophrastus, and Anaxagoras. Later portions continue with Spartan discipline and the virtues of Greek and Roman women, while discussing painters such as Zeuxis and kings like Philip of Macedon and Ptolemy. The whole is held together by loose thematic grouping rather than continuous narrative.
grc.aelius_aristides.orationes: The Orationes is a collection of Greek prose speeches by Aelius Aristides. The work opens with a hymn to Zeus, framed as thank-offerings made in fulfilment of a vow after escape from a storm at sea. In this opening piece, the speaker laments the belatedness of his sacrifice and calls upon the Muses for aid. The hymn proceeds to celebrate Zeus as self-generated and eternal, first cause and craftsman of the cosmos. It recounts his creation and ordering of earth, sea, air and aether, along with his adornment of the heavens with stars. Further orations follow in the collection.
grc.aeschines.against_ctesiphon: This forensic oration by Aeschines was delivered before Athenian jurors after Philip's death, prosecuting Ctesiphon for proposing a decree to honour Demosthenes with a golden crown. The speech opens by urging jurors that the laws safeguard democracy and free speech, arguing the decree is illegal because Demosthenes still owes an account of his offices. Aeschines also objects to ordering Demosthenes' proclamation in the theatre before the assembled Greeks, then indicts Demosthenes across four phases of his political career. He alleges bribery in the Peace of Philocrates and betrayal in the Theban alliance, further charging impiety over the sacred plain of Cirrha and cowardice at Chaeronea. The closing sections contrast Demosthenes with Solon, Aristides, Themistocles, and Miltiades, urging the jurors to deny the crown as punishment for his conduct.
grc.aeschines.on_the_embassy: On the Embassy is a defence speech by the Athenian orator Aeschines, which answers a prosecution brought by Demosthenes on charges of bribery connected with the peace made with Philip of Macedon. The speech opens with a plea to the Athenian jurors, asking them to hear the defendant with goodwill and reminding them of the magnitude of his danger. The greater part of the speech refutes the charges in order, recounting the making of the peace and the first and second embassies. Aeschines defends his conduct toward Cersobleptes and the Phocian cities, as well as the Amphictyonic settlement, while supporting his case with decrees, letters, and witnesses. He portrays Demosthenes' own conduct as envoy in hostile terms, and the speech ends with an appeal for acquittal that invokes his family, military service, and record of goodwill.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon: The Agamemnon, a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, opens with a watchman on the royal palace roof at Argos awaiting the chain of beacon fires announcing the fall of Troy. A chorus of Argive elders recalls the expedition against Troy and the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, before a herald's report brings news of the king's victory. Agamemnon's homecoming with the captive prophetess Cassandra follows, and Clytemnestra, avenging her daughter, lures her husband onto a costly robe and kills him. She slays Cassandra with him, acting together with her lover Aegisthus, whose father Thyestes was ruined by Atreus. The play stands as the first part of a trilogy tracing the curse on the house of Atreus. It closes with the triumphant pair exchanging threats with the defiant chorus, which looks ahead to the return of Agamemnon's son Orestes.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: This prose hypothesis accompanies Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon, opening by recounting how Agamemnon promised Clytemnestra a beacon signal on the day of victory. She then posted a paid watchman, and the report of the fire brings together the elders who form the chorus. The summary follows the drama's course, including Agamemnon's return with Cassandra and her prophecy of death. It details the king's murder and the quarrel in which Clytemnestra and Aegisthus defend the killing. The text closes with didascalic information, recording that the play was produced under the archon Philocles in the 78th Olympiad. Aeschylus took first prize with the Agamemnon, Choephoroi, Eumenides, and the satyr-play Proteus, while the choregos was Xenocles of Aphidnae, and a list of the dramatis personae follows.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides: The Eumenides, a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, concludes the Oresteia, which dramatizes the cycle of vengeance. The play opens with the Pythia's prayer at Delphi, where she discovers Orestes seated at the omphalos as a suppliant. The sleeping Erinyes surround him in the sanctuary, and the drama follows his pursuit for killing his mother Clytemnestra. He flees under Apollo's protection to Athens, where Athena institutes a trial for bloodshed on the Areopagus. Apollo testifies, and an equal count of votes settles the case, so Athena's ballot acquits Orestes of the charge. In the closing movement, she persuades the resentful Furies to accept a home in Attica, establishing them as the Eumenides with cult honors. The play ends with a torchlit procession, and the goddesses bless the city with fertility and civic concord.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides_hypothesis: This anonymous prose hypothesis, or plot argument, introduces the Eumenides, the final play of Aeschylus's Oresteia. Its date remains uncertain, though it accompanies the drama in transmission. The summary begins with Orestes fleeing the Erinyes at Delphi under Apollo's direction. He reaches Athens and takes refuge at the shrine of Athena. After his acquittal through the goddess's counsel, he returns to Argos. There he appeases the angry deities and renames them the Eumenides, or the Kindly Ones. A closing remark notes that the story appears in neither of two poets.
grc.aeschylus.persians: The Persians is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus that dramatizes the reaction of the Persian court to the defeat of Xerxes' invasion of Greece. It opens with a chorus of Persian elders at Susa recalling the muster of the king's vast host and voicing anxiety for news of his return. The queen mother Atossa recounts an ominous dream before a messenger arrives to tell of the annihilation of the Persian fleet at Salamis. The ghost of Darius, summoned by offerings, interprets the disaster as divine punishment for hubris and prophesies a further defeat at Plataea. The drama closes as Xerxes himself returns in rags to join his elders in a sustained lament over the ruin of Asia.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: This short prose hypothesis, or plot summary, of ancient date was transmitted as the prefatory argument to Aeschylus's Persians and is anonymous. It opens by citing Glaucus's account of Aeschylus's plots, which reports that the Persians reworked Phrynichus's Phoenissae ('Phoenician Women') and quotes the play's first line. The summary then sets the drama at the tomb of Darius and outlines its subject, Xerxes' invasion of Greece with vast land and naval forces. Xerxes, it recounts, was defeated by sea at Salamis and on land at Plataea before fleeing back across to Asia. Concluding notes record Aeschylus's victory in the archonship of Menon with the Phineus, Persians, Glaucus Potnieus, and Prometheus. They also distinguish the first Persian expedition under Darius, repulsed at Marathon, from the second under Xerxes at Salamis and Plataea.
grc.aeschylus.seven_against_thebes: This Greek tragedy by Aeschylus dramatizes the assault of the Seven from Argos on Thebes. It opens with Eteocles rallying the citizens of Cadmus' city to man the walls, as a seer reports that the enemy is preparing an imminent attack. In the long central scene a scout describes, gate by gate, the devices blazoned on the shields of the seven Argive champions. Eteocles assigns Theban defenders to meet them, while the chorus of Theban women prays to the city's gods amid an argument with the king over their panic and supplications. A messenger then announces that Eteocles and his brother Polynices have slain each other at the seventh gate. Antigone and Ismene lament the dead, and in the closing exchange Antigone defies a decree of the council forbidding Polynices burial, vowing to bury him herself.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: The Suppliant Women (Hiketides) is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date by Aeschylus, built around a chorus of suppliant maidens rather than a dominant individual protagonist. The play opens as the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, land at Argos after fleeing Egypt to escape marriage to their cousins, the sons of Aegyptus. They take refuge at the altars of the local gods, and King Pelasgus, recognizing their Argive descent through the lineage of Io, refers their plea to the citizen assembly. When the assembly votes to shelter them, an Egyptian herald's attempt to seize the maidens by force is repelled. The drama closes with the refugees settled in the city, offering thanksgiving to the gods of Argos and praying that Zeus avert the hated marriage.
grc.andocides.on_the_mysteries: On the Mysteries is a forensic speech in which the Athenian orator Andocides defends himself against a charge of impiety arising from the profanation of the Eleusinian Mysteries and the mutilation of the Herms. He opens with an appeal for the jurors' goodwill and a promise to recount every relevant event from the beginning, covering the successive informations laid over the secret rites and the panic that followed the mutilation of the Herms. The narrative details Diocleides' false denunciation that saw his kinsmen imprisoned and Andocides' own naming of the actual offenders, which he presents as an act that saved both his family and the city. Andocides contends that the decree of Isotimides under which he stands charged has been invalidated by the amnesty decrees and oaths sworn after the overthrow of the Thirty. He adds invective against his chief enemies, Callias son of Hipponicus and Alcibiades, before closing with a public exhortation that Athens accept peace with Lacedaemon. He reviews earlier treaties to argue that peace has been salvation for the democracy where war has been its overthrow.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris is an anonymous Greek navigational treatise of uncertain date, and its title means the measurement of the Great Sea in stades. The opening preface addresses a most honoured brother, promising an exact account of the Mediterranean coasts from Alexandria to the Pillars of Heracles and Gades. The body consists of numbered entries giving distances between ports, anchorages, headlands, and islands, while notes describe harbours, watering places, and shelter from particular winds. Routes follow the North African coast through Cyrenaica to Carthage, passing through Syria, Cilicia, and the southern shores of Asia Minor. The text also takes in Rhodes, the Aegean islands, Cyprus, and Crete.
grc.apollodorus.library: The Library is a Greek prose compendium of mythology attributed to Apollodorus, whose date and authorship remain uncertain to modern scholars. The narrative opens with the rule of Uranus over the universe, then details his offspring by Ge and the usurpation by Cronus. From there the account runs through the Titanomachy and the Gigantomachy, also covering the assault of Typhon before turning to genealogical saga. The text recounts Deucalion and the flood, along with the voyage of Jason, describing the twelve labours and later campaigns of Heracles. The Theban cycle follows, moving from Cadmus and Dionysus to Oedipus, and continues through the Seven Against Thebes and the Epigoni. The work also traces the Arcadian and Spartan lines, including Atalanta, and covers the Trojan house from Dardanus to Priam and Paris. The early kings of Athens are also included in the narrative, and the surviving account breaks off amid Theseus's youthful exploits on the road from Troezen.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica is a Greek mathematical treatise on conic sections by Apollonius of Perga, composed during the Hellenistic period by a geometer of that era. The preserved lines set out propositions in the Euclidean manner, where each proposition consists of a general enunciation followed by a demonstration. The text deals with tangents and secants drawn from external points, which are applied to sections of a cone and to circumferences of circles. The hyperbola receives particular attention in the work, as propositions involve its asymptotes and its opposite sections. Ratios of divided straight lines determine where lines meet or touch the curve.
grc.apollonius_rhodius.argonautica: The Argonautica is a Hellenistic Greek epic in four books attributed to Apollonius of Rhodes, which recounts Jason's voyage with the Argonauts to Colchis to win the Golden Fleece. The poem opens with a prayer to Apollo to sing of the men of old, and it follows the muster of heroes at Pagasae and their outward voyage. The narrative covers the abandonment of Heracles and Hylas in Mysia, and it also details the passage of the Symplegades and the court of Aeetes. Medea's love for Jason and her flight with him form the central drama, and the story concludes with the Argo's arrival back at the Greek shore.
grc.archimedes.arenarius: The Arenarius, or Sand-Reckoner, is a Greek treatise by Archimedes dedicated to King Gelon, which opens by recalling the opinion that grains of sand are infinite in number. The author undertakes to refute this view through geometric demonstration, adopting figures deliberately larger than earlier estimates for the earth's circumference. It also uses larger values for the diameters of the sun and moon, while an experiment with a long rule and a small cylinder gauges the sun's apparent diameter. The text proves that the sun's diameter exceeds the side of a chiliagon, and a system of orders and periods of numbers is defined on myriads of myriads. This allows quantities far beyond ordinary nomenclature to be named, establishing bounds for the diameter of the cosmos as usually conceived. Larger bounds are set on the hypotheses of Aristarchus of Samos, who makes the earth circle the sun and places the fixed stars far away. The final section shows the number of grains filling Aristarchus's sphere, which is less than a myriad of myriads of the eighth order.
grc.archimedes.de_corporibus_fluitantibus: De Corporibus Fluitantibus is Archimedes' Greek hydrostatic treatise, cast as postulates, propositions, and proofs, with some portions supplied in Latin. It opens with a postulate on fluid behaviour under pressure, deducing that the surface of a fluid at rest is spherical and shares its centre with the earth. The following propositions set out how solids behave in fluid, where bodies of equal weight rest wholly submerged. Lighter bodies float partly above the surface and are driven upward, while heavier bodies sink while losing weight in the fluid. The closing portion determines equilibrium positions for segments of a right-angled conoid, showing when they right themselves, tilt, or rest with their base just touching the surface. The text appeals to the Equilibria and the mechanical elements for centres of gravity.
grc.archimedes.de_lineis_spiralibus: Archimedes' On Spirals (De Lineis Spiralibus) is a Greek geometrical treatise written in the Doric dialect, opening as a letter to Dositheus that recalls the death of Conon. The author surveys earlier problems, proving some and showing others to be false, while the body presents lemmas on uniform motion and sequences of lines. It also covers tangents and neuses to circles before defining the spiral, and the main theorems establish ratios of radii and the property of the tangent. They rectify the circumference and calculate the areas enclosed by the spiral, where the first turn bounds one third of the area of the first circle. Successive turns stand in simple multiple ratios, and the treatise concludes by comparing areas cut off between radii with sectors.
grc.archimedes.de_planorum_aequilibriis: Archimedes' De Planorum Aequilibriis, or On the Equilibrium of Planes, is a treatise on statics that derives the law of the lever from seven postulates on suspended weights. The work also examines the centre of gravity of plane figures, including propositions on commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes. Written in the Doric dialect of ancient Greek mathematics, the text features forms like τᾶς and σαμεῖον, which differ from Attic literary Greek. The treatise provides the canonical formulation of key mechanical terms, including κέντρον τοῦ βάρεος, ἰσορροπέω, and ῥέπω. Later Greek authors drew on this vocabulary in their own discussions of the lever and balance.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: The Problema Bovinum is a short Greek arithmetical problem in verse that its introductory note presents as a challenge devised by Archimedes and sent to those pursuing such questions in Alexandria, in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene. It opens with an address to a stranger, asking him to reckon how many bulls and cows of four colours, white, dark, yellow and piebald, grazed the fields of Sicily, their several numbers bound by stated fractional ratios. A further demand raises the difficulty: the white and dark bulls together must form a square number and the yellow and piebald a triangular number, with the promise that whoever satisfies every condition will be judged outstanding in wisdom. A closing prose scholion restates the rules for each colour and appends numerical totals for the bulls and cows of the four herds, expressed in Greek alphabetic numerals.
grc.archimedes.quadratura_parabolae: The Quadratura Parabolae, a short treatise by Archimedes, is transmitted in Greek as a letter addressed to Dositheus. It concerns the area of a segment bounded by a straight line and a parabola. The work opens with a preface lamenting the death of Conon and announcing the central theorem. This theorem states that every such segment is four-thirds of the triangle with the same base and equal height. The body first establishes the result mechanically using a lever, then proceeds through inscribed triangles in a continued ratio of four to one. A supporting lemma shows that magnitudes in quadruple progression sum to four-thirds of the greatest, and the treatise closes with definitions of the segment's base, height, and vertex, ending with a final proof by exhaustion of the main result.
grc.aretaeus.curatione_acutorum_morbum: De curatione acutorum morborum ('On the Cure of Acute Diseases') is the Latin title under which a Greek medical treatise ascribed to Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a physician of uncertain date, has been transmitted. The treatise itself is composed in prose of a markedly Ionic coloring. The material gathered here gives a detailed clinical account of acute convulsive disorders, setting out the warning signs, the seizure itself, and the aftermath of epilepsy. It then takes up the spasms of tetanus in its rigid, backward-arching (opisthotonic) and forward-curving forms. Further sections discuss the causes of these spasms and their incidence by season, age, and sex. These sections also weigh the physician's limited prospects of aiding those the disorders strike.
grc.aristophanes.clouds: Aristophanes' comedy Clouds ('The Clouds') opens at night with the elderly farmer Strepsiades lamenting debts incurred through his son Pheidippides' passion for horses. He resolves to seek instruction at the neighbouring Thinkery of Socrates to master specious argument and evade his creditors. There, comic displays of Socrates' natural philosophy, astronomy, and geometry alternate with Strepsiades' own hapless schooling. The chorus of Clouds, which replaces Zeus, advises him to send his son in his place. Pheidippides masters the Unjust Argument, which defeats the Just Argument in an agon contrasting old and new education. He then turns his rhetoric against his father, defending the beating of parents and threatening his mother. Repenting of the sophistic training he sought, Strepsiades burns down the Thinkery and drives Socrates and Chaerephon from the roof.
grc.aristophanes.ecclesiazusae: Ecclesiazusae ('The Assemblywomen') is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes, which opens before daybreak with Praxagora addressing a burning lamp. She and her fellow plotters disguise themselves in men's cloaks, beards, and heavy shoes, rehearsing their plan to pack the Assembly and carry the vote. This action hands the city over to female government, where Praxagora's programme abolishes private property and institutes common messes in public buildings. It also replaces marriage with an ordered community of partners, in which the old have first claim on the young. Later episodes show the new laws at work in daily life, as a husband is left behind at home while his wife governs. Reluctant citizens are compelled to surrender their possessions to the common store, and a young man is dragged off by two rival elderly women, each claiming priority under the statute. The play ends with the chorus preparing a communal feast, cataloguing its outlandish ingredients and inviting citizens and spectators to join.
grc.aristophanes.frogs: Aristophanes' Frogs (Batrachoi) is an Attic comedy of uncertain date, and its title refers to the frog chorus that appears in the underworld. Dionysus and his slave Xanthias banter as the god disguises himself in Heracles' lion-skin and club, asking his way down to fetch Euripides. He crosses the lake with Charon amid the croaking of the frogs, then joins the procession of initiates who hymn Iacchus. He endures humiliations, including a whipping contest with Xanthias in Heracles' stead, before Aeschylus and Euripides dispute the tragic throne before Pluto. The bulk of the play is their agon over prologues, lyrics, and the moral worth of poetry, which Dionysus settles in Aeschylus' favour. Choral passages frame the contest and close with the poet's departure, including a parabasis on the treatment of deserving citizens and blessings for Athens.
grc.aristophanes.knights: Aristophanes' Knights is a political comedy named for its chorus of Athenian cavalry, and the action opens in the house of Demos, the crotchety old man who personifies the Athenian people. Two slaves, ousted from their master's favour by the tanner Paphlagon, resolve to find him a rival, and they recruit a vulgar sausage-seller from the agora to stage escalating contests before Demos. These include rival professions of devotion, gifts, mutual accusations, and duels of oracles, and the sausage-seller eventually exposes Paphlagon's extortions and usurps his position. A lengthy parabasis defends the poet's art and laments the decline of earlier comic dramatists, and the play closes with Demos restored to the hearty simplicity of the age of Miltiades and Aristides. Paphlagon is condemned to peddle sausages at the city gates.
grc.aristophanes.lysistrata: Lysistrata is a comedy by Aristophanes, first performed at Athens during the Peloponnesian War, and the title names the heroine who leads the women in their campaign for peace. The play opens with Lysistrata and Calonice assembling a congress of women from Athens and its allies, who swear an oath to withhold sex from their husbands until peace is made. The women also seize the Acropolis and its treasury to enforce their resolve, and the action follows the standoff between the women and their men. This includes failed attempts to storm the citadel and a debate before the council of old citizens, while the plot also tracks the tribulations of individual couples such as Cinesias and Myrrhine. Finally, Spartan envoys arrive, equally afflicted by the women's campaign, and after the disputing parties present their claims, the goddess Reconciliation brings the sides together. The play closes with united songs of thanksgiving and a Lakonian dance in celebration of the restored peace.
grc.aristophanes.peace: Peace is a Greek Old Comedy by Aristophanes, whose title names the goddess the protagonist seeks to rescue. Trygaeus fattens a dung beetle on barley cakes to fly to heaven, where he finds the goddess Peace held captive while war ravaged the land. He brings her back to earth, and the chorus of farmers rejoices in the return of rural life. Satirical scenes mock war-mongers, oracle-mongers, and other public figures, while comic notices also mention poets such as Sophocles and Cratinus. The play concludes with a wedding hymn as Trygaeus marries Opora, and the company is then invited to share a festive meal.
grc.aristophanes.wasps: Aristophanes' Wasps, belonging to the tradition of Athenian Old Comedy, features a chorus of elderly jurors likened to wasps because of their sting. The plot centers on Philocleon, an old man addicted to jury service, and his son Bdelycleon, who confines his father at home in a desperate attempt to cure him of this mania. The action includes a mock trial of a dog and a debate over the meagre pay of jurors, followed by a parabasis in which the chorus defends the martial exploits of the older generation. Philocleon eventually relapses into wilder habits at a symposium, leading to drunken brawling in the streets, and the play closes with a dancing contest involving the sons of Carcinus.
grc.aristotle.analytica_priora: The Analytica Priora, a Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on the syllogism, serves as the instrument of demonstrative argument and defines its subject as demonstration. The text lays out basic notions of proposition, term, and syllogism, distinguishing between perfect and imperfect forms of these structures. It details syllogistic theory, including the three figures and their valid moods, and covers the conversion of propositions and syllogisms built on necessary or possible premises. Later sections treat syllogisms from opposed premises and argument from false premises, while the text examines circular demonstration, begging the question, and refutation. It explores the search for middle terms as causes and the construction of definitions, asking how the first principles of demonstration come to be known. These principles arise from perception through memory and experience, and they are grasped at last by a state of mind more certain than science.
grc.aristotle.de_caelo: De Caelo ('On the Heavens') is a Greek treatise by Aristotle on the physical cosmos. It opens by defining natural science as the study of bodies, magnitudes, and their movements. Early chapters cite Pythagorean doctrine to argue that body alone counts as perfect magnitude. The text distinguishes simple local motions as circular, upward, and downward. It concludes that circular motion belongs to a divine body prior to the elements. The opening defers the question of the universe's infinite magnitude to treat its parts first.
grc.aristotle.de_generatione_animalium: Aristotle's treatise on the generation of animals explores how living things come to be, opening by asking what causes serve the coming to be of parts connected with generation. The work argues that male and female are the principles of generation, with the male supplying form and the principle of motion, while the female supplies matter. It examines semen, menstrual fluid, and the reproductive organs of blooded and bloodless animals, and it also covers spontaneous generation, the role of heat, and the development of the embryo. The text discusses birds' eggs, gestation periods, and the causes of resemblances and monstrosities, as the five books move from general theory to detailed causal explanations of particular phenomena.
grc.aristotle.de_interpretatione: Aristotle's De Interpretatione ('On Interpretation') is a short prose treatise on the logic of predication. It opens by defining the name and the verb as conventional signs that carry no truth value alone. The text then examines affirmation, negation, and the relations between contradictory and contrary propositions. It also analyzes modal statements concerning necessity, possibility, and impossibility. A famous section asks whether claims about future events, like a sea battle, are already true or false. The work closes with an analysis of the opposition between beliefs and assertions.
grc.aristotle.de_sophisticis_elenchis: Aristotle's De Sophisticis Elenchis ('On Sophistical Refutations') examines arguments that seem valid but are actually fallacies. The work defines these apparent refutations and the sophists who profit from them. It distinguishes four kinds of reasoning: didactic, dialectical, peirastic, and eristic. The main body outlines the aims of contentious disputants and classifies fallacies. Six types depend on language, while others arise from outside it. The text offers practical guidance on questioning and solving such arguments. It closes by noting that no such inquiry had existed before.
grc.aristotle.divisiones_aristoteleae: This short Greek collection of dialectical divisions is transmitted under Aristotle's name, whose uncertain date and authorship remain matters of scholarly debate. The work opens with a passage quoted from Diogenes Laertius, which reports Aristotle dividing goods into those of the soul, body, and external sources. Brief chapters follow, covering friendship, constitutions, justice, the sciences, medicine, and law, while also addressing discourse, rhetoric, music, nobility, beauty, the soul, virtue, and rule. Benefaction, happiness, truth, punishment, and pleasure complete the list of topics, and several subjects appear twice in closely parallel versions. The compilation closes with discussions of priority, simultaneity, contraries, and negation.
grc.aristotle.epistulae: The Epistulae is a brief collection of six Greek letters attributed to Aristotle, whose date and authorship remain uncertain. The opening letter counsels a ruler to trust in virtue rather than the shifting turns of fortune, while warning against tyrannical rule and grandiloquent speech. The remaining letters urge benefaction and mercy toward the unfortunate, invoking Theophrastus on gratitude and recommending swift reconciliation after an injury. A short closing note addresses the acroamatic discourses, remarking that these works are intelligible only to those who heard them. This formulation plays on the ancient distinction between exoteric and esoteric writings, and throughout, the pieces are gnomic moral essays in epistolary form.
grc.aristotle.magna_moralia: The Magna Moralia ('Great Ethics') is a Greek treatise on ethics attributed to Aristotle. Its authorship remains disputed, and the work is of uncertain date. It places the study of character within the broader field of politics. The text argues that happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. This activity must be sustained over the course of a complete life.
grc.aristotle.meteorologica: Aristotle's Meteorologica defines its subject as the remaining part of natural philosophy, following the study of first causes, celestial bodies, and the elements. The work surveys the region between the earth and the heavens, treating shooting stars, comets, and the Milky Way. Later sections cover clouds, rain, snow, hail, dew, and frost, while winds, earthquakes, rivers, springs, and the sea are also examined. The cause of the sea's salinity is explained, and thunder, lightning, hurricanes, and thunderbolts receive attention. Halos, rainbows, mock suns, and rods are discussed, explained through the reflection of sight. The mixture of moist vapour and dry exhalation is key, and a final book examines the affections of bodies, covering combination, solidification, melting, and kindred processes. The composition of homogeneous materials is also analyzed, including metals, flesh, and bone.
grc.aristotle.nicomachean_ethics: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, a Greek treatise in ten books, asks what the human good is and how it may be attained. The work opens by claiming that every art, inquiry, action, and choice aims at some good. It identifies the highest good, studied by politics, as happiness or eudaimonia. The body defines happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. It examines moral virtues as means between excess and deficiency. Specific virtues such as courage, temperance, magnanimity, and justice are treated alongside intellectual virtues. The text also considers pleasure, weakness of will, and friendship. It concludes by ranking the contemplative life as the most complete form of happiness. The final section turns to the question of legislation and civic education.
grc.aristotle.physica: The Physica, or Physics, is Aristotle's treatise on natural philosophy, which investigates the principles and causes of things that exist by nature and are subject to change. The work opens by arguing that knowledge depends on grasping first causes and elements, and it then surveys the four causes, necessity, chance, and the infinite. The text also examines place, the void, and time as the number of motion, while considering continuity, infinite divisibility, and the species of change and motion. The closing books establish that motion is eternal and identify circular local motion as the first kind, concluding that there must be a first unmoved mover without magnitude.
grc.aristotle.politics: Aristotle's Politics is a Greek philosophical treatise on the polis and the forms of association that constitute it, opening by arguing that every polis is a natural community directed toward the good life. It asserts that man is by nature a political animal, then treats the household and slavery while critiquing earlier schemes for ideal states. The work classifies constitutions into kingship, aristocracy, and polity, and also examines oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny. It analyzes the deliberative, magisterial, and judicial parts of each regime, and examines the causes of constitutional change and revolution. The means of political stability are discussed, and the work ends with the education of the citizen body. It closes on the proper use of leisure and the ethical effects of music.
grc.aristotle.αριστοτέλους_φυσικά_προβλήματα: This large Greek collection of scientific and medical problems is transmitted under Aristotle's name. Its date remains uncertain, and the text is arranged by subject into short entries. Each item poses a why question and offers one or more attempted explanations. The work opens with medical issues such as why great excesses cause disease. It also asks why changes in season and winds aggravate or cure illnesses. Later series cover mechanics, motion, and the rounded shapes of plant and animal parts. The collection concludes with bodily matters like the effects of rubbing and gymnastic practice.
grc.aristotle.φυσιογνωμονικά: This short Greek treatise on physiognomy, preserved in the Aristotelian corpus, is attributed to Aristotle, though its date remains uncertain. The work argues that mental dispositions accompany bodily states, as seen in drunkenness and illness, and it defines the art while criticizing earlier methods based on animal genera and ethnic groups. The main body catalogues signs from movement, shape, colour, hair, skin, voice, and body parts, referring each sign to an animal type or to male and female dispositions. The text closes with remarks on bodily size and proportion, noting that the face and eyes yield the clearest signs.
grc.arrian.cynegeticus: Arrian's Cynegeticus is a short Greek prose treatise on hunting with hounds, serving as a supplement to Xenophon's work of the same name. The author addresses Xenophon son of Gryllus directly in the opening, noting that Xenophon did not know the Celtic breed of dogs. The text also mentions the Scythian and Libyan horses, while the body offers practical guidance on judging and feeding hounds. It covers exercising, tethering, and breeding these animals, giving special attention to the swift Celtic coursing dogs. The work describes the pursuit of the hare without nets, detailing the conduct of hunters on horseback and on foot. Celtic and Libyan methods for taking larger game are also explained, closing with injunctions to sacrifice to Artemis Agrotera, including examples from Homer and Celtic votive customs.
grc.bacchylides.dithyrambs: The Dithyrambs of Bacchylides are fragmentary choral songs preserved in papyrus remains, and the title refers to hymns originally performed in honor of Dionysus. The opening fragments, though much broken, narrate the Greek expedition against Troy, naming Theano, Odysseus, and Menelaus among the dramatis personae. Other poems explore gnomic reflection on Zeus, Justice, and Hybris, while the collection also draws on episodes from other myth cycles. These include Theseus carried by dolphins to the hall of Nereus, and the birth of Dionysus to Semele at Cadmus' Thebes. Finally, it depicts Idas' seizure of Marpessa at Sparta.
grc.bacchylides.epinicians: The Epinicians ('victory songs') gather the choral odes of the Greek lyric poet Bacchylides. These songs were composed to honour victors at athletic contests. Each poem typically pairs praise of the victor, his family, and his city with an extended mythological narrative. Such narratives are drawn from heroic legend, as in an ode recounting Minos' arrival with fifty ships. Many of the odes are preserved only in fragmentary form, with long lacunae interrupting both metre and sense. Others survive as short excerpts.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.epistulae: This volume gathers the Greek letters of Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century bishop of Cappadocia, and opens with letters to Gregory of Nazianzus that recall their studies at Athens. These early pieces question whether fortune and necessity rather than human choice govern events, and they also recount the writer's travels after leaving the city. A following letter defends withdrawal from the world and sets out the discipline of the solitary life, identifying silence, scriptural reading, prayer, fasting, simple diet, and night vigils as means of purifying the soul. Elsewhere the collection ranges more widely, addressing friends, clergy, and civic officials, while these later letters cover personal consolation, ascetic counsel, and the affairs of the church.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epitaphius: The Epitaphius Adonidis ('Lament for Adonis') is a Greek bucolic lament for the dead Adonis, attributed to Bion of Phlossa and of uncertain date. It opens with the repeated cry 'Woe for Adonis, fair Adonis is lost', which the Erotes take up as Cypris is roused from her couch to mourn her lover. The youth has been gored in the thigh by a boar on the mountains, and the poem follows Aphrodite's frantic search for him through wood and crag. There follows the weeping of nymphs, rivers, springs, and flowers, and her address to the dying youth and to Persephone, who detains him below. His blood is transformed into the rose and her tears into the anemone, before Hymenaeus, the Charites, and the Moirai join the mourning. The poem ends with the command that Cythera stay her cries for today, to weep again when a year has passed.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epithalamium: This fragmentary Greek epithalamium, or wedding song, is attributed to the bucolic poet Bion of Phlossa, who wrote thirty-two lines in dactylic hexameters. The work, which breaks off mid-sentence, is framed as an exchange between the herdsmen Lycidas and Myrson. One speaker asks why a sweet Sicilian pastoral melody is being performed, recalling the song Polyphemus once sang for Galatea. The poem then turns to the story of Achilles on Skyros, recounting Paris' abduction of Helen and the general muster of the Achaeans. Achilles alone lay hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes, disguising himself as a girl and performing women's work. He shared the chamber and bed of Deidameia, addressing her at night as his sole companion before complaining that Dionysus has parted them.
grc.callimachus.epigrams: Callimachus of Cyrene composed these short Greek poems in the early third century BC while active in Alexandria. The collection is written mostly in elegiac couplets and opens with a stranger consulting the sage Pittacus on a choice of brides. It then moves to laments for the poets Heraclitus of Halicarnassus and the cynic Timon. The remaining verses include funerary pieces for the drowned, the young, and the aged. Votive epigrams record offerings to Artemis, Demeter, Aphrodite, and the Graces of Queen Berenice. Erotic and convivial pieces on boys, women, and the pains of love also appear throughout. Verse on poets and poetry recurs, praising Aratus's subtle phrasing while dismissing hackneyed public themes.
grc.callimachus.hecala: Callimachus' Hecale is a Hellenistic epyllion, a short epic poem written in Greek hexameters, which survives only in fragments gathered from ancient quotations and testimonia. The collection opens with an epigram by Crinagoras praising the work, which was composed in answer to critics who mocked the poet for never having written a long work. The surviving verses follow Theseus' defeat of the Marathonian bull and his stay with the old woman Hecale, while brief quotations describe her household, her preparations for her guest, and her country speech. Later fragments trace a crow's narrative of its estrangement from Athena, and they also cover Hecale's death and the aetiology of the Athenian deme named in her honour.
grc.callimachus.hymns: The Hymns of Callimachus are six hexameter poems by a Hellenistic Greek poet. They follow the Homeric manner and address Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, Delos, Athena, and Demeter. The first hymn asks what is fitting to sing of Zeus at libations. It recounts his disputed birth in Arcadia and Crete and praises his gift of justice to kings. The remaining poems mingle invocation with extended narrative. They cover Apollo's slaying of Python, Artemis's hunt, Leto's wandering, Athena's bath, and Demeter's vengeance on Erysichthon. The last two hymns use a literary Doric dialect for ritual processions.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.μαθηματικὴ_σύνταξις: The Mathēmatikē Syntaxis, or Mathematical Treatise, is a comprehensive astronomical work by Claudius Ptolemy, commonly known as the Almagest, and it consists of thirteen books. The opening section addresses Syrus and defends the certainty of mathematics, arguing that the heavens move spherically while the earth remains central and motionless. The remaining books provide trigonometric tools and spherical astronomy for the system, then treating solar and lunar theory, including the calculation of eclipses. The text also catalogs fixed stars and details the motions of the five planets, with observational data and numerical tables running throughout the entire treatise. The work closes with an epilogue declaring the account of the heavens complete.
grc.clement.exhortation: This short Greek Christian exhortation on daily conduct is attributed to Clement. Its date remains uncertain, and it survives as a single continuous piece. The text urges quietness in word and deed to prevent the mind from falling prey to haste and passion. It then moves through bearing, speech, and deference to elders, while firmly refusing falsehood and deceit. The instruction culminates in constant prayer and hymnody, directing all works and words toward God and Christ. It closes with counsel on temperance, endurance under sickness, and mercy toward the afflicted.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.protrepticus: The Protrepticus, an early Christian apologetic work by Clement of Alexandria, urges Greeks and other pagans to abandon their traditional religion for the Christian faith. The text opens with the legend of Orpheus charming animals with his song, which Clement turns against pagan beliefs by arguing that the divine Logos tames humanity. The work systematically exposes Greek cult and myth as scandalous fictions or dead practices, treating the mysteries of Demeter, Dionysus, and Cybele with particular scorn. The oracles are declared dead, and the Olympic gods are dismissed as deified men or demons, while philosophical cosmologies are criticized as mere worship of the elements. Clement cites Greek poets and philosophers as witnesses for one true God, and the argument culminates in an appeal to the Hebrew prophets and Christ. It closes with a vision of Christian mysteries that supersede the pagan ones.
grc.demetrius.elocutione: A Greek treatise on prose composition and style, transmitted as Peri hermēneias (De Elocutione), attributed to Demetrius and of uncertain date. It opens by comparing the division of prose into clauses (kōla) with the division of poetry into metres, and explains how clauses and commata combine into periods. The work proceeds through the plain, grand, elegant, and forceful kinds of style, discussing rhythm and euphony, figures and similes, charm, jest, hyperbole, and allegory, word choice, and the guarded figure (eschematismenon), with illustrations drawn from Homer, Sappho, Plato, Xenophon, and other poets, philosophers, historians, and orators. It closes with remarks on smooth, hiatus-avoiding composition and on the ungraceful (acharis) in diction and arrangement.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_3: This Attic forensic oration by Demosthenes is the third of his three speeches against Aphobus, delivered in the fourth century BC during a dispute with one of his guardians. The work answers a suit for false witness brought by Aphobus against Demosthenes' supporters, recalling how easily he refuted Aphobus's falsehoods at the earlier trial. He predicts that the present jury will likewise recognise the man's shamelessness, defending witnesses who testified that Aphobus acknowledged the slave Milyas had been freed. The speech presses Aphobus's repeated refusal to submit the relevant household slaves to torture, while reviewing the provisions of the will, including the eighty-mina dowry and furniture. It closes on the arbitrators' assessment of the loss at ten talents.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_2: This Athenian forensic speech is transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus as the second oration Against Boeotus. The speaker, Mantitheus, contests a claim on his deceased father's estate. He argues that Boeotus and his brother Pamphilus were fraudulently passed off as the old man's sons. Their mother Plangon orchestrated this deception through perjury. The text recounts the first marriage and dowry arrangements of the speaker's mother. It details the deceptive oath sworn at the Delphinium and the father's refusal to acknowledge the pair. The forced introduction to the phrateres is presented as the consequence of that deception.
grc.demosthenes.against_midias: Against Midias is a courtroom speech delivered by Demosthenes in the Athenian law courts, where he prosecutes Midias for hubris, a charge of insolence arising from an assault. The victim was serving as a chorus sponsor at the Dionysia festival, and the speaker notes that Midias' insolence towards all citizens is notorious. He explains how the assembly condemned the defendant in a probolē before the trial, setting the assault within the context of the religious festival. The text reads out the laws governing probolai and conduct during the Dionysia, broadening into a sustained attack on Midias' whole career. This includes his dealings with Aristarchus and a catalogue of his offences directed against individuals, the laws, and the gods. The orator warns against the wealthy friends who will intercede for him, urging the jury to give a verdict that vindicates the laws and preserves the security afforded to every citizen alike.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_30: This short forensic speech belongs to the Demosthenic corpus and was written in Attic Greek for delivery before an Athenian jury. It addresses a private suit against Onetor, the brother-in-law of Aphobus and son of Timocrates. The speaker opens by recounting his fruitless efforts to settle differences with Aphobus and Onetor before resorting to litigation. The case concerns Onetor's claim that a plot of land was pledged to him in lieu of a dowry. The speech argues that the dowry was never paid and that the wife's supposed abandonment is a fiction. It contends that the pledge is a pretext to deprive the speaker of property recovered in his judgment against Aphobus. The speaker supports these contentions with depositions, witnesses, and offers to interrogate slaves under torture. He also builds a chronological argument from the dates of the marriage, the alleged abandonment, and the original lawsuit.
grc.demosthenes.against_phormio: This courtroom speech from the Demosthenic corpus was delivered in an Athenian commercial court, where the prosecuting merchant Chrysippus sues Phormio over a maritime loan of twenty minas. The case concerns a voyage to the Pontus and the subsequent shipwreck of the vessel, during which the shipmaster Lampis claimed that Phormio repaid the gold in the Bosporus. Chrysippus argues that the cargo was never laden as the contract required, and he also contends that Lampis gave false testimony after sharing the money. The speech defends the admissibility of the suit under emporic rules, describes an attempted arbitration before Theodotus, and cites various laws. Chrysippus accuses Lampis of illicitly exporting grain to Acanthus during a shortage, while he reviews his own services to the city in the grain trade. The speech closes with an appeal to protect lenders and credit.
grc.demosthenes.against_polycles: Against Polycles is a courtroom speech from classical Athens attributed to Demosthenes. The title names the defendant, who is prosecuted for refusing to take over a trireme. The speaker argues that the case concerns the whole city, not just the litigants. He recounts outfitting the vessel at his own expense and serving under the general Timomachus. The speech details convoy duty in the Hellespont and northern Aegean, as well as an episode involving Callippus and Callistratus. It closes with a plea for reimbursement and punishment of a citizen who defied the rules of succession.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_2: This short forensic speech is attributed to Demosthenes and addresses a prosecution for false witness. It belongs to the series of inheritance disputes over the estate of the banker Pasion. The speaker, Apollodorus, prosecutes Stephanus for giving false witness on behalf of Phormion. The text opens by anticipating Stephanus' defense regarding the scope of his testimony. It argues that Stephanus swore falsely about the contents of a document held by Phormion. The speaker cites statutes on wills, heiresses, and witness procedure to show the testimony was unlawful. The closing appeal urges the judges to punish the witness for testifying against the law.
grc.demosthenes.against_timocrates: Against Timocrates is an Athenian forensic speech in the Demosthenic corpus, serving as a public prosecution for proposing an illegal law. The orator declares Timocrates the sole cause of the trial, claiming he defrauded the city of money it was about to recover. The measure would allow citizens condemned to state imprisonment for unpaid fines to obtain release by furnishing sureties. This action would annul verdicts already rendered, undermining the courts, the council, and the city's finances. The speaker, an associate of Euctemon, first rehearses earlier actions against Androtion and his circle, then expounds the statutory procedure for legislation that Timocrates flouted. The speech shows point by point that the new measure contradicts standing statutes on theft, mistreatment of parents, and military desertion. It closes with digressions on Androtion's public record and the melting down of dedicatory crowns for phialai. The orator also discusses Athenian statesmen who submitted to imprisonment and the Locrian practice of legislating with a halter around the neck. Finally, he cites Solon's comparison of the laws to the city's coinage.
grc.demosthenes.exordia: This collection gathers exordia, or opening sections, for speeches delivered to the Athenian assembly. The texts are transmitted under the name of the orator Demosthenes, though their date and authorship remain uncertain. The first piece features a speaker who rises only after others have finished, ready to add counsel where their advice has fallen short. The remaining preambles address the assembly directly and work through a recurrent repertoire of themes. They urge the listeners to hear all who wish to advise and to keep to the matter at hand. They also warn against flattery and argue that policy demands preparation rather than confident words. Several pieces touch on diplomatic affairs involving Sparta, Arcadia, Mytilene, Rhodes, and Philip of Macedon.
grc.demosthenes.for_phormio: This forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus defends Phormion, a former slave and business manager of the banker Pasion, in an Athenian court. Pasion had leased his bank and shield factory to Phormion before his death, and the will also left his widow and the guardianship of his younger son to Phormion. The opening concedes that Phormion is inarticulate, so his friends instruct the judges, and the argument traces the history of the lease, the will, and the estate division. It details the earlier suit, arbitration, and Apollodorus' formal release of claims, arguing that a new suit is inadmissible after such a release. Contracts, laws, and testimony support this legal position, while the speech also recounts Apollodorus' income and expenditure. It defends the marriage of a banker's widow to a freedman using precedents, and the closing appeal asks the judges to save a man useful to the city.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_2: The Second Olynthiac is a short deliberative oration by Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly amid the war between Olynthus and Philip of Macedon. It opens by treating the emergence of peoples willing to fight Philip, above all the Olynthians, as a manifest sign of the gods' goodwill toward Athens. The bulk of the speech argues that a power built on perjury, deception and injustice must soon collapse, cataloguing Philip's betrayals of Amphipolis, Potidaea, the Thessalians and the Phocians, and probing the weakness of his kingdom, the hardship and resentment of his subjects and soldiers, and the disreputable circle of flatterers around him. Turning to Athens, it rebukes the citizens' idleness, their hesitancy over contributions and personal service, and the partisan conduct of the symmories, before closing with practical proposals: an embassy to the Thessalians, contributions from all according to their means, and common, resolute prosecution of the war.
grc.demosthenes.on_organization: This short deliberative speech by the fourth-century Athenian orator Demosthenes is addressed to the assembly. It is known as On Organization, a title that refers to the systematic arrangement of the city's military forces. The speaker opens by discussing public money and the two-obol payments that prompted the meeting. He argues that accepting the dole is useless unless citizens also organize the army. Demosthenes urges that hoplites, cavalry, and other troops be enrolled under a chosen general. He contrasts the modest lives of the men of Salamis and Marathon with contemporary luxury. The speech closes by asserting that safety depends on arms rather than lawcourts.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_chersonese: This deliberative oration, titled On the Chersonese, was delivered to the Athenian Assembly, addressing the crisis created by Philip of Macedon's campaigns in Thrace. The speech also concerns the Athenian command of Diopeithes in the Chersonese, and Demosthenes opens by urging speakers to judge the city's interest rather than personal feelings. He argues that Philip is already at war with Athens despite his denials, surveying Philip's encroachments in Thrace, Euboea, and the Hellespont. He defends Diopeithes against accusations that threaten to dissolve his force, while criticizing the Athenians' ease-loving inaction and the orators who paralyze policy. Demosthenes urges payment of the war tax and maintenance of the standing army, closing with a defense of his own courage and a summary of his proposals.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_crown: On the Crown, a forensic oration by Demosthenes, was spoken in the trial over Ctesiphon's decree awarding him a golden crown. Aeschines had prosecuted that decree as illegal, and the speech opens with a prayer for the judges' goodwill. Demosthenes then answers Aeschines' slanders and reviews his public life, examining his opposition to Philip of Macedon. The oration covers the Peace of Philocrates, the embassies, and the Amphictyonic quarrel, while also discussing the alliance with Thebes and the resulting war. Demosthenes defends the legality of the crown decree, arguing that the Theban alliance was the city's finest policy. The speech closes with invective against Aeschines' parentage and conduct, ending with a final prayer to the gods.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_false_embassy: Demosthenes' On the False Embassy is a forensic speech delivered in an Athenian court, which prosecutes Aeschines for bribery and misconduct during embassies to Philip of Macedon. The title refers to the false reports Aeschines allegedly gave about the mission, and the opening urges jurors to rely on their oath and justice rather than on the defendant's friends. The body recalls Aeschines' early denunciations of Philip and narrates the negotiations for the peace of Philocrates, while charging that Aeschines wasted crucial time, took bribes, and betrayed Phocis, Thrace, and the Hellespont. The speaker calls other ambassadors as witnesses and reads out letters from Philip, and closing sections anticipate counter-arguments, including a threatened prosecution by Charidemus. They dismiss Aeschines' acting career and famed voice as irrelevant to his public conduct, and the speech presses for a conviction that will serve as a warning to corrupt envoys.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_1: The First Philippic is a deliberative speech by Demosthenes addressed to the Athenian assembly, concerning the growing threat posed by Philip of Macedon. The speaker defends his decision to address the crowd before the usual advisers, arguing that Athens suffers from negligence rather than from enemy strength. The text recalls past victories against Sparta to highlight current failures, criticizing the habit of reacting only after fresh outrages occur. A detailed program for permanent preparedness forms the greater part of the speech, including fifty triremes, ten fast vessels, and a standing force of two thousand men. The plan calls for continuous campaigns under an accountable general, closing with an appeal to vote for these measures. It urges the Athenians to wage war in deeds rather than in decrees.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_3: The third of Demosthenes' Philippics is a deliberative speech delivered in the Athenian assembly, warning that Philip of Macedon is already at war with the Greeks despite his professions of peace. The speaker complains that endless talk since the peace has let affairs drift toward ruin, showing that Philip's seizure of cities and territories amounts to open war. These conquests range from Olynthus and Phocis to Thessaly, Euboea and the Chersonese, contrasting old Athenian severity toward bribed traitors with present corruption by Macedonian gold. He recounts how Olynthus, Eretria and Oreus fell by heeding Philip's partisans, urging the Athenians to arm and equip themselves. The speech also calls for embassies to the Peloponnese, Rhodes, Chios and the Persian King.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_4: This deliberative speech in Attic Greek is attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes, who addresses the assembly during a crisis with Philip II of Macedon. He announces that he will say what he judges advantageous for the city, while the body rehearses Philip's encroachments in Thrace, Euboea, Megara, and Olynthus. These actions argue that Philip has already broken the peace and is at war with Athens, so the orator denounces the citizens' indolence and the politicians who take Philip's pay. He urges steady military and financial preparation, including the reallocation of the theoric funds, and recommends an embassy to the Persian King. The speech closes by warning that Greece will fall into servitude unless the Athenians mend their ways.
grc.diogenianus_of_heraclea.παροιμίαι_δημώδε: This Greek compilation presents popular proverbs as drawn from the collection of Diogenianus of Heraclea, whose writer is of uncertain date. The text opens with a short treatise on proverbs, discussing the term's etymology and definition along with its kinship to the fable. This introduction also covers various types of sayings, including Aesopian and Carian forms, with illustrative verses from poets such as Archilochus and Aristophanes. The bulk of the work is an alphabetical catalogue running from alpha to the end of the Greek alphabet. Each proverb is glossed with its sense and commonly supplied with an explanatory story drawn from myth, history, comedy, or everyday life. Examples range from the gardens of Adonis to Midas' ass's ears, with cross-references to kindred sayings recurring throughout the text. Quotations from authors such as Plato, Menander, Solon, and Lucian are woven into the explanations.
grc.dionysius_calliphontis.dionysii_callipho: The Descriptio Graeciae is a short prose periegesis attributed to Dionysius son of Calliphon, whose date remains uncertain and who is otherwise obscure. The work opens with a preface addressed to Theophrastus, where the author announces a rapid account of the whole of Hellas. The surviving text proceeds as a coastal circuit beginning at Ambracia, moving through Acarnania, Aetolia, Locris, and Phocis. Delphi, Parnassus, and the Corycian cave are described in this region, while the itinerary continues through Boeotia to Megara and the Peloponnese. Thebes, Plataea, and the oracle of Trophonius are noted along the way, with places listed with their sanctuaries, mountains, rivers, and distances. The style is compressed and dense with toponymy, and the preserved text is damaged by lacunae and an interrupted sequence, resuming later with the island of Crete.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isocrate: Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote this Greek essay to examine the orator Isocrates, whose title De Isocrate means On Isocrates. It begins with a summary biography covering his birth, schooling, and long career as a teacher. He died shortly after the battle of Chaeronea at nearly a hundred years of age. The discussion then weighs Isocrates against Lysias, crediting him with purity and grandeur in his diction. Dionysius notes a periodic, quasi-poetic rhythm, but judges Isocrates inferior to Lysias in charm and concision. Isocrates is considered superior in the arrangement of his subject matter, and individual speeches are surveyed in the text. These include the Panegyricus and the address to Philip, while the Areopagiticus and the Archidamus are also examined. Criticisms of his ornate style by earlier writers are reported, and the essay ends with extended specimens of his work. The exordium of On the Peace is analysed, and the forensic Trapeziticus is also examined for its manner.
grc.epictetus.discourses: The Discourses, or Diatribai, were recorded in Greek by Arrian, a pupil of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus. Arrian explains in a prefatory letter that he transcribed his master's lectures from memory as notes for his own use. The surviving text presents these teachings as dialogues between Epictetus and unnamed visitors or questioners. The work develops Stoic ethics chiefly through the distinction between what lies within our power and what does not. It covers topics such as providence, freedom, friendship, and purity, while illustrating points with examples from Socrates and Roman public life.
grc.epictetus.enchiridion: The Enchiridion, meaning a handbook, is a compact Greek manual of Stoic ethical teaching by the philosopher Epictetus. It is arranged as a sequence of very short chapters that guide the reader through practical philosophy. The work opens with the division between things that are and are not in our power.
