This foundation grounds freedom and happiness in judgment, impulse, and desire alone. The remaining chapters gather precepts on handling impressions, desire, and aversion. They also address meeting death, loss, and insult with equanimity. Further sections cover duties arising from familial and social roles. The text includes guidance on piety toward the gods and the proper use of divination. It concludes with verses on following Zeus and providence willingly.
grc.epicurus.epistula_ad_herodotum: The Epistula ad Herodotum is a letter of the philosopher Epicurus, one of three letters and a set of principal doctrines transmitted by Diogenes Laertius, addressed to a correspondent named Herodotus. It opens by explaining its purpose: to provide an epitome of Epicurus's writings on nature so that those unable to work through the longer books may retain the most important doctrines in memory. The body of the letter expounds Epicurean physics in sequence, covering the criteria of knowledge, the eternity of the whole, bodies and void, indestructible atoms moving in an infinite universe, the birth and dissolution of innumerable worlds, the role of images in vision, hearing and smell, the soul as a fine-parted mortal body, qualities, accidents and time, the natural origin of language, and celestial phenomena explained by multiple possible causes rather than divine agency. It concludes by directing attention back to sense-perceptions and feelings, through which fears concerning the gods and death are dispelled and tranquility of life secured.
grc.epicurus.gnomologium_vaticanum_epicureum: The Gnomologium Vaticanum Epicureum is a Greek collection of some eighty short Epicurean sayings, and its title identifies the work as a Vatican manuscript of Epicurean maxims. It is attributed to Epicurus, though its compilation date remains uncertain, and the text opens with an aphorism stating that the blessed and immortal being has no troubles of its own. It does not give such troubles to others, and the remaining maxims cover death, pain, and pleasure, while they also address the classification of desires. Friendship, justice, and mutual trust receive further attention, and the collection discusses fate, necessity, and dreams. It highlights the wealth, freedom, and self-sufficiency that philosophy makes possible, and several sayings are addressed directly to individual friends. The work closes with reflections on the wise man's freedom from disturbance.
grc.euclid.elements: Euclid's Elements is a Greek mathematical treatise that presents geometry as a deductive system. The title refers to the fundamental principles from which the entire work is derived. It begins with definitions of basic geometric entities and five postulates. The body of the text consists of propositions, each accompanied by a formal proof. Early examples include the construction of an equilateral triangle on a given line.
grc.euripides.alcestis: Alcestis is a Greek tragedy by Euripides that opens with Apollo recounting his service to Admetus, king of Pherae. He tricked the Fates into allowing Admetus to escape death if a substitute died in his place. Alcestis, the king's wife, accepted this role and bids farewell to her household before dying. Admetus quarrels with his aged father Pheres, who refused to die for him, and receives the visiting Heracles. Learning whose death he has intruded upon, Heracles wrestles Death at Alcestis' tomb. He leads back a veiled woman, who is revealed to Admetus as his wife restored to life.
grc.euripides.andromache: Euripides' Andromache is a Greek tragedy that opens with Hector's widow taking refuge at the altar of Thetis, where she is enslaved to Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles, after the fall of Troy. The Spartan Hermione, Neoptolemus' barren wife, threatens to kill Andromache and their child, Molossus, while Menelaus arrives to support his daughter and seizes the boy as a hostage. He forces Andromache from her sanctuary, but the aged Peleus intervenes and drives him off, after which a messenger reports that Neoptolemus has been killed at Delphi through the scheming of Orestes. Orestes arrives and carries Hermione away to Sparta, and Peleus mourns over his grandson's corpse before Thetis appears from above. She commands the burial at Delphi and the marriage of Andromache to Helenus, and she also orders the continuation of the Molossian royal line and her own reunion with the now immortalized Peleus.
grc.euripides.bacchae: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, dramatising the arrival of the god Dionysus in Thebes and the resistance to him of the young king Pentheus. The play opens with Dionysus, in mortal disguise, declaring his intention to prove his divinity and punish the house of Cadmus for denying that Zeus fathered him on Semele. Pentheus imprisons the disguised god, who escapes as the palace is destroyed by miracles, and a messenger then reports both the wondrous rites of the Theban women on Mount Cithaeron and their savage attacks on the local settlements. Lured by Dionysus, Pentheus dresses as a woman to spy on the rites, is led to Cithaeron, and is torn apart by the maddened maenads, his mother Agaue returning in triumph with his head; the recognition of her deed, the exile of Cadmus and Harmonia, and Dionysus' final pronouncement of their transformation into serpents close the play.
grc.euripides.cyclops: The Cyclops is the only satyr drama to survive complete from Greek tragedy, offering Euripides' comic treatment of the Odyssey episode where Odysseus blinds the man-eating Polyphemus. The play opens with Silenus lamenting his situation as the Cyclops' herdsman beneath Mount Aetna, where he and his sons the Satyrs have passed from the service of Dionysus into slavery. When Odysseus and his crew arrive seeking provisions, Silenus trades cheese and lambs for wine, but Polyphemus returns and rejects the Greeks' appeal to the obligations of hospitality. He then cooks and devours two of the sailors, while Odysseus refuses to flee without his companions and gets the giant drunk with a potent wine of Dionysus. Under the assumed name Nobody, he burns out the giant's single eye with a heated stake, and the hero escapes by ship while the Cyclops recalls an oracle of his blinding. The Satyrs go over to the service of Bacchus.
grc.euripides.fragmenta: This volume gathers the surviving fragments of the Greek tragic poet Euripides, preserving single lines and short segments from lost tragedies. Substantial portions of the Melanippe plays are included, and the collection also contains a chorus in honour of Peace. It opens with brief gnomic utterances on poverty and wealth, proceeding as a series of quotations from the dramatic corpus. These include laments, moral maxims, and lyrics on the seasons, while dramatic scenes of recognition and crisis are also present. The material ranges from isolated lines to extended dialogue passages.
grc.euripides.hecuba: Hecuba is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, probably first performed in the years after the Athenian expedition against Macedonia, though its exact date remains uncertain. The play opens with the ghost of Polydorus, youngest son of Priam and Hecuba, who recounts how his Thracian guest-friend Polymestor murdered him for the gold he carried from Troy. Hecuba, enslaved among the victorious Greeks, then learns that her daughter Polyxena is to be sacrificed on the tomb of Achilles. When her son's corpse washes ashore, she exacts a brutal revenge on Polymestor, blinding him and killing his two sons. The drama concludes with a trial scene before Agamemnon, in which Polymestor defends his crime and prophesies Hecuba's transformation and the murder of Agamemnon by Clytemnestra.
grc.euripides.helen: Helen, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, dramatizes the alternative tradition in which the real Helen never went to Troy. In the prologue, she explains how Hermes carried her to Egypt while a phantom went to Troy. She now dreads being forced into marriage by Theoclymenus, the son of Proteus. Teucer passes through, and a shipwrecked Menelaus arrives to recognize his wife. The seer Theonoe confirms that the report of Menelaus's death is false. Feigning that the castaway comes to announce his own end, they obtain a ship for funeral rites. They escape, though the deception is soon discovered by the king. The Dioscuri appear to restrain Theoclymenus from killing Theonoe. They foretell divine honors for Helen and a dwelling on the Isles of the Blessed for Menelaus.
grc.euripides.heracleidae: The Heracleidae, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, dramatises the flight of Heracles' children from the persecution of Eurystheus. Set in Athens at the altar of Zeus Agoraios, the refugees seek sanctuary there from their pursuer. The plot follows their appeal to Demophon and Acamas, while an oracle demands the sacrifice of a maiden. Macaria offers herself for this purpose, and the aged Iolaus arms himself for battle. Eurystheus is defeated through Iolaus' miraculous rejuvenation, and a dispute follows over the captive king's life. Alcmene condemns him while Hyllus insists on sparing him, and Eurystheus prophesies that his tomb will protect Athens.
grc.euripides.hippolytus: Hippolytus, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, is edited and translated by David Kovacs in a forthcoming Harvard University Press edition running to 1,448 lines. The play opens with Aphrodite announcing from above her resolve to destroy the chaste Hippolytus, son of Theseus, because he honors Artemis and scorns her. The action follows Phaedra's anguished and carefully concealed passion for her stepson, the nurse's fatal betrayal of the secret, and Phaedra's suicide. Her death leaves a written charge accusing Hippolytus of assaulting her, and Theseus, believing the dying woman, curses his son with one of the three wishes Poseidon granted him. A monstrous bull from the sea terrifies Hippolytus' horses and drags him to a mortal injury. Artemis then reveals Phaedra's innocence and the young man's purity, consoles him as he dies, promises him enduring cult honors at Troezen, and reconciles him with his repentant father.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_tauris: Iphigenia in Tauris is a Greek tragedy by Euripides that tells of Iphigenia, who was spirited away by Artemis at the moment of her sacrifice at Aulis. She serves unwillingly as priestess among the Taurians, a land whose king, Thoas, obliges her to put Greek castaways to death on the goddess's altar. The play opens with her expository prologue recounting her lineage, the events at Aulis, her rescue by Artemis, and an ominous dream concerning her brother Orestes. Orestes and Pylades then arrive, sent by Apollo to steal the statue of Artemis from the temple, and are captured and brought forward for sacrifice. They are recognized through the letter Iphigenia means to send to Argos, and brother and sister contrive an escape disguised as a purification rite by the sea. At the close, Athena's epiphany halts Thoas's pursuit, secures safe passage for Orestes and the image, and ordains the cult of Artemis Tauropolos in Attica together with Iphigenia's service in the Brauronian rites.
grc.euripides.orestes: Orestes is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, first performed in 408 BC, where the title names the central figure who suffers after killing his mother Clytemnestra. Electra opens the play by recounting the cursed history of the house of Atreus, describing how the Furies afflict Orestes as he lies ill and awaits a vote. The drama follows his failed appeals to Menelaus and his subsequent condemnation, after which Orestes attempts a suicide pact with Electra and seizes Hermione as a hostage. Helen is nearly murdered before her deification averts the act, and the palace burns, while Apollo appears to fix Orestes' marriage and trial.
grc.euripides.phoenissae: Phoenissae, a Greek tragedy by Euripides of uncertain date, dramatizes the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices for the throne of Thebes. Named for its chorus of Phoenician captive women, the play opens with Jocasta tracing the misfortunes of the house of Cadmus. As the Argive host musters before the city, Antigone surveys the seven champions while the oracle demands the death of Creon's son Menoeceus. The assault is repulsed, and the brothers kill each other in single combat, leading Jocasta to kill herself over their deaths. Creon denies Polynices burial, and Antigone resolves to defy his edict, while the blind Oedipus departs into exile toward Colonus.
grc.euripides.rhesus: Rhesus is a Greek tragedy transmitted among the plays of Euripides, though its authorship and date remain disputed. The title names the Thracian king who arrives as a Trojan ally during the tenth year of the war. The story draws on the Doloneia of Iliad Book 10 to dramatize a single night in the Trojan camp. Hector sends the scout Dolon to spy on the Greek ships, but Odysseus and Diomedes kill him. The heroes then raid the camp, slaying Rhesus in his sleep and carrying off his white horses. The play closes with the Muse mourning her son and foretelling Achilles' death.
grc.euripides.trojan_women: A Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatising the immediate aftermath of the fall of Troy. It opens with Poseidon surveying the ruined city, describing Priam's death at the altar of Zeus and the Trojan women gathered as captives before the gates, among them Hecuba. The action follows the allotment of the captive women to their Greek masters, including Andromache, who is assigned to Achilles' son. Cassandra gives vent to prophetic outbursts, Menelaus and Helen hold their debate, and the child Astyanax is put to death. It ends with Hecuba and the chorus lamenting the burning of the city as they are led away to servitude in Greece. In its laments for the women of Troy, the play draws on the epic tradition of the city's fall.
grc.flavius_josephus.antiquitates_judaicae: Antiquitates Judaicae ('Jewish Antiquities') is a twenty-book historical work in Greek prose by Flavius Josephus. The author wrote it after separately composing his account of the Jewish war against Rome. In the preface, Josephus explains that the work sets out the whole ancient history and constitution of the Jewish people. He notes that the text renders Hebrew writings into Greek and that his patron Epaphroditus urged its completion. The narrative runs from the creation of the world and the laws attributed to Moses. It carries the account down to the final years before the war with Rome.
grc.flavius_josephus.josephi_vita: The Vita, meaning life, is a short Greek autobiography by Flavius Josephus that serves as an appendix defending his conduct during the Jewish War. The text opens with a genealogy tracing his priestly and Hasmonaean descent, then details his education and examination of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes. An embassy to Rome on behalf of imprisoned priests follows this early account, while the greater part narrates his command in Galilee at the outbreak of the revolt. It also covers his feuds with John of Gischala and Justus of Tiberias, describing his maneuvering among the cities and factions of the region. The work closes with a polemic against Justus's history, including an account of his fortunes under Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian. The text ends with a valediction to his patron Epaphroditus.
grc.gaius_romanus.fragmenta: Greek fragments attributed to Gaius, a Roman church writer of uncertain date, transmitted in the quotations of Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History and preserving part of the dialogue he held with Proclus, a champion of the Phrygian or Montanist heresy. The collection opens with Eusebius's report that Proclus concurred in an earlier discussion of the death of Philip and his daughters, whose tombs lay at Hierapolis in Asia. In the surviving exchange Gaius points to the 'trophies' of the apostles who founded the Roman church at the Vatican and on the Ostian road, enumerates only thirteen epistles of Paul apart from that to the Hebrews, and reproves Cerinthus for teaching an earthly kingdom of Christ and fleshly pleasures in Jerusalem after the resurrection. Further passages recount how Natalius, a confessor who accepted a salaried bishopric from the disciples of Theodotus the cobbler, was flogged through the night by angels and crawled back to communion with bishop Zephyrinus, and how the same heretics emended the divine scriptures while placing their confidence in the syllogisms of Aristotle, the geometry of Euclid and the authority of Galen rather than in the ancient rule of faith.
grc.galen.de_atra_bile: Galen's Greek treatise On Black Bile (De Atra Bile) examines the melancholic humour within ancient medicine. It opens by surveying earlier treatments, praising Hippocrates and censuring Erasistratus. The work distinguishes black bile from other humours by its sensible qualities. It explains how the humour forms in hot and dry bodies and climates. Galen traces disorders such as melancholy, cancers, and varicose veins. A sustained polemic defends the necessity of humoral theory to medical practice.
grc.galen.de_dignoscendis_pulsibus: De Dignoscendis Pulsibus, a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, deals with how the pulse is to be recognised and distinguished by touch. The work presents itself as the second of four parts of a complete account of pulse theory, where the first covers genera and species. The third addresses their causes, while the fourth explains their significance for practice, a division that has left diagnosis neglected. Accurate diagnosis of diastole, systole, and the differing qualities of the arterial beat demands many years of disciplined practice. Galen illustrates this claim from his own experience as a young student of medicine, describing his slow attainment of certainty in distinguishing the movements of the artery.
grc.galen.de_dignotione_ex_insomniis: Galen wrote this short Greek treatise on diagnosis from dreams, transmitted under the title De Dignotione ex Insomniis, which explains how dreams may be read as signs of the body's underlying condition. The text opens by linking dream images to humoral correspondences, such as fire for yellow bile and smoke for black bile, while also noting the importance of timing and recent food in interpreting these visions. The discussion then addresses the difficulty of separating somatic dreams from those with mantic foreknowledge, and anecdotes illustrate this challenge, including a wrestler who dreamed of standing in a pool of blood. Dreams of drinking, eating, and intercourse are read as signs of thirst, hunger, and seminal abundance, and the closing explanation holds that the soul enters the body's depths in sleep to perceive its condition. Visions of burdens, running, or flying correspond to the quantity and corruption of the prevailing humours.
grc.galen.de_methodo_medendi: De Methodo Medendi is a Greek treatise on therapeutics by Galen, which is addressed to a friend named Hiero. Its opening section takes the form of a preface, where the author explains his long hesitation to write on the therapeutic method. He complains of an age in which patients favour obsequious and flattering physicians over the truly skilful. The text also delivers an extended invective against Thessalus, who professed to teach medicine in six months and vilified Hippocrates and the ancient Asclepiads. The preface recalls the old rivalry among the medical schools of Cos, Cnidus and Italy, illustrating its argument with quotations from Hesiod on the two kinds of strife.
grc.galen.de_optima_doctrina: De Optima Doctrina is a Greek polemical treatise by Galen that targets the doctrine associated with Favorinus, who argued that the best teaching involves arguing with equal force on both sides of every question. The opening reports Favorinus' account of the Academic suspension of judgment, both older and newer, claiming pupils may judge opposing arguments without first learning any criterion of knowledge. Galen contends that nature has furnished all people with trustworthy criteria in the senses and the intellect, without which neither teacher nor pupil can judge anything. The argument notes that Favorinus contradicts himself in his own writings on the cataleptic impression, while the closing pages liken the teacher to a trainer or craftsman who corrects a learner's errors. This figure leaves the learner's natural faculties intact, and Galen restates his promise to equip pupils with the instruments and criteria by which true accounts are found and false ones detected.
grc.galen.de_ossibus_ad_tirones: Galen's De Ossibus ad Tirones is a short Greek treatise on osteology addressed to novices in medicine who are just beginning their studies. The work opens by arguing that a physician must know each bone in itself and understand its arrangement with the others to treat injuries correctly. The text then defines the skeleton and the technical vocabulary of its connections, distinguishing between arthrosis and symphysis along with their kinds and subdivisions. The author describes the forms of synarthrosis, including suture, gomphosis, and harmonia, while also detailing unions made through cartilage, sinew, or flesh. A corresponding distinction is drawn among nerves, tendons, and ligaments, and once these preliminary definitions are concluded, the treatise proceeds to the bones individually. It begins this survey with the skull.
grc.galen.de_rebus_boni_malique_suci: De rebus boni malique suci ('On the Good and Bad Juices') is a short Greek medical treatise on diet by Galen, a physician of the Roman imperial period. The opening describes successive famines in provinces subject to Rome, where people driven to eat unwholesome foods suffered skin sores of many kinds, fevers, dysentery and mental disturbance. From such observations it argues for the Hippocratic doctrine that diseased bodily humours are the cause of illness. It closes with an autobiographical passage in which Galen recalls his father's supervision of his childhood diet and the recurring autumnal illnesses of his youth. He credits his continued good health to a regimen of moderation and exercise.
grc.galen.de_semine: This Greek treatise, attributed to Galen and preserved in the Kühn edition, examines the nature and function of semen in both sexes. It opens by asking whether semen provides only an efficient principle of generation, as Aristotle held, or also a material one, as Hippocrates supposed. The author undertakes to decide this dispute through observation and dissection rather than plausible argument. Evidence from animal experiments, the testimony of women, and anatomical dissections of pregnant beasts supports the claim that both parents contribute to the embryo. The work then traces embryonic development, including the formation of membranes and principal organs, and the causes of resemblance to either parent. It repeatedly refutes Aristotle, Athenaeus, Herophilus, and other earlier authorities on the generative parts, including the disputed role of the testes and spermatic vessels.
grc.galen.de_typis: Galen's short Greek treatise On Types (De typis) opens with the author remarking that many have treated the theory of periodicity in disease more diffusely, and announcing his intention to give a briefer, more sharply defined account, suited to newcomers to medicine. The work defines a typos as the ordered alternation of exacerbation and remission in an illness, observes that most diseases but above all fevers exhibit such periodicity, and distinguishes first from second, standing from moving, and simple from compound types. Its main body characterises the quotidian, tertian, quartan and semitertian fevers in turn, setting out their symptoms, pulses, attendant signs, seasonal prevalence, dangers and duration, with quotations from Hippocrates and a report of Agathinus's differing explanation of the semitertian's name. A concluding section treats doubled types and the ways in which quotidian, tertian, quartan and quintan fevers may be interwoven, illustrated by a worked example of a recurring daily pattern of exacerbations and remissions.
grc.galen.de_venereis_ap_oribasium: This short Greek treatise on sexual intercourse, attributed to Galen, was transmitted through excerpts compiled by the physician Oribasius. The text rejects the Epicurean view that sex is never beneficial to health, arguing that intercourse at long intervals leaves a person feeling lighter and freer in breathing. It sets out proper timing and bodily conditions for the act, describing contrary effects on strong and weak constitutions, including exhaustion, feverishness, and melancholy. The work closes with corrective measures for those harmed by abstinence or overindulgence, including preparatory exercise, cold baths when the season permits, and a lighter, moister, moderately warming diet.
grc.galen.quos_quibus_catharticis_medicament: This Greek treatise by the second century physician Galen is titled Quos quibus catharticis medicamentis et quando purgari oporteat, which means which patients are to be purged with which cathartic drugs and when. It begins by noting that purging healthy bodies is laborious and quickly weakening because the drug finds the blood wanting and melts the flesh instead. The text then matches the humours requiring evacuation, namely phlegm, bitter and black bile, and serous residue, to the chronic diseases they cause. It illustrates this practice with cases of gout, epilepsy, melancholy, and a cancerous condition of the breast checked by annual purging. Later sections set out the timing of purgation by season, region, age, and habit, along with the preparation of patients through trial emetics and rest. The work also details the use of hellebore and colocynth, the draught of ptisan following the drug, and the blending of purgatives with fragrant ingredients to protect the stomach.
grc.galen.thrasybulus_sive_utrum_medicinae_s: This short treatise by Galen is addressed to a friend named Thrasybulus, who asked whether the healthful belongs to medicine or gymnastics. Galen promises to set his oral answer down in writing, examining how such problems should be framed and defined. The argument maintains that one art concerns the body, divided into therapeutic and preservative parts, with gymnastics assigned to the latter. The materials of this art include food, drink, evacuations, and training, supported by appeals to Hippocrates, Plato, and Erasistratus. Galen distinguishes the natural healthy condition from the athletic condition, condemning athletic training and its trainers as a counterfeit art. The work closes by explaining why the whole art bears the name medicine.
grc.galen.περὶ_τῶν_ἐν_ταῖς_τροφαῖς_δυνάμεων: Galen's treatise On the Powers of Foods examines how foodstuffs affect digestion and health. It insists that knowledge of a food's faculty rests on disciplined experience rather than speculative argument. The opening chapters correct earlier dietary writers, quoting Diocles and invoking Erasistratus and Mnesitheus. The argument turns repeatedly to Hippocratic writings, above all the Epidemics and the book On Diet. Galen weighs the attribution of that text while discussing digestibility and the humours. The work forms part of his wider physiological project and refers to his own studies on mixtures.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ὑπέρ_παλαμήδους_ἀπολ: This Greek prose defence speech is attributed to Gorgias of Leontini. It presents the legendary Palamedes speaking at Troy in reply to a charge of treason brought by Odysseus. The speaker argues that the alleged crime was impossible because no contact or payment could have escaped notice. He also claims he had no motive in tyranny, wealth, honour, or safety. Palamedes catalogues his services to mankind in letters, laws, numbers, and the arts of peace. The speech closes with an appeal to the judges to decide by truth and deeds rather than slander.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.christus_patiens: The Christus Patiens is a Greek tragedy on the Passion, burial, and Resurrection of Christ, attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus and of uncertain date. It opens with a prologue spoken by the Virgin, who sets the deception of the first mother in Eden as the cause of her Son's redemptive death and begins her lament in the role of tragic mother. The action moves through Judas' betrayal, Peter's denial, the trial before Pilate, and the crucifixion, which the Mother and the Galilean women mourn amid cosmic portents, to the piercing of the side and the burial by Joseph and Nicodemus. After the tomb is sealed and guarded, the women find it empty, the risen Christ appears to Mary Magdalene and then to the disciples gathered behind closed doors, and the play closes with a prayer of the evangelist John to the Mother of God.
grc.heraclitus_of_ephesus.fragmenta: This volume gathers the surviving fragments of Heraclitus of Ephesus, a Presocratic philosopher whose exact dates remain uncertain. The text follows the arrangement of Hermann Diels' Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, with Bywater's numbering noted alongside. Each fragment is preserved as a quotation from later Greek and Latin writers, with the citing source clearly identified. The collection opens with the famous saying on the logos, the account that governs all things. Subsequent fragments explore the unity of opposites, the ever living fire, and the ceaseless flux of the river. They also address the one divine law, the role of war, and the critique of earlier sages. Aphorisms on the soul, sleep, and human folly complete the set.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.catoptrica: The Catoptrica ('On Mirrors') is a Greek treatise on reflected vision attributed to Hero of Alexandria. The preserved opening assumes that nature does nothing in vain or to no purpose. From this premise, it argues that reflection must occur at equal angles. A geometrical proof supports the claim by showing that a ray broken at unequal angles travels a longer path than one at equal angles. The work as a whole develops the geometry of reflection across plane, spherical, and other curved mirrors. It proves propositions concerning the courses of visual rays and the properties of the images formed.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.dioptra: The Dioptra is a Greek treatise on surveying attributed to Hero of Alexandria. It details the construction of a geared sighting instrument and the measurements it enables. The opening preface defends the utility of dioptrics and argues that one instrument suffices for all tasks. The body proceeds through numbered problems, including establishing differences of level along water conduits. It covers joining inaccessible points, taking distances, and driving tunnels through mountains. Closing chapters add a spring-flow gauge and a reckoning of the distance from Alexandria to Rome.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.geodaesia_sp: This short Greek treatise on geodesy, or land measurement, is attributed to Hero of Alexandria, who opens with elementary definitions of the point, line, surface, plane, angle, and circle. The text then traces the invention of measurement to Egyptian surveyors who re-marked fields after the Nile flood, defining the terms and genera of plane geometry used by these surveyors. It tabulates linear measures from the finger to the schoinos and parasanges, setting out conversions between areas measured in orguiai and the seed measures of land in modii and litrai. The treatise closes with worked numerical problems on finding the areas and sides of squares, oblongs, and triangles, including right-triangle constructions ascribed to the methods of Pythagoras and of Plato. It also covers the computation of a triangle's area from its three sides.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.pneumatica: This Greek treatise on pneumatics, preserved among the works of Hero of Alexandria, expounds the theory and construction of devices that operate through air, fire, and water. The title Pneumatica refers to the study of air and its mechanical properties, and it opens with a long physical argument defending the existence of dispersed vacua and the compressibility of air. This section draws on phenomena such as drinking vessels, medical cupping glasses, and the diving of swimmers, while the bulk of the work describes a long series of contrivances with numbered diagrams. These include bent siphons, vessels that pour wine or water at will, and altar figures that libate, along with dragons that hiss when fire burns, singing birds, and trumpets. Temple doors that open by fire on the altar, the water organ, and an aeolipile are also detailed, and fountains, measuring vessels, self feeding lamps, and surgical suction instruments complete the list. Each device is explained by appeal to the pressure and movement of trapped air, and the text closes with an animal automaton that appears to drink after being cut, which is operated by hidden tubes and valves.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.stereometrica: The Stereometrica, a Greek collection of worked problems in solid mensuration, is attributed to Hero of Alexandria, though its date remains uncertain. The text opens with numerical rules for finding the volume and surface of a sphere, which derive from Archimedes' demonstration that a circumscribing cylinder is half again the sphere. The work then proceeds through long series of solved exercises for cones, truncated cones, cylinders, and columns, and also covers cubes, wedges, obelisks, and pyramids with square, triangular, and polygonal bases. Later sections turn to the measurement of theatres, amphitheatres, vaults, and apses, and the author also addresses apsed niches, pools, wells, jars, ships, granaries, and grain stores. Capacities are reckoned in modii and Italian sextarii, while short procedures derive heights from shadows and gauge pipes, sails, and roof tiles. The text also settles questions of weights and measures, and the demonstrations cite Archimedes and Euclid's Elements, with a closing section of elementary arithmetic teaching the multiplication of feet and fractional measures.
grc.herodianus.συμπόσιον: The Symposium is a very short Greek grammatical work by Herodian, transmitted only as a string of brief entries. Each entry explains an individual word through etymology, opening with a derivation of the word for onion. A longer note follows on the word for appearance, debating the aspiration of trochaic neuter nouns. This note quotes a rule making their initial vowel smooth, while remaining entries cover terms for foods and seasonings. They also include names for vessels of the table, with words like crab, vinegar, and bread appearing in the list. Each term is given a derivation from another word, and occasional Homeric quotations are included in the notes. Remarks ascribed to Philoxenus also stand alongside the text, which is cited from Herodian's own Symposium.
grc.herodotus.histories: The Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus is a Greek prose work in nine books that opens with a proem announcing its aim of preserving the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians. The author also sets out the cause of the war between them, and the narrative begins with Persian and Phoenician accounts of a chain of abductions. These stories of Io, Europa, Medea, and Helen explain the origin of East West enmity, and the text then turns to Croesus of Lydia and the rise of Persia under Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius. The narrative of Persian expansion is interwoven with long ethnographic and geographical digressions that cover Egypt, Scythia, and other lands. The work also includes histories of Greek states such as Athens and Sparta, and it details the Ionian revolt and the invasions of Darius and Xerxes. The text recounts the battles of Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea, and it concludes with the Greek counteroffensive, the Athenian capture of Sestos in the Hellespont, and the punishment of the Persian governor Artayctes.
grc.hesiod.theogony: The Theogony, a Greek epic poem of uncertain date attributed to Hesiod, opens with an invocation of the Heliconian Muses. They encounter the poet tending sheep on the mountain, giving him a laurel sceptre and an inspired voice. The poem traces beginnings from Chaos, Gaia, and Eros through generations of Night, Pontus, and Ocean. It details the overthrow of Uranus by Cronus and the birth of Aphrodite, followed by catalogues of Nereids, Oceanids, rivers, and monsters. The central narrative follows Cronus's swallowing of his children and Zeus's rise to power, covering the war with the Titans, the punishment of Prometheus, and the making of Pandora. The text concludes with the defeat of Typhoeus, Zeus's distribution of honours, and a catalogue of goddesses who bore children to mortal men.
grc.hippocrates.aphorismi: The Aphorisms is a collection of terse medical maxims in ancient Greek, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates, though its date is uncertain. The text is arranged in seven distinct sections, opening with the celebrated dictum that life is short and the art long. The work then moves through rules for diet, sleep, and the use of purgative drugs, while also considering the bearing of seasons, winds, and the ages of life on health. Later sections gather prognostic signs drawn from sweats, urine, and dreams, including observations on surgery, epilepsy, and the diseases of women.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_et_locis: On Airs, Waters, and Places is an ancient Greek medical treatise from the Hippocratic collection, attributed to Hippocrates, though its date remains uncertain. The work addresses the travelling physician who must assess an unfamiliar city, opening by declaring that a correct investigation of medicine requires attention to seasons, winds, waters, and a city's position. The text traces how exposure to hot or cold winds and the sun shapes the bodies and illnesses of its inhabitants, classifying waters from rain, snow, springs, and marshes, noting their distinct medical effects. The author shows how seasonal signs and star risings can foretell the diseases of the coming year, while warnings are given about the dangerous moments of seasonal change. The closing section compares Asia and Europe, arguing that climate and political institutions explain differences in physique and courage, and ethnographic accounts describe the Macrocephali, the Phasians, the Sauromatae, and the nomad Scythians. Their bodily peculiarities are explained by their environment and way of life.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_locis: On Airs, Waters, Places is an ancient Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates, whose title signals the environmental factors that shape human health and character. The text instructs physicians to examine seasons, winds, waters, and local customs, then details how specific climates affect the bodies of different populations. It also classifies various water sources as either harmful or wholesome, predicting yearly health trends by tracking seasonal transitions and star risings. The closing chapters compare the peoples of Asia and Europe, discussing groups such as the Long-heads and Scythian nomads. The treatise argues that climate and terrain determine physical traits and customs.
grc.hippocrates.de_capitis_vulneribus: De Capitis Vulneribus, a Greek surgical treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, addresses injuries to the cranium and their treatment. The text opens with an account of skull shape and suture courses, which resemble the letters T, H, or X. The work classifies cranial wounds as fractures, contusions, depressions, or indentations, and explains how to detect hidden injuries through questioning and inspection. Detailed directions follow for incision, dressing, and trepanation, while warnings address the proper handling of the saw and drill. The author notes the dangers posed to the membrane surrounding the brain, and the treatise ends with remarks on the thinner bones of children. It lists signs of a fatal outcome, such as fever and convulsions, and further technical guidance completes the operation safely.
grc.hippocrates.de_diaeta_in_morbis_acutis: De Diaeta in Morbis Acutis is a Greek medical treatise from the Hippocratic corpus, attributed to Hippocrates, though its exact date remains uncertain. The text opens by criticizing the Cnidian opinions for recording symptoms without prognostic observations, and it also faults their reliance on a very small number of remedies. The work argues against prolonged fasting at the start of acute illnesses, while detailing the introduction of barley gruel and its strained juice. The author warns against sudden changes in a patient's habitual diet, and he also discusses the discriminating use of various drinks. These include sweet, dark, and white wines, along with hydromel and water, and the treatise concludes with an account of bathing and its specific benefits.
grc.hippocrates.de_flatibus: De Flatibus, meaning Breaths, is a short Greek prose treatise on the causes of disease. It is transmitted under the name of Hippocrates and its date remains uncertain. The text opens by describing medicine as a laborious art and asking what single cause might explain all illnesses. It then argues that air, drawn into the body with food and drink, is the source of every ailment. The author explains fevers, rigors, hernias, and abscesses as effects of breath moving through the veins and flesh. The work closes by claiming to have demonstrated that breath is the dominant cause of all diseases.
grc.hippocrates.de_fracturis: On Fractures is a Greek surgical treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates, though its exact date remains uncertain. The work details the management of broken and displaced bones, beginning by criticizing physicians who fail to extend fractures properly. It then explains the mechanics of reduction and bandaging, covering injuries to the forearm, upper arm, thigh, and shin. Later chapters address compound fractures and the use of levers, while the author also discusses diet and the signs of bone exfoliation.
grc.hippocrates.de_prisca_medicina: De Prisca Medicina, a Greek treatise attributed to Hippocrates, argues that medicine rests on long accumulated experience. The author rejects abstract postulates that reduce disease causes to single elements. He traces the art's origin in the discovery of a diet suited to human nature. This development moved from raw foodstuffs to prepared bread, porridge, and blended drinks. The text defends the regimen of the sick through various discussions. It examines fasting, repletion, and the effects of heat and cold.
grc.hippocrates.jusjurandum: The Jusjurandum, or Hippocratic Oath, is a short Greek composition transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus, though its date and authorship remain uncertain. It is attributed to Hippocrates and records a physician swearing a formal pledge of professional conduct. The text opens with an invocation of Apollo the healer, Asclepius, Hygieia, and Panacea. The body sets out obligations to the teacher and a commitment to treat the sick for their benefit. It prohibits giving deadly drugs or abortive pessaries and cutting patients for stone. The oath also demands sexual propriety, confidentiality, and purity of life and art, closing by promising lasting repute to those who keep the pledge.
grc.homer.hymns: The Homeric Hymns are thirty-three hexameter poems transmitted under Homer's name. Their date remains uncertain, and they address the major gods of the Greek pantheon. The opening fragment honours Dionysus, weighing conflicting accounts of his birth before Zeus confirms the Nysan version. Four long narratives recount Persephone's abduction, Apollo's founding of his cult, Hermes' theft of cattle, and Aphrodite's seduction of Anchises. Shorter hymns invoke deities such as Ares, Helios, Selene, and the Dioscuri. The collection closes with the Dioscuri, called upon as saviours of sailors in winter storms.
grc.homer.iliad: The Iliad ('The Poem of Ilium') is a Greek epic poem in twenty-four books of dactylic hexameter, attributed to Homer and of uncertain date. A quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over a captive woman opens the poem and sets its declared subject, the wrath of Achilles and the suffering it brings upon the Achaeans. The narrative follows Achilles' withdrawal from the fighting before Troy and the mounting reverses suffered by the Greek forces. Patroclus dies at Hector's hands, and Achilles returns to battle to kill Hector before Priam ransoms his son's body. The poem closes with the nine days of mourning and the Trojans' funeral rites for Hector, ending with his burial and the funeral feast in Priam's house.
grc.homer.odyssey: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic poem in twenty-four books, attributed to Homer and of uncertain date. It opens with an invocation to the Muse for the tale of the man of many devices who wandered long after the sack of Troy. Poseidon's anger kept him from his home, and the poem begins with a council of the gods. Telemachus then voyages to Pylos and Sparta in search of news of his father. Odysseus, released from Calypso's island, recounts his wanderings among the Phaeacians. He describes encounters with the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, and the cattle of the Sun. Returned unrecognised to Ithaca, he is sheltered by Eumaeus and reunites with Telemachus. He endures the insolence of the suitors in his own hall before the contest of the bow. The poem closes with their slaughter, the testing and reunion with Penelope, and a truce brought about by Athena.
grc.isaeus.speeches: This collection contains twelve forensic speeches in Attic Greek, which are attributed to Isaeus, an Athenian logographer and teacher of Demosthenes. The works were probably composed in the fourth century BC, and all but one speech concerns contested inheritances. They were written for delivery by clients in Athenian courts, where the arguments address wills, adoption, and claims of kinship. Each speech builds a case through legal argument, appealing to the laws of Athens and examining witnesses. The texts also attack the opposing litigants' claims to legitimate birth.
grc.isocrates.speeches: The Speeches of Isocrates gather twenty-one separate Greek prose discourses by the Athenian rhetorician. The opening speech is a protreptic address to the young Demonicus, son of Hipponicus. It sends him paternal counsel on piety toward the gods and honour for his parents. The text also advises on disciplined care of body and soul and the company he should keep. The collection ranges from such advisory pieces to public and forensic orations. All are cast in the long, carefully balanced periods characteristic of Isocrates' prose.
grc.libanius.declamations_13-30: This collection of declamations in Greek by Libanius gathers rhetorical speeches composed on themes drawn from Greek history and from imagined situations. They are fictional pieces written as school exercises in rhetorical imitation rather than for actual forensic delivery. The opening speech has the Corinthians address the Greeks in accusation of Athens over the siege of Potidaea. Much of the collection then takes its material from the era of Demosthenes and Philip. In these speeches a Demosthenes figure laments the disaster at Chaeronea, contemplates death, and answers Philip's demands upon Athens. Others move to invented courtroom pleas, including that of a poor man who asks the council for hemlock to escape the misery of a newly enriched neighbour settled beside him.
grc.libanius.declamations_31-51: This volume contains twenty-one Greek declamations by the rhetorician Libanius. They are numbered thirty-one to fifty-one within his collected works. Such pieces are fictitious display speeches used for rhetorical training. They are delivered in the voices of imagined speakers before courts or councils. The first speech is addressed to a city council by a man whose property has been repeatedly confiscated. He recounts his father's teaching on frugality and argues that death is preferable to living on after the loss of his estate.
grc.libanius.orations_26-50: This volume gathers a series of orations by the fourth century Greek sophist Libanius. The speeches are written in an Atticizing style and address imperial governors and officials. The opening address is directed to Icarion, a governor of Antioch who resents the city's attachment to his predecessor Proclus. Libanius argues that recent disorders in the baths and theaters stem from a few troublemakers rather than the citizens as a whole. Later pieces combine civic complaints with personal quarrels, most prominently a sustained invective against Silvanus, son of Gaudentius. This former pupil is depicted as repaying his teacher's kindness with insults, mockery of his lameness, and open hostility. The collection closes with a petition to an emperor protesting the abuses of officials who compel provincials to furnish donkeys, labor, and goods for public building works.
grc.lucian.alexander: Lucian's Alexander, also known as Alexander the False Prophet, is a Greek prose satire addressed to his friend Celsus. The author compares his task of recording the life of Alexander of Abonoteichus to the cleansing of the Augean stables. The narrative traces Alexander's early dependence on a Tyanean magus and his partnership with Cocconas of Byzantium, a writer of choral songs. It details the founding of an oracle at Abonoteichus, where a tame snake is presented as the newborn Asclepius under the name Glycon. The text exposes the cult's devices, including a rigged goose egg, a mechanical snake head, and tampered sealed questions. It also highlights the hostility toward Epicureans and Christians, which culminates in the burning of Epicurus's book. The account closes with Alexander's death at seventy from a festering foot, contrary to his own prophecy of a hundred and fifty years.
grc.lucian.contemplantes: Charon, or the Inspectors, is a short satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, whose title refers to the pair who survey human life from a high vantage point. Charon is granted a single day's leave from ferrying the dead, and he persuades a reluctant Hermes to guide him over the upper world. They stack Pelion on Ossa and Oeta on Parnassus to see clearly, observing cities swarming like beehives while hopes and fears hover overhead. The Fates spin each person's fragile thread, and they foresee the impending falls of kings such as Croesus, Cyrus, and Polycrates. Below them, Solon converses with Croesus on the uncertainty of happiness, while the tour also takes in tombs and funeral offerings. It notes the vanished splendour of Nineveh, Babylon, Mycenae, and Troy, and the dialogue closes as Charon descends again, musing that human strivings leave the ferryman himself unremarked.
grc.lucian.dearum_iudicium: The Dearum Iudicium, a short comic prose dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, offers a pointed satirical reworking of the epic judgement of Paris, the myth that precipitates the Trojan War. Zeus instructs Hermes to carry a golden apple to Paris, a young shepherd on Mount Ida, who must decide which of Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite is the most beautiful. The goddesses travel across Phrygia, exchanging jealous banter and mutual disparagement along the way, while Paris deliberates nervously and asks to inspect the undressed competitors before making his choice. Hera offers lordship of all Asia, while Athena promises victory in war, and Aphrodite offers the hand of Helen, a prize that already appeals to Paris. He awards the apple to Aphrodite, who promises to serve as matchmaker with the help of Eros, Himeros, Pothos, and the Charites, a decision that sets the abduction leading to Troy in motion.
grc.lucian.dialogi_meretricii: Lucian of Samosata wrote this collection of short Greek prose dialogues, which are set among the courtesans of Athens. The opening scene features Thais and Glycerion discussing a soldier lover that the courtesan Gorgona has lured away. Later scenes track the fortunes and stratagems of the trade, including jealous suitors and haggling over fees. Mothers coach their daughters into prostitution, while hired witches and forged letters complicate lovers' quarrels. One extended episode describes the wealthy Megilla, who lives as a man with her female companion. Another follows a soldier whose lurid tales of single combat terrify his mistress and her maid into flight.
grc.lucian.icaromenippus: Lucian of Samosata wrote Icaromenippus, a title meaning Menippus with wings, which is a satirical dialogue where Menippus the Cynic recounts his flight to a friend. He fashioned wings from an eagle and a vulture to escape contradictory philosophical teachings, pausing on the moon to meet the shade of Empedocles. Menippus then gained sharp sight to survey human affairs from above, mocking the pettiness of kings, philosophers, and ordinary people. Zeus later denounced the squabbling philosophical sects at the Moon's prompting, promising to destroy them after overhearing the day's prayers. Hermes finally returned Menippus to earth, where he resolved to carry his findings to the philosophers in the Stoa.
grc.lucian.patriae_encomium: This short Greek prose encomium, known as the Patriae Encomium or praise of the fatherland, is attributed to Lucian of Samosata. It argues that the native land deserves the highest honor in human life, opening by conceding the proverb that nothing is sweeter than one's home. The text then asks if anything more august and divine can be named, answering that the fatherland is the cause and teacher of all sacred things. He treats the native land as a common mother dearer than any parent, which the gods cherish for the places of their birth. People repay it through education, wealth, and public service, while exiles and the aged long to end their days in its soil. Lawgivers impose banishment as the harshest penalty for the greatest wrongs, and generals rally troops with the cry that the war is for the fatherland, a name that makes the coward brave.
grc.lucian.podagra: Lucian of Samosata wrote Podagra, a short Greek dramatic satire that travesties the diction and metres of tragedy. The title means gout, a condition the speaker personifies as a hateful child of Cocytus. This monstrous figure was born of the Fury Megaera and nursed with the milk of Alecto. The afflicted speaker leans on his staff to deliver a sustained tragic style invocation. He catalogues the disease's fire and bitterness in the joints and veins. The monody closes as the speaker is summoned out of doors toward the sunlight.
grc.lucian.rhetorum_praeceptor: The Rhetorum Praeceptor, a short Greek satirical monologue by Lucian of Samosata, features a self-styled master of eloquence instructing an eager youth. The young man asks how he may become a rhetor and be admired as a sophist, prompting the teacher to promise a road far easier than the steep path traced by Demosthenes and Plato. He prescribes boldness, ignorance, and shamelessness as essential travelling gear for instant success, while a stock of showy Attic words and contempt for classical reading complete the toolkit. The satire closes with the teacher's confession of a disreputable career, recounting his low birth, a fraudulent marriage, and a flourishing practice as a losing advocate.
grc.lucian.toxaris_vel_amicitia: A Greek prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, carrying the alternative title On Friendship, in which Mnesippus, a Greek, and Toxaris, a Scythian, discuss friendship. The opening exchange turns on the Scythian cult of Orestes and Pylades, with Mnesippus questioning the worship of foreigners who had plundered the country and slain its king. Toxaris defends his people's honours to men they judge good and beneficent, and goes on to describe the bronze stele in the Oresteion recording the friends' deeds. In the temple enclosure, painted scenes show the shipwreck, the sacrifice to Artemis averted, and the fight during their escape. The rest of the work consists of stories of devoted friendship, told on the Greek and the Scythian side in turn.
grc.lucian.verae_historiae: Lucian of Samosata's Verae Historiae is a Greek prose narrative whose preface declares the narrator describes things he neither saw nor suffered. He claims these events do not exist and could never have existed, telling readers to believe none of it. The work is offered openly as fiction, ridiculing earlier poets and prose writers like Ctesias, Iambulus, and Homer's Odysseus. These authors recorded marvellous voyages and fabulous peoples, while the narrative follows the narrator and his fifty companions. They travel beyond the Pillars of Heracles into the western ocean, landing on an island after seventy-nine days adrift in a storm. It bears an inscription of Heracles and Dionysus, where a flowing river of wine is found and fish taste and colour of the wine.
grc.lycurgus.against_leocrates: This eisangelia charges Leocrates with treason for abandoning Athens after Chaeronea, and it opens with a hypothesis summarising the legal case. Lycurgus invokes Athena and other city gods, pledging a just and pious accusation against the defendant. He argues that Leocrates fled with money, slaves, and ancestral sacred objects, going to Rhodes and then Megara. He lived there for more than five years before returning, though his defence claimed he had sailed out on trade. Lycurgus corroborates the charge with witnesses, documents, and the decree of Hypereides, the ephebic oath, and the oath sworn at Plataea. He reinforces his case with exempla from Codrus, the Persian Wars, Euripides' Erechtheus, Homer, Tyrtaeus, and Simonides, reviewing earlier Athenian and Spartan treatment of traitors before urging the jurors to condemn Leocrates to death.
grc.novum_testamentum.actus_apostolorum: The Actus Apostolorum, or Acts of the Apostles, is the fifth book of the New Testament, written in Koine Greek prose from the Imperial era. The text opens with a dedication to Theophilus and an account of Jesus' ascension, then describes the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost and the founding of the church in Jerusalem. The narrative follows the apostles through Peter's preaching, the martyrdom of Stephen, and the conversion of Saul, while also covering the admission of Gentiles and the Jerusalem council. Paul's missionary journeys across Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece form the later focus of the work. The book closes with Paul's arrest, trials before Roman governors and King Agrippa, and a stormy voyage to Malta. It ends with his preaching under guard in Rome.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_colossenses: The Epistle to the Colossians is a New Testament letter in Greek of uncertain date, presented as written by the apostle Paul with Timothy to the community at Colossae. Paul was imprisoned when he composed this message to the believers, opening with a salutation and thanksgiving for the Colossians' faith and love. This leads into a hymnic declaration of Christ as the image of the invisible God, who is described as the firstborn of all creation and the agent of reconciliation. Paul then details his labor and suffering for the various churches, warning readers against being taken captive by empty philosophy. He also advises against judging one another by rules of food, drink, and festivals, arguing that believers have died and been raised with Christ. The closing movement offers ethical exhortation to seek the things above, telling readers to strip off the old self and clothe themselves in compassion. They are also urged to show humility and love in their daily lives, while a household code addresses wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves, and masters. The letter includes counsel on prayer and conduct toward outsiders, with greetings sent from associates including Tychicus, Onesimus, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas. Paul instructs the church to exchange the letter with the community at Laodicea, and the final greeting is written in Paul's own hand.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_i: The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a Greek letter from the Imperial era, attributed to Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, and Sosthenes. It addresses the church of God at Corinth, opening with thanksgiving and a plea to end factional loyalties. The letter then tackles disorder within the community, covering wisdom, immorality, marriage, and spiritual gifts. A sustained argument for the resurrection of the dead follows, and the work closes with travel plans and personal greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_ii: 2 Corinthians is a Greek epistle from the Roman imperial period, addressed by Paul and Timothy to the church at Corinth and Achaia. The letter opens with a blessing on the God who comforts his servants, and Paul explains a change in his travel plans. He counsels leniency toward a repentant offender, then defends his apostolate as a ministry of the new covenant. This ministry is marked by suffering, integrity, and the word of reconciliation, while later chapters urge the Corinthians to finish their collection for the poor in Jerusalem. Paul answers rival preachers with an ironic boast of his hardships and visions, warning of censure during his impending third visit to the community. The work concludes with exhortations to restore the community and a threefold benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_ephesios: The Epistle to the Ephesians is a New Testament letter in Greek prose, attributed to the apostle Paul and addressed to the saints in Ephesus. It opens with a salutation and a blessing over God's grace, then gives thanks for the recipients' faith and love. The first half presents redemption through Christ's blood, revealing the mystery of God's will to unite all things in Christ. It describes the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile into one new humanity, portraying the church as Christ's body and a temple. This temple is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, while the latter half moves into ethical exhortation. It urges the putting off of the old self and truthfulness, calling for mutual kindness and purity. A household code governs wives, husbands, children, parents, and slaves, and the text also uses the image of the whole armor of God. This armor defends against spiritual powers, and the letter closes with word that Tychicus will report on the writer's affairs. It ends with a benediction of peace and grace.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_hebraeos: The Epistle to the Hebrews is a Greek prose letter from the Imperial era whose author remains unknown and which lacks a standard opening salutation. It addresses a community of Jewish believers, declaring that God now speaks through a Son who surpasses angels. Christ is presented as a high priest after the order of Melchizedek, set above Moses and the Levitical priesthood. The old covenant's repeated sacrifices are contrasted with Christ's single offering, and the author describes his entry into the true heavenly sanctuary. Warnings against unbelief are interwoven with appeals to enter God's rest, while a catalogue of faithful figures runs from Abel to the prophets. Final exhortations urge endurance, discipline, and obedience to leaders, and personal notices and greetings from Italy close the letter.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philemonem: This short Greek prose letter belongs to the New Testament and dates from the Imperial era. It is attributed to the apostle Paul, who writes jointly with Timothy. The text is addressed to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church meeting in Philemon's house. Paul opens with a greeting and thanks Philemon for his faith and love. He then intercedes for Onesimus, a former slave who became Paul's spiritual child during imprisonment. Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother rather than a slave. He offers to cover any debt Onesimus may have incurred and expresses confidence in Philemon's compliance. The letter asks for lodging in hope of Paul's release through the recipients' prayers. It closes with greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, followed by a benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_romanos: The Epistle to the Romans is a Greek Christian letter ascribed to the apostle Paul, addressed to the believers in Rome during the imperial period. The text opens with a salutation in which Paul greets the community, announcing that the righteousness of God is revealed through faith. The body argues that Jew and Greek alike stand under sin, justified by faith apart from the works of the law. This theme is traced through the example of Abraham, covering the reconciliation won by Christ against Adam's transgression. The letter discusses liberation from sin and the law through baptism and the Spirit, noting God's continued purpose for Israel alongside the Gentiles. The Spirit assures believers that nothing separates them from the love of God, urging the offering of the body as a living sacrifice. It calls for mutual love and subjection to governing authorities, advising forbearance between the strong and the weak. Paul sets out his plans to visit Rome en route to Spain, ending with greetings to named members of the community.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_i: The First Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter written in Greek prose during the Imperial era, and it is attributed to the apostle Paul. Addressed to his associate Timothy at Ephesus, the text opens with a charge for Timothy to remain there and restrain teachers of divergent doctrine. It also warns against endless genealogies that distract from the purpose of the law, and the remainder sets out detailed instructions for the ordering of congregational life. These include directions for public prayer and the conduct of men and women, and the letter also lists qualifications for overseers and deacons. It addresses the enrolment and support of widows, and further guidance covers the treatment of elders and slaves. The text warns against ascetic pretension and the love of money, and it closes with a charge to guard the deposit of faith until the appearing of Christ.
grc.novum_testamentum.apocalypsis: The Apocalypse (Revelation), the final book of the New Testament, is an early Christian apocalypse in Greek prose from the Imperial period. It presents itself as the revelation of Jesus Christ, delivered through an angel to a servant named John. After an epistolary greeting, a vision commands John to write messages of praise and rebuke to seven churches in Asia. The remainder recounts his visions on Patmos and in heaven, where a Lamb opens a sealed scroll and seven seals, trumpets, and bowls of wrath follow. A dragon and two beasts appear, and the visions move on to the fall of Babylon. After a thousand-year reign and the final judgment, the new Jerusalem descends, and the book closes with promises of Christ's imminent return.
grc.novum_testamentum.iacobi: The Epistle of James is a Greek New Testament letter from the Imperial era, sent in the name of James, who calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. It addresses the twelve tribes in the Dispersion, proceeding as a chain of moral and paraenetic discourses rather than a sustained argument. The text teaches endurance under trial, prayer for wisdom, and impartiality toward rich and poor, while later sections set out the harmony of faith and works through the examples of Abraham and Rahab. They also warn against the untamed tongue and the danger of quarrels and friendship with the world, closing with a call to bring back anyone who wanders from the truth.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannes: The Gospel of John is the fourth of the four canonical Gospels in the New Testament, written in Greek prose during the Roman Imperial period by an author of uncertain identity. The text opens with a prologue that hails the Word, or Logos, which was with God in the beginning, and this Word became flesh to bring grace and truth in place of the law given through Moses. The account follows Jesus from the witness of John the Baptist and early signs like the water made wine at Cana, moving through long discourses on the bread of life and the good shepherd into the farewell speeches. The work closes with the passion narrative, covering the arrest, trial, and crucifixion of Jesus, and it ends with resurrection appearances to Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and the disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_ii: The Second Letter of John is a brief New Testament epistle written in Greek prose, composed at an uncertain date during the Imperial period. The author identifies himself only as the Elder, and the letter opens with a greeting to the elect lady and her children. The writer expresses joy at their conduct and urges them to love one another, reminding them to keep the commandments heard from the beginning. The text warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, telling the addressee not to welcome these individuals into the house. The letter closes with a hope of speaking face to face, ending with greetings from the children of the addressee's elect sister.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_iii: The Third Letter of John is a brief Greek epistle from the New Testament, belonging to the group of three Johannine letters. The author, who identifies himself only as the elder, writes in prose during the Imperial era. He opens with a greeting to Gaius, expressing love in the truth and praying for his health and prosperity. The body praises Gaius for his hospitality, welcoming travelling missionaries with faith, while contrasting him with Diotrephes. Diotrephes is a domineering church figure who refuses the elder's representatives and expels members from the congregation. The letter commends Demetrius as a good man, attested by all people and the truth, and closes with hopes for a face to face visit, declining ink and pen to pass on mutual greetings among friends.
grc.novum_testamentum.iudae: The Epistle of Jude is a brief New Testament letter written in Greek prose during the Imperial era. It is counted among the catholic epistles and attributed to Judas, the brother of James. The author addresses a community beloved in God the Father and urges them to contend for the faith. He warns against intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ, citing examples like Sodom and Gomorrah. The text also references Michael's dispute over the body of Moses and the prophecy of Enoch. It concludes with exhortations to build up faith and a doxology to the only God.
grc.novum_testamentum.marcus: The Gospel of Mark, the second of the four canonical gospels, is a prose narrative written in Greek during the Roman imperial period. Tradition attributes the text to Mark the evangelist, and the story opens with the preaching and baptism of John the Baptist. It then describes the baptism of Jesus and his temptation in the wilderness, while the main body follows Jesus through Galilee and surrounding regions. He calls the twelve, heals the sick, and expels unclean spirits, and he also teaches the crowds in parables. The journey to Jerusalem brings temple confrontations and an eschatological discourse, and the last supper leads into the betrayal, trial, and crucifixion. The account closes with the women fleeing the empty tomb, and shorter and longer endings are appended to this conclusion.
grc.novum_testamentum.matthaeus: The Gospel of Matthew is a Greek prose narrative in the New Testament that opens with a genealogy of Jesus traced from Abraham through David. An infancy narrative follows, including the visit of the magi and the flight into Egypt, before the story tracks Jesus from his baptism by John and temptation in the wilderness. His Galilean ministry features preaching, healing, and exorcism, punctuated by extended discourses such as the Sermon on the Mount and the parables of the kingdom. The narrative later turns toward Jerusalem, where the entry into the city and temple confrontations occur, followed by an apocalyptic discourse on the destruction of the temple and the end of the age. This leads into the Last Supper, betrayal, trial before Pilate, crucifixion, and burial, closing with the women at the empty tomb and appearances of the risen Jesus. He commissions the disciples to baptize all nations.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_i: The First Epistle of Peter is a prose letter in the Greek New Testament, attributed to the apostle Peter and dating from the imperial period. It addresses the elect exiles of the Dispersion in five provinces, opening with a blessing on the living hope secured by Christ's resurrection. The body urges holiness, mutual love, and good conduct among the nations, presenting believers as living stones and a royal priesthood. The letter then counsels submission to earthly authorities and frames suffering as a share in Christ's passion, while baptism is figured in the deliverance through the flood. Closing sections instruct elders to shepherd the flock and counsel humility, with greetings sent through Silvanus from Babylon together with Mark.
grc.oppian.halieutica: The Halieutica, a Greek didactic poem in five books, comprises 3,506 lines of hexameter verse attributed to Oppian. He addresses it to a Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, whose identity and date remain uncertain. The poem opens with a proem contrasting the perilous craft of the fisherman with easier hunts, invoking Zeus, Poseidon, and Hermes. It surveys the breeding grounds and habits of sea creatures, detailing their loves, fights, and cunning devices. Specific examples include the mating of the moray and viper, sponge hunters, and the dolphin's friendship with a youth of Lesbos. Later books focus on fishing techniques, describing hooks, nets, traps, spears, poisons, and the hunting of tunny and swordfish, concluding with a prayer for the emperor and an invocation to Eros.
grc.oppian_of_apamea.cynegetica: The Cynegetica, a Greek didactic epic in four books attributed to Oppian of Apamea, is addressed to the young Antoninus, son of Domna and Severus. Bidden by Calliope and Artemis to sponsor a song of the chase, the young man receives this comprehensive guide to hunting. The first book treats the hunter's equipment and dress, the seasons and hours suited to the hunt, and the breeds, mating and training of horses and dogs. It also includes an excursus on legendary hunters such as Perseus, Castor and Polydeuces, Meleager, Atalanta, Hippolytus and Orion. The second and third books survey the generations of wild beasts, the horned game, elephants, the rhinoceros and smaller creatures. They then describe the great carnivores, lion, pard, lynx, tiger, bear and wild boar, with close attention to their courtship, parturition and parental behaviour. The final book turns to methods of capture, covering pit traps, nets, fire and mounted drives for lions. It details the luring of panthers with springs of drugged wine, which occasions an extended account of Dionysus, the Bacchants and Pentheus. The book concludes with the taking of bears and gazelles with nets and snares.
grc.pausanias.description_of_greece: Pausanias composed this periegesis, or descriptive tour, of mainland Greece in ten books. The work surveys the country region by region through its cities, sanctuaries, and monuments. Book one begins at Cape Sounion and the harbors of Athens before entering the city. Later books cover the Peloponnese, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia, Elis, and Arcadia. The text then returns to central Greece with Boeotia and Phocis, closing in the Ozolian Locrians. Temples, statues, and tombs are interwoven with local myths, cult practices, and historical anecdotes.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_mutatione_nominum: De Mutatione Nominum ('On the Change of Names') is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus. It expounds the seventeenth chapter of Genesis and the divine appearances to Abraham. The work argues that the truly Existent is unnameable and unknowable. It suggests that scriptural titles designate distinct divine powers such as kingship and creative beneficence. The text interprets successive scriptural renamings as moral and psychological readings of virtue. It also treats the promised birth of Isaac as joy generated in the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_posteritate_caini: De Posteritate Caini, a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, expounds the Genesis narrative of Cain's departure from God and his descendants. Opening with Genesis 4:16, where Cain dwells in the land of Naid, it argues that the Mosaic narrative must be read figuratively because God has no face. The exposition follows Cain's line, including Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methuselah, and Lamech, taking each name as a personification of impiety, vanity, or bodily passion. Cain's founding of a city is read as a doctrine making the mind the measure of all things, while later sections set the Cainites against Seth, the other seed raised in place of Abel. Extended allegories of watering and irrigation feature Hagar and Rebecca at the well, and the treatise closes with the drunkenness of Lot's daughters, Onan, and Phinehas. It ends with praise of peace as the fount of happiness and long life.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sobrietate: De Sobrietate, a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, expounds the scriptural account of Noah's drunkenness in Genesis 9. The work frames sobriety as the watchfulness of the rational soul, opening with the verse where Noah wakes from wine. He learns what his younger son has done, and the text first praises the sober mind. It then reads scriptural talk of younger and older as moral conditions, including examples like Ishmael, Isaac, Rachel, and Leah. Joseph and the naming of Abraham as elder also appear, while the latter half interprets the curse of Canaan. This curse represents vice in motion rather than at rest, and the blessings of Shem and Japheth are also expounded. The wise man calls on God to enlarge the mind, seeking to dwell in the purified house of the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_specialibus_legibus_lib: De Specialibus Legibus is a four-book Greek treatise by the first-century Alexandrian Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, which expounds the individual precepts of the Mosaic law as the species that fall under the ten commandments. Philo had treated those commandments as the genera in an earlier work, and the text opens with a defence of circumcision against those who deride the practice. It then addresses the worship of the one God and the prohibition of images, while the remaining books pass in order through the rest of the Decalogue. This includes the Sabbath, duties to parents, marriage, and judicial procedure, with each precept supplied with a rational or symbolic explanation. The treatise closes with the laws of warfare and a praise of justice and equality.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_virtutibus: De Virtutibus, a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, expounds the virtues as embodied in the Mosaic law. The work falls into sections on courage, humanity, repentance, and nobility, opening by passing from a preceding discussion of justice to courage. True manliness is defined as knowledge that scorns poverty, dishonour, mutilation, and disease, and this firm and high-hearted soul scorns the furious rage that the many admire. The bulk of the work follows the law's humane injunctions concerning female captives, runaway and debt slaves, enemies and their beasts of burden, and newborn animals. The text then treats repentance and, at length, nobility, arguing from the patriarch Abraham, from Tamar, and from Jacob's handmaids. Genuine good birth derives from virtue and worship of the one God rather than from ancestry.
