grc.philo_judaeus.de_vita_mosis_lib_iii: De Vita Mosis presents the third book of Philo Judaeus' Greek treatise, which was edited in Cohn's Berlin edition of 1902 and runs to 627 lines. Philo, a Jewish author writing in Greek, ranks Moses above Greek sages as a lawgiver while recasting the biblical narrative in the idiom of Greek biography. The account follows Moses from his Chaldaean lineage and Egyptian birth through exposure on the Nile, detailing his adoption by the king's daughter and royal education in mathematics and philosophy. The text also covers the enslavement of his people, and the opening prologue defends Moses against the mockery of Greek men of letters. It announces an account drawn from sacred books and elders of the nation, standing among the fullest ancient Greek treatments of Moses. This work bridges scriptural narrative and the conventions of Greek paideia, biography, and encomium.
grc.philo_judaeus.legatio_ad_gaium: A Greek historical narrative by Philo of Alexandria, who writes as a member of the embassy sent by the Jews of Alexandria to the emperor Gaius Caligula. The work opens with a meditation on the instability of fortune against the steadfastness of nature and divine providence, naming the people Israel as 'he who sees God.' It then traces Gaius's accession after Tiberius, the empire's initial rejoicing, his grave illness, and his growing demand for divine honours, before turning to the order to erect a colossal statue of the emperor in the Jerusalem Temple and the grief and danger this brought upon the nation. The account culminates in the envoys' humiliating audiences before Gaius in Rome, his mockery of their ancestral customs, their narrow dismissal, and closes with a promise to narrate the emperor's subsequent reversal of fortune.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.heroicus: Heroicus is a Greek dialogue by Philostratus the Athenian, in which a Phoenician merchant is delayed by contrary winds on the Hellespont coast near Troy. He meets a vinedicker who lives in communion with the restored hero Protesilaos, claiming the hero dwells on his land and helps him cultivate it. The rest of the work is largely the vinedicker's report of Protesilaos' conversations, where the hero describes the true deeds and characters of the Greek and Trojan warriors. He corrects what he takes to be Homer's and the poets' inventions, and he also recounts marvels, oracles, and cult practices connected with the heroes. Topics range from Palamedes and Ajax to the careers of Odysseus, Hector, and Achilles, and the dialogue closes as the vinedicker declines to speak of the underworld's rivers.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vitae_sophista: The Vitae Sophistarum, meaning Lives of the Sophists, is a Greek prose work by Philostratus the Athenian. It presents a record of celebrated sophists in two books, dedicated to Antonius Gordianus. The preserved selection includes the dedicatory letter and the opening of the first book. Philostratus surveys the history of sophistic rhetoric in these pages. He distinguishes an older tradition founded by Gorgias of Leontini from a second sophistic associated with Aeschines. The text illustrates this character with anecdotes about Prodicus, Chaerephon, and Demosthenes.
grc.pindar.odes: Pindar's Carmina gathers the epinician odes of the Greek lyric poet in four books. These volumes are named for the festivals where the celebrated victors won their prizes. The collection opens with an ode for Hieron of Syracuse that moves from splendour to myth. Each poem praises an athletic victor and his city while weaving in heroic legend. The sequence ends with a tale of Perseus, Medusa, and Athena's invention of the flute.
grc.plato.cleitophon: The Cleitophon is a short dialogue attributed to Plato, featuring a single sustained speech by Cleitophon, son of Aristonymus. He responds to a report that he disparaged Socrates while praising Thrasymachus, opening by admiring Socrates' exhortations. Cleitophon compares these words to a god's speech on the tragic stage, arguing they rouse men to care for their souls. He then complains about the lack of clear teaching, noting that he repeatedly questioned Socrates and his companions about justice. Proposed answers such as benefit, advantage, friendship, and harmony collapsed under examination, leaving Socrates appearing able only to exhort. The dialogue ends with a pointed challenge, as Cleitophon asks what treatment the soul requires to reach virtue, declaring he will go to Thrasymachus if Socrates does not answer.
grc.plato.cratylus: Plato's Cratylus is a Greek dialogue in which Socrates examines whether names possess a natural correctness or are fixed only by convention. The title refers to Cratylus, one of the two interlocutors who debate this issue with Socrates. The conversation opens with Cratylus claiming that names belong to things by nature, while Hermogenes argues they are whatever a community agrees to call them. Socrates then offers a long series of etymologies for names of gods, heroes, and cosmic entities, as well as words for virtue and vice. He argues that original name-makers imitated the essences of things in sounds and letters, though he allows for names distorted by usage or borrowed from foreign tongues. The discussion closes with Socrates qualifying the theory, noting that names are likenesses of things but can be fitted well or badly. He concludes that things must ultimately be studied through themselves rather than through names, which may mislead those who follow them.
grc.plato.crito: The Crito ('The Crito') is a short Socratic dialogue set in Socrates' prison cell in Athens. Crito arrives before dawn with news that the ship from Delos is expected, signaling the day of execution. He urges escape, citing public opinion, the danger to his friends' fortunes, and the upbringing of Socrates' children. Socrates maintains that one must never return injustice for injustice, whatever the many believe. In reply, the personified Laws of Athens claim he tacitly agreed to obey them by remaining in the city. They argue that rearing children there and never leaving means flight would wrong the laws, the city, and himself. The dialogue closes with Socrates resolved to remain and accept death, saying that in this the god leads.
grc.plato.euthydemus: Plato's Euthydemus is a Greek dialogue in which Socrates recounts a meeting at the Lyceum, telling Crito about the sophist brothers Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. These men claim to teach virtue and refute any questioner, describing eristic displays against the young Clinias and Ctesippus. They use verbal tricks to argue that only fools learn, while claiming that contradiction and false statement are impossible. The brothers further assert that Socrates is fatherless and related to dogs, prompting Socrates to offer his own protreptic account of philosophy. He defines it as the knowledge of right use, seeking a single royal or political knowledge of good use. This search exposes false lovers of wisdom, ending with Socrates advising the brothers to converse only with paying pupils. He also exhorts Crito to test philosophy itself rather than judge it by bad practitioners, encouraging his sons to pursue this path.
grc.plato.gorgias: Plato's Gorgias is a dialogue set in Athens where Socrates examines the nature of rhetoric, and the title names the celebrated rhetorician who serves as the primary interlocutor. Socrates and Chaerephon arrive late at Callicles' house after Gorgias has given an exhibition, and Socrates first draws from Gorgias the claim that rhetoric produces persuasion before crowds. He then answers Polus's defense of the tyrant's power to do what he pleases, arguing that doing injustice is worse than suffering it and that punishment benefits the wrongdoer. Callicles rejects this as conventional morality and champions the natural right of the stronger, while Socrates replies with an account of self-control and the ordered soul. He closes with a myth of the dead judged naked before Rhadamanthus, Minos, and Aeacus, urging that justice and virtue be practiced in life and in death alike.
grc.plato.hippias_minor: The Hippias Minor, a Socratic dialogue by Plato, features Eudicus prompting Socrates to question the sophist Hippias of Elis about Homer's judgment of Achilles and Odysseus. These portraits frame the ensuing argument, which first asks whether the truthful and the false speaker are one and the same. It draws on arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy to argue that only the capable man can both lie and tell the truth. Socrates then turns to whether one who errs or wrongs voluntarily is better than one who does so involuntarily. He tests this claim through examples from running, wrestling, the crafts, and the faculties of body and soul. The dialogue ends unresolved, with Socrates professing himself unsettled by the argument's apparent conclusion that the deliberate wrongdoer, if such a person exists, would be the good man.
grc.plato.laches: Plato's Laches is a short Socratic dialogue in which Lysimachus and Melesias seek counsel on their sons' education. They ask the generals Nicias and Laches whether training in fighting in armour is beneficial. Socrates redirects the inquiry to examine the nature of courage, the virtue such training aims to instil. Laches defines courage as endurance of the soul, while Nicias offers knowledge of what is to be feared. Both definitions are tested and found wanting, leaving the group in perplexity. They resolve to seek a teacher for themselves and their sons and to meet again the next day.
grc.plato.leges: Plato's Laws is a long dialogue in twelve books conducted between an unnamed Athenian Stranger, Cleinias of Crete, and Megillus of Sparta. The title refers to the work's focus on legislation as the men walk from Cnossos towards the shrine of Zeus. They ask whether the laws of Crete and Sparta were given by a god or by men. The discussion then moves through the full design of a projected colony at Magnesia, covering education, choral song, gymnastics, and military training. It also addresses marriage, religious worship, and the trial of impiety, including criminal and civil statutes, courts, and penalties. The text ends by proposing a Nocturnal Council of elder guardians modelled on the union of intelligence and sensation in the soul to watch over the whole constitution.
grc.plato.lysis: The Lysis is a Socratic dialogue in which Plato examines the nature of friendship. It opens with Socrates walking outside the city walls between the Academy and the Lyceum, where Hippothales and a group of youths draw him into a newly built wrestling school. After telling Hippothales that a lover should humble rather than flatter his beloved, Socrates questions the boys Lysis and Menexenus about who can be a friend to whom. He tests the claims that like is friend to like and that opposite attracts opposite. He then asks whether what is neither good nor bad becomes a friend of the good through the presence of evil. Each proposal collapses in its turn, and the conversation ends unresolved when the boys' attendants call them home at dusk.
grc.plato.menexenus: Plato's Menexenus is a Socratic dialogue of uncertain date that opens with a chance meeting between Socrates and the young Menexenus after a council session. The council must choose a speaker for the public burial of the war dead, and after playful talk about funeral rhetoric, Socrates recites a long oration. He delivers this speech in the voice he attributes to Aspasia, praising the autochthonous birth of the Athenians and their ancestral constitution. The oration recounts the city's wars from Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea, continuing through campaigns against fellow Greeks to recent conflicts with Sparta and Persia. The speech closes with exhortations to the sons of the fallen and offers consolation to their parents. A brief closing exchange returns the oration to its ironic frame, and Socrates promises further political speeches learned from Aspasia.
grc.plato.meno: Meno, a Platonic dialogue, features Socrates and the Thessalian visitor Menon, a nobleman trained by Gorgias, inquiring whether virtue can be taught. Menon asks if virtue arises by teaching, practice, or nature, and the conversation moves through the demand for a definition. Socrates demonstrates recollection by solving a geometrical problem with one of Menon's slaves, arguing that knowledge is true belief tethered by an account of the cause. Using the method of hypothesis, Socrates concludes that virtue is a kind of wisdom, and since no teachers of virtue exist, it must arise by divine dispensation. The dialogue ends with an injunction for Menon to win over the Athenian Anytus.
grc.plato.parmenides: The Parmenides is a philosophical dialogue by Plato of uncertain date, opening with a frame conversation in which Cephalus of Clazomenae and his companions induce Antiphon to recite a reported meeting. This meeting involves a young Socrates, Zeno, and the aged Parmenides, where Socrates questions Zeno's defence of the Eleatic thesis and puts forward an account of Forms. He meets searching objections from Parmenides concerning the participation of sensible things in Forms, and is then set an exercise in dialectic. The remainder of the work consists almost entirely of Parmenides' prolonged examination of two hypotheses, namely 'if the One is' and 'if the One is not'. This examination derives contrary and often paradoxical consequences for the One itself, as well as consequences for the others with respect to unity and plurality. The dialogue concludes that the One and the others are and are not in every way, and that they both appear and do not appear.
grc.plato.phaedo: Plato's Phaedo, a dialogue on the death of Socrates, is framed as a narrative by Phaedo of Elis to Echecrates. The story takes place in Socrates' prison cell on the day he drinks the hemlock. Socrates first explains why a philosopher should face death willingly, then offers arguments for the soul's survival from the cycle of opposites. He also draws on recollection and the soul's kinship with the invisible, while Simmias and Cebes raise objections that reopen the question of the soul's endurance. Socrates answers by recounting his turn toward explanations through Forms, and a final argument presents the soul as the principle of life and therefore immortal. The closing movement includes a myth of the true earth and the underworld, ending with the death scene and Socrates' last words about a debt to Asclepius.
grc.plato.phaedrus: Plato's Phaedrus is a Greek dialogue in which Socrates converses with the young Phaedrus, who has heard a speech by Lysias urging a youth to favour a non-lover over a lover. As they walk beside the Ilissus, Socrates offers rival speeches on love, which culminate in a palinode and the myth of the winged soul. The work then turns from love to rhetoric, examining how speeches are composed and criticising written discourse by contrast with the living dialogue of dialectic. It also recounts the story of the Egyptian god Theuth's invention of writing, before closing with Socrates' prayer to Pan and instructions to send messages to Lysias and Isocrates.
grc.plato.protagoras: Plato's Protagoras is a Socratic dialogue in Greek prose. It recounts how Hippocrates roused Socrates before dawn to pay the visiting sophist Protagoras of Abdera for instruction. The opening exchange follows the two to the house of Callias, where Protagoras is lodging. Socrates questions what such paid teaching would make of a pupil. The dialogue as a whole takes up whether virtue can be taught. This leads into debate between Socrates and Protagoras over the nature and unity of virtue.
grc.plato.respublica: Plato's Respublica, or Republic, is a Socratic dialogue in ten books that opens with Socrates' descent to the Piraeus for a festival. He is detained at the house of Cephalus, where they discuss old age, and the conversation turns to the question of justice. The dialogue then constructs an ideal city in speech, treating the education and way of life of its guardians. The analogy between city and soul is explored, and the rule of philosophers is examined. The allegories of the sun, the divided line, and the cave appear, followed by the degeneration of constitutions and the figure of the tyrant. A criticism of poetry and the immortality of the soul are discussed, and the work closes with the myth of Er, where souls choose their next lives before drinking from the river of Lethe.
grc.plato.sophista: Plato's Sophist is a dialogue set the day after the Theaetetus, where an unnamed Stranger from Elea, a companion of Parmenides and Zeno, joins Socrates. The Stranger takes Theaetetus as his respondent to define the sophist through dichotomous division, using the angler as a paradigm to classify acquisitive and imitative arts. Midway, the hunt pauses for a prolonged examination of being and non-being, surveying earlier theories and the 'gigantomachy' between materialists and idealists. It argues that false speech becomes possible once being, sameness, difference, rest, and motion are distinguished as the greatest kinds. The dialogue closes by narrowing the divisions to a final definition, identifying the sophist as an ironic imitator who is ignorant of what he imitates. He produces appearances in short private arguments through contradictory speech.
grc.plato.statesman: A dialogue by Plato, opening with a short frame in which Theodorus and Socrates arrange for a visiting Stranger, questioned by young Socrates, to define the statesman by division. The work follows the Stranger's method of diaeresis through successive attempted definitions of the statesman's art, including a long myth of cosmic reversal and the age of Kronos, a parable in which the king is first mistaken for a shepherd and the definition is then corrected, and an extended analogy comparing statesmanship to the art of weaving. The dialogue separates the royal science from rival claimants such as generals, judges and orators, classifies forms of constitution and examines whether law or expert knowledge should rule, discusses measurement and the mean in speech and action, and closes by defining the true statesman as the one who binds courageous and moderate temperaments together into a single fabric for the city.
grc.plato.theages: Theages is a brief Socratic dialogue in the Platonic corpus, attributed to Plato and of uncertain date. The title names the young man whose desire for wisdom prompts the conversation. Demodocus of Anagyrus asks Socrates for a private word, and they withdraw to the stoa of Zeus Eleutherios. Socrates questions Theages about the specific kind of wisdom he seeks, contrasting expertises like steersmanship and medicine with the political knowledge of Themistocles and Pericles. After jesting that the boy aims at tyranny, Socrates disclaims any such knowledge himself. The closing portion describes the daimonion, a divine sign that has attended Socrates since childhood, which only ever dissuades, as shown in stories of Charmides and Aristides. The dialogue ends with an agreement to test their companionship, planning prayers and sacrifices to placate the sign if it opposes the association.
grc.plato.timaeus: Plato's Timaeus opens with Socrates summarizing the ideal city from the previous day, after which Critias reports the ancient victory of Athens over Atlantis. This tale is traced back to Solon and Egyptian priests, while the bulk of the work is Timaeus' long cosmological discourse. A divine craftsman shapes the visible universe as a living likeness of an eternal model, explaining the world-soul and its planetary circuits. The discourse also covers the generation of time and the four elements, which are built from triangles and regular solids. The characterless receptacle receives all becoming, and the construction of the human body and its mortal soul follows. The dialogue closes with discussions of sensation and breathing, addressing disease and the transmigration of degenerate souls, while the completed cosmos is hailed as one visible living god.
grc.plutarch.aemilius_paulus: Plutarch's Life of Aemilius Paulus opens with a preface shared with its companion Life of Timoleon, where the author explains his habit of writing parallel lives as mirrors for the ordering of his own character. The narrative follows Lucius Aemilius Paulus from his patrician Roman lineage and early magistracies, tracing his commands in Iberia and against the Ligurians to his election in his sixties. He was chosen to lead the war against Perseus of Macedon, and central chapters recount the campaign culminating in the battle of Pydna. This includes the lunar eclipse before the engagement and the breaking of the Macedonian phalanx, while Perseus's flight, betrayal, and surrender conclude the military action. The closing sections cover Aemilius's tour of Greece and the devastation of Epirus, and they also detail his three-day triumph and the deaths of his two young sons. His address to the people on the instability of Fortune follows these events, and the text ends with Perseus's captivity, Aemilius's censorship, and his final illness.
grc.plutarch.amatorius: Plutarch's Amatorius is a Greek dialogue on love of uncertain date, where Autobulus recounts conversations held at the festival of Eros in Thespiae. The discussion begins with the abduction of the young Bacchon by the wealthy widow Ismenodora, which prompts an argument over whether pederastic or conjugal love better deserves the name of Eros. Protogenes's father defends Eros as a god and a teacher of virtue, drawing on Platonic doctrine and an Egyptian teaching about three Erotes. An extended analogy compares Eros to the sun, while stories of lovers' courage illustrate his case, ranging from Cleomachus of Thessaly and Epaminondas to the Galatian Camma. The dialogue closes with Peisias leading the bridal procession, and the company departs to salute the god and attend the wedding.
grc.plutarch.an_seni_respublica_gerenda_sit: This Greek dialogue by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, features a conversation with his friend Euphanes. Euphanes quotes Pindar to ask whether old age is a proper season for public life. Plutarch argues that age brings prudence, authority, and experience to the statesman. He cites Greek and Roman examples, including Pericles, Cato, and Cicero, to support this view. The text weighs which offices an elder should keep and how to speak without envy. It concludes that political engagement is a lifelong way of life for a rational being.
grc.plutarch.animine_an_corporis_affectiones: This short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia, asks whether the affections of the soul are worse than those of the body. The work answers that psychic disorders are graver because they escape the sufferer's awareness, opening with Homer's verdict that no creature is more wretched than man. The argument uses medical analogy to show that bodily diseases announce themselves clearly, while the soul's maladies deceive their bearers, who take them for virtues. The essay cites the Aesopic fox, Democritus, and the madness of Agave, closing by figuring passions as wintry storms that wreck a man's life.
grc.plutarch.antony: Plutarch's Greek biography of Mark Antony, one of the Greek Parallel Lives and composed as a comparison with the Life of Demetrius, opens with the statesman's ancestry. It recalls a grandfather put to death in Marius's purge and the young Antony's extravagance under Curio, before turning to his campaigns in the East. Antony's service as Caesar's ally and general leads on to Caesar's assassination, his ascendancy at the funeral oration, and the triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and its proscriptions. After his marriage to Octavia, the narrative dwells at length on the liaison with Cleopatra that estranged him from Rome. A disastrous Parthian expedition, the naval defeat at Actium, and the final collapse at Alexandria lead to Antony's suicide. The account closes with Cleopatra's death, the fate of their children, and the later fortunes of the family down to Nero.
grc.plutarch.bruta_animalia_ratione_uti: A Greek prose dialogue transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch, it takes its premise from the Circe episode of the Odyssey, in which the sorceress turns Odysseus's companions into beasts. Odysseus asks Circe to restore his men to human form, but she produces instead Gryllus, one of the swine, who refuses and undertakes to defend the animal way of life. The ensuing debate measures the reason and virtue of beasts against those of humanity. Gryllus contends that animals possess courage, justice, and the other virtues untaught and according to nature, while human reasoning serves appetite and ambition. From the name of its principal animal speaker the work is also known as the Gryllus.
grc.plutarch.caesar: Plutarch composed this Greek biography of Julius Caesar as part of his Parallel Lives, pairing him with Alexander to compare their lives and characters. It opens with Caesar's marriage to Cornelia and the enmity that Sulla felt toward him, tracing his perilous youth, including his capture by pirates and his rhetorical studies at Rhodes. He rises through the Roman magistracies amid the Catilinarian debate and the Bona Dea scandal, and his alliance with Pompey and Crassus brings him the consulship and the Gallic command. The central portion covers the wars in Gaul, Germany, and Britain, where the revolt of Vercingetorix and the siege of Alesia stand out in this section. The story then turns to the rupture with Pompey and the crossing of the Rubicon, and the civil war proceeds through Pharsalus, Alexandria, Zela, Thapsus, and Munda. Caesar's dictatorship for life and his reform of the calendar follow these victories, and the conspiracy of Brutus and Cassius leads to his murder in the senate-house. He dies on the Ides of March at the base of Pompey's statue, and the text closes with the omens that appeared before Brutus at Philippi.
grc.plutarch.caius_gracchus: A Greek biographical work by Plutarch, belonging to his Lives of Roman statesmen, which opens with Caius Gracchus withdrawing from public life after his brother Tiberius's death, reluctant to take up the political cause that had cost Tiberius his life. The narrative follows his quaestorship in Sardinia, his tribunates and legislative programme of grain distributions, judicial reform, colonies and roads, his rivalry with Livius Drusus and the senate's counter-moves, and his colonial foundation at the site of Carthage. It concludes with the armed confrontation under the consul Opimius, the death of Caius and his ally Fulvius Flaccus, the reprisals that followed, and the later fortunes of his mother Cornelia.
grc.plutarch.camillus: This Greek prose biography is one of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, a collection of paired biographies. It traces the career of the Roman statesman Marcus Furius Camillus, who is recorded as a second founder of Rome. The narrative opens with the paradox of a five-time dictator who never held the consulship. It follows his early distinction against the Aequi and Volscians and the ten-year siege of Veii. The text recounts the Gallic invasion, the burning of Rome, and Camillus's return from exile. He defeats the Gauls and restores the city, later handling the demagogue Manlius Capitolinus. The work concludes with his death in the plague that followed his final compromise.
grc.plutarch.cicero: This Greek biography of the Roman orator Cicero by Plutarch belongs to his Parallel Lives, opening with traditions about his parentage and the unflattering origin of his family name. The narrative follows his education in Greek philosophy and rhetoric, detailing his quaestorship in Sicily and the prosecution of Verres. His consulship saw him expose the Catilinarian conspiracy and execute the ringleaders, while the account continues with his exile engineered by Clodius and his triumphant return. It covers his governorship of Cilicia and his wavering between Pompey and Caesar, ending with his speeches against Antony and his proscription and murder.
grc.plutarch.cleomenes: Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes is a Greek prose biography from his Parallel Lives, continuing the story begun in the Life of Agis. The narrative opens after the death of Leonidas II, detailing the forced marriage of Agiatis to the young Cleomenes. His character and education under the Stoic Sphaerus are sketched before the main plot follows his seizure of power. He cancels debts and redistributes land to restore old Spartan discipline, then campaigns against the Achaean League and Aratus. He captures Argos and Corinth before losing to the Macedonian king Antigonus, while his brother Eucleidas dies at Sellasia. Cleomenes flees to Egypt, is detained at the court of Ptolemy in Alexandria, and a failed uprising leads to the suicides of his companions. His mother Cratesicleia and her children are executed, and a serpent coils about his exposed body at the end.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pericles_and_fabi: This formal comparison, known as a synkrisis, concludes Plutarch's paired Lives of Pericles and Fabius Maximus. It opens by noting that both men left many fine examples of political and military virtue. The text first weighs their generalship, contrasting Pericles at the head of a fortunate Athens with Fabius supporting a Rome battered by defeats. It cites specific deeds such as Fabius' rescue of Minucius and Pericles' nine trophies. The discussion then moves to their civic conduct, setting Fabius' gentleness toward Minucius against Pericles' ostracism of Cimon and Thucydides. It also considers their disinterestedness with money before closing on Pericles' buildings, whose magnificence the comparison places above all earlier Roman display.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_sertorius_and_eum: This short formal comparison, known as a synkrisis, closes Plutarch's paired Lives of Sertorius and Eumenes by declaring that everything memorable about the two men has now been gathered. Both were exiles and foreigners who continually commanded large and warlike armies of many peoples, with Sertorius holding his command by the willing deference of his allies. Eumenes won supremacy through his deeds amid contests over leadership, and the text contrasts their characters, noting that Eumenes was warlike and contentious though he might have lived securely and with honour. Sertorius was mild and peace-loving, yet no peace was permitted him, so each was driven into the opposite role. The piece closes with their deaths, Sertorius slain unsuspecting through his trust in his friends, while Eumenes was caught while trying to flee and reduced to pleading with his captor for his body and life.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_solon_and_publico: This brief Greek prose piece by Plutarch serves as the formal synkrisis, or comparison, that closes his paired lives of Solon and Publicola. It opens by noting that each statesman was the other's imitator and witness, and the author cites Solon's answer to Croesus on happiness as spoken more fittingly of Publicola than of Tellus. The body weighs their careers point by point, starting with Publicola's distinguished lineage and a death mourned by all Rome, while his wealth was justly gained and generously spent. He borrowed from Solon's laws in framing the constitution, and he also doubled the senate and displayed a rooted hatred of tyranny. This hatred was shown in the expulsion of the kings and the unmasking of the Tarquins' conspiracy, while Solon is credited with the cancellation of debts that secured the citizens' freedom. His constitution was more brilliant in its beginning, though Publicola preserved his and proved the more fortunate at the last, and the piece closes by observing that a statesman's deeds must be judged against the circumstances before him. Publicola won his greatest contests in person and turned the formidable Porsenna from enemy into friend.
grc.plutarch.conjugalia_praecepta: The Conjugalia Praecepta is a Greek ethical essay by Plutarch, which opens as a wedding gift to a newly married couple. The author explains that philosophy offers a discourse on marriage no less worthy than song, and he prays that Aphrodite be attended by the Muses, Hermes, Peitho, and the Graces. The body of the work consists of a long succession of short precepts, maxims, and anecdotes, which draw on figures such as Solon, Socrates, Cato, Philip, and Olympias. These stories address the conduct and harmony of husband and wife, and recurring themes include the avoidance of quarrels and the wife's modesty. The text also covers household management, common property, and friends, while urging the control of jealousy, gossip, and the restraint of luxury. The closing chapters are addressed to the bride Eurydice and the groom Pollianus, urging philosophy and education as the finest adornment of a wife, and the author cites learned and celebrated women from Theano and Sappho to Claudia and Cornelia.
grc.plutarch.de_animae_procreatione_in_timae: Plutarch's De animae procreatione in Timaeo, a Greek philosophical treatise preserved within his Moralia, focuses on Plato's account of the world soul's generation in the Timaeus. It begins by surveying how earlier Platonists like Xenocrates and Crantor interpreted the relevant passage. The main argument posits a third principle alongside god and matter, a pre-cosmic soul that the demiurge orders. This view is defended against rival readings and the tension between the Phaedrus and the Timaeus. The text also includes excursuses on the origin of evil in Stoic and Epicurean thought. The closing chapters trace the mathematical construction of the world soul through number series and means, concluding with reflections on the harmony ordering the planets and the cosmos.
grc.plutarch.de_cohibenda_ira: Plutarch's De Cohibenda Ira, meaning On Restraining Anger, is a short Greek dialogue featuring a conversation between Fundanus and Sulla about controlling temper. Fundanus explains how he tamed his own quick anger over time, while the speakers compare anger to a disease needing continuous treatment. They argue that reason must be cultivated in advance, because a person in rage admits no outside counsel. The text uses medical and nautical imagery, and it also includes anecdotes and verses about slight provocations. The dialogue is preserved among Plutarch's moral essays.
grc.plutarch.de_herodoti_malignitate: Plutarch's short Greek essay On the Malice of Herodotus, part of the Moralia and addressed to an Alexander, serves as a sustained polemic against Herodotus's Histories. The text warns that Herodotus's easy style conceals a malignant character, with bias directed chiefly against the Boeotians and Corinthians. It catalogs signs of malice such as harsh word choice and gratuitous disgraceful episodes, while noting the omission of noble deeds and the preference for worse accounts. Plutarch proceeds through the Histories book by book, from Io and the Trojan War to the Persian Wars, arguing that Herodotus defames leading Greek states and diminishes their achievements. These include the battles of Marathon, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, and Plataea. The work closes by conceding the sweetness of Herodotus's narrative, likening his hidden slander to a beetle among roses.
grc.plutarch.de_liberis_educandis: The De Liberis Educandis, a Greek moral essay attributed to Plutarch, offers precepts for rearing freeborn children within the Moralia corpus. It begins by proposing an inquiry into upbringing, starting with the choice of a wife and conception circumstances. The text then passes through infant nursing, nurse selection, and the choice of paedagogues and teachers. Training of the body and memory follows, advocating disciplined praise and reproach rather than blows. Later sections treat tongue restraint, anger, truthfulness, and the disputed question of the company of lovers. The perils of adolescence and flatterers are examined, and arranging marriages concludes the practical advice. Anecdotes from Lycurgus, Socrates, and Themistocles illustrate these points, while the work closes with a catalogue of unstable goods. These include nobility, wealth, beauty, strength, and health, but education alone is held to be an immortal and divine possession.
grc.plutarch.de_stoicorum_repugnantis: De Stoicorum Repugnantiis is a Greek philosophical treatise by Plutarch that argues Stoic doctrine is at odds with itself, especially in Chrysippus's writings. It opens by demanding that a philosopher's life display the same harmony with his teaching that Aeschines required of the orator and the law. The work then turns to a long catalogue of Stoic inconsistencies, showing Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus praising the active life while spending their days in secluded study. Chrysippus is made to contradict himself over the order of philosophical instruction, the unity of virtue, and law and justice. He also argues on both sides regarding pleasure, the wise man's earnings, and friendship, while the longest sections attack his physics and theology. They charge that his accounts of fate, providence, and the gods conflict with one another, and his views on the cosmos's growth and its position in the void also clash with his earlier statements.
grc.plutarch.epitome_libri_de_animae_procrea: This short Greek epitame condenses Plutarch's treatise On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus, which is preserved among the Moralia. The work summarizes the author's extensive study, reporting what Plato and the Platonists laboured over regarding the making of the soul. It introduces geometrical, musical, and arithmetical theorems to support its argument, tracing the shaping of matter by soul and the bestowal of soul on the universe. The text also addresses evil as a growth of matter and criticizes Posidonius, insisting that Plato makes the soul ordered by number rather than being a number. The account closes with the world-soul blended from indivisible and divisible substance, where the same and the different are mixed through intermediate natures. Finally, the world's body is harmonised from the four elements.
grc.plutarch.fabius_maximus: This Life by Plutarch, written in Greek as part of his Parallel Lives, treats the Roman statesman Fabius Maximus, who is paired with the Life of Pericles. Fabius was a dictator famed for his cautious strategy of attrition against Hannibal during the Second Punic War, and the narrative traces his lineage from Heracles. It describes his deliberate, slow-tempered character and his first consulship, which included a triumph over the Ligurians, before he was appointed dictator after Lake Trasimene. He avoided battle with Hannibal despite the mockery of his master of horse, Minucius, who later received equal command but was defeated. The catastrophic battle of Cannae followed under Terentius Varro and Paullus, and Fabius subsequently recaptured Tarentum through an act of betrayal. He later quarreled with Scipio Africanus over the plan to invade Africa, and the life closes with his death before the war ended.
grc.plutarch.instituta_laconica: The Instituta Laconica, meaning Ancient Customs of the Spartans, is a brief Greek miscellany preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch. Written under the Roman Empire, it gathers short notices of Lycurgan institutions and everyday Laconian practice. The text opens with the rule of silence at the common messes, where the eldest diner points to the doors. He declares that no word spoken within may pass beyond them. The collection then runs through diet, bodily hardship, and the upbringing of boys. It covers trained theft, music, burial rites, and military custom, including scarlet cloaks and sacrifices after victory. The work closes with anecdotes of magisterial punishments and the annual flogging of youths at the altar of Orthia. It also notes the leisure secured by helot labour and Sparta's eventual subjection under Rome.
grc.plutarch.lacaenarum_apophthegmata: The Lacaenarum Apophthegmata, or Sayings of Spartan Women, is a short Greek collection of anecdotes preserved in Plutarch's Moralia. It opens with Argileonis, mother of Brasidas, questioning visitors from Amphipolis about her son's worthy death. The text next gives Gorgo's warnings to her father Cleomenes against Aristagoras. The body consists of terse replies by named and anonymous Laconian mothers, wives, and daughters. These women send sons to war with their shield, disown cowards, and answer questions on marriage with pointed brevity. A few entries carry short epigrams, and the collection closes with sayings of Spartan women in captivity.
grc.plutarch.lucullus: Plutarch's Greek Life of Lucullus opens with the ancestry of Lucius Licinius Lucullus, detailing his youthful prosecution of Servilius the augur, who had accused his father. The narrative follows his early service under Sulla and a naval mission to Egypt, Cyrenaica, and Cyprus, before he commands the war against Mithridates and Tigranes, including the siege of Sinope. The text covers the crossing of the Euphrates and the march into Armenia, later treating his orderly administration of Asia and his sumptuous retirement. He kept a library open to Greek scholars and adhered to the Old Academy of Antiochus, while his political influence gradually faded as Pompey rose to prominence. The work closes with the failing mind of his last years, setting a report of death by poisoning beside other accounts. His devoted brother arranged for his burial.
grc.plutarch.maxime_cum_princibus_philsopho_: Plutarch wrote this short Greek treatise, preserved among the Moralia, whose Latin title means a philosopher should converse especially with men in power. The work argues that seeking such company is not driven by a love of glory, but that shunning rulers actually betrays ambition and servility. He maintains that philosophy sown in a ruler's soul benefits many people at once, illustrated by anecdotes of Anaxagoras and Pericles, Plato and Dion, and Pythagoras among the leading men of Italy. The essay also cites Cato and Athenodorus, as well as Scipio and Panaetius, while analogies from doctors, priests, farmers, and shipwrights further support the argument. The discussion closes with Plato's Sicilian voyages and his encounter with Dionysius, where his teaching met a mind still drinking in the dye of tyranny. Noble words gain the force of laws when they hold the minds of men in command.
grc.plutarch.nicias: Plutarch's Life of Nicias is a Greek biography of the Athenian general and statesman Nicias, son of Niceratus, who is explicitly paired with the Life of Crassus to invite comparison of the Sicilian and Parthian disasters. An opening preface explains the author's decision to keep his treatment of events already narrated by Thucydides deliberately brief, while the life surveys Nicias's wealth from the Laurium silver mines and his lavish festival dedications at Athens and Delos. It also notes his pious and superstitious temperament before following his commands in the Peloponnesian War, covering his negotiation of the peace that bears his name and his rivalry with Alcibiades over Athenian policy. The narrative closes with his reluctant leadership of the Sicilian expedition and the siege of Syracuse, where a lunar eclipse checked the retreat, leading to the destruction of the army at the Asinarus river. Nicias was captured and executed, and the Athenian prisoners met their fate in the quarries.
grc.plutarch.non_posse_suaviter_vivi_secundu: Non posse suaviter vivi secundum Epicurum ('It is not possible to live pleasantly according to Epicurus') is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch. It is preserved among his moral essays and directed against the Epicurean Colotes. The work reverses Colotes' charge that life is impossible under other doctrines. Instead, the speakers argue that a pleasant life is impossible on Epicurean principles. The discussion contrasts bodily pleasures with the abiding joys of noble action and philosophy. It also examines Epicurus' teachings on the gods, providence, and the soul's survival.
grc.plutarch.otho: Plutarch's Life of Otho is a Greek biography of the Roman emperor whose rule followed the murder of Galba and was undone by civil war against Vitellius. The work is drawn from Plutarch's Lives and opens with Otho sacrificing on the Capitoline and pardoning Marius Celsus, an adherent of the slain Galba. From there the narrative follows his conciliatory settlements in the senate and with survivors of Nero's and Galba's reigns, alongside the mutinous violence of his soldiers. The war in northern Italy against the generals of Vitellius culminates in a confused and bloody defeat near Bedriacum. It closes with Otho's speeches refusing to prolong a struggle of Romans against Romans, his disciplined suicide at Brixellum, and the mourning of his troops. Plutarch reports having seen the modest tomb and epitaph, and he records a verdict that Otho lived no better than Nero yet died more nobly.
grc.plutarch.philopoemen: Plutarch's Life of Philopoemen, one of the Greek biographies in his series of Lives, treats the Megalopolitan general and statesman who rose to lead the Achaean League in the Hellenistic age. The work opens with Cleander of Mantinea, whose friendship with Philopoemen's father leads him to raise the orphaned boy, and with the philosophers Ecdemus and Megalophanes, who direct his education toward politics and action. It goes on to portray his austere habits, his rejection of athletic training, his farming near Megalopolis, and the career that made him the foremost commander of the Achaeans, including his victories over the Spartan tyrants Machanidas and Nabis, a disputed generalship for the Gortynians in Crete, a naval expedition against Nabis, and uneasy relations with Titus Flamininus and Rome. The narrative closes with his capture by the Messenian rebel Dinocrates, his death by poison in prison, the vengeance of the Achaeans under Lycortas, his funeral in which Polybius carries the urn, and a final notice of the honors his statues enjoyed even after Mummius sought to destroy them.
grc.plutarch.platonicae_quaestiones: Platonicae Quaestiones, preserved in Plutarch's Moralia, poses ten aporiae from Plato's dialogues, which Plutarch resolves in his own expository voice. The first question asks why the god commanded Socrates to act as a midwife, forbidding him from begetting children while requiring him to assist others. This answer frames the elenchus as a purgative remedy for the soul, describing philosophy as recollection rather than direct teaching. Later questions examine the naming of the supreme god as father and maker, and they also address the unequal divisions of the line in the Republic. The text explores the birth of body from soul, the rectilinear figures of the elements, and the priority of straight to curved. It considers the wing of the soul in the Phaedrus, presents antiperistasis as a single cause of effects ranging from thunder to magnetism, and discusses the sowing of souls as instruments of time in the Timaeus. Finally, the composition of logos from nouns and verbs alone is analyzed, with mathematical, physical, and grammatical arguments applied to the Platonic wording throughout.
grc.plutarch.publicola: Plutarch composed this Greek prose biography of Publius Valerius Publicola as part of his paired lives, explicitly matched with the life of Solon. The work traces Publicola's lineage and original name before detailing his role in the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus. It describes the institution of the consulate under Brutus and Collatinus to replace the kingship, following the suppression of a royalist conspiracy. The narrative includes the exploits of Horatius Cocles at the wooden bridge and Cloelia among the hostages. Later sections cover Publicola's measures for liberty, his repeated consulships, the consecration of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter, and the Sabine wars. It concludes with the reception of Appius Claudius and Publicola's death and public funeral.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_convivales: Plutarch's Quaestiones Convivales, or Table Talk, presents a series of sympotic dialogues framed as letters sent to the Roman Sossius Senecio. The opening preface explains the project of gathering remembered dinners in Rome and Greece, while raising the first problem about whether philosophy is fitting at a drinking party. The remaining books pose new questions at each sitting, covering physics, medicine, and natural history, and they also include literary puzzles from Homer and discussions of rites and customs. A closing sequence addresses the Muses, music, and the art of dance, and the debates recur among a familiar company, above all Plutarch's brother Lamprias and the philosopher Ammonius.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adulator_ab_amico_inter: Plutarch wrote this Greek ethical essay for Antiochus Philopappus, which is preserved in the Moralia under the Latin title Quomodo adulator ab amico internoscatur. The text opens by citing Plato to argue that self-love makes every man his own first flatterer, opening the way for external flatterers. The main body shows how flattery counterfeits friendship through shared pleasures, imitation of tastes, eager services, and sham frankness. The author collects signs that expose the counterfeit, such as inconstancy, servility towards the rich, and the praising of vices as virtues. Later chapters turn to the genuine frankness that belongs to true friendship, prescribing when reproof should be sharp and when it should be gentle. The work closes by recommending the cutting away of self-love and urging the pursuit of self-knowledge as the surest safeguard against flattery.
grc.plutarch.regum_et_imperatorum_apophthegm: Attributed to Plutarch and of uncertain date, the Regum et Imperatorum Apophthegmata is a Greek collection of brief anecdotes. It records the memorable replies, witticisms, and judgements of rulers and generals. The work opens with a short preface addressed to the emperor Trajan. This introduction argues that a man's spoken words display his character more directly than his deeds. The sayings proceed in loose chronological order from the Persian kings through the tyrants of Sicily. They continue to the Macedonian dynasts and Athenian statesmen, Spartan kings, and Theban generals. The collection concludes with Roman leaders from the early Republic down to Caesar and Augustus. The material is grouped under the names of individual rulers. Each entry is a compact episode in which an answer to a question, an insult, or a crisis serves as a portrait of its speaker.
grc.plutarch.solon: Plutarch's Life of Solon is a Greek biographical account of the Athenian lawgiver, poet, and sage, opening with antiquarian discussions of his ancestry. The text cites Didymus for the claim that his father was Euphorion, contrasting this view with the common tradition of Execestides and noting his Codrid descent. The narrative covers his early trading voyages, poetry, and the tripod episode, placing him among the Seven Sages and detailing his leadership in recovering Salamis. The story turns to the Cylonian pollution and Epimenides' purification of Athens, events that led to the conflict between debtors and creditors that brought him the archonship. His central reforms included the seisachtheia, which cancelled outstanding debts, and he established a mixed constitution ranking citizens in four property classes. A wide body of laws addressed marriage, funerals, water rights, and public conduct, while the biography also recounts his travels in Egypt and Cyprus. His celebrated meeting with Croesus vindicates his warning to count no man happy until the end, and the closing chapters describe his return to an Athens slipping under Peisistratus. His unsuccessful resistance and death during the tyranny are detailed, and the text ends with the implausible story that his ashes were scattered on Salamis.
grc.plutarch.theseus: Plutarch's Life of Theseus, a Greek prose biography from his Parallel Lives, is paired with the life of Romulus and opens with a methodological preface. Addressed to Sosius Senecio, the work explains how to sift mythical elements while following Theseus from his concealed birth at Troezen to his overland journey to Athens. He clears the road of malefactors such as Periphetes, Sinis, Sciron, and Procrustes, and is recognized by Aegeus despite the schemes of Medea. Later portions recount the Cretan tribute and his voyage to slay the Minotaur, where Ariadne aids him, but a forgotten sail brings Aegeus to his death. The text describes his unification of Attica and the reordering of its civic institutions, and it also covers the founding of the Isthmian games and the war with the Amazons. His friendship with Peirithous leads to a battle with the Centaurs, and Theseus makes a fatal descent to the underworld before the abduction of Helen. The Life closes with his imprisonment, return, and exile to Skyros, where he dies at the hands of Lycomedes and receives honors at Athens. Cimon eventually recovers his remains for proper burial in the city.
grc.plutarch.tiberius_gracchus: Plutarch's Life of Tiberius Gracchus is a Greek prose biography from the Plutarchan Lives, presenting the elder brother within the Roman pairing with Gaius announced at its opening. The text establishes the family's standing through Tiberius and Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, while contrasting the brothers' looks, speech, and habits before following Tiberius's career. He serves under Scipio at Carthage and holds the quaestorship under Mancinus, and the narrative covers the negotiated surrender to the Numantines and his tribunate. The preserved portion ends with his defence of the agrarian law against the propertied class, breaking off in the conflict with the tribune Marcus Octavius. Polybius, Fannius, and Gaius Gracchus's memoir are invoked as authorities, and the work includes allusive touches such as the Dioscuri comparison of the brothers' oratory. It also features the celebrated passage likening landless Italians to beasts without a share in the land.
grc.plutarch.vitae_decem_oratorum: The Vitae decem oratorum, meaning Lives of the Ten Orators, is a work of uncertain date attributed to Plutarch. It was transmitted with the Moralia and contains brief biographies of the ten canonical orators of Athens. The text opens with Antiphon of Rhamnus, recounting his family, teaching, and execution. It then proceeds through Andocides, Lysias, Isocrates, Isaeus, Aeschines, Lycurgus, Demosthenes, Hyperides, and Dinarchus. The sequence closes with notices of Demochares and Lycophron son of Lycurgus. Each life records ancestry, deme, teachers, political career, trials, and manner of death. The entries also tally genuine and spurious speeches, comment on style, and append anecdotes and public decrees.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.placita_philosophorum: The Placita Philosophorum ('Opinions of the Philosophers') is a Greek compendium of philosophical doctrines attributed to Plutarch. It opens by dividing philosophy into physical, ethical, and logical parts after the Stoics and Peripatetics. The text then defines nature before turning to the principles and elements proposed by individual thinkers. It proceeds topic by topic through the natural world, recording the doctrines of Thales, Anaximander, Pythagoras, and others. Each section juxtaposes conflicting opinions, presenting the disputed teachings of successive schools in brief, systematic form.
grc.polyaenus.strategemata: Polyaenus' Strategemata ('Stratagems') is a Greek collection of military ruses. The Macedonian author dedicates the work to the emperors Antoninus and Verus. He presents it as an aid in their war against the Persians and Parthians. The text comprises eight books and some nine hundred short anecdotes. These entries are arranged roughly in chronological order by commander. The final book gathers the exploits of women, from queens to citizen wives.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_mundo: This Greek cosmological treatise, attributed to Aristotle though its authorship and date remain uncertain, is composed as a letter addressed to Alexander. It opens by praising philosophy as a divine expedition of the soul to behold the whole of things. The work then surveys the spherical heavens, the aether, and the seven planetary circles, while also describing the five concentric elements with the earth at rest at the centre. It turns next to the seas, continents, and meteorological phenomena such as winds and thunder, and terrestrial and maritime disturbances, including earthquakes. The treatise closes with an account of the divine power that preserves cosmic harmony, likening God to a Persian great king, a lawgiver, and a chorus-leader. His many names are gathered as Zeus, necessity, and fate.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: This Greek prose periplus of the Euxine Sea is of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted anonymously and attributed to Arrian, which explains the designation Pseudo-Arrian. The text opens at the sanctuary of Zeus Ourios on the Thracian side of the Bosporus, tracing the right, Asian shore through Bithynia, Paphlagonia, Pontus, and Colchis to the Cimmerian Bosporus. The route then rounds Lake Maeotis and returns along the left, European coast, passing the Tauric Chersonese and the mouths of the Ister to end at Byzantium. Coastal points are enumerated in sequence with distances in stadia and miles, including notes on harbours, anchorages, navigable rivers, and the safety of particular shores. Woven into the itinerary are notices of Greek colony foundations and various peoples, including the Scythians, Sarmatians, Taurians, and Mossynoeci. The text also records mythical associations, such as the island of Achilles and the Amazons of the Thermodon, mentioning Iphigenia in the Tauric land and citing Herodotus, Xenophon, and earlier geographers.
grc.pseudogalen.de_theriaca_ad_pamphilianum: This Greek pharmacological treatise is transmitted under the name of Galen, though its date remains uncertain. It is cast as an address to Pamphilianus, who asked the author to explain the theriac antidote. The work argues that theriac serves not only against venomous bites and poisonings but also as a preventive for health and longevity. It cites Roman magnates who take the drug at the new moon and a plague in Italy that it stemmed. The central section lists conditions such as fevers, coughs, dropsy, and jaundice, specifying dosage and season for each. It closes with recipes for Hedyochrus, squill troches, and the composite antidote attributed to Andromachus.
grc.pseudolucian.χαρίδημος_ἢ_περὶ_κάλλους: The Charidemus, or On Beauty, is a short Greek dialogue transmitted under Pseudo-Lucian's name, and its date remains uncertain. The text is attributed to the circle of Lucian, where Hermippus meets Charidemus, who agrees to report a symposium held by Androcles in the Peiraeus. The guests there praised the beauty of the youth Cleonymus, which prompted a series of speeches from Phylon, Aristippus, and Charidemus. They argue that beauty is the most divine and honoured of goods, supporting this claim with mythological examples, including Zeus's pursuit of Ganymede and the judgement of Paris. Charidemus's closing speech emphasizes beauty's supremacy over every other excellence, and the dialogue ends with Hermippus thanking his companion for the account.
grc.pseudomenander.sententiae_corresponds_to: The Greek Sententiae, or single-line moral maxims, are transmitted under the name of the comic poet Menander, whose ascription is pseudepigraphic. The collection, of uncertain date, preserves a Greek version corresponding to the Arabic tradition of the Menander Sentences. It opens with the precept that one who is human ought to think human thoughts, continuing through several hundred brief sayings. Most of these lines are single verse lines arranged alphabetically by initial letter, urging moderation, self-control, and justice. They give particular attention to friendship, wealth, and poverty, while also addressing marriage, women, and household management. The collection further considers piety toward the gods and the workings of fortune, time, and speech.

This short Greek collection of one-line gnomic sayings is preserved under the name of the comic poet Menander. It corresponds to the Greek wording of one of the Arabic versions of the Sentences of Menander. The compiler and date of the collection remain unknown. It opens with a counsel to speak and learn good things eagerly and to put piety towards God first. The remaining monostichs, composed in iambic trimeters, urge mastery of tongue and temper, honour towards parents, elders and friends, and endurance of poverty. They also warn against ill-gotten gain, wariness towards women and pleasure, and the value of silence and self-knowledge. The collection closes with sayings on the greatness of a gift given at the right moment and on old age as a prayed-for evil.
grc.pseudoplutarch.de_fluviis: The De Fluviis is a short Greek prose treatise of uncertain date that is a work of geographical paradoxography devoted to rivers and the mountains beside them. It opens with the Hydaspes in India, where a tale of incest and royal suicide explains the river's renaming. The text then proceeds river by river through the known world, taking in the Ismenus and Achelous in Greece. The Nile in Egypt and the Tigris and Indus further east are also described in these entries. Each entry gives the water's earlier name and a mythological aetiology, where divine lust or transgression ends in drowning and a change of name. The corresponding story of the adjacent mountain is also told, and the text catalogues stones and plants found in or near the water. These are credited with marvellous protective, erotic, or medicinal powers, and throughout, the narratives are supported by citations of named authorities. Historians and local writers are invoked by book number for each account.
grc.pseudoscymnus.scymni_chii_ut_fertur_peri: This Greek verse periegesis, transmitted under the name of Pseudo-Scymnus, has uncertain authorship and date, though it is addressed to a king named Nicomedes. The prologue defends comic iambic metre for a brief account, invoking the model of Apollodorus's chronicle dedicated to Attalus. It lists key geographers, including Ephorus, Eratosthenes, Demetrius of Callatis, and Timaeus, before conducting a coastal circuit beginning at the Pillars of Heracles. The route passes through Iberia, Tartessus, Celtica, Massalia, Italy, Sicily, the Adriatic, Illyria, Epirus, mainland Greece, the Peloponnese, and Crete. The journey includes Thessaly, Macedonia, Thrace, the Propontis, the Black Sea, the Maeotis, and the Tanaïs, ending amid coastal towns in northern Asia Minor, such as Sinope and Heracleia. Throughout, the poem records city foundations and their founders, details rivers, islands, harbours, and emporia, and notes the customs of Greek and barbarian peoples.
grc.quintus_smyrnaeus.fall_of_troy: The Fall of Troy is a Greek epic in fourteen books attributed to Quintus Smyrnaeus, which continues the Trojan story from the end of the Iliad to the city's destruction. The poem opens after Hector's death, as the Trojans cower behind their walls, and the Amazon queen Penthesileia arrives to aid them, but she dies at Achilles' hands. The narrative then traces the coming and slaying of Memnon, followed by Achilles' death, the contest for his arms, and Ajax's suicide. Neoptolemus and Eurypylus arrive before the stratagem of the wooden horse, and the poem closes with the sack of the city and the Greeks' departures. The gods obliterate the fortifications and disperse the fleet with storms.
grc.sappho.fragments: These fragments of Greek lyric poetry were composed by Sappho in an Aeolic dialect. They preserve pieces of songs on love, desire, and the worship of Aphrodite and other gods. The collection also covers weddings, girlhood companions, and mythological figures like Helen and Adonis. It opens with an appeal to Hera for the safe return of Charaxus. A nearly complete hymn summoning Aphrodite stands nearby among the longer pieces. Elsewhere, preservation is poor, with many items reduced to single broken lines or isolated words.
grc.septuaginta.aggaeus: The Aggaeus, or Haggai, is a short prose book of prophetic oracles in the Septuagint, belonging to the Minor Prophets in the Greek Old Testament. The text opens with a word of the Lord in the second year of Darius, delivered through the prophet to Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest. They are rebuked for dwelling in panelled houses while the house of the Lord lies waste, and the remaining oracles urge the people to rebuild the temple. They promise that the glory of the latter house will surpass the former, while questions of purity are put to the priests to show that the people's works are defiled. The text recounts blighted harvests and failing stores before closing with a promise of cosmic shaking, in which the thrones of the nations are overthrown and Zorobabel is chosen as a signet.
grc.septuaginta.amos: Amos, the Greek Septuagint version of the prophetic book attributed to a herdsman of Tekoa, uses the Greek form of the prophet's name as its title. The book sets his activity in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam, opening by introducing the words Amos saw concerning Jerusalem two years before the earthquake. The text proceeds through judgement oracles against Damascus, Tyre, Edom, and Moab, then turns on Judah and Israel, denouncing the sale of the poor and the corruption of worship. Visions of coming ruin and a confrontation with the priest Amaziah follow, and the work closes with a promise that the fallen tent of David will be rebuilt.
grc.septuaginta.canticum: The Canticum is the Song of Songs as transmitted in the Greek Septuagint, a Hellenistic translation of the Hebrew love poem ascribed to Solomon. The text opens with a superscription and the woman's plea for her lover's kiss, then proceeds as a cycle of lyric dialogues between the woman and her beloved. Refrains adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem punctuate these exchanges, which include the woman searching the city streets for her absent lover. The procession of Solomon's palanquin with its armed escort also appears, while extended songs of mutual praise draw from garden, orchard, and vineyard imagery. The poem closes with love's strength compared to death, and an exchange over the vineyard of Solomon follows. The beloved's flight to the mountains of spices ends the work.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_theodotionis: The Book of Daniel is a Greek version attributed to Theodotion, which was transmitted with the Septuagint and written in prose. The narrative opens with Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem, where Daniel and his three companions are deported to the Babylonian court. The story follows Daniel's rise as an interpreter of dreams, and episodes include the great statue, the fiery furnace, and the lions' den. The furnace story is expanded by the prayer of Azariah, while the latter part turns apocalyptic and recounts visions of beasts. It also describes the wars of the kings of the north and south, and the book closes with Michael's arising and a command to seal it.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_translatio_graeca: The Old Greek version of the biblical book of Daniel, preserved in the Septuagint, is an anonymous prose rendering of Hellenistic origin. It opens with Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem and the deportation of Daniel and his three companions to the Babylonian court. The narrative follows their fortunes under successive foreign kings, including Daniel's interpretation of royal dreams and the survival of his friends in the fiery furnace. The latter part of the book turns apocalyptic, recounting visions of beasts and the seventy weeks of years. It ends with a final angelic revelation of future wars and the resurrection of the dead.
grc.septuaginta.ecclesiasticus: Ecclesiasticus, also known as Sirach, is a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book preserved in Greek, and its prologue identifies Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem as the original author. His descendants later transmitted and gathered his sayings into this final form, and the text opens with a prose preface describing its origin and contents. The main body offers maxims on the fear of the Lord and family duties, and it also addresses friendship, speech, wealth, and the discipline of children. Longer poems are interspersed throughout the practical instructions, and one such poem features a self-praise of Wisdom and her dwelling in Israel. A later section eulogizes famous men of Israel from Enoch to the high priest Simon, and the work closes with a prayer of thanksgiving and an autobiographical account.
grc.septuaginta.epistula_jeremiae: The Epistle of Jeremiah is a short Hellenistic prose work transmitted in the Septuagint and attributed to the prophet Jeremiah. Cast as a letter to Jewish exiles carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, it announces they will remain captive for seven generations. God will eventually lead them out in peace, while the body launches a sustained satirical attack on idols. These silver, gold, and wood artefacts are fashioned by craftsmen and guarded by priests, yet they cannot speak, see, or move. Their cults are marked by impurity and corruption, and a refrain asserts they are not gods to be feared. The closing verses contrast these idols with celestial bodies and weather, noting that the sun, moon, stars, and wind carry out the commands of the true God. The text ends by declaring that a righteous man without idols stands far from reproach.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_a: Esdras A, conventionally known in English as 1 Esdras, is an anonymous Greek prose work of uncertain Hellenistic date, preserved in the Septuagint. It retells the history of Judah in a form closely related to Chronicles, opening with Josiah's Passover celebration in Jerusalem. The narrative follows the last kings of Judah from Josiah's death in battle against the Pharaoh of Egypt. It continues through the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the subsequent exile of the people, turning to Cyrus's decree. Interwoven with the return are lists of repatriates and correspondence obstructing the work, alongside the tale of three bodyguards. Their contest over wine, kingship, women, and truth wins Zerubbabel royal favor, leading to the temple's completion and dedication. Ezra's later mission under Artaxerxes ends with his prayer over mixed marriages, concluding with the dismissal of foreign wives and the public reading of the law.
grc.septuaginta.ezechiel: Ezechiel is the Hellenistic Greek translation of the biblical book of the prophet Ezekiel, transmitted as part of the Septuagint corpus. The work opens with the prophet's vision of the divine chariot-throne by the river Chebar, where he is commissioned to speak to a rebellious house of Israel. The narrative moves through oracles of judgement and symbolic acts against Jerusalem, including visions of corruption within the temple and the departure of the divine glory. Sayings on the watchman's duty and individual responsibility also appear, while a long sequence of oracles targets foreign nations such as Ammon, Moab, and Egypt. The closing portion turns to consolation and restoration, featuring the valley of dry bones and the reunion of Judah and Joseph. A single Davidic ruler is promised for the reunited tribes, and the campaign of Gog of Magog is described. An extended vision of a new temple concludes the text, including detailed measurements and cultic regulations for priests and prince. A life-giving river and the division of the land among the twelve tribes are also detailed.
grc.septuaginta.isaias: The Septuagint is a Hellenistic era Greek translation of the Hebrew prophetic book, presenting Isaiah son of Amoz's prophecies against Judah and Jerusalem. The text covers the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, opening with a vision and a summons for heaven and earth to listen. The prophet complains that the Lord refuses the sacrifices of a rebellious people, and the work then denounces injustice and idolatry within Judah. It includes oracles against foreign powers such as Babylon, Assyria, and Egypt, while narrative episodes describe Isaiah counseling Ahaz and Hezekiah during the Assyrian threat. These stories cover the siege of Jerusalem and the king's illness, and the closing stretch brings oracles of consolation and restoration. It features songs of a suffering servant and promises of Zion's renewal, with visions of a new heaven and earth concluding the text.
grc.septuaginta.jeremias: The Greek version of Jeremiah preserved in the Septuagint is of Hellenistic date, opening with the word of God that came to Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth in Benjamin during the reign of Judah's kings. The prophecies denounce the idolatry and injustice of Judah and Jerusalem, announcing sword, famine, and exile from the north, while recording the prophet's clashes with priests and rival prophets. The text details symbolic acts such as the buried linen girdle, the potter at his wheel, and the shattered earthenware flask, before turning to sustained oracles against the surrounding nations. These oracles include Egypt, Philistia, Edom, and Ammon, as well as Kedar, Damascus, Moab, and Elam, but above all they target Babylon, framed by the cup of wrath that all peoples must drink. The book closes with the narrative of Nabouchodonosor's siege and the fall of Jerusalem, recounting the assassination of Gedaliah and the flight of the remnant to Egypt. Words of comfort to Baruch and promises of return follow, finally promising restoration and a new covenant.
grc.septuaginta.joel: The Greek Septuagint version of the prophetic book of Joel is a Hellenistic era translation of a Hebrew biblical text. It opens with the word of the Lord coming to Joel son of Bathuel and a summons to the elders. The prophecy describes a devastating locust plague, figured as agricultural ruin and an invading army. It calls the priests and people to fasting, mourning, and repentance before the day of the Lord. The Lord promises restored harvests, the outpouring of the Spirit, and the gathering of nations for judgment. The book closes with Egypt and Edom laid waste, Judah settled forever, and the Lord dwelling in Zion.
grc.septuaginta.jonas: The Book of Jonah appears in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Jewish scriptures, which was produced during the Hellenistic period by translators whose names are not recorded. The text presents its story in continuous narrative prose rather than oracular material, opening with the Lord commanding Jonah son of Amathi to preach against Nineveh. The prophet instead flees by ship toward Tarshish, prompting a divinely raised storm, and the sailors throw him into the sea, where a great fish swallows him. From its belly he prays for three days and nights before being cast up on dry land, and under a second commission he preaches in Nineveh, and the city repents in sackcloth and fasting. God relents, which provokes Jonah's anger and a closing lesson on divine pity, and this lesson is taught through a springing and withering gourd.
grc.septuaginta.josue: The Greek book of Joshua appears under its Septuagint title, Josue, which is the Hellenistic prose rendering of the Hebrew biblical text. Its translators remain anonymous, and the hero is named Jesus, or Iesous, son of Nave. The narrative opens with the Lord charging Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan into the promised land. It proceeds through the spies at Jericho, the miraculous river crossing, and the city's fall. Later events include Achan's offense, the capture of Ai, and the treaty with the Gibeonites. The text also details campaigns against southern and northern kings, including the battle of Gibeon. The latter part consists largely of registers, such as lists of conquered kings and tribal boundaries. It closes with Joshua's exhortations at Shechem and notices of his death and burial.
grc.septuaginta.judith: Judith is an anonymous Hellenistic narrative preserved in Greek within the Septuagint, and its title names the widow who saves her people from the Assyrian threat. The story opens in the twelfth year of Nebuchadnezzar, who rules the Assyrians at Nineveh, and he overthrows Arphaxad, king of the Medes, before sending his general Holofernes westward. Holofernes punishes nations that refused to join his war and besieges the city of Bethulia, where the defenders weaken until Judith prays for strength and enters the enemy camp. She beheads the general as he lies drunk after seeking her favor, and the book closes with the rout of the Assyrian army and Judith's hymn of praise. She later makes a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and lives a long, honoured life, dying at Bethulia at the age of one hundred and five.
grc.septuaginta.kritai: The Kritai, meaning Judges, is the Greek Septuagint version of the biblical book, a prose narrative from the Hellenistic period. The story begins after Joshua dies, as Israelites ask the Lord for a leader to guide them against the Canaanites. The text describes the partial conquest and settlement of the region, then follows a recurring cycle of apostasy and foreign oppression. Deliverance comes through a succession of leaders, including Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Barak, Gideon, Abimelech, Jephthah, and Samson. The book closes with appendices on Micah's shrine, the Danites, the Levite's concubine, and the war against Benjamin. Throughout, Israel's unfaithfulness is set against the raising of saviours, with the refrain noting that there was no king in Israel.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_b: 2 Maccabees is a Hellenistic era Greek Jewish historical work transmitted in the Septuagint, presenting itself as an abridgment of a five book history by Jason of Cyrene. The text opens with two letters from Jerusalem to the Jews of Egypt, concerning the observance of the days of the purification of the temple. The narrative recounts the attempted seizure of the temple treasury by Heliodorus, detailing the hellenizing measures and persecutions under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. The story includes the martyrdoms of the aged Eleazar and of seven brothers and their mother, following the rise of Judas Maccabaeus and his campaigns against Nicanor, Timothy, and Gorgias. The account covers the death of Antiochus and the rededication of the temple, closing with the wars under Lysias and Demetrius and the defeat of Nicanor.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_d: 4 Maccabees is a Greek prose treatise from the Hellenistic era. Its title means 'Four Maccabees,' though the work is not a historical narrative. It argues that devout reason holds absolute sovereignty over the passions. The text defines reason, wisdom, and the cardinal virtues before offering proof. It narrates the martyrdom of the priest Eleazar, seven brothers, and their mother. These deaths under Antiochus Epiphanes show that obedience to the Law conquers suffering.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_i: First Maccabees is an anonymous Hellenistic Jewish historical narrative transmitted in Greek within the Septuagint, and its date remains uncertain. It belongs to the tradition of biblical historiography, opening with the conquests of Alexander the Great and the accession of Antiochus Epiphanes. His edicts against Jewish law and the plundering of the temple provoke a revolt led by the priest Mattathias and his five sons.
