The narrative follows Judas Maccabeus through his victories and the rededication of the altar, but he dies in battle. Leadership passes to his brothers Jonathan and Simon, who conduct campaigns, negotiate with rival Syrian kings, and send embassies to Rome and Sparta. The work closes with Simon holding the high priesthood and military command, removing the Seleucid yoke, until he is murdered by his son-in-law Ptolemy, leaving his son John as heir.
grc.septuaginta.nahum: The Book of Nahum appears here in its Greek form, one of the twelve minor prophets as rendered in the Septuagint. This Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures was produced in the Hellenistic period by translators whose identities remain unknown. The text opens with a superscription identifying it as an oracle of Nineveh and a vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. A theophanic hymn follows, describing the Lord as jealous, avenging, slow to anger, and terrible in wrath. The prophecy then announces the doom of the Assyrian capital, where God restores the splendour of Jacob and Judah. The city falls amid plunder, panic, and the flight of her soldiers, while closing oracles denounce the city of blood as a sorceress and harlot. They picture her merchants scattered like locusts and her rulers asleep, stating that her wound is incurable and that all who hear of her ruin will clap their hands.
grc.septuaginta.odae: The Odae, or Odes, form a collection of prose canticles transmitted in Greek biblical manuscripts, and they are appended to the Psalms in the Septuagint tradition. The collection opens with the song of Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea, and it proceeds through canticles and prayers drawn from other biblical books. These include the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, and the prayers of Hannah, Hezekiah, Jonah, and Habakkuk. The prayer and song of the Three Youths and the Prayer of Manasseh also appear, and New Testament canticles of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon are included as well. The collection closes with a morning hymn of praise, and the date of the compilation as a distinct collection is uncertain.
grc.septuaginta.proverbia: The Paroimiai, or Greek Proverbs, is a Hellenistic prose rendering of the biblical collection attributed to Solomon son of David. It opens with a superscription and a preamble promising knowledge of wisdom, discipline, and the interpretation of proverbs, riddles, and sayings. The body consists chiefly of paternal instructions to a son on prudence, justice, restraint, and the dangers of the adulterous woman. These are interspersed with speeches of personified Wisdom, including an account of her presence at the creation of the world. Long runs of aphorisms on speech, wealth, poverty, friendship, and kingship also appear throughout the text. Toward the end stand numerical and observational sayings, the words of King Lemuel taught by his mother, and a poem praising the virtuous woman.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi: The Psalms in their Greek Septuagint version form the collection of Hebrew psalms as it passed into Greek biblical use. This translation was made in the Hellenistic period and includes superscriptions ascribing many poems to David. The collection opens with a beatitude on the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Subsequent psalms range over laments, thanksgivings, royal hymns, and wisdom admonitions. They also include long recitals of Israel's history from the plagues of Egypt through repeated apostasy. The sequence closes with hallelujah hymns summoning instruments to praise the Lord. A short appended psalm narrates David's youth, his anointing, and his beheading of the Philistine.
grc.septuaginta.ruth: Ruth is the Greek version of the biblical book of that name, rendered anonymously into Greek in the Hellenistic period as part of the Septuagint. The narrative opens with a famine that drives Elimelech and his family from Bethlehem to Moab, where the deaths of the men leave his wife Naomi alone with her Moabite daughters-in-law. Naomi's return to Bethlehem at the barley harvest shapes the rest of the book, and Ruth gleans in the field of the kinsman Boaz, approaching him at the threshing floor. She is married to him after he settles the right of redemption before the elders at the gate, and the birth of their son Obed is greeted by the women of Bethlehem as a restoration of Naomi. A closing genealogy traces Obed's line through Jesse to David the king.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_theodotionis: Susanna is a narrative in Hellenistic biblical prose set among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, preserved in the Greek version attributed to Theodotion. The story opens with Susanna, the beautiful and God-fearing wife of the wealthy Joakim, whose garden becomes the scene of the central crisis. Two elders appointed as judges are consumed with desire for her, and they accost her as she bathes alone, denouncing her as an adulteress. The assembly condemns her to death, but God stirs the spirit of the young Daniel, who separates the two witnesses and exposes their false testimony. He asks questions about the tree under which they claim to have caught the lovers, leading to the elders being put to death according to the law of Moses. Susanna's innocence is vindicated, and Daniel's standing among the people grows.
grc.septuaginta.threni_seu_lamentationes: The Greek Lamentations, transmitted in the Septuagint under the title Threni, is a biblical book of Hellenistic date and uncertain authorship. The title Threni means Lamentations. The work consists of five laments over the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of Judah. The first four are arranged as acrostics on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. It opens with the cry of how the city once crowded with people now sits solitary like a widow among the nations. The text moves from the city's mourning and the Lord's outpoured wrath through confession of sin and reflections on suffering. It ends with a closing communal prayer that God, enthroned for ever, would turn his people back and renew their days as of old.
grc.septuaginta.tobias: The Book of Tobit, known in Greek as Tobias, is a Hellenistic Jewish prose narrative of uncertain date and authorship preserved in the Septuagint. The story opens with the first-person account of Tobit, a man of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, who recounts his almsgiving, burial of murdered kinsmen, blindness, and prayer for death. The narrative then follows his son Tobias, who is sent to recover a deposit in Media under the disguised angel Raphael, and who catches a fish in the Tigris. Tobias marries his kinswoman Sarah at Ecbatana, where he burns the fish's organs to drive off the demon Asmodeus, who had slain her seven previous husbands. The couple returns with the money and the bride to heal Tobit's sight with fish gall, after which Raphael reveals his identity. Tobit chants a hymn of praise with prophecies of Nineveh's fall, and the book closes with his final instructions and the deaths of Tobit, Anna, and Tobias in Ecbatana.
grc.septuaginta.zacharias: The Zacharias of the Septuagint is the Greek version of the biblical book of Zechariah, a collection of prophecies attributed to Zechariah son of Barachias of the line of Addo. The oracles are set in the reign of Darius, and the translation was made in the Hellenistic period. The book opens with the word of the Lord coming to the prophet in the second year of Darius, summoning a people chastened like their fathers to turn back to the Lord. A series of night visions follows, including horsemen among the shady mountains and four horns with smiths, a man with a measuring line, and the high priest Jesus accused and reclothed. A golden lampstand is fed by two olive trees, and a flying scroll is seen, while a woman is borne in a measure to Babylon and four chariots are described. These visions are interspersed with oracles on the rebuilding and repopulation of Jerusalem, covering the crowning of the high priest and fasts turned to joy. Later chapters turn to shepherds who destroy the flock and the thirty pieces of silver, describing the breaking of the two staffs and a sword roused against the shepherd. The assault of the nations on Jerusalem is detailed, and the Lord stands on the Mount of Olives, with living waters flowing from the city and all peoples ascending yearly to keep the feast of tabernacles.
grc.sophocles.ajax: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, dramatizing the fate of Ajax after the arms of Achilles are awarded to Odysseus. In the prologue Athena shows Odysseus how she has turned Ajax's murderous rage upon the army's flocks and herds, which he slaughtered believing them the Atreidae and their followers. She holds him deluded inside his tent, and the play goes on to depict his recognition of his disgrace and his suicide. After the laments of Tecmessa and the chorus, a quarrel breaks out between Teucer, Agamemnon and Menelaus over Ajax's burial. It is Odysseus who finally intervenes to bring the quarrel to a settlement.
grc.sophocles.antigone: This Greek tragedy by Sophocles is set in Thebes after the deaths of Eteocles and Polynices, who killed one another during the war for the city. Antigone tells her sister Ismene of Creon's edict forbidding the burial of Polynices, declaring her resolve to bury him in defiance of the law. Antigone is caught and condemned despite her appeal to divine ordinance, while the pleas of Haemon and the warning of Teiresias fail to turn Creon in time. Antigone hangs herself, and Haemon and Eurydice kill themselves, leaving Creon to lament his ruin. The play closes with the chorus reflecting that wisdom comes only through suffering, noting that reverence is owed to the gods and that great words bring great blows upon the proud.
grc.sophocles.ichneutae: The Ichneutae, a satyr play by Sophocles that survives only in papyrus fragments, opens mid-speech with a proclamation of a reward for finding Apollo's stolen cattle. A tracker recounts following traces through Thessaly, Boeotia, and other lands toward Cyllene, where the satyrs, sent under their father Silenus to hunt the herd, reach a cave. From this cave issues a sound never before heard among mortals, and the nymph Cyllene explains that the infant Hermes concealed there has killed a tortoise and fashioned the lyre from its shell. Later fragments consist largely of exchanges over the theft, in which the satyrs, Silenus, and Cyllene dispute the child's deed, while the close of the play is badly damaged.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_at_colonus: Oedipus at Colonus, a tragedy by Sophocles, dramatizes the final episode of the Oedipus story. The blind hero arrives in Attica led by his daughter Antigone, reaching a grove at Colonus where he asks to be set down. Learning the spot is inviolable ground of the Eumenides, he takes it as his promised resting place. He gains the protection of Theseus and the Athenians, while Creon attempts to force him back to Thebes. Creon carries off Antigone and Ismene, and Polynices appeals to his father, which ends in a curse. These events supply the conflicts of the central action, and the closing scenes follow Oedipus away to a hidden grave. He vanishes from sight, an end reported by a messenger, while Antigone and Ismene lament their loss as they prepare to return to Thebes.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_tyrannus: Oedipus Tyrannus, a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, follows the ruin of the king of Thebes within a single day. The plague stricken city supplicates Oedipus, who sends Creon to Delphi, where the oracle demands that the killer of Laius be found and driven out. The search brings Oedipus into angry conflict with the seer Tiresias, who also accuses Creon of plotting against him. Jocasta recalls an abandoned child, and Oedipus remembers a killing at a crossroads, while a messenger from Corinth and an aged herdsman complete the evidence. Oedipus is revealed as Laius' murderer and Jocasta's son, so Jocasta takes her own life, and Oedipus blinds himself. He passes under Creon's charge into exile after leaving his daughters, and the chorus reflects that no man should be counted happy before his life ends.
grc.sophocles.philoctetes: Philoctetes is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles that dramatises the attempt to obtain the bow of Heracles. The weapon is held by Philoctetes, who has been marooned on Lemnos for ten years with a festering snake bite. The play opens on the desolate shore where Odysseus coaches Neoptolemus in the deceit required to win the bow. After gaining trust and seizing the weapon, Neoptolemus is overcome by conscience and reverses the treachery. Heracles then appears to command Philoctetes to sail to Troy, promising him healing and victory. The drama turns throughout on the conflict between expedient cunning and honourable integrity.
grc.sophocles.trachiniae: The Trachiniae ('The Women of Trachis') is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles. It dramatises the final catastrophe of Heracles through the story of his wife Deianira. The play opens with Deianira at Trachis lamenting her long separation from her husband. She recounts her wooing by Heracles and the river-god Achelous. A messenger soon brings news of his victories and of the captive Iole. Deianira sends him a robe soaked in the poisoned blood of the centaur Nessus. When she learns what she has done, she kills herself. The dying Heracles extracts a promise from his son Hyllus to burn him on Mount Oeta.
grc.soranus.de_signis_fracturarum: De Signis Fracturarum ('On the Signs of Fractures') is a short Greek medical treatise transmitted under the name of Soranus. It opens by defining the cranial fracture and distinguishing its principal varieties, such as fissure, incision, depression and splintering. The text then works through the skeleton site by site, from nose, jaw and clavicle to spine, sternum, ribs, pelvis and the bones of the limbs. It describes the visual and tactile signs by which each kind of fracture is diagnosed. The work ends with general criteria for judging the danger of fractures complicated by open wounds, protrusion of bone, or involvement of vital parts.
grc.soranus.gynaeciorum_libri_iv: The Gynaeciorum Libri IV is a four book Greek treatise on women's medicine by the physician Soranus, whose date remains uncertain. The text survives in the Teubner edition of Johannes Ilberg, and its opening divides the discipline while defining the ideal midwife. It cites literacy, memory, and steady nerves, and it specifies physical traits such as long, slender fingers and short trimmed nails. The work then covers the anatomy of the womb, and it details the management of pregnancy and childbirth. It details the care of the newborn, including swaddling, bathing, nursing, and the timing of teething and weaning. Later chapters address pathological conditions, discussing the causes and correction of uterine prolapse at length. The text closes by cataloguing affections of the female parts, among them abscesses, ulcers, cancers, and fistulas.
grc.themistocles.epistulae: The Epistulae ('Letters') is a pseudepigraphic collection of Greek letters attributed to Themistocles, the Athenian statesman of the Persian Wars. These texts are of uncertain date and are preserved in Rudolf Hercher's Epistolographi Graeci of 1873. The opening letter, addressed to Aeschylus, recounts his ostracism and sympathetic encounters with Argive friends on the way to Delphi. Other letters to Pausanias, Aristides, and Polygnotus rehearse his exile at Argos and his flight via Corcyra to the court of Admetus in Molossia. They also describe his perilous voyage to Asia and the honours granted to him at the Persian court. A final short note orders the dispatch of silver kraters and golden thuribles by a trustworthy carrier.
grc.theocritus.epigrams: The Epigrams are short Greek poems transmitted under the name of Theocritus. They are composed in literary dialects with marked use of Doric. The pieces include dedications to gods such as Pan, Priapus, and Aphrodite. They also contain epitaphs for figures ranging from herdsmen to physicians and sophists. Verses on statues, votive offerings, and choregic victories complete the set. These varied works stand as a brief epigrammatic complement to the bucolic poetry of the Theocritean corpus.
grc.theocritus.idylls: The Idylls are thirty short poems by Theocritus, written mostly in the Doric dialect, and the title means 'little poems' or 'songs' in Greek. The opening piece features a goatherd and the herdsman Thyrsis, who sings of the sufferings of Daphnis for a wager. The collection includes pastoral singing matches, laments, and love talk among herdsmen, while it also contains urban mimes, such as Syracusan women at the festival of Adonis. Encomia praise patrons like Hiero and Ptolemy, while an epithalamium honors Helen, and mythological episodes concern Hylas, Heracles, and the Cyclops. Closing poems describe a speaker's bondage to Eros, who drags him by a yoke.
grc.theophrastus.characters: The Characters of Theophrastus is a Greek collection of brief ethical portraits, each focusing on a single disreputable type of person. A prologue addressed to Polycles announces the plan of setting down the ways of men by kinds, while the speaker claims ninety-nine years of observation of human nature. Each sketch opens with a compact definition of a character, then catalogues the tell-tale words and gestures that betray that type in ordinary life. The behaviours described are drawn from dinner parties, the agora, and the bathhouse, and they also include dealings with friends, slaves, and tradesmen. The whole forms a systematic taxonomy of everyday vice.
grc.tryphiodorus.the_taking_of_ilios: The Taking of Ilios (Iliou Halosis) is a short Greek epic in hexameters by Tryphiodorus, of uncertain date. It opens with a prayer to Calliope to sing of the end of the ten years' war, then recounts the building of the Wooden Horse by Epeius at Athena's prompting, the Greeks' feigned departure for Tenedos, Sinon's deception of Priam, and the Trojans' fatal resolve to haul the horse into their city despite Cassandra's prophecies. The latter part describes the night of the sack: the warriors emerging from the horse, the slaughter of Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios and of Astyanax on the walls, the violation of Cassandra by Ajax, the sparing of Antenor's house and the rescue of Aeneas, and the Greeks' departure with Helen and the captives after burning Ilios.
grc.zenobius_sophista.ἐπιτομὴ_ἐκ_τῶν_ταρραίο: This Greek epitome of proverbs is transmitted under the name of the sophist Zenobius. Its title records that it was compiled from the collections of Tarrhaeus and Didymus. The work opens with the entry 'Abydenon epiphorema' and proceeds alphabetically. Each saying is glossed with its meaning and often its origin story. Entries cite poets, historians, comic writers, and oracles as witnesses. The narratives range from the labours of Heracles to Athenian institutions.
grc.aelian.epistulae_rusticae: The Epistulae Rusticae, or 'Rustic Letters', is a short collection of twenty fictitious letters in Greek attributed to Aelian. The text is composed in a polished literary style that is shot through with rustic vocabulary and dialect forms. These letters are exchanged among imagined country dwellers, and the opening letter, from Euthykomides to Blepaios, recounts a flirtation with a girl among the vines. It closes with a jesting oath by the great mysteries of Pan, while the remaining letters are self contained vignettes of rural life. Farmers trade banter and seasonal gifts of fruit and wine, and a beekeeper mourns his absconded swarms, while neighbours quarrel over water and stolen grapes. The misanthrope Knēmōn trades insults with his well meaning correspondent Kallippidēs, and other senders write of hunting, a bride swapped for a courtesan, and a neighbour who has abandoned his farm for the sea trade. They also describe the honest virtues of the farming life.
grc.aelian.ἀποσπασμάτια: This collection of short Greek excerpts, transmitted under the name of Aelian, consists chiefly of fragments from his works On Providence and On Divine Manifestations. The text also includes pieces of uncertain position drawn from the Suda and later commentators such as Eustathius. The volume opens with brief notices of the frugal lives of Chrysippus of Soli and Cleanthes. The body of the work gathers moralising anecdotes that show divine providence at work. The impious, including Epicurean philosophers, tyrants, temple robbers, and oath breakers, meet with punishment. The pious are protected through dreams, oracles, providential rescues, and the healings of Asclepius. Scattered among these stories are episodes from Greek and Roman history, accounts of sacrilege, and short glosses on rare words.
grc.aelius_aristides.ars_rhetorica: This Greek treatise on rhetoric, of uncertain date, is transmitted under the name of Aelius Aristides. It opens by enumerating the virtues of political discourse, among them solemnity, force, sweetness, and clarity. Each virtue is then shown to arise from thought, figure, and diction, the lessons being illustrated chiefly from Demosthenes, with Isocrates and Thucydides also drawn on. Along the way it treats the kinds of discourse and their mixtures, the subjects of deliberative oratory, praise and blame, and the periodic arrangement of clauses and sentences. The latter part turns to the plain style, setting its thoughts, figures, rhythms, and diction against those of political oratory largely through extended analysis of Xenophon. The work closes with discussions of the beginnings of a discourse, the conveyance of character, and the special case of Homer.
grc.aelius_herodianus.on_enclitics: Aelius Herodianus wrote this brief Greek grammatical treatise on enclitic words and their accentuation, opening by distinguishing the enclined word, the enclitic particle, and the synenclitic sequence. The text then examines the parts of speech that admit enclisis, among nouns only the indefinite tis is discussed, while verbs include phemi and eimi. Pronouns, interrogative adverbs, and conjunctions also feature in the analysis, and rules explain how enclitics surrender or shift their accents and raise the grave accent of the preceding word. Examples are drawn chiefly from Homer, with citations of Hesiod and Callimachus, and the closing line notes that the remaining material of the treatise has dropped out.
grc.aelius_theon.progymnasmata: A Greek rhetorical treatise, the Progymnasmata of Aelius Theon, a handbook of preliminary exercises for students of rhetoric that has been transmitted together with the Ars rhetorica printed in Spengel's Rhetores Graeci. The work opens by urging that orators should first train in philosophy and the general curriculum before pleading causes, mocking those who skip such preparation, and announcing that it will set out the exercises to be practised before one undertakes full hypotheses, together with definitions and methods of use for each. The body of the treatise treats the exercises in turn, beginning with chreia and continuing through myth, narrative, and the methods of refutation and confirmation, with detailed instructions on clarity, brevity and plausibility in narration, the treatment of evidence and topics, and the varied ways of paraphrasing and recasting material. Extensive illustrative passages are drawn from Homer, Hesiod, Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Demosthenes, Lysias and Isocrates, while guidance is also given to teachers on choosing models, correcting pupils' work, avoiding rhythmic or ornate composition, and adapting instruction to the natural strengths of individual students.
grc.aeschines.against_timarchus: In this Athenian forensic speech the orator Aeschines prosecutes Timarchus under the law subjecting public speakers to scrutiny, seeking to bar him from the assembly for a dissolute life. Aeschines opens by denying that he has ever injured any citizen and casts himself as avenger of the city, the laws, and himself against Timarchus' lawless demagogy. He then recites the archaic laws governing the upbringing of boys, conduct in schools and gymnasia, prostitution, and hubris. A long narrative follows of Timarchus' alleged career as the kept companion of Misgolas, Pittalakos, and Hegesander, his squandering of his patrimony, and his misconduct in public offices and embassies. The later portion attacks Demosthenes as the author of Timarchus' defense and contrasts honourable love with hired prostitution through examples drawn from Homer and tragedy. It closes with an exhortation to the jurors to punish wrongdoers for the sake of civic order.
grc.aeschylus.libation_bearers: The Libation Bearers (bearers of drink offerings), a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, is the second play of his Oresteia and dramatizes Orestes' revenge for the murder of his father Agamemnon. It opens at Agamemnon's tomb, where Orestes and his sister Electra meet and join a chorus of captive women in lament, prayer, and invocation of the dead king. Acting on an oracle of Apollo, Orestes and his companion Pylades gain entry to the palace in disguise, where they kill Clytemnestra's lover Aegisthus and then Clytemnestra herself. Orestes displays the net in which Agamemnon died and asserts that his deed was just, but the avenging Furies become visible to him alone. The play ends with Orestes driven mad and fleeing toward Apollo's seat at Delphi, while the chorus wonders where the house's cycle of bloodshed will end.
grc.aeschylus.prometheus_bound: Prometheus Bound is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date, attributed to Aeschylus. It opens with Power and Force compelling a reluctant Hephaestus to rivet the fire-thief Prometheus to a desolate crag in Scythia, as punishment for his gifts to mortals. The rest of the play consists almost entirely of the chained Titan's encounters with successive visitors, among them the chorus of Oceanids, Oceanus, the heifer-maiden Io and Hermes. Hermes demands the secret prophecy that threatens Zeus's rule, while Prometheus foretells Io's wanderings, the hero who will one day free him, and his own eventual reconciliation with Zeus. Refusing throughout to submit, he is engulfed with his chorus by thunder, earthquake and storm in the closing cataclysm.
grc.aesop.fabulae: This collection of Greek prose fables is transmitted under the name of Aesop, though its date remains uncertain. The title refers to the legendary fabulist to whom these stories are attributed. Many narratives survive in parallel recensions, and most end with a brief moral comment. The volume opens with the tale of the goods asking Zeus how to reach men. It then runs through a long series of short stories featuring animals, gods, and ordinary humans. Familiar tales include the fox and the sour grapes, the frogs begging for a king, and the north wind and the sun. Other stories involve a farmer who tells his sons to dig for treasure in a vineyard. Hundreds of briefer anecdotes also appear, with morals touching on greed, ingratitude, and flattery. Many fables recur in variant versions, differing in wording, detail, and the moral appended.
grc.aesop.αισώπειων_μύθων_συναγωγή: This collection of Greek prose fables is transmitted under the name of Aesop, though its date remains uncertain. It opens with the fable of the Good and the Evil Things, in which goods descend from heaven one by one while evils assail humanity in a body. The work then runs through several hundred short narratives, drawn mostly from the doings of animals such as foxes, wolves, lions, and eagles. It also features human types including fishermen, farmers, astrologers, and debtors, with each fable typically closing with a one-line moral maxim. Alongside these stand fables of Zeus, Hermes, and Prometheus, as well as anecdotes attached to named figures like Aesop, Demades, Socrates, and Stesichorus. The collection concludes with an extended account of the Choice of Heracles.
grc.agatharchides.ex_agatharchidis_de_maris_: Agatharchides of Cnidus, a Greek prose writer of the Hellenistic age, composed a five-book geography and ethnography of the Red Sea and its coasts. The work survives only in abridged form as a series of summaries. The opening excerpts consider Ptolemy's institution of elephant hunting and the rival explanations of why the Red Sea bears its name. They also include a polemic against earlier mythographers. The sequence then ranges over Egypt and the sufferings of its gold-mine convicts. It continues with the coasts of the Troglodytes and the fish-eating Ichthyophagi, the Arabian Gulf and its tribes, and accounts of exotic animals and the cause of the Nile's summer flood.
grc.alcidamas.ὀδυσσεύς: This Greek prosecution speech is attributed to Alcidamas, though its date remains uncertain. It presents Odysseus accusing Palamedes of treason before the assembled Greeks at Troy. The speaker alleges that Palamedes conspired with Alexander, citing an inscribed arrow and a shield emblem as evidence. He repeatedly dwells on Palamedes' character as a sophist and philosopher. The latter part digresses into the stories of Nauplius, the violation of Auge by Heracles, and the birth of Telephus. It also recounts Alexander's voyage to Greece that ended in the abduction of Helen. The piece belongs to the tradition of rhetorical exercises composed on themes from the Trojan War.
grc.anacharsis.epistulae: The Epistulae attributed to Anacharsis is a short pseudepigraphic collection of Greek letters ascribed to the Scythian sage of Greek tradition and is of uncertain date. The collection opens with a letter to the Athenians, where the writer answers their mockery of his imperfect Greek by arguing that a man's worth lies in judgement and deeds rather than in purity of speech. The remaining letters are composed in the persona of a plain-spoken barbarian and are addressed to figures including Solon, Cyrus and a king of the Lydians. These letters defend Scythian frugality and hospitality while denouncing drunkenness, envy and the pursuit of wealth. One extended rebuke is illustrated by the parable of a ship on the Danube that founders under stolen cargo. The closing letter to the Lydian king declares that the writer has come to Greece to learn its customs and has no need of gold.
grc.andocides.against_alcibiades: This political speech, transmitted in the corpus of Andocides, is titled Against Alcibiades, and it is cast as an Athenian ostracism contest in which the speaker, Alcibiades, and Nicias compete for exile. The text opens with reflections on the danger of meddling in public affairs, while also noting the duty of a good citizen to risk himself for the many. The speaker protests that he should not be ruined by slander after four acquittals, and the bulk of the work attacks Alcibiades' life and character. It cites his mistreatment of his wife and dealings in Callias' household, and the speaker also mentions the coercion of the painter Agatharchus and the assault on Taureas. He notes a son begotten on a captive Melian woman, and the text further criticizes the doubling of the allies' tribute and the extravagance of Olympic victories. Against this, the speaker sets his own embassies and self-funded liturgies, arguing that ostracism serves the city only if the worse man is exiled, and he concludes that Alcibiades, a tyrant in deed while posing as a democrat, must go.
grc.andocides.on_the_peace: This deliberative speech in Attic Greek is attributed to the Athenian orator Andocides, who addresses the assembly with a charge against politicians. They favour peace in name while opposing the terms for its conclusion, and the speaker presents himself as part of an embassy sent with full powers to Sparta. He surveys earlier peace settlements with Lacedaemon, including the peace of fifty years, the Thirty Years' Peace, and the peace made by Nicias. He argues that the democracy was never overthrown under any of these agreements, and that a peace on equal terms differs from the truces dictated by a victor. The text then weighs the case for continuing the war over Corinth and Boeotia, dismissing the value of the Argive alliance and recalling past misjudgements. These include dealings with the Great King, the desertion to Amorges, and the Sicilian expedition, while the favourable terms now on offer are contrasted with those imposed after defeat. The speech closes by inviting the assembly to amend the written terms and urges them to choose for themselves between peace and war within forty days.
grc.anonymous.geographiae_expositio_compendi: This short anonymous Greek compendium of geography, of uncertain date, offers a schematic account of the inhabited world. It opens with the earth's circumference in stadia and the length and breadth of the inhabited world, measured from the Ganges to the Sacred Promontory beyond Lusitania. Having divided the earth into Europe, Libya and Asia by isthmuses and straits, the work surveys the peoples and regions of each continent. The largest islands, mountains and rivers are then ranked, and the oceans and inland seas are described with their principal gulfs and their dimensions in stadia and miles. A closing section treats the twelve winds and gives the lengths, breadths and coastlines of the world's main seas, straits and islands.
grc.antiphon.speeches: This collection gathers six speeches in Attic Greek attributed to Antiphon, an orator of uncertain date. The corpus contains forensic orations for prosecution and defence in homicide cases. It also includes the tetralogies, which are paired sets of model speeches arguing alternately for and against a single murder charge. The collection opens with a young prosecutor's case against his stepmother. He accuses her of poisoning his father, while his half-brothers and their mother appear for the defence.
grc.antisthenes.αἴας: This short Greek rhetorical speech is attributed to Antisthenes, though its date remains uncertain. It presents Ajax, son of Telamon, contesting the award of Achilles' arms before the assembled Greeks. He claims the prize against Odysseus, protesting that absent judges cannot rightly adjudicate matters known only to eyewitnesses. Ajax contrasts his open conduct, such as bearing Achilles' body from battle, with his rival's secrecy and greed. He accuses Odysseus of a nocturnal theft of a goddess's image and a willingness to endure indignity for gain. The speaker urges the judges to decide by deeds rather than words, noting that war is settled by action.
grc.antisthenes.ὀδυσσεύς: This short Greek oration, attributed to Antisthenes, features Odysseus defending his claim to Achilles' arms. He addresses the assembled Greeks rather than Ajax alone, asserting that his services exceed those of any other warrior. The speech contrasts Odysseus' craft with Ajax's brute strength, citing the recovery of a stolen goddess image. He also claims credit for entering enemy walls alone and guarding the army like a pilot. Ajax's armor and courage are dismissed as the recklessness of a wild boar. The oration closes by predicting a wise poet will portray Odysseus as the sole taker of Troy.
grc.apollodorus.epitome: The Epitome is an abridged continuation of the Bibliotheca, a Greek mythographic handbook attributed to Apollodorus. Its date remains uncertain, and the text opens mid-narrative with Theseus' roadside killings. It follows his career through the Minotaur, Ariadne, and the Amazons. The story then turns to the houses of Pelops and Atreus. The narrative runs through the Trojan cycle, from the judgment of Paris to the capture of Troy. It closes with the returns of the Greek leaders, including Agamemnon's murder and Odysseus' death.
grc.apollonius_dyscolus.περὶ_ἀντωνυμίας: A Greek grammatical treatise by Apollonius Dyscolus, of uncertain date, on the pronoun (Περὶ Ἀντωνυμίας). It opens with a preface defending concise exposition and a review of the names given to the pronoun by Aristarchus, the Stoics and others. The main discussion defines the pronoun as a word standing in place of a noun and representing definite persons, then takes up its division into deictic and anaphoric classes, the three grammatical persons and their combinations, the possessive and reflexive derivatives, questions of number, case, gender and accentuation, and the contrast between orthotone and enclitic forms. Individual forms are examined dialect by dialect, chiefly Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic and Boeotian, with Homeric and lyric quotations as evidence, and the argument repeatedly refutes rival views, including Stoic classifications and the readings of Aristarchus and Zenodotus.
grc.appian.civil_wars: Appian's Civil Wars is a Greek prose history in five books dealing with the internal conflicts of the Romans. The opening survey traces civil strife from early disputes involving the plebs and senate over laws, debts, and land. The narrative moves through the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, covering the dictatorship of Sulla and the rivalry of Caesar and Pompey. The story reaches the triumvirate of Antony, Lepidus, and Octavian, concluding with the war around Actium. The account closes with Antony's defeat and the taking of Egypt, elevating Octavian as Augustus, ruler of Rome and the nations under her.
grc.archimedes.ad_eratosthenem_methodus: This Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes is cast as a letter to Eratosthenes, opening by recalling theorem statements sent earlier without proofs. The author explains why he now publishes the mechanical method behind them, setting out a method where figures are cut into parallel slices. These slices are balanced against one another on a lever, and results are first surmised mechanically and then confirmed by strict geometric demonstration. A series of lemmas on centers of gravity follows this explanation, and the procedure is then applied to a sequence of specific theorems. One theorem states that a segment of a right-angled conoid is four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and height, while another shows that a sphere is four times the cone on its greatest circle. The circumscribed cylinder is half again the sphere, and comparable results are given for spheroids and segments of spheres, closing with a solid cut from a cylinder shown to be one-sixth of the enclosing prism.
grc.archimedes.fragmenta: This short collection of Greek fragments is transmitted under the name of Archimedes. It opens by contrasting the five regular solids known to Plato with the thirteen semiregular polyhedra credited to Archimedes. The text then lists each of those thirteen in turn, detailing their faces, angles, and edges. It also notes the regular solid from which each is generated by truncation. A further fragment discusses a fourteen-faced solid that Plato is said to have known. The closing piece, framed around Ptolemy, explains why stars appear larger near the horizon by appealing to refraction in the moist air about the earth, with reference to Archimedes' work on mirrors.
grc.aretaeus.signorum_acutorum_morbum: This Greek medical treatise, attributed to the Cappadocian physician Aretaeus, examines the signs of acute diseases, though its date remains uncertain. The opening section traces the premonitory symptoms of epilepsy from visual flashes to the final outcome, while later chapters describe tetanus and suffocating throat affections. These include synanche and cynanche, as well as pleurisy and peripneumonia, and the text also covers the spitting of blood, syncope, cholera, and intestinal obstruction. Closing portions address inflammatory fevers of the liver and disorders of the kidneys and bladder, concluding with suffocation arising from the womb and the condition known as satyriasis.
grc.aristophanes.acharnians: Aristophanes wrote this comic play, first produced in 425 BC, to satirize the ongoing Peloponnesian War, and the title refers to the Acharnians, a group of charcoal burners who oppose the protagonist. Dicaeopolis, an Attic farmer weary of conflict, arranges a private peace with Sparta, and he opens his own marketplace to enemy traders after the assembly refuses to discuss peace. Ambassadors recount their extravagant missions to Persia before he seals a thirty-year truce, and this act draws the wrath of the Acharnians, who pursue him in anger. To defend himself, he borrows tragic rags from Euripides and dresses as a beggar, arguing that the war sprang from petty private grievances like the Megarian dispute. He deflects his pursuers by holding a basket of charcoal hostage, and the second half follows the private peace in action with various scenes. Megarians sell their daughters disguised as piglets in the market, and a Boeotian trades eels for a captured informer in a separate deal. Festive celebrations of the wine god provide a moment of relief, and the bride receives a marriage-bed aphrodisiac as part of the festivities. General Lamachus marches off to a winter campaign while Dicaeopolis departs, and Dicaeopolis leaves for a drinking party and returns victorious from his feast. Lamachus limps home wounded just as Dicaeopolis arrives back.
grc.aristophanes.birds: Aristophanes wrote this comedy about two Athenians, Pisthetairos and Euelpides, who leave their city to live among birds. They wander a trackless wild, guided by a crow and a jackdaw, seeking Tereus, a man transformed into a hoopoe. Tereus advises them to build a city in the air, named Nephelokokkygia, which intercepts sacrificial smoke. This settlement forces the Olympian gods to negotiate, and a procession of human visitors, including a poet, an oracle-monger, and the geometer Meton, arrives. The birds claim in a formal address that they are older than the gods, and divine envoys, from Iris to an embassy of Poseidon and Heracles, are rebuffed. Pisthetairos is finally granted the goddess Basileia in marriage and elevated as supreme ruler.
grc.aristophanes.thesmophoriazusae: Aristophanes wrote this comedy about Euripides, who faces death for slandering women in his tragedies, while the women gather at the Thesmophoria, a festival honoring the goddesses of marriage. Agathon, a fellow tragedian, refuses to help Euripides by entering the assembly in disguise, so Euripides' kinsman is shaved and dressed as a woman to smuggle into the meeting. He answers the women's charges until his sex is discovered and he is seized, taking a baby that is actually a wine-skin as a hostage to delay his arrest. Euripides then arrives in disguises parodying his plays Helen and Andromeda, while Echo repeats his laments as he promises to speak well of women. The captives are freed, and the Scythian archer is duped into chasing the kinsman, while a dancing girl also flees through the streets as the chorus bids farewell.
grc.aristotle.categoriae: Aristotle's Categoriae opens by distinguishing homonyms, synonyms, and paronyms, then divides what is said into simple and composite expressions. The text lists the ten categories under which terms spoken without combination fall, and the body takes up these categories in turn. It dwells at greatest length on substance, distinguishing primary individual substances from secondary ones, and then treats quantity, quality, and relation. The author notes what is proper to each, and the closing chapters examine the four modes of opposition. They also cover the senses in which one thing is prior to or simultaneous with another, concluding by discussing the six species of motion and the various senses of having.
grc.aristotle.constitution: This Greek treatise on the history and workings of the Athenian constitution has been transmitted under Aristotle's name, though its authorship has long been debated. It opens with Athens' earliest kings and the mythical origins of its institutions before turning to the reforms of Draco, Solon, and Cleisthenes. The narrative then passes through the tyranny of Peisistratus and his sons and the successive oligarchic and democratic regimes down to the author's own day. The latter part sets out in detail the machinery of the contemporary democracy, from the council and the magistracies to the courts. It also describes the procedures by which citizens, jurors, and officials were enrolled and held accountable. The work concludes with an account of how judges are selected by lot and how verdicts are reached in the Athenian lawcourts.
grc.aristotle.de_anima: Aristotle's De Anima ('On the Soul') ranks the inquiry into the soul among the highest subjects, surveying earlier doctrines before offering its own account of the soul. The work defines the soul as the first actuality of a natural body endowed with life, then proceeds through the soul's faculties in order of generality. The nutritive faculty is shared by plants and animals, while sensation is examined sense by sense, and the treatise also covers imagination, desire, and thought. It treats the interdependence of soul and body along the way, distinguishing a mortal passive intellect from an active intellect that is separable and immortal. The text closes with a discussion of the cause of animal movement and the senses of taste and touch.
grc.aristotle.de_insomniis: This short Greek treatise on dreams, attributed to Aristotle, opens by asking whether dreams belong to the thinking or perceptive faculty of the soul. The author argues that dreaming is neither bare sensation nor opinion but a function of imagination, which shares its subject with perception yet differs in its specific activity. The body of the work explains how sense impressions leave behind movements in the organs, and these residual motions persist after the original stimulus has ceased. The text illustrates this with after images from bright objects and flowing water, and it also cites strong noises, smells, and a clouded mirror held by a menstruating woman. Normally, waking perception drowns out these faint movements, but in sleep, the idle senses allow them to surface. Dreams are strong and clear for healthy people but distorted for the feverish or drunk, and they are also distorted for the melancholic, while none occur after meals or in young children, though some rare individuals never dream at all. The work closes by defining the dream as a phantasm arising from these movements, and it distinguishes this from the faint perceptions and stray thoughts that can accompany slumber.
grc.aristotle.de_iuventute_et_senectute_de_v: This Greek prose treatise by Aristotle is known by the Latin title De Iuventute et Senectute, De Vita et Morte, which translates as On Youth and Old Age, On Life and Death. It belongs to his writings on natural philosophy concerning functions shared by living things, and it opens by announcing an account of youth, old age, life, and death. The work also undertakes an inquiry into the causes of respiration, while the argument locates the nutritive and sensitive soul in the middle of the body. In blooded animals, this seat is the heart, while bloodless ones have an analogue, and death is treated as the loss of innate heat. Old age represents the gradual exhaustion of this heat from want of nourishment, whereas violent death is its quenching by an opposing cold. The discussion explains how plants and animals must continually cool this heat by means of food, water, or air, and the text ends at the point of passing on to a fuller explanation of breathing.
grc.aristotle.de_longitudine_et_brevitate_vi: This short Greek treatise by Aristotle examines the causes of long and short life in living things, opening by setting out problems for inquiry. It asks whether one cause governs longevity in both animals and plants, and whether long life belongs to the healthy constitution. The argument considers what is easily destroyed in natural compounds, holding that life depends on a warm and moist principle that must be neither small nor readily dried up. This principle explains why large land animals such as man and the elephant are the longest-lived of animals, and why warm regions, males, and fatty or whole-blooded creatures outlast others. Trees, whose parts are perpetually renewed, surpass all living things in the length of their existence. The work closes by announcing that youth, old age, life, and death remain to be treated for the study of animals to be complete.
grc.aristotle.de_partibus_animalium: De Partibus Animalium is a four book treatise by Aristotle that examines the causes behind the various parts of animals. The opening section addresses the education needed to judge well and outlines the method proper to natural inquiry. Aristotle argues that form and purpose rank above matter while rejecting the dichotomous division of animal kinds. The remaining books begin with homogeneous constituents such as blood, marrow, fat, and bone before moving to principal organs. The heart, lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and bladder are discussed, followed by external parts of blooded animals. Teeth, horns, tongue, eyes, limbs, and the organs of speech and respiration are examined in this section. The discussion then passes to insects, crustaceans, shellfish, molluscs, fish, birds, and egg laying quadrupeds. Throughout, the work asks what each part is for and why animals are constituted as they are.
grc.aristotle.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: De Sensu et Sensibilibus, meaning On Sense and Sensibles, is a short Greek treatise attributed to Aristotle, belonging to the minor natural works that examine living things as affections common to soul and body. The text presents itself as a continuation of the enquiry into the soul found in the De Anima, turning to powers such as sense, memory, pleasure, and pain that belong to animals. The argument first examines the sense organs, allotting each to an element, and refutes accounts of vision as an emanation of fire. Colour is defined as the limit of the transparent in a determinate body, and varieties of colour and flavour are derived from mixtures of white and black. Sweet and bitter are also mixed according to numerical ratios, while smell is treated as intermediate between touch and sight. Its kinds are distinguished, and pleasant odours of flowers are assigned to man, a connection that involves respiration and the cooling of the brain. The closing discussion asks whether perception proceeds through a medium, considers whether several objects can be perceived at the same instant, and addresses the unity of the common faculty that judges them.
grc.aristotle.de_somno_et_vigilia: Aristotle's short Greek treatise De Somno et Vigilia ('On Sleep and Waking') examines the nature of these states, asking whether they belong to the soul, the body, or both, and why they occur. The text also poses puzzles about dreams, their causes, and their potential to foretell the future, which are referred for treatment in other works. The author argues that sleep and waking are affections of the common faculty of sense, possessed by all animals that have touch, though by no plants. A physiological explanation follows, describing how vapours from food rise by innate heat, cool in the brain, and recoil to seize the primary sense organ. Sleep is defined as this seizure, which prevents sensory activity, and it occurs of necessity for the sake of preservation, since rest preserves the animal.
grc.aristotle.eudemian_ethics: The Eudemian Ethics is a Greek ethical treatise by Aristotle that inquires into happiness and the character of the good life. Its opening takes its cue from the Delian inscription distinguishing the good, the beautiful, and the pleasant. The work asks how living well is acquired, whether by nature, learning, habituation, or chance. It insists that a life must be ordered toward a definite end. The body of the text treats the virtues of character as means between excess and deficiency. It examines liberality, magnanimity, and justice, and then explores friendship at length in its various kinds and conditions. The treatise concludes with an account of good fortune and of kalokagathia as perfect virtue. Its final standard is the contemplation of God.
grc.aristotle.fragmenta_deperditae_partis_pr: This work, attributed to Aristotle, preserves fragments of the lost first part of the Constitution of the Athenians, whose title means the political constitution of Athens. The text survives chiefly through quotations in later lexicographers, scholiasts, and Plutarch, opening with an account of Athens' earliest kingship and the citizens' renaming as Ionians after Ion. Lexicographical notes on Apollo Patroos accompany this opening section, while the remaining fragments concern Theseus, who is credited with the synoikismos and the first move toward democracy. He also divided the people into eupatridae, geomoroi, and demiourgoi, and the text sets out the pre-Cleisthenic organisation of the citizen body into four tribes. It further details twelve trittyes or phratries and thirty gene of thirty men apiece, whose members were called gennetai, followed by a notice of Theseus' death at Scyros and the recovery of his bones after the Persian Wars. A closing editorial remark states that other fragments do not belong to the treatise.
grc.aristotle.poetics: Aristotle's Greek treatise examines poetry in general and its principal kinds, opening by announcing a complete treatment of the poetic arts. The author distinguishes forms of imitation by their medium, objects, and manner, including epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, and music. The text traces the origins of poetry in the human instinct for imitation and rhythm, defining tragedy and enumerating its six parts. Extensive discussion follows on plot, covering unity of action, reversal, and recognition, while the author considers the kind of hero who best serves the tragic effect. Pity and fear are identified as proper to the genre, and later sections take up character and diction, including metaphor. Methods for answering objections to particular poems are set out, and epic is weighed against tragedy in the final analysis. The work concludes that tragedy achieves the aims of poetic imitation more fully than epic.
grc.aristotle.topica: The Topics is a Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on dialectic, setting out a method for reasoning from accepted opinions about any problem proposed. Its opening defines syllogism, distinguishes the demonstrative, dialectical and eristic varieties, and states the purposes of the inquiry for exercise, debate and the philosophical sciences. The greater part of the treatise collects strategies of argument concerning the four predicables of definition, property, genus and accident. It shows how propositions about each predicable may be established and refuted, and what counts as a correctly laid-down definition or property. The final book prescribes the roles of questioner and answerer in a dialectical exchange and classifies the faults of faulty reasoning. The work closes with advice on training, the choice of interlocutors and the ready command of propositions and definitions.
grc.aristotle.μηχανικά: The Μηχανικά is a short Greek treatise on mechanics transmitted under Aristotle's name, of uncertain date. It opens by defining mechanics as the art that assists human purposes in what lies contrary to nature, and traces all such effects to the properties of the circle, from which the balance and the lever derive. The remainder consists of a long series of problems treated in question-and-answer form, explaining by the principle of the lever the working of balances, pulleys, the wedge, oars and rudders, nutcrackers, forceps, ship's windlasses, and human movements such as rising from a seat. Later problems concern projectiles, why thrown objects stop moving, and why bodies carried in whirling water drift toward the centre.
grc.aristoxenus.elementa_harmonica: The Elementa Harmonica, a Greek theoretical treatise on the science of melody, is opened by Aristoxenus, who ranks harmonics first among musical science branches. He defines its goal as the theory of systems and tones, then criticises the achievements of earlier writers such as Eratocles. The argument proceeds through the ordered movement of the voice, offering definitions of note, interval, and system. The text examines the three genera of melody, namely enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic, and details the divisions of the tetrachord. Principles governing consonance, succession, and melodic composition are also discussed, closing with demonstrations of melodic paths from each kind of interval. It also covers the three species into which the fourth can be cast.
grc.arrian.anabasis: Arrian's Anabasis is a Greek prose history of Alexander the Great in seven books, and the title means 'The March Up' or 'The Expedition'. The author opens with a preface explaining his method of reconciling sources, recording as true whatever Ptolemy and Aristobulus agree upon about Alexander. Where they differ, he chooses the more credible and noteworthy account, and the narrative follows Alexander from his accession to the Macedonian throne. He was a young man of about twenty when Philip died, and the story covers campaigns against the Thracians, Triballi, and Illyrians. It then describes the crossing into Asia and major battles with Persians, while later books detail the reduction of coastal cities and Egypt. The conquest of the Persian heartland is also recounted, and the text includes hard-fought campaigns in Bactria and Sogdiana. These involved Spitamenes and the Scythians, including the siege of the Sogdian rock, and the account then turns to India and the return westward. The work closes with Alexander's death in Babylon, presenting divergent accounts of his final days and rumours of poisoning. A long final assessment of his character and achievements concludes the text.
grc.artemidorus.onirocriticon: Artemidorus of Daldis composed the Onirocriticon, a Greek treatise on interpreting dreams as signs of future events, and the title means the art of judging dreams. The work opens with a preface that defends dream divination against its critics, then distinguishes the meaningless enypnion from the true dream, or oneiros. True dreams are classified as either theorematic, fulfilling exactly what is seen, or allegorical, signifying one thing through another. The main body proceeds through manifold images, including animals, bodily acts, gods, and journeys, and for each, it states the outcome portended to dreamers of differing condition, from slaves to rulers. A concluding series of actual dreams with their observed fulfillments rounds off the treatise.
grc.aspasius.in_ethica_nicomachea_paraphrasi: Aspasius's Greek exposition of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics begins by weighing ethical and political philosophy against theoretical wisdom, judging the former necessary for living well while the latter is superior in honor. The text then follows Aristotle's argument section by section, introducing art, method, action, and deliberative choice, which lead toward the good with happiness as the human end. The work treats the moral virtues at greatest length, focusing on liberality, magnificence, and magnanimity, which is understood as greatness of soul measured by honor. The closing portions are devoted to friendship and its division into kinds, which are grounded in the good, the pleasant, and the useful. The author also examines equality and superiority between friends, such as parents and children, and considers the correspondence of friendship and justice with constitutions from kingship to tyranny. Finally, he addresses the claims of kinship and mutual benefit, including disputes over the repayment of favors.
grc.athenaeus.deipnosophists: This Greek prose dialogue features Athenaeus addressing Timocrates with an account of a sumptuous banquet hosted by the wealthy Roman Larensis, who gathers a diverse group of guests. Attendees include grammarians, philosophers, physicians, and musicians, and the dinner talk moves from fish and vegetables to music and jests. It also covers drinking cups, the wealth of kings, and ships, while long quotations from poets, historians, and philosophers thread through the conversation. Comic poets are especially prominent in these citations, and as the meal proceeds, the diners treat of parody and comedy. They also discuss proverbs, rare words, and the vocabulary of lamps and torches, and the evening closes with a libation and a paean to Hygieia, Health.
grc.babrius.fabulae_aesopeae: Babrius, a poet of uncertain date, composed a collection of Aesopic fables in Greek verse. He recasts traditional tales of animals and men in short limping iambics. The prologue is addressed to a boy named Branchus. It recalls the mythic ages when beasts spoke and mortals kept company with gods. Babrius then announces that the fables of our wise old Aesop will be set down. The individual fables are brief narratives, each furnished with a short moral lesson.
grc.barnabas.barnabae_epistulae: This Greek Christian epistle, of uncertain date and attributed in tradition to Barnabas, opens by rejoicing in the spiritual gifts of its addressees. The writer then undertakes to share a portion of the knowledge he has received, arguing that literal observances of the Mosaic law were never what God desired. These practices, including sacrifice, fasting, and circumcision, are read as figures pointing to Christ, while the text warns that evil days precede the approaching end. It concludes with a teaching on two ways, contrasting the path of light with the way of darkness, and closes by asking to be remembered by those who profit from its exhortation.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.de_legendis: This Greek exhortation to young men is attributed to Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea, and sets out how pagan learning may profit readers raised in the Christian life. It opens with the speaker commending his counsel by goodwill toward the youths and long experience of human affairs, promising the safest road for those just entering upon life. The present human life is distinguished from the life to come, with external studies valued only as preparation, like leaves adorning the fruit of truth. In support of this, the work cites Moses and Daniel, men who first disciplined their minds in Egyptian and Chaldean learning before turning to divine things. A review follows of what should be accepted and what passed over in the poets, with examples of self-command and endurance drawn from Socrates, Pericles, Euclides and Alexander. It closes with warnings against sloth, wealth, pleasure and love of reputation, urging that virtue be gathered from every source as provision for the journey.
grc.callimachus.aetia: The Aetia, a four book elegy by the Hellenistic Greek poet Callimachus, explains the origins of cults, rites, festivals, and local customs. The work survives only in papyrus fragments and quotations by later writers, and the extant material opens with ancient epigrams and testimonies about the poet. A dream prologue follows, where the poet is carried to Helicon to question the Muses, and books one and two range over aetiologies of heroes, foundations, and rituals. These include the Locrian maidens sent to Troy, Coroebus, and Phalaris' bull, while book three preserves the longest continuous narrative, the courtship of Acontius and Cydippe on Ceos. This story is woven together with an account of the island's settlement, and book four carries the poem on to further local aetiologies, such as the Deipnias festival and the hero Androgeos.
grc.carmina_delphis_inventa.carmina_delphis_: Carmina Delphis Inventa gathers Greek cult songs for Apollo recovered from the Athenian treasury at Delphi, printing surviving musical notation beneath the words. It includes a Latin editorial apparatus on harmonies and opens with a decree honouring the Athenian composer Cleochares, son of Bion. Cleochares wrote the city's ceremonial hymns, and the poems themselves are of uncertain date. One hymn invokes Apollo as the son of Zeus who slew the serpent guarding the tripod. It also recalls the god's repulse of the Galatian war host, while other pieces call on Helicon and the daughters of Zeus. They summon singers to the twin peaks of Parnassus, and the collection closes with prayers for the safety of Bacchic bands and the flourishing of musical contests.
grc.chariton.de_chaerea: Chariton's Chaereas and Callirhoe is a Greek prose romance of uncertain date, and the narrator identifies himself as Chariton of Aphrodisias, a clerk to the rhetor Athenagoras. He announces an account of a love affair that befell at Syracuse, where the story opens with the marriage of Callirhoe, daughter of the Syracusan general Hermocrates, to the young Chaereas. Jealous rivals provoke a quarrel in which he strikes his bride so that she collapses, and she is buried as dead, but tomb robbers free her and sell her into slavery at Miletus. The wealthy Dionysius marries her there, while Chaereas searches the seas for her, and he is shipwrecked, enslaved, and finally brought to trial before the Persian king Artaxerxes at Babylon. An Egyptian revolt interrupts the trial, leading to Chaereas's naval command and victories, and the couple reunites on Aradus and returns to Syracuse laden with Persian spoils.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.eclogae_prophetica: The Eclogae Propheticae, a short Greek miscellany by Clement of Alexandria, gathers notes on prophetic and other biblical passages despite its uncertain date. It opens with the hymn of the three young men in the fiery furnace, which Clement reads as evidence for the purity of the heavens and waters. He also sees this text as proof of the ordered ranks of angelic powers, before the collection ranges across allegorical interpretations of Genesis, Daniel, Hosea, and the Psalms. The work discusses baptism through water, spirit, and fire, along with fasting and prayer, while covering the soul's purification from matter and its advance toward divine knowledge. It closes with notes on angels and the restoration of souls in ranks, addressing the fate of exposed infants as reported from the Apocalypse of Peter. The final section also considers the significance of stars, day and night, and particular psalm verses.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.paedagogus: The Paedagogus, a Christian instructional treatise by Clement of Alexandria, presents the divine Word as the tutor who trains human souls in virtue and sobriety. The opening chapters define the educator's office, noting his philanthropy and equal guidance of men and women, while he instructs through law and prophets. He heals the passions before higher teaching begins, and the body of the work turns to practical daily conduct, regulating eating, drinking, and behaviour at table. It also covers music, laughter, and the use of garlands, ointments, and jewellery, with further rules addressing hairstyle, public deportment, and the manner of men, women, and children in church. The text closes by gathering commandments from the Decalogue, prophets, and apostles into a summary, which is followed by a prayer and a hymn of thanksgiving to Christ.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.quis_dives_salvetu: Quis Dives Salvetur ('Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?') is a Greek homily by Clement of Alexandria on the question whether the wealthy can attain salvation. It opens with a censure of those who flatter the rich with encomia, before turning to the Gospel episode in which a rich man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life and is told that it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The main body expounds that passage, arguing that the command to sell all one has must be understood chiefly of the passions of the soul rather than of outward property, that wealth is an indifferent instrument to be used rightly, and that almsgiving, love of God and neighbour, illustrated from the parable of the Good Samaritan, and true repentance leave the rich a path to eternal life. The work closes with the story of the apostle John pursuing and reclaiming a young man turned bandit chief, offered as a great example of repentance, followed by a doxology.
grc.colluthus.rape_of_helen: The Rape of Helen is a Greek poem in epic hexameters by Colluthus, an author of uncertain date, which recounts the events leading to Helen's journey from Sparta to Troy. The work opens with a prayer to the nymphs born of the river Xanthus, who are asked to tell of the shepherd Paris and the first beginning of the strife. The narrative moves from the wedding of Peleus and Thetis to the arrival of Paris, when Eris, barred from the feast, casts a golden apple among the goddesses. Hermes brings Paris from Mount Ida for the famous judgment, where Hera offers rule over Asia, while Athena offers prowess in war. Aphrodite offers the hand of Helen, which Paris chooses, and the remainder follows Paris by ship to Sparta, where Helen, persuaded by Aphrodite's command, departs with him by night. The poem closes with Hermione searching in vain for her vanished mother, and it also shows Cassandra tearing her hair as Troy opens its gates to Paris.
grc.cratetis_epistulae.epistulae: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to the Cynic philosopher Crates, of uncertain date. The opening letter urges its recipient to hasten to greet Diogenes while he still lives. The remaining letters, mostly brief and gnomic, exhort their addressees to a Cynic life of toil, cold water, plain food and the rough cloak. They argue that philosophy teaches justice better than law, and defend the name of 'dog' as a badge of endurance rather than a reproach. Among them are advice to women disciples on philosophy, adornment, childbirth and the rearing of children, and a warning against drunkenness illustrated from Homer. A longer narrative epistle recounts Diogenes' capture by pirates and his conduct when exposed for sale in the slave market.
grc.demosthenes.against_androtion: Against Androtion is a forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus, delivered in an Athenian court to support Euctemon's prosecution of the politician Androtion. The case concerned a decree that conferred a crown on the Council, while the speaker promised to help Euctemon win redress. He also vowed to defend the city against such abuses of power, contending that the Council could not lawfully be crowned. The argument asserts that the Council had failed to build the triremes required by law, and the speech surveys Androtion's public career. He is accused of dragging defaulters and even metics from their homes with the aid of the Eleven, and the text details his insults. It further describes his melting down of allied dedicatory crowns to make gold phialai inscribed with his own name, while closing appeals urge jurors to convict.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_1: This forensic oration by Demosthenes is the first of his speeches against Aphobus, whom he sued for mismanaging the estate left by his father. The speech opens by noting that Aphobus refused arbitration and evaded family friends, then recounts how the father died leaving a son of seven and a daughter of five. The mother had a dowry of eighty mnas and property of nearly fourteen talents, and three guardians were entrusted with this estate. The speech itemizes the property, including two workshops and household goods, and lists sums on deposit with bankers and out at maritime interest. Testimony is read aloud to reckon up money allegedly taken by Aphobus, Demophon, and Therippides, while the argument covers the unpaid dowry, a concealed will, and a claim of buried treasure. The oration closes with a warning of a penalty of a hundred mnas, appeals to the laws and the jurors' oath, and pleads for pity on a household wronged by its protectors.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristocrates: This forensic speech by Demosthenes was composed for an Athenian court. It serves as a prosecution against Aristocrates, who proposed a decree. The decree made anyone who killed the mercenary commander Charidemus liable to seizure without trial. The speaker disclaims private enmity and declares that his real concern is that Athens securely hold the Chersonese. The argument shows the decree to be contrary to the Athenian homicide laws, from Draco's code to the procedures of the Areopagus and the other homicide courts. It reviews at length Charidemus's career in the service of Cotys, Cersobleptes, and other Thracian dynasts, his alleged betrayals of Athenian interests, and the machinations by which the decree was brought forward. The closing sections contrast the honors lavished on Charidemus with the treatment of earlier benefactors such as Miltiades and Themistocles and urge the jurors to annul the decree.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_1: This forensic prosecution speech, attributed to Demosthenes, is brought against Aristogiton, a public debtor who nonetheless presents himself in court as an informer and accuser of others. The opening observes that Lycurgus, the joint prosecutor, has already stated the legal case, and that the verdict will turn less on arguments than on the jurors' attitude toward wickedness. The speech then catalogs Aristogiton's misdeeds, among them his betrayal of his father in prison and the sale of his sister. It also dwells on his treatment of Zobia, who sheltered him after his escape, and on his assault on a fellow prisoner and theft of a document. The speaker attacks Aristogiton's professed goodwill toward the people, likening him to a scorpion or viper in the city's midst. It closes by urging the jurors, in view of the citizens and foreigners watching their verdict, to impose either death or a fine he cannot pay.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_2: This Athenian forensic oration, attributed to Demosthenes, appears in his corpus as the second speech in the prosecution of Aristogiton. Lycurgus had already exposed the defendant's character in the earlier case, and the speaker asserts that Aristogiton owes money to the public treasury. He stands disfranchised and is barred by law from addressing the people, so the orator argues that convicted lawbreakers must be excluded from public life. The text compares the injury to the city with a helmsman's error ruining a ship, appealing to Solon's swift punishments for demagogues. It also cites penalties once paid by Aristides, Miltiades, and Pericles, while recounting how Aristogiton twisted Hyperides' decree into a personal privilege. This decree had restored rights to citizens after the disasters at Chaeronea, and the oration reviews Aristogiton's barren record as a politician. It closes by urging jurors to defend the laws that govern the cosmos.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_1: This Athenian forensic speech from a private suit is transmitted among the orations of Demosthenes, where it is generally counted among the private speeches of the corpus. The speaker, Mantitheus, opens by disclaiming any meddlesome fondness for litigation, explaining that he has sued his half-brother Boeotus to prevent him from claiming the same name. The argument contends that their father Mantias registered the boys as Boeotus and Mantitheus respectively, since a father has sole legal authority to give or revoke his children's names. The bulk of the speech enumerates the practical confusion two identically named citizens would cause, while it rebuts the anticipated charge that the name was imposed under provocation or mockery. The text closes with hostile characterisation of Boeotus and appeals to the laws and jurors' oaths.
grc.demosthenes.against_callippus: Forensic speech in Greek from the corpus attributed to Demosthenes, written for the defense in an Athenian private suit over a money deposit left with a bank. The opening observes that no opponent is harder to refute than a man of reputation who lies boldly and can produce witnesses. The narrative then explains that Lycōn of Heraclea left sixteen minae and forty drachmae with the banking house of Pasiōn, to be repaid to Cephisiadēs, a metic of Scirus, whom Archebiades was to present, and argues that Callippus, proxenos of the Heracleots, inspected the bank's record at the time, stayed silent for more than five months, and later fabricated both a claim to the money and a suit for damages. The speaker contests Callippus's account of an oath before the arbitrator Lysitheides, discredits the relatives testifying for him, and supports his case with documents, laws, and witness testimony before closing with a plea for acquittal.
grc.demosthenes.against_dionysodorus: Against Dionysodorus is an Athenian forensic speech by Demosthenes, which addresses a commercial suit over a maritime loan. The speaker presents himself as a partner in a bottomry loan, and this loan of three thousand drachmae was advanced to Dionysodorus and Parmeniscus. The defendants were bound by contract to return the ship to the Piraeus, but they sailed to Rhodes and sold the grain cargo there. They acted in concert with the agents of Cleomenes, who had cornered the Egyptian grain trade. The speech then reads out the contract and a formal challenge, and it rebuts the defendants' claims of shipwreck and concessions from other lenders. The orator urges the jurors to enforce the stipulated penalty of double repayment, arguing that the verdict will determine confidence in maritime agreements and the security of the city's commerce.
grc.demosthenes.against_eubulides: This forensic speech, transmitted among the private orations of Demosthenes, answers a prosecution by Eubulides on a charge of falsely claiming Athenian citizenship. The defendant opens by protesting against Eubulides' slanders and asking for a hearing equal to the one granted his accuser. He then recounts the night-time scrutiny held in his deme of Halimous, alleging that Eubulides and his associates contrived the vote against him. The speaker establishes his citizen birth by tracing the genealogy of his mother's family and producing testimony from kinsmen, phratries and demesmen. His enrolment in the deme and his preliminary selection for the priesthood of Herakles are offered as further proof. After censuring Eubulides' record of expelling citizens for money, the speaker closes by pleading to keep his civic status and bury his mother in the ancestral tombs.
grc.demosthenes.against_lacritus: This Athenian forensic speech, transmitted within the corpus of Demosthenes, addresses a commercial suit known as a dikē emporikē. The speaker, Androcles of Sphettus, a merchant who lent money for a voyage to the Black Sea, opens with a general attack on the Phaselites as inveterate defaulters in maritime lending. The text recounts a loan of thirty minas to Artemon and Apollodorus of Phaselis, where a written contract stipulated a cargo of Mendean wine. After Artemon died, the action was brought against his brother and heir, Lacritus, a pupil of Isocrates who denied liability for the debt. The body of the speech sets the contract terms against the brothers' conduct, citing a cargo far short of the stipulated three thousand jars and a second unauthorized loan on the same security. The speaker mentions the failure to bring return freight to Athens, and a claimed shipwreck near Panticapaeum is contradicted by witness testimony, while the collateral was pledged to a Chian creditor. The speech closes with an appeal to the jurors to uphold the binding force of maritime agreements.
grc.demosthenes.against_leochares: This forensic oration, attributed to Demosthenes, was delivered in an Athenian inheritance suit concerning the estate of the childless Archiades. The speaker accuses Leochares of lodging a false diamartyria, or challenge, which asserts that Archiades left legitimate sons.
