The speech traces the descent of the Otryneis from Euthymachus, listing his sons Meidylides, Archippus, and Archiades. The speaker argues that male kinship makes him and his father the nearest heirs, attacking the irregular enrolments that placed Leochares as an adopted child. The text cites Solon's law regarding the disposal of estates by adopted sons, while witness testimony and deme registers support the speaker's position. The jurors are asked to reject the challenge and assign the inheritance to the closest kin.
grc.demosthenes.against_macartatus: Against Macartatus is an Athenian courtroom speech in Greek, attributed to Demosthenes, and delivered in an inheritance dispute over the estate of Hagnias. The speaker recalls earlier contests with the same opponents and announces a full narrative of the affair, tracing the descent of both parties from Bouselos of Oinoe. The widow Philomache won the estate at law, while her rivals produced forged wills, and her son was adopted into the house of Euboulides and enrolled among the phrateres. The case is supported by testimonies and laws of Solon on inheritance and the epiklerate, while accusations of collusion and perjury run through the speech against Theopompus and his son Macartatus. They are also charged with uprooting more than a thousand olive trees from the land, and the speech closes with an appeal to the jurors to protect the boy. It asks them to keep the household of Hagnias from desolation.
grc.demosthenes.against_nausimachus_and_xeno: This forensic speech in Attic Greek is attributed to Demosthenes, though its date remains uncertain. It was delivered in an Athenian court by one of two orphan brothers, who faced prosecution by Nausimachus and Xenopeithes over the administration of their inheritance. The speaker begins by describing a legal motion to have the case ruled inadmissible, arguing that their father had already been sued by the same men and released from those actions. The greater part of the speech relies on the settlement and the father's subsequent death, citing laws forbidding renewed litigation over released claims and the five-year limit for orphans to sue former guardians. He contrasts the opponents' present written charge with their earlier complaint, while also attacking their squandered estates and poor record in liturgies. The speech closes with the reading of testimony, laws, and the original charge, ending with a plea that the brothers be left in possession of their property.
grc.demosthenes.against_olympiodorus: This private forensic speech by the Athenian orator Demosthenes addresses a jury court where the plaintiff sues his brother-in-law Olympiodorus over a disputed inheritance. The text opens with a defense of the painful necessity of litigating against a kinsman, then recounts the death of the childless Comon and the subsequent funeral. The men divided the estate under written contracts and mutual oaths, which were deposited with Androcleides for safekeeping. Joint litigation against rival claimants ended in Olympiodorus' victory, but he refused to share the proceeds as the oaths required. This included money obtained through a tortured slave, while laws, contracts, and testimony are cited throughout the argument. The closing sections rebut the defendant's excuses and press for the contracts to be opened, attacking Olympiodorus' treatment of his wife, her sister, and their daughter. He also denounces the defendant's life with a hetaera, and the speech ends with an appeal for a just verdict.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_31: This forensic speech belongs to the Demosthenic corpus, addressing private actions from fourth century BC Athens. The text arises from lawsuits against former guardians, opening by recalling an earlier argument. Onetor never paid the dowry owed to Aphobus, and the speaker announces an exposure of falsehoods. The argument tracks Onetor's shifting statements, where he first placed valuations on the house and estate. He later changed the dowry amount to a talent, removing boundary markers once litigation began. These acts prove the dowry was never paid, showing Onetor's conduct as guarantor involved collusion.
grc.demosthenes.against_phaenippus: This forensic speech, attributed to Demosthenes, addresses an Athenian jury concerning a suit arising from an antidosis, a procedure for exchanging public liturgies. The text opens with praise for Solon's law governing such exchanges, then details the speaker's formal challenge to Phaenippus and his inspection of the estate at Cytherus. The body documents Phaenippus' defiance, including the late filing of his sworn valuation, while he unsealed marked storehouses and carted off grain, wine, and timber. Phaenippus produced debts and a dowry claim to inflate his liabilities, and the speech supports these claims with inserted laws, witness depositions, and the valuation itself. The closing plea asks jurors to compel the exchange and relieve the speaker, who is impoverished by misfortunes in the silver mines and assessed three talents.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_1: This forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus addresses a private suit of false witness, where Apollodorus, son of Pasion, speaks against Stephanus of Acharnae before the Athenian jurors. He claims that Stephanus's testimony and Phormion's outrages have wronged him, and the core of the argument examines a deposition regarding a challenge and a purported will. Apollodorus has the witness statements, the challenge, the will, and the bank lease read out, arguing that these documents are fabricated and that the testimony contradicts itself. The speech then shifts to invective, highlighting Stephanus's servile origins and greed, while it also details Phormion's alleged mistreatment of Apollodorus's mother. The closing appeal asks the jurors to punish the false witness as a warning to others.
grc.demosthenes.against_theocrines: Against Theocrines is a forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, delivered in an Athenian court to support a denunciation. The speaker explains that his father was fined ten talents after Theocrines laid an information against a ship of Micon. He then abandoned the case for money, leaving the prosecution to his son. The body of the speech assembles charges against Theocrines, citing his repeated acceptance of payment to withdraw prosecutions. It also notes his unpaid fines owed to the state and details his betrayal of the speaker's father. This occurred in a case concerning an illegal decree, further addressing the misconduct of his brother in public office. Laws, decrees, a stele, and witness testimony are read into the argument. The closing urges jurors to enforce the laws against a professional sycophant. It asks them to aid a young man pleading his father's cause.
grc.demosthenes.erotic_essay: The Erotic Essay, a short Greek epideictic oration attributed to Demosthenes, is composed in the voice of a lover addressing the young Epicrates. The speaker regards him as the most attractive and promising of the city's youth, and the oration opens with a frame announcing a composition. This style is meant for display rather than the courtroom, aiming to praise the youth and counsel him on education and the conduct of life. The main body celebrates Epicrates' beauty and his moderation towards his admirers, while highlighting his manliness shown in his choice of training with arms. A chariot-race victory further demonstrates his character, and the text cites mythological exemplars and figures such as Pericles and Alcibiades. It also mentions Timotheus and Solon as men formed by association with philosophers, closing with an exhortation to take up philosophy and choose friends with care for a leading part in the city's affairs.
grc.demosthenes.for_the_megalopitans: This deliberative oration by Demosthenes was delivered before the Athenian assembly, addressing the question of aiding the Megalopolitans of Arcadia against the Lacedaemonians. The speaker opens by rebuking both the Arcadian and Lacedaemonian envoys, criticizing them for trading accusations instead of advising on the common interest. The argument then holds that Athens' true policy is to keep both Thebes and Sparta weak, taking up the claim that alliance with the Megalopolitans would make enemies of Sparta. It also addresses the claim that such an alliance would hinder the recovery of Oropus, considering the charges brought against the Megalopolitans and Thebans for their earlier dealings. The oration reviews proposals for restoring Thespiae, Orchomenus, and Plataea, and also considers pulling down the old stelai. Appeals to the oaths sworn for the Messenians lead to the closing admonition, urging the city not to abandon the Megalopolitans or any weaker state to a greater.
grc.demosthenes.funeral_speech: This Greek funeral oration, known as an epitaphios, is attributed to Demosthenes and was composed for the public burial of Athenians who fell in war. The speaker opens by professing the difficulty of finding adequate praise for men who chose a noble death over life. The speech then surveys the autochthonous nobility of the Athenian people and the mythical exploits of their ancestors. It recounts the repulse of the Amazons, Eumolpus, and the Heraclids, along with the burial of the Seven against Thebes. The narrative moves to the Persian Wars and the valour of the recently fallen, whose defeat is recast as a victory of spirit that preserved the freedom of all Greece. The closing sections credit the democracy with fostering such courage, recalling a hero of each of the ten Attic tribes as a model for the dead. The speech ends with consolation to parents and orphans before dismissing the mourners to perform the customary rites.
grc.demosthenes.letters: This collection gathers Greek prose letters attributed to Demosthenes, which are addressed to the council and people of Athens. The first letter begins with a prayer to the gods, presenting the writer as an exile offering political counsel. He urges concord among citizens and forbearance toward former opponents, while also calling for united Greek action now that Alexander is dead. The correspondence combines formal salutation with sustained advice on public affairs, and it also touches on the question of the writer's own return home.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_1: This speech by Demosthenes addresses the Athenian assembly as the first of the Olynthiac orations, urging the city to defend Olynthus against Philip of Macedon. The orator argues that good counsel matters more than money, presenting the war as a rare opportunity to act. He lists missed chances at Euboea, Amphipolis, and Pydna, warning that Olynthus falling would allow Philip to march on Attica. He proposes sending soldiers to save the Olynthic cities, also suggesting ravaging Philip's own territory. The speech closes by urging the use of military funds, calling for rich and poor to serve as needed.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_3: This deliberative speech, the third of Demosthenes' Olynthiac orations, addresses the Athenian assembly to urge vigorous military aid to Olynthus against Philip of Macedon. The orator complains that talk of punishing Philip has distracted the city from saving its allies, while he reviews past delays and missed opportunities since Philip's siege in Thrace. Flattering politicians are blamed for the city's passivity, and the speech proposes appointing lawmakers to suspend laws concerning the theoric fund. This measure would return money and citizens to military service, and the closing section contrasts the discipline and conquests of ancestors like Aristides and Pericles with the private luxury of present day statesmen. It ends with a call for Athenians to serve in person and restore the civic order.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_halonnesus: This Athenian deliberative speech by Demosthenes dates from the age of Philip II of Macedon, and it was composed in answer to a letter in which Philip professed to be giving Athens the island of Halonnesus. The speaker begins by insisting that Philip's complaints cannot bar Athenians from giving counsel at the bema, and he undertakes to examine both the letter and the arguments of Philip's ambassadors. The text then rebuts the letter point by point, denying that Halonnesus is Philip's to give, and it exposes his proposals on pirates and commercial treaties as devices to consolidate his seizures at Potidaea and Amphipolis. The speech cites his actions at Pherae, Ambracia, and in Cassopia as proof that his professed care for Greek freedom is empty, and it recalls the decree of Philocrates and the earlier embassy under Python. It attacks Philip's encroachments on the Chersonese in favour of Apollonides of Cardia, and the speaker closes by reserving a further reply to the ambassadors' arguments.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_liberty_of_the_rhodia: This Athenian deliberative oration by Demosthenes urges the assembly to restore the exiled democracy of Rhodes, whose government had been overthrown by oligarchs acting with the support of Mausolus of Caria. The speech opens by defending the right of every counsellor to speak freely on matters of great consequence, then reviews the recent war provoked by Chios, Byzantium, and Rhodes. He recalls the precedent of Timotheus' aid to Ariobarzanes and the liberation of Samos, while noting that the King's success in Egypt would leave Artemisia free to secure Rhodes for herself. The closing sections broaden into a defence of democracy at large, presenting oligarchic revolution as the common enemy of all who value freedom. The oration calls on Athens, as protector of Greek liberty, to act worthily of her ancestors.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_navy: This deliberative speech, preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes, urges the Athenian assembly to prepare its navy against the Persian king. Its date remains uncertain, though the text opens by criticizing speakers who offer empty praise of Athens' ancestors. The orator argues against immediate war, noting that the Greeks are divided and Athens would bear the brunt of the conflict. Instead, he proposes making the city's power visibly ready through specific naval and financial measures. He suggests enrolling two thousand men in symmories and assigning three hundred triremes to them by lot. Ship sheds should be redistributed by tribe and trittys, while monetary contributions are deferred until danger becomes manifest. The speech concludes by urging Athens to let its deeds, rather than words spoken at the bema, prove worthy of its ancestors.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_peace: This Athenian deliberative oration by Demosthenes addresses the assembly during a tense period following a peace with Philip of Macedon. The speaker begins by confessing the difficulty of advising on present affairs and censuring the Athenians for acting only after events have gone against them. He then defends his past counsel, recalling his opposition to the Euboean expedition in aid of Plutarchus and his denunciation of Neoptolemus. The speech reviews the promises made when the oaths of peace were sworn and the circumstances of the Phocian surrender. The greater part argues that Athens should preserve the existing peace and judge each question on its merits. It warns against being drawn into a common war under Amphictyonic auspices over Delphi and Phocis, urging a weighing of quiet security against the perils of quarrelling over Oropus, Amphipolis, and the islands.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_trierarchic_crown: A short Greek oration attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes, the Trierarchic Crown belongs to the corpus of classical Attic oratory. Addressed to the council, the speaker pleads for a crown in recognition of his service as a trierarch. He contrasts his own expenditure in fitting out and fully manning a trireme with the conduct of rivals who hired substitutes for the liturgy and failed to equip their ships. Drawing on earlier Athenian practice, including the punishment of trierarchs after a naval defeat, he argues that those who discharge public duties deserve honour. Those who neglect them merit censure rather than reward.
grc.demosthenes.philip: This short Greek letter in the Demosthenes corpus is written in the voice of Philip II of Macedon, addressing the Athenian council and people, though its authorship and date remain uncertain. Philip opens by announcing his intent to state grievances plainly, claiming to have suffered wrongs despite repeated embassies and noting his observance of oaths. The body serves as a catalogue of complaints, citing the ten month imprisonment of the herald Nicias and condemning Athens for tolerating pirates and the Thasians. It further lists raids and enslavements by the general Diopeithes in Thrace, mentioning an embassy sent to the Persian king to incite him against Macedon. Philip also references decrees concerning Teres and Cersobleptes, grants of citizenship to Evagoras of Cyprus and Dionysius of Syracuse, and the disputed status of Halonnesus, which he says he took from the pirate Sostratus. He ends by defending his title to Amphipolis as ancient, basing this claim on conquest and acknowledgments in Athenian letters and treaties, urging that the quarrel be settled by argument and arbitration rather than by arms.
grc.didymus_alexandrinus.mensurae_marmorum_a: This short Greek treatise on the measurement of marble and timber is attributed to Didymus Alexandrinus, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens by distinguishing linear, planar, and solid modes of measurement, and it also sets out the differences among various cubits. The body consists of worked problems computing the solid contents of marble slabs, addressing round, half-round, square, and triangular timbers, along with the diagonals of square pieces. Conversion rules follow among the cubit, the Ptolemaic foot, the Roman foot, palms, and digits, including the ratios of the Ptolemaic and Roman feet to the royal cubit. The work closes with procedures for converting lengths and areas measured in cubits, palms, and digits into plane measurements.
grc.dinarchus.against_aristogiton: This forensic prosecution speech, attributed to Dinarchus, targets Aristogeiton on a charge of taking bribes following a report from the council of the Areopagus. The report arose from the aftermath of the Harpalus affair, and the speaker declares the case astonishing because a notorious wrongdoer now stands judgment. The argument surveys Aristogeiton's record of earlier crimes and imprisonment, while also noting his debts to the state and denunciation by Lycurgus. The text rebuts appeals to spare him for his ancestors' sake, invoking the ancestral expulsion of Arthmius of Zeleia as a precedent. The convictions of Demades and Demosthenes are also cited, treating bri-taking as a betrayal of the city. The speech closes by urging the judges to condemn him to death, serving as both punishment and a cleansing of corruption.
grc.dinarchus.against_demosthenes: This forensic speech by Dinarchus prosecutes Demosthenes before an Athenian jury, concerning money brought into the city by Harpalus. Dinarchus announces that the demagogue has been caught taking gifts from his enemies, arguing that the case now rests with the jurors. The speaker defends the investigation and verdict of the Areopagus council, recounting Demosthenes' alleged misdeeds, including the betrayal of Thebes. He also details his flight after the battle of Chaeronea, highlighting failures on embassies and the sale of favors and citizenships. Dinarchus contrasts Demosthenes with earlier benefactors such as Timotheus and Conon, urging the conviction and death penalty set down in a decree by Demosthenes himself. The speech closes by handing the prosecution to the remaining accusers.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.ad_ammaeum: This short Greek treatise, cast as a letter from Dionysius of Halicarnassus to Ammaeus, sets out to refute the claim that Demosthenes modelled his speeches on Aristotle's rhetorical treatises. It opens with Dionysius reporting a Peripatetic who promised to show that Demosthenes, having learned the art from Aristotle, transferred its precepts into his own orations. Dionysius then reconstructs, from the biographers, the chronology of Demosthenes' public career, which runs from the Against Androtion through the deliberative speeches against Philip. This chronology he sets beside the life of Aristotle as handed down. Calling the philosopher himself as witness, he argues from passages in the rhetorical handbooks, whose examples are drawn from the Olynthiacs, On the Crown, and other speeches. The conclusion drawn is that Demosthenes' forensic and deliberative orations were composed before Aristotle's treatises.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.antiquitates_: The Antiquitates Romanae of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a Greek prose history of Rome running from the city's legendary origins to the war with Pyrrhus. It opens with a methodological preface in which the author defends his choice of subject, arguing that Rome's dominion surpassed in extent and duration the earlier empires of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Macedonians, Athenians and Spartans. The narrative then covers the regal period and the early Republic, with sustained attention to the struggles between patricians and plebeians and to the speeches of statesmen, ambassadors and tribunes that shaped them, including the conflict surrounding Gaius Marcius. The work closes with episodes of the early third century, among them Pyrrhus' campaigns and defeat, the censorship of Fabricius, an embassy to Ptolemy Philadelphus, and the subjugation of the Brettii and other Italian peoples.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_antiquis_o: Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote this Greek critical essay for Ammaeus, titled De Antiquis Oratoribus, which means On the Ancient Orators. The author praises his own age for restoring philosophical rhetoric, arguing that a theatrical Asianic manner had replaced it after Alexander's death. Dionysius attributes this shift to the educating influence of Rome, and the essay surveys that transformation across the Greek cities. It examines six orators whom Dionysius judges the finest, with the older group including Lysias, Isocrates, and Isaeus. The later group features Demosthenes, Hyperides, and Aeschines, and each man's life, character, and style receive detailed attention.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_demosthene: Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote this Greek rhetorical treatise in the first century BC, taking the form of a letter addressed to Ammaeus. The work examines the style of Demosthenes, opening with a taxonomy of literary diction. Dionysius distinguishes the austere style of Thucydides from the plain style of Lysias, while noting the mixed middle style practiced by Isocrates and Plato. Each category is illustrated with lengthy quotations and criticism, supporting the central argument that Demosthenes imitated no single model. Instead, he wove the finest features of all these styles into one flexible manner, comparing passages from Isocrates, Plato, Herodotus, and Demosthenes. These comparisons demonstrate his superiority in the grander genres, concluding with an analysis of Demosthenic word arrangement, melody, rhythm, variation of periodic form, and delivery, while answering the hostile criticisms of Aeschines point by point.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_dinarcho: This short Greek treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus assesses the orator Dinarchus, whom the author previously skipped in his studies of ancient orators. He now finds the man worthy of a separate account, recounting Dinarchus's Corinthian origins and his move to Athens. There, he associated with Theophrastus and Demetrius of Phalerum, and wrote speeches for fifteen years after Alexander's death. He later fled to Chalcis under Cassander's oligarchy, and in old age, he sued Proxenus over entrusted money. Dionysius characterizes the style as imitative rather than original, resembling the work of Lysias, Hyperides, and Demosthenes. The author establishes dates using a list of Athenian archons, and the work ends with catalogues of speeches attributed to Dinarchus. These include genuine public speeches, spurious ones, and private ones, each cited by its opening words. The text gives grounds for accepting or rejecting each attribution.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_lysia: This Greek critical essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus examines the style of the Attic orator Lysias, opening with a life that notes his Syracusan parentage and birth at Athens. The text records his sojourn in Thurii and his return to Athens as a prolific writer of courtroom, deliberative, and display speeches. The main body takes up his stylistic virtues in turn, beginning with purity of Attic diction, plain words, clarity, and brevity. The analysis continues with vividness, characterisation, and propriety, before addressing persuasiveness, while pervasive charm is treated as the surest test of genuine Lysian authorship. The essay also covers his powers of invention and arrangement, assessing his standing in the judicial, deliberative, and epideictic kinds of oratory. Extended excerpts illustrate the argument, including the speech against Diogeiton, the Olympic oration urging the Greeks against Dionysius of Syracuse, and a deliberation on preserving the ancestral constitution. Speeches on Lysias's name, such as those for Nicias and Iphicrates, are questioned, and the essay closes by announcing Isocrates as the next orator in chronological order.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydide: Dionysius of Halicarnassus addresses this critical essay to Quintus Aelius Tubero, explaining that he now offers a fuller study of Thucydides at his correspondent's request. The work surveys earlier historians to show how Thucydides set himself apart, praising the justice and restraint of the factual narrative. He then faults the composition, including the division by seasons and uneven treatment of battles, while also critiquing the style for its archaic vocabulary and dense diction. Dionysius illustrates these points with the Corcyrean stasis and several key speeches, closing by rejecting the defense of Thucydides' obscurity. The essay commends the parts that stay within ordinary usage, crediting Demosthenes alone with successfully imitating this manner.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.epistula_ad_p: This Greek letter from Dionysius of Halicarnassus is addressed to Pompey, who is called Geminus in the text. It opens by answering a complaint that Dionysius had accused Plato while weighing Demosthenes against Isocrates and Plato. The author then defends comparison as the surest method of critical testing, noting that many before him, including Aristotle, had censured Plato. Dionysius examines Plato's style at length, praising his plain and precise manner while finding the ornate, figurative, and dithyrambic vein defective, using examples from the Phaedrus. The letter closes with critical estimates of Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Philistus, and Theopompus, and it also references the author's memoranda on imitation addressed to Demetrius.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.libri_secundi: These Greek fragments preserve parts of the second book of Dionysius of Halicarnassus's treatise On the Ancient Orators. The text survives as a short series of scholia and critical notices. It opens with a note on a metaphor in Demosthenes that is more tragic than the political phrasing in the speech On the Embassy. Other fragments address the prooemium of that speech, calling it epilogic and unduly ornate. They also praise a colon borrowed from Euripides for its sound judgement. Finally, the text censures Aeschines for his use of specific phrases regarding bodies and virtue.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnassus.de_compositio: This short Greek rhetorical treatise on the arrangement of words is transmitted in epitomized form under the name of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. The work opens as a birthday gift from the writer to a young friend named Rufus Melitius. It is offered as equipment for every profitable use of language, defining synthesis as the fitting placement of words into clauses and periods. The author ranks this skill above the mere choice of words as the source of charm, persuasion, and power in style. He examines the sounds of letters and syllables, along with the rhythms and metres that run through even unmetrical prose. The text also considers the imitation of nature's sounds, distinguishing three styles of harmony: the austere, the polished, and the well-blended. Each style is illustrated with extended quotations from Homer, Pindar, Thucydides, Sappho, and Isocrates. The discussion covers the propriety of arrangement suited to subject and feeling, addressing how prose can carry hidden measures and verse can loosen its metre toward the freedom of prose.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.de_imitatione_: The surviving fragments of Dionysius of Halicarnassus' treatise On Imitation set out how a writer should study and emulate earlier Greek authors. It opens with definitions of rhetoric, of imitation and of emulation, and a plea for close reading of the ancients, illustrated by the story of the plain wife made beautiful by gazing at portraits and by Zeuxis painting his Helen from the finest features of the maidens of Croton. The body of the work reviews the qualities to be drawn from individual models, characterising Hesiod, Pindar, Simonides, Stesichorus and Alcaeus among the poets, Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides among the tragedians, Herodotus, Thucydides, Philistus, Xenophon and Theopompus among the historians, Plato and Aristotle among the philosophers, and Lysias, Isocrates, Lycurgus, Demosthenes, Aeschines and Hyperides among the orators. Short closing pieces contrast Gorgias' poetic manner with Lysias' plainness and argue that the apparent artlessness of Lysias' style is itself highly wrought.
grc.epictetus.gnomologium_epicteteum_e_stoba: This collection gathers Greek moral maxims attributed to Epictetus from the anthology of Stobaeus, opening with a saying that compares a life entangled with fortune to a turbulent winter torrent. In contrast, the soul that keeps company with virtue is likened to an ever-flowing spring, while the remaining sayings are mostly brief aphorisms built on similes. They treat the opposition of virtue to fortune, wealth, and luxury, and also address moderation in food, drink, and conviviality. The text explores true freedom of the soul against bodily slavery, considering household order and friendship as against flatterers. The duty of just judgment is also examined, and the conduct of the citizen and statesman concludes the work. It ends with the image of a man who benefits his city as unprompted as the rising sun.
grc.epicurus.ratae_sententiae: The Ratae Sententiae, or Principal Doctrines, is a short Greek collection of forty numbered maxims that sets out the central ethical teachings of Epicurus. Diogenes Laertius transmitted these sayings in his life of the philosopher, and they address the blessed and untroubled nature of the gods. The maxims also treat death as nothing to us and the measure of pleasure and pain, while discussing the need to study nature to dispel fear. They classify desires as natural, necessary, or vain, and finally examine the role of friendship and justice in the secure life. Some of the sayings are accompanied by brief explanatory glosses in parentheses.
grc.euripides.heracles: Euripides' tragedy Heracles opens in Thebes, where the hero's wife Megara, their children, and his aged father Amphitryon shelter at an altar of Zeus. The usurper Lycus, who has killed the ruling house of Creon, prepares to put them to death. Heracles, away in the underworld fetching Cerberus, returns in time to slay Lycus and rescue his household. Madness sent by Hera then drives him to murder his own wife and children. On waking, bound to a pillar, he confronts the deed in a long scene of grief and despair. Theseus arrives, argues him out of suicide, and leads him to Athens for purification, leaving the destroyed family to lament their fate in Thebes.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_aulis: This Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizes the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, opening with Agamemnon recounting the oath binding Helen's suitors to an old retainer. He also describes the muster of the Greek armament and Calchas' oracle, which demands the death of his daughter in exchange for sailing. Menelaus intercepts Agamemnon's letter countermanding the summons to his wife, and Clytemnestra arrives with Iphigenia and the infant Orestes under the pretense of marriage to Achilles. The hero discovers the misuse of his name and rages at the deception, then resolves to defend the girl against an army clamoring for the sacrifice. Iphigenia ultimately chooses to die freely for the sake of Greece, and a messenger reports that Artemis substituted a deer and carried the maiden away. This act releases the fleet for Troy as Agamemnon sends Clytemnestra home.
grc.eusebius_caesarea.historia_ecclesiastica: This Greek church history in ten books is attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea, and it narrates the story of the Christian church from the incarnation and apostolic age down to Constantine's victory over Licinius. Book 1 opens with a chapter by chapter outline of its contents, then arguing from prophecy for the pre-existence, incarnation, and ancient roots of the Christian name. The text turns next to Herod, the census of Quirinius, John the Baptist, and Jesus, while later books trace the succession of bishops in Jerusalem, Rome, Alexandria, and other sees. They also cover the careers of figures such as Clement, Origen, and Dionysius, and the narrative addresses arguments with heresies including Marcion and Montanus. It details the series of persecutions under Roman emperors, and the work ends with the conversion of Constantine, the Edict of Milan, and the rebuilding of churches.
grc.flavius_josephus.contra_apionem: Contra Apionem, a two book apologetic treatise written in Greek by Flavius Josephus, is addressed to Epaphroditus and responds to those who slander the Jewish people. Josephus notes that his Antiquities has already established the antiquity of the Jews, and he now writes briefly against critics who distrust his account because Greek historians record nothing of them. The first book defends the careful transmission of Jewish records and outlines the twenty two books of the Hebrew scriptures, citing Egyptian, Phoenician, Chaldean, and Greek writers as witnesses to early Jewish history. The author then refutes the hostile Egyptian narratives of Manetho, Chaeremon, and Lysimachus, while the second book answers the specific accusations of Apion and Apollonius Molon. It closes with a summary of the Mosaic constitution, its theocratic government, priesthood, and laws, arguing that this law has remained unaltered and has spread among many peoples.
grc.flavius_josephus.de_bello_judaico_libri_: The Bellum Judaicum is a seven book history by Flavius Josephus, who introduces himself as Josephus son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem. He first fought against the Romans and later accompanied them, recounting the great war between the Jews and the Romans. The work covers the turmoil after Nero through the revolt and Roman campaigns, ending with the siege and destruction of Jerusalem under Titus. Josephus presents the text as a Greek rendering of an earlier account composed in his ancestral language for peoples beyond the Euphrates. He defends the accuracy of his history against critics, accusing them of flattering the Romans or slandering the Jews. The narrative stresses the role of internal tyrants and factions in the city's fall, joining the historian's account of events to the author's lament for his homeland.
grc.galen.ad_glauconem_de_methodo_medendi: This Greek medical treatise by Galen, addressed to a friend named Glaucon, frames its advice as a general method for treating diseases. The work opens by defending the need for physicians to know each individual patient's constitution, outlining a dialectical method for dividing diseases into genera and species. Galen praises Hippocrates, Mnesitheus, and Plato for their use of such division, then proceeds systematically through various types of fevers. It covers simple ephemeral fevers arising from fatigue, insomnia, grief, and anger, detailing their signs in pulse, urine, and complexion. The author also examines periodic fevers such as tertian, quartan, quotidian, and continuous forms, discussing the diagnosis and dietary treatment of these conditions. The treatise turns next to fevers accompanied by symptoms like vomiting, syncope, and hemorrhage, discussing when evacuation of blood or humors is safe. It closes with accounts of local diseases and swellings, including inflammations, erysipelas, herpes, and scirrhus, as well as oedema, abscesses, fistulae, and gangrene. The author gives methods of treatment by purging, venesection, plasters, and surgery, ending with a promise of a fuller work on the powers of drugs.
grc.galen.an_in_arteriis_sanguis_contineatur: This short Greek treatise by Galen argues that arteries naturally contain blood, written against Erasistratus and his followers who held that these vessels carry only pneuma. Galen opens with a syllogistic proof that blood must already be present in the vessels, then answers the objection that subtle pneuma could pass out unobserved. The argument supports his case with appeals to the visible behaviour of exposed arteries, and it also relies on anatomical observations of the mesenteric vessels. A demonstration with a cannula and ligature shows that the pulse ceases beyond the ligature, proving that arterial dilatation stems from a power of the heart rather than from transmitted pneuma. Along the way, Galen defends the use of logical method in medicine, and he also criticizes the reasoning of both Skeptics and Dogmatists. The work closes with the anatomical demonstration of the ligated artery.
grc.galen.de_anatomicis_administrationibus: This Greek anatomical manual was written by the physician Galen during the reign of the emperor Antoninus. The opening section explains that Galen rewrote his anatomical books after the originals were lost in Rome. He undertook this task at the specific request of the consul Flavius Boethus. The text then proceeds as a sustained practical instruction in the art of dissection. It leads the dissector from the skeleton, studied on human bones or apes, through muscles, vessels, and nerves. The guide continues to the viscera of the chest and abdomen, including the peritoneum and organs of nutrition. Later parts describe procedures on living animals, such as exposing the beating heart and sectioning nerves. These experiments also involve dissecting the brain's coverings, ventricles, and contained vessels.
grc.galen.de_antidotis: Galen's De Antidotis is a Greek pharmacological treatise on antidotes, which are drugs physicians administer internally to counteract poisons and venomous bites. The work opens with a definition of the antidote, then accounts for two famous compound preparations, the Mithridatium of Mithridates of Pontus and the theriac of Andromachus, Nero's archiater. The greater part of the text gives detailed instructions for compounding the theriac, covering the selection and testing of ingredients such as vipers' flesh, squill, and opium. Warnings about adulteration and notes on the regions that yield the best simples are included, while recipes in prose and verse are drawn from Andromachus, Damocrates, and Criton. Closing sections assemble further antidotes ascribed to named physicians and rulers, including the Mithridatium itself and remedies for the bites of vipers, scorpions, and mad dogs.
grc.galen.de_causis_morborum: Galen's treatise on the causes of disease opens by recalling an earlier work that classified ailments by species and genus. It announces that the causes of each disease will now be examined, beginning with the simple parts of the body. The discussion first takes up the causes of diseases of immoderate heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. It lists sources such as excessive exercise, putrefaction, and exposure to sun or cold. The text explains how fevers, apoplexies, and comas arise from these conditions. It then treats compound diseases and the affections of organic parts, covering faulty conformation from conditions in the womb. It also addresses the careless rearing of infants, corruption of cavities, and abnormalities of position. The work ends with the common genus of dissolution of continuity, including fractures, wounds, and contusions. It anticipates a following account of the differences of symptoms.
grc.galen.de_constitutione_artis_medicae_ad_: Galen writes to Patrophilus, whose eagerness to learn the healing art he serves by setting down memoranda. This second of two works shows how the single method that founds every productive art also constitutes medicine. The text first classifies the arts as theoretical, practical, productive, and acquisitive, then establishes medicine as a productive art of the corrective kind. This discipline repairs the body as a builder mends a damaged house rather than creating something new. The argument requires knowledge of the body's parts in their substance, size, shape, and number, and it also demands understanding of their activities and uses. The discussion passes from anatomy through the four elements and the mixtures that yield health and disease, then moves to the therapeutic method, whose general aim is that contraries cure contraries. Worked diagnoses such as pleurisy illustrate this approach, and an account of prognosis describes it as a weighing of disease against nature. Brief sketches of the preventive and recuperative branches of hygiene complete the demonstration, showing that medicine, like the other productive arts, is built from the concept of its end.
grc.galen.de_consuetudinibus: This short Greek medical treatise by Galen defends habit as a legitimate therapeutic indication, opening by answering detractors of this doctrine. It appeals to Hippocrates on acute diet and to Erasistratus on paralysis, while recounting the death of Aristotle of Mytilene, who refused a cold drink. The bulk of the text seeks the cause of habit's power, arguing that repeated use of foods and drinks produces a qualitative alteration in the body. This reasoning extends to external agents such as heat, cold, and sun, and also covers gymnastic training of body and mind, citing Plato's Timaeus. The closing section discusses habitual evacuations, nosebleeds, and haemorrhoids, explaining these not from habit itself but from the causes of the original evacuations.
grc.galen.de_crisibus: Galen's Greek treatise On Crises addresses the diagnosis and prognostication of turning points in disease, declining to fix a single definition of crisis. Instead, he undertakes to teach how such events may be discerned, moving the argument through the four periods of illness from beginning to decline. The text examines signs of concoction shown in urine, sputum, and bowel evacuations, while also discriminating fever types and predicting the timing of a crisis. Galen sustains quotation and exegesis of Hippocratic passages from the Aphorisms, Prognostic, and Epidemics, attacking later physicians such as Thessalus who neglect these doctrines.
grc.galen.de_curandi_ratione_per_venae_secti: This Greek medical treatise by Galen is concerned with treatment by venesection, or bloodletting, and is directed in part against physicians of the Erasistratean school who rejected the practice. It opens by asking what a physician must settle before bleeding anyone: which conditions require evacuation, which call for venesection in particular, and which patients can bear the loss of blood. Galen then considers the choice of vein and incision point, the quantity of blood to be drawn, and its timing by season, age and bodily strength. He also distinguishes evacuant from revulsive uses of bleeding, illustrating the argument with case histories from his practice at Rome. A closing section extends the discussion to arteriotomy and reports operations performed at Pergamum and elsewhere, some undertaken on the strength of dreams. Throughout, Galen invokes Hippocratic authority and attacks the doctrines of Erasistratus and his followers, among them Chrysippus of Cnidus.
grc.galen.de_diebus_decretoriis: De diebus decretoriis, meaning On Critical Days, is a Greek medical treatise by Galen that examines the days on which crises in disease occur and how far they can be trusted. The opening argues that a sudden resolution of illness counts as a genuine crisis only when accompanied by visible evacuations, such as sweats, abundant urine, haemorrhages, or discharges. Convalescents must accordingly be kept under strict regimen, and crises are then classified as complete or incomplete, trustworthy or unreliable, dangerous, clear, obscure, or plainly foreshadowed. The seventh day is presented as the most reliable crisis day, while those on the sixth, twelfth, and sixteenth are rare, incomplete, or generally unfavourable. In support of this scheme, the treatise appeals to Hippocrates and to the accumulated experience of earlier physicians, including Archigenes, Heracleides of Tarentum, Philotimus, and Diocles.
grc.galen.de_difficultate_respirationis: This Greek treatise by Galen addresses the condition of difficult breathing, arguing that dyspnoea is a disturbance affecting respiration. It parallels the way such disturbances impact sensation and movement, while Galen examines the natural components of breathing. He considers the pauses that occur between inspiration and expiration, classifying forms of dyspnoea as either simple or compound. These conditions arise in the speed, size, or spacing of the breath, and the author criticizes newer physicians. He notes that Hippocrates and older medical writers used different terms for these defects, departing from customary names.
grc.galen.de_elementis_ex_hippocrate: This Greek treatise, attributed to Galen in the second century AD, examines the elements of bodies according to Hippocrates, who is claimed to have first established this doctrine correctly. It argues that the hot, cold, dry, and wet are the fundamental constituents of all things, distinguishing elements as they appear to the senses from those in nature. The author uses the experience of pain to show that man cannot be composed of a single principle, while refuting rival theories, including those of the atomists and monists. The text also critiques physicians like Athenaeus of Attalia and Asclepiades for placing elements too near to sense, before a second book discusses the four humours, which are blood, phlegm, and the two biles. These are presented as the elements proper to animals with blood, covering embryonic formation, the varieties of blood, and the selective attraction of drugs. It concludes by grounding nutrition and evacuation in a faculty that draws like to like.
grc.galen.de_foetuum_formatione: Galen's brief Greek treatise, On the Formation of the Foetus, examines embryonic development by criticizing philosophers who lacked anatomical evidence, contrasting them with Hippocrates. Galen quotes Hippocrates' observational account of a six-day embryo at length, while the body describes the membranes and vessels surrounding the foetus. These include the chorion, amnion, allantois, and umbilical veins and arteries, which he argues form first from the seed, drawing the mother's blood like plant roots. The liver and heart follow, with the brain and sense organs appearing last, against Stoic and Peripatetic doctrines, Galen distinguishes the principles of generation from those of governance. The work closes by asking about the forming cause, an artisan of supreme skill, whom he confesses himself unable to determine.
grc.galen.de_hirudinibus_revulsione_cucurbit: This brief Greek treatise by Galen outlines four therapeutic procedures. It begins with practical directions for catching and applying leeches to draw blood. The text also details the care of the bitten area and how to stop bleeding. Revulsion is described next as a method to divert violent flows of humours. The cupping-glass is then discussed regarding its use in inflammatory conditions. Finally, incision and scarification are presented as lighter alternatives to frequent venesection.
grc.galen.de_inaequali_intemperie: De Inaequali Intemperie ('On Uneven Imbalance') is a short Greek treatise by Galen that examines anomalous dyscrasia, an imbalance of bodily qualities that afflicts one part differently from another. The opening chapters distinguish such irregular imbalances from uniform ones, illustrating these conditions with erysipelas, phagedaena, herpes, and elephantiasis. The text then surveys the body's structures from the largest visible parts down to the homogeneous tissues. The remainder follows a hot flux invading a muscle to explain how inflammation and pain arise. It describes recovery through dispersion or concoction into pus, noting which cavities offer safer sites for suppuration. Hippocratic sayings on pain arising during alteration of nature are invoked along the way.
grc.galen.de_instrumento_odoratus: The De Instrumento Odoratus is a Greek treatise by Galen that examines the anatomy and physiology of the organ of smell. It begins by distinguishing the perception of odours from the faculty that effects it, and Galen then asks whether the nose itself can be that organ. He traces the nasal passages, the ethmoid bone, and related membranes, which connect the mouth, pharynx, and brain. Using anatomical observation and experiments with odorous substances, he argues for a deeper seat of olfaction in the anterior cavities of the brain. Galen also rejects a hypothesis reported from Aristotle, which held that breathing uncovers special odour-bearing pores. Instead, he maintains that odours are perceived only during inhalation.
grc.galen.de_locis_affectis: Galen's De Locis Affectis ('On the Affected Locations') is a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date within his oeuvre that opens by explaining why physicians distinguish the precise bodily parts, topoi, affected by disease, since treatment varies according to those differences. The work then develops a systematic method for diagnosing hidden rather than visibly apparent diseased locations, drawing on anatomical knowledge of each organ's substance, position, and function, and proceeds organ by organ through the head and brain, nerves, spinal marrow, lungs and chest, heart, liver, spleen, stomach, intestines, kidneys, bladder, uterus, and external genitalia, illustrating each discussion with case histories from Galen's own practice and with critiques of predecessors such as Archigenes, Erasistratus, and Asclepiades.
grc.galen.de_marcore: De Marcore ('On Marasmus') is a brief Greek medical treatise by Galen that defines marasmus as the destruction of a living body through dryness. A simple form arises from starvation, while compound forms are accompanied by excessive heat or cold, as in certain fevers and in old age. The treatise opens with a digression recalling a philosopher who promised to rear infants immune to aging, an anecdote illustrating how plausible but unproved arguments persuade. Galen then investigates the cause of aging and rejects the doctrine that innate heat consumes the body as a flame consumes its fuel. He also engages with a Hippocratic saying on the killing power of the heat that shaped the body.
grc.galen.de_morborum_differentiis: Galen composed this Greek medical treatise, transmitted under the Latin title De Morborum Differentiis, which sets out a systematic classification of diseases for the reader. It opens by defining disease as an affection contrary to nature that impairs bodily function, distinguishing it from both symptom and cause. The text argues that health is a due symmetry of the body's elements, while disease is described as the asymmetry of those same elements. The argument then enumerates the primary simple diseases of the homoiomerous parts, which are first presented as excess and defect of porosity. This view relies on the hypothesis of passive elements, and the author then considers the four dyscrasias of hot, cold, wet and dry. These arise on the hypothesis of active qualities, and the discussion passes to the diseases of the organic parts. These arise from defects of shape, number, size, composition or continuity, with examples ranging from inflammations, ulcers, tumours and abnormal growths to fractures, dislocations and amputations. The treatise ends by showing how compound diseases of whole organs are built up, and these complex conditions are constructed out of the simple affections described earlier. The text also separates what is disease proper from what is merely its cause or symptom.
grc.galen.de_motu_musculorum: This Greek medical treatise by Galen examines the movement of muscles, identifying them as the organs of voluntary motion. The text surveys their great number and varied shapes, while also detailing their points of attachment to bone. Galen distinguishes tendons, ligaments, and nerves in the process, describing the tendon as a mixed nature between ligament and nerve. The work traces powers of motion and sensation from the brain, which travel through nerves into the muscle body. The muscle is also nourished by artery and vein, and the author sets voluntary movements apart from natural ones. He contrasts these with the movements of arteries and veins, closing with a physiological account of the tendon that explains how it binds muscle to bone, allowing the muscle to draw in movement.
grc.galen.de_nervorum_dissectione: This short Greek treatise by Galen examines the dissection of the nerves, noting that all physicians agree nerves are the sole source of voluntary motion and sensation. The author states that these structures originate in the brain and spinal cord, and the main body proceeds pair by pair through the cranial nerves, numbered after Marinus. It then traces the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral pairs from their bony exits, mapping their distribution among muscles, sense organs, and viscera. Galen repeatedly points out where earlier anatomists went astray, and the work closes with a compressed summary for beginners. Exact detail is referred to Galen's fuller anatomical procedures.
grc.galen.de_parvae_pilae_exercitio: Galen's short Greek treatise On Exercise with the Small Ball argues that this activity surpasses all other forms of gymnastics for health. Addressed to Epigenes, the opening concedes that earlier philosophers and physicians have said enough about gymnastics in general. It observes, however, that ball exercise in particular has never been adequately explained. The text praises the exercise for its accessibility, since it requires only a small ball rather than the wealth and leisure demanded by hunting. It also trains every part of the body evenly while sharpening the mind through the attention needed to catch and throw. The treatise discusses how the exercise can be intensified or softened to suit the old, the young, and the convalescent. It likens the quick seizure and guarded retention of the ball to a general's skills. The conclusion weighs these advantages against the dangers of other pursuits, which injure runners, riders, and wrestlers. Ball exercise, properly practised in moderation, brings benefit without hazard to body and soul alike.
grc.galen.de_placitis_hippocratis_et_platoni: De Placitis Hippocratis et Platonis ('On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato') is a treatise by the physician Galen. It argues that Hippocratic medicine aligns with Platonic teaching on the soul. The text opens in the midst of an extended anatomical argument. Galen appeals to dissection and vivisection to show that the left ventricle holds blood. He also demonstrates that psychic pneuma resides in the ventricles of the brain. The author presses this case against Chrysippus, Erasistratus, and Aristotle. These thinkers are charged with placing the ruling part of the soul in the heart.
grc.galen.de_plenitudine: Galen writes this Greek treatise on fullness, or plethos, which examines the excess of fluids in the body and its vessels. The text opens by surveying and ridiculing the definitions of quantity offered by contemporary physicians, some of whom measure it against the capacity of the containing vessels, while others rely on the dynamic power of the body. The discussion then distinguishes these two senses and criticises Erasistratus' account of how plethora arises and is diagnosed, and it also attacks the Stoic and Herophilean doctrines of the cohesive cause. The author dissects the cluster of symptoms by which the empiric doctors justified phlebotomy, including bodily weight, tension, swelling and redness of the veins, sluggishness, a sedentary life and suppressed evacuations. The closing sections set out how the several kinds of humoral excess are recognised, identified through colour, pulse, sleep, appetite and previous regimen, and contributory factors such as season, region and the density of the patient's body are also considered.
grc.galen.de_praenotione_ad_epigenem: This Greek medical treatise by Galen is concerned with prognosis and is addressed to Epigenes. It opens with a denunciation of physicians who pursue favour through flattery, display, and attendance on the wealthy, and who persecute those claiming foreknowledge of the course of disease. The main part is a narrative account of the quartan fever of Eudemus, a Peripatetic philosopher whom Galen attended in Rome. Galen records his pulse-based predictions of the fever's critical days and his disagreements with rival physicians over treatment, notably their administration of theriac. The account also refers to anatomical demonstrations on voice and respiration given before distinguished Romans, among them men of consular rank.
grc.galen.de_praesagitione_ex_pulsibus: Galen's Greek treatise De Praesagitione ex Pulsibus ('On Prognosis from the Pulse') teaches how to draw prognostic signs from the pulse. It defines prognosis to cover present and past conditions as well as things to come. The discussion centers on the pulse conventionally called 'great.' It examines how changes in size, speed, and density arise from causes such as bodily constitution, thinness, exercise, and bathing. The text also treats the examination of patients who conceal their condition. It includes an anecdote in which Galen detects that a wealthy man has secretly taken medicine despite his denials. The argument presupposes Galen's earlier treatises on the diagnosis, differences, and causes of pulses.
grc.galen.de_propriorum_animi_cuiuslibet_aff: This short Greek ethical treatise by Galen serves as a reply to an interlocutor who sought a summary of a book Galen wrote for Antonius the Epicurean. That earlier work focused on watchfulness over one's own passions, and the text distinguishes errors, which arise from false opinion, from the passions. It argues that self-love blinds everyone to his own failings, following the fable of Aesop's two sacks and sayings of Plato. It prescribes entrusting self-knowledge to an impartial observer who should be neither loved nor hated and will report one's faults. The author also counsels patience under criticism, and practical directions follow for testing such a companion's honesty. They also cover treating able critics as paedagogues, in Zeno's phrase.
grc.galen.de_ptisana: Galen wrote this short Greek treatise on the preparation and medical use of ptisan, which refers to a barley gruel and its juice. He notes that physicians often serve the drink without defining its limits, so he sets out its proper boiling, powers, and administration. He discusses choosing pure water and sound barley that is neither too new nor too old, while detailing the correct cooking method. The text describes the properties of the well-boiled ptisan, whose smoothness, moistness, and power to cleanse and nourish make it suited to acute fevers. The work closes with qualifications on when and how much to give the drink, explaining how dosage should be graduated from the juice alone to the whole ptisan.
grc.galen.de_pulsibus_ad_tirones: Galen addresses Teuthras in this short Greek treatise on the pulse, promising to outline what beginners need to know while leaving the fuller art for other works. The text explains which arteries are palpable and why the wrist is the most convenient site, then details elementary differences in size, speed, force, and the texture of the arterial coat. The author also covers regularity, periodic order, and compound deviations such as the worm-like and ant-like pulses, while a second part lists factors that alter the pulse in health, including sex, temperament, age, and season. It also notes the effects of climate, pregnancy, sleep, exercise, bathing, food, wine, and water, before the final and longest section treats pathological changes in the pulse. It gives the characteristic signs of emotions, pain, inflammation, and a long list of diseases, which range from pleurisy and empyema to phrenitis, lethargy, tetanus, paralysis, dropsy, and jaundice. The work closes with a discussion of the effects of hellebore.
grc.galen.de_purgantium_medicamentorum_facul: Galen wrote this Greek medical treatise on the action of purgative drugs, which translates as On the Faculties of Purging Medicines. He argues that cathartics possess an attractive power proper to each humour, a force that draws out that specific humour alone from the veins. Galen directs the argument against Erasistratus, who allowed no such faculty, and also challenges the followers of Asclepiades, who held that purgatives transform all humours indiscriminately. The treatise invokes Hippocratic authority for the doctrine of attraction, repeatedly challenging opponents to public demonstrations on patients with jaundice and dropsy. The goal is to decide matters by deeds rather than long speeches.
grc.galen.de_sanitate_tuenda: Galen's Greek treatise De Sanitate Tuenda ('On the Preservation of Health') outlines the hygienic aspect of medicine, arguing that preserving health must precede the treatment of disease. The author defines health as a due proportion of elementary qualities in the body's parts, while surveying innate harms from conception, such as the progressive drying of old age. External factors also threaten the body's integrity, and the text examines how food, drink, respiration, and the pulse replenish lost substance. Digestion transforms nutriment into matter resembling the body, and the formation and evacuation of residues keep the body free of corruption.
grc.galen.de_sectis_ad_eos_qui_introducuntur: Galen's short Greek treatise De Sectis ('On the Sects') introduces newcomers to the principal schools of ancient medicine and to the disputes among them. It opens by defining medicine as knowledge of the healthy and the diseased, and by naming its two earliest sects, the Empiric and the Logical or Dogmatic. The Empiricists, it explains, derive their remedies from accumulated experience, while the Dogmatists proceed by reasoning or 'indication' from hidden causes, ages, seasons, and bodily conditions. Each school accuses the other of inadequacy over anatomy, dialectic, and demonstration. A final section presents the Methodist school, with its 'commonalities' of constriction and flux, its dismissal of causal inquiry, and its boast of teaching the whole art in six months. The treatise closes with a dogmatic speaker's rebuttal, addressed to the beginners for whom the work is written.
grc.galen.de_sophismatis_seu_captionibus_pen: Galen wrote this short Greek treatise on fallacies arising from wording, which is preserved under the Latin title De Sophismatis seu Captionibus penes dictionem. The work sets out Aristotle's six modes of verbal sophism, including homonymy, amphiboly, accent, and combination. Galen also covers division and figure of speech, judging Aristotle's supporting argument entirely obscure. The explanations of earlier interpreters are likewise unsuccessful, so Galen argues that diction has a single virtue, clear signification. Its single vice is ambiguity, meaning every fallacy dependent on language ultimately arises from a word's double meaning.
grc.galen.de_substantia_facultatum_naturaliu: This Greek fragment by the second-century CE physician Galen addresses a specific philosophical problem. It defends Plato against charges of inconsistency regarding the nature of animals and plants. The text reconciles ordinary statements with the doctrine of the Timaeus. Galen then distinguishes natural faculties from psychic powers. He argues that bodies arise from a thorough mixture of the four elements. Questions about the soul's substance and immortality need not be settled by the physician.
grc.galen.de_symptomatum_differentiis: Galen's De symptomatum differentiis, meaning On the Differences of Symptoms, is a Greek medical treatise that follows a separate treatment of diseases and their causes to complete the account of abnormal bodily conditions. The work opens by defining the symptom and distinguishing it from disease, cause, and related terms, while defending these precise usages against less exact medical vocabulary. The body divides symptoms into three genera: abnormal dispositions, impairments of activities, and phenomena attending excretions, with impairments traced through psychic and natural faculties, including sensation, movement, and reasoning. Examples range from blindness and pain to indigestion, atrophy, and disordered discharges, showing that symptoms arise from diseases as their causes. They often follow one another in sequence, like a row of tiles set in motion.
grc.galen.de_temperamentis: This Greek medical treatise by Galen examines temperatures, or the mixtures of elementary qualities in bodies, opening by showing that bodies are composed of hot, cold, dry, and wet qualities. The text then surveys earlier doctrines that recognize only four or five such mixtures, while Galen argues that the best-tempered constitution must be counted first among nine kinds. He discusses how mixtures are diagnosed by touch and reason, noting the balance found in the skin of the hand, and covers variations of temperament with age, season, and race. Later books treat the qualities of foods and drugs, distinguishing what nourishes from what alters the body, and explain why some substances act hot or cold only in potentiality. The text closes by summarizing how things potentially hot, cold, dry, or wet are to be tested and judged.
grc.galen.de_theriaca_ad_pisonem: Galen addresses a friend named Piso in this Greek prose treatise on the theriac, a compound antidote against venomous bites and poisons. The opening praises Andromachus, a Cretan physician esteemed by the emperors of his time and credited with a treatise on the antidote. It also recounts Galen's observation of Piso tending his own son's injury. Later sections celebrate the drug's reputation and power, explaining how a batch may be tested for adulteration using cockerels and purgatives. The text condemns vendors who trade on its name. The closing portion credits the emperor Marcus with habitual use of the remedy and praises the liberality with which the reigning emperors dispense medicines. It recounts cures such as those of Antipater and of Arrhia.
grc.galen.de_totius_morbi_temporibus: In this short Greek treatise Galen examines the 'times' of a disease as a whole, meaning the phases through which it passes. He distinguishes four phases, analogous to the ages of living creatures: genesis or onset, ascent, acme, and decline. The discussion rehearses disputes among physicians over how these phases are to be defined and whether some diseases lack one or another of them. Galen then applies the scheme to individual conditions such as inflammation, fever, ulcers, and ophthalmia. The stage a disease has reached, he holds, is recognized through signs of defective or completed digestion in the evacuations, urine, and sputum. Hippocratic sayings on the timing of remedies such as venesection, clysters, and purging are cited in the course of the argument about treatment at each phase.
grc.galen.de_tremore_palpitatione_convulsion: Galen wrote this short medical treatise on four abnormal bodily motions, opening by objecting to Praxagoras for classing them indiscriminately as affections of the arteries. The body of the text defines each condition and marks it off from its neighbours, tracing tremor to weakness of the power that moves and carries the body. Palpitation results from the gathering of thick vaporous pneuma in hollow parts such as muscles or skin, while rigor involves a sudden and painful whole-body chilling of the innate heat. Convulsion stems from over-tension of the nerves and muscles caused by excess moisture, dryness, or inflammation, and Galen weighs the views of earlier physicians and philosophers, including Herophilus, Hippocrates, Plato, and Asclepiades. He cites Hippocratic case material and reports observations of his own, closing the treatise with an account of the different treatments the conditions require.
grc.galen.de_tumoribus_praeter_naturam: Galen's short Greek treatise, De Tumoribus Praeter Naturam ('On Tumours Contrary to Nature'), examines the varieties of abnormal swelling. It begins by analyzing the term onkos to distinguish mere increase, such as fatness, from swellings that damage function. The argument follows inflammation in detail, asserting that the swollen part is filled with blood rather than pneuma. It then passes to abscesses, fistulas, and cystic growths like atheromata, steatomata, and melicerides. Later sections cover anthrax, gangrene, cancer, erysipelas, and other conditions including oedema and scirrhus. The work closes with the claim that no kind of abnormal swelling has been left undiscussed.
grc.galen.de_uteri_dissectione: Galen's De Uteri Dissectione is a Greek anatomical treatise that opens with a programme of topics to be treated. These include the uterus's position, size, and shape, as well as its suspension, nourishment, and the vessels that weave it. The discussion proceeds through the organ's placement between the bladder and the rectum, recording earlier descriptions of its horn-like processes by Herophilus, Diocles, and Eudemus. Later sections treat its attachments, ligaments, and nourishing vessels, while the work also examines its two coats and the cervix with its changes over the reproductive cycle. It concludes with the chorion, amnion, and allantois, ending with a promise of a separate account of the embryo's anatomy.
grc.galen.de_utilitate_respirationis: De Utilitate Respirationis, meaning On the Use of Breathing, is a Greek medical-philosophical treatise by Galen that investigates why living creatures breathe and what benefit the process confers. The opening section catalogues the answers of earlier doctors and philosophers, among them Asclepiades, Praxagoras, Philistion, Diocles, Hippocrates, and Erasistratus. The body of the work tests these doctrines against observable phenomena, examining breath-holding, suffocation, and the movements of the heart and arteries. Galen also considers the extinction of flames cut off from air, observing the breathing of people in baths, during exercise, and at different ages. The text refutes Erasistratus' account at length, concluding that the chief use of respiration is the preservation of innate heat. The moderation of this heat is also a primary function, while the nourishment of the psychic pneuma through inspiration is a secondary benefit.
grc.galen.de_venarum_arteriarumque_dissectio: De Venarum Arteriarumque Dissectione is a Greek anatomical treatise by Galen, which opens as a note to his friend Antisthenes. Galen promises a synopsis of the vascular system, likening this network to a tree with roots, a trunk, and branches. The account first follows the portal vein from the liver to the stomach, intestines, and spleen, then traces the hollow vein upward to the heart, neck, and head, and downward to the legs. The text also covers arteries arising from the left cavity of the heart, including the aorta, while Galen distinguishes superficial from deep vessels and records variations among individual specimens. He notes which veins run without accompanying arteries and defers fuller detail to other dissections, closing the survey with the vessels of the unborn animal, specifically the umbilical arteries and vein.
grc.galen.de_victu_attenuante: This short Greek treatise by Galen examines the thinning regimen, a diet designed to attenuate thick and viscous humours. It argues that many chronic illnesses, such as nephritis, arthritis, and epilepsy, can be relieved by this diet alone. The text surveys various foods, including pungent vegetables, seeds, cereals, and fish, to grade their effects on the humours. It also covers roots, tree fruits, and preserved items, closing with an account of honey and specific wines. The author names the Ariousian, Lesbian, Falernian, and Theraean wines, along with milk, in this final section. Throughout, Galen insists that the physician must control both the occasion and the measure of use. He commends oxymel, honey tempered with vinegar, as the drink most suited to this regimen.
grc.galen.institutio_logica: Galen, a physician and philosopher, wrote this Greek introduction to logic, which is transmitted under the title Institutio Logica, or logical instruction. Its date remains uncertain, and the work opens by explaining how things are known through perception, understanding, and demonstration. It then defines propositions, axioms, and syllogisms, proceeding through categorical and hypothetical propositions. The treatise also covers the figures and moods of the syllogism, while Galen discusses proof and relational arguments used in mathematics. He draws on Stoic, Peripatetic, and Aristotelian doctrine, with examples from Plato, Euclid, and medicine appearing throughout. The text closes with criticism of Chrysippean and Peripatetic classifications, and it also rejects forms of syllogism that Galen judges redundant.
grc.galen.quod_optimus_medicus_sit_quoque_ph: This short Greek treatise by Galen argues that the best physician must also be a philosopher, opening by comparing most physicians to athletes who long for Olympic victories yet undertake none of the training needed to win them. The author praises Hippocrates in words while noting that his followers neglect the studies he prescribed, and the discussion then examines why those who extol Hippocrates neither read nor understand his writings. Their failures in logical method, knowledge of the body, and prognosis are ascribed to the love of money and pleasure, and the text sets out what a true physician requires, including contempt for wealth, self-discipline, and tireless effort. It concludes that the logical, physical, and ethical parts of philosophy are all indispensable to medicine, and whoever would practise the art worthily in Hippocrates' manner must philosophise rather than quarrel over names.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ἑλένης_ἐγκώμιον: The Encomium of Helen ('In Praise of Helen') is a short prose defence of Helen of Troy by Gorgias of Leontini. Gorgias undertakes to free Helen from the censure of the poets by showing that she deserves no blame for the voyage to Troy. After an opening meditation on praise and blame as the fitting honours of city, body, soul, and speech, the speaker recounts Helen's parentage and beauty. He then examines four causes of her journey, the designs of gods and fortune, abduction by force, persuasion by speech, and love kindled through sight, acquitting her in each case. The treatment of persuasion presents speech as a great dynast and as a drug upon the soul, illustrated from poetry, incantation, debate, and painting. The speech closes with the declaration that it is both Helen's encomium and its author's plaything.
grc.hermogenes.progymnasmata_dub: This ancient Greek handbook covers the progymnasmata, or preliminary rhetorical exercises, and is attributed to Hermogenes, though its date remains uncertain. The text begins with the myth, arguing that fable shapes young souls toward virtue, and illustrates this point using fables of the nightingale, the fox, and Aesop. The treatise then defines and classifies the standard sequence of exercises, which include narrative, chreia, gnome, and refutation, among other forms. Each definition is paired with a worked specimen to show elaboration, and examples range from monkeys debating a city to Medea betraying the golden fleece.
grc.hermogenes.περὶ_τῶν_στάσεων: This Greek rhetorical treatise, attributed to Hermogenes, examines the stases, or issues, of civic disputes, though its date remains uncertain. It ranks the division of civic questions as the greatest part of rhetoric and defines the civic question. The text distinguishes the persons and things open to examination, then sorts questions that can sustain a dispute. A method follows, moving through the logical stases of conjecture, definition, counterplea, and transference. The work continues with legal stases arising from written instruments, antinomy, ambiguity, and syllogism. It concludes with practical stases concerning the lawful, the just, the expedient, and the possible.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.belopoeica: The Belopoeica, a Greek technical treatise attributed to Hero of Alexandria, details the design and construction of various artillery engines. It opens with a philosophical preface that frames engine-making as a path to peace, while criticizing earlier writers for recording dimensions without explaining how the machines were built. The body distinguishes straight-spring arrow-shooters from palintone stone-throwers, tracing development from the hand bow to torsion machines. The author describes frames, washers, sinew springs, and bases in detail, and assembly, tensioning, and maintenance procedures are also covered. The work closes with rules for scaling engines from the spring-hole diameter, including a geometrical method for finding two mean proportionals.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_automatis: This Greek treatise by the mechanician Hero of Alexandria details the construction of automata in two books, distinguishing between self moving shrines called hypagenda and stationary display boards known as stata. The first book offers practical directions for level ground, light materials, cords, and axles, and it also describes a moving shrine of Dionysus where an altar kindles and dancing Bacchae perform. The second book explains the stationary boards through a tableau of the myth of Nauplius, which includes ships under repair, a sailing expedition, dolphins, and a beacon fire. The narrative continues with the wreck of the fleet, the appearance of Athena, and a thunderbolt striking Ajax, while Hero evaluates the earlier treatment of this myth by Philon of Byzantium. The work closes with a note on timing motions by a steady flow of water.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_mensuris: The De Mensuris is a short Greek treatise on measurement attributed to Hero of Alexandria, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens by dividing measures into three kinds, namely the linear, the planar, and the solid. The bulk of the work consists of worked numerical examples that compute the volume or capacity of pits, wells, stones, and beams.
