Other objects include columns, walls, ships, and cisterns, which are also measured in these examples. The closing sections form a glossary of weights, coins, and dry and liquid measures, defining units such as the talent, mina, shekel, and drachma. The text also explains the Hebrew, Greek, and Roman names for these units.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.mechanicorum_fragment: This short collection preserves Greek fragments from the Mechanics of Hero of Alexandria, which survive as excerpts and paraphrases often referring to Hero's own demonstrations. The compiler notes that he encountered corrupted and incomplete copies of the original books, and the text opens with the problem of moving a given weight by a given force. This is illustrated by the gear train of the Baroulkos, with stated ratios of drums and axles, and the passage also includes a hand-turned screw and a report of Archimedes' saying about moving the earth. A mechanical construction for finding two mean proportionals between two given straight lines follows, and an epitome of the five mechanical powers then describes the wheel and axle, lever, and wedge. The screw is also covered, with the construction and use of each device, and a further fragment demonstrates the centre of gravity of a triangle. The collection ends with descriptions of lifting machines with one to four uprights, and it also details sled-like turtles for hauling heavy loads over the ground.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.metrica: The Metrica is a Greek treatise on geometric mensuration by the Alexandrian mathematician and engineer Hero of Alexandria, whose date of composition remains uncertain. The work opens with a preface tracing geometry to the measuring and dividing of land, recalling the achievements of Eudoxus and Archimedes. The author announces a collection of useful results from earlier writers alongside his own contributions, proceeding from plane figures to solid bodies. It covers triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons up to the dodecagon, while the circle, ellipse, and parabola are also treated. A general rule for a triangle's area from its three sides is demonstrated through the inscribed circle, and solid bodies include prisms, cylinders, cones, and pyramids. The sphere and its segments are discussed, including the five Platonic solids and irregular objects measured by water displacement, with a concluding section treating the division of lands and figures in prescribed ratios.
grc.heronis_alexandrini.liber_geeponicus_sp: The Liber Geeponicus is a Greek collection attributed to Hero of Alexandria, though its exact date remains uncertain. It opens with definitions of plane and solid figures, covering circles, triangles, and quadrilaterals. The bulk of the work serves as a practical manual of mensuration, where worked problems compute areas, perimeters, and volumes for various geometric shapes and structures. These include squares, triangles, circles, pyramids, and regular polygons, and the text also provides rules for converting among body-based measures like the foot and cubit. Further sections measure land in iugera and differentiate soils of differing quality, while they treat measures of lime, stone, timber, and walls. A general rule connects the side and diameter of any regular polygon, and reckonings for stored wheat and barley in modii and sextarii are also provided. Headings naming Hero and a section bearing Euclid's name mark the collection as a composite, and grain reckonings authenticated in the prefecture of a Modestus further confirm this status.
grc.hesiod.works_and_days: Works and Days is a didactic poem by the Greek poet Hesiod, whose date remains uncertain, but the text frames itself as advice to his brother Perses. The two men had recently disputed their family inheritance, and the poem opens with an invocation to the Pierian Muses and to Zeus. This god raises the low and abases the proud, and he also sends mankind both the bad and the good Strife. The text recounts the myths of Prometheus and Pandora, and it also describes the five races of men, from gold to iron. A fable of the hawk and the nightingale warns rulers against injustice, while the greater part of the work offers practical instruction. It covers ploughing, sowing, harvesting, and seafaring, and the poem closes with a calendar of favourable and unfavourable days.
grc.hippocrates.coa_praesagia: The Coa Praesagia, a prognostic treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, is attributed to Hippocrates, though its date remains uncertain. It sets out numbered maxims on signs that predict fatal, dangerous, or hopeful outcomes, opening with shivering fits that follow chills and their accompanying symptoms. The work then proceeds through fevers, critical days, and signs of the head, eye, and ear, before covering the tongue, sputum, voice, respiration, throat, chest, and abdomen. It also addresses haemorrhages, spasms, quinsy, pleurisy, empyema, consumption, and liver disease, followed by dropsy, dysentery, bladder complaints, apoplexy, and wounds of the head and body. The treatise concludes with disorders grouped by age, ailments of women, and various discharges.
grc.hippocrates.de_alimento: De Alimento ('On Nutriment') is a short Greek medical treatise of uncertain date attributed to Hippocrates. It opens by defining nutriment as one and yet many, single in kind but manifold in its wet and dry forms. The text surveys how nourishment reaches every tissue, humour, and organ within the body. It also examines the unity of beginning and end in all things, along with various evacuations. The work discusses the porosity of the body and its respiration, as well as the rooting of veins in the liver. It further details the nourishment of the embryo and infant through blood and milk. The treatise closes with remarks on the assimilation of liquid and solid nutriment.
grc.hippocrates.de_arte: De Arte, meaning On the Art, is a short Greek treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus. It is attributed to Hippocrates and serves as a defence of medicine. The work rebukes those who deny that medicine is a genuine art. It defines the practice as removing suffering and blunting the violence of disease. The text answers objections regarding luck, failure, and the refusal of hopeless cases. It concludes by showing that hidden ailments can be overcome through reasoning and observable signs.
grc.hippocrates.de_genitura: This short treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus is ascribed to Hippocrates. It offers a physiological account of human generation across eleven chapters. The text opens with the doctrine that seed is the strongest part of the body's moisture. It traces this substance through veins and spinal marrow, explaining nocturnal emissions and the infertility of eunuchs. The argument then turns to women, describing female seed and pleasure in intercourse. It details how the stronger and more abundant seed determines the child's sex and resemblance to its parents. The work closes by attributing small stature and deformity to a narrow womb or injury to the mother.
grc.hippocrates.de_humoribus: This brief Greek medical treatise, attributed to Hippocrates and preserved in the Hippocratic Corpus, has an uncertain date and uses an aphoristic style rather than continuous argument. The text opens with the colours of the humours and rules for drawing them off, then catalogues signs of evacuations and crises in urine, sputum, stools, sweat, and dreams. Later sections discuss the timing of purgation relative to critical days and paroxysms, while also noting deposits of humours in joints and elsewhere. The work treats the effects of winds, waters, and seasonal changes on disease, and it examines constitutions suited to each season and age. It closes with remarks on haemorrhoids and the thick white urine of Antigenes.
grc.hippocrates.de_liquidorum_usu: This short Greek treatise on the therapeutic use of liquids is attributed to Hippocrates, whose uncertain date places it within the Hippocratic Corpus. The text opens by distinguishing drinking water from sea water, then sets out the effects of hot and cold affusions on the body. The author details the care needed to judge the proper degree of heat, while later sections treat sea water and vinegar for wounds, itching, and skin conditions. They also discuss the astringent and softening properties of sweet and dark wines, addressing many affections including erysipelas, gouty swellings, and tetanus. The work covers head injuries and disorders of the eyes, ears, and womb, closing by summarising the modes of application. These include pouring liquids, anointing with oils, and applying leaves or plasters, each judged by whether cold or heat proves beneficial or injurious.
grc.hippocrates.de_natura_hominis: De Natura Hominis, a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date attributed to Hippocrates, opens by attacking those who reduce human nature to a single element. The author rejects physicians who identify man with blood, bile, or phlegm alone, maintaining that the body contains four humours whose balanced mixture constitutes health. Their excess, deficiency, or separation breeds disease, and the text traces their seasonal predominance. Later chapters set out treatment by opposites and attribute epidemic disease to the air men breathe. They describe the courses of the principal veins and where phlebotomy should be performed. The text also interprets signs in sputum, urine, and stools, distinguishing four types of fever according to the bile from which each arises.
grc.hippocrates.de_salubri_diaeta: De Salubri Diaeta, meaning On a Salubrious Diet, is a short Greek prose treatise from the Hippocratic corpus, attributed to Hippocrates, though its exact date remains uncertain. The text opens by prescribing a seasonal regimen for laypeople, urging copious eating and undiluted wine in winter, while softer and wetter fare is recommended for spring and summer, with gradual transitions between these regimes. Later chapters adapt diet, exercise, bathing, and clothing to bodily type, age, and locality, providing specific regimens for the fat who wish to grow thin and the thin who wish to grow fat. The work also sets out the seasonal use of emetics and clysters, along with guidance for infants, women, and athletes, before closing with the maxim that a sensible man should know how to benefit himself in sickness.
grc.hippocrates.praeceptiones: The Praeceptiones, a short treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, is attributed to Hippocrates, though its date remains uncertain. It offers counsel on the theory and conduct of medicine, beginning by distinguishing time from the critical moment, or kairos. Healing must rest on experience joined with reason, not just plausible argument, and the text advises learning from observation and even from laymen. It urges physicians to cooperate with one another and to moderate their fees, while avoiding pretension and affected obscurity in their speech. The treatise closes with brief remarks on signs and symptoms in disease.
grc.hippocrates.prognosticon: The Prognosticon is a Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates, though its date remains uncertain, and the title means a prediction or forecast. It opens by declaring that the best physician practises prognosis, foretelling symptoms so patients will trust him, while conceding that not all the sick can be saved. The body sets out signs for judging recovery and death in acute diseases, including the face, posture, hands, breathing, sweats, and the hypochondrium. It also covers dropsies, sleep, bowel movements, urine, vomits, and sputum, and chapters address the days of suppuration and the critical days of fevers. Pains of the head, ears, and throat are also discussed, and the work closes by urging physicians to master and weigh all signs against one another. It notes that these signs hold true in every land and season.
grc.hippocrates.vectiarius: This Greek surgical treatise, attributed to Hippocrates and appearing in the Hippocratic Corpus, has an uncertain date. It opens with an anatomical survey of bones and their articulations, running from the fingers through the leg, spine, ribs, shoulder, and arm. The bulk of the work treats dislocations throughout the body, covering the ribs, jaw, shoulder, hip, knee, and foot. The author sets out diagnostic signs and methods of reduction, while also detailing bandaging and apparatus such as levers and stretching benches. Rules of diet and prognosis are included, with repeated warnings of gangrene and death appearing where reduction fails or is misapplied. The text closes with general observations on which joints slip most readily, noting practitioner errors and describing deformities left by congenital or untreated dislocations.
grc.isidore_of_charax.mansiones_parthicae: The Mansiones Parthicae, a short Greek itinerary attributed to Isidore of Charax, an otherwise obscure author of uncertain date, records the overland route from the Euphrates to the eastern Parthian provinces. It opens with the crossing at Zeugma and the road down the river through Apameia, proceeding station by station through Mesopotamia and Babylonia to Seleucia on the Tigris. The route continues across Media and the Caspian Gates to Hyrcania, Parthia, Aria, and Sakastane, where the author names villages, fortified posts, Greek foundations, rivers, temples, and royal residences. Distances are given in schoeni, and the itinerary ends at Alexandropolis in Arachosia, the stated limit of Parthian rule. The surviving corpus closes with fragments of Isidore, including an account of pearl-fishing in the Persian Gulf and notices of Persian kings quoted from Athenaeus and Lucian.
grc.isocrates.letters: This collection contains nine short letters in classical Attic prose attributed to Isocrates. Most are cast as epistles of counsel addressed to rulers and dynasts. The opening letter urges a powerful addressee, at war with Carthage while Spartan supremacy recedes, to weigh the safety of the Greeks. It asks him to consider the perils of rash boldness against the pursuit of martial glory. The letters reflect on the limits of advising in writing rather than in person. They also examine the difference between flatterers and honest counsellors, and the conditions under which a death in battle brings honour rather than disgrace.
grc.libanius.declamations: Libanius, a fourth-century AD rhetorician from Antioch, composed these imaginary courtroom speeches, which follow the Greek tradition of rhetorical display on fictitious legal situations. The settings are largely classical Athens, and the collection opens with a speech by a companion of Socrates. He pleads before Athenian jurors against the philosopher's condemnation, urging them to judge by their oath rather than by hostility. The remaining declamations feature a varied cast of hypothetical litigants, including one husband who asks the council for release from his wife's incessant chatter. Another man laments the theft of treasure he had buried for safekeeping, and each speech elaborates the arguments and emotional appeals appropriate to its imagined case.
grc.libanius.orations: The Greek orations gathered here date from the fourth century CE and are the work of Libanius of Antioch, a sophist and teacher of rhetoric. The opening oration is autobiographical, narrating his upbringing in a prominent Antiochene family, his education, and his career. It was composed to correct opposing verdicts, since some counted his fortune the happiest and others the most wretched. Subsequent speeches carry the self-defence further, answering complaints from rivals, students, and the city over his teaching and conduct, and rebutting slanders against the emperor Julian. The collection closes with an oration in defence of the pantomime dancers, addressed to Aristides. This final speech presents the art as a public schooling in the deeds of myth and history, after the manner of the poets and tragedians.
grc.libanius.orations_1-11: Orations 1-11 gathers the opening speeches of Libanius, a Greek rhetorician of Antioch. The text is printed from Richard Foerster's Teubner edition. The first oration is an autobiography in which he corrects those who call him either the most fortunate or the most wretched of men. He narrates his family history at Antioch, his orphaned childhood, and his ardour for the study of rhetoric. Libanius frames his life through allusion to earlier Greek literature. He cites Aristophanes' Acharnians outright and recalls his memorization of the ancient orators.
grc.lucian.abdicatus: Lucian of Samosata composed this short forensic speech in Greek, which belongs to his collection of rhetorical declamations. The speaker is a young physician answering his father's lawsuit, where the father seeks to disinherit him a second time. The son protests that he was cast off once before, but was readmitted after curing his father's madness. Now he faces renewed expulsion for refusing to treat his stepmother, whose case he judges to be incurable. He argues that a father who voluntarily took back a son has exhausted his legal power of renunciation, and that decisions rendered in court must stand. He maintains that medicine is a free art, so no one may be commanded against a physician's judgment.
grc.lucian.adversus_indoctum_et_libros_multo: This short Greek satirical invective by Lucian targets a wealthy but ignorant man who buys fine old books hoping mere possession will pass for culture. The speaker charges that his conduct defeats his own purpose, as he cannot distinguish valuable ancient books from worm-eaten rubbish. A string of analogies drives the point home, including a man with wooden feet buying costly clogs and Thersites appearing in Achilles' armour. Euangelos of Tarentum is flogged from the theatre at Delphi, while he wears a gem-studded cithara. The tale of Orpheus' lyre and its ill-fated purchaser Neanthus follows, and Dionysius composes verses on Aeschylus' writing-tablet. Demetrius the Cynic tears a copy of the Bacchae, and Pyrrhus suffers a flatterer-induced delusion of resembling Alexander. The speech closes with advice to sell the library to the educated, comparing the owner to the dog in the manger who neither eats the barley itself nor allows the horse to do so.
grc.lucian.anacharsis: This short dialogue by Lucian features the Scythian sage Anacharsis and Solon, who discuss the training of Athenian youths in a lively exchange. Anacharsis questions the value of young men wrestling in the mud, finding their physical contests to be a form of madness. Solon defends these exercises as preparation for civic life, describing education in letters, music, and the laws. The conversation also covers athletic prizes and Spartan customs, with Anacharsis objecting from his own cultural perspective. The pair eventually withdraws to the shade, arranging to continue the discussion the next day.
grc.lucian.bacchus: Lucian's short Greek prose piece, the Bacchus, frames a myth as a defence of unexpected styles of discourse. The speaker recounts Dionysus' campaign against the Indians, who first ridicule his army of maenads, satyrs, Pan, and Silenus. They are eventually routed when the forces meet in battle. The narrator compares this reaction to how people treat unfamiliar speech, expecting only satiric and comic matter. A second story describes a grove with three springs that affect boys, men, and old men differently. The aged receive a sudden torrent of eloquence from the waters. The piece closes with a jest that any foolishness is due to drunkenness, while wisdom is Silenus' favour.
grc.lucian.calumniae_non_temere_credundum: Calumniae Non Temere Credundum, meaning On Not Readily Believing Slander, is a short Greek essay by Lucian of Samosata that argues against the credulity allowing calumny to flourish in human affairs. The text opens with a vivid image of ignorance pouring a mist over the world, which blinds people, causing them to stumble over what lies at their feet. They also dread what is far off, a dynamic that supplies tragedy with its disasters, while Lucian takes the painter Apelles as his model for this inquiry. Apelles was slandered before Ptolemy and barely escaped harm, and he depicted Calumny in an allegory, which Lucian follows in his own analysis. The essay defines slander as an accusation made in the accused's absence, credited without any opportunity for rebuttal, and Lucian anatomizes the roles of the slanderer, the slandered, and the credulous listener. He supports this analysis with anecdotes from Ptolemy's court and from the life of Alexander, citing wronged figures ranging from Bellerophon and Hippolytus to Aristides and Socrates. The essay closes by prescribing that every charge be examined on its own merits, with reason posted as the doorkeeper of the ears, as in Homer's tale of the Sirens. Lucian looks to a time when lives are illuminated by truth, where slander would find no ground to stand on and would flee to the pit.
grc.lucian.cataplus: Lucian's Cataplus ('The Downward Journey') is a short comic dialogue set on the shore where the dead embark for the underworld. Charon complains to Clotho that the ferry stands ready while Hermes lingers above among the living. When Hermes finally arrives, he brings the newly dead, including the tyrant Megapenthes and the cobbler Mikyllos. Megapenthes begs for more life and pleads in vain to learn the fate of his possessions and household. The poor cobbler goes gladly, laughing at the equality of death while the tyrant laments his abandoned riches. Before Rhadamanthys, the philosopher Kyniskos indicts the tyrant, whose lamp and couch testify against him. He is condemned to be bound beside Tantalus and denied the water of Lethe, so that he must remember forever what he was.
grc.lucian.de_domo: This short Greek prose piece, attributed to Lucian and transmitted under the title De Domo, meaning On a House, serves as a rhetorical exercise. It defends the delivery of formal speeches in praise of a splendid building, arguing that a cultivated viewer who meets a beautiful hall with silence is a philistine. Settings of great beauty naturally call forth eloquence, as shown by Alexander's longing to bathe in the Cydnus, while Socrates' conversation by the Ilissus offers a further instance. The argument proceeds to praise the proportions, light, and judicious use of gold in the house, contrasting these qualities with the ostentatious but artless luxury of the Persian kings. The piece closes with the figure of the modest woman, who wears gold only in measured ornament.
grc.lucian.de_luctu: Lucian's De Luctu begins by observing common people at funerals, who lament death as unbearable while ignorant of its true nature. The text mocks the popular underworld drawn from Homer and other poets, describing Pluto, Persephone, the rivers, and the Acherusian lake. It details Cerberus, the judges, and the fates of the wicked, which sustain specific funeral customs, including the obol for the ferryman. The corpse is washed, anointed, and garlanded by hired wailing women, before a long imagined speech follows in which the dead son rebukes his grieving father. He catalogues the hunger, disease, and old age he has escaped, exposing the folly of the lament through this dialogue. The piece closes with a survey of national burial customs, noting the Greek burning, the Persian burying, the Egyptian mummifying, the Scythian eating, and the final funeral feast.
grc.lucian.de_mercede: De Mercede, a short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, is addressed to the young Timocles. The speaker promises to describe the hardships of those who serve rich households for a salary, drawing on the accounts of men who have endured such lives. The main body likens paid friendship to slavery, cataloguing the humiliations and servile flattery that dependents face at lavish dinners. They receive the worst food and wine while attending forced walks and journeys, and the fee itself is often petty. A comic inset recounts the Stoic TheSmopolis minding a patroness's lapdog on a journey, while later passages touch on women who keep rhetoricians and philosophers as ornaments. They also note the envy and slander that meet the dismissed dependent, and the work closes with a spoken allegory of Wealth's house. The suitor enters led by Hope and passes through Deceit, Servitude, Toil, and Old Age, leaving naked and despairing. The god is blameless, and the responsibility lies with the chooser.
grc.lucian.de_sacrificiis: This brief satirical essay in Greek is by Lucian of Samosata, the second-century CE rhetorician and satirist. It mocks the anthropomorphic piety of traditional cult, arguing that gods who need offerings, sulk when slighted, and sell their favours for hecatombs are less than noble. To make the point it rehearses mythic exempla drawn largely from Homer and the poets. Among them are Artemis's vengeance on Oeneus, Chryses' bargaining with Apollo, and Apollo's servitude to Admetus and Laomedon. Zeus's overthrow of Cronus and his many amours, the births of Athena and Dionysus, the lameness of Hephaestus, and Prometheus chained on the Caucasus supply further examples.
grc.lucian.de_saltatione: De Saltatione is a Greek dialogue by the satirist Lucian of Samosata, in which Lycinus defends pantomime dance against Crito's attacks. Crito rebukes Lycinus for his devotion to the theatre, dismissing the art as frivolous and effeminate. Lycinus replies with a sustained encomium tracing dancing to the primal movement of the cosmos. He catalogues mythological subjects like Heracles and the Trojan war, detailing the memory and bodily discipline required. Anecdotes about celebrated and ridiculous dancers carry the argument to its close. Crito is eventually won over and asks to share Lycinus' seat at the theatre.
grc.lucian.de_syria_dea: This brief prose treatise, attributed to Lucian and written in Ionic Greek, describes the great sanctuary of the Syrian goddess in a city near the Euphrates. The narrator, presenting himself as an Assyrian, promises an account of the temple and its rites, drawing on his own observation and the testimony of the local priests. An early digression covers ancient shrines in Phoenicia, including the Adonis rites at Byblus, while the body recounts foundation legends involving Deucalion, Semiramis, Derketo, and Stratonice. The text then details the precinct, colossal phalli, and gold-clad images of Hera and Zeus, along with the self-moving oracle of Apollo and the clergy. It also notes the Galli, who castrate themselves, and the sacred lake with its venerated fish, before closing with great festivals, processions to the sea, and the spring rite of burning trees. Practices of tattooing, self-laceration, and castration are described, along with the dedication of consecrated locks of hair.
grc.lucian.deorum_consilium: Lucian of Samosata wrote this short satirical dialogue in Greek, where Zeus convenes an assembly of the gods to hear complaints about the crowd of mortals and foreigners lately admitted to divinity. Momus is urged to speak with frankness and derides the newcomers in turn, mocking Dionysus and his rustic retinue, Asclepius, and Heracles, the last of whom Zeus silences. The speaker also targets Egyptian animal cults, bogus oracles, and the philosophers' empty personifications such as Virtue and Fortune, while reproaching Zeus himself for setting the precedent through his own amours. The dialogue closes with the reading of a decree appointing seven judges to review each god's credentials, who will expel the unqualified to their ancestral tombs or Tartarus and restrict each deity to its proper function.
grc.lucian.dialogi_marini: The Dialogi Marini is a collection of brief dramatic dialogues in Greek, set among the sea gods and sea-nymphs of myth. Variously dated to the second century AD, the work is attributed to Lucian of Samosata. The opening dialogue between Galateia and Doris mockingly appraises the Cyclops Polyphemos as a lover. An exchange between Polyphemos and Poseidon recounts his blinding by Odysseus. Later pieces carry the theme of divine passion through encounters of Poseidon, Proteus, and Menelaos. The collection concludes with a pair of winds describing Zeus's abduction of Europa to Crete.
grc.lucian.dialogi_mortuorum: The Dialogues of the Dead is a collection of short comic dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, set almost entirely among the shades in the underworld. The work opens with Diogenes instructing Polydeuces to summon Menippus down to Hades, where satraps, tyrants, and rich men are now recognizable only by their weeping. The remaining scenes range widely through myth and history, as Hermes and Charon process the new arrivals while Pluto and Minos hold court. Alexander, Hannibal, and Scipio dispute military precedence, and Diogenes contrasts his enduring fame with Mausolus' vast monument. Helen survives only as a nameless skull, and Protesilaus wins a single day's return to his bride. Menippus tours the famous dead, from the Seven Sages and Empedocles to Socrates and Tiresias, while the Cynics Diogenes, Crates, and Antisthenes laugh at the reversals.
grc.lucian.dipsades: The Dipsades ('The Thirsty Serpents') is a short comic piece in Greek prose by Lucian. It opens among the scorched southern sands of Libya, waterless, fruitless, and uninhabited except by the tent-dwelling Garamantes. These people venture out to hunt wild asses, ostriches, and elephants when rain briefly tames the heat. From there the piece catalogues the land's monstrous serpents before settling on one whose bite kindles an insatiable and incurable thirst. An epitaph illustrates the affliction, likening a dead traveller to Tantalus and the Danaids. It closes playfully as the speaker, confessing no firsthand knowledge of Libya, compares his growing thirst for the audience's attention to the doomed thirst of the serpent's victim.
grc.lucian.electrum: Lucian's short satirical dialogue opens with a recollection of the myth that poplars on the river Eridanus weep amber for Phaethon. The speaker had once hoped to gather these tears, but sailing up the river in later life, he finds neither trees nor gems. When he retells the tale of Phaethon, local boatmen ridicule him for trusting the poets, as they have never heard the name. His second expectation, that Apollo's musical swans haunt the banks, meets the same dismissal from the locals. The piece closes with the moral that believing poets, who inflate everything toward the grandiose, leads to such disappointments. The speaker warns that his own plain discourse holds out no such treasures to his listener.
grc.lucian.eunuchus: Lycinus arrives from the marketplace in high spirits to tell Pamphilus about a lawsuit between rival philosophers. The dispute concerns a well paid chair of philosophy maintained at the king's expense, which had been vacant since the death of a Peripatetic. The elderly Diocles opposes the candidacy of Bagoas, a eunuch who is said to know the doctrines but is derided as unfit for philosophy. Bagoas argues that judgment should fall on the soul rather than the body, appealing to Aristotle's admiration for the eunuch tyrant Hermias of Atarneus. He also jests that were philosophers judged by their beards, the goat would be preferred, and after proposals to examine the candidate bodily, general laughter ensues. The verdict is inconclusive, sending the case off to Italy, while Diocles prepares an added charge of adultery and Bagoas remains confident of victory.
grc.lucian.gallus: This short comic Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata opens with the poor cobbler Micyllus cursing a cock whose crowing cut short a dream of boundless wealth. The bird answers in human speech, revealing itself as the soul of Pythagoras, which has passed through many lives from Euphorbus at Troy to Aspasia and Crates. Using a feather of Hermes, it leads Micyllus by night into the houses of the rich, including the tanner Simon, the moneylender Gniphon, and the wealthy Eucrates. The bird displays the anxieties and hidden miseries that accompany their fortunes while narrating its own past lives and the lavish banquet of Eucrates' dream. At daybreak, Micyllus is persuaded that his humble poverty is happier than the wealth he had previously coveted.
grc.lucian.harmonides: This brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata opens with the aulete Harmonides asking his teacher Timotheus how he might win renown. Harmonides has already mastered the technical demands of the instrument but seeks further fame. Timotheus replies that seeking approval directly from the crowds is a slow and uncertain business. He advises that the surest path is to win the judgment of a few acknowledged experts. The narrative adds that Harmonides died uncrowned at his first competition at the Dionysia. He burst a breath vessel in his eagerness to perform. A closing speaker extends this lesson beyond musicians to all who display themselves publicly. Applying it to his own pursuit of reputation in speech, he resolves to submit his work to one supremely learned man. This single approval outweighs the votes of the multitude.
grc.lucian.hercules: Lucian of Samosata wrote this short prose piece, which takes its departure from a painting of the Celtic Heracles, whom the Gauls call Ogmius. He is portrayed as a shrunken old man in the god's lion-skin, carrying his club and bow while a Celtic bystander explains the image. The god draws a crowd of men by golden and amber chains fastened from their ears to his pierced tongue. The Celts take him for Heracles rather than Hermes because he is eloquence itself, and his winged arrows are words that wound the soul. The closing pages turn the figure back on the aging author, who defends his return to public rhetorical display after long retirement. Invoking Hippoclides' remark that such things are no concern of his, he asks the gods for a fair wind and relaunches his refurbished little boat upon the sea.
grc.lucian.hermotimus: In this dialogue, Lycinus meets Hermotimus hurrying to his Stoic teacher after twenty years of study. He draws the man into a conversation about the path to philosophy. Lycinus questions the promised rewards of the sect and presses the problem of choosing among rival schools. He argues through analogies that testing every doctrine would outrun a human lifetime. Anecdotes about Hermotimus's harsh teacher undercut the school's pretensions. The man ends by renouncing philosophy and resolving to live the common life.
grc.lucian.hippias: Lucian composed this short Greek encomium to praise an engineer named Hippias. The speaker argues that true wisdom is best shown through deeds rather than words alone. He cites physicians, musicians, generals, and master builders as earlier examples of such men. The greater part of the piece offers a detailed praise of Hippias's bathhouse. It describes the levelling of the site, the firm foundations, and the various rooms. The speaker ends by listing the bath's virtues and repaying the craftsman with his speech.
grc.lucian.iudicium_vocalium: In this short Greek mock-forensic oration, Lucian stages a courtroom trial in which the letter Sigma prosecutes the letter Tau before the seven vowels sitting as judges. It opens with a written charge, laid under the archon Aristarchus of Phalerum, in which Sigma alleges violence and robbery in Tau's usurpation of his place in spelling. Sigma's speech catalogs his grievances through comic examples of words disfigured by the substitution, and it reports the parallel complaints of Delta, Theta and Zeta. Beyond these individual wrongs, Sigma broadens his case into a supposed tyranny over human speech, complete with a fanciful derivation of crucifixion from the letter's shape. The oration ends with Sigma demanding that Tau be punished by suffering death in its own form.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_confuatus: This satirical Greek dialogue by Lucian features Zeus being cross-examined by the Cynic Cyniscus, whose title signals the central act of questioning the supreme deity. Cyniscus begins by asking whether the Fates celebrated by Homer and Hesiod truly fix all events, arguing that this leaves no room for divine intervention or the power of prayer. He presses Zeus on why the wicked prosper while men like Phocion and Socrates suffer, and why thunderbolts strike the innocent more often than temple robbers. Cyniscus suggests that if all is fated, Minos should sentence Heimarmene rather than Sisyphus, claiming the gods are merely instruments of the Fates, like a carpenter's tools. Zeus responds with evasion, indignation, and threats before finally falling silent, and he departs by denouncing his questioner as a bold sophist.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_tragoedus: This comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata parodies tragedy, epic, and political oratory, opening with Zeus pacing in distress while Hera, Athena, and Apollo press him for an explanation. He reveals that the Stoic Timocles and the Epicurean Damis are disputing in Athens about divine providence, prompting an assembly of the gods to observe the debate. Hermes issues a proclamation stitched together from Homer, and the divine statues take their seats by material worth, with Egyptian idols outshining the bronzes of Myron and Phidias. Momus speaks with his habitual bluntness, and Apollo delivers an oracle so opaque that Momus takes it as plain abuse. Word arrives that Timocles and Damis are about to renew their debate, and the gods eavesdrop from a cloud as Timocles defends providence using the order of the heavens and the image of a well-governed ship. Damis replies with the gods' loves and feuds in Homer, along with ambiguous oracles that ruined Croesus, and he also cites the discordant worship of the nations and the mismanagement of the world-ship. The assembly carries on until Timocles, out-argued and out of temper, drives his opponent away with insults.
grc.lucian.marcrobii: Lucian of Samosata wrote this short Greek essay as a birthday gift for Quintillus, prompted by a dream to send examples of men who lived long lives. He begins by discussing races famed for longevity, such as the Seres and Chaldaeans, before turning to specific individuals arranged by their occupation. Kings and generals appear first, including Numa, Hiero, and Mithridates, while philosophers, historians, and poets follow, with Lycurgus closing the list. Each entry notes the age attained and often includes a brief anecdote, such as Isocrates composing a speech at ninety-six. Sophocles proved his sanity by reading a play in his old age, and Lucian promises to write separately about long-lived Romans and Italians.
grc.lucian.muscae_encomium: The Muscae Encomium is a short mock encomium in praise of the fly by Lucian of Samosata. It opens by setting the insect's size against that of gnat and bee and by describing its delicate, iridescent, membranous wings and its melodious flight. The speech then surveys the fly's anatomy and bloodsucking proboscis, its birth from a worm, its lifelong table companionship with humankind, its cunning evasions of the spider, and the boldness for which Homer repeatedly likens his heroes to it, before turning to the fly's revival from ashes as proof of the soul's immortality, its freeloading ease, its nomadic sleeping habits, the myths and poetesses named Myia, and the long-lived soldier-flies. It ends by cutting the discussion short with the proverb about making an elephant out of a fly.
grc.lucian.navigium: A comic dialogue of Lucian of Samosata, opening as Timolaos explains to Lykinos why he and his companions hurried to the Piraeus to view a colossal Egyptian grain ship newly arrived there. The conversation dwells on the vessel's gigantic dimensions, its Isiac figurehead and gilded ornaments, the multitude of its crew, and the captain's account of a storm-tossed voyage from Egypt in which a star of the Dioscuri saved the ship near the Chelidonian islands. When the strayed companion Adiamantos is overtaken on the road back to Athens, he confesses that he had been lost in a daydream of sudden wealth, and the friends successively frame extravagant mock wishes: a fleet of grain ships, a self-won kingdom extending to the Euphrates, and rings granting health, invisibility, strength, flight, eternal youth, and universal charm. Lykinos deflates each fantasy in turn by exposing the anxieties, dangers, and brevity that attend riches and power, and the party reaches the Dipylon gate laughing at the emptiness of such dreams.
grc.lucian.necyomantia: Lucian of Samosata presents a satirical dialogue in which the Cynic Menippus, wearing a grotesque costume of cap, lion-skin, and lyre, arrives among his friends from the world below. He recounts his journey to Hades, where contradictions between poets and laws, along with fruitless philosophical wrangling, left him unable to decide how to live. He sought out Mithrobarzanes, a Babylonian Magus, who purified him with lengthy rites and led him down through the marshes of the Euphrates into the underworld. There, Menippus watches Minos try the dead and sees kings and moneylenders stripped of their rank, while attending an assembly where the dead vote that the rich should return to life as beasts of burden. Tiresias whispers that the best life is the plain, unpretentious one of the ordinary man, and with his question answered, he escapes back to the surface through the sacred cave of Trophonius. He finds himself suddenly at Lebadeia.
grc.lucian.philopseudes: The Philopseudes, a Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian, features Tychiades asking Philocles why some men love falsehoods without any obligation to do so. Philocles recounts a visit to the ailing Eucrates, where several philosophers and a physician gather to trade marvels. These include a Babylonian exorcist healing a snakebite and a Hyperborean magician conjuring the dead. Other tales involve a walking bronze statue, a descent into Hades, and an Egyptian priest turning a doorbolt into a servant. Tychiades punctuates each story with skeptical mockery before leaving the company in disgust. The frame closes with Philocles noting that Tychiades has passed the infection of falsehoods to him, concluding that truth remains the surest antidote to such lies.
grc.lucian.pro_imaginibus: The Pro Imaginibus is a short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata that serves as an apology for extravagant praise in an earlier encomium. That earlier work had likened a woman to Hera and Aphrodite, which she rebukes as an affront to divine honour. The greater part of the work takes the form of a mock trial where Polystratus prosecutes Lycinus. He argues that elevated comparison is the essence of true encomium rather than flattery, citing Homer and Phidias. Alexander's refusal to have Mount Athos carved into his image is also noted in the text. The dialogue closes with Lycinus delivering his defence as if in the woman's presence, turning her piety into grounds for higher praise.
grc.lucian.prometheus: This short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata is set on the Caucasus. It opens with Hephaestus and Hermes surveying the cliffs for a suitable spot on which to nail the condemned Prometheus. Chained to the rock and awaiting the eagle, the Titan demands a hearing, and the piece unfolds as a mock forensic exchange. Hermes prosecutes, charging him with cheating Zeus over the sacrificial portions, with fashioning humankind, and with stealing fire. In reply Prometheus defends each exploit at length, portraying the god's wrath as petty ingratitude. The exchange closes with the Titan hinting that the secret of Thetis may yet purchase his release, and foretelling the coming of a Theban archer to save him.
grc.lucian.prometheus_es_in_verbis: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian, entitled Prometheus Es in Verbis, in which a speaker answers a critic who likens him to Prometheus for fashioning what seem to be living creations out of lowly clay. He weighs and largely rejects two flattering readings of the name, that his works are masterfully wrought and that they are original creations like Prometheus's moulding of mankind, illustrating the peril of mere novelty with the story of Ptolemy son of Lagus, whose exhibition in Egypt of a gold-harnessed Bactrian camel and a piebald man ended in ridicule. The greater part of the piece turns on his experiment of yoking Dialogue, a stately companion of philosophical walks, to Comedy, the Dionysiac mocker of philosophers who trips to anapaestic measures, a hybrid as monstrous as the hippocentaur unless the mixture is harmonious. He closes by resolving to stand by what he has once chosen, since to change one's mind is the work of Epimetheus, not of Prometheus.
grc.lucian.saturnalia: This short satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata explores the festival of the Saturnalia. The priest Cronosolon asks Cronos for riches, but the god explains that wealth belongs to Zeus. Cronos grants only the temporary equality of slaves and masters during his seven-day reign. The conversation shifts to mythological banter about Cronos devouring his children and the vanished golden age. He then commissions the priest to draft a comic code of laws for the festival. The work closes with letters debating the claims of the poor and the burdens of wealth.
grc.lucian.soleocista: The Solecist is a short comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, whose title refers to a person who makes grammatical errors. It opens with a question about whether an expert can avoid such mistakes, then stages a contest where the expert is repeatedly caught in errors. He fails to notice his own faults while censuring those of others, and the piece also includes anecdotes about Socrates of Mopsus from Egypt. These stories gently mock the barbarisms and false Atticisms of his companions, and the dialogue closes with a discussion of easily confused words and forms. It breaks off with the remaining lessons deferred to another occasion.
grc.lucian.symposium: Lucian of Samosata composed this satirical Greek dialogue, which opens with Philo asking Lycinus to confirm a story of recent violence. Lycinus then narrates a wedding banquet held for Aristaenetus' daughter and the moneylending philosopher Eucritus. The guests included members of rival philosophical schools, a grammarian, and a rhetor. Their evening moved from table talk and a slanderous letter to quarrels over seating and food. The gathering eventually descended into a drunken melee involving broken skulls and an overturned lamp. The account closes with the wounded bridegroom led home in bandages and the company dispersing.
grc.lucian.zeuxis: This short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata examines the tendency of audiences to admire novelty at the expense of genuine artistry. It opens with the narrator leaving after reading a discourse, showered with congratulations from hearers who praise only its originality. The bulk of the work consists of two illustrative stories, the first concerning the painter Zeuxis and his picture of a female centaur suckling twin young. The narrator sees the picture in a copy at Athens, where the spectators admire the unheard-of subject rather than the craftsmanship. The second story tells of Antiochus surnamed Soter, whose victory over the Gauls was won when the unexpected sight of sixteen elephants threw the enemy into confusion. In closing, the speaker treats his own case as a third instance, complaining that the strangeness of his subject wins applause while the real merits of his writing pass unnoticed.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.excerpta: These short excerpts, transmitted under the name of Nicomachus of Gerasa, deal with Greek music theory and are of uncertain date. The opening section recounts the legend of the lyre's invention by Hermes, tracing the instrument's transmission through Orpheus, Linus, Amphion, and Terpander. The remainder sets out arithmetical demonstrations of the ratios governing the tone, the fourth, and the fifth, explaining why the outer strings bear the names hypate and nete. These strings are assigned to the Moon and Saturn, and the text also tabulates the note names of the greater perfect system across its five tetrachords. A closing passage maps the five tetrachords onto the celestial spheres and the tetraktys, appealing to Plato's Laws, where harmonics is placed last among the sciences.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἐγχειρίδιον_ἁρμονικ: The Ἐγχειρίδιον Ἁρμονικῆς, or Manual of Harmonics, is a short Pythagorean treatise on music theory written by Nicomachus of Gerasa in twelve chapters for a lady who requested a summary. He explains that he composed it while travelling and promises a fuller treatment later, opening with a list of headings and an apology for its brevity. The text covers the distinction between continuous and intervallic voice, as well as the naming of notes from the seven planets. The chapters also detail Pythagoras's discovery of numerical ratios through the blacksmith experiment, examining the diatonic division of the octave and the harmonic doctrine of Plato's Timaeus. The work includes the testimony of Philolaus and the tuning of the octave by ratios, concluding with an account of the fifteen-note double-octave system. Finally, it defines the three genera of melody, namely diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic.
grc.nonnus_of_panopolis.dionysiaca: The Dionysiaca is a Greek epic poem written in dactylic hexameters by Nonnus of Panopolis at an uncertain date. Devoted to the life of the god Dionysus, it opens with an invocation of the Muse to sing of Semele. She was killed by a thunderbolt, and Zeus carried the infant Dionysus in his thigh until birth. The poem follows the god from his upbringing through a long campaign against the Indians, filled with battles, transformations, divine interventions, and love affairs. It includes his union with Ariadne, and the epic closes with Dionysus's apotheosis and the establishment of his worship. Rites and dances celebrated at Athens honor him together with Iacchus.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_galatas: The Epistle to the Galatians is a letter in the Greek New Testament, written in Koine prose during the Imperial period. It is addressed to the churches of Galatia under the name of the apostle Paul, who opens by claiming his commission directly from Jesus Christ. He rebukes the Galatians for turning to a different gospel so quickly, while the body defends his apostolic independence from the Jerusalem leaders. This defense uses autobiographical narrative, including the confrontation with Cephas at Antioch, and argues that justification comes through faith in Christ rather than works of the law. He draws on the example of Abraham and the contrast between promise and law, supported by the allegory of Hagar and Sarah. The letter concludes with ethical exhortations to stand in freedom, urging readers to walk in the Spirit and bear one another's burdens, ending with a note in Paul's own hand and a final blessing.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philippenses: The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek New Testament letter written by Paul and Timothy to the Christian community at Philippi. It opens with a salutation of grace and peace, followed by a thanksgiving for the Philippians' partnership in the gospel. The writer describes his imprisonment and tension between departing to be with Christ and remaining for the community. This leads to an exhortation to unity and humility, grounded by a hymnic passage on Christ's self-emptying, death, and exaltation. The middle chapters cover travel plans involving Timothy and the ailing Epaphroditus, along with warnings against opponents and an autobiographical passage. In that passage, the writer counts his pedigree and attainments as loss for the knowledge of Christ. The closing sections urge steadfastness, continual rejoicing, and prayer free from anxiety, while calling for reconciliation between Euodia and Syntyche. The letter thanks the Philippians for the material support they sent, ending with greetings from those with Paul, including the saints of Caesar's household, and a benediction of grace.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_ii: The second letter to the Thessalonians is a prose epistle of the New Testament, written in the names of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. It addresses the church of the Thessalonians, opening with thanksgiving for the recipients' growing faith and love. This gratitude is offered amid persecutions and a vision of judgment, while the body corrects a report that the day of the Lord has already come. Instead, it sets out a prior rebellion and the revelation of the man of lawlessness, whom the Lord will destroy at his appearing. The text urges believers to stand firm and hold fast to their traditions, while requesting prayer for the spread of the gospel. Members are commanded to work quietly and eat their own bread, avoiding idleness, and the letter prescribes withdrawal from the disobedient, coupled with admonition. It ends with a prayer for peace and a greeting in Paul's own hand.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_titum: The Epistle to Titus is a short Greek prose letter from the New Testament, presenting a message from Paul to his coworker Titus during the Roman imperial period. The text opens with Paul identifying himself as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, greeting Titus as his genuine child in the shared faith. The body instructs Titus to appoint blameless elders in each Cretan town, while silencing false teachers who upset households for shameful gain. Paul counsels various groups on orderly conduct, grounding these exhortations in divine grace, and emphasizes salvation by mercy rather than works. The letter closes with warnings against quarrels and genealogies, ordering Titus to shun divisive persons after repeated admonition. Travel plans involving Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos are noted, and the text ends with final greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.lucas: The Gospel of Luke is a Greek prose narrative preserved in the New Testament, which recounts the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus in an Imperial-era biblical idiom. The text opens with a preface addressed to Theophilus that explains the aim of an orderly account, followed by the annunciations and births of John the Baptist and Jesus under Herod and Augustus. The narrative then traces Jesus's baptism, temptation, and Galilean ministry of preaching, healing, and parables, including the good Samaritan and the prodigal son, the sending out of the disciples, and the long journey toward Jerusalem. The final chapters cover his entry into the city, teaching in the temple, and the Last Supper, and they also describe his betrayal, trial before Pilate and Herod, crucifixion, and burial. The account concludes with the women's discovery of the empty tomb, appearances on the road to Emmaus, and the ascension from Bethany.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_ii: The Second Epistle of Peter is a Greek New Testament letter attributed to the apostle Simon Peter, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens with a greeting from Symeon Peter, who addresses those who share his faith and urges them to cultivate virtue and knowledge. The author also calls for self-control, endurance, godliness, and love to complete their character, while affirming the apostolic witness to Christ's transfiguration and the reliability of prophecy. It then turns to a sustained denunciation of false teachers, using scriptural examples of divine judgment, such as the flood and Sodom, to illustrate this warning. The closing chapter answers scoffers who mock the promise of Christ's return, proclaiming that the day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will be dissolved by fire, leading to new heavens and a new earth.
grc.orphica.fragmenta: This volume gathers Greek fragments attributed to Orpheus and the Orphic poets, whose date and authorship remain uncertain. The texts survive as quotations in later authors, ranging from Plato and Aristotle to Damascius. The collection opens with a report from Plato's Philebus, which cites Orpheus' injunction to cease song in the sixth generation. The material is chiefly theological in nature, including cosmogonic and theogonic verses on Ocean and Tethys. It also features Night, the serpent Chronos, and the cosmic egg, with Phanes appearing alongside statements on the soul's divine origin. The body is described as a prison for the soul, while notices of rites and initiations are ascribed to Orphic books. Gold funerary tablets from Petelia and Eleutherna are included, addressing the dead at the spring of Memory. A papyrus paraphrase of an Orphic Demeter hymn is also present, and allegorical explanations of Orphic doctrine complete the collection.
grc.paradoxographus_florentinus.mirabilia_de: The Paradoxographus Florentinus, an anonymous Greek collection of marvels concerning waters, is named for its Florentine manuscript, and its date remains uncertain. The text opens with a spring at Potniae near Thebes whose water drives horses mad, then continues as a terse catalogue of springs, lakes, and rivers with strange properties. These waters are said to intoxicate, petrify, or make drinkers hate wine, while the collection also describes lakes with floating islands and sunken cities visible beneath the surface. Combustible naphtha is located across Greece, Asia, Africa, and Italy, and many entries close with the name of a source authority such as Isigonos, Ctesias, Aristotle, or Theopompus. Several entries quote epigrams said to be inscribed at the springs themselves.
grc.phalaridis_epistulae.epistulae: This collection of Greek prose letters is attributed to Phalaris, the tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, and the date of composition remains uncertain. The texts are written in the tyrant's own voice and are addressed to poets, philosophers, physicians, and various Sicilian cities. The opening letter thanks the physician Polyclitus for curing an incurable disease, and it also rebukes citizens who accuse the benefactor of treachery. Phalaris reports victories over Leontini and other towns throughout the collection, and he sends gifts, loans, and invitations to Acragas to his correspondents. The letters console the family of Stesichorus on the poet's death, and Phalaris instructs his wife Erytheia and son Paulola in several passages. He answers charges of cruelty, most notably regarding the brazen bull, which was devised by Perilaus, whom Phalaris claims to have executed.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_abrahamo: De Abrahamo, a Greek philosophical exposition by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, rewrites the Genesis narrative of Abraham as part of a larger series on the Mosaic laws. The work opens by introducing the five books of the law and three pre-Abrahamic figures, Enos, Enoch, and Noah, who stand for hope, repentance, and righteousness. The main course follows Abraham from his migration out of Chaldaea to the death of Sarah, reading each episode on both a literal and an allegorical level as the soul's progress toward God. The text closes with praise of Abraham's faith and his standing as the first elder of the race, noting his fulfilment of the divine law without written instruction.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_aeternitate_mundi: Philo Judaeus wrote this Greek treatise to argue that the cosmos is eternal and incorruptible, opening by invoking God as the source of knowledge. It surveys earlier opinions on whether the world is generated and perishable or eternal, covering Democritus, Epicurus, and the Stoic doctrine of conflagration and palingenesis. Aristotle, Plato's Timaeus, Hesiod, and the Mosaic account of Genesis also receive attention, while the remainder assembles proofs that no cause within or without can destroy the world. The text weighs the arguments of Critolaus and answers the Stoic case for ekpyrosis and rebirth, reporting that Boethus of Sidon and Panaetius abandoned the conflagration doctrine. It closes by replying to objections drawn from mountain formation and the shrinking of the sea, addressing the mutability of elements and living kinds, along with the alleged youth of the arts.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_agricultura: This Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus reads Genesis 9:20–21 as an allegory of the soul, opening by distinguishing the husbandman Noah from the mere tiller of the ground. The latter figure represents the wicked man who labours only for the body, while the argument proceeds through paired terms to clarify these spiritual roles. Jacob and Moses serve as shepherds of the soul's flock, and God acts as the shepherd of the cosmic whole through his firstborn Logos. The text contrasts the skilled horseman with the unskilled rider, where the passions are horses, and the serpent of Dan bites the horse's heel. Virtue is presented as the only truly sacred contest, and the work closes on Noah's having only begun the art of cultivation. It draws lessons on beginnings without ends and on voluntary and involuntary transgression, showing how virtue is planted, advanced, and brought to completion.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_cherubim: De Cherubim is a Greek allegorical commentary on Genesis by Philo Judaeus, which opens by citing Genesis 3:24, where cherubim and a flaming sword guard the tree of life. Philo distinguishes being cast out from being sent forth, a key interpretive move, and reads Hagar's departures as the removal of encyclical education once Sarah, virtue, has borne fruit. The cherubim and fiery sword are expounded as the two spheres of the heavens with the sun, and they also symbolize God's two eldest powers, goodness and sovereignty, joined by the Logos. The closing part takes Cain, whose name means possession, as the mind born of sense-perception, which claims created things as its own, yet God alone truly owns all things. Humans are merely settlers and sojourners, with the divine Logos serving as the instrument of creation.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_confusione_linguarum: De Confusione Linguarum is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus that expounds the confusion of tongues in the Tower of Babel narrative of Genesis 11:1–9. The work opens as a continuation of a preceding discussion, quoting the biblical passage in full, and it also answers critics who deride the ancestral laws. The body surveys and rejects rival accounts of the episode, including the myth of the Aloeidae who piled mountains to reach heaven. It also rejects the fable that animals once spoke a single language, and the text then reads the story allegorically of the soul. The builders' one speech becomes the harmonious consensus of the wicked in wrongdoing, and the tower is a citadel of vice and impiety. God's descent is a figurative expression for a God who fills all things, and He works through ministering powers and is the cause of goods alone. The treatise closes with an analysis of confusion as the dissolution of the alliance of vices, which is distinguished from mere mixture. It ends with the scattering of the impious builders as God's dispersal of impiety from the world.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_congressu_eruditionis_g: Philo Judaeus wrote this Greek allegorical treatise on Genesis 16:1–6, which opens by citing the scriptural passage about Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar. The text identifies Sarah with virtue, which appears barren yet remains fertile in good deeds, while Hagar represents the encyclical studies, including grammar, geometry, music, and rhetoric. The mind must pass through these preliminary disciplines to receive the true offspring of virtue, and later sections explore numerical symbolism, focusing on the pre-eminence of the number ten. This discussion covers the tithe and related laws on firstfruits, festivals, and sacrifices, which are illustrated by stories of Abraham, Melchisedek, and the wilderness wanderings. The work closes by interpreting Hagar's affliction as a salutary hardship, representing the divine discipline imposed on the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_decalogo: Philo Judaeus, a Jewish writer, composed this Greek philosophical treatise titled De Decalogue, which means the Ten Commandments. The work presents these commandments as the summary heads of the Mosaic law, opening by asking why the laws were given in a deep wilderness rather than in cities. The author dwells at length on the perfection of the number ten and describes the theophany at Sinai, where the divine voice sounded from fire to a purified people. The main body discusses each commandment in turn, first covering the five duties concerning God, his name, the sabbath, and parents. It then addresses the five prohibitions against adultery, murder, theft, false witness, and desire, treating them as the heads of whole classes of particular laws. A closing section explains why the commandments were issued as bare injunctions without specified penalties because God is the cause of goods alone.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_fuga_et_inventione: De Fuga et Inventione is a Greek allegorical commentary by the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria, which interprets Genesis 16:6–12. The treatise identifies three causes of flight, namely hatred, fear, and shame, and traces these motives through the scriptural careers of Jacob and Hagar. It examines the Mosaic law on involuntary homicide and the six cities of refuge, detailing their number, location, and connection with the Levites and the high priest. The second half explores the complementary themes of seeking and finding, illustrated by Joseph and Isaac, who finds wisdom without seeking. The text also analyzes the several senses of 'well' or 'spring' in Scripture and closes with a symbolic reading of the names and places in Hagar's story.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_gigantibus: Philo Judaeus, a Jewish philosopher, wrote this Greek prose treatise titled De Gigantibus, which means 'On the Giants'. The work offers an allegorical exposition of Genesis 6:1-4, addressing the passage on the multiplication of mankind. Philo interprets the 'angels of God' as bodiless souls, some of which descend into bodies while others remain in the service of the creator. He argues that the divine spirit cannot dwell in flesh, and wisdom requires detachment from the body and its pleasures. The giants are not mythological beings, but figures for men 'of the earth', 'of heaven', and 'of God'. These groups are exemplified by lovers of pleasure, students of the arts, and priestly prophets such as Abraham. The treatise ends by reading Nimrod as the soul's desertion from God, and Babylon, whose name means 'migration', represents the change of mind with which every defection begins.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_josepho: De Josepho ('On Joseph') is a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish-Hellenistic writer Philo Judaeus. It presents the biblical Joseph as the exemplar of the political life. The work follows earlier lives of Moses, which focused on learning and ascetic practice. The narrative begins with Joseph's youthful dreams and his sale to merchants bound for Egypt. It traces his servitude, imprisonment, and rise to governor of Egypt. The story concludes with his reconciliation with his brothers and his death at age one hundred and ten. Allegorical commentary runs throughout, comparing the politician to a dream interpreter.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_migratione_abrahami: De Migratione Abrahami is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus that examines the divine command for Abraham to leave his land, kindred, and father's house. The text quotes Genesis 12:1–3 at its outset to frame this discussion, interpreting the summons as the soul's threefold migration away from the body, sense-perception, and spoken utterance. This movement allows the mind to advance toward the intelligible and toward God, while the treatise works verse by verse through the call of Abraham. It considers the gifts promised to the wise, including a great nation, blessing, and a magnified name, and explores the relation between inner thought and the speech that expresses it. The author weighs the worth of literal observance alongside symbolic meanings, warning against the danger of the 'mixed multitude' of confused opinions that accompanies the exodus from the life of the senses. Later passages attack the Chaldean doctrine that the visible cosmos is divine, tracing Abraham's progress out of Haran, which is figured as the cave of sense-experience, and continuing on to Sychem.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_opificio_mundi: De Opificio Mundi, a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish author Philo Judaeus, examines the creation of the world as narrated in the opening chapters of Genesis. The work opens by contrasting Moses with other lawgivers who set down bare laws or veiled truth in myth, noting that Moses began his legislation with the noblest subject, an account of the world's generation where law and cosmos accord. The argument follows the six days of creation, moving from the intelligible world to the visible one, and details the making of heaven, the elements, plants, animals, and man as the image of God. Extended discussions cover the properties of the numbers six, four, and seven, along with the sanctity of the seventh day, while the text closes with the first man, paradise, and the serpent as a symbol of pleasure. It concludes with five doctrines drawn from the cosmogony, including that God exists, is one, and exercises providence over the single, generated world.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_plantatione: Philo Judaeus, a Jewish exegete, composed this Greek treatise as part of a series of allegorical commentaries on Genesis. The work opens by shifting from general agriculture to viticulture, focusing on Noah as the first to plant a vineyard. God is portrayed as the supreme planter, with the cosmos rooted in the divine Logos. The rational soul is likened to a garden where senses and virtues are divinely cultivated. Later sections interpret Eden and Abraham's grove as symbols of the soul's virtues and God's eternal nature. The text concludes with a philosophical debate on whether the wise man can fall into drunkenness.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_praemiis_et_poenis_et_d: Philo Judaeus opens this Greek treatise by dividing the oracles delivered through Moses into cosmogony, history, and legislation. The work announces its subject as the prizes set before the good and the penalties laid upon the wicked. The first part interprets patriarchal figures as victors in sacred contests, assigning hope, repentance, and justice to Noah's line. Faith, joy, and the vision of God go to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while Moses alone receives kingship, lawgiving, prophecy, and the high priesthood. The twelve tribes draw their privileges from the blameless house of the founders, and the treatise sets out the goods promised to the obedient. These include victory over enemies, material plenty, fertility, bodily soundness, and the rest that sabbaths and sabbatical years afford. Against these stand the curses that overtake transgressors, ranging from failed harvests, drought, and locusts to enslavement, sickness, and panic in battle. The desolation of a land deprived of its fallow rest is also mentioned, and the text ends with the assurance that repentance can avert the curse. Scattered exiles who return to the ancestral way of life will be forgiven and brought back to their homeland in sudden and unexpected freedom.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sacrificiis_abelis_et_c: De Sacrificiis Abelis et Caini ('On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain') is a Greek allegorical commentary by Philo Judaeus. It interprets the offerings of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4. The text opens with a meditation on the soul gaining Abel and shedding Cain. It then allegorizes the brothers as warring dispositions within a single mind. Pleasure and Virtue each solicit the mind with rival promises in a personified scene. Later sections examine Cain's faults in offering sacrifice only after days. The work reads Mosaic laws on firstborns and unleavened loaves as rules for consecrating the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_somniis_lib_iii: A Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus, De Somniis ('On Dreams') Book III offers a philosophical and allegorical interpretation of the divinely sent dreams recorded in Genesis. It opens by distinguishing two classes of God-sent dreams and takes as its subject the second kind. In such dreams the human mind, set in motion by the mind of the whole, appears to be god-possessed and to foresee the future. Its principal example is Jacob's dream of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven (Genesis 28:12–15). Philo expounds the vision through symbolic readings of its details, taking the well called 'of the oath' as an image of knowledge. The discussion extends to the four elements of the cosmos and to the boundless nature of learning.
grc.philo_judaeus.quis_rerum_divinarum_heres: Philo Judaeus, the Alexandrian Jewish writer, composed this Greek philosophical commentary on Genesis 15, presenting an allegorical exposition of the biblical narrative. The treatise opens with Abraham's petition to God, where his question about inheritance becomes an inquiry into who is worthy to become heir of divine things. It then moves through discussions of the wise man's boldness before God, while the author examines the meaning of names such as Masek, Damascus, and Eliezer. He also explores the division of the soul and the four kinds of ecstasy, interpreting the cutting of sacrificial animals and the seven-branched lampstand. The text concludes with the covenant promise of the land stretching from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, reading the story as an account of the soul's migration from the senses toward the intelligible realm.
grc.philo_judaeus.quod_deterius_potiori_insi: Quod deterius potiori insidiari soleat is a Greek allegorical commentary on Genesis 4:8 by Philo Judaeus, which opens with Cain luring Abel into the plain. Philo interprets this as a symbol of rivalry, reading it alongside Joseph sent to his brothers and Isaac meditating in the field. These stories form a contest between self-love, figured in Cain, and the love of virtue, figured in Abel. The argument holds that the wicked man who attacks the better destroys himself, since killing Abel means killing the finest part of his own soul. The virtues themselves remain imperishable, even as the attacker perishes, while later sections expound the voice of Abel's blood, the meaning of blood, and the soul's substance. They also discuss the curse on Cain, the tilling of the ground, and the sevenfold vengeance, which serves as an allegory of the seven parts of the irrational soul. The text closes with the mark set upon Cain, a sign of a folly that escapes death but knows every other calamity.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.de_gymnastica: This Greek treatise on athletics by Philostratus the Athenian is of uncertain date, and it ranks gymnastics among the branches of wisdom rather than mere craft. The author sets down memoranda for those who train athletes, giving the origins of Greek contests such as foot races and boxing. It also covers the pentathlon, wrestling, and pankration, while stories of athletes from Peleus and Milo to Glaukos and Arrhichion are interspersed throughout. The text then turns to the trainer's art, discussing judging an athlete's inborn nature from his parents and physique. It also classifies bodily types and temperaments, and the author manages training cycles, diet, oiling, dust, sun, and apparatus. The treatise closes with a picture of robust ancient training, denouncing the luxury and corrupt diet of the author's own day, and it also criticizes bought victories that caused the discipline to decline.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.epistulae_et_d: Philostratus the Athenian, a Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period, composed this collection of short Greek love letters and two prose declamations. The opening letters send roses to a beloved, using the flower to symbolize spring, desire, and beauty that quickly withers. Subsequent letters address unnamed boys and women, as well as named friends, Epictetus, and the empress Julia Augusta. These texts praise the poor lover, love for a foreigner, blushes, and long hair, while lamenting its cropping. They also discuss the study of erotic poetry and the proper character of epistolary style. The work concludes with two dialexeis, or declamations, in which the author, a Lemnian, professes devotion to his native Lemnos and Imbros, and argues that law and nature are kindred rather than opposed.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vita_apollonii: The Vita Apollonii is a Greek prose biography in eight books by Philostratus the Athenian, which recounts the life of the sage Apollonius of Tyana. The narrator claims to have compiled the text from the travel notes of Damis of Nineveh, the subject's will, and other written accounts. The opening defends the project by surveying earlier figures in the Pythagorean and divine-man tradition, denying that Apollonius was a magician. The narrative follows Apollonius from his birth at Tyana, marked by an omen of the Egyptian god Proteus, to his ascetic Pythagorean discipline. It details his journeys to Babylon and India, where he travels, teaches, and intervenes across Greece, Egypt, and Ionia. This includes his encounter with Vespasian at Alexandria and his trial before Domitian in Rome, followed by his miraculous escape from imprisonment. The closing books describe his public vindication at Olympia and his counsel to Nerva, while rival traditions address his death and possible immortality at Ephesus, Lindus, and Crete.
grc.philostratus_the_lemnian.imagines: The Imagines (Eikones, 'Images') is a Greek prose collection attributed to Philostratus the Lemnian, made up of rhetorical descriptions of individual paintings. A prologue sets the scene at a gallery in a seaside suburb of Naples. There the speaker, a guest of Aristodemus of Caria, expounds the pictures to his host's young son and a circle of studious youths. The subjects are mythological and Homeric, beginning with the contest of fire and water at the Scamander from Iliad 21 and continuing with figures such as the personified Comus. Each description discusses in detail how its painting renders the story, the figures, and the effects of colour and light.
grc.phlegon.de_mirabilibus: This short Greek prose work, the De Mirabilibus, is attributed to Phlegon and preserves a single narrative episode told as a report addressed to a king. The story recounts how Philinnion, a young woman, returned from the dead to visit Machates, who was a guest lodging in her family's house. The account follows the alarm of her parents, Charito and Demostratus, and details Machates' production of the ring and breastband she had left with him. The text describes the opening of her tomb and the chthonic purifications ordered after her final disappearance. It closes with the narrator's offer to send further witnesses and particulars to the king.
grc.plato.alcibiades_2: This short Socratic dialogue opens with Socrates meeting Alcibiades on his way to pray, warning that people often ask the gods for evils they mistake for goods. The Oedipus story illustrates this dangerous error in human judgment, and the discussion then classifies various forms of folly and examines practical skills. Socrates argues that generalship, rhetoric, and manual crafts are useless without knowledge of the good, depicting a city governed by such expertise as full of disorder. He praises the Spartan custom of praying only for good things, and he also recounts how Athenians consulted the oracle of Ammon about their failures.
