Citations from Homer and Euripides support the claim that gods refuse wicked offerings, and the dialogue closes with Alcibiades agreeing to postpone his sacrifice. He resolves to clear the mist from his soul before acting.
grc.plato.apologia: Plato's Apologia presents the defence Socrates spoke before an Athenian jury, who faced charges of impiety towards the city's gods and of corrupting the young. The speech opens with Socrates confronting the slanders of both early and recent accusers, asking the jurors to bear with his plain, unpolished manner of speech. As a seventy-year-old appearing in court for the first time, he sets the tone for his argument, then cross-examines Meletus on the specific details of the indictment. Socrates recounts the Delphic oracle's answer that no one was wiser than he, which launched his lifelong mission of examining politicians, poets, and craftsmen. He also defends his divine sign, his poverty, and his conduct under the Thirty, proposing maintenance in the Prytaneum as a counter-penalty after the verdict. He refuses exile or silence, issues a warning to his condemners, and concludes with reflections on death and a request regarding his sons.
grc.plato.charmides: Plato's ancient Greek dialogue features Socrates, Critias, and the young Charmides, who is set in the palaestra of Taureas at Athens. This location is chosen immediately after Socrates returns from the fighting at Potidaea, where Critias presents his nephew Charmides. He does so under the pretext of a headache remedy, and the ensuing discussion pursues the question of what sophrosyne is. The speakers examine a succession of candidate definitions, including modesty, quietness, doing one's own things, and self-knowledge. They also consider knowledge of knowledge itself, which completes the examination of these philosophical concepts.
grc.plato.euthyphro: Euthyphro is a short Platonic dialogue in which Socrates questions a man who claims exact knowledge of divine matters. The scene is set at the stoa of the Athenian king-archon, where Socrates reports the indictment for impiety brought against him by Meletus. He learns that Euthyphro has come to prosecute his own father for murder. Socrates then asks for a definition of the pious, and each of Euthyphro's successive answers is tested and found wanting. The argument repeatedly circles back on itself without reaching a settled definition. The dialogue ends aporetically as Euthyphro hurries away.
grc.plato.hipparchus: Hipparchus is a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and printed in Burnet's Oxford text. It opens with Socrates and an unnamed friend attempting to define the lover of gain, while also seeking to settle whether gain itself is good. A string of elenctic exchanges dismantles the friend's successive accounts, which rely on analogies with the farmer, horseman, and helmsman. The two eventually concede that everyone loves gain, identifying the reproached lover as one who profits from things the good do not dare to touch. A later digression praises Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, as a benefactor who brought the poems of Homer to Athens, giving the dialogue its title. Its aporetic handling of value and profit affords close parallels with other Platonic works, and it also connects with later Greek discussions of acquisition.
grc.plato.hippias_maior: The Hippias Major ('Greater Hippias') is a Socratic dialogue of Plato in which Socrates questions Hippias of Elis, a travelling sophist celebrated for his eloquence, memory and earnings. It opens with Hippias's boasts about his lucrative embassies and public displays, until Socrates, prompted by a challenger who had confounded him, asks what the beautiful itself is. Socrates puts a series of proposed answers to the test, among them a beautiful maiden, gold, and the fitting or appropriate. The useful and beneficial, and the pleasure received through sight and hearing, are refuted in turn, and Socrates's own attempts fare no better. The discussion ends without a definition, in perplexity, on the proverb that beautiful things are difficult.
grc.plato.ion: Plato's Ion is a short Socratic dialogue in which Socrates questions Ion of Ephesus, a prize-winning rhapsode who recites and interprets Homer. The text opens with Socrates inquiring about Ion's visit to the festival of Asclepius at Epidaurus, where he asks about Ion's success in the rhapsodic contest. Socrates then presses whether Ion's command of Homer alone amounts to a craft, arguing by analogies with painting, sculpture, and music that rhapsody is not a craft. Instead, it is a divine inspiration conveyed like the power of a lodestone, which flows from the Muse through the poet and the rhapsode to the audience. Socrates tests whether the rhapsode knows the several arts Homer describes, including chariotry, medicine, fishing, and divination, and also asks whether rhapsody and generalship are the same. Socrates leaves Ion to choose between being deemed unjust or divine.
grc.plato.lovers: The Lovers (Erastai) is a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato, though its authenticity is disputed and its date uncertain. It opens with Socrates entering the school of the grammarian Dionysius, where two well-born youths and their admirers are quarrelling about Anaxagoras and Oenopides. Asked whether philosophy is a fine thing, the disputants define it as the pursuit of learning in many arts and crafts. Socrates cross-examines the definition through the analogy of the pentathlete, who ranks second in every contest, arguing that a dabbler is useless while genuine craftsmen are to hand. He drives the argument towards the unity of justice, temperance, statesmanship and kingship as a single art of judging rightly. The dialogue closes abruptly, with one interlocutor silenced by shame and the other still objecting that matters stand otherwise.
grc.plato.philebus: Plato's Philebus is a Socratic dialogue asking whether pleasure or intelligence constitutes the good for human life. It opens with Socrates restating the dispute between Philebus, who holds that enjoyment is the good for all living creatures, and the advocates of thought, knowledge, and true reasoning. The discussion then moves through questions of method and the four classes of being to a detailed classification of pleasures, including mixed and false varieties. There follows an account of the kinds of knowledge and the construction of a blended life in which both pleasure and intelligence participate. The argument concludes that the good is to be sought in measure, proportion, and truth, with mind placed closest to it and pleasure ranked far below. A closing exchange leaves a few remaining points of the summary to be supplied on a later occasion.
grc.plato.symposium: Plato's Symposium is an ancient Greek dialogue opening with Apollodorus recounting a dinner party at the tragedian Agathon's house after a dramatic victory. The guests agreed to moderate their drinking and instead deliver speeches in praise of Eros, with Phaedrus, Pausanias, the physician Eryximachus, and Aristophanes each offering their views on Love. Aristophanes told a myth of primordial split beings seeking their lost halves, while Agathon celebrated Love's youth and beauty in his own speech. Socrates questioned Agathon and reported the teaching of the priestess Diotima of Mantinea, describing Love as a daimon between mortal and divine. The soul's ascent toward Beauty itself was also part of this teaching, and the evening was interrupted by the drunken Alcibiades, who praised Socrates instead. He likened Socrates to satyrs and Silenus figures and recounted failed attempts to seduce him, as the party broke up toward dawn. Socrates argued that one man could write both comedy and tragedy, then proceeded to the Lyceum as on other days.
grc.plato.theaetetus: Plato's Theaetetus is a dialogue devoted to the question of what knowledge is, opening with Eucleides of Megara telling Terpsion that Theaetetus is dying of wounds and dysentery. Eucleides mentions that he once wrote down an account of Socrates' conversation with the youth, which a slave then reads aloud. In this record, Socrates questions Theaetetus before the geometer Theodorus, who proposes that knowledge is perception, true judgement, or true judgement with an account. Socrates tests each definition through discussions of Protagoras, Heraclitean flux, and Socratic midwifery, while also exploring memory as a wax tablet and knowledge as an aviary of birds. The enquiry ends aporetically, with no definition accepted, as Socrates departs to answer the indictment of Meletus. He arranges to meet Theodorus again the next morning, concluding the philosophical investigation without a final resolution.
grc.plutarch.ad_principem_ineruditum: A brief moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to an uneducated ruler and known by its Latin title Ad Principem Ineruditum. It opens with the story of the Cyrenaeans who begged Plato to write laws for them and were refused, on the ground that legislating is hard for men so fortunate. From there the essay argues that a ruler must take philosophy as an attendant counsellor and guardian, first ordering his own soul before governing others, since the true king obeys the law, the living reason enthroned within him, and imitates the god who orders all things rather than brandishing sceptre and thunderbolt. Plutarch supports the argument with a broad range of exempla, Theopompus moderating the Spartan kingship, Alexander and Dionysius, Epaminondas keeping watch while Thebes feasted, Cato's death at Utica, the fearful tyrants Clearchus and Aristodemus, and closes with reflections on how power exposes untrained souls and how in rulers punishment, driven by anger, outruns accusation and proof.
grc.plutarch.adversus_colotem: Plutarch wrote this polemical treatise for Saturninus to answer Colotes, an Epicurean who had argued that other doctrines make life impossible. The work opens with the arrival of Colotes' book, which was addressed to King Ptolemy, and friends urged a reply after reading it together. Plutarch then takes up the accusations one by one, defending Democritus, Empedocles, Parmenides, and Plato against the charges. The text also addresses Socrates, Stilpon, and the Cyrenaics, while examining Arcesilaus and the suspension of judgement. Plutarch holds that the Epicurean position undermines itself, and the closing section contrasts Epicurean withdrawal with civic duty. It catalogues the public deeds of those Colotes had attacked.
grc.plutarch.agesilaus: Plutarch's Life of the Spartan king Agesilaus opens with his lineage, his upbringing in the city's training system despite a lameness he bore cheerfully, and his contested accession over Leotychides. The narrative follows his campaigns against Persian forces in Asia Minor, his estrangement from Lysander, and his command at the Battle of Coronea. The rise of Thebes under Epaminondas, the Spartan defeat at Leuctra, and the Theban invasion of Laconia occupy the later chapters. The work closes with Agesilaus's mercenary expedition to Egypt, where he served Tachos and then Nectanabis, and with his death at eighty-four on the journey home.
grc.plutarch.agis: Plutarch's Life of Agis profiles the Spartan king who sought to restore the Lycurgan constitution. The work opens with a reflection on the dangers of seeking glory, illustrated by the careers of the Gracchi. Agis and Cleomenes are then presented as a pair of Lacedaemonian demagogue kings comparable to those Roman reformers. The narrative follows Agis's proposals to cancel debts and redistribute land, which met strong resistance from King Leonidas and the wealthy. It details the treachery of Agesilaus, the burning of debt records, and Agis's campaign supporting the Achaeans against the Aetolians. The life concludes with his arrest, summary trial, and execution by strangling alongside his mother and grandmother.
grc.plutarch.alcibiades: Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades is a biographical account of the Athenian statesman and general, opening with his lineage from Eurysaces and the Alcmaeonids. The text details his upbringing under the guardianship of Pericles, while also noting his boyhood attachment to Socrates. The narrative follows his entry into politics and rivalry with Nicias, covering the ostracism of Hyperbolus and the Argive alliance. Alcibiades advocates for the great Sicilian expedition, but accusations of mutilating the Herms and profaning the Mysteries lead to his exile. He defects to Sparta and deals with Tissaphernes, before a triumphant recall brings naval victories at Abydus and Cyzicus. He wins at Byzantium but suffers renewed disgrace after Notium, and the work closes with the fall of Athens. It traces his wanderings in Thrace, Bithynia, and Phrygia, where he dies in a burning house. The final chapters attribute this death to Lysander or Pharnabazus.
grc.plutarch.alexander: Plutarch opens by declaring that he writes lives rather than histories, gathering signs of character from small words and deeds. The narrative follows Alexander from his birth amid portents, his schooling under Aristotle, and the taming of Bucephalus. It details his accession at twenty, the destruction of Thebes, and the expedition proclaimed against Persia. The main course covers the crossing into Asia, the victories at the Granicus, Issus, and Gaugamela, and the siege of Tyre. It also recounts the founding of Alexandria, the journey to the oracle of Ammon, and the capture of the Persian court. Alexander adopts Persian dress and customs while facing crises over Philotas, Cleitus, and Callisthenes. The army then moves into India, where Alexander fights Porus and endures a devastating return march through Gedrosia. The story concludes with the deaths of Hephaestion and Alexander in Babylon, along with rumors of poisoning and the fates of Roxane, Stateira, and Arrhidaeus.
grc.plutarch.amatoriae_narrationes: Amatoriae Narrationes, a short Greek collection of five local tales, is transmitted with the Moralia and attributed to Plutarch, though its date remains uncertain. The first story concerns Aristocleia of Aliartos, a Boeotian maiden who dies violently before her wedding, while the remaining narratives follow a pattern of desire, abduction, and retribution through local legend. Actaeon of Corinth is killed by his admirer Archias, an event that leads to the founding of Syracuse, and other tales include the outrage against Skeadas's daughters at Leuktra. The collection also recounts the killing of Phokos by Callirhoe's rejected suitors, as well as the deaths of the Spartan Alkippos's daughters and their mother Damokrita. Each tale is set in a named Boeotian or Peloponnesian town, and they close with vengeance, a divine sign, or a foundation bound to the disaster.
grc.plutarch.an_recte_dictum_sit_latenter_es: A short Greek philosophical essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, which takes up and refutes the Epicurean maxim lathe biōsas, 'live unnoticed.' The opening remarks on the paradox that Epicurus, in urging withdrawal from public life, did not himself conceal the precept, since to proclaim it was already to seek fame. The argument then likens hidden vice to sickness concealed from the physician, insists that virtue needs recognition in order to act, citing Epaminondas, Themistocles, Camillus, and Dion as benefactors who could not have helped humanity in obscurity, and treats knowledge as the light that gives honour and effective exercise to the virtues. It closes with a vision of the afterlife in which the wickedly obscure are punished not with bodily torments but in a realm of darkness, oblivion, and utter loss of reputation.
grc.plutarch.an_virtus_doceri_possit: Plutarch wrote this short moral essay, preserved in the Moralia under the title Whether Virtue Can Be Taught, which opens by asking why prudence and right living are held to be untaught, while singing, letters, and farming are learned. The author compares good men who exist in name only to centaurs or giants, and the argument then ranges over examples from crafts, households, and public life. It includes anecdotes about Diogenes, Aristippus, and Iphicrates, along with a reference to Plato on harmony, and contends that forbidding instruction would abolish virtue altogether. Denying its teachability while granting it to minor accomplishments resembles the Scythians blinding their slaves, and the essay closes by presenting prudence as the guiding order of all other arts. It argues that these arts are of no avail unless their practitioners are themselves trained and orderly, like educated attendants at a dinner.
grc.plutarch.an_vitiositas_ad_infelicitatem_: This short Greek moral essay by Plutarch appears in the Moralia, asking whether vice alone can make a person unhappy. It opens with a case from Euripides, describing a man with brief and insecure wealth who has no leisure to enjoy his Tantalus-like riches. The argument claims that vice needs no instruments to cause wretchedness, being more violent than fire or iron. Fortune and Vice are staged as rival contractors, bidding to make a man unlucky, while Fortune threatens poverty, slavery, poison, and the pyre. Figures like Socrates and Diogenes meet these threats with composure, and the essay closes by denying that Fortune can complete misery without vice. Vice alone softens and hollows out its victims, making even the rich and secure wretched.
grc.plutarch.aratus: Plutarch composed this Greek biography for his Lives, opening with an address to Polycrates as an ancestral model for his children. The narrative follows Aratus of Sicyon from his childhood escape from the tyrant Abantidas to the moonlit scaling of Sicyon's walls to overthrow Nicocles. It recounts Aratus's city joining the Achaean League and his covert capture of the Acrocorinthus, followed by campaigns against the tyrants of Argos and Megalopolis. The text covers his feud with Lydiades and the war with Cleomenes of Sparta, noting how the appeal to Antigonus Doson placed Corinth back in Macedonian hands. Aratus's growing estrangement from Philip V is noted, whose slow poison is said to have killed him, before a closing notice describes the honors paid to Aratus at Sicyon. This includes the annual Arateion and the madness of his son under Philip's drugs, ending with Philip's own downfall at Roman hands.
grc.plutarch.brutus: Plutarch's Life of Brutus is a Greek prose biography of Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Julius Caesar. It opens with Brutus's claimed descent from Junius Brutus, who expelled the Tarquins. The text also notes conflicting ancient reports about his ancestry through his mother Servilia. The narrative follows his upbringing under his uncle Cato and his attachment to the Old Academy of Plato. It details his terse Laconic manner in Greek letters and his mission to Cyprus on Cato's behalf. Finally, it describes his choice to join Pompey in the civil war against Caesar.
grc.plutarch.caius_marcius_coriolanus: Plutarch composed this Greek biography of the Roman patrician Gaius Marcius Coriolanus as part of his collection of Lives. The narrative opens with the distinction of the Marcian house and the orphaned Marcius's upbringing by his widowed mother Volumnia. His rise follows youthful military distinction and the capture of Corioli, whence he takes the surname Coriolanus. The story then traces his conflict with the plebs over grain and his failed bid for the consulship. These events lead to his prosecution, exile, and generalship for the Volscians alongside Tullus Aufidius. He campaigns through Latium to the walls of Rome, where the supplication of the Roman matrons led by his mother turns him back. Digressions treat the plebeian secession and Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly. They also cover Roman religious scruples over interrupted rites and customs of personal naming. The broken standing of Coriolanus among the Volscians ends in his violent death at Antium.
grc.plutarch.caius_marius: Plutarch composed this Greek biography of the Roman general Gaius Marius as part of his Parallel Lives. The work opens with a discussion of Roman naming customs and Marius's humble origins at Cirrhaeaton near Arpinum. It then traces his career from early service under Scipio Aemilianus through his tribuneship. The narrative follows his rise to command in the war against Jugurtha and his successive consulships against the Cimbri and Teutones. These campaigns included the battles at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae. The account concludes with his political rivalry with Sulla, exile, violent return to Rome alongside Cinna, a seventh consulship, and his death seventeen days into it, ending with the downfall of his son Marius.
grc.plutarch.cato_minor: Plutarch's Greek biography profiles Cato the Younger, a Roman senator known for his stubborn defense of the republic. The opening traces his lineage from Cato the Censor and gathers anecdotes of his severe temperament as an orphaned child under Sulla. The narrative then follows his public career, covering his austere private life and service in Rome's offices. It details his mission to convey royal treasure from Cyprus and his quarrels with Cicero, Clodius, Pompey, and Crassus. The text concludes with his suicide at Utica as Caesar approached, along with brief notices of his children at Philippi.
grc.plutarch.cimon: Plutarch pairs the Greek Life of Cimon with the Life of Lucullus in his Parallel Lives, justifying this union by noting that both generals shared valour and unfinished campaigns. The text opens with an anecdote about Damon of Chaeronea, an ancestor of Plutarch, whose murder of a Roman officer nearly ruined the city until Lucullus intervened. The narrative then traces Cimon's career from his obscure youth and devotion to his sister Elpinice, following his leadership of the Delian League and the victory at the Eurymedon. The account details the capture of Eion and Skyros and the return of Theseus's bones, while Cimon's lavish public generosity and philolaconian politics eventually led to his ostracism and recall. The work closes with his death during the expedition to Cyprus and the veneration of his memory.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aegisalius_pompey: This short Greek synkrisis, or formal comparison, is attributed to Plutarch and serves as the closing section of his paired biographies of the Spartan king Agesilaus and the Roman general Pompey. The text opens by announcing that the writer will quickly review the points of difference between the two men, beginning with their contrasting rises to power before weighing their specific actions. The essay examines their dealings with Sulla and Lysander, along with their transgressions in civil life, and also considers their political virtue and moments of good fortune or error. Finally, it compares their generalship, noting Pompey's abandonment of Rome and defeat at Pharsalus, which are set against Agesilaus's defence of a weakened Sparta and his later conduct in Egypt. The author acknowledges faults on either side and traces each man's failures to his character.
grc.plutarch.comparison_agis_cleomenes_gracc: This short Greek composition by Plutarch serves as the formal comparison closing his paired Lives of Agis and Cleomenes and of the Gracchi. It weighs the Spartan kings against the Roman brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, opening by noting that the narrative has ended. The text first examines the natural gifts and upbringing of the two pairs, then assesses their continence with money. It also considers their political innovations, achievements in war, deaths, conduct of revolutions, and the specific charges brought against them. The work closes by awarding first place in virtue to Tiberius, finding Agis the least at fault of the Spartans. It ranks Gaius and Cleomenes together in daring, completing the final assessment of these historical figures.
grc.plutarch.comparison_alcibiades_coriolanu: Plutarch wrote this short comparative essay in Greek as the formal closing to his paired Lives of Alcibiades and Coriolanus. The text opens by judging their military exploits as evenly matched, with neither commander holding a decisive advantage in daring or generalship. It then contrasts their political careers, pitting Alcibiades' brilliant but demagogic charm against Coriolanus' proud and unyielding oligarchic temper. The essay weighs their conduct over money and the resentment each aroused at home. It also examines the disasters each brought upon his city through anger and their differing ends in exile. Plutarch concludes that Coriolanus surpassed Alcibiades in temperance and self-command, deserving to be ranked with the purest of the Greeks.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_demosthenes_with_: Plutarch wrote this short Greek synkrisis, or formal comparison, to conclude his paired Lives of Demosthenes and Cicero. The text weighs the rhetorical powers and styles of the two orators. It then turns to their characters as these appear in their speeches. The author treats their humour, gravity, and self-display. Further sections contrast the authority each held and how he used it. They also compare their conduct toward money and royal gifts, and the differing circumstances of their flights and downfalls.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_dion_and_brutus: Plutarch's Comparison of Dion and Brutus serves as the formal conclusion to his paired biographies, weighing the Syracusan statesman against the Roman tyrannicide in Greek. It opens by noting that both men achieved great things with slight advantages, as Dion lacked a partner of Cassius's calibre and advanced his own fortune for the war. The work sets their dissimilar tyrants side by side for comparison, judging Dionysius's open tyranny an easier mark than Caesar's popular rule. The author then assesses their conduct as generals and the purity of their motives, also examining their choice of friends and partisans. Dion's trust in corrupt associates contrasts with Brutus's single minded purpose, and the piece closes with an anecdote about a bronze statue of Brutus at Mediolanum. Caesar threatened the city but smilingly praised the Gauls for their fidelity, ordering the statue to remain in its place.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lucullus_and_cimo: This short formal comparison in Greek closes Plutarch's paired biographies of Lucullus and Cimon, opening by judging Lucullus fortunate in his end, since he died before the civil wars he foresaw. His country was still free, a lot shared with Cimon, and the remainder weighs the two men point against point. It contrasts their use of wealth and taste for luxury, while comparing their successes by land and sea. Cimon won a single-day victory combining land battle and naval action for Greece, whereas Lucullus campaigned beyond the Taurus and across the Tigris. He captured Tigranocerta, Cabira, Sinope, and Nisibis, and the text also notes their standing with soldiers and allies. Both men experienced political prosecution and ostracism, concluding that both were favoured by the gods, the one shown what to achieve, the other what to guard against.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lycurgus_and_numa: Plutarch composed this brief Greek comparison, known as a synkrisis, to accompany his lives of Lycurgus and Numa Pompilius. The text opens by gathering the points of difference between these two ancient lawgivers. It first outlines their shared qualities, including moderation, piety, and divine sanction for their legislation. The author then weighs their contrasts, such as Numa's acceptance of kingship versus Lycurgus's voluntary surrender of it. Further differences include the harsher task of taming Sparta against Numa's gentler ordering of Rome. The piece closes by noting that Lycurgus's laws endured for five hundred years, while Numa's peace collapsed soon after his death.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_philopoemen_and_t: This brief Greek synkrisis weighs the Achaean general Philopoemen against the Roman Titus Quinctius Flamininus, rounding off the pair of lives devoted to these two figures. Plutarch opens by conceding Titus's superiority in the magnitude of his services to Greece, having defeated Philip and liberated the Greek cities when Philopoemen had withdrawn to Crete. The argument then sets their failings side by side, ascribing Philopoemen's missteps to ambition and a hot temper, while Titus's stem from contentiousness. The text credits Philopoemen with far wider and more personal military experience, gained in countless battles and through his own redesign of arms and tactics. He proved no less effective as a private citizen than as a commander, and the essay ends by finding the balance hard to determine. It proposes to award the Greek the crown of martial skill and the Roman that of justice and goodness.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_theseus_and_romul: Plutarch's Comparison of Theseus and Romulus is the short formal synkrisis that closes the paired biographies of the two founders in his Lives. The title means a formal comparison of the two heroes. It opens by weighing their first motives, contrasting Theseus's self-chosen ambition from a secure kingship at Troezen with Romulus's flight from servitude. The comparison then proceeds point by point through their exploits against tyrants and robbers, their daring in war, and the love of Ariadne. It also examines their divergent political temperaments, their lapses toward brother and son, and the founding and unification of cities. The text concludes on matters divine, contrasting Romulus's providentially favored preservation with the oracle to Aegeus that cast Theseus's begetting as against the will of the gods.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_apollonium: This Greek essay, preserved in Plutarch's Moralia, consoles Apollonius on the early death of his son, who is described as disciplined, pious, and philanthropic. The speaker concedes that some grief is natural but argues for rational moderation, citing Homer, Pindar, Euripides, and Socrates to show that death is no evil. Plato's myth of the judgement of souls from the Gorgias is also incorporated, and stories of divine favour and comely fathers like Pericles and Demosthenes follow. The text suggests untimely death may spare future suffering, closing by urging Apollonius to honour his son through grateful memory.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_uxorem: Plutarch wrote this Greek letter of consolation to his wife Timoxena after their infant daughter died, and the text was transmitted with the Moralia, a collection of his ethical essays. It opens with news of the child's death and directions for a simple burial, then appeals to his wife to moderate her sorrow. He argues that excessive grief is both irrational and harmful to the mind, while praising Timoxena's composure before visitors and recalling the daughter's affectionate nature. Plutarch warns against ostentatious lamentation and urges that the mind dwell on the bright parts of a life. A closing section appeals to Dionysiac teaching on the soul's immortality and to ancestral custom concerning the burial of very young children.
grc.plutarch.crassus: Plutarch's Life of Marcus Licinius Crassus opens with the Roman triumvir's frugal upbringing, then turns to the avarice that Romans regarded as his dominant vice. The narrative traces his vast fortune built from Sulla's proscriptions and cheap ruined houses, detailing his flight to Spain and eight months hidden in a seaside cave. His service under Sulla and rivalry with Pompey for public standing follow, leading into a continuous account of the gladiatorial war led by Spartacus. This section covers the outbreak at Capua and the defeats of Roman commanders, describing Crassus' appointment, the decimation of troops, and the wall across the Bruttian isthmus. The final battle saw Spartacus die while Pompey claimed credit for ending the war, and the life closes with the joint consulship and reconciliation engineered by Caesar. The triumvirate and the conference at Luca are also recounted, detailing Crassus' Syrian command and Parthian invasion against omens and warnings. The disaster of the desert march and the death of his son Publius are noted, concluding with his own death amid Surena's treachery at Carrhae. The insulting mock triumph and grotesque scenes at the Parthian court follow, ending with the retribution that later overtook Surena and Hyrodes.
grc.plutarch.de_alexandri_magni_fortuna_aut_: This Greek declamatory essay from Plutarch's Moralia stages a contest between Fortune and Virtue, asking which force deserves credit for Alexander's conquests. It opens with Fortune personified, claiming Alexander as her own peculiar work, and she provokes an answer on behalf of philosophy. The argument that follows attributes his empire instead to his virtue, including his schooling under Aristotle and his founding of cities. He mingled Macedonians and Persians in one common civic life, and his magnanimity toward the family of Darius also stands out. The text notes his maxims and patronage of artists, while it lists a long catalog of wounds and hardships. The closing contention is that Fortune opposed rather than aided him, thus his greatness belongs to virtue and not to chance.
grc.plutarch.de_amore_prolis: De Amore Prolis, meaning On Affection for Offspring, is a Greek prose treatise by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia. The work argues that parental love is natural and freely given, contrasting this with the laws, honours, and incentives that induce humans to marry and rear children. The author relies on copious natural observation to make his case, describing the kingfisher's woven nest, the viviparous sharks, and the bear's licking of her formless cubs. The text also notes the partridge's diversion of hunters and the care shown by hens, dogs, and horses. It closes by setting the beasts up as witnesses against a human nature that alone appears to love for a price.
grc.plutarch.de_capienda_ex_inimicis_utilita: Plutarch wrote this short Greek moral essay for Cornelius Pulcher, exploring the theme of turning hostility to one's advantage. The text notes that public life is never free of envy and strife, where friendships and enmities interweave in complex ways. Profiting from enemies therefore deserves serious examination, as the discussion ranges widely across several key points. Enemies watch a man's affairs more closely than friends do, and their scrutiny encourages vigilance and self-improvement. Abuse and insult can serve as correction, while flattery often silences candid friendship. Enduring reviling without anger exercises self-command, and showing fairness toward an enemy purges envy. Praising a rival's merits helps achieve this goal, and such actions prevent contentiousness from being spent on friends. Instances from Greek and Roman history illustrate the argument, with Chilon and Socrates appearing in these examples. Themistocles, Cicero, and Cato are also cited.
grc.plutarch.de_communibus_notitiis_adversus: This Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, preserved within the Moralia, opens with Lamprias telling Diadoumenus that his Stoic friends have disturbed him. They philosophize contrary to the common conceptions shared by all humankind, and the work then systematically prosecutes Stoic doctrine on those grounds. It examines the Stoic account of goods and indifferents, as well as the paradoxes concerning the sage. The text also challenges the claim that vice is useful to the whole, and it further critiques the theology of the conflagration in which only Zeus survives. The dialogue addresses physical teachings on mixture, the infinite division of bodies, and time, while also considering growth, the soul, and the elements. Chrysippus is quoted extensively throughout the text, and his formulations are repeatedly charged with overturning universal preconceptions that the Stoics themselves claim to follow.
grc.plutarch.de_cupiditate_divitiarum: This short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, is devoted to the love of wealth. It opens with an anecdote about the trainer Hippomachus, who remarks that a long-armed boxer should take down a hanging crown. This image applies to those who marvel at fine estates and heaps of silver, acting as though happiness were for sale. The argument is illustrated with anecdotes of Aristippus, Demades, and Phocion, showing that wealth cures no evil but the love of wealth itself. Greed is an insatiable sickness of the soul that calls for purgation, and no one is poor who has enough. The acquisitive man is filled with desires for gold, ivory, and emeralds, passing his life in debts, lawsuits, and anxiety. Plutarch distinguishes the petty miser from the rapacious kind, who takes from others what he cannot use. He condemns parents who bequeath avarice to their children, and the essay closes by contrasting wealth with virtue and wisdom. Wealth is blind without spectators and stages banquets for an audience, while virtue and wisdom keep their own light even when no one is watching.
grc.plutarch.de_curiositate: A short Greek moral treatise by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia and known by its Latin title De Curiositate, on polypragmosyne, the invasive curiosity that hunts out other people's affairs and misfortunes. It opens with the image of a dark and unhealthy house that cannot be fled but can be brightened by shifting the light and rearranging the doors, a figure applied to the treatment of the disease of curiosity. The argument portrays the busybody who scrutinizes others' failings while remaining blind to his own, likens him to the Lamia that stores her eyes in a vessel at home, and sets the vice beside envy, spite, adultery, and slander. Anecdotes from myth and history, from Oedipus and Aristippus to Alexander and Plutarch's recollection of Rusticus under Domitian, give way to practical training: small exercises of restraint such as ignoring wall inscriptions and postponing the opening of letters, and the deliberate turning of inquisitiveness toward nature, plants, and history.
grc.plutarch.de_defectu_oraculorum: Plutarch's De defectu oraculorum, a dialogue from the Moralia, opens with a mythical account of eagles and swans converging on the Delphic omphalos. Epimenides offers an ambiguous oracle about this event, while a company at Delphi asks why the oracles of Greece have fallen silent. The group includes Lamprias, the philosopher Ammonius, and the grammarian Demetrius returning from Britain, with the widely traveled Spartan Cleombrotus also joining the discussion. Successive speakers weigh depopulation and the daimones who mediate between gods and humans, and they also consider the report of the great god Pan's demise. The conversation then ranges over Platonic cosmology and debates over the number of worlds, examining the significance of the five regular solids before turning to physical explanations. Mantic exhalations rising from the earth are discussed alongside the temperament required of the Pythia, and the recent fatal breakdown of a prophetess at the shrine is also noted. The question whether Apollo is to be identified with the sun remains open at the close.
grc.plutarch.de_e_delphos: De E Delphos, a Greek dialogue by Plutarch preserved among the Moralia, opens with the narrator sending excerpts of his Pythian discourses to friends. He recalls how guests about to leave Delphi caught him near the temple, reviving a question first debated there in the time of Nero. The company asks why the single letter E is inscribed in the temple of Apollo, and Ammonius, Lamprias, Theon, Eustrophus, and Nicander successively interpret the letter. They view it as the numeral five, supported by Pythagorean and Platonic speculation on fives in number, music, geometry, the senses, and the soul. They also read it as the dialectical connective 'if', or as a token of the alternating regimes of Apollo and Dionysus. In the closing discussion, the E is finally read as 'Thou art', a salutation owed to a god who alone, timeless and unchanging, truly is, standing against the 'Know thyself' addressed to mortals swept through birth and destruction.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium: De Esu Carnium, a Greek prose diatribe attributed to Plutarch, appears in the Moralia and argues for abstinence from animal flesh. The speaker asks what passion led humans to eat meat, suggesting early humans ate flesh only out of desperate necessity. Since the earth now yields abundance, slaughter is wanton, and human teeth and digestion mark the body as unfit for meat. Cooking and seasoning merely disguise the act of murder, while heavy meat diets are said to dull the intelligence of the soul. The text closes by invoking Diogenes eating a raw octopus and cites an Athenian prosecution for flaying a ram alive. It includes Empedocles' doctrine of souls atoning for bloodshed and treats the Dionysian myth of the Titans as a riddle concerning the punishment of the irrational element in human nature.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium_2: This Greek prose essay by Plutarch forms the second book of his work On the Eating of Meat, arguing for abstinence from animal flesh and opening with an exhortation to purify the mind. The author likens the habit of eating freshly slaughtered meat to a hook lodged fast in pleasure, maintaining that flesh eating arises from gluttony and luxury rather than necessity. The text catalogues brutal culinary practices and traces how unrestrained appetite corrupts the senses, also arguing that such habits breed lawlessness in every other pleasure. Plutarch then takes up the question of justice toward irrational animals, appealing to the abstinence taught by Pythagoras and Empedocles. The essay weighs the doctrine of the transmigration of souls, noting that even an unproved belief warrants caution in killing. He rebuts the Stoic denial of any justice toward animals, closing by urging each person to examine his own passions on the question.
grc.plutarch.de_exilio: De Exilio (On Exile) is a consolatory essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia and addressed to a friend banished from Sardis. It opens by arguing that speeches, like friends, prove their worth by being present and useful in misfortune, so that consolation should teach rather than join in lamentation. Exile, it contends, is no genuine evil, since grief rests on judgment rather than on things themselves, and the whole earth, or even the cosmos, is a person's true fatherland. Along the way it cites celebrated exiles such as Themistocles, Diogenes, Thucydides and Xenophon, who flourished away from their native cities. The essay praises the leisure, quiet and freedom of island life and answers Euripides' attacks on exile. It closes with the thought that the soul itself is an exile from heaven, making all humankind wanderers and strangers.
grc.plutarch.de_fato: Plutarch's short treatise On Fate, addressed to Piso, opens with a promise to set out concisely what appears true concerning fate. It distinguishes fate as activity from fate as substance, tracing the former in Plato's ordinance of Adrasteia in the Phaedrus, the laws spoken by the god in the Timaeus, and the speech of Lachesis in the Republic, and defining the latter as the world-soul distributed among Clotho, Atropos, and Lachesis. The argument presents fate as a finite, cyclical order comparable to a divine law that governs universals while particulars follow in their train, then sets fate in relation to providence, chance, the spontaneous, the possible, and what is up to us, treating chance as an incidental cause on the model of the Phaedo's account of the sacred ship to Delos and ranking providence in three grades, from the first god through the celestial gods to the earthbound daimones who oversee human affairs. It closes by summarizing the headings to be tested against the opposing doctrine that places everything under fate through prior causes, cosmic sympathy, divination, the sage's acceptance of events, and the principle that every assertion is either true or false.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna_romanorum: A rhetorical essay in Greek by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, which takes up the question whether Roman hegemony was the work of Fortune or of Virtue. It opens with the two personified powers, long rivals in great contests, meeting in a personified courtroom to plead their claims, and with the speaker's proposal that they more plausibly joined forces, as fire and earth combine in Plato's cosmos, to fashion the greatest of human achievements. The body of the work summons Roman witnesses for Fortune, Numa Pompilius, Aemilius Paullus, Sulla, Caesar and Augustus among them, and then turns to Rome's own history for evidence, from the exposure and she-wolf nurture of Romulus, through Numa's long peace, the cults and epithets of Fortune in the city, and Servius Tullius's rise from a captive household, to the Gallic sack repelled by the sacred geese, Caesar's storm-borne crossing against Pompey, and the triumph of Augustus over Antony and Cleopatra. Throughout, temples, omens and anecdotes, such as Caesar committing his sails to his own Fortune, are marshalled as testimony that Rome's empire was wrought by Virtue and Fortune together.
grc.plutarch.de_fraterno_amore: De Fraterno Amore, a Greek ethical treatise by Plutarch, examines the affection and concord owed between brothers. The work opens with a dedication to Nigrinus and Quintus, using the Spartan dokana as an emblem of a shared yet indivisible bond. The argument surveys sources of quarrels, including competition for parental favor, property disputes, inequality, and interference from wives and flatterers. It sets out how elder and younger, abler and less fortunate siblings should conduct themselves. Historical exempla, such as Athenodorus' forbearance toward Xenon, Ariamenes' submission to Xerxes, and Attalus' restoration of the kingdom to Eumenes, illustrate the rewards of magnanimity.
grc.plutarch.de_garrulitate: Plutarch's Greek moral essay On Talkativeness opens with the claim that philosophy can scarcely cure garrulity, since its medicine is speech and the garrulous listen to no one. The argument first exposes the fault as ridiculous, hateful, and dangerous, illustrating the harm with anecdotes of ruined friendships and betrayed confidences. Aristotle is badgered by a bore, and Zeno bites off his tongue, while a barber earns the wheel for reporting a Sicilian disaster. Idle talk lets Sulla into Athens and nearly undoes a plot against Nero, and Fulvius is driven to suicide after revealing Augustus' secret. The latter part turns prescriptive, praising silence and Laconic brevity, and it sets out exercises of restraint, such as letting others answer questions first. Readers should proportion each reply to the questioner's need, avoiding well-worn battle stories and travel reminiscences, and writing rather than speaking is advised, as is keeping company with elders. The essay closes on the Simonidean maxim that a man often repents of speaking, but he never repents of holding his peace.
grc.plutarch.de_genio_socratis: This Greek dialogue by Plutarch is set in Thebes before the fall of a Spartan backed oligarchy, opening with Caphisias, brother of Epameinondas, recounting a conspiracy to Archidamus. The plot targets the ruling archons Archias and Leontidas, and the narrative follows the assassination of these tyrants and the freeing of prisoners. It also covers the surrender of the Cadmea fortress, while philosophical discussions on Socrates' daimonion and omens thread through the story. The Pythagorean Theanor arrives concerning Lysis during these debates, and Timarchus later descends into the cave of Trophonius. There he beholds cosmic islands, the Styx, the moon, and guiding daimones.
grc.plutarch.de_gloria_atheniensium: This Greek essay by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia, weighs the glory of Athens' generals against that of its poets, historians, and orators. It opens with a saying of Themistocles to his commanders, noting that removing men of action leaves no writers. A catalogue of Athenian exploits follows, ranging from Pericles and Cimon to Thrasybulus and Conon. The argument then considers Simonides' comparison of painting with silent poetry and the vividness of Thucydides. Anecdotes about Homer, Pindar, Menander, and Corinna illustrate the city's lack of a renowned epic or lyric poet. The text also addresses the splendour of tragedy and the victories celebrated by festivals. It closes by subjecting the orators, above all Isocrates and Demosthenes, to an unfavourable comparison with military achievement.
grc.plutarch.de_invidia_et_odio: This short Greek treatise from Plutarch's Moralia contrasts the passions of envy and hatred, opening by allowing that the two seem scarcely to differ. It then distinguishes them at length, noting that hatred springs from the impression of another's wickedness and can extend even to animals. Envy is felt only by human beings toward human good fortune and admits no justification, as the discussion traces how the passions grow. Envy fastens on rising virtue and reputation, while hatred fixes on deepening vice, and overwhelming success extinguishes envy but not hatred, as Alexander's fate shows. The means which dissolve enmity leave envy untouched, defining hatred as a settled intent to do harm. The envious begrudge their neighbours' prosperity without wishing them ruin, casting shade on a tall house rather than tearing it down.
grc.plutarch.de_iside_et_osiride: Plutarch's treatise On Isis and Osiris, preserved among the Moralia, takes the form of a letter addressed to Clea, a priestess at Delphi. It opens by claiming that the highest gift from the gods is truthful knowledge of them, then retells the Egyptian myth of Osiris and Typhon in summary form. This narrative covers the birth of the gods on the five epagomenal days, and it also details Typhon's murder and dismemberment of Osiris. The story continues with Isis's quest for his body and the conflict between Horus and Typhon, after which Plutarch subjects this myth to a series of philosophical interpretations. Successive explanations identify the gods with the Nile's inundation and the powers of moisture and drought, and they also link them to solar and lunar phenomena. The text further connects the deities to the two opposing principles governing the cosmos, drawing comparisons with Persian dualism and Chaldaean doctrine, while the author cites the views of Pythagoreans, Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics. The final sections treat the sacred animals of Egypt and ritual dietary observances, and they also examine the symbolism of priestly garments and daily incense offerings. Each element is interpreted through a mixture of natural philosophy and moral allegory, and the author insists that these rites be read with reverent understanding rather than literally.
grc.plutarch.de_primo_frigido: De Primo Frigido, a short Greek dialogue from Plutarch's Moralia, is addressed to Favorinus and opens by asking whether cold is a primary power. The speaker argues that cold has degrees, is directly sensed, and produces real effects such as freezing, contraction, and hardening. These observations suggest that cold cannot be a mere absence of heat, so the text examines rival doctrines that assign the primary cold to air or water. These claims are tested against observations of frost, snow, rivers, and wells, while contrasting climates of regions such as Libya and Scythia are also considered. The dialogue concludes that the earth itself is the primary principle of cold, closing with counsel to hold judgement in suspense where matters remain uncertain.
grc.plutarch.de_pythiae_oraculis: De Pythiae Oraculis ('On the Oracles of the Pythia') is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch set at the sanctuary of Delphi. The scene opens as Basilocles greets Philinus, who has spent the day showing Diogenianus the local votive offerings. Their conversation moves from the blue sheen of bronze dedications to omens attached to statues of Hieron and Lysander. The central question asks why the Pythia no longer delivers oracles in verse and whether the prophetic power has left the shrine. Theon leads the response by defending the oracle's continued operation and comparing the Pythia's inspiration to the moon receiving sunlight. He explains the shift from verse to plain speech as a consequence of changes in Greek life and language.
grc.plutarch.de_recta_ratione_audiendi: Plutarch wrote this short Greek moral essay for a reader named Nicander. It explains how young people should receive philosophical instruction through lectures. The title means 'How a Young Man Should Hear Lecturers.' The opening warns that freedom without education enslaves a person to their appetites. The main body teaches listeners to remain silent and weigh the content of speech rather than the speaker's reputation. It also advises curbing envy and asking only questions that serve understanding. The essay concludes by urging that praise be measured and sincere. It asserts that hearing well is the beginning of living well.
grc.plutarch.de_se_ipsum_citra_invidiam_laud: This short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to Herclanus, explores how a public figure may speak of his own merits without incurring envy. The title means 'On Self-Praise', and the text opens by observing that self-praise is universally condemned as tasteless and illiberal. Yet few refrain from it in practice, as noted by Euripides and Pindar, and the discussion then surveys the circumstances in which such praise becomes legitimate. These include defence against accusation, adversity, or injury, as well as the wish to rouse or restrain an audience. The essay details devices that blunt the offensiveness of self-praise, including ascribing success to fortune or divine favour, acknowledging minor faults or humble origins, and shifting praise from ability to character. The text closes with warnings about deceptive occasions where the habit insinuates itself, such as praising others, recounting one's own deeds, censuring contemporaries, or accepting praise from those present.
grc.plutarch.de_sollertia_animalium: De sollertia animalium is a Greek prose dialogue by Plutarch that appears in the Moralia and features a contest between champions of the chase and the sea. Younger members of a Chaeronean circle debate whether land or marine creatures show greater intelligence, with Optatos serving as the arbiter of this intellectual contest. Autoboulos opens the discussion by fearing that a recent encomium of hunting has fired the young men's passion, noting that the debate follows a prior inquiry into whether all animals share in reason. Aristotimos pleads the land animals' cause with catalogues of elephants, dogs, ants, bees, and foxes, while Herakleon answers for the sea with the stratagems of fish against nets and hooks. He also cites the tunny's arithmetic and the dolphin's friendship toward humans, and the interlocutors weigh whether justice can extend to animals, canvassing Stoic and Epicurean denials alongside the positions of Empedocles and Pythagoras. Tales of dolphins rescuing men are also included in this ethical inquiry, and the speeches close with judgment reserved for the arbiter, as Soclarus proposes to ask Optatos to join the two cases against those who strip animals of reason.
grc.plutarch.de_tranquilitate_animi: Plutarch's De Tranquillitate Animi, a Greek moral essay on euthymia, opens as a letter to Paccius, where the author excuses a delayed reply to his correspondent's request for advice on peace of mind. The writer offers reflections gathered from his own notebooks to address this specific inquiry, arguing that contentment depends not on withdrawal from activity but on the right disposition of the soul. It criticises the Epicurean counsel of inaction and treats the pitfalls of ambition and envy, while also covering the acceptance of one's own nature and circumstances. The text further discusses the premeditation of misfortune and death, as well as the corrosive effect of remorse, illustrating these points with anecdotes and quotations drawn from poets and philosophers. The work closes by likening the tranquil life to a continuous festival in which the world itself is a sacred temple.
grc.plutarch.lycurgus: Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus recounts the career of the semi-legendary Spartan lawgiver, noting that even his genealogy, travels, and dates are disputed among ancient historians. The narrative traces his regency for the infant Charilaus and his journeys to Crete, Asia, and Egypt, after which he returned to reform Sparta under the sanction of a Delphic oracle. He established the council of elders, a redistribution of land, an iron currency, and the common messes, while further sections describe the training of girls and boys, marriage customs, and the Laconic brevity of speech. The text also covers military and musical practice, the treatment of the helots, and the disputed institution of the krypteia, before closing with Lycurgus's second consultation at Delphi and the oath binding his countrymen to the constitution until his return. His deliberate death followed, after which his laws are said to have endured for some five hundred years.
grc.plutarch.marcellus: Plutarch's Life of Marcellus recounts the career of Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the Roman general who fought the Gauls of northern Italy and later opposed Hannibal during the Second Punic War. The biography opens with his lineage, his martial temperament, and early distinctions such as rescuing a brother in Sicily and winning election as aedile. It then follows his campaigns against the Insubres and Gaesatae, culminating in his killing of the Gallic king in single combat and his dedication of the spoils to Jupiter Feretrius. The narrative turns to the battles with Hannibal at Nola and the siege and capture of Syracuse, dwelling at length on the war machines of Archimedes and the mathematician's death. Marcellus shows clemency toward the conquered Syracusans and removes Greek art to Rome, while holding repeated consulships and fighting further engagements with Hannibal. The work ends with his death in an ambush and a notice of his descendants, down to the Marcellus who was nephew and son-in-law of Augustus.
grc.plutarch.marcus_cato: Plutarch's Life of Marcus Cato begins with the subject's Sabine origins and frugal rural upbringing, following Cato the Elder through military service from age seventeen in the war against Hannibal. His political rise came under the patronage of Valerius Flaccus, leading to a consulship and governorship of Hither Spain, which was crowned with a triumph and his part in the victory over Antiochus at Thermopylae. A censorate marked by sumptuary measures and the expulsion of Lucius Quinctius Flamininus from the senate followed, while apothegms, courtroom prosecutions, and hostility to Greek philosophy and luxury were woven through the account. He also cared for his son's education and worked as an orator and author, before the Life closes with the aged Cato's insistence that Carthage must be destroyed. It ends with his death as the Third Punic War began.
grc.plutarch.numa: Plutarch's Life of Numa recounts the career of Numa Pompilius, the Sabine successor of Romulus as king of Rome. The text opens with a survey of conflicting chronological traditions about Numa's era, including the report that he was an associate of Pythagoras. It then narrates the disappearance and deification of Romulus, the interregnum, and Numa's election from among the Sabines. Numa reluctantly accepted the throne after favorable omens, before moving through his religious and civic legislation. This included the pontificate, the Vestal Virgins, bloodless sacrifice, and the temples of Fides and Terminus. The work closes with Numa's gentle death, the burial of his sacred books, and a contrast with the violent fates of the kings who followed him.
grc.plutarch.pelopidas: Plutarch's Pelopidas, a Greek biographical parallel life, narrates the career of the Theban general Pelopidas. It opens with a preface on commanders who expose themselves to danger and on the famous friendship between Pelopidas and Epameinondas. The narrative recounts his role in liberating Thebes from the Spartan-occupied Cadmea, his command of the Sacred Band, and the victories at Tegyrae and Leuctra that broke Spartan supremacy. Later sections follow his campaigns, his embassy to the Persian king Artaxerxes, and his death fighting the tyrant Alexander of Pherae. The life closes with the assassination of Alexander by the tyrant's wife Thebe. Pelopidas is paired with the life of the Roman Marcellus, with whom he is compared for his boldness in battle and his death in the service of his city.
grc.plutarch.phocion: This Parallel Life recounts the career of Phocion, an austere fourth-century Athenian general whose unbending integrity ran counter to Macedonia-dominated politics. The text opens by setting his virtue against Cato the Younger, whose similarly rigid character brought him no favour amid Rome's corrupt times. The narrative follows his blunt interventions in the assembly and his resistance to Demosthenes, while also detailing his refusal of Harpalus's gold and his counsel against the Lamian War. Phocion was finally condemned on a treason charge, which he met with undisturbed composure, and he drank hemlock alongside his companions, causing the people to feel belated remorse. His wife buried his ashes at their hearth, and his son executed his accusers, while the work closes by reflecting that the city's treatment of Phocion recalled its condemnation of Socrates.
grc.plutarch.pompey: Plutarch composed this Greek biography of Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus as part of his Parallel Lives, opening with the Roman people's early loathing of Pompey's father, Strabo. This hostility contrasts sharply with the son's winning appearance and manner, which drew comparison with portraits of Alexander. The narrative follows his rise under Sulla, including commands in Sicily and Africa, and his triumph over Sulla's objection. He fought the Spanish war against Sertorius, cleared pirates from the Mediterranean, and defeated Mithridates, capping his sweeping settlement of the eastern provinces with a third triumph. Later chapters cover his dominance in Roman politics and his alliance with Caesar and Crassus, which eventually led to civil war and his defeat at Pharsalus. He was murdered on the Egyptian shore at the order of Ptolemy's courtiers, and the text closes with the fate of his assassins and the burial of his remains.
grc.plutarch.pyrrhus: Plutarch's Life of Pyrrhus is a Greek biographical account of the Epirot king and general, tracing his turbulent career from childhood to his death in battle. The text opens with the legendary genealogy of the Molossian kings, then describes the infancy of Pyrrhus, who is smuggled out of Epirus and saved at the Illyrian court of Glaukias. The narrative follows his seizure of the throne and his service under Demetrius and Ptolemy, detailing his brief conquest of Macedonia and his western wars against Rome. These conflicts include the battles at Heraclea and Asculum, and the account also covers his war against the Carthaginians in Sicily. After his failed invasion of the Peloponnese, the work closes with his death amid the confused street fighting at Argos.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_graecae: Plutarch's Greek Questions, preserved among the Moralia, gathers brief answers to obscure local terms and customs. The title refers to inquiries concerning the Greek world. The work opens by asking who the konipodes and artynoi of Epidaurus were. It explains the council of one hundred and eighty men and their dusty feet. Other items address the punishment of adulterous women at Cyme and magistrates called the forgetful at Cnidus. The collection also covers Delphic festivals, the month Bysios, and the origins of proverbial sayings. It closes with the wagon rollers of Megara, whose ancestors overturned a ceremonial procession into a lake.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_naturales: The Quaestiones Naturales is a short Greek treatise by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia, made up of brief question-and-answer discussions of natural and physical puzzles in the tradition of the Peripatetic problemata. It opens by asking why sea water does not nourish trees, weighing one possible explanation after another, some drawn from Plato, Anaxagoras and Democritus. The same pattern of 'why' question, rival hypotheses and appeal to earlier authorities carries the work through such varied topics as the superiority of rainwater and thunderstorms for seeds, the salting of livestock, the breeding and behaviour of pigs, bears and other animals, the conditions that defeat tracking at the full moon or in frost, and the effects of cold and wine on must and vines, with quotations from writers including Empedocles, Aristotle, Heracleitus, Aratus and Alcman. Each question is handled on its own, so that the whole reads as an unordered series of explanations rather than a connected argument.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_romanae: The Quaestiones Romanae ('Roman Questions') is a treatise by the Greek author Plutarch. It is transmitted among his Moralia and consists of a long series of short questions. Each question concerns Roman religious, social, or political customs. The text opens by asking why a Roman bride is bidden to touch fire and water. Subsequent inquiries range over wedding and funeral rites, festivals, and civic institutions. Explanations are commonly given in the alternative, with earlier writers such as Varro and Cicero cited by name. The treatments mix etymology, mythology, and philosophical speculation about the meaning of Roman practice.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adolescens_poetas_audir: This prose treatise from Plutarch's Moralia is addressed to Marcus Sedatus on behalf of his son Cleander, arguing that young men beginning to read the poets should be trained in moral judgement rather than kept from poetry altogether. The opening treats poetic reading like diet, drawing on Philoxenus' remark about the choicest meats, while Plutarch describes poetry as a medicine that mixes pleasure and profit. He sets out ways of steering the young reader by distinguishing praise from blame in Homer, and the essay also covers understanding the poets' imitation of flawed characters. Plutarch suggests supplementing objectionable statements with philosophical doctrine and attending to the poets' own hints of disapproval, urging that poetry, so handled, serves as a preparatory discipline that leads the young gently towards philosophy.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_quis_suos_in_virtute_se: This ethical essay by Plutarch, preserved within the Moralia, is addressed to Sossius Senecio and explores how a philosopher can recognize his own progress toward virtue. The text opens by asking how improvement can be perceived while vice still weighs the soul down like lead, and it rejects the idea that the shift from folly to wisdom happens in a single instant. The main body lists observable marks of advance, such as steady study and mildness in disputation, and it also notes a changed manner of reading that values the useful over the ornamental. The author further highlights willingness to accept criticism and to confess one's own faults, and calm dreams, tempered passions, and zealous imitation of good men are also cited. The argument is illustrated with anecdotes from figures like Sextius, Diogenes, and Demosthenes.
grc.plutarch.romulus: Plutarch's Life of Romulus, written in Greek as part of the Parallel Lives, recounts the founding of Rome. It opens with a survey of conflicting ancient accounts of the city's name and origins before turning to the exposure and nurture of Romulus and Remus. The narrative then covers the overthrow of Amulius, the founding of the city, the rape of the Sabine women, and the wars with Acron and the Sabines under Tatius. After the joint kingship comes the establishment of Rome's political and religious institutions, along with various etymologies of Roman customs and place-names. The life closes with Tatius's death, Romulus's increasingly autocratic rule, his mysterious disappearance in a storm, and the senator Julius Proculus's report of his apotheosis as Quirinus. A final discussion turns to Romulus's age at death and to the divine honours paid to men of virtue.
grc.plutarch.septem_sapientium_convivium: Plutarch's Greek dialogue, preserved in the Moralia, is titled Septem Sapientium Convivium, or the Dinner of the Seven Wise Men. The narrator Diocles promises Nicarchus a truthful account of the famous banquet, noting that earlier reports erred and the company was larger than the traditional seven sages. The scene is a reception prepared by Periander of Corinth at a sanctuary of Aphrodite near Lechaeum, where Thales, Solon, Bias, Pittacus, Chilon, Cleobulus, and Anacharsis recline alongside Aesop and other guests. Their table talk ranges over monarchy, tyranny, and the best constitution, and they also discuss household economy and the proper measure of food and drink at symposia. Narrated episodes intersperse the conversation, including Arion's rescue by dolphins and the death of Hesiod, before the gathering ends with libations to the Muses, Poseidon, and Amphitrite.
grc.plutarch.sertorius: Plutarch's Sertorius is a Greek biographical narrative from his collection of Lives, which treats the Roman general Quintus Sertorius, who fought under Caepio and Marius against the Cimbri and Teutones. He later sided with Cinna in the civil wars and built a power in Spain after Sulla's victory, while the work opens with a proem on the recurrence of similar fates in history. It pairs Sertorius with other one-eyed commanders, including Philip, Antigonus, and Hannibal, and the narrative follows his flight to Spain and Mauretania and his excavation of Antaeus' tomb. He won over the Lusitanians using a tame white doe and schooled noble boys at Osca, then proclaimed a senate of exiles and waged a prolonged guerrilla war against Metellus and Pompey. This conflict included battles at the Sucro and near Lauron, along with negotiations with Mithridates of Pontus, before the story closes with his assassination by Perpenna at a banquet. Pompey later executed the conspirator after burning Sertorius' correspondence unread.
grc.plutarch.sulla: Plutarch's Life of Sulla begins with the subject's patrician descent and impoverished youth, noting his fierce gray-eyed appearance and lasting fondness for jesters and actors. The text recounts his first fame as quaestor under Marius in the war against Jugurtha, following his rivalry with Marius and command against Mithridates. This includes the siege of Athens and victories at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, after which he settles with the king and returns to Italy to win the civil war against Cinna's followers. His dictatorship is marked by proscriptions, legislation, and voluntary abdication, while a closing section covers his final years, marriage to Valeria, and painful lingering death. It also describes his elaborate funeral and the epigram weighing his fortune.
grc.plutarch.timoleon: Plutarch's Life of Timoleon is a Greek biographical work of uncertain date that opens with a prologue explaining that Lives serve as a mirror for shaping one's own virtue. The author also announces the pairing of Timoleon with Aemilius Paulus before the narrative follows Timoleon from the assassination of his brother Timophanes. This event occurred after Timophanes made himself tyrant at Corinth, and Timoleon then withdrew from public affairs for twenty years. He was later elected to lead an expedition for the relief of Syracuse, crossing to Sicily where he received the surrender of the tyrant Dionysius. He defeated Hicetas and his Carthaginian allies, and a decisive victory followed at the river Crimisus. Timoleon extinguished the remaining tyrannies of the island, refounding Syracuse with settlers summoned from Greece, and the Life closes with his blindness and honoured retirement at Syracuse, ending with his death and a public funeral in the marketplace.
grc.plutarch.παροιμίαι_αἷς_ἀλεξανδρεῖς_ἐχρῶν: Attributed to Plutarch, the Παροιμίαι αἷς Ἀλεξανδρεῖς ἐχρῶντο is a Greek paroemiographic collection in which each entry cites a proverb and explains the circumstances in which it applies, usually with an anecdote or aition drawn from Greek history, myth, or custom. It opens with the saying Οἴκοι τὰ Μιλήσια ('Milesian affairs belong at home'), glossed through the story of Aristagoras of Miletus and his ostentatious embassy to Sparta. The remaining entries, most introduced by the formula ἐπὶ τῶν ('said of those who...'), range over boastfulness, avarice, cowardice, luxury, stupidity, and other failings, explaining sayings such as Τιθωνοῦ γῆρας and Ἀμαλθείας κέρας through myth, and others through local customs, cults, and institutions of cities like Sparta, Corinth, Samos, Syracuse, and Massalia. The date of compilation is uncertain, the collection being transmitted under Plutarch's name.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.de_musica: This Greek treatise in dialogue form is attributed to Plutarch, though scholars regard it as pseudonymous and of uncertain date. The work opens at a banquet hosted by Onesicrates during the Kronia, where guests are invited to speak on music. The kitharode Lysias surveys the mythical and historical origins of the art, treating figures such as Olympus, Marsyas, and Terpander. He also covers the aulodic and kitharodic nomes, later rhythmic innovations, and the supposed degeneration of music in the hands of poets like Timotheus. Soterichus then ascribes the invention of music to Apollo rather than any human discoverer. He discusses the harmoniai, expounds Pythagorean teaching on cosmic harmony, and reviews music's religious and educational uses before the host dismisses the company.
grc.polybius.histories: Polybius composed this universal history in Greek to explain how Rome came to rule the inhabited world, examining the specific constitution that enabled this rapid expansion within fifty-three years. A programmatic preface defends history as training for political life and sets the start at the 140th Olympiad, which marks when wars in Macedon, Syria, and Italy first connected global affairs. The narrative follows Rome through the Hannibalic war and conflicts in Greece, Asia, and Africa, ending with the capture of Carthage and the settlement among the Greeks. Analytical digressions discuss Roman institutions, military organization, and the qualities of a general, while the text also covers campaigning by day and night on land and sea. The work closes with notices of Greek affairs and the author's recapitulation of its scope.
grc.pseudo_dicaearchus_messeniushe.dicaearch: This short Greek geographical description, known as a periegesis or circuit, covers central Greece and is transmitted under the name of Dicaearchus of Messana, though its title assigns it to Athenaeus. The date of the text remains uncertain, and it opens with a traveller's approach to Athens and a survey of the city. The author describes Athens as dry, ill planned, and poor in houses, yet the city is adorned with the Odeion, the theatre, the Parthenon, and the unfinished Olympieion. Remarks follow on its produce, continual spectacles, and the hazards awaiting foreign visitors, before the account proceeds by measured stages to Oropus, Tanagra, Plataea, Thebes, and Anthedon. It notes roads, soils, products, and water supply along the way, while each people is sketched in pointed, often satirical characterisations. The narrative crosses to Chalcis in Euboea and turns aside for an excursus on Mount Pelion, detailing its rivers, trees, medicinal plants, the Cheironian cave, and the sanctuary of Zeus on the mountain's summit. The extant portion closes with an argument that Hellas was originally a city of Thessaly, and poetic quotations reinforce the claim that Greece proper extends from the Peloponnese to the territory of the Magnetes.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: This Greek periplus, meaning a sailing manual, served merchant captains on the Erythraean Sea, and it is transmitted anonymously but handed down under the name of Arrian. The date of the text remains uncertain, and it opens on the Barbaric coast of East Africa, describing the Fish-Eaters' settlements. The narrative mentions the hunting station of Ptolemais Theron and the port of Adulis, from which ivory moved inland to the metropolis of the Axumites. The text then rounds the whole ocean, taking in the Arabian shore, and covers Muza, Eudaimon Arabia, Kane, and the frankincense country. The route continues through the Persian Gulf and into India, tracing the coast from the Indus delta and Barygaza to the pepper ports of the Limyrike. The journey proceeds to Taprobane, the mouth of the Ganges, and the far lands of Chryse and Thin, closing with regions beyond that are hard of access and unexplored. Throughout, the work records harbours, anchorages, local rulers, and peoples, and it also details sailing seasons, winds, currents, and the imports and exports of each market.
grc.pseudogalen.de_fasciis: This pseudo-Galenic Greek treatise on bandages, known as De fasciis, is of uncertain date and authorship, and it was transmitted among the works of Galen. The text opens by invoking Hippocratic teaching on the speed, rhythm, and cleanliness proper to every art, and it defends the use of varied and ornamental bandages against critics who judged them useless or harmful. The work classifies bandages by material, form, length, width, and manufacture, and it states the qualities a good bandage must possess and explains where each wrapping should begin and end. The text details the purposes of bandaging, from holding parts together to correcting dislocations, and a long practical catalogue follows, giving step-by-step instructions for individually named bandages. These cover the head, face, eyes, ears, jaw, shoulder, chest, groin, and waist.
grc.pseudogalen.de_remediis_parabilibus: The De remediis parabilibus is a Greek medical handbook of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Galen, which focuses on inexpensive remedies that do not require an elaborate pharmacy. The text opens with a prooemion addressed to Glaucus, arguing that medicine must serve travelers and rural dwellers, before treating ailments of the head, including headache, hair, ears, eyes, and face. The author moves part by part through the teeth, mouth, stomach, and liver, and treatments for the spleen, kidneys, bladder, and bowel disorders follow. The handbook also covers women's conditions and the bites of venomous animals, closing with a discussion of poisons and their antidotes. A second book is addressed to Solon, proceeding from the hair to the feet in the same order, and it adds dressings for wounds and cosmetic preparations. Amulets and incantations appear alongside the recipes, and the book ends with dietary and hygiene instructions for preserving health.
grc.pseudogalen.introductio_seu_medicus: This Greek medical treatise, of uncertain date and authorship, is transmitted under Galen's name. It is titled Introductio sive Medicus, which means Introduction, or The Physician. The work opens with an account of medicine's discovery, crediting Asclepius, Egyptian experience, and Hippocrates. It then outlines the three starting points of medicine and its three main sects. The text distinguishes the rationalist, empiricist, and methodist schools by their leaders and doctrines. It further defines medicine as an art or science and divides it into five parts.
