grc.pseudolucian.δημοσθένους_ἐγκώμιον: The Encomium of Demosthenes ('In Praise of Demosthenes') is a short Greek prose dialogue handed down under the name of Lucian and of uncertain date. It opens with the narrator meeting the poet Thersagoras in a colonnade, where Thersagoras has been composing verses as an offering for Homer's birthday. The two compare Homer and Demosthenes, weighing the orator's force, style, and political career against the poet's. Thersagoras then produces a memorandum from the Macedonian court, cast as a little drama, in which Antipater recalls his and Philip's admiration for Demosthenes. In the memorandum Archias reports the orator's defiance and his death by poison in the sanctuary of Poseidon on Calauria. The work closes with Antipater ordering the body sent to Athens and the narrator resolving to repeat the document's contents to his listeners.
grc.pseudolucian.κυνικός: This Greek dialogue, transmitted under the name of Lucian, is generally regarded as spurious by scholars, and its date remains uncertain. The text presents a conversation between Lycinus and an unnamed Cynic philosopher, where Lycinus questions the Cynic about his long hair, beard, threadbare cloak, and barefoot life. He objects that such a way of living is not frugality but destitution, no better than the lot of beggars. The Cynic answers at length, distinguishing sufficiency from need and attacking luxury, greed, and the pursuit of pleasure. He argues that these vices are the source of wars and strife, while appealing to the gods' provision. The philosopher also cites Heracles and Theseus as exemplars of hardy self-mastery, noting the ancients' rejection of softness and vindicating his own dress and unshorn appearance. He claims this look is fitting for good men and even for the gods, whose statues are depicted in the same guise.
grc.pseudolucian.λούκιος_ἢ_ὄνος: This short Greek comic narrative is transmitted under the name of Lucian, though its authorship and date remain uncertain. The first-person narrator, Lucius, travels to Thessaly and lodges at Hypata with the miser Hipparchus. His eagerness to witness magic brings him into contact with a supposed sorceress and her circle. After an affair with his host's maid Palaestra, he pursues the promised wonders of witchcraft. The tale moves toward the transformation into an ass announced by its title, told in a colloquial and racy style.
grc.pseudolucian.φιλόπατρις_ἢ_διδασκόμενος: The Philopatris, meaning Lover of the Fatherland, is a short Greek comic dialogue also titled Didaskomenos, or The Learner. Transmitted under the name of Lucian, its authorship remains uncertain. Triephon finds his friend Critias pale and distraught, prompting an inquiry into his state. Triephon, who has been baptised by a Galilaean, ridicules the Olympian gods and their myths. He expounds a Christian doctrine of creation, providence, and the recording of deeds in heaven. Critias objects using Homeric references to fate and the Moirai, then recounts rebuking prophets and astrologers in the marketplace for slandering the fatherland. A third speaker, Cleolaus, arrives with news of the fall of Susa and the defeat of the Persians, closing the dialogue in patriotic celebration.
grc.pseudolucian.ἀλκυών: The Halcyon is a brief Greek Socratic dialogue attributed to Lucian, though its authorship and date remain uncertain. The title refers to the kingfisher, a bird central to the myth recounted within the text. Socrates and Chaerephon walk by the sea near Phalerum when a mournful cry draws their attention. Socrates tells the story of Alcyone, daughter of Aeolus, who was transformed into a halcyon after her husband Ceyx died. He links the bird to the midwinter calm known as the halcyon days. The conversation widens into a reflection on the smallness of mortal judgment before divine power. Human weakness is contrasted with nature's marvellous handiwork, as exemplified in the bee. Socrates vows to share the story of the bird's devoted love with Xanthippe and Myrto. The two men then turn from the shore toward the city.
grc.rufus_of_ephesus.de_renum_et_vesicae_aff: A Greek medical treatise by Rufus of Ephesus on the diseases of the kidneys and bladder, De Renum et Vesicae Affectionibus opens by announcing that it will set out, ailment by ailment, what afflicts these organs, how to recognise each condition, and how to treat it. It first contrasts inflammation of the kidneys with inflammation of the bladder, describing the sufferers' postures and pains, the signs of each affection, and remedies of diet, rest, venesection, poultices, and diuretic drugs. Later chapters pass to haemorrhage of the kidneys and a wasting disorder of unquenchable thirst with constant urination, then to the gravest bladder complaints, including suppuration, ulceration, itching, paralysis, and the weak bladder that cannot retain urine. Throughout, treatments are prescribed in detail, from warm baths, clysters, and topical ointments to castoreum and phlebotomy, and the work closes with the exercise, massage, and warming regimens recommended for the disabled and incontinent bladder.
grc.rufus_soph.ars_rhetorica: Attributed to the sophist Rufus, the Ars Rhetorica is a short Greek handbook of uncertain date that defines rhetoric as the art of disposing any proposed speech well and persuasively. The text distinguishes four rhetorical kinds, namely judicial, deliberative, encomiastic, and historical, while its treatment focuses chiefly on the judicial speech and its four parts. These parts are the proem, narration, proof, and epilogue, and the handbook begins with a catalogue of sources for the proem. These sources include the speaker, opponents, jurors, and the circumstances of the case, and it then lists the virtues of clarity, concision, and plausibility in narration. Four modes of telling are also distinguished in this section, and the discussion of proof covers arguments from persons, things, and examples. It also includes inartificial evidence such as documents, laws, and contracts, and the enthymeme and maxim follow the argument in this part. The work closes with remarks on propositions and specific figures, and it defines the epilogue as a recapitulation aimed at amplification or anger.
grc.scylax_of_caranda.periplus_scylacis: This Greek periplus, or coastal sailing survey, is attributed to Scylax of Caranda, and its date remains uncertain to modern scholars. The text begins at the Pillars of Heracles on the European side, proceeding coast by coast while naming peoples, cities, harbours, and rivers. Sailing distances are given in days, nights, and stades, and the circuit runs from Iberia through Liguria, Italy, and the Adriatic. It continues to the Greek mainland, Thrace, and Scythia, then follows the shores of the Euxine and Maeotis. The Asiatic coast is traced from the Sauromatae through Colchis and Paphlagonia, passing the Troad, Ionia, Caria, Lycia, and Cilicia. The journey reaches Cyprus, Phoenicia, and Egypt, and closing sections follow the African coast from the Canopic mouth of the Nile. The path passes Cyrene, the Syrteis, and Carthage, returning to the Pillars of Heracles. The work ends with totals of sailing times, including computations for open-sea crossings among the Aegean islands. A ranked list of the largest islands concludes the text.
grc.septuaginta.abdias: The Book of Obadiah is a brief prose prophecy of uncertain date, preserved in the Greek version of the Hellenistic Septuagint. The text bears the name of the prophet Obadiah, and it opens with a message of the Lord against Idumaea. A report is heard from the Lord, and an envoy is dispatched to the nations, who are summoned to war against her. The oracle derides Edom's self-confidence in its rocky strongholds, threatening the thorough despoliation of the region. The text condemns Edom's conduct on the day of Jerusalem's fall, when Edom rejoiced over Judah's ruin and helped cut off the fugitives. Judgment is announced on the principle of exact retribution, and the day of the Lord is foretold for all the nations. The prophecy closes with deliverance on Mount Zion, where the house of Jacob is described as fire consuming the house of Esau. The surrounding lands are repossessed, and the kingdom becomes the Lord's.
grc.septuaginta.baruch: Baruch is a Hellenistic Jewish book of the Septuagint, written in Greek prose. It is attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, though its date remains uncertain. The text opens with a narrative frame in which Baruch reads the book to King Jehoiachin and the exiles in Babylon. These exiles send silver to Jerusalem with instructions for sacrifices and for prayer on behalf of Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar. The body consists of a communal confession of sin, a poem on the location of wisdom, and a lament by widowed Jerusalem. It closes with oracles of consolation telling Jerusalem to look eastward for her scattered children to return.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_translatio_grae: Bel and the Dragon is a short narrative in Greek prose of Hellenistic date, preserved among the additions to Daniel in the Septuagint. It opens by introducing Daniel as a priest and companion of the king of Babylon, in whose city the Babylonians worship the idol Bel. Daniel demonstrates that the daily offerings set before Bel are consumed by the idol's hidden priests rather than by the god. He then destroys a living dragon the Babylonians venerate by feeding it a cake of pitch, fat, and hair, and the enraged populace throws him into a lions' den. An angel carries the prophet Habakkuk from Judea to bring Daniel food in the den. After six days the king finds Daniel alive, releases him, and casts his accusers to the lions in his place.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_b: This Greek text preserves the Hebrew book of Ezra–Nehemiah within the Septuagint, presenting an anonymous prose narrative of uncertain date. The story follows the Judean exiles returning from Babylon, opening with the decree of Cyrus of Persia. The exiles go up to Jerusalem to rebuild the house of the Lord, laying the temple foundations and completing the building under Darius. They face opposition from the peoples of the land, while the priest Ezra arrives under Artaxerxes to teach the law of Moses. He also dissolves marriages with foreign women, and Nehemiah then obtains leave from the same king to rebuild the walls. He acts against the hostility of Sanballat and Tobiah, as long registers of returnees, priests, Levites, and settlers punctuate the account. The narrative closes with Nehemiah enforcing Sabbath observance and tithes, and he also enforces separation from foreign wives.
grc.septuaginta.esther: The Greek Book of Esther is a Hellenistic biblical text of uncertain date that opens in the second year of Artaxerxes with Mordecai's dream. This Jew from the Babylonian captivity serves in the Persian court at Susa, where he dreams of two dragons and a spring that becomes a great river. The story then recounts the fall of Queen Astin and the rise of Esther, while Haman plots to destroy the Jews. Mordecai and Esther avert this danger through fasting and prayers, leading to Esther's bold approach to the king. Haman is executed, and the extermination decree is reversed, so the Jews ultimately defeat their enemies and institute the days of Phrurai. Mordecai provides an allegorical interpretation of his dream, and a colophon names Dositheus and Lysimachus of Jerusalem, who brought and translated the epistle under Ptolemy and Cleopatra.
grc.septuaginta.habacuc: This Greek rendering of the biblical prophecy of Habakkuk, one of the Twelve Prophets in the Septuagint, was made in the Hellenistic era. It opens with the prophet's cry of complaint over injustice, to which God replies that the bitter and swift Chaldaeans will be stirred up as an instrument of judgement. Dialogues over divine justice and a series of woes against greed, bloodshed, and idolatry then lead into the 'Prayer of Habakkuk'. This hymn, marked by interlude refrains, depicts God's theophany from Teman and Mount Paran in the imagery of the divine warrior. The book closes with the prophet's resolve to rejoice in the Lord though the fig tree, vine, and fields fail.
grc.septuaginta.job: The Book of Job in Greek is a prose biblical rendering transmitted anonymously within the Septuagint during the Hellenistic period. The story opens with Job, a wealthy and blameless man in the land of Ausitis, whose righteousness is tested before the heavenly court at the devil's prompting. Consequently, his children, herds, and health are stripped away while he holds to his integrity, leading to cycles of disputation. Job curses the day of his birth and argues over divine justice with three friends, namely Eliphaz, Baldad, and Sophar. Their exchange is followed by the speeches of Eliou, after which the Lord questions Job from a cloud concerning creation, the beasts, and the sea-monsters. Job submits in humility to this divine address, and an epilogue doubles his possessions, adding seven sons and three daughters named Hemera, Kasia, and Amaltheia's horn. An appended note identifies him with the Edomite king Jobab, the fifth from Abraham, and describes the book's translation from the Syriac.
grc.septuaginta.michaeas: The Michaeas preserves the Septuagint Greek rendering of the biblical prophecy of Micah, which was made from the Hebrew during the Hellenistic period. It belongs to the collection known as the Twelve Prophets and opens with the word of the Lord coming to Micah the Morashtite. This event occurred in the days of Joatham, Achaz, and Ezekias, kings of Judah, and announces judgement upon Samaria and Jerusalem for idolatry and sin. Subsequent oracles condemn land seizure, rapacious magistrates, venal priests, and false prophets, setting these faults against promises of the exaltation of the mountain of the Lord. There, nations shall beat swords into ploughshares, and a ruler to come from Bethlehem will also shepherd his people. A later section takes the form of a divine indictment, recalling the exodus and the Balak episode, and culminates in the demand to do judgement and love mercy. Readers are also told to be ready to walk with the Lord God, while the book closes with laments over social collapse and family strife. It describes the prophet's patient endurance of the Lord's wrath, and a final hymn praises the God who pardons iniquity. This God casts sins into the depths of the sea, showing truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham.
grc.septuaginta.osee: The Book of Hosea opens with the word of the Lord coming to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah, while Jeroboam son of Joash rules Israel. The prophet receives a command to take a wife of fornication, whose children will bear names that signify divine judgement. Translated into Greek during the Hellenistic period, the text alternates between denunciation and promise throughout its narrative. Israel and Ephraim are arraigned for idolatry and corrupt worship, and they are also condemned for seeking help from Assyria and Egypt. Priests, princes, and the general population all stand condemned, and Judah receives a warning as well. Oracles of destruction target Samaria and its calf, giving way to repeated calls to return to the Lord. The collection closes with a penitential summons that offers promises of healing and fruitfulness. A short wisdom saying concludes the work, describing the straight ways of the Lord, on which the righteous walk while sinners stumble.
grc.septuaginta.sapientia_salomonis: Sapientia Salomonis, or the Wisdom of Solomon, is a Greek Jewish wisdom book from the Hellenistic period, preserved in the Septuagint and ascribed to Solomon, though its actual author is not named. The text opens with an exhortation to those who judge the earth to love righteousness, urging them to seek the Lord with singleness of heart. It reflects on the persecution of the righteous and the folly of the impious, while also addressing the hope of immortality. A first-person prayer follows, in which Solomon prizes wisdom above wealth, power, and health, and the text then praises wisdom's divine nature and her guidance of figures from Adam through the patriarchs and the Exodus. The latter part retells the departure from Egypt at length, contrasting the preservation of the Israelites with the plagues visited on the Egyptians. The book denounces idolatry as the source of every evil, closing with God's magnification of his holy people.
grc.septuaginta.sophonias: The Book of Zephaniah, one of the twelve Minor Prophets, was rendered from the Hebrew in the Hellenistic period. The text opens with a superscription placing the word of the Lord in the days of Josiah. Oracles of judgement follow against Judah and Jerusalem for idolatry and injustice, portraying the day of the Lord as wrath. A summons calls the meek to seek righteousness before that day arrives, while judgement is pronounced on Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Cush, Assyria, and Nineveh. The prophet laments Jerusalem's corruption, yet her just Lord will leave a humble remnant. The book closes with nations calling on the Lord, inviting the daughter of Sion to rejoice because her king is in her midst.
grc.sextus_empiricus.adversus_mathematicos: The Adversus Mathematicos of Sextus Empiricus, a Greek prose work of uncertain date, sets out the case of Pyrrhonian Scepticism against the liberal arts and the dogmatic philosophers. It opens by distinguishing the Epicurean from the Pyrrhonian grounds for opposing the so-called encyclical studies, and argues that nothing is teachable: neither the thing taught, nor the teacher, nor the learner, nor the manner of learning. From there the argument runs through the individual disciplines of grammar, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astrology, and music, and through the logical, physical, and ethical doctrines of the dogmatists, treating among other questions the existence of signs, the criterion of truth, and causes, and pressing opposing arguments to equal strength and suspension of judgement. The work closes by extending the case against teaching to the art of living and by completing the whole exposition of the sceptical undertaking.
grc.sophocles.electra: This Greek tragedy by Sophocles dramatizes the revenge of Orestes and Electra, who avenge the murder of their father Agamemnon. The play opens at daybreak before the palace at Mycenae, where Orestes arrives in disguise to obey the Delphic oracle. He sets in motion a false report of his own death, while most of the action follows Electra as she maintains public mourning. She quarrels with her sister Chrysothemis and with Clytemnestra, and news of Orestes' death plunges her into despair. A token from their father restores the living Orestes to his sister, and Clytemnestra is killed within the house. Aegisthus is lured back to die where Agamemnon was slain.
grc.soranus.vita_hippocratis_secundum_soranu: This Greek biography of Hippocrates is attributed to Soranus of Cos, though its date remains uncertain. It begins by tracing the physician's Coan genealogy, linking his descent to Heracles and Asclepius. The text then follows his career, noting his move to Thessaly after a dream. It details his cures of Perdiccas of Macedon, Democritus of Abdera, and plague-stricken cities. The narrative also records his refusal of Persian gifts and the civic honors he received. It closes with his death near Larissa, the honey found at his tomb, and his surviving sons and pupils.
grc.strabo.geography: Strabo's Geography is a Greek prose survey of the inhabited world in seventeen books, opening by defending geography as a proper part of philosophy. The author hails Homer as the founder of the discipline, citing earlier practitioners from Anaximander and Hecataeus down to Eratosthenes. The work proceeds region by region across Iberia, Gaul, Italy, and Greece, continuing into Asia and Africa to describe lands, peoples, cities, and rivers. Strabo digresses freely into myth, local history, and ethnography, which is evident in his extended treatment of Boeotia, Phocis, and Delphi. Throughout, he weighs and corrects the accounts of earlier geographers, relying on his own observation and more recent information. The closing books follow the North African coast from Mauretania, passing through Carthage and the Syrtes to reach Cyrenaica, ending with an outline of the Roman provinces organized under Caesar Augustus.
grc.strabo.strabonis_geographiae_chrestomath: This Greek chrestomathy condenses Strabo's seventeen books of Geography into brief notices, each introduced by the word that, a standard feature of such epitomes. The text opens by claiming that Homer first ventured to write geography, then discussing the encircling Ocean, its tides, and the coasts named in the poems. The body ranges over mathematical, astronomical, and philosophical foundations, also covering Eratosthenes, the relation of poetry to truth, and the cults of Greece, Phrygia, and Thrace. Regional entries follow on Crete, the Cyclades, the Taurus, and Strabo's fivefold division of Asia, with Egypt treated next, with attention to the fish and animals of the Nile. The work closes in Libya and Mauretania with ethnographic notes and the resources of Carthage, ending with a notice of the seventeen books of Strabo's geographical chrestomathy.
grc.theophrastus.concerning_odours: This short Greek treatise by Theophrastus explores the nature of smells and the art of perfumery, arguing that odour arises from mixture. The author distinguishes pleasant scents from foul ones, noting the dullness of human smell compared to other animals. The text surveys the causes and varieties of odour in plants, animals, and minerals, focusing heavily on the making of unguents. Specific scents such as rose, cypros, iris, nard, and myrrh are detailed alongside Egyptian and megaleion types. The work covers colouring, ageing, and storage in lead and alabaster vessels, describing physical effects ranging from headaches to purgation. Later sections discuss animal smells and examine Democritus's explanation of odour, concluding by describing the blending of dry aromatics for scenting clothes and bedding.
grc.theophrastus.de_lapidibus: Theophrastus wrote this Greek prose treatise on stones, minerals, and earths, opening by dividing substances consolidated in the earth into those formed from water and those formed from earth. The author argues that stones arise from pure matter solidified by heat or cold, while later chapters survey the behaviour of stones under fire and describe precious and seal stones. These include emerald, carbuncle, lyngourion, and amethyst, along with their localities, and the text also covers the working of stone for carving, polishing, and the touchstone assay of gold. Subsequent sections treat earths and mineral pigments such as ochre, miltos, kyanos, and cinnabar, discussing their sources, preparation, and uses in painting, fulling, and building. The work closes with a discussion of gypsum and its adhesive properties.
grc.theophrastus.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: Theophrastus wrote this Greek treatise on the senses and their objects. It begins by contrasting the views that perception works through the like or the opposite. The author then surveys thinkers such as Parmenides, Empedocles, Plato, and Democritus. He reports their accounts of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch while pressing objections. Later chapters examine the sensibles themselves, including Democritus's atomic explanations of flavours and colours. The work closes with a critique of Plato's definitions of heat, cold, and sound.
grc.theophrastus.fragmenta_varia_13190: This volume gathers fragments of Theophrastus of Eresus, a pupil of Aristotle, whose material survives through quotations and paraphrases by later Greek authors. Clement of Alexandria, Simplicius, and Stobaeus are among the key transmitters, and the opening excerpts report Theophrastus's views on sensation and the divine. These sections precede discussions of first principles, motion, and place, after which the fragments range over topics in rhetoric and legislation. They include notes on Athenian legal practice and the sale of property, while later sections address questions of probability and style in rhetoric. The collection also features notices from a treatise on love, and scattered reports on birds, fishes, and serpents appear throughout. The volume closes with natural history notes on locusts and snakes, covering the hoarded remedies of animals and three kinds of honey.
grc.theophrastus.περί_ὀσμών: In this short Greek treatise on smells, Theophrastus argues that odours, like juices, arise from mixture, and that earth, being most mixed, is the most odorous of the simple bodies. The treatise then classifies pleasant and foul smells, observing that smell is the dullest of the senses, though many animals perceive odours humans miss. A survey of the natural odours of plants, animals and inanimate things follows, before the discussion turns to the perfumer's craft, which occupies the greater part of the work. Theophrastus describes the oils and spices compounded into unguents such as rose perfume and iris, and considers why perfumes flavour wine yet spoil food. He goes on to cover the storage of perfumes in lead and alabaster vessels and their medicinal powers. It closes with the smells of animals, a criticism of Democritus's account of odour, and the preparation of dry aromatic mixtures for scenting clothes and bedding.
grc.theophrastus.περὶ_φυτῶν_αἰτιῶν: Theophrastus opens this Greek treatise by noting that plant generation has been described before, then he sets out to assign the specific causes proper to each mode of growth. The early chapters examine propagation from seed, cuttings, layers, and branches, explaining why date palms sprout in several ways while dry trees rarely grow from anything but seed. Later sections address cultivation, covering sowing seasons, weather, frost, and soil effects on yield, and the text also compares the vigour and keeping power of seeds from trees, cereals, and garden plants. The work closes with a long account of plant juices and odours, arguing that soil, climate, and locality determine why some plants are fragrant and others insipid.
grc.thucydides.peleponnesian_war: The Athenian historian Thucydides opens by naming himself and declaring that the war of the Peloponnesians and Athenians was the greatest upheaval the Greeks had yet experienced. He states that he began recording this conflict from its very outset, and the work proceeds through an archaeological sketch of early Greece and the growth of Athenian power. It then details the causes of hostilities, the plague at Athens, and the debates over Mytilene and Plataea, while the narrative covers the frequent interventions of Sparta and the alliance of Athens with Argos, Mantinea, and Elis. The great expedition against Syracuse ends in disaster for Athens, and later books follow the oligarchic coup at Athens and the shifting allegiance of Alcibiades. Persian involvement on both sides and naval warfare around Ionia and the Hellespont are also recorded, with campaigns, speeches, treaties, and oaths appearing in detail throughout the text. The narrative breaks off in the twenty-first year of the war, before its conclusion, and the work is transmitted in eight books.
grc.aelius_herodianus.περι_καθολικης_προσῳδι: Περὶ Καθολικῆς Προσῳδίας, a Greek grammatical treatise on accentuation, is attributed to Aelius Herodianus and survives as an epitome. This abridgement presents itself as a summary of Herodian's fuller treatment, with a prefatory summary describing twenty books arranged by the terminations of accented words. The list includes nouns, verbs, pronouns, articles, prepositions, adverbs, and conjunctions, while a closing book addresses vowel quantities and breathings. The surviving exposition defines prosody and sets out rules for placing the acute and circumflex accents, and it also treats enclitics, diacritics, word length, and dialectal forms. These rules are illustrated chiefly from Homeric verses.
grc.aeschines_sp.ἐπιστολαί: This is a short collection of Greek letters of uncertain date, transmitted with the works of the Athenian orator Aeschines and attributed to him. The opening letter, addressed to Philocrates, recounts a voyage from Attica that, after calls at Ceos and Delos and successive shifts of wind, ends with the writer's arrival at Rhodes. Written in exile to Ctesiphon and to the Athenian council and people, the remaining letters offer self-defence over his condemnation and his quarrels with Demosthenes and his partisans. They also urge the Athenians not to renew the war after Alexander's death. Among their anecdotes are the lineage of Cleocrates and Cimon's abduction of Callirhoe beside the Scamander. The collection closes with an apologia for the writer's political career and an appeal on behalf of his children.
grc.alcidamas.περὶ_σοφιστῶν: This short Greek prose speech, attributed to Alcidamas, announces a formal indictment of written speeches and the sophists who rely on them. It opens by attacking men who display wisdom through books yet cannot speak extemporaneously, arguing that composition is an easy attainment and therefore of slight worth. The practiced extempore speaker can also write, but not conversely, a point illustrated by analogies of weight-lifting, running, and javelin-throwing. The ability to speak is needed at every moment of life, whereas composition suits only rare occasions. Written speeches burden the memory and break down in court, unable to accommodate unforeseen arguments or the desires of hearers. A written logos is merely an image of true speech, like a statue or painting, agreeable to view but of no practical use. A closing section answers the objection that the speaker condemns in writing what he practices himself, explaining that he composes only for display before large audiences and as a record of his progress. The speech ends by recommending constant exercise in extempore speech, treating writing as an occasional pastime.
grc.andocides.on_his_return: Andocides delivered this oration to the Athenian assembly after the fall of the Four Hundred, pleading for his restoration and the renewal of his immunity. He complains that enemies judge him by past misfortunes rather than the city's good, asking the Athenians to show human understanding for his suffering. The body recounts his choice to inform against outrages to save his father, detailing his exile and the services he rendered to redeem himself. He fitted out rowers and supplies for the fleet at Samos, sharing in the naval victory that saved Athens from the Peloponnesians. He also frustrated attempts to keep grain from Cyprus out of the Piraeus, but upon his return, he was arrested and denounced by Pisander. The speech closes by requesting the reconfirmation of Menippus's decree of safety, invoking his family's hereditary devotion to the democracy, as his great-grandfather Leogoras went into exile with the people rather than join the tyrants.
grc.appian.foreign_wars: The Foreign Wars is a Greek prose compilation transmitted under the name of Appian, which gathers his narratives of Rome's wars against foreign enemies. The work opens with Aeneas' flight from Troy and his settlement in Latium, then traces the line of Alban kings and Romulus' foundation of Rome. The narrative moves through early wars against the Latins and Volscians, giving an extended account of Hannibal's campaign in Italy. This includes the betrayal of Tarentum and the siege of Capua, while the text closes with the Mithridatic war. It recounts Mithridates' flight and death, and it also details Pompey's campaigns as far as the Caucasus and Judaea.
grc.aratus.phaenomena: Aratus composed the Phaenomena, a didactic poem in Greek hexameters, to explain the stars and weather. The title means 'Appearances,' referring to the visible signs of the heavens. The work opens with an invocation of Zeus, the benevolent source of all signs granted to humankind. The first and longer part describes the constellations of the northern and southern sky. It also covers the great circles of the celestial sphere and the zodiac. A second part, known as the Diosemeia, treats weather prognostics for sailors and farmers.
grc.archimedes.de_conoidibus_et_sphaeroidibu: This Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, written in the Doric dialect, examines solids of revolution, specifically right and obtuse-angled conoids and oblong and flattened spheroids. The work opens as a letter announcing proofs for both earlier and more recent theorems, then supplies definitions for these solids, their axes, vertices, centres, and segments. The body states lemmas from proportion theory and conic geometry before proving key propositions, which use inscribed and circumscribed figures built from cylinders to establish volumes. For instance, a segment of a right conoid cut perpendicular to the axis is half the cone on the same base, while segments cut in any planes are in duplicate ratio of their axes. Half of an oblong spheroid cut through its centre is double a cone, and the text also determines which plane sections are circles, parabolas, or ellipses. It proves that a tangent plane touches such a solid at a single point, and a closing set of problems includes cutting a segment equal to a given cone, cylinder, or sphere.
grc.archimedes.de_sphaera_et_cylindro: Archimedes' Greek treatise on the sphere and cylinder opens with a dedicatory letter to Conon. It announces results sent earlier, chiefly that a sphere's surface is four times its greatest circle. The letter also notes that a circumscribing cylinder is half again as large in volume. After a preface of definitions, axioms, and lemmas, the first book proves areas of pyramids, cones, and cylinders. It concludes that a sphere equals four times the cone over its great circle. The second book consists largely of problems, such as finding a plane figure equal to a spherical surface.
grc.archimedes.liber_assumptorum: The Liber Assumptorum, or Book of Lemmas, is a short collection of geometrical propositions in Greek attributed to Archimedes, though its date remains uncertain. The text opens with a proof concerning two internally tangent circles that have parallel diameters, showing that lines drawn from the point of contact to the ends of those diameters form a single straight line. The remaining propositions explore the geometry of the circle and the semicircle, addressing tangents from external points and chords that intersect at right angles. The work also examines areas and diameter ratios of figures bounded by semicircular arcs, including the arbelos and the lune. One proposition poses a problem requiring the ratio between a semicircle's diameter and that of the circle inscribed in its arbelos. The collection closes with two porisms, one of which establishes that a side of the regular pentagon inscribed in a circle is cut in extreme and mean ratio.
grc.archytas_of_tarentum.fragmenta: These fragments preserve the words of Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher whose surviving text is transmitted in literary Doric Greek through later authors. The collection opens with a long treatise on mathematics or harmonics, which calls astronomy, geometry, arithmetic, and music sister sciences. The pitch of sound is explained through the speed of motion, where rapid movement produces sharp notes, while slow movement creates heavy ones. Shorter fragments define the three musical means as arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic, and they distinguish learning from another person from discovering by oneself. The discovery of calculation is credited with ending civil strife by establishing equality, and the collection closes with an inventory of titles ascribed to him. These range from works on principles, being, the soul, and wisdom to a treatise on cookery, and letters exchanged with Plato and Dionysius are also listed. Testimonies to writings on machines and agriculture complete the list.
grc.aristophanes.plutus: The Plutus ('Wealth'), a comedy by Aristophanes, opens with the slave Carion grumbling as he escorts his master home from Apollo's oracle. The god has bidden the man to follow Wealth himself, blind and helpless, when he might as well have cured him. The plot turns on the restoration of Wealth's sight, after which he bestows riches on the just and abandons sycophants and wrongdoers. Poverty, however, warns that a world rid of her would be destitute. Subsequent scenes bring the healed god to the temple of Asclepius, and an elderly woman is undone when her young lover, no longer dependent on her money, deserts her. The play closes with Plutus reinstated in his former seat within the temple, led in procession with torches and sacred vessels.
grc.aristotle.de_memoria_et_reminiscentia: This short Greek treatise by Aristotle examines memory and recollection, and it is transmitted as one of the essays of the Parva Naturalia. The work opens by turning from the senses to the nature of memory, asking what memory is and where it arises in the soul. Aristotle argues that memory is a lasting state of the perceptive faculty, arising from imagination and bound up with the perception of time. The text explains poor memory in the very young and the very old, using the analogy of an imprint made in the soul. The remainder treats recollection as a deliberate act of searching, resembling a syllogism moving from a starting point to what is sought. Movements in the soul proceed by similarity, contrast, or contiguity, and this act is found among known animals only in human beings, ending with a summary of its conclusions on both topics.
grc.aristotle.economics: The Economics is a short Greek treatise on household management attributed to Aristotle, whose title means the art of managing a household. It opens by distinguishing economics from politics and tracing the natural constitution of the home, where the author examines the conjugal relation, children, property, and slaves. He then surveys the duties of the household head toward wife, offspring, servants, and possessions, followed by provisions on training, discipline, and resource management. The work distinguishes four kinds of economy, namely royal, satrapic, political, and private, before closing with anecdotes showing how rulers and cities raised money in wartime. These examples range from Cypselus of Corinth to Alexander's commanders.
grc.aristotle.metaphysics: Aristotle's Metaphysics is a Greek prose treatise in fourteen books on first philosophy. It investigates being qua being and the principles and causes of things. The work opens with the claim that all human beings by nature desire to know. It traces the ascent from sensation and memory through experience to art and science. The text then sets out the aporiai concerning first principles and examines the four causes. It analyses substance as matter, form, and the composite, together with potentiality and actuality. Later books argue for an unmoved first mover and examine the doctrines of Plato's followers and the Pythagoreans on separate Forms and numbers.
grc.aristotle.res_publica_atheniensium: This Greek treatise on the Athenian state, transmitted among Aristotle's works, has an uncertain date to modern scholars. It opens amid the Cylonian conspiracy's aftermath and addresses the harsh oligarchic order of the hektemoroi preceding Draco and Solon. The historical first half traces the development of the Athenian constitution, covering Draco's code, Solon's reforms, the Pisistratid tyranny, and Cleisthenes' reorganization. The narrative continues through the oligarchic upheavals of the late fifth century down to the author's own day. The second half sets out the working constitution in detail, describing the council of five hundred and its supervision of magistrates and finances. It also details the nine archons and their religious and judicial duties, further explaining the military and festival offices. Finally, it outlines the courts, including the allotment of jurors, the use of ballots and water clocks, and the conduct of trials.
grc.aristotle.rhetoric: Aristotle's Rhetoric is a Greek prose treatise on the art of persuasion, opening by defining rhetoric as the counterpart of dialectic. The author criticizes earlier handbooks for ignoring proof, and the work then sets out the three species of oratory. These are deliberative, forensic, and epideictic, and the text also identifies the sources of persuasion in character, emotion, and argument. A central book analyzes the passions, from anger and fear to shame and pity, while examining the ages and characters of audiences as material for enthymematic reasoning. The final book treats style and arrangement, covering correctness of language, metaphor, and simile, and it also addresses periodic composition and the parts of a speech. It offers guidance on questioning, answering, and the use of the laughable.
grc.aristotle.virtues_and_vices: This short Greek ethical treatise, attributed to Aristotle though its date remains uncertain, circulates within the Aristotelian corpus under the title Virtues and Vices. The work opens by ranking the noble among praiseworthy things and the base among blameworthy ones, adopting the Platonic division of the soul into three distinct parts. Phronesis is assigned to the rational part, while gentleness and courage belong to the spirited, and temperance and self-control are linked to the appetitive part. Justice, liberality, and magnanimity apply to the soul as a whole, and the text then defines each virtue and its corresponding vice in turn. It catalogues the traits and behaviours that accompany these states, concluding by characterizing virtue as a well-ordered disposition of the whole soul. This state is likened to a model of a good constitution, while vice is described as the contrary of this ordered state.
grc.aristotle.περί_χρωμάτων: This short Greek treatise on colours, transmitted under the name of Aristotle, has an uncertain date but investigates how colours arise in the natural world. The text opens by defining simple colours as those following the four elements, where air and water are naturally white, while fire and the sun are yellow. Earth is also white, though it appears variegated through staining, and the remainder derives many colours from the mixture of these simples. It also considers the varying strength of reflected light, discussing blackness, shadow, and the hues of sea and sky. The author then examines the ripening and changing colours of fruits and flowers, and finally describes the colouring of hair, wool, and feathers in animals. This includes the greying and whitening that occur with age, and the work closes by observing that the whole inquiry is best grasped from the mingling of sunlight and firelight.
grc.aristotle.ἐκ_τοῦ_περὶ_ἀκουστῶν: This short Greek treatise on sound and the voice, of uncertain date, was transmitted as an excerpt from a work titled On Things Heard. The text is attributed to Aristotle, and it begins by claiming that every voice and noise arises when bodies set the air in motion. The author rejects the idea that air is given a shape, arguing instead that it is driven and compressed. A general mechanics of sounding follows, explaining how a blow of air carries voice to the ear. The qualities of sound, such as pitch and hardness, are traced to the lung and windpipe. Examples are drawn from human and animal voices, as well as from musical instruments. Natural phenomena like rivers and thunder also illustrate the principles. The text closes with an account of how rapid impacts produce continuous sound.
grc.arius_didymus.liber_de_philosophorum_sec: This Greek doxographic epitome, attributed to Arius Didymus and preserved by Stobaeus, surveys the ethical doctrines of the ancient philosophical schools. It opens with an account of happiness as activity in noble and preferred actions, then passes through notices of Xenophanes and Philo of Larissa. There follow definitions of character and of the passions as framed by the followers of Plato, by Zeno, and by Aristotle. The longest portion sets out Stoic ethics at length, covering the four primary passions and their many species together with the paradoxes concerning the wise man. The Stoic section also contains discussions of friendship, of law, and of the city. It ends with Aristotle and the later Peripatetics, whose doctrines cover virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency, the classification of goods, and finally household management and constitutional matters.
grc.callistratus.statuarum_descriptiones: This collection contains fourteen rhetorical descriptions of artworks, attributed to Callistratus, whose date remains uncertain. The first piece depicts a statue of a pipe-playing Satyr in a grotto near Egyptian Thebes. The sequence then proceeds through further statues, including Scopas' Bacchante, Praxiteles' Eros, and a drunken Indian. It continues with Narcissus at the spring, Lysippus' personification of Opportunity, and Orpheus on Helicon. The list also includes Dionysus, the vocal colossus of Memnon, Asclepius, an ephebe, a Centaur, and Medea. The collection closes with a painting of Athamas and Ino amid a storm-tossed sea, filled with dolphins and sea deities. Each description sets the artwork in a landscape or sanctuary, dwelling on how stone, bronze, or pigment can seem alive. They show the figures breathing, moving, and displaying the passions of the soul.
grc.chionis_epistulae.epistulae: These seventeen Greek letters, attributed to Chion of Heraclea, present a correspondence between the young Heracleote and his father, as well as with Plato. The opening letter, sent from Byzantium, addresses parental anxiety over his prolonged absence, asking his father to view his education as a pledge of future excellence. The narrative follows his voyage from the Black Sea toward Athens, where he is detained at Byzantium and witnesses Xenophon restraining the Greek soldiery from sacking the city. A storm subsequently drives him to Perinthus before he reaches his destination, where he describes his philosophical life with Plato and Speusippus. The sequence concludes with his return to a Heraclea oppressed by the tyrant Clearchus, where Chion begins to conspire against the tyrant. He writes a farewell to Plato on the eve of the attempt, embracing the prospect of a noble death for his city's freedom.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.musica: This short Greek collection of definitions and notes on music is transmitted under the name of Claudius Ptolemaeus, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens with a numerical scheme of the cosmic system, assigning ratio-numbers to the standing notes of the spheres. These range from the moon and Hermes to Aphrodite, the Sun, Ares, Zeus, Kronos, and the fixed stars. The remainder gathers memoranda on music theory at large, defining music, melody, and harmonics. It lists the kinds of rhythm and metrical feet, such as dactylic, iambic, and paeonic, with their time values. It measures tones, semitones, and dieses in twelfths of a tone after Eratosthenes, describing the qualities of the four elements. It identifies the three things subject to rhythm: word, melody, and bodily movement. It provides a table of the lyre's notes for the left and right hands in kithara-playing. It closes with a remark on the manly Dorian and mournful Phrygian rhythms.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.excerpta_ex_theodo: This Greek compilation, transmitted under the name of Clement of Alexandria, preserves the Gnostic teaching of Theodotus, a follower of Valentinus. It opens with a Valentinian exposition of the Saviour's words, which are read through the myth of Sophia and the spiritual seed. The text then moves through the whole Valentinian system, including the emanation of the aeons and Sophia's fall. It covers the unknowable Father, the Monogenes, the Saviour, and the psychic Christ, while examining the three natures of human beings descended from Adam. The Demiurge and the creation of the world are described, and the meaning of baptism and its liberating power are explained. Short notes on other Gnostic teachers, including followers of Basilides, are interspersed throughout, alongside running exegesis of individual scriptural passages ranging from the transfiguration and John's prologue to the wedding garment and the money of Caesar.
grc.cleonides.εἰσαγωγὴ_ἁρμονική: The Eisagōgē harmonikē, a short Greek treatise on musical theory, is attributed to Cleonides, though its date remains uncertain. It defines harmonics as the science of the harmonized, divided into seven parts, including notes, intervals, genera, systems, tonos, modulation, and melopoeia. The body of the text defines these elements in turn, treating the eighteen notes of the system as fixed or movable. The three genera are diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic, and their tetrachordal divisions use six colourings expressed in numerical fractions of the tone. The arrangement of tetrachords forms the lesser and greater perfect systems, and the treatise sets out the species of the octave with their traditional names. These are Mixolydian, Lydian, Phrygian, Dorian, Hypolydian, Hypophrygian, and Hypodorian, and it also lists the thirteen tonoi counted according to Aristoxenus. Quotations from Terpander and Ion illustrate the term, and the work closes with the four kinds of modulation. This includes change of tonos and of melopoeia, which has ethical characters suited to tragedy, laments, or hymns. It is the practical employment of conduction, interweaving, repeated striking, and sustained tone.
grc.demades.on_the_twelve_years: On the Twelve Years is a short forensic defense attributed to the Athenian orator Demades, whose title refers to the twelve years of political activity under scrutiny. A statesman of the age of Philip and Alexander answers charges before an Athenian court, comparing the juror to a physician who must know the cause of a disease. He defends the peace he wrote with Philip and the honors he conferred on him, acts of necessity that won back two thousand captives without ransom. He also secured a thousand citizens without a herald, while vilifying Demosthenes as a bitter sycophant. The orator insists that decisions taken in war cannot be judged by the standard of present peace, with aphoristic sayings on fortune, rhetoric, and the taming of Alexander scattered through the argument. The speech closes on further such sententiae.
grc.demosthenes.against_apatourius: This short Athenian forensic speech belongs to the Demosthenic corpus, and it was delivered by a defendant in a maritime commercial suit. The speaker supports a paragraphe, a plea that the case is inadmissible, citing laws granting merchants prompt commercial dikai. These rules allow disputes over alleged contracts to be settled by the paragraphe procedure, which recounts dealings with Apatourius and the fugitive Parmenon of Byzantium. A loan of thirty minae was raised from the banker Heraclides on his guarantee, and the ship and children were taken in pledge for this debt. All contracts were mutually released once the debt was paid, but the original written agreements subsequently vanished from view. A disputed arbitration by Aristocles was held in Parmenon's absence after an earthquake destroyed his family, and the speaker denies ever having stood guarantor for Parmenon. He argues from the passage of time and the annual term allowed for guarantors, concluding that his paragraphe was entered rightly. Apatourius has sued falsely and contrary to the laws.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_2: This forensic speech by Demosthenes is the second of two delivered against Aphobus, concerning the estate that the speaker's dying father entrusted to Aphobus and two fellow guardians. The orator opens by announcing his intent to refute Aphobus' many falsehoods, beginning with the claim that the grandfather owed money to the state. The father allegedly refused to lease the house for fear of penalty, and the argument shows that the family's wealth was openly held and liberally assessed for liturgies. The guardians concealed the will by which alone the truth could be learned, misappropriating the workshop, the slaves, and other assets while lodging contradictory accounts. The speech recalls how the father placed his children and property in the three men's hands, exposing the antidosis contrived to bar the speaker's lawsuits. The orator pleads on behalf of the impoverished mother and sister, closing by urging the jurors to grant the speaker his day in court.
grc.demosthenes.against_callicles: Against Callicles is a short Athenian forensic speech transmitted among the works of Demosthenes, whose uncertain date features a landowner answering a private suit for damages. The plaintiff, a neighbour named Callicles, claims harm from rainwater draining between their farms, and the opening laments the burden of a wicked and grasping neighbour. It recounts Callicles' record of vexatious litigation, including suits routed through a cousin, a brother, and the slave Callarus. The argument maintains that the disputed walling was built by the speaker's father more than fifteen years earlier, when Callicles' father lived beside him and never objected. The land is planted with vines and figs and holds ancestral tombs, so it cannot be a gully, and the alleged spoilage of grain and oil was trivial, with testimony and a formal challenge read out in support. The speech closes with an appeal to the jurors not to abandon a man being driven from the city by sycophants.
grc.demosthenes.against_evergus_and_mnesibul: This forensic speech by Demosthenes, composed for an Athenian jury in a suit for false testimony, praises laws allowing injured parties to sue perjured witnesses. The speaker, a former trierarch, asks jurors to hear the affair from its beginning, recounting how he was compelled by decree and law to recover naval equipment owed to the state by Theophemus. His seizure of pledges led to blows between the two men, and Theophemus retaliated by plundering the speaker's house and property. Against this background, he prosecutes Theophemus's brother Evergus and brother-in-law Mnesibulus, whose testimony that Theophemus had once offered to surrender a female slave for the torture-test proved decisive in the earlier assault trial. The speech argues that this testimony is demonstrably false because the slave was repeatedly demanded and never produced, supporting the narrative throughout with the reading of decrees, laws, and depositions.
grc.demosthenes.against_nicostratus: This Athenian forensic oration belongs to the private class within the corpus attributed to Demosthenes, arising from an apographē for state confiscation. The speaker insists he registered slaves claimed by Arethusius as a wronged man, not a professional informer, citing the estate size. He recalls a long friendship with Nicostratus, detailing his ransom after capture by a trireme and sale at Aegina. The text covers loans and a mortgage extended to him, followed by injuries including a judgment in default. It describes an ambush near the stone quarries and a successful action for false summons, where the jury imposed a talent fine. The closing portion marshals witnesses to establish that the slaves belong to Arethusius, recounting mutual challenges for public torture.
grc.demosthenes.against_spudias: This Greek forensic oration of uncertain date is transmitted among the private speeches of the Demosthenic corpus, where a plaintiff sues his brother-in-law Spudias before an Athenian jury. The speaker explains that he and Spudias married two sisters, the daughters of Polyeuctus, compelling him to litigate over the property that man left behind. The speech recounts Polyeuctus's marriage settlements and dowry arrangements, detailing a thousand drachmae of dowry still outstanding and secured by boundary stones on a house. He lists further grievances, including the price of a slave with interest and money lent to Polyeuctus's widow, as well as pledged jewellery, a tent never returned, and a mina spent on the Nemesia. Spudias allegedly refuses to honour or disputes all of these claims, prompting the speaker to answer anticipated defences with laws, wills, deposited documents, and witness testimony. The oration weighs the rival valuations of the dowry goods and closes by urging the jurors not to let Spudias prevail through false accusations.
grc.demosthenes.against_zenothemis: This short Athenian forensic speech, transmitted within the Demosthenic corpus, arises from a maritime loan on a grain cargo shipped from Syracuse. The speaker cites the laws under which he lodged a paragraphe, a formal objection, arguing that Zenothemis' suit is inadmissible because no written contract existed. The narrative shows Zenothemis and the shipowner Hegestratos conspiring to scuttle the vessel, intending to defraud the lenders of the cargo. Hegestratos drowned when the plot failed, and Zenothemis then sought to divert the ship at Cephallenia. Later, Zenothemis laid claim to the grain at Athens, while the latter part of the speech introduces evidence and testimony. It also attacks Zenothemis' record in other litigations, closing with the speaker's report that Demosthenes, his kinsman, declined to intervene.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_2: This speech by Demosthenes warns the Athenian assembly that Philip of Macedon is exploiting the peace to expand his power. He argues that Philip is actively preparing against their city while orators merely denounce his aggression. The text surveys Philip's conduct since the peace, including his favour to the Thebans and dealings with the Messenians. It also details his interventions in Thessaly and his interactions with the Argives and Lacedaemonians. Demosthenes contends that all these actions converge on a design against Athens. He recalls the peace embassies and the surrender of Phocis and Thermopylae, demanding that the responsible ambassadors answer for their unfulfilled promises.
grc.demosthenes.reply_to_philip: The Reply to Philip is a short Athenian assembly speech by Demosthenes, framed as an answer to a letter from Philip of Macedon. The orator charges that Philip never made peace in earnest but only postponed the war, and his letter now openly admits the breach. The speaker argues that Philip should be neither feared nor resisted half-heartedly, as divine favour lies with Athens against an oath-breaker. Distrust of the king spreads among the Thessalians, Thebans, and the cities he has attacked, while the Persian king could be persuaded to finance an Athenian-led coalition. The Macedonian kingdom is depicted as inherently fragile, depending on the king's own campaigning yet resented by his subjects who sacrifice their lives and families to his love of glory. The court dreads him as much as his enemies do, and flatterers and mercenary captains share this fear. The speaker attributes the losses of the former war to negligence, noting that politicians bought with Philip's gifts also share the blame. He urges the Athenians to spare neither public nor private resources, taking the field with better generals than before. The orator calls for rallying the other Greeks to the alliance by deeds rather than words.
grc.dinarchus.against_philocles: This Greek courtroom oration by Dinarchus prosecutes Philocles for bribery and treachery concerning the money Harpalus brought into Attica. The speaker recalls that Philocles was repeatedly condemned by the Areopagus, yet he took bribes while holding the generalship over Mounichia and the ship-shdes. He had sworn to keep Harpalus out of the Peiraeus, but now stands trial only for the assessment of his penalty. The speech treats the charges as admitted rather than disputed, weighing fine, death, and confiscation. The orator presses for the harshest sentence, warning that a commander who sells his trust would as readily betray the fleet, the harbors, and the city itself.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_compositio: Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote this Greek rhetorical treatise for Rufus Metilius, comparing the opening dedication to Helen's gift of the peplos. He defines arrangement, arguing it takes priority over word choice, and demonstrates its power by rearranging passages from Homer and Herodotus. The text surveys the three tasks of fitting, shaping, and modifying words, while also analysing the contributions of melody, rhythm, variation, and propriety. Extended discussions cover letters, syllables, and rhythmical feet, and Dionysius classifies three general types of arrangement. The austere style is exemplified by Pindar and Thucydides, while the smooth and flowery type includes Sappho and Isocrates. The well-blended mean is shown by Homer, Stesichorus, Herodotus, and Demosthenes, and the treatise closes with an argument that good prose contains concealed metres, showing how verse can resemble prose.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isaeo: The essay begins by gathering what is known of Isaeus the logographer, noting his disputed origins as Athenian or Chalcidian and his training under Isocrates. The author also mentions Isaeus' role as teacher of Demosthenes and the silence of earlier writers about his life. The text then treats his exclusive practice of forensic oratory and his distinctive style, which largely imitates Lysias yet differs in greater artifice of composition and emotional effects. Isaeus thus appears as the source from which Demosthenes' power grew, and extended comparisons of passages from speeches of the two orators illustrate the contrast between Lysias' natural simplicity and Isaeus' technical elaboration. These include the speech for Eumathes the metic and the Callimachus concerning the estate of Ferenicus. The work ends with brief assessments of other rhetoricians such as Isocrates, Gorgias, and Alcidamas, explaining why Dionysius of Halicarnassus took Lysias and Isaeus as his exemplars, and announcing a further discussion of Demosthenes, Hyperides, and Aeschines.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.ars_rhetorica: A Greek treatise on rhetoric attributed to Dionysius of Halicarnasus, the work opens with praise of festivals as a gift of the gods and, in an address to one Echecrates, teaches how a festival speech should commend the presiding god, the city, the contest, the crown, and the king. It then passes in turn through the chief occasions of epideictic oratory: wedding speeches and the speech in the bridal chamber, addresses on the day of a child's birth, words of welcome to governors arriving in a city, public and private funeral orations, and exhortations delivered to athletes at the games. The latter part is devoted to figured speeches, in which a speaker says one thing while meaning another, with extended analyses of passages from Demosthenes, Thucydides, Plato, Xenophon, Euripides, and Homer. A closing section catalogues the faults that disfigure rhetorical exercises in character, judgment, technique, and diction, and proposes those four criteria as the standard for judging any speech.
grc.epictetus.fragments: This volume gathers short Greek fragments, dialogues, and maxims transmitted under the name of Epictetus, with several pieces headed as drawn from Arrian's compilations. The opening dialogue asks whether a philosopher must study the physical composition of things, taking up the Delphic precept to know oneself. Later excerpts treat what lies within our power and what does not, addressing acceptance of nature, friendship, pleasure, wealth, and moderation. Some sections are marked as coming from Arrian's protreptic lectures or the memorabilia of Epictetus, while others are noted as excerpts from Rufus on friendship. The collection closes with a string of aphorisms on friendship and household order, covering wealth, sound judgment, and the conduct of citizens and rulers.
grc.euripides.medea: Medea, a Greek tragedy of the fifth century BCE by Euripides, opens with the Nurse's lament that Jason has forsaken Medea, the Colchian princess who once saved him. He means to marry the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth, and both Medea and her children have been condemned to exile. Creon, fearing her reputation for cunning, grants her a single day's delay, and her quarrel with Jason, who defends the new marriage as advantageous to the family, ends in stalemate. Assured of asylum by Aegeus, king of Athens, Medea sends her children to the bride with a poisoned robe and golden crown that destroy both princess and father. She then kills her own sons so that Jason is left wholly bereft. The play closes with Medea above the house in the chariot of the Sun, refusing Jason the children's bodies for burial and foretelling his dishonourable death before departing for Athens.
grc.euripides.suppliants: Suppliants is a classical Greek tragedy by Euripides that opens at Eleusis, where the childless mothers of the Seven who fell before Thebes supplicate Demeter. Aethra, the mother of Theseus, pleads their cause with her son, and he wins the Athenian assembly's approval to recover the dead. He rebuffs the herald sent by Creon in a debate on monarchy and democracy, defeats the Thebans in battle, and brings the bodies back for cremation. The play then presents the mothers' laments and Evadne's self-immolation on the pyre of her husband Capaneus. Athena's closing epiphany imposes an oath of peace on Adrastus and foretells the vengeance of the dead men's sons.
grc.galen.de_comate_secundum_hippocratem: Galen begins by asking what the name coma signifies in Hippocrates, considering whether it means drowsy sinking into sleep, sleep itself, or a lethargic torpor. He reviews the divergent answers of earlier interpreters on this point, drawing chiefly on the third book of the Epidemics and on the Prognostic. He argues that Hippocrates repeatedly pairs coma with sleeplessness, suggesting the word cannot simply mean sleep or drowsiness. Galen distinguishes two kinds of sinking, which he calls kataphora, one being the heavy sleepiness proper to lethargic patients. The other is a heavy but rousable, sleepless torpor that occurs in cases of phrenitis, and he maintains that both conditions fall under the name of coma. A final discussion defends the interrogative force of Hippocrates' phrase 'are they phrenitic?', reading this hesitation as a sign of an early stage of illness that may end either in lethargy or in phrenitis.
grc.galen.de_compositione_medicamentorum_sec: Galen's De Compositione Medicamentorum Secundum Locos ('On the Composition of Drugs According to Parts') arranges compound recipes by the body regions they treat. The text argues that therapy depends on the patient's constitution and the nature of the affected part, not just the disease. It begins with remedies for the head, covering scalp and hair complaints such as alopecia and baldness. The work then moves to dentifrices and mouth remedies, followed by plasters and ointments for sciatica, gout, and arthritis. Many formulas are ascribed to earlier physicians like Andromachus, Asclepiades, and Heras. Galen comments on the powers, proportions, and correct preparation of these ingredients.
grc.galen.de_experientia_medica: Galen's De Experientia Medica, or On Medical Experience, is a Greek polemic against the Empirical school, taking the form of a dialogue that opens and closes in mid-argument. A speaker mocks an Empiricist opponent who still awaits further observations before conceding anything, while the debate demands that Empiricists state how many observations suffice for a reliable generalisation. The text faults them for supplying no measure of the often, and it also weighs their appeals to Democritus and Plato. It concludes that countless similar observations cannot establish a medical doctrine, because no measure of frequency exists across differing patient conditions.
grc.galen.de_simplicium_medicamentorum_tempe: Galen's Greek treatise, De Simplicium Medicamentorum Temperamentis ac Facultatibus ('On the Temperaments and Powers of Simple Medicaments'), explains how single drugs act on the body. The work relies on the primary qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness to describe these effects. It begins by defining key terms and distinguishing simple medicines from compound ones. Galen rejects the Sceptic and Empiric view that such powers are unknowable, arguing instead that they stem from elemental qualities. He proposes a method for testing each drug by its observed effect on the patient. This judgement must rest on the substance itself rather than on colour or texture. Examples like pepper, hellebore, henbane, and mandrake illustrate the classification of drugs by their heating or cooling degrees.
grc.galen.de_venae_sectione_adversus_erasist: Galen wrote this Greek prose treatise to defend phlebotomy against the school of Erasistratus, which declined to employ the practice. He asks why an author so meticulous over trifles like vegetable recipes ignored venesection, a stance Galen finds difficult to justify. The text reports objections from Erasistratus' followers and Chrysippus of Cnidus, and it also rehearses the Erasistratean physiology where fever arises from blood in the arteries. Galen answers with Hippocratic passages and the concordant practice of physicians of every sect, arguing that drawing blood is easier to control than drugs, clysters, or fasting. The closing argument turns Erasistratus' own admissions against him, since he concedes the need to evacuate plethora, so venesection remains the speedy remedy.
grc.galen.natural_faculties: This Greek treatise by Galen examines the natural faculties that govern living bodies. It distinguishes between the soul's works, like perception, and nature's works, such as growth. The text argues that every body part holds innate attractive, retentive, alterative, and expulsive powers. Galen demonstrates these through digestion, blood formation, and the function of organs like the stomach. He criticizes Erasistratus and Asclepiades for denying such inherent powers. Hippocrates and Aristotle provide the authoritative framework for this physiology of alteration.
grc.galen.protrepticus: This Greek prose protreptic by Galen urges young men to devote themselves to education in the arts. It opens by asking whether irrational animals share in reason, concluding that man alone is rational. The argument contrasts the unstable goddess Fortune with Hermes, the master of reason. It depicts the ruin that overtakes those who pursue wealth, noble birth, and beauty. A sustained attack on athletic training follows, showing its uselessness for war, health, and livelihood. The text closes by commending the liberal arts, and above all medicine, as the worthiest object of a young man's labour.
grc.galen.synopsis_librorum_suorum_de_pulsib: Galen wrote this Greek synopsis to defend the practice of creating concise summaries, arguing that students avoid long treatises but suffer from poor abridgments by others. This work compresses his sixteen-book study of the pulse into a single overview, defining the pulse as the perceptible expansion of the artery. It surveys differences in size, speed, strength, and rhythm, explaining how to distinguish these traits by touch. Later chapters discuss causes and variations by sex, age, and season, covering the prognostic value of pulse diagnosis in fevers. The text names aberrant forms such as the wave-like and gazelle-like pulses, criticizing Herophilus and Erasistratus for their theories on pulse timing and movement. The treatise breaks off before its exposition is complete.
grc.hanno.periplus_hannonis: The Periplus of Hanno is a short Greek narrative of uncertain date that presents the report of a Carthaginian sent beyond the Pillars of Heracles. His mission was to found cities of the Libyphoenicians on the Atlantic coast, and the story opens with the decision to equip sixty penteconters. These ships carried some thirty thousand men and women, along with grain and provisions, as the fleet travels down the coast through settlements like Thymiaterion and the island Kernē. They meet the friendly Lixitae and their Ethiopian neighbours, and the journey continues past lakes and great rivers teeming with crocodiles and hippopotamuses. The crew witnesses nocturnal fires and a burning, impassable country, and they also see a mountain called the Chariot of the Gods. An island resounding with flutes, cymbals, and drums adds to the wonders, and in the Horn of the South, three hairy women are seized. Their interpreters call these women Gorillas, and their skins are carried back to Carthage. Dwindling stores finally end the voyage, and the narrative closes with this return rather than any formal conclusion.
grc.hippocrates.de_articulis: De Articulis, a Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates, addresses dislocated and subluxated joints despite its uncertain date. The work opens with the shoulder, distinguishing directions of humeral head slippage and comparing reduction methods. The author ranks a shaped wooden lever best among techniques like the heel and ladder. The discussion proceeds joint by joint through the elbow, wrist, fingers, jaw, nose, ear, spine, ribs, hip, knee, ankle, and foot. Each section details signs of displacement, leverage, extension, and bandaging techniques for these specific areas. Extensive passages cover the fatal danger of reducing open dislocations, gangrene, amputation, and wasting from unreduced cases. The text notes congenital deformities such as club foot and includes digressions on anatomy, patient constitution, and cattle physiology. Further digressions concern the legendary Amazons and a quotation from Homer.
grc.hippocrates.de_morbis_popularibus: This Greek medical treatise, attributed to Hippocrates though its date remains uncertain, is conventionally titled in Latin as De Morbis Popularibus, which means the Epidemics. The text opens with a record of the seasons and weather at Thasos near the autumn equinox, then describes the year's constitution and the disorders that prevailed during that time. The work proceeds through general descriptions of epidemic ailments, fevers, consumption, and other conditions, while also discussing the types of fever and the critical days on which crises and recoveries fall. The largest portion consists of individual case histories of named patients in several towns, where each case is traced day by day through symptoms, excretions, crises, and final outcomes.
grc.hippocrates.de_officina_medici: De Officina Medici ('The Physician's Workshop') is a short Greek treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus. It is attributed to Hippocrates, though its date remains uncertain. The text opens with a reflection on knowledge gathered through the senses. It then lists the elements of the surgical setting, including the patient, operator, instruments, and light. The bulk of the work prescribes the physician's posture, bearing, and hand training. It also sets out detailed rules for bandages, splints, and the reduction of fractures.
grc.hippocrates.epidemiarum: Epidemiarum, meaning Epidemics, is a Greek medical treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates, though its exact date remains uncertain. The text records seasonal constitutions, weather patterns, and prevailing diseases in specific locations, and it also includes detailed clinical case histories from various regions. The work begins at Thasos with a year of seasonal conditions and a fatal outbreak of phthisis among the young, then moves through other years and places. It describes fevers, bowel complaints, and other epidemic ailments, which are interleaved with brief notes on individual patients, including wrestlers, women in childbirth, children, and wounded men. The author sets down their symptoms, crisis days, outcomes, and occasional treatments in sequence.
grc.hippocrates.prorrheticon_i: The Prorrheticon, a collection of short statements attributed to Hippocrates, offers signs for foretelling the course of disease despite its uncertain date. It opens with indicators present at the onset of illness, such as drowsiness and head pains, which combined with wakefulness point specifically to phrenitis. The main body catalogues indications for acute fevers, delirium, tremors, and sweats, while also examining the tongue, urine, bowel discharges, loss of voice, and nosebleeds. Each sign is marked as fatal, doubtful, or favourable, with occasional reference to named patients from Cos. Toward the end, the terse entries give way to fuller discussions that instruct physicians in questioning patients about menstruation, the womb, and chronic complaints.
grc.libanius.declamations_1-12: This volume gathers twelve declamations by Libanius, which are Greek speeches cast as pleas before courts or assemblies. They are delivered in the personae of figures from myth and classical history, beginning with a defence of Socrates at his trial. A companion of the philosopher answers the charges of Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon while addressing the Athenian jurors in this imagined setting. The remaining declamations carry the same form through other subjects, featuring speakers drawn from the Trojan cycle and Athenian public life. One such speaker is Achilles, who justifies his anger and refuses the gifts and marriage alliance offered by Agamemnon. At the close, Timon laments that love for Alcibiades has overthrown his misanthropy, treating both legendary and historical characters within the fixed shape of an imagined address to judges or listeners.
grc.lucian.de_astrologia: Lucian composed this short Greek dialogue in an archaizing Ionic style, where the speaker complains that learned men neglect astrology, which he champions as the oldest science. He traces the art from the Ethiopians, who first observed the moon and planets, to the Egyptians, who fixed the zodiacal signs and the measures of time. The knowledge passed to the oracle of Ammon and the Babylonians, and it finally reached the Greeks through Orpheus. A long central sequence rereads Greek myths as distorted memories of celestial knowledge, featuring Tiresias' double nature and the golden ram in the strife of Atreus and Thyestes. Bellerophon, Phrixus, Daedalus, Icarus, and Pasiphae are also discussed, while Phaethon and Endymion join the divine parentages of Minos, Aeneas, and Autolycus. Cronus' slow course and episodes in Homer and Hesiod are examined, and the oracles of Delphi and Didyma and Odysseus' consultation of Tiresias are included. Lycurgus' Spartan laws complete the list of examples, and the dialogue closes by rebutting objections that astrology is impossible or useless. The stars' movements bring foreknowledge that makes coming goods and evils easier to bear.
grc.lucian.de_parasito_sive_artem_esse_paras: Lucian of Samosata composed this short comic dialogue featuring Tychiades and the parasite Simon, who concedes he knows no conventional craft but claims mastery of dining at other men's tables. He offers a mock serious defense of parasitism as a genuine technē, arguing that this practice surpasses both rhetoric and philosophy in value. Simon cites philosophers like Aeschines, Aristippus, and Plato as historical examples, while claiming Homeric heroes, notably Nestor and Patroclus, as members of this group. The parasite is compared favorably with orators in both war and peace, and Simon extols his freedom from fear, ambition, and the love of money.
