He presents the parasite as a blessing and guardian to the rich man he attends, and Tychiades finally declares himself Simon's first pupil in the art.
grc.lucian.dialogi_deorum: Lucian of Samosata wrote the Dialogues of the Gods in Greek, a title that translates to Dialogues of the Gods. These miniature comic pieces are staged among the Olympians, conducted in everyday colloquial speech. The collection opens with Prometheus bargaining with Zeus for his release, while he is chained on the Caucasus. The dialogues then range over Zeus' love affairs with Ganymede, Io, Semele, and Danaë, and they also cover Hera's jealous quarrels and Ixion's cloud bride. The text recounts the births of Athena, Dionysus, and Heracles, and it describes the net in which Hephaestus traps Ares and Aphrodite. Apollo mourns for Hyacinthus in one of these scenes, while Pan claims divine parentage and Hermes laments his endless errands. Throughout, the gods appear as a quarrelsome and amorous household, and their mythic exploits are recounted as gossip, bickering, and domestic comedy.
grc.lucian.herodotus: Lucian of Samosata wrote this short Greek prose piece under the title Herodotus. It opens with a wish to imitate even one of Herodotus's excellences, such as the beauty of his language or the wit of his judgment. The narrative recounts how Herodotus sailed from Caria and read his nine books before the Greeks at Olympia. This act won him a pan-Hellenic reputation and inspired later sophists to follow the same route to fame. The text also describes at length a painting by Aetion of the marriage of Alexander and Roxane. Lucian closes by likening his own presentation of works to Macedonians to Herodotus's recitation.
grc.lucian.hesiod: This brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata features a conversation between Hesiod and an unnamed critic. The critic charges Hesiod with breaking the promise made in his verse that the Muses granted him knowledge of things past and to come. He notes that Hesiod recounted the births of the gods and gave farming counsel yet never foretold anything useful to life. Hesiod replies that the Works and Days offers practical instruction on agriculture, seasons, and labour rather than divination. He argues that the Muses bestow their gifts as they please and that poets fill out their lines for metre and euphony without incurring a duty of literal completeness. The exchange closes with the retort that Hesiod's claimed inspiration was not even reliable, having left its promised foreknowledge unfulfilled.
grc.lucian.imagines: Lucian of Samosata composed this Greek dialogue as a conversation between Lycinus and Polystratus, who begins by describing how a beautiful woman left him standing in a state of frozen awe. He then constructs a detailed verbal portrait of her physical form, drawing on celebrated sculptures, including the Cnidian Aphrodite of Praxiteles and works by Phidias. The text also references famous painters to add color to the image of the woman, who is identified as Panthea, the companion of a king. The second half of the dialogue turns to her inner qualities, praising her education, wisdom, and temperance in high fortune. The piece closes with a proposal to combine body and soul into a single written portrait, which is meant to be more lasting than any work of brush or chisel.
grc.lucian.phalaris: Phalaris is a pair of rhetorical speeches in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, staged at Delphi over the question of whether to accept a bronze bull dedicated by Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas. It opens as the tyrant's envoys address the Delphians, relaying his request that the god receive the offering, and they also plead that his reputation for cruelty is undeserved. The envoys then narrate Phalaris's seizure of power amid faction at Acragas, describing his professed moderation and his justification for punishing plotters. The story of Perilaus, the craftsman who devised the bull as an engine of torture, is also told, and he was shut inside it as its first victim. A Delphian speaker closes the work by arguing that the dedication must be received, since the sanctuary has never examined the character of donors, and doing so now would profane established custom.
grc.lucian.pro_lapsu_inter_salutandum: Lucian of Samosata wrote this short prose piece about a slip of the tongue, where the speaker greeted a patron at daybreak with the wrong word. He used 'hugiainein' where custom demanded 'chairein', an error that left him rebuked before the onlookers. The bulk of the work is the written apology he resolves to compose, which surveys greetings and letter openings in antiquity. The text notes the use of 'chairein' in Homer and drama, while Plato replaced it with 'eu prattein'. Pythagoreans and Epicureans preferred 'hugiainein', and anecdotes involve Alexander, Hephaestion, Antiochus, Ptolemy, Pyrrhus, and Augustus. The argument turns the lapse into a propitious omen, attributing the slip to the favour of Hygieia or Asclepius, and closes with the apology addressed to Asclepius.
grc.lucian.pseudologista: The Pseudologista is a short Greek invective by Lucian of Samosata, in which a speaker denounces a malicious critic who taunted him as a barbarian. The critic also jeered at the speaker's declamations, prompting a threat of repayment in the biting iambs associated with Archilochus. The speaker appeals to a Menandrian prologue figure, who supports frank speech while the speaker rehearses the man's notorious conduct. The closing portion recounts an anecdote from Olympia involving a sophist who passed off a written speech about Pythagoras as his own improvisation. This text was patched together from borrowed material, and the audience recognised each stolen passage.
grc.lucian.quomodo_historia_conscribenda_sit: The Quomodo Historia Conscribenda Sit ('How History Should Be Written') is a satirical treatise on the craft of historiography by Lucian of Samosata, cast as advice to a friend named Philo. It opens with the comic story of the Abderites, who fell into collective madness and declaimed Euripides after a performance of the Andromeda, a condition Lucian likens to the epidemic of would-be historians that followed a recent war between Romans and Parthians. The greater part of the essay mocks the faults of these contemporaries, among them bombastic prologues, servile imitation of Thucydides and Herodotus, flattery, implausible exaggeration, and gross errors of geography. It then turns to positive precepts: the historian should be politically perceptive, fearless and impartial, devoted above all to truth, writing for posterity rather than present applause, and setting out events in plain, clear diction, carefully ordered and proportioned like a sculptor shaping given material.
grc.lucian.scytha: The Scythian is a short prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, in which a Syrian speaker recounts the story of Toxaris, a man of common Scythian stock. Toxaris came to Greece before Anacharsis, seeking Greek learning, and he died at Athens, where he received heroic honours as a healer. In the Ceramicus, he greets the newly landed Anacharsis, who is bewildered and on the point of sailing home. Toxaris leads him to Solon, presenting the aged lawgiver as Greece entire, and Anacharsis is then initiated and made a citizen of Athens. The speaker compares his own later arrival with Anacharsis' perplexity, reporting Athenian counsel to attach himself to an eminent father and son.
grc.lucian.tyrannicida: This short Greek declamation by Lucian takes the form of a defense speech, where the speaker claims a public reward for killing two tyrants in a single day. He tells the judges that he cut down the tyrant's son with his own sword, then led the aged father to slay himself with the same blade. The bulk of the work answers an objector who insists the reward belongs only to the man whose hand did the killing. He recounts his storming of the acropolis and defeat of the bodyguard, dwelling on the son's harsher tyranny and the father's doting subjection to him. He dramatizes the old man's lament over his dying child and his trembling suicide, arguing that whoever supplies the cause of death counts as the killer under the law. He closes by asking the judges to weigh the design and entire outcome of the deed rather than the exact manner of the tyrant's death.
grc.lucian.vitarum_auctio: Vitarum Auctio, a short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, features Zeus ordering Hermes to prepare a marketplace for an auction of philosophers' lives. A would-be purchaser examines each lot in turn, beginning with a long-haired Pythagorean who teaches the harmony of the universe and transmigration. The tour continues to a dog-like Cynic and a drunken Cyrenaic hedonist, followed by a laughing philosopher from Abdera and a weeping one from Ephesus. An Athenian expounds the theory of forms and community of women, while an Epicurean gourmet and a Stoic expert in syllogisms and paradoxes appear next. A double-natured Peripatetic and a Pyrrhonian skeptic who professes ignorance of everything round out the list, as the exchanges trade in mockery of each school's doctrines and jargon. The lots are variously bought, refused, or left unsold, and at the close, Zeus and Hermes dismiss the crowd, promising to auction the lives of ordinary and tradesman-like men on the following day.
grc.maximus_of_tyre.dialexeis: The Dialexeis of Maximus of Tyre is a collection of philosophical lectures composed in Greek. It is also transmitted under the title Philosophumena, which means philosophical discourses. The work consists of orations on ethical and philosophical subjects. The first oration contrasts the actors of Dionysus with the philosopher. This philosopher plays many roles in a civic drama directed by god. The opening text argues that the philosopher's logos must adapt to every occasion of human life. It illustrates this point with Homeric quotations and analogies drawn from musical harmonies, rivers, and athletic contests.
grc.niciae_epistula.epistula: This single Greek letter is attributed to Nicias, the Athenian general in Sicily, and is addressed to the Athenians during the campaign against Syracuse. The text opens by reminding the recipients that earlier deeds are known from previous letters, then reports the arrival of the Spartan Gylippus with reinforcements. A battle was lost before the walls, and the siege works were abandoned, while the greater part recounts the decay of the fleet and its crews. Rotten hulls, casualties, desertion, and the hostility of the countryside caused this decline, and the weakness of the remaining allies is also described. The letter closes with an urgent demand for fresh land and naval forces, money, and a successor commander due to the writer's kidney illness. A warning follows that decisions must be taken at once with the coming of spring.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_ii: The Second Letter to Timothy is one of the Pastoral Epistles in the Greek New Testament, framed as a letter from the apostle Paul, who is imprisoned and near death. The recipient is his beloved associate Timothy, though the exact date remains uncertain, and Paul opens by recalling Timothy's sincere faith, which he inherited from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to rekindle his spiritual gift and not be ashamed of the gospel or Paul's chains, using images of the soldier, athlete, and farmer to guide the reader. The letter also warns against vain disputes and teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus, while Paul describes the vices that will prevail in the last days and appeals to remain in the inspired scriptures. He solemnly charges Timothy to preach the word in season and out of season, closing with Paul's sense that his hour of departure has come. He asks Timothy to bring Mark, his cloak, and the parchments, reporting on companions who have left or stayed before offering a final benediction of grace.
grc.philip_ii_king_of_macedonia.epistulae: This brief Greek collection presents royal letters attributed to Philip II of Macedon, whose opening letter addresses the council and people of Athens. It announces Philip's campaigns in Phocis and warns the Athenians to abide by their sworn agreements, while the remaining pieces deal chiefly with relations with Athens. A long letter catalogs grievances, including the imprisonment of the herald Nicias and the conduct of the general Diopeithes. It also covers the dispute over Halonnesus and rival claims to Amphipolis, and shorter notes to the Thebans and Peloponnesian allies take up peace overtures. They also include a summons to arms against the Locrians who had violated the sanctuary at Delphi, and the collection closes with a correspondence with Aristotle. Philip announces the birth of a son and asks that Aristotle rear and educate him, and a reply on virtue and the conduct of rule follows.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_ebrietate: De Ebrietate, a Greek allegorical treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, opens by recalling what other philosophers had said about drunkenness in a preceding book. The author then turns to what Moses the Lawgiver holds on the subject, surveying the Law's differing commands concerning wine. It covers the Nazirites, the priests, and the disobedient son condemned to be stoned, interpreting drunkenness as a figure for folly from lack of education and insatiable appetite. Biblical episodes are expounded as symbols of vice and knowledge, including Noah's nakedness, Jacob and Esau, and Lot with his daughters. These are set against the sobriety of those who follow right reason and virtue.
grc.philo_judaeus.in_flaccum: This Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus examines the fall of Aulus Avillius Flaccus, who served as Roman prefect of Alexandria and Egypt under Tiberius and Gaius. The text opens by ranking Flaccus as heir to Sejanus's designs against the Jewish nation, then catalogues his capable and orderly early administration. With Tiberius's death and Gaius's accession, the prefect degenerates, and the narrative follows his connivance at mob violence against the Alexandrian Jews. It details the desecration of their synagogues and the public floggings, during which Jewish women were forced to eat pork. Flaccus also obstructed an embassy bearing a decree of homage to the emperor, which King Agrippa eventually secured. The work closes with Flaccus's arrest at a banquet, his banishment to Andros, and his violent death, presented as retribution for the innocent blood he shed, framing these events as proof that the Jewish nation did not lack divine aid.
grc.plato.alcibiades_1: This Socratic dialogue, attributed to Plato, features a conversation between Socrates and the young Alcibiades, who is about to make his first appearance in Athenian public life. Socrates begins by explaining his long attachment to the youth, noting that a daimonic opposition has ceased, and then questions Alcibiades' political ambitions. He shows that Alcibiades cannot define justice or identify the many as competent teachers, turning the discussion to self-knowledge and the care of the soul. Socrates warns that Alcibiades must prepare for a contest against the kings of Sparta and Persia, presenting himself as the only genuine lover of his soul. He concludes that only virtue, cultivated through mutual self-examination, will secure the happiness of both men and the city.
grc.plato.critias: Plato's Critias is a short, unfinished dialogue that continues the Timaeus, in which Critias describes a war fought nine thousand years before his time. The conflict pitted primordial Athens against the island of Atlantis, and the work opens with Critias asking for indulgence after Timaeus' speech. It then recounts the ancient constitution of Athens, where the warrior class lived in common around the temple of Athena and Hephaestus. The text also notes the pristine fertility of Attica before attention turns to the island of Atlantis. Poseidon united with Cleito and divided the land into ten kingdoms, which were assigned to his sons. The royal city featured concentric rings of land and water, containing temples, palaces, canals, and harbours. The narrative details the military organisation and royal laws, but corruption eventually overtook the kings as their divine element waned. The story breaks off just as Zeus gathers the gods to judge the Atlantians.
grc.plato.epinomis: The Epinomis ('After the Laws') is a short Greek dialogue attributed to Plato. It serves as an appendix to the Laws and reopens the conversation of the Athenian Stranger, Cleinias, and Megillus. The text addresses the question left unfinished there, which is what learning makes a human being truly wise. The speaker surveys practical arts such as farming, building, generalship, and medicine. He argues that none of these yields wisdom, which rests instead on number and mathematics. Astronomy crowns this mathematical study and leads to a theology of the celestial bodies. The work closes by prescribing this study, pursued through piety, as the proper discipline of the nocturnal council.
grc.plato.minos: This short Socratic dialogue, attributed to Plato though its date remains uncertain, features Socrates discussing the nature of law with an unnamed companion. They begin by asking what law is and whether it is simply what a city decrees, then examine and revise that initial suggestion. The argument claims that law aims at the discovery of truth, and it also asserts that the writings of doctors, gardeners, and kings serve as the laws of their arts. The variation of laws among peoples shows that most have not found what truly is, and the text then offers an encomium of Minos, defended against Homer and Hesiod. Minos is presented as a pupil of Zeus and a beneficent lawgiver, whose unchanging Cretan laws were slandered by Athenian poets because of the tribute. The dialogue closes with Socrates asking what the good lawgiver distributes to the soul, and the companion is unable to answer this final question.
grc.plutarch.apophthegmata_laconica: This Greek collection brings together brief sayings of Spartan kings and citizens, preserved among the Moralia ('Moral Essays') of Plutarch. It opens with the answers of Agasicles, among them his reason for refusing to study under the sophist Philophanes, before turning to Agesilaus. The terse replies of Agesilaus are interleaved with episodes from his campaigns against Tissaphernes and the Persian king and with his dealings with Greek cities. Later sections gather remarks of Cleomenes, Labotas, Leotychidas, and other royal and private Spartans on command, warfare, piety, and laconic brevity of speech. The work closes with anecdotes of anonymous Laconians, including their answers to Philip of Macedon and Antipater and vignettes of Spartan conduct at Olympia and elsewhere.
grc.plutarch.aquane_an_ignis_sit_utilior: Aquane an Ignis Sit Utilior, meaning whether water or fire is the more useful, is a short Greek treatise by Plutarch preserved among his Moralia. The work opens with Pindar's verdict that water is best, a view weighed against natural philosophers who make fire the first principle of all things. The body of the text consists of antithetical arguments, where the case for water rests on its constant necessity for all creatures. It also cites its priority over the fire later ascribed to Prometheus, while water supports the growth of plants and crops. It is harmless and equally available to rich and poor, and the sea's power to join humankind in exchange is also noted. The opposing case credits fire with sustaining the heat on which life depends, highlighting the invention of the crafts under Hephaestus. Fire extends the usable day, and it notes the kinship of sight, the keenest sense, to flame.
grc.plutarch.aristides: The Aristides is one of Plutarch's Greek biographies of the Athenian statesman surnamed the Just. It opens by weighing conflicting reports about Aristides' poverty and answering the objections of Demetrius of Phalerum. The narrative then follows his long rivalry with Themistocles and his part at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea. The battle at Plataea is recounted in unusual detail, down to the dispute over the award of valour. Later chapters cover his assessment of the allies' tribute after Athens assumed command. They also include anecdotes of his incorruptibility, his death, and the public honours paid to his family.
grc.plutarch.comparationis_aristophanes_et_m: This brief Greek comparison of the comic poets Aristophanes and Menander is preserved among the Moralia attributed to Plutarch. The essay opens by pronouncing Menander by far the superior poet in general terms. It then censures Aristophanes' diction as coarse and ill-suited, citing antitheses and jumbled stylistic registers. Quotations from his plays illustrate these faults. Menander's language is praised for its blended consistency, fitting every character, age, and circumstance. This quality is compared to a craftsman's product that fits all wearers. Remarks on their audiences contrast Aristophanes' bitter, biting salt with the universal charm of Menander. That charm made Menander at home in theatres, schools, and symposia.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aristides_cato: The synkrisis appended to Plutarch's paired Lives of Aristides and Cato the Elder opens by noting that their differences are hard to discern amid many great resemblances. Both men rose to office and renown without inherited advantage, and the text then weighs the pair point by point, beginning with their different entries into public life. It contrasts the still modest wealth of Athens with the grandee politics of Rome, and their military records are next examined, with Aristides serving at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea. Cato distinguished himself in Spain and in the war against Antiochus, and the comparison turns to their political fortunes, setting Aristides' ostracism by Themistocles against Cato's escape from repeated public prosecutions. Further sections compare their household economy and attitude to money, and the author defends Aristides' voluntary poverty as a mark of self-sufficiency while questioning Cato's thrift. The discussion also takes up self-praise, frankness, and political ambition, and the comparison ends with their marriages, charging that Cato's wedding in old age to the daughter of a serving man brought scandal upon his reputation for temperance.
grc.plutarch.comparison_demetrius_antony: This short formal comparison, known as a synkrisis, closes Plutarch's paired Lives of Demetrius and Antony. It opens by noting that great reversals of fortune befell both men, proposing to weigh their power and prominence first. Demetrius inherited an empire largely made by his father Antigonus, while Antony raised himself from obscure origins to claim Caesar's place. The author then sets their careers point against point, matching Demetrius' liberation of Greek cities against Antony's war on Cassius and Brutus. Their generosity, luxury, and love affairs are also compared, with Cleopatra's hold on Antony likened to Omphale's stripping of Heracles. The piece examines their marriages, acts of impiety, and treatment of parents, considering breaches of sworn agreements and the differing ways each lost his cause. The comparison ends by finding neither man's death praiseworthy, judging Demetrius' endurance of captivity the more disgraceful.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lysander_sulla: This brief comparison by the Greek author Plutarch formally closes the paired Lives of Lysander and Sulla, opening by turning from the two biographies just completed to the synkrisis. The body sets the men's common rise from obscurity against their different roads to power, with Lysander gaining command in a well-ordered Sparta while Sulla emerged amid the corruption and faction of Rome. The text then compares their conduct toward friends, their attitudes to money and pleasure, and their private morals, weighing military achievement next. This section contrasts Lysander's two naval victories and his inglorious death before Haliartus with Sulla's many pitched battles, including his twice holding Rome and his storming of the Piraeus. Each man's treatment of Athens supplies a final point of moral contrast, and the closing verdict judges that Sulla accomplished more while Lysander erred less. It awards the primacy in self-control and temperance to Lysander and in generalship and courage to Sulla.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_nicias_and_crassu: This short Greek prose synkrisis, or formal comparison, concludes Plutarch's paired Lives of the Athenian Nicias and the Roman Crassus. It opens by weighing the two men's wealth, finding Nicias' mining revenues less disreputable than Crassus' gains. Those gains came from Sulla's proscriptions and his fire-brigade speculation. The comparison then proceeds point by point through their public expenditure, political conduct, and commands. It contrasts the Sicilian expedition with the Parthian campaign before touching on their attitudes to divination. The piece closes with an assessment of their deaths, judging Crassus' end the more blameless.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pelopidas_and_mar: This short Greek essay by Plutarch is the formal comparison that closes his paired lives of Pelopidas and Marcellus. It opens with the judgment that the two men matched one another in courage, industriousness, fiery temper, and magnanimity. They differed chiefly in that Marcellus inflicted slaughter on the cities he subdued, while Pelopidas and Epaminondas never killed a captive or enslaved a city. The essay then weighs their campaigns, setting Marcellus's victory over the Celts and capture of Syracuse against Pelopidas's exploits at Tegyra and Leuctra and his liberation of Thebes. It also considers their conduct against Hannibal and Sparta, asking what credit each man deserved for his deeds. Plutarch ends by lamenting the irrational deaths of both in battle, for Pelopidas was buried by the allies for whom he fell, Marcellus by the enemies by whom he fell.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_timoleon_and_aemi: Plutarch's Comparison of Timoleon and Aemilius Paullus concludes the paired Lives of the Greek liberator of Sicily and the Roman conqueror of Macedon. This formal synkrisis opens by noting that both men won famous victories over distinguished foes, with Aemilius defeating the Macedonians and the line of Antigonus, while Timoleon overcame the Carthaginians and the tyrants of Sicily. The argument then weighs their unequal circumstances, judging Timoleon's successes more creditable because he achieved them with mercenary troops against broken tyrants and a great Carthaginian force. Plutarch praises the purity and justice of both commanders, remarking that no Greek general who touched Sicily, Dion alone excepted, escaped corruption. Further points treat their disinterestedness and bearing, as Aemilius enriched himself by not a drachma from the kingdom he overthrew, while Timoleon accepted rewards but did not need them. Aemilius proved unbowed by good fortune or the calamity of his children's deaths, whereas Timoleon's remorse over his brother reveals a gentler and more yielding disposition.
grc.plutarch.de_amicorum_multitudine: This short Greek moral essay by Plutarch appears in the Moralia, arguing that seeking many friends is a maimed and blind kind of philia. The text opens with an anecdote about Menon the Thessalian, whose sweeping catalogue of virtues for every age and station draws a sharp remark from Socrates. A man who names many virtues knows none, just as one who falls into many friendships may possess none. The argument plays on the images of Briareus's hundred hands and Argus's watchful eyes, comparing affection divided among many to a river split into thin and weak streams. No one can attend to many friends' competing claims at once, and many friends also bring many enemies in their train. The essay recalls famous pairs such as Theseus and Pirithous, Achilles and Patroclus, and Orestes and Pylades, concluding that friendship arises from likeness of character. This bond demands a steadfast disposition rather than the Proteus-like versatility of the man who conforms himself to everyone, making such a firm friend rare.
grc.plutarch.de_faciae_quae_in_orbe_lunae_ap: Plutarch's Greek dialogue, De facie quae in orbe lunae apparet, opens mid-conversation as Sulla asks the assembled speakers to review opinions about the lunar face. The group includes the narrator Lamprias, Lucius, Pharnaces, Apollonides, Theon, and the mathematician Menelaus, who attack rival explanations involving reflection from the outer ocean. They argue instead for a moon compounded of earth and ether, lit by the sun and marked by deep hollows. Later portions treat the geometry of eclipses, the earth's shadow, and questions of weight and cosmic position. The text also asks whether the moon could sustain inhabitants, vegetation, and its own dew, before closing with Sulla's retelling of a stranger's tale. There, Cronus sleeps guarded by daimones, and an afterlife assigns earth to the body, the moon to the soul, and the sun to the mind.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna: De Fortuna, a short Greek essay preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch, argues that human affairs are governed by reason and good counsel rather than by chance. The text opens by voicing the claim that fortune directs mortal things, then rebuts it with paired exempla. Aristides enduring poverty and Scipio refusing the spoils of Carthage stand against Philocrates, Lasthenes, and Euthycrates corrupted by Philip's gold. Alexander's restraint is set against Priam's ruin, while the argument contends that crafts accomplish their works by rule, measure, and skill rather than luck. Prudence is accordingly the greatest of the arts, and man, physically naked and defenceless among the beasts, prevails over them through reason, memory, and technique. The essay draws on sayings of Sophocles, Plato, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Aeschylus, Hesiod, and Demosthenes, closing with the thought that wealth, fame, and success apart from prudence become sources of harm and disgrace to their possessors.
grc.plutarch.de_sera_numinis_vindicta: Plutarch's dialogue On the Delays of Divine Vengeance, preserved among his Moralia, examines why the gods defer punishment of the wicked. The conversation opens just after an Epicurean speaker has departed, and Plutarch then discusses the question with his companions Patrocleas, Timon, and Olympichus. They argue that postponement allows for repentance and correction, and they also claim that vice itself torments the evildoer. The dialogue culminates in the tale of Thespesius of Soli, who is revived after an apparently fatal fall and reports on the afterworld.
grc.plutarch.de_superstitione: De Superstitione is a short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, which treats the passion of deisidaimonia. The text opens by dividing ignorance concerning the gods into two distinct currents, where atheism arises in harsh temperaments, while superstition develops in softer ones. Atheism is defined as a false judgment that produces apathy toward the divine, whereas superstition is a passion born of false belief that fills victims with dread. It robs them of sleep through frightful dreams and drives them to degrading purifications, laments, and self-mortification. Furthermore, it causes the divine to be conceived as cruel and vengeful, illustrated by historical exempla including Midas, Aristodemus, and Nicias at the lunar eclipse. The essay also cites the Jews keeping the sabbath under siege and Carthaginian child sacrifice, closing with a warning that those fleeing superstition too quickly may leap over the piety that lies between and fall into atheism.
grc.plutarch.demetrius: Plutarch wrote this Greek prose biography of Demetrius Poliorcetes, the son of Antigonus and king of Macedon, opening with a prologue that defends the portrayal of men whose great natures carry both vices and virtues. It announces that the book will treat Demetrius alongside Antony, and the narrative follows his first campaigns under his father and his victory over Ptolemy at Salamis in Cyprus. He was received at Athens as a saviour and god, and the siege of Rhodes won him the title Besieger of Cities. The story continues through the disaster at Ipsus, where Antigonus fell, and Demetrius seized the Macedonian throne. He then waged renewed wars against Pyrrhus, Lysimachus, and the Greek cities, and his final defeat and capture by Seleucus led to three years of captivity in the Chersonese. He died there, and his son Antigonus conveyed his remains to Demetrias in a royal funeral procession.
grc.plutarch.galba: Plutarch composed this Greek biographical account of an elderly Roman aristocrat, who was proclaimed emperor after Nero fell and murdered within months. The text opens with a reflection on military discipline, drawing on the disorder of Roman armies and the rapid succession of rulers. The narrative follows Galba's noble lineage and wealth, detailing his governorship of Spain and the revolt of Vindex that led to his acclamation. Intrigues by Nymphidius Sabinus at Rome are described, and his march to the city is recounted while growing resentment among soldiers is noted. They were denied their promised donative, and the story closes with the adoption of Piso, the German legions proclaiming Vitellius, and Otho's conspiracy. Galba was assassinated in the Forum, and a concluding assessment of his character follows.
grc.plutarch.mulierum_virtutes: Plutarch's essay on the virtue of women opens as a letter to Clea, rejecting Thucydides' saying about the silence of a good woman. The author argues that the same virtue belongs to men and women, adducing the Roman custom of public funeral praises. The remainder assembles historical and legendary episodes of female heroism, where Trojan women burn the ships in Italy. The women of Phocis, Chios, and Argos fight Cleomenes, while Persian and Celtic women also appear in these tales. Cloelia escapes with the hostages, and the tyrannicides Camma, Aretaphila, and Xenocrite are included. The collection closes with domestic examples, including Stratonice, Chiomara, and Timoclea's defiance of Alexander, plus Eryxo and the wife of Pytheas, with some episodes reported in variant versions and earlier authorities occasionally cited.
grc.plutarch.parallela_minora: This short Greek collection of paired anecdotes is transmitted within Plutarch's Moralia. It opens with a preface that defends ancient history against critics who dismiss it as mere myth. The compiler explains that he has set a more recent Roman parallel beside each older Greek story. He cites the specific writers who recorded both sides of these comparative narratives. The pairs cover battle accounts, self-sacrifices, tales of tyrants, and city foundation legends. Each item closes with a named source, and the same stories reappear on both sides.
grc.plutarch.pericles: Plutarch pairs the Athenian statesman Pericles with Fabius Maximus in this Greek biographical essay, which opens with a methodological discussion of how virtuous deeds arouse emulation in the reader. Pericles' distinguished ancestry and unusual physical appearance are noted before his education under Anaxagoras, and his cautious entry into politics involved rivalry with Cimon and Thucydides son of Melesias. He consolidated power through pay for jury service and public building works, and the text details the construction programme overseen by Phidias, including the Parthenon and Propylaea. Accusations against his associates and his relationship with Aspasia are also examined, while the Samian revolt and the coming of the Peloponnesian War receive substantial treatment. The Megarian decree and Pericles' refusal to lift it are discussed, and the final portion follows the war's outbreak and the plague that destroyed his family. His brief restoration and death conclude the narrative, and the closing assessment notes that Athens was great in deed under his rule.
grc.plutarch.praecepta_gerendae_reipublicae: Plutarch's Praecepta Gerendae Reipublicae, a Greek treatise preserved in the Moralia, addresses Menemachus, a young man of good family entering public life. The work contrasts philosophers who merely exhort with the practical statesman, covering motives for entering politics and reading the character of citizens. It discusses the proper use of speech and rhetoric, advising on the choice of entry into public life. The author examines the selection and treatment of friends, while also addressing the handling of rivals and enmities. The treatise considers conduct under Rome's imperial power, further exploring relations with co-officials and the dangers of ambition and flattery. It closes with counsel on stirring civic concord, urging the avoidance of faction and the quelling of private quarrels before they inflame whole cities, illustrated by anecdotes and sayings from Greek and Roman history.
grc.plutarch.themistocles: Plutarch composed this Greek prose biography as part of his Parallel Lives, focusing on the Athenian statesman and general Themistocles. It begins with his undistinguished parentage, noting an Athenian father and a mother of disputed origin, before tracing his political rise and rivalry with Aristides. He persuaded the city to fund warships with silver from Laurium, and Plutarch details his leadership at Artemisium and Salamis against Xerxes. The text also covers the rebuilding of the walls and the fortification of the Piraeus, while later chapters address his ostracism and accusations of collaboration with Persia. These charges arose from the treason of Pausanias, and the life concludes with his flight through Greece and death at Magnesia. Anecdotes and conflicting traditions from earlier historians run throughout the text, and the final sections note his children, tomb, and the honors retained by his descendants.
grc.plutarch.titus_flamininus: This life of the Roman consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus forms one of Plutarch's paired biographies, serving as the counterpart to his account of Philopoemen. The text opens with a description of Titus's bronze statue in Rome and his quick, ambitious character. The narrative traces his early service in the war against Hannibal and his capture of Tarentum. It also covers his unusually early consulship and his command against Philip V of Macedon. The story culminates in the defeat of the Macedonian phalanx and his proclamation of the Greeks' freedom at the Isthmian games in Corinth. Later chapters treat his restrained settlement of the war with the Spartan tyrant Nabis. They also discuss his diplomacy among the Greek cities when Antiochus invaded Greece. The work further details his role in Hannibal's death in Bithynia. It concludes with the humiliation of his brother Lucius at Cato's hands and a formal comparison of Titus and Philopoemen.
grc.polyaenus.excerpta_polyaeni: The Excerpta Polyaeni is a collection of military stratagems attributed to Polyaenus, a Macedonian author of uncertain date. The work opens with an encomium of the ideal general, listing virtues such as endurance, courage, prudence, and piety. The remainder consists of brief anecdotes, each introduced by the formula 'How'. These stories feature generals from Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Carthaginian, and Roman history. Figures like Philip, Alexander, Hannibal, and Caesar defeat enemies through feigned retreats, ambushes, and forged letters. The entries are grouped by subject, moving from field ruses and discipline to sieges, naval engagements, and acts of treachery.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_spiritu: This short Greek physiological treatise, transmitted under Aristotle's name with the title De Spiritu, has uncertain authorship and date. It opens by asking how the innate pneuma persists and grows, considering whether it is nourished through respiration or digestion. The body raises puzzles about respiration and its cooling function, while examining the pulse as a movement distinct from breathing and nutrition. The author discusses the conveyance of nourishment through veins and arteries to flesh, bone, and sinew, and addresses the purposes served by bones in movement and support. The treatise concludes by rejecting the notion that a single kind of fire acts alike in all bodies, asking whether innate heat operates as instrument, material, or both.
grc.pseudogalen.ad_gaurum_quomodo_animetur_f: Ad Gaurum (Πρὸς Γαῦρον περὶ τοῦ πῶς ἐμψυχοῦνται τὰ ἔμβρυα, 'On How Embryos Are Ensouled') is a Neoplatonic treatise of uncertain date and authorship, falsely attributed to Galen and cast as a disputation addressed to a certain Gaurus. It opens by surveying the longstanding perplexity over whether the embryo is an animal or lives only in the manner of a plant, whether potentially or actually alive, and over when the soul may be said to enter the body. The argument then marshals Plato's Timaeus and Phaedrus to distinguish the vegetative from the self-moving soul, rebuts Hippocratic, Stoic (notably Chrysippus's spermatic logoi) and popular explanations, including tales of the father or womb snatching a soul from the air and Chaldaean doctrines of the eastern 'gate of souls', and answers objections drawn from foetal movement and maternal cravings. Its own thesis, supported by analogies of the ship and its steersman, musical harmony, the magnet and naphtha, is that neither parent transmits the rational soul, that embryos live a merely plant-like life in the womb, and that the completed body receives its proper soul from outside at birth, while the closing section, on whether like proceeds from like, survives in damaged condition.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_theodotionis: Bel and the Dragon is a short prose addition to the Book of Daniel, surviving in the Greek Septuagint tradition, specifically in the version associated with Theodotion. The narrative opens with the death of Astyages and the accession of Cyrus, after which the honoured Daniel disputes with the king over the worship of the idol Bel. He proves the idol to be clay and bronze by strewing ashes in its temple, exposing the priests, along with their wives and children, who secretly consume its offerings. The king has them slain and gives Bel over to Daniel, who dismantles its temple, before the story turns to the great dragon venerated by the Babylonians. Daniel kills it with cakes of pitch, fat, and hair, and in consequence, he is cast into the lions' den for six days. The prophet Habakkuk, carried from Judaea by an angel of the Lord, brings him food.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_g: This Hellenistic Greek prose narrative, preserved in the Septuagint as the third book of Maccabees, recounts the peril and deliverance of the Jews in Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator. The story opens with Ptolemy marching to Raphia to defeat Antiochus, who had seized his territory, and then visiting Jerusalem to attempt entering the inner sanctuary. This act provokes divine punishment, and the narrative turns to the persecution of Jews in Alexandria, including a decree to brand them with the ivy mark of Dionysus. Ptolemy imprisons them in the hippodrome and releases five hundred elephants maddened with wine and frankincense, but the aged priest Eleazar prays for deliverance. Two angels turn the beasts against the king's troops, and the work closes with the release of captives and the establishment of annual days of commemoration.
grc.septuaginta.malachias: Malachias is the Greek Septuagint version of a short biblical prophecy attributed to the prophet Malachi, whose Hebrew original is of uncertain date. Rendered into Greek during the Hellenistic period, the text opens as a burden of the word of the Lord to Israel delivered by an angel. The work proceeds through disputations where God rebukes priests for blemished sacrifices and profaning the covenant of Levi. He also condemns the people for faithlessness, wrongful divorce, and withheld tithes, while promising a refining day of the Lord. The text foretells a sun of righteousness and anticipates Elijah the Thesbite before the great and manifest day. It closes with an admonition to remember the law of Moses.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_i_sive_chronic: The First Paralipomenon ('Things Omitted'), or Chronicles, is a Greek biblical book preserved in the Septuagint, rendered from Hebrew into Greek by an anonymous translator in the Hellenistic period. It opens with an unbroken chain of genealogies running from Adam through Noah and Abraham to the twelve tribes. These are followed by the priestly and Levitical houses, the settlers of Jerusalem, and notices of the Edomite kings and the return from Babylon. The narrative portion recounts the death of Saul, David's anointing at Hebron, his capture of Zion, and his victories over the Philistines and neighboring nations. There follow the transfer of the ark to Jerusalem, the census and ensuing plague, and David's extensive military, cultic, and administrative preparations for the temple Solomon is to build. It closes with David's assembly of all Israel, his charge to Solomon and provision for the temple service, Solomon's enthronement, and David's death after forty years of reign.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi_salomonis: The Psalms of Solomon are a collection of Greek prose psalms of Hellenistic date, transmitted with the Septuagint corpus and bearing Solomon's name in the title, though the works are anonymous. The opening psalm cries out to the Lord in affliction as sinners press upon the speaker, recalling the profanation of Jerusalem's holy places and the mockery of its captors. Across the collection the poems lament the arrogant foreign ruler who trampled the sanctuary as well as the sins of Jerusalem's own people. They denounce hypocrites and the insolent rich, while giving voice to the prayers of the pious poor. Later pieces express confidence in God's just judgment, hope for a purified Zion gathered from exile, and the promise of a Davidic king and resurrection for those who fear the Lord.
grc.soranus.de_fasciis: Soranus composed this short Greek surgical treatise on bandages, which survives in some sixty numbered sections. The text opens mid instruction, detailing how to wind a bandage across the brow and over the crown of the head. It then proceeds part by part through the body, prescribing the application of specific named bandages. The sequence moves from the skull and face, covering the eyes, nose, jaw, and cheeks, to the chest and shoulder. It continues to supports for the breast, groin, and genitals, before addressing the arm, hand, and lower leg. Each entry states the manner of application and the injury it suits, keyed to numbered illustration plates.
grc.tryphon_i_grammaticus.περὶ_τρόπων: This short Greek treatise on tropes, known as peri tropōn ('On Tropes'), is attributed to the grammarian Tryphon, whose date remains uncertain. The text opens by defining phrasis as diction that conveys heightened signification, dividing it into kuriologia and tropos. The author then enumerates fourteen principal tropes, including metaphor, catachresis, allegory, and riddle, proceeding through each figure. Each is defined and illustrated chiefly from Homer, with some examples also coming from tragedy, comedy, and lyric poetry. A final section catalogues twenty-seven further figures of diction, ranging from hyperbole and emphasis to irony and sarcasm. It also includes wit and proverb, briefly distinguishes komma from kolon, and assigns stylistic characters to Thucydides, Demosthenes, Lysias, and other orators.
grc.xenophon.anabasis: The Anabasis ('The March Up-Country') is a Greek prose narrative by Xenophon that opens with the rivalry between Cyrus the Younger and his elder brother Artaxerxes. It recounts how Cyrus secretly assembled a Greek mercenary force under cover of campaigns against the Pisidians and Tissaphernes. The work takes its name from the army's march up-country from Sardis into the interior of the Persian empire. After Cyrus' death in battle the narrative follows the fortunes of the Greek soldiers, and Xenophon himself appears among those who lead the retreat.
grc.archimedes.dimensio_circuli: The Dimensio Circuli, or Measurement of a Circle, is a brief Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes. It consists of three propositions on the geometry of the circle. The first proves that every circle equals a right triangle with a leg equal to the radius and a base equal to the circumference. The second establishes that the area of a circle has to the square on its diameter the ratio of 11 to 14. The third and longest proposition demonstrates that the circumference of any circle exceeds three times its diameter by less than a seventh and by more than ten seventy-firsts.
grc.aristotle.de_divinatione_per_somnum: This short treatise by Aristotle, transmitted among the Parva Naturalia, examines divination through dreams, noting that such claims are neither easy to dismiss nor to credit. The text distinguishes dreams as causes, signs, or mere coincidences of future events, while reputable physicians watch dreams closely for signs of bodily conditions. Most dreams, especially those about distant events, are judged to be coincidences, which explains why so many of them fail to come true. The author holds that dreams are daimonic rather than sent by the gods, arising from faint natural movements that the sleeping mind perceives more readily at night. Prophetic aptitude belongs to ordinary, excitable, and melancholic characters rather than the wisest, and the best judge of dreams is one who can discern resemblances in distorted images. The closing sentence recalls that sleep, dreaming, and divination have all been discussed.
grc.artaxerxis_epistulae.epistulae: These two royal letters, written in Greek and attributed to the Persian king Artaxerxes, are preserved among the Greek epistolographers. The first purports to be the decree ordering the extermination of the Jews throughout the empire at Haman's instigation. The second announces the revocation of that decree, the crucifixion of Haman at Susa, and the granting of peace and honour to Mordecai and Esther on the thirteenth of Adar. Together the letters retell the story of the Book of Esther in the king's own voice, in the elevated prose of an imperial rescript. The date at which the two letters were composed remains a matter of uncertainty.
grc.critias.fragmenta: The Fragmenta gather the surviving remains of Critias of Athens, son of Callaeschrus, who was a poet, sophist, and politician serving among the Thirty. These texts reach us through quotations in authors such as Athenaeus, Plutarch, and Galen, opening with an elegiac passage praising the songs of Anacreon. The collection also includes sympotic verse on the kottabos and a poem honouring Alcibiades, while substantial prose fragments discuss the constitutions of Sparta and Thessaly. Other prose pieces address the nature of love, virtue, and aphorisms, and tragic speeches from plays like Peirithous and Sisyphus are also preserved. Some of these are transmitted under Euripides' name, and lexical and grammatical notes on individual words complete the remains.
grc.demosthenes.against_pantaenetus: This courtroom speech by Demosthenes, delivered in an Athenian private action, opens with the speaker's defence of the preliminary plea, or paragraphe, which argues that the suit brought by Pantaenetus is inadmissible. The greater part of the oration recounts the underlying affair, including a joint loan of a hundred and five minae made to Pantaenetus for the purchase of a mining workshop and thirty slaves at Maroneia. The narrative also covers the tenancy of the workshop under Mnesicles and the quarrel between Pantaenetus and the partner, which ended in the partner's victory at law, followed by a settlement in which Pantaenetus released the speaker from every charge. The speaker then answers each count of the new indictment, producing laws, witness testimony, and formal challenges that show both the release and the mining statutes bar the suit. The speech closes with a character defence of lending money and a plea that a settlement once made should stand.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_accession_of_alexande: This short deliberative speech in Attic Greek is attributed to Demosthenes, dating from Alexander's accession and addressing the Athenian assembly. The speaker concedes that urging the Athenians to abide by their oaths is right in principle, but argues that Alexander violated the Common Peace. He cites the installation of tyrants at Messene and Pellene, along with the dissolution of democracies in the Peloponnese. The forcible escort of shipping to Tenedos and the provocative entry of a Macedonian trireme into the Piraeus are also mentioned. Since justice, expediency, and the treaty clauses condemn these acts, he urges a vote for war.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydidis: De Thucydidis Idiomatibus is a short Greek rhetorical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, cast as a letter to Ammaeus of uncertain date. Dionysius explains that he now gathers examples to show Thucydides' distinctive style, following earlier works addressed to Aelius Tubero. The author characterizes the language as a mixture of prose and poetry, featuring archaic, poetic, and foreign words alongside common usage. The text surveys grammatical figures with passages quoted from the History, including exchanges of nouns for verbs and active for passive voice. It also notes shifts between singular and plural, as well as between genders and cases, highlighting personification of abstractions and long parenthetical insertions. The treatise identifies strained antitheses in the manner of Gorgias, concluding with demonstrations of four instruments of style: poetic vocabulary, variety of figures, harshness of harmony, and speed of expression.
grc.epicharmus.fragmenta: The Fragmenta of Epicharmus gathers the surviving remains of the Greek poet's verse, composed in the Doric dialect. The pieces are short and largely gnomic or dialectical in character. They treat subjects such as the usefulness of maxims and the ceaseless change of all things. Other fragments explore the difference between perceiving through the senses and understanding. The collection also addresses the presence of intelligence in living creatures. These fragments stand embedded in excerpts from later ancient writers who quote them. The volume closes with a passage in which Epicharmus foretells that his sayings will one day be recast in new dress.
grc.euripides.ion: Euripides' Ion is a Greek tragedy that opens with Hermes recounting Apollo's union with Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus of Athens. The exposed infant was carried to Delphi and reared as a servant in Apollo's temple. The action centres on the grown Ion's meeting with Creusa and her husband Xuthus, who have come to the oracle seeking heirs. Xuthus is instructed to claim the youth as his own son, while Creusa, believing herself wronged, attempts to poison him. The plot fails, and tokens of exposure establish Creusa as Ion's mother. Athena then appears to explain Apollo's design and to foretell that Ion's descendants will become the Ionians, while Xuthus' line will found the Dorians and Achaeans. The play closes with the family preparing to leave Delphi for Athens, where Ion is to take up his ancestral rule.
grc.eutropius.breviarium_historiae_romanae: A Greek version of the Breviarium Historiae Romanae, the compressed history of Rome from the foundation of the city composed by Eutropius. The work recounts how Roman power grew from the humblest beginnings to a dominion without equal in memory, opening with the birth of Romulus to Rhea Silvia and Mars and his founding of the settlement on the Palatine hill. The narrative proceeds reign by reign through the seven kings, Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus, down to the rape of Lucretia, the expulsion of the Tarquins and the end of the monarchy.
grc.galen.de_bono_habitu: This short Greek treatise by Galen examines euexia, a term meaning good condition of the body, and begins by distinguishing hexis, a stable state, from the qualified conditions of euexia and cachexia. Simple good condition is defined as the perfection of health found in the best-constituted bodies, which is contrasted with the merely relative condition of athletes such as Milo or Achilles. The author draws on Hippocrates and Plato to explore what these two kinds share and where they diverge, noting that they both possess good mixture of parts, sound functioning, and good humours. Their difference lies in the proportion or disproportion of blood and flesh, and the text concludes with a physiological account of how excessive repletion harms the body. It explains how overfilled veins smother innate heat and can rupture vessels in the lung, liver, and chest.
grc.galen.de_humero_iis_modis_prolapso_quos_: This brief Greek medical treatise by Galen addresses shoulder dislocations that Hippocrates did not describe. The title refers to the specific types of joint displacement under discussion. Galen contrasts the single mode recorded by Hippocrates with additional modes known to later physicians. He recounts five cases he witnessed, one in Smyrna during his student years and four in Rome. Their frequency reflects the size of those cities and the unskilful practices of doctors and wrestling trainers. The work then describes reduction techniques, including countertraction, a broad chest strap, slings, and the Hippocratic bench. It closes with a discussion of how muscle tension or laxity and bodily condition affect the ease of dislocation and reduction, with remarks on the interpretation of Hippocratic wording.
grc.galen.de_usu_partium_corporis_humani_ixi: This Greek prose treatise by the second-century physician Galen examines teleological anatomy. The work argues that each bodily part exists for the sake of the soul's activities. The excerpt presents the opening argument, which defines a part as something with its own outline yet joined to others. It surveys how animal endowments like horns, tusks, speed, and strength match their natures. Humans, alone naked and unarmed yet rational, receive hands in place of natural weapons. Galen follows Aristotle in holding that man possesses hands because he is wisest, with the hand serving as an organ before all organs as reason is an art before all arts. Hippocrates, Plato, and Aristotle are invoked by name throughout this argument.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.theological_oration: The Theological Orations of Gregory of Nazianzus form a sequence of five Greek orations on the doctrine of the Trinity. The first opens with a rebuke of clever disputants who turn argument into a game, laying down that only the purified may philosophise about God at the proper season and within limits. The subsequent discourses treat the incomprehensibility of the divine essence and the weakness of human knowledge of God. These texts defend the Son's eternal generation and consubstantiality with the Father against objections drawn from scripture while expounding the names ascribed to him. The orations argue at length for the divinity of the Holy Spirit and detail his procession from the Father. The sequence closes with an account of the unity of the one divinity in three hypostases, ending with a doxology to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
grc.herodian.ab_excessu_divi_marci: Herodian's Ab Excessu Divi Marci ('From the Death of the Divine Marcus') is a Greek history of the Roman empire. It covers the period from the death of Marcus Aurelius to the accession of Gordian III. The opening proem criticises earlier historians for favouring elegance over truth. It then introduces Marcus's deathbed anxieties for his young son Commodus. The narrative proceeds through a rapid sequence of reigns, including Commodus, Pertinax, Didius Julianus, and Septimius Severus. It continues with Caracalla, Macrinus, Elagabalus, Alexander Severus, and Maximinus Thrax, recounting assassinations, civil wars, and foreign campaigns against Parthians, Persians, and Germans, while noting the growing political power of the army in imperial succession.
grc.hyperides.speeches: These forensic speeches and fragments were composed by the Athenian orator Hyperides, who was active in the fourth century BC. The surviving material consists of excerpts from addresses delivered to Athenian jurors. They include a defence against a public indictment, a charge known as eisangelia. Other pieces concern private causes involving marriage, adoption, and inheritance. The public charges alleged range from the betrayal of the dockyards to the seizure of a stronghold. Much of the wording survives only in passages quoted by later grammarians, notably Pollux, so the speeches are preserved discontinuously.
grc.lucian.bis_accusatus_sive_tribunalia: Lucian of Samosata wrote this Greek dialogue under the Latin title Bis Accusatus sive Tribunalia. The title translates as Double Indictment, or Tribunals. Zeus complains to Hermes about the endless toil of divine rule. He also laments suits lodged by the arts and sciences against mortals who abandoned them. These cases have lain untouched through the gods' supposed idleness. Hermes is sent to proclaim a day of court, and Justice is appointed to sit in judgment on the Areopagus over the accumulated cases.
grc.lucian.demonax: Lucian of Samosata composed this short biographical encomium for the Cypriot philosopher Demonax, whom he knew at Athens and presents as a model of philosophical life. He claims his age was not wholly without men worthy of remembrance, naming the athlete Sostratus and, above all, Demonax. The body sketches Demonax's origins and his self-directed turn to philosophy, where he refused any single school and displayed mildness, frankness, and ready wit. He successfully defended himself before the Athenian assembly against charges of impiety, and the text then offers a long series of apophthegms and repartees. These exchanges involve sophists, philosophers, and officials such as Favorinus and Herodes Atticus, before the work closes with the philosopher's death at nearly a hundred. He received a public burial and lasting honours from the Athenians, and Lucian notes that he has recorded only a few episodes from many, which is enough to show what sort of man Demonax was.
grc.lucian.fugitivi: Lucian of Samosata composed this short comic prose dialogue, traditionally titled the Runaways, which is cast as a conversation between Zeus and Philosophy. It opens with the two recalling an aged enthusiast who burned himself alive on a pyre at Olympia. Philosophy then recounts her mission from Zeus to civilize humankind among various ancient peoples. She laments that impostors now dress and brawl in the philosophers' manner while living in greed and debauchery. Zeus, Philosophy, Hermes, and Heracles descend to a city on the Hebrus to hunt the fugitives. A herald's proclamation, with Orpheus's help, identifies three runaway slaves who had taken up the Cynic guise, and the capture, punishment, and return of Cantharus, Licythion, and Miropnoun to their masters close the piece.
grc.lucian.lexiphanes: Lexiphanes ('The Word-Fancier') is a short satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which the title character affects an ostentatiously archaic and outlandish style of speech. It opens with Lexiphanes presenting to his friend Lycinus a freshly minted anti-symposium written against Plato's Symposium and asking for a judgment on it. At Lycinus' urging he recites a long specimen, a narrative of exercise, bathing, drinking, and a sumptuous dinner party. The piece is a grotesque jumble of rare, technical, and invented words that bewilders its hearers. Lycinus pronounces the speech a disease and brings in the physician Sopolis, whose emetic literally purges the offending vocabulary. The dialogue closes with precepts directing the offender to form his style on the best poets, orators, Thucydides, and Plato.
grc.lucian.nigrinus: The Nigrinus of Lucian is a short satirical dialogue framed by an opening letter addressed to the philosopher Nigrinus. In it Lucian undertakes to report to a friend a conversation he once heard, and the dialogue proper presents the narrator's account of a visit to Nigrinus. Nigrinus, a Platonist living in Athens, praises philosophy and the frugal, frank, poverty-embracing life of the Athenians while deriding the luxury of Rome. Its episodes cover sycophants and flatterers of the rich, gluttony and elaborate baths, extravagant funerals and wills, and the mania for chariot-racing. The satire also targets philosophers who peddle virtue, and throughout it runs the recurring image of philosophy as a healer's well-aimed arrow. The work closes with the narrator declaring himself wounded by the words and asking his friend to seek with him a common cure, after the manner of Telephus.
grc.lycophron.alexandra: This Greek dramatic monologue in iambic trimeters, attributed to Lycophron and of uncertain date, is spoken throughout by a servant of Priam. He reports to the king the prophecies uttered by his captive daughter Cassandra, who was once struck dumb but has broken into prophecy. The poem opens with the servant explaining that she veils her meaning in deliberately obscure and riddling language. Her vision sweeps from the judgment of Paris through the Trojan War and the deaths of heroes on both sides. It then follows the wanderings of the returning Greeks, above all Odysseus, and the fortunes of Aeneas and his descendants, ending with the future greatness of Rome. At the close the frame resumes, as Cassandra withdraws again into her prison and the servant ends his report with a prayer for his master's house.
grc.marcus_aurelius.m._antonius_imperator_ad: This Greek prose work, conventionally known as the Meditations, carries the original title M. Antonius Imperator ad Se Ipsum, meaning Marcus Aurelius, To Himself. The text opens with a book of thanks to family, teachers, and the gods, then offers sustained Stoic exhortation on the governance of the mind. The author also addresses the acceptance of fate and the transience of all things, while these notes record where the entries were written. Such locations include among the Quadi on the river Granua and at Carnuntum, forming a private commonplace book of short maxims and self-addresses. The whole is distributed across the twelve books in which the tradition transmits it.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.problemata_arithmet: This short collection contains six numbered arithmetical problems, which are preserved with the Introduction to Arithmetic of Nicomachus of Gerasa. The text attributes these problems to Nicomachus, and the first item provides a rule for summing consecutive numbers. It distinguishes between an odd and an even count of terms, while the remaining items offer quicker methods for such sums. They include a rule for series in equal difference, and a ten number puzzle is said to have been set by King Leo. The text also features a trick for discovering a secret number, and it presents a testament apportioning gold coins among six children.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_i: The First Letter to the Thessalonians is a Greek prose epistle from the Imperial era, opening with a salutation from Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the local church. The authors express thanks for the converts' faith, love, and endurance, while recalling the missionaries' toil and persecution in Macedonia. The text rejoices in Timothy's report of the Thessalonians' steadfastness, exhorting readers to holiness, sexual restraint, and brotherly love. It also urges quiet work and esteem for their leaders, teaching that the dead in Christ will rise first at the Lord's descent from heaven. The letter warns that the day of the Lord comes like a thief, urging watchfulness and mutual encouragement among the believers. Short closing commands address rejoicing, prayer, and testing prophecy, concluding with a greeting and a final benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_i: The First Epistle of John is a Greek prose letter from the Imperial era. It is traditionally attributed to John, though the text names neither author nor audience. The opening prologue presents the word of life as manifested in Jesus Christ. The body alternates ethical exhortation with polemic against antichrists and false spirits. A sustained meditation declares that God is love and that it reaches perfection in believers. The letter closes with assurance of eternal life and a warning against idols.
grc.plato.epistles: This Greek collection of thirteen letters is transmitted under Plato's name, and most are addressed to Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, and the circle of Dion. Shorter notes go to other friends and correspondents, while the opening letters rebuke Dionysius for ingratitude and refuse his gifts. They also reflect on a philosopher's reputation and conduct in dealings with power, and the longest central letter gives an autobiographical account of Plato's voyages to Sicily. It details his hopes and disappointments at the Syracusan court, and a digression explains why the deepest philosophical teaching cannot be set down in writing. The later letters arrange practical affairs, money, gifts, and marriage settlements, and they also cover journeys and close with greetings and instructions to Iatrocles.
grc.plutarch.epitome_argumenti_stoicos: This short Greek epitome, attributed to Plutarch though its date remains uncertain, presents an argument against the Stoics. It opens by contrasting Pindar's impervious Caeneus with the Stoic sage, who is struck and tortured yet remains fearless and unconquerable. The argument examines Stoic paradoxes, comparing the overnight conversion of a vicious man into a sage with Euripides' Iolaus. It also notes Athena's removal of Odysseus' ugliness and likens the claim that virtue brings instant wealth and kingship to the horn of Amalthea. Finally, the text contrasts this with Heracles, who always needs necessities, ending with the Stoic begging for food while shouting that he alone is rich.
grc.pseudogalen.de_optima_secta_ad_thrasybul: The De optima secta, a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date and authorship, was transmitted among the works of Galen and addressed to a certain Thrasybulus. It asks how the doctrines of medicine are to be judged, opening by stipulating that every medical thesis must be true, useful, and consistent with its assumed principles. The body of the work sets out what the Logical, Empiric, and Methodist schools hold in common and what distinguishes each. It then refutes the Empiric reliance on observation, recorded history, and transition to the similar, while the author also challenges the Methodist doctrines of the commons, the uselessness of symptoms, and the seasons of disease. The Rationalist position, which grasps hidden causes through reason, is vindicated throughout as the soundest.
grc.pseudolucian.ἔρωτες: The Erotes is a short Greek prose dialogue attributed to Lucian and of uncertain date; it opens with Theomnestus regaling Lycinus with erotic tales at dawn as the pair celebrate a festival of Heracles. At Lycinus's prompting they agree to weigh love of women against love of boys, and Lycinus recounts a voyage to Italy that brought him, with his companions Charicles of Corinth and Callicratides of Athens, to the temple of Aphrodite at Cnidus, where they admired Praxiteles' statue and heard a temple attendant tell of a youth who defiled it. Charicles then delivers a set speech defending heterosexual love and attacking women's vanity and luxury, while Callicratides answers with a defence of pederasty that invokes Socrates, Achilles and Patroclus, and Orestes and Pylades; Lycinus awards the victory to Callicratides, allowing marriage to all but reserving philosophic love for the wise. Theomnestus responds with a racy speech on the ascending stages of physical love before Lycinus cuts the discussion short so that the party may attend the god's sacrifice.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_b: Paralipomenon B, the second book of Chronicles in the Septuagint, is a prose narrative of Hellenistic date whose translator remains unnamed. The text opens with Solomon's accession and his prayer for wisdom at Gibeon, describing the building and dedication of the temple at Jerusalem. It records the king's wealth and glory, then follows the kings of Judah from Rehoboam to Zedekiah, detailing alternating religious reform and apostasy. The narrative recounts wars with neighbouring peoples, Assyria, and Babylon, while also noting temple restorations and prophetic rebukes. The story ends with the burning of the temple, concluding with the deportation to Babylon and Cyrus's proclamation permitting the exiles to return.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_translatio_graeca: The Greek Susanna is a short prose narrative of uncertain date from the Hellenistic period, preserved in the Septuagint among the additions to the Book of Daniel. The story opens in Babylon with the household of the wealthy Joakim, whose wife Susanna is the beautiful and God-fearing daughter of Helcias. She walks daily in his garden, where two elders appointed as judges covet her and try to force themselves upon her. They falsely accuse her of adultery when she refuses, and the assembly assents to her condemnation, but the youthful Daniel receives a spirit of discernment from an angel. He separates the elders and cross-examines each about the tree beneath which they claim to have seen the supposed lovers, and their contradictory answers expose the lie. The law's penalty is carried out on them as false witnesses, Susanna is vindicated, and a closing admonition praises the piety of the young.
grc.sextus_empiricus.pyrrhoniae_hypotyposes: The Pyrrhoniae Hypotyposes ('Outlines of Pyrrhonism') is a Greek prose treatise by the sceptical philosopher Sextus Empiricus. Its date remains uncertain, but the work offers a systematic account of Pyrrhonian scepticism. The first book opens with a list of chapters and then treats the division of philosophy into dogmatic, Academic, and sceptical tendencies. It also examines the concept, principles, criterion, and end of scepticism. The text details the ten, five, and two modes that lead to suspension of judgement and tranquillity. It further distinguishes scepticism from the Heraclitean, Democritean, Cyrenaic, and Protagorean philosophies, as well as from the Academy and empirical medicine.
grc.theophrastus.enquiry_into_plants: Theophrastus wrote this short Greek prose treatise on weather signs, which was transmitted alongside his Enquiry into Plants. The opening announces a collection of signs for rain, winds, winter storms, and fair weather, and these observations come from the author and trustworthy informants. The text also explains star risings and the divisions of time, while the greater part catalogues prognostics from the sun, moon, stars, and clouds. It also notes haloes, thunder, lightning, mountains, and the sea, and the author distinguishes rain from wind and southerly or northerly weather. Later sections gather signs of winter and fair weather, and the treatise closes with predictions for whole years and seasons.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.fragmenta: These fragments belong to Bion of Phlossa, a Greek bucolic poet whose surviving texts are written in the Doric dialect. They include short poems, epigrams, and isolated lines that cover themes of love, song, and pastoral life. The collection opens with a dialogue about the seasons, arguing that spring is the sweetest time of year. A young bird-catcher then sees Eros for the first time, and Aphrodite brings Eros to be taught music. The poems reflect on the brevity of mortal toil, and they also praise the blessedness of mutual love. A prayer to Hesperus follows these meditations, and the poet reproaches Aphrodite for her son's harshness. Apollo makes vain efforts to heal a stricken lover, and the Cyclops woos Galatea in a later scene. Aphoristic verses link Eros and the Muses, and a handful of single-line remains conclude the collection.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.apotelesmatica_tetra: The Tetrabiblos is a Greek treatise in four books on astrology, the art of prognostication from the celestial bodies. Ptolemy opens with an address to Syrus that defends the possibility and usefulness of such prediction. He insists on its merely probable character and distinguishes it from the certain knowledge of astronomy. Book 1 sets out the physical doctrine of planetary natures, zodiac signs, aspects, and houses. Book 2 treats mundane or national astrology, covering climates, peoples, eclipses, and the weather. Books 3 and 4 turn to genethlialogy, the judgment of nativities, proceeding from parents and length of life. They cover bodily form, disease, the soul, wealth, rank, marriage, and the quality of death.
grc.demosthenes.against_conon: This Athenian forensic speech, written by Demosthenes for a private suit for assault, was brought by the young Ariston against his attacker, Conon. Ariston opens by explaining that he has recovered from severe beatings that nearly killed him during a hostile quarrel at Panakton. The speech then describes a night-time attack near the Leokorion in the agora, where Conon, his son Ctesias, and their companions knocked Ariston down and stripped him. They also beat him before witnesses, and medical experts documented his injuries, which later sections argue make Conon liable under laws on outrage and stripping. The text exposes the perjured evidence of Conon's drinking companions, closing with a formal challenge to a solemn oath and an appeal to the judges.
grc.demosthenes.against_leptines: An Athenian public prosecution speech by Demosthenes, written for the opponents of Leptines' law repealing the exemptions from liturgies held by benefactors of the city, among them the son of Chabrias. The opening addresses the jurors on the question whether it profits the city to annul the law, and the argument then sets out the wrongs the measure would do, stripping honours already granted and making future gratitude unsafe. In support the speaker surveys the grants of citizenship and exemption conferred on such men as Leucon of Bosporus, Epicrates of Cyrene, the Corinthian exiles, the Thasians, the Byzantines, Conon and Chabrias, reading out the decrees in their favour and recounting the deeds of Chabrias at length. Further sections defend the honouring of benefactors against appeals to Spartan and Theban practice, invoke Solonian legislation on how laws are to be framed, exhibit the substitute statute proposed in place of Leptines' measure, and note that its terms would expose to severe penalties any who asked a reward for services.
grc.euripides.electra: This Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizes the revenge of Orestes and Electra, who seek vengeance against the murderers of their father, Agamemnon. The play opens with a prologue delivered by a peasant, who explains how Agamemnon was slain upon his return from Troy. Orestes was smuggled into exile to protect him from danger, while the forced marriage of Electra was meant to forestall any avenger. Orestes and Pylades arrive in disguise and meet Electra at a spring, where an old servant helps them recognize one another. The siblings kill Aegisthus at a country sacrifice, then lure Clytemnestra to the house with false news of childbirth, where they kill her as well.
