The drama closes with the appearance of the Dioscuri, who pronounce the matricide a mistake and send Orestes to stand trial in Athens, while Electra is given in marriage to Pylades.
grc.lucian.apologia: The Apologia is a short Greek dialogue in which Lucian of Samosata answers the charge of inconsistency levelled against him after his invective upon men who attach themselves to rich households for pay. It opens with Lucian voicing, as though for his friend Sabinus, the objection that the author of so fierce a condemnation of salaried dependence has now himself accepted such a position. Sabinus then presses the case at length, likening him to a tragedian off stage and to a monkey betrayed by a fig, while Lucian replies by distinguishing his salaried judicial and secretarial office in the Roman administration of Egypt from servile attendance on a private patron, and by arguing that everyone acts for reward, kings not least. The dialogue ends on a lighter note, with Lucian conceding that he is no sage and waving his critics away with the words 'Hippocleides does not care.'
grc.lucian.de_morte_peregrini: This short satirical epistle is addressed to Cronius by Lucian of Samosata, who recounts the life of the Cynic Peregrinus, who styled himself Proteus. The opening mocks the old man's love of glory and reports his recent death by fire, while the narrative traces his career, including adultery and flight in Armenia. It also details the murder of his aged father and a sojourn among Christians in Palestine, before Peregrinus wandered through Egypt, Italy, and Greece, marked by theatrical asceticism. The account follows the narrator to Elis and Olympia, where Peregrinus announces his intention to burn himself, and his follower Theagenes extols him amid rival harangues and invented oracles. After the games, the narrator witnesses the night-time cremation at nearby Harpina, and the letter closes with the mocking aftermath, including a tale that a vulture rose from the pyre. It also mentions plans for statues and cult, and an anecdote about the dead man's fear of pain.
grc.lucian.piscator: Lucian of Samosata composed this satirical dialogue to defend his public mockery of the philosophers, opening with ancient thinkers like Plato and Aristotle rising from the dead to stone a reviled offender. This figure is Parrhesiades, Lucian's spokesman, who had previously put philosophy up for auction and ridicule, and he secures a formal trial before Philosophy herself. Philosophy arrives at the Acropolis with personified Truth and Justice, while Diogenes proseces the case and Parrhesiades argues that his abuse targeted only charlatans seeking money and vanity. Philosophy acquits him and enrolls him as a friend of the sect, and a second hearing then summons the philosophers with promises of pay and honours. It crowns the few genuine ones and puts the impostors to flight, ending with Parrhesiades fishing from the wall with a hook baited with gold. He lands a string of fraudulent Cynics, Platonists, Aristotelians, and Stoics to be branded.
grc.lucian.somnium: The Somnium is a short Greek prose work by Lucian of Samosata, where the speaker recounts a formative dream from his boyhood to a live audience. His father deliberates with friends over what trade the boy should learn, eventually apprenticing him to an uncle skilled in sculpting. The uncle's harsh correction of the boy's first botched stroke sends him home in tears, and that night, two women contend for him in a vivid dream. The rough-handed Sculpture and the radiant Paideia, or Education, vie for his favor, and he judges for Paideia, who rewards him with a winged ascent over cities and nations. He wakes to a changed appearance that astonishes his father, and the speaker rebukes scoffers among his hearers. He explains that he has told the story so that the young may take his rise from obscure origins as an example, urging those tempted by poverty to abandon learning to pursue education.
grc.lucian.timon: This comic Greek dialogue by Lucian dramatises the story of Timon of Athens, the legendary misanthrope. Zeus, roused by complaints that his thunderbolt has gone cold, sends Hermes and Plutus to Timon. The hero, stripped of fortune by ungrateful flatterers, now digs the land in solitary bitterness. Along the way, the gods discuss the inconstancy of wealth and the virtues of Poverty. When Timon uncovers a buried treasure, he drafts a code of total withdrawal from mankind. His former hangers-on soon return to court his renewed riches, but he drives them off with his mattock.
grc.plutarch.artaxerxes: Plutarch composed this Greek biographical life of the Persian king Artaxerxes II, who bore the surname Mnemon, and the opening distinguishes this second Artaxerxes, son of Darius and Parysatis, from a gentler earlier namesake. It also sets the stage for his rivalry with his brother Cyrus, whose bid for the throne and death at the battle of Cunaxa are followed. Plutarch weighs the conflicting accounts of Ctesias, Dinon, and Xenophon on this event, then turns to the fate of the captured Greek generals and Parysatis's vengeance against them. Her poisoning of Queen Stateira is also described, and the later course covers the war with Sparta, which ended with the King's Peace of Antalcidas. It also details the unsuccessful Egyptian and Cadusian campaigns, during which Artaxerxes married his daughter Atossa, and the conspiracies of Teribazus led to the execution of the crown prince Darius. The king died at ninety-four after a reign of sixty-two years.
grc.aristotle.de_respiratione: De Respiratione is a short Aristotelian treatise on why animals breathe, opening by reviewing earlier natural philosophers who held that all living creatures respire. Aristotle argues that fish and many bloodless animals plainly do not, and the bulk of the work sets out his own explanation of the process. Innate heat in the heart must be tempered by cooling, so lunged animals achieve this by breathing air, while gilled animals take in water. The text explains why air-breathers suffocate in water and fish die on land, describing the working of the lungs, gills, windpipe, and heart. The course of life is traced from generation and youth through old age to natural death, and a final section considers the pulse and heartbeat alongside respiration. It touches on the border between natural philosophy and medicine in questions of health and disease.
grc.demosthenes.against_timotheus: Against Timotheus is a Greek forensic speech preserved among the orations of Demosthenes, argued in an Athenian private suit concerning debts owed to the speaker's deceased father, a banker of the Piraeus. The defendant was the general Timotheus, and the opening appeals to the judges not to find it strange that a son prosecutes a man his father once helped freely. The narrative then details successive transactions, including a first loan for Timotheus' departure as general and a second of a thousand drachmas raised at Calaureia. These funds kept the Boeotian trierarchs supplied and were repaid to the shipmaster Philip, while the account also covers freight money for timber from Macedonia and the valuation of two silver phialai deposited at the bank. Supporting the account with witnesses, bank memoranda, and inferences from Timotheus' embarrassments, the speaker rebuts claims that the money was lent to Antimachus or a Boeotian navarch. He explains his refusal of the oath Timotheus offered and closes by asking the judges to help him recover the sums his father left.
grc.demosthenes.against_neaera: This fourth century BCE Athenian forensic speech, preserved among the orations of Demosthenes, charges Neaera, a Corinthian courtesan, with xenia, a violation of guest friendship. The prosecutor alleges that she lived as the wife of the citizen Stephanus and passed off her daughter as an Athenian. The opening frames the suit as a response to injuries and plots by Stephanus, while the body recounts Neaera's early career as a slave prostitute in Corinth. It details Stephanus's blackmail of her lovers and the marriage of her daughter Phano to Theogenes, who performed the city's secret rites before the scandalised Areopagus. The prosecutor then challenged Stephanus to test household slaves under torture, which he refused, and the closing appeal urges jurors to convict in defence of the laws and the gods. This final plea also seeks to protect the standing of citizen women.
grc.libanius.orations_51-64: This group of speeches by Libanius, the fourth-century AD rhetorician of Antioch, carries the numbers 51 to 64 in the standard collection of his works. The first opens as a direct address to the emperor on justice and the twin supports of arms and laws. It then denounces the throngs who besiege governors at their houses, baths, and tables, along with the letters and intermediaries that corrupt their verdicts. Elsewhere in the range a panegyric weighs an emperor's sons, sent east and west after their father's death, against Cyrus, Darius, and Alexander to their advantage. A long defence of pantomime dancing, addressed to an Aristides, sets the dancer beside the poets and orators as a teacher of audiences in justice and endurance.
grc.lysias.speeches: Lysias was an Athenian orator active in the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE. Thirty-four forensic and deliberative speeches are transmitted under his name, though several are of uncertain authenticity. The corpus opens with On the Murder of Eratosthenes, a defense of a husband who killed an adulterer. The remaining speeches address private litigation concerning homicide, inheritance, and property. They also include public orations on political matters, such as defenses against confiscations and calls for civic concord.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἀριθμητικὴ_εἰσαγωγή: The Arithmetikē Eisagōgē, a Greek treatise on Pythagorean number theory, is attributed to Nicomachus of Gerasa, though its date remains uncertain. It opens by defining philosophy as the love of wisdom, arguing that mathematical sciences lift the mind from the sensible to the intelligible. Nicomachus appeals to Pythagoras, Plato, and Archytas to support this claim, while the body of the text classifies numbers in themselves and their ratios. It covers even and odd, prime, composite, and perfect numbers, and also examines figurate and polygonal numbers, illustrated with letter-number diagrams. The treatise then treats quantity in relation, cataloguing various means, and a set of short appended problems follows the main text. These cover the summation of series and a riddle ascribed to a king Leo, and they also include a trick for divining a number held in someone's mind. Finally, they address the division of gold cups among a dying man's children.
grc.callimachus.iambi: Callimachus of Cyrene, the third-century BCE poet and scholar of the Alexandrian Library, wrote thirteen Iambi in the manner of the archaic satirist Hipponax. The first poem brings Hipponax back from the dead to rebuke the quarrelling scholars of Alexandria. The collection survives only in pieces, recovered from papyri such as the Oxyrhynchus papyrus edited by A. S. Hunt in 1910 and from ancient summaries, and this text keeps the editor's notes on its sources beside the fragments.
grc.philo_judaeus.legum_allegoriarum_libri_i: Philo of Alexandria, the Jewish philosopher of the early first century CE, wrote the Allegories of the Laws as a running allegorical commentary on Genesis 2 and 3. Verse by verse he reads the creation of man, the garden, the serpent and the fall as an account of the soul, its mind and its senses, and the struggle between reason and pleasure. The work opens with the completion of heaven and earth in Genesis 2.1.

it.dante.inferno: The first cantica of Dante's Commedia comprises thirty-four cantos. In 1300, the poet finds himself lost in a dark wood. Virgil guides him down through the nine circles of Hell. Each circle punishes a specific class of sin with a mirroring penalty. The damned tell their stories as the travellers descend. They reach the frozen centre of the earth.
it.dante.purgatorio: The second cantica comprises thirty-three cantos set on the mountain of Purgatory. Here, souls are cleansed of the seven capital vices as they ascend its terraces. Virgil guides Dante to the summit, which is the earthly paradise. At this point, Virgil departs and Beatrice takes his place.
it.dante.paradiso: The third cantica, thirty-three cantos in total, ascends through the spheres of the heavens. Beatrice serves as the guide for this final section of the poem. The journey concludes with the poet's vision of God. Its subject matter is theology, light, and the limits of speech. The text repeatedly stages the poet's inability to report what he saw.

fro.chanson_de_roland: The oldest surviving French epic consists of about four thousand assonanced lines. It is preserved in an Oxford manuscript from the twelfth century. Roland commands Charlemagne's rearguard and is betrayed at Roncevaux. He refuses to sound his horn for help until his men are lost. The poem ends with Charlemagne's vengeance and the trial of the traitor Ganelon.

gmh.nibelungenlied: This Middle High German heroic epic, dating from about 1200, runs to some 2,400 stanzas. The poem falls into two halves, and the first of these tells of Siegfried's courtship of Kriemhild. It also recounts his dragon-won invulnerability and his murder at the hands of Hagen. The second half turns to Kriemhild's marriage to Etzel and to the annihilation of the Burgundians at his court.

en.blake.songs_of_innocence: Songs of Innocence is a collection of short lyric poems by William Blake, whose title refers to the state of childhood purity that the verses celebrate. It opens with an Introduction where a piper is bidden by a laughing child on a cloud, and he plucks a hollow reed to write down his happy songs for every child. The lyrics are largely in simple quatrains and other brief measures, voiced by or about children and their guardians. Shepherds, lambs, and a black child of the southern wilds appear, while a young chimney sweep is comforted by an angelic dream. Charity children file into St Paul's, while infants and nurses play, and pastoral delight and maternal tenderness frame scenes of cradle-song and springtime. A divinity identified with the lamb and the child watches over them, and the collection closes with the assurance that God shares every human sorrow.
en.bunyan.pilgrims_progress: John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is a prose allegory presented as a dream narrative, where the title refers to the journey of the protagonist, Christian, toward the Celestial City. The story opens with a sleeping narrator who sees a ragged man carrying a heavy burden, and this man, Christian, flees the doomed City of Destruction to escape coming judgment. He is directed by Evangelist to the wicket-gate and begins a long journey, passing through the Slough of Despond and the Interpreter's house. At the cross, his burden falls away, and he climbs Hill Difficulty, reaching Palace Beautiful and fighting Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation. He also crosses the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and his townsman Faithful joins him, but they are arrested at Vanity Fair. Faithful is condemned by Lord Hate-good and burned at the stake, and Hopeful then becomes Christian's new companion. They pass By-ends and the silver mine of Demas, and Giant Despair imprisons them in Doubting Castle until the key called Promise frees them. They rest on the Delectable Mountains and in the land of Beulah, and finally, they cross the river of death and enter the Celestial City. Ignorance is turned away at the gate because he lacks a certificate.
en.carroll.alice_in_wonderland: Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland is a Victorian prose fantasy recounting a young girl's adventures in a nonsensical underground world. It opens with Alice following a hurried White Rabbit down a rabbit-hole into a hall of locked doors, where potions and cakes alternately shrink and enlarge her. Among her encounters are a sorrowful Mouse, a hookah-smoking Caterpillar, and the peppery Duchess with her grinning Cheshire Cat. She later joins an endless tea-party with the Hatter and March Hare, plays croquet with the tyrannical Queen of Hearts, and hears the Mock Turtle's lament. The story closes with a chaotic trial of the Knave of Hearts for stolen tarts, where Alice grows to full size and denounces the court as a pack of cards. She then wakes on the riverbank to find that the whole adventure has been a dream.
en.coleridge.rime_of_the_ancient_mariner: Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a narrative poem in archaic ballad style, and the title refers to the old sailor who narrates the tale. An ancient mariner detains a wedding guest on his way to the feast, and he begins the story of a ship driven southward into icy seas. The mariner shoots the albatross that had befriended the crew, and under a becalmed sky a spectre ship wins the sailors' lives. Death and Life in Death crew this ghostly vessel, and the mariner alone survives and is cursed among his dead shipmates. He blesses water snakes unawares and is then able to pray, and the albatross falls from his neck after this moment of grace. Angelic spirits and mysterious voices work the ship homeward, and the vessel sinks in a whirlpool near the coast. A hermit shrives the mariner before he is condemned to wander, and he is seized by agony that forces him to tell his tale. The wedding guest departs a sadder and a wiser man, and he has heard the moral that prayer avails for those who love all things.
en.cowper.task: The Task is a long reflective poem in blank verse, divided into six books, whose title refers to the humble subject matter the poet undertakes at a lady's command. It opens in a mock-heroic vein with a history of the sofa, from which the poet turns to the country walks that frame the whole work. He meditates on nature, rural retirement, and the changing seasons along the Ouse, while the digressive course ranges widely to survey city luxury and fashionable folly. The poem also addresses corrupt public life and the slave trade, and extended passages treat domestic happiness, gardening, and winter scenes. It closes with a portrait of the contented retired man, arguing that true freedom comes through God alone, and a vision of a restored creation ends the work.
en.edgar_allan_poe.the_raven: The Raven is a narrative poem by Edgar Allan Poe, composed in stanzas of insistent internal rhyme. The structure builds around the single word refrain Nevermore, and the poem opens on a bleak December midnight. A grieving scholar broods over books and the memory of the lost Lenore, hearing a tapping at his chamber door. He finds a stately raven perched on a bust of Pallas, moving from amused speculation to anguished questioning. He asks if there is any balm for his sorrow, wondering if he will clasp Lenore in a paradise beyond death. The raven answers every question with Nevermore, leaving the bird above the chamber door with its shadow cast on the floor, so the speaker's soul shall be lifted nevermore.
en.keats.eve_of_st_agnes: The Eve of St Agnes is a narrative poem by the English Romantic poet John Keats, written in the early nineteenth century in Spenserian stanzas. It opens on a bitter wintry night, as an aged beadsman says his prayers in a castle chapel while a baronial feast is prepared above. Madeline observes the rituals that, by an old superstition, are to bring a sleeping virgin a vision of her future husband on St Agnes' Eve. Porphyro, her lover from a hostile family, is led by the aged Angela into her chamber, where he spreads a lavish feast and wakes her from her dream. The lovers escape through the sleeping household into the storm, and the poem closes with the baron's nightmarish visions and the deaths of Angela and the beadsman.
en.keats.fancy: Fancy is a short lyric in rhymed couplets by John Keats, whose title refers to the personified power of imagination that drives the poem. It opens with the maxim that pleasure is never at home, while the speaker addresses a hearer seated at a winter fireside. He dispatches Fancy to gather the pleasures of the scattered seasons, mingles May blossoms, summer swarms, and autumn fruit with the muffled snow outside. The poem closes by bidding Fancy find a mistress likened to Ceres' daughter, then returns to its opening claim that delight melts at a touch.
en.keats.hyperion: Keats's Hyperion is an unfinished epic in blank verse that dramatises the overthrow of the Titans by the younger gods. The poem opens with the fallen Saturn sitting silent in a shadowy vale, while Thea mourns the loss of his dominion nearby. They move to a cavern where the defeated Titans gather in grief, and Oceanus argues that a race more strong in beauty must rightly succeed them. Clymene recalls hearing Apollo's new music, and Enceladus calls for a second war, at which moment the sun-god Hyperion appears in disconsolate splendour. The third book shifts to Apollo on Delos, who pours out his anguish and hunger for knowledge to Mnemosyne. He is deified in an agony of dying into life, shrieking as the narrative breaks off abruptly.
en.keats.isabella: Isabella is a narrative poem by John Keats that retells a tale from Boccaccio's Decameron. The story follows the secret love of Isabel and Lorenzo within a Florentine merchant household. Their brothers murder Lorenzo in the Apennine forest to force Isabel into a noble marriage. She later digs up his body and buries his head in a garden pot. A basil plant grows above the grave, fed by her tears. The brothers flee in banishment after recognizing the victim's face in the stolen pot.
en.keats.lamia: Lamia is a narrative poem in rhymed couplets by Keats, which tells how a serpent becomes a beautiful woman who wins the love of the young Corinthian Lycius. The story opens in a fabled Cretan forest, where Hermes searches for a hidden nymph and grants the serpent Lamia a human body in exchange for revealing the nymph's whereabouts. Lamia then makes her way to Corinth, where she enthrals Lycius and conjures a palace and marriage feast. The philosopher Apollonius arrives uninvited and fixes her with a penetrating gaze, causing her serpent nature to be exposed and she vanishes with a scream. Lycius is found dead upon the couch, and an appended note quotes Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, which tells the tale of Menippus Lycius and the lamia at Corinth.
en.keats.lines_on_the_mermaid_tavern: The poem is a short lyric in octosyllabic couplets by the early nineteenth-century poet John Keats. It opens with an apostrophe to the souls of dead poets, asking whether any Elysium they knew, happy field or mossy cavern, could be choicer than the Mermaid Tavern. Keats pictures the tavern, celebrated in legend as a haunt of Elizabethan poets, with its Canary wine and venison pies dressed as if for Robin Hood and Maid Marian. It then tells a fanciful tale of the tavern's sign-board flying away, until an astrologer records on sheepskin that the poets drink in glory beneath a new old sign. With the Mermaid now set among the constellations of the Zodiac, the opening stanza returns at the close as a refrain, framing the whole in the same teasing question.
en.keats.ode_on_a_grecian_urn: Ode on a Grecian Urn is a five-stanza lyric ode by Keats that speaks in apostrophe to an ancient Greek vessel. The poem opens by hailing the urn as a sylvan historian and asks what leaf-fring'd legend haunts its shape. Middle stanzas dwell on scenes where soft pipes play melodies that remain unheard and a bold lover is forever short of a kiss. Boughs and an unwearied melodist stay in perpetual spring while a priest leads a garlanded heifer to a green altar. A little town is left eternally silent as the close addresses the Attic shape as a Cold Pastoral. It muses on the urn's endurance against old age and ends with the maxim that beauty is truth.
en.keats.ode_on_melancholy: Ode on Melancholy is a thirty-line lyric by the English Romantic poet John Keats, whose opening stanza forbids the sufferer of melancholy all recourse to death and mourning. It lists Lethe, wolf's-bane, nightshade, and yew-berries among the forbidden remedies, then advises that when the melancholy fit falls sudden from heaven, the sufferer should glut his sorrow on a morning rose. He should also look to the rainbow of the salt sand-wave and the globed peonies, while the final strophe sets Melancholy in the very temple of Delight. She dwells with Beauty that must die and Joy that is ever bidding adieu, and her sovran shrine is seen only by him whose strenuous tongue can burst Joy's grape. This allows him to taste the sadness of her might.
en.keats.ode_to_a_nightingale: John Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' is a lyric ode in eight stanzas, where the speaker's heart aches as he hears the bird singing of summer. He seeks escape first through wine and then on the viewless wings of poesy, which carries him away from a world of weariness, fever, and death. He enters a dark, fragrant forest to contemplate an easeful death, while the nightingale is hailed as an immortal bird whose voice has sounded since ancient days. It cheered Ruth amid the alien corn and charmed magic casements on perilous seas, until the word forlorn tolls him back to his sole self. The fading anthem leaves him asking whether he wakes or sleeps.
en.keats.robin_hood: John Keats's short lyric 'Robin Hood' opens with the declaration that the days of the greenwood are gone, and their hours are old and gray. Their minutes are buried under the leaves of many years, and the poem catalogues what has vanished with the outlaw band. This includes the bugle, the bow, and the morris dance, as well as the song of Gamelyn and the tough-belted outlaw idling in the green shawe. Keats imagines Robin and Marian restored to a changed world where he would craze to see his oaks felled. She would weep that her wild bees sing no more and honey cannot be got without hard money. A closing litany bids honour to the bow-string, the bugle-horn, Lincoln green, and Little John, and it also honours Maid Marian and all the Sherwood clan before inviting the speakers to try a burden in their memory.
en.milton.comus: Comus is a masque by Milton, a dramatic entertainment in blank verse interspersed with lyric song and dance. The title refers to the sorcerer who serves as the work's antagonist. An Attendant Spirit opens the piece by explaining that the Lady must be protected from Comus, son of Bacchus and Circe. His enchanted liquor transforms travellers into beasts, creating a perilous threat in the tangled wood. The brothers search for her and debate the value of chastity while she remains captive. In the enchanter's palace, she meets his pleas for pleasure with a firm defence of temperance. The glass breaks, though he escapes with his wand, and the river-nymph Sabrina dissolves the spell. The company arrives at Ludlow Castle, where the children are restored to their parents. The Spirit's epilogue ends the piece with the declaration that virtue alone is free.
en.milton.il_penseroso: John Milton's Il Penseroso, a lyric in rhymed octosyllabic couplets, celebrates the contemplative life under Melancholy's patronage. The speaker banishes vain deluding joys and hails Melancholy as a sage goddess, attended by Peace, Quiet, Leisure, and Contemplation. The poem explores nocturnal pleasures, including the nightingale's song and the wandering moon, alongside midnight study of Platonic and Hermetic lore. It turns to dawn in twilight groves and mysterious dreams, closing with a hope for a studious old age in a peaceful hermitage. This life is devoted to star and herb and may attain prophetic strain.
en.milton.l_allegro: L'Allegro ('The Cheerful One') is a lyric poem by John Milton. It opens by banishing Melancholy and summoning the goddess Mirth, Euphrosyne. The work belongs to the English mirth and melancholy tradition. The poem traces a day of cheerful delights from dawn to night. It moves from rural fields to cities and the stage. The speaker resolves to live with Mirth.
en.milton.lycidas: Lycidas is a pastoral elegy by John Milton that mourns the drowning of a young shepherd-poet, whose title refers to the deceased friend imagined as lost at sea. The poem is composed in irregularly rhymed pentameter stanzas, beginning with the speaker plucking laurel and myrtle before their season. The speaker calls on the Muses to sing for one dead ere his prime, moving through memories of shared shepherding and the absence of nymphs. A dialogue with Phoebus addresses the theme of fame, while sea-gods report the fate of the perfidious bark. The lament of Camus follows a stern rebuke of negligent clergy, delivered by the Pilot of the Galilean lake. A catalogue of flowers is gathered to strew the Laureat Herse, closing in consolation as Lycidas rises through divine might. He joins the company of the saints and becomes Genius of the shore, while the frame returns to the uncouth Swain who has sung from dawn to sunset. He departs to fresh woods and pastures new.
en.milton.paradise_lost: Milton's Paradise Lost is a blank-verse epic in twelve books on the fall of humanity. It opens with an invocation to the heavenly Muse announcing man's first disobedience and the loss of Eden. The narrative follows Satan and the rebel angels from their fall into Hell through the infernal council at Pandemonium, Satan's voyage across Chaos to the newly created world, and the assembly in Heaven at which the Son offers himself for mankind's redemption. Raphael warns Adam and recounts the war in Heaven and the creation before Satan, in the serpent, seduces Eve, and the poem concludes with judgement on the first parents, Michael's prophetic visions of human history, and their expulsion from Paradise.
en.milton.paradise_regained: Paradise Regained is a short epic poem in four books of blank verse by John Milton, which dramatizes the temptation of Christ in the wilderness as the act that reverses Adam's fall. The title means the restoration of paradise to all mankind through one man's obedience, and the poet opens by turning from the fall of man to sing this recovery. Satan resolves to try the newly baptized Son of God after a council of fallen angels, and over forty days, the Tempter assays hunger with a conjured banquet and offers riches and glory. He also presents the empires of Parthia and Rome and the philosophy of Athens, and at last, he assails the Saviour with a night of storms and a dare to jump from the Temple. Unshaken, the Son of God refutes each solicitation, and Satan falls baffled from the pinnacle, after which angels bear the victor to a celestial feast before Christ returns to his mother's house.
en.milton.sonnets: This small collection of sonnets by John Milton is written in English and Italian, including a single canzone among the shorter poems. The opening piece invokes the nightingale as a herald of successful love, placing the speaker in the joint service of the Muse and of Love. The Italian poems follow the amorous conventions of the Petrarchan tradition, praising a lady whose name honours the valley of the Rhine. One addresses his friend Diodati on an unexpected fall in love, while another defends the choice to write of love in a foreign tongue. The English sonnets offer meditations on youth, time, and the will of Heaven, and they also include an appeal to an armed officer to spare the poet's house.
en.shakespeare.a_midsummer_night’s_dream: A Midsummer Night's Dream is a five act comedy by William Shakespeare, whose title suggests the fantastical events that unfold during a single night. The play opens in Athens as Duke Theseus prepares to marry Hippolyta, while Egeus demands that his daughter Hermia wed Demetrius or face death. Hermia and Lysander flee into a wood outside the city, where the fairy king Oberon and queen Titania quarrel over a changeling boy. A misapplied magic flower entangles the affections of four young Athenians, and the weaver Bottom is transformed with an ass's head. He becomes the object of the charmed Titania's devotion, and the lovers are restored and wed by the end. Amateur tradesmen perform Pyramus and Thisbe before Theseus, and the fairies bless the bridal house as Puck invites the audience to take the whole as a dream.
en.shakespeare.hamlet: This English tragedy by William Shakespeare opens at midnight on the battlements of Elsinore. Sentries and Horatio meet the apparition of the recently dead king of Denmark. The ghost tells Prince Hamlet that his uncle Claudius murdered him and married the widow Gertrude. Hamlet feigns madness while hesitating over revenge and stages a play to test the king's conscience. The drama moves through the killing of Polonius and Hamlet's dispatch to England with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. He escapes at sea, and the plot reaches its climax in a fencing match with an envenomed foil and poisoned cup. This final scene leaves the king, the queen, Laertes, and Hamlet dead as Fortinbras of Norway arrives to take the throne.
en.shakespeare.richard_iii: Richard III is a history play by William Shakespeare, which opens with the Duke of Gloucester declaring that he is determined to prove a villain. The action traces his ruthless rise to power through a series of crimes, including the murder of his brother Clarence in the Tower. He woos Lady Anne over a corpse while scheming against the queen's family as Edward IV dies. Richard gains the crown through staged reluctance and then kills his nephews, prompting Buckingham to rebel. Ghosts visit Richard and Richmond before the battle, where Richard cries for a horse as Richmond slays him. The play ends with the union of the houses of York and Lancaster.
en.shakespeare.sonnets: Shakespeare's Sonnets comprise a sequence of 154 poems written in iambic pentameter, and the majority follow the English form of three quatrains and a closing couplet. The opening group urges a fair young man to marry and beget heirs, aiming to preserve his beauty against time and decay. The sequence then follows the poet's devoted attachment to this young friend, treating his worth, absence, and reconciliation with unusual directness. The poems also address betrayal by the friend with the poet's own mistress, exploring the rivalry of other poets and the claim that verse confers immortality. From sonnet 127 onward, the addressee becomes a dark-complexioned woman, and the later poems explore desire, lust, deceit, and disillusionment. The collection closes with two allegorical sonnets on Cupid's brand, which is quenched in a fountain whose healing bath proves powerless against love.
en.spenser.faerie_queene: Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene is a long allegorical romance epic composed in the late sixteenth century. The title refers to the fairy queen, Gloriana, who serves as the poem's dedicatee and stands for Queen Elizabeth. The work is cast in the nine line Spenserian stanza and opens with the Redcrosse Knight. He rides out with the veiled lady Una to prove his prowess against a dragon. The six completed books follow virtuous champions such as Redcrosse for Holiness and Guyon for Temperance. These knights face monsters and magicians while Prince Arthur repeatedly intervenes in their aid.
en.swift.gullivers_travels: Jonathan Swift's prose satire presents itself as the truthful memoir of the ship's surgeon Lemuel Gulliver, who opens with a mock publisher's note and a letter protesting editorial alterations. The narrative then follows four voyages through a series of strange lands, beginning with a shipwreck that leaves Gulliver prisoner among the tiny Lilliputians, whose court factions caricature English politics. Later voyages take him to Brobdingnag, a land of giants whose king condemns European institutions, and he also visits the flying island of Laputa and the islands of Glubbdubdrib and Luggnagg. The final voyage brings him to Houyhnhnmland, where rational horses govern the brutish Yahoos, and the work closes with Gulliver back in England, estranged from his family and humankind. A concluding chapter defends his veracity and his declared design of reforming readers.
en.wordsworth.prelude: The Prelude is Wordsworth's long autobiographical poem in blank verse, cast in fourteen books and addressed throughout to Coleridge as 'O Friend!'. The title refers to the poem's function as a preface to a larger, unfinished work, while the narrative follows his childhood among the lakes and fells of the Lake District. It also covers his school days, undergraduate years at Cambridge, and a walking tour through the Alps, before the later books treat his disillusionment with the French Revolution and the moral crisis that followed. This period ends with the gradual restoration of imaginative faith through remembered 'spots of time', and the poem culminates in the ascent of Snowdon and valedictions to his sister and Coleridge.
en.world_english_bible.new_testament: This is the New Testament of the Christian Bible in the King James Version, the early modern English translation named after King James I. The work opens with the Gospel according to Matthew, beginning with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David and son of Abraham, and the account of his birth. Across the four gospels the narrative follows his teaching and miracles to his crucifixion and resurrection. The Acts of the Apostles then traces the growth of the early church from Pentecost through the missionary labours of Peter and Paul. A series of epistles, running from Paul's letters to the congregations through the general letters of Hebrews, James, Peter and John, instructs and admonishes the first Christian communities. It ends with the Book of Revelation, an apocalyptic vision of judgment and the new heaven and earth.
en.world_english_bible.pentateuch: The Pentateuch, meaning the five books, comprises the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the King James Version and traditionally ascribed to Moses. Genesis opens with the creation of the world in six days, then follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Exodus recounts the Israelites' bondage and their deliverance under Moses, followed by the covenant and the giving of the Law at Sinai. Leviticus codifies sacrifice, priesthood, and purity, while Numbers records the census and the years of wandering in the wilderness. Deuteronomy restates the law in Moses' farewell discourses, closing with his death in Moab and the charge given to Joshua.
en.world_english_bible.revelation: The Book of Revelation, given here in the King James translation, is the apocalyptic work that closes the Christian New Testament. Its date is uncertain, and the prophet who names himself John places his visions on the island of Patmos. The text opens with a vision of the glorified Christ commanding John to send letters to seven churches in Asia. The body of the work unrolls a chain of visionary scenes, including the heavenly throne and the Lamb opening a book sealed with seven seals. It also features the sounding of seven trumpets and the pouring out of seven vials of wrath. The dragon Satan and two beasts bearing the number six hundred sixty six appear before the destruction of the harlot Babylon. The narrative closes with the binding of Satan, a final battle, and the last judgment. It ends with the descent of the new Jerusalem into a new heaven and new earth, followed by exhortations to keep the words of the prophecy.
en.blake.songs_of_experience: William Blake's Songs of Experience gathers short lyric poems in quatrains and other brief stanzas, opening with an Introduction where the Bard calls upon the Earth to rise from despair. The poems treat childhood, repressed desire, institutional religion, and social misery, with works like 'The Chimney-Sweeper' and 'London' exploring these heavy themes. Short emblem pieces on flowers, insects, and beasts stand beside ballad-like narratives, while 'The Tyger' interrogates the tiger's creator. 'The Little Girl Lost' tells a story, and a sequence of paired dramatic voices debates the nature of love. The collection closes with 'The Voice of the Ancient Bard' summoning youth toward the morn.
en.keats.ode_bards_of_passion: This ode by John Keats addresses the bards of passion and mirth. It tells them they have left their souls on earth while living again in heaven. The heavenly souls commune with the spheres, fountains, and trees. They sit on Elysian lawns where the nightingale sings divine truth. The earth-born souls speak to mortals of sorrows, delights, and passions. They teach wisdom even though the bards are far away. The lyric closes by hailing the bards as double-lived in regions new.
en.keats.ode_to_psyche: Ode to Psyche is a lyric poem by Keats written in irregular stanzas. The speaker apologizes to the goddess for revealing her secrets in tuneless numbers. He then describes a vision of Cupid and Psyche embracing in a flowered glade. The poem laments that Psyche lacks the temples and altars of older gods. She is too late for the antique vows of the faded hierarchy. The speaker vows to build a fane in an untrodden region of his mind.
en.keats.to_autumn: To Autumn is a short lyric ode by John Keats, which addresses the personified season in three eleven-line stanzas. It opens with an apostrophe to autumn as the close bosom-friend of the maturing sun, and they conspire to load the vines, cottage-trees, gourds and hazel shells with ripeness. The second stanza pictures the drowsy season amid the harvest, where it rests on a granary floor or sleeps in a half-reaped furrow. The closing stanza insists that autumn has its own music, cataloguing the gnats mourning among the river sallows. The bleating lambs and hedge-crickets join the red-breast's soft treble, while gathering swallows twitter in the rosy light of the stubble-plains at day's end.
en.milton.arcades: Arcades is a short pastoral entertainment by John Milton, presented to the Countess Dowager of Derby at Harefield. Noble members of her family approach her seat of state in pastoral dress, singing in praise of her almost divine presence. The Genius of the Wood then addresses the singers, hailing them as descendants of Arcadia. He describes his guardianship of the grove against blighting winds and cankered worms, and tells of the celestial harmony by which the Sirens lull the daughters of Necessity. This harmony holds nature to her law, and he leads them onward with songs toward the lady's glittering state. The piece closes with lyrics bidding the Arcadian nymphs and shepherds forsake their old hills for a better soil where they may serve a rural queen surpassing all Arcadia.
en.world_english_bible.prophets: The Prophets division of the King James Bible contains twenty-one Old Testament books in English. It follows the traditional order from Joshua to Malachi. The narrative opens after Moses dies, with God commanding Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan. It then traces the conquest of Canaan and the rule of the judges. The story continues through the united monarchy under Samuel, Saul, David, and Solomon. The division splits into the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, which fall to Assyria and Babylon. The latter portion presents the prophets, from Isaiah's oracles to Malachi's closing promise.
en.shelley.adonais: Adonais is a pastoral elegy written in Spenserian stanzas, where Shelley uses the classical name to mourn a young poet. The poem opens with a summons to weep for the dead youth, while also rallying Urania, his mighty mother, to his grave. The course of the poem takes in the lament of nature, featuring a procession of personified mourners, including a self-portrait of the poet. The text attacks the reviewer held responsible for the young poet's death, then turns toward consolation, welcoming the dead poet by Chatterton, Sidney, and Lucan. The speaker feels his own spirit drawn to follow Adonais to the abode of the Eternal.
en.world_english_bible.writings: The Writings, or Ketuvim, form the third division of the Hebrew Bible in the King James translation, gathering thirteen books of narrative, poetry, and wisdom literature. It opens with the tale of Ruth, a Moabite who follows Naomi and enters David's lineage, before covering the royal histories of Chronicles and the post-exilic restoration in Ezra and Nehemiah. Esther's deliverance in Persia follows these historical accounts, and the volume turns to wisdom and lyric books, including Job, the Psalter, and Solomon's proverbs. Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and Lamentations complete this section, while the collection closes with Daniel's court narratives and his visions of empires.
en.browning.sonnets_from_the_portuguese: Sonnets from the Portuguese is a sequence of love sonnets by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, written in Petrarchan form and addressed by a woman speaker to her beloved. The opening sonnet sets the sweet years of Theocritus's song against the melancholy years of the speaker's life, until a figure that seems to be Death is revealed as Love. From there the sequence traces a movement from grief, self-doubt, and the pull of the grave toward the acceptance of an earthly union. The speaker weighs worldly opposition and the threat of separation against vows of constancy that neither sea, tempest, nor heaven's distance can dissolve. It closes with poems that measure love against old griefs, childhood faith, and lost saints. A final gift of flowers leaves their roots, the speaker says, in her own.

ar.abid_ibn_al_abras.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Abid ibn al-Abras (died c. 555), counted among the ten Mu'allaqat in the longer canon, a poem of desolation, wisdom and the hunt. 92 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.abu_firas.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Abu Firas al-Hamdani (died 968), the warrior prince of Aleppo and cousin of Sayf al-Dawla, including the Rumiyyat written in Byzantine captivity. 10 poems and 103 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.abu_nuwas.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Abu Nuwas (died c. 814), the Abbasid master of the wine song, the hunt and the profane epigram, whose khamriyyat lie behind the wine imagery of Persian lyric. 5 poems and 41 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.abu_tammam.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Abu Tammam (died 845), the Abbasid court poet and compiler of the Hamasa, whose ode on the conquest of Amorium (the sword is truer than the books) opens this small selection. 2 poems and 79 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.al_asha.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of al-A'sha Maymun (died c. 625), the wandering singer of pre-Islamic Arabia whose wine and praise poems circulated from Yemen to Hira. 132 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.ali_ibn_abi_talib.diwan_wikisource: The diwan attributed to Ali ibn Abi Talib (died 661), the fourth caliph and first Shi'i imam: wisdom verses and pious counsel gathered under his name by later compilers and quoted throughout Persian and Urdu literature as his. 161 poems and 751 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.amr_ibn_kulthum.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Amr ibn Kulthum (died c. 584), the Taghlibi chieftain, apart from his Mu'allaqa, which the corpus holds separately. 4 poems and 28 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.amr_ibn_kulthum.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Amr ibn Kulthum (died c. 584), the boast of the Taghlib before the king of Hira, whose refrain of tribal pride was said to be the Taghlib's one poem. 103 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.antara.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Antara ibn Shaddad (died c. 608), the black warrior poet of Abs, love for Abla and battle in one poem, the ode behind the popular Romance of Antar. 75 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.barudi.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Mahmud Sami al-Barudi (died 1904), the Egyptian soldier-statesman exiled to Ceylon after 1882, who revived the Abbasid manner and opened the neoclassical school that Shawqi completed. 11 poems and 285 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.bashshar.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Bashshar ibn Burd (died 783), the blind Persian-born poet of Basra who first bent the classical qasida toward the new Abbasid style. 2 poems and 48 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.busiri.burda: Al-Busiri's Qasidat al-Burda ("The Poem of the Mantle"), a 160-verse panegyric ode to the Prophet Muhammad composed in 13th-century Mamluk Egypt. According to the traditional account, al-Busiri, paralyzed by illness, saw the Prophet in a dream, who wrapped him in his mantle (burda) and healed him; the poem became one of the most widely memorized, recited, and commented-on texts in the Islamic world, and the model for a long tradition of imitations (see shawqi.nahj_al_burda).
ar.harith_ibn_hilliza.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of al-Harith ibn Hilliza (died c. 570), the Bakri chieftain's answer to Amr ibn Kulthum before the king of Hira, the two poems being the classic pair of tribal pleading. 164 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.hassan_ibn_thabit.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Hassan ibn Thabit (died c. 674), the poet of the Prophet, who defended Muhammad in verse against the Meccan satirists and whose elegies on him were a model for later praise poetry. 10 poems and 186 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.hatim_al_tai.diwan_wikisource: The poems attributed to Hatim al-Ta'i (died c. 578), the pre-Islamic chieftain whose name became the Arabic and Persian byword for generosity. 37 poems and 359 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.ibn_sahl.diwan_wikisource: The diwan of Ibn Sahl al-Andalusi (died 1251), the Seville poet of Jewish birth whose love lyrics and muwashshahs are among the most musical verse of Muslim Spain. 154 poems and 2,323 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.ibn_zaydun.nuniyya: The Nuniyya of Ibn Zaydun (died 1071), the Cordoban poet's farewell to the princess Wallada, the most famous love poem of Muslim Spain and a model for later poems in the same rhyme. 48 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.imru_al_qais.diwan_wikisource: The diwan of Imru' al-Qais (died c. 550), the wandering prince who is by tradition the first of the Arab poets, apart from his Mu'allaqa, which the corpus holds as a separate text. 31 poems and 1,074 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.imru_al_qais.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qais (died c. 550 CE), traditionally reckoned first among the seven (or ten) pre-Islamic "Suspended Odes" that stand as the founding masterpieces of classical Arabic poetry. It opens with the genre-defining atlal scene -- the poet halting to weep over the traces of an abandoned campsite -- before moving through love episodes, a famous storm description, and boasts of the poet's own prowess, in the qasida form that shaped Arabic ode-writing for a millennium.
ar.jamil_buthayna.diwan_wikisource: The poems of Jamil ibn Ma'mar, called Jamil Buthayna after the woman he loved (died 701), the chief poet of the Umayyad Udhri school of chaste love whose story and verses fed the Persian and Urdu romance of hopeless devotion. 95 poems and 716 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.kaab.banat_suad: Ka'b ibn Zuhayr's Banat Su'ad ("Su'ad has departed"), the seventh-century ode that gave the Burda tradition its name. According to the traditional account Ka'b, a pre-Islamic poet under sentence for satirizing the Prophet, recited it in Medina as a plea for pardon and was rewarded with the Prophet's own mantle (burda). It opens as a classical love-lament and camel-journey poem before turning to praise, and it became the model that al-Busiri and, through him, Ahmad Shawqi answered (see busiri.burda and shawqi.nahj_al_burda). 59 verses; text from Arabic Wikisource.
ar.khansa.diwan_wikisource: The elegies of al-Khansa (died c. 645), the greatest woman poet of early Arabic literature, whose laments for her brothers Sakhr and Mu'awiya, killed in tribal fighting before Islam, set the pattern for the Arabic marthiya. 69 poems and 709 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.labid.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Labid ibn Rabi'a (died c. 661), the poet who lived on into Islam, with its famous opening on the effaced encampment and the long boast of the tribe. 176 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.maarri.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri (died 1057), the blind skeptic of Ma'arrat al-Nu'man, from the Saqt al-Zand and the Luzumiyyat, the collection in which he bound himself to a double rhyme throughout. 6 poems and 54 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.mutanabbi.diwan_wikisource: The diwan of al-Mutanabbi (died 965), the most quoted poet of the Arabic language: panegyrics for Sayf al-Dawla of Aleppo and Kafur of Egypt, satires, elegies and the proverbial single verses that Persian, Turkish and Urdu poets carried into their own traditions. 286 poems and 5,407 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line with the two hemistichs separated by a bar.
ar.nabigha.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani (died c. 604), the court poet of the Lakhmids of Hira, an apology to the king al-Nu'man that became the model of the Arabic poem of excuse. 100 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.nawawi.arbain: The Forty Hadith of al-Nawawi (died 1277), the standard short collection of the sayings of the Prophet on the essentials of faith, memorized across the Islamic world and quoted constantly in Persian and Urdu verse (deeds are by intentions; none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself). 42 hadith from Arabic Wikisource, one hadith per line, without the commentary that accompanies them there.
ar.nawawi.riyad_al_salihin: Riyad al-Salihin (The Gardens of the Righteous) of al-Nawawi (died 1277), the most widely read collection of hadith on conduct and devotion, some 1,900 sayings of the Prophet arranged by topic. With the Qur'an it is the main Arabic source for the quotations and allusions in Persian and Urdu religious and Sufi poetry. 1,887 hadith from Arabic Wikisource, one hadith per line.
ar.quran.abasa: He Frowned (42 verses, Meccan), opening with a gentle rebuke of Muhammad for turning from a blind man, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, to focus on a wealthy Meccan he hoped to persuade -- one of the Quran's clearest self-critical moments -- followed by reflections on food, creation, and resurrection.
ar.quran.ad_duha: The Morning Brightness (11 verses, Meccan), a short sura of reassurance to Muhammad during a pause in revelation, recalling God's past care for him as an orphan and urging kindness to orphans and the needy in turn.
ar.quran.ad_dukhan: Smoke (59 verses, Meccan), named for a smoke that will be a sign preceding judgment, focused on the night the Quran was first revealed (traditionally Laylat al-Qadr) and Pharaoh's destruction as a pattern of divine justice.
ar.quran.adh_dhariyat: The Scattering Winds (60 verses, Meccan), named for winds that scatter dust, opening with a series of oaths and retelling Abraham's angelic visitors (who announce Isaac's birth and warn of Lot's people's destruction) as a sign of resurrection's certainty.
ar.quran.al_adiyat: The Chargers (11 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by galloping war-horses, condemning human ingratitude and love of wealth, and warning that graves will be overturned and hearts' secrets exposed.
ar.quran.al_ahqaf: The Sand Dunes (35 verses, Meccan), named for the region inhabited by the people of 'Ad, warning the Quraysh of the fate of earlier disbelieving nations and including a passage on kindness owed to parents.
ar.quran.al_ahzab: The Confederates (73 verses, Medinan), named for the coalition of tribes that besieged Medina in 627 CE (the Battle of the Trench), and also addressing Muhammad's household and marriages, adoption law, and the concept of Muhammad as "seal of the prophets."
ar.quran.al_ala: The Most High (19 verses, Meccan), praising God's creative and guiding power, urging Muhammad's ease in reciting and remembering the revelation, and closing with a comparison of this transient world to the everlasting hereafter, echoed in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses.
ar.quran.al_alaq: The Clot (19 verses, Meccan), traditionally identified as containing the Quran's first revealed verses ("Read, in the name of your Lord who created"), describing man's creation from a clinging clot and rebuking a figure (traditionally Abu Jahl) who tried to stop Muhammad from praying.
ar.quran.al_anam: Cattle (165 verses, Meccan), named for a passage on pagan superstitions about livestock, and centrally concerned with arguing for God's oneness (tawhid) against polytheism, including Abraham's search for God among the stars, sun, and moon before recognizing their Creator.
ar.quran.al_anbiya: The Prophets (112 verses, Meccan), a rapid survey of the missions of numerous prophets -- Abraham, Lot, Noah, David, Solomon, Job, Jonah, Zechariah, and others -- as a unified argument that all prophets preached the same message of monotheism.
ar.quran.al_anfal: The Spoils of War (75 verses, Medinan), revealed after the Battle of Badr (624 CE), addressing the division of war spoils and reflecting on that decisive early Muslim victory as a sign of divine aid, alongside rules of engagement and alliance.
ar.quran.al_ankabut: The Spider (69 verses, Meccan), named for a simile comparing those who take protectors other than God to a spider's fragile web, and reviewing the trials of Noah, Abraham, Lot, and other prophets as reassurance to persecuted early Muslims.
ar.quran.al_araf: The Heights (206 verses, Meccan), named for a barrier between Paradise and Hell where the fates of some souls are undecided. It retells the stories of several prophets sent to peoples who rejected them -- Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb, and Moses at length, including the Exodus and the golden calf.
ar.quran.al_asr: Time (3 verses, Meccan), one of the shortest and most quoted suras: an oath by time itself, declaring that all humankind is in loss except those who believe, do good, and counsel each other to truth and patience.
ar.quran.al_balad: The City (20 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by "this city" (Mecca), reflecting on the hardship of human life and urging freeing slaves and feeding the needy as "the steep path" to righteousness.
ar.quran.al_baqara: The Cow (286 verses, Medinan), the longest sura in the Quran, named for a story within it about a cow sacrificed by the Israelites. It covers an enormous range of legal, narrative, and doctrinal material -- the story of Adam, Abraham and the Kaaba, the direction of prayer (qibla), fasting, warfare, marriage and divorce law, usury, and the closing "Throne Verse" (Ayat al-Kursi) and final two verses recited widely for protection.
ar.quran.al_bayyina: The Clear Proof (8 verses, Medinan), addressing Jews, Christians, and polytheists together, arguing that a clear proof -- the Quran and Muhammad's recitation -- has now come to settle their prior disagreements over scripture.
ar.quran.al_buruj: The Constellations (22 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by the sky's constellations and recalling the martyrdom of believers burned in a trench by a persecuting king (traditionally linked to the Najran Christians), affirming God's power over their persecutors.
ar.quran.al_fajr: The Dawn (30 verses, Meccan), opening with oaths by the dawn and ten nights, recalling the destroyed peoples 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh as warnings against arrogance in wealth, and describing the soul's peaceful return to God.
ar.quran.al_falaq: The Daybreak (5 verses, Meccan), one of the two closing "protective" suras (al-mu'awwidhatan), a short prayer for refuge with the Lord of the daybreak from the evil of darkness, sorcery, and envy.
ar.quran.al_fath: Victory (29 verses, Medinan), revealed after the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628 CE), which the sura frames as "a clear victory" despite its apparent concessions, and praising the believers who pledged loyalty to Muhammad under the tree (Bay'at al-Ridwan).
ar.quran.al_fatiha: The Opening (7 verses, Meccan). The short prayer that opens the Quran and is recited in every unit (rak'ah) of the five daily Muslim prayers: praise of God, an acknowledgment of the Day of Judgment, and a plea for guidance on "the straight path."
ar.quran.al_fil: The Elephant (5 verses, Meccan), recalling the year of Muhammad's birth (traditionally 570 CE), when an army with war elephants attacking Mecca (led by the Abyssinian Abraha) was destroyed by flocks of birds pelting it with stones.
ar.quran.al_furqan: The Criterion (77 verses, Meccan), named for the Quran's role as a criterion distinguishing truth from falsehood, defending Muhammad against Meccan objections to his prophethood and describing the qualities of "the servants of the Merciful."
ar.quran.al_ghashiya: The Overwhelming Event (26 verses, Meccan), contrasting the toil and torment of the damned with the ease and comfort of Paradise's inhabitants, and closing by pointing to camels, sky, mountains, and earth as signs for reflection.
ar.quran.al_hadid: Iron (29 verses, Medinan), named for iron's usefulness to humankind mentioned within it, urging charitable spending, describing the light of believers on the Day of Judgment, and reflecting on monasticism among earlier Christians.
ar.quran.al_hajj: The Pilgrimage (78 verses, Medinan), addressing the rites of the hajj to Mecca, alongside the resurrection, permission for the wronged to fight in self-defense, and a closing call to strive in God's cause.
ar.quran.al_haqqa: The Reality (52 verses, Meccan), describing the Day of Judgment ("the Reality") and the fates of destroyed peoples ('Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh, the people of Lot, Noah's people), and defending the Quran against accusations of being a poet's or soothsayer's words.
ar.quran.al_hashr: The Exile (24 verses, Medinan), revealed after the expulsion of the Jewish tribe Banu Nadir from Medina, and closing with a celebrated passage of divine names and attributes.
ar.quran.al_hijr: Al-Hijr (99 verses, Meccan), named for the rock-cut dwellings of the Thamud people at al-Hijr, retelling the creation of Adam, Iblis's refusal to bow to him, and destruction narratives including Lot's people, as warnings to Muhammad's Meccan opponents.
ar.quran.al_hujurat: The Private Apartments (18 verses, Medinan), a sura of social and interpersonal etiquette: respect toward Muhammad, verifying reports before acting on them, reconciling disputes between believers, and prohibitions on mockery, suspicion, and backbiting.
ar.quran.al_humaza: The Slanderer (9 verses, Meccan), condemning the backbiter and slanderer who hoards wealth thinking it will make him immortal, and describing his punishment in the "Crushing Fire" that reaches the heart.
ar.quran.al_ikhlas: Sincerity (4 verses, Meccan), a compact statement of strict monotheism -- God is one, eternally self-sufficient, neither begetting nor begotten, without equal -- traditionally described as equivalent in merit to one-third of the entire Quran.
ar.quran.al_imran: The Family of Imran (200 verses, Medinan), named for the family of Mary's father, and largely concerned with the birth of Mary and Jesus, debate with Christians over Jesus's nature, and reflection on the Muslim defeat at the Battle of Uhud as a test of faith.
ar.quran.al_infitar: The Cleaving (19 verses, Meccan), describing the sky splitting apart as a sign of the Day of Judgment, and the two recording angels who note every deed.
ar.quran.al_insan: Man (31 verses, Medinan), also called ad-Dahr ("Time"), describing man's creation from a mixed fluid drop and the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, traditionally linked by exegetes to Ali and Fatima's charity.
ar.quran.al_inshiqaq: The Splitting Open (25 verses, Meccan), describing the sky splitting and the earth flattening out on Judgment Day, and the moment each soul receives its record of deeds in the right or left hand.
ar.quran.al_isra: The Night Journey (111 verses, Meccan), named for Muhammad's night journey from Mecca to "the farthest mosque" (traditionally identified with Jerusalem) in its opening verse, followed by ethical injunctions (kindness to parents, honesty, humility) and warnings against the pride of Iblis and of past nations.
ar.quran.al_jathiya: Crouching (37 verses, Meccan), named for nations crouching (kneeling) before God on the Day of Judgment, arguing from natural signs -- the alternation of night and day, rain, the sea -- for God's oneness and warning against those who take their own desires as their god.
ar.quran.al_jinn: The Jinn (28 verses, Meccan), describing a group of jinn who overheard the Quran being recited and believed, reporting their reaction and affirming God's oneness to their own kind.
ar.quran.al_jumua: Friday (11 verses, Medinan), instituting the Friday congregational prayer and its etiquette, and criticizing those entrusted with the Torah who fail to uphold it.
ar.quran.al_kafirun: The Disbelievers (6 verses, Meccan), a short, firm declaration of religious separation from Meccan polytheists, closing with the famous line "to you your religion, and to me mine."
ar.quran.al_kahf: The Cave (110 verses, Meccan), named for the story of youths who took refuge in a cave and slept for centuries (the "Sleepers of Ephesus" tradition), and also containing the story of Moses's journey with the mysterious figure al-Khidr and the account of Dhu'l-Qarnayn ("The Two-Horned One") and the wall against Gog and Magog.
ar.quran.al_kawthar: Abundance (3 verses, Meccan), the shortest sura in the Quran, in which God grants Muhammad "al-Kawthar" (abundance, traditionally understood as a river in Paradise), instructing him to pray and sacrifice in gratitude and declaring that it is his enemy, not he, who will be cut off without posterity.
ar.quran.al_layl: The Night (21 verses, Meccan), opening with oaths by night and day, distinguishing the generous, God-fearing believer from the miserly denier, and promising ease for the one path and hardship for the other.
ar.quran.al_maarij: The Ascending Stairways (44 verses, Meccan), describing the psychological character of anxious, ungenerous humanity contrasted with the steadfast qualities of true believers, and the reality of the coming judgment.
ar.quran.al_maida: The Table Spread (120 verses, Medinan), named for the disciples' request that Jesus call down a table of food from heaven as a sign. Traditionally held to include the Quran's final revealed legal verses, it covers dietary law, contracts, criminal penalties, and relations with Jews and Christians.
ar.quran.al_masad: The Palm Fiber (5 verses, Meccan), a sharply worded condemnation of Muhammad's uncle Abu Lahab ("Father of Flame") and his wife for their hostility to him, the only sura naming a specific opponent by name.
ar.quran.al_maun: Small Kindnesses (7 verses, Meccan), condemning those who deny the faith by mistreating orphans, failing to feed the poor, praying carelessly for show, and withholding even small acts of neighborly kindness.
ar.quran.al_muddaththir: The Cloaked One (56 verses, Meccan), traditionally among the earliest revelations, commanding Muhammad to "arise and warn," and describing the fate of a wealthy disbeliever who dismissed the Quran as mere sorcery.
ar.quran.al_mujadila: The Pleading Woman (22 verses, Medinan), named for a woman who disputed with Muhammad over an unjust pre-Islamic divorce formula (zihar), which the sura reforms, alongside guidance on private conspiratorial conversation (najwa).
ar.quran.al_mulk: The Dominion (30 verses, Meccan), opening in praise of God's sovereignty over creation and life and death, and traditionally recommended for nightly recitation as protection in the grave.
ar.quran.al_muminun: The Believers (118 verses, Meccan), opening with a description of the qualities of successful believers (humility in prayer, chastity, honesty), followed by the creation of man, Noah's mission, and a warning against sectarian division.
ar.quran.al_mumtahina: She That Is To Be Examined (13 verses, Medinan), named for the examination of women migrants' sincerity before their integration into the Muslim community, addressing loyalty and boundaries between Muslims and their opponents while permitting kindness to non-hostile non-Muslims.
ar.quran.al_munafiqun: The Hypocrites (11 verses, Medinan), describing the false profession of faith and disloyalty of hypocrites within the early Muslim community at Medina.
ar.quran.al_mursalat: Those Sent Forth (50 verses, Meccan), built around the repeated refrain "woe that Day to the deniers," describing the Day of Judgment through a series of oaths by winds and angelic messengers.
ar.quran.al_mutaffifin: Those Who Give Short Measure (36 verses, Meccan), condemning merchants who cheat with unequal weights and measures, and contrasting the fate of the wicked (recorded in Sijjin) with the righteous (recorded in Illiyyin).
ar.quran.al_muzzammil: The Enshrouded One (20 verses, Meccan), addressed to Muhammad wrapped in his cloak, instructing night prayer and patient endurance of his opponents' rejection.
ar.quran.al_qadr: The Night of Decree (5 verses, Meccan), a short sura celebrating Laylat al-Qadr, the night the Quran began to be revealed, described as "better than a thousand months," when angels descend with divine decree.
ar.quran.al_qalam: The Pen (52 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by the pen and what is written, defending Muhammad's character against accusations of madness, and telling a parable of owners of a garden who lost their harvest through selfishness.
ar.quran.al_qamar: The Moon (55 verses, Meccan), opening with the moon splitting as a sign, and structured around a repeated refrain ("how [terrible] was My punishment and My warning") applied to the destroyed peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot, and Pharaoh.
ar.quran.al_qaria: The Calamity (11 verses, Meccan), naming the Day of Judgment "the Calamity" and describing it through the image of scattered moths and carded wool, then weighing each soul's deeds on a scale.
ar.quran.al_qasas: The Story (88 verses, Meccan), centered on an extended retelling of Moses's life from infancy (set adrift on the Nile) through his flight to Midian, marriage, and call to prophethood, alongside the story of the arrogant, wealthy Qarun (Korah) swallowed by the earth.
ar.quran.al_qiyama: The Resurrection (40 verses, Meccan), affirming bodily resurrection against skeptics, describing the moment of death and the soul's departure, and the vivid contrast of radiant and downcast faces on Judgment Day.
ar.quran.al_waqia: The Inevitable Event (96 verses, Meccan), describing the Day of Judgment and dividing humanity into three companies -- the foremost, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left -- with detailed description of each group's fate.
ar.quran.an_naba: The Great News (40 verses, Meccan), opening by asking what people are disputing about -- "the great news," the resurrection -- and describing creation as evidence, then Hell and Paradise in vivid detail.
ar.quran.an_nahl: The Bee (128 verses, Meccan), named for a passage on the bee as a sign of God's providence, part of a broader catalogue of natural blessings -- rain, livestock, ships, the compass points -- offered as evidence for gratitude and belief.
ar.quran.an_najm: The Star (62 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by the star and describing a vision of revelation (traditionally linked to Muhammad's ascension, mi'raj), and rejecting the pagan Meccan goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat as powerless idols.
ar.quran.an_naml: The Ant (93 verses, Meccan), named for an ant that warns its colony as Solomon's army passes, part of an extended Solomon narrative that includes the hoopoe bird's report of the Queen of Sheba and her eventual submission to Solomon's God.
ar.quran.an_nas: Mankind (6 verses, Meccan), the Quran's final sura and the second of the two protective suras, a prayer for refuge with the Lord of mankind from the whispered evil of a retreating tempter, among jinn and among men.
ar.quran.an_nasr: Divine Support (3 verses, Medinan), traditionally understood as revealed near the end of Muhammad's life, announcing God's help and the coming triumph of Islam and instructing praise and seeking forgiveness in response.
ar.quran.an_naziat: Those Who Pull Out (46 verses, Meccan), opening with oaths by angels associated with death and resurrection, retelling Moses's confrontation with Pharaoh briefly, and describing the Day of Judgment.
ar.quran.an_nisa: Women (176 verses, Medinan), one of the Quran's major legal suras, addressing inheritance shares, marriage and dower, orphans' property, and the treatment of women, alongside passages on warfare, hypocrisy, and interfaith relations with Jews and Christians.
ar.quran.an_nur: Light (64 verses, Medinan), a legal and social sura addressing slander and the requirement of witnesses (revealed in connection with an accusation against Muhammad's wife Aisha), modesty in dress and conduct, and the celebrated "Verse of Light" comparing God's guidance to a lamp in a niche.
ar.quran.ar_rad: Thunder (43 verses, Medinan), named for thunder's praise of God mentioned within it, addressing God's signs in nature, the fate of disbelieving nations, and the contrast between temporary worldly life and the reality of the hereafter.
ar.quran.ar_rahman: The Most Merciful (78 verses, Meccan or Medinan by different accounts), built around the refrain "which of your Lord's favors will you both deny," addressed to jinn and humankind together and cataloguing blessings in creation and the delights of Paradise.
ar.quran.ar_rum: The Byzantines (60 verses, Meccan), opening with a prediction that the defeated Byzantines (Romans) will be victorious again within a few years -- fulfilled after their reversal against the Persians -- offered as a sign of God's power over historical events.
ar.quran.as_saff: The Ranks (14 verses, Medinan), named for believers fighting in ranks "as though a solid structure," urging commitment matched by action and recalling Jesus's foretelling of a messenger to come after him named Ahmad.
ar.quran.as_saffat: Those Ranged in Ranks (182 verses, Meccan), named for angels described as standing in ranks, and containing an extended account of Abraham's near-sacrifice of his son, alongside brief mentions of Noah, Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Lot, and Jonah.
ar.quran.as_sajda: The Prostration (30 verses, Meccan), named for a prostration verse within it, treating creation, resurrection, and the contrast between the reward of believers and the punishment of those who deny the Day of Judgment.
ar.quran.ash_shams: The Sun (15 verses, Meccan), built from a chain of cosmic oaths (the sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth, soul) affirming that the soul's purification or corruption determines its fate, illustrated by the story of the Thamud's slaughter of a sacred she-camel.
ar.quran.ash_sharh: The Opening Up (8 verses, Meccan), also called al-Inshirah, reassuring Muhammad that God has relieved his distress and eased his burden, with the celebrated refrain "with hardship comes ease."
ar.quran.ash_shuara: The Poets (227 verses, Meccan), retelling the missions of Moses, Abraham, Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb in a recurring refrain structure, and closing by distinguishing the Quran from the poetry of the pagan poets its opponents compared it to.
ar.quran.ash_shura: Consultation (53 verses, Meccan), named for its instruction that believers' affairs be conducted by mutual consultation (shura), alongside themes of prophetic continuity across religions and patience under persecution.
ar.quran.at_taghabun: Mutual Disillusion (18 verses, Medinan), named for the Day of Judgment as a day when gains and losses of this life are revealed to have been misjudged, urging trust in God and warning against being distracted by wealth and children.
ar.quran.at_tahrim: The Prohibition (12 verses, Medinan), addressing a domestic episode in Muhammad's household and closing with the exemplary figures of Pharaoh's wife Asiya and Mary as models of righteous women.
ar.quran.at_takathur: Rivalry in Worldly Increase (8 verses, Meccan), a short, sharp rebuke of the competitive accumulation of wealth and status that distracts people until death, warning that they will be questioned about their worldly pleasures.
ar.quran.at_takwir: The Overturning (29 verses, Meccan), opening with a rapid sequence of cosmic upheavals marking the Day of Judgment (the sun darkened, stars falling, seas boiling over), and including a defense of Muhammad's prophethood and of the angel Gabriel who brought the revelation.
ar.quran.at_talaq: Divorce (12 verses, Medinan), setting out the waiting period (iddah), maintenance, and procedural rules for divorce.
ar.quran.at_tariq: The Night Star (17 verses, Meccan), opening with an oath by the piercing night star, arguing for resurrection from the analogy of man's creation from a fluid, and God's power to bring him back.
ar.quran.at_tawba: Repentance (129 verses, Medinan), the only sura not opening with the Quran's customary "In the name of God" invocation. It addresses the treatment of treaty-breaking polytheists, hypocrites within the Muslim community, and the campaign to Tabuk.
ar.quran.at_tin: The Fig (8 verses, Meccan), opening with oaths by the fig, the olive, and Mount Sinai, affirming that man was created "in the best of forms" but can fall to the lowest, except those who believe and do good.
ar.quran.at_tur: The Mount (49 verses, Meccan), named for Mount Sinai invoked in its opening oaths, describing the rewards of Paradise for the righteous and rebutting the Meccans' accusations against Muhammad's prophethood.
ar.quran.az_zalzala: The Earthquake (8 verses, Medinan), describing the earth's violent shaking on the Day of Judgment, when it will testify to everything done upon it, and every soul will see the full weight of even its smallest deeds.
ar.quran.az_zukhruf: Ornaments of Gold (89 verses, Meccan), named for worldly gold ornaments dismissed as insignificant beside true guidance, arguing against the Meccans' objection that the Quran was not revealed to a "great man" of the two cities, and recounting Abraham's rejection of his father's idolatry and Moses versus Pharaoh.
ar.quran.az_zumar: The Throngs (75 verses, Meccan), named for the throngs of the saved and the damned entering Paradise and Hell in its closing verses, centrally an argument for sincere, exclusive devotion to God against those who take other intercessors.
ar.quran.fatir: Originator (45 verses, Meccan), also called al-Mala'ika ("The Angels") for its opening reference to angels as God's messengers, arguing from creation and natural signs for God's oneness and warning against the deception of Satan.
ar.quran.fussilat: Explained in Detail (54 verses, Meccan), also called Ha Mim Sajda, arguing for the Quran's clarity and divine origin against Meccan rejection, and including the peoples of 'Ad and Thamud as warning examples.
ar.quran.ghafir: The Forgiver (85 verses, Meccan), also called al-Mumin ("The Believer") for a secret believer in Pharaoh's court who argues for sparing Moses, opening with divine attributes including forgiveness and framing Pharaoh's downfall as a warning.
