ar.quran.hud: Hud (123 verses, Meccan), named for the Arabian prophet Hud sent to the people of 'Ad, one of several destruction narratives here (Noah, Hud, Salih, Abraham and Lot, Shu'ayb, Moses) illustrating a recurring pattern: a prophet warns, the people reject him, and destruction follows.
ar.quran.ibrahim: Abraham (52 verses, Meccan), named for Abraham's prayer for his descendants and for Mecca late in the sura, concerned broadly with gratitude versus ingratitude toward God and the fates of past disbelieving peoples.
ar.quran.luqman: Luqman (34 verses, Meccan), named for the sage Luqman's ethical counsel to his son (gratitude, avoiding arrogance, moderation in voice and gait), framed by broader arguments for God's oneness from creation.
ar.quran.maryam: Mary (98 verses, Meccan), centered on the annunciation and virgin birth of Jesus to Mary, followed by shorter accounts of Abraham, Moses, Ishmael, and Idris, framed as a family of prophets united in worship of the one God.
ar.quran.muhammad: Muhammad (38 verses, Medinan), also called al-Qital ("Fighting"), addressing the conduct of war against those who obstruct God's path, the fate of hypocrites, and a description of the rivers of Paradise.
ar.quran.nuh: Noah (28 verses, Meccan), a sustained retelling of Noah's centuries-long call to his people to abandon idolatry, their refusal, and his prayer for their destruction by flood.
ar.quran.qaf: Qaf (45 verses, Meccan), opening with a single disconnected letter, focused on resurrection and God's complete knowledge of every soul, including the image of two recording angels seated at each person's shoulders.
ar.quran.quraysh: Quraysh (4 verses, Meccan), calling on the Quraysh, Mecca's dominant tribe, to worship the God who secured their prosperous trading caravans and protected them from hunger and fear.
ar.quran.saba: Sheba (54 verses, Meccan), named for the kingdom of Sheba and the collapse of its Ma'rib dam as punishment for ingratitude, alongside the story of Solomon's death (undetected by the jinn working for him until his staff, which his body leaned on, was eaten by a worm) and warnings to Mecca's disbelievers.
ar.quran.sad: Sad (88 verses, Meccan), opening with a single disconnected letter, and centered on David's repentance after a moment of judgment and Solomon's love of horses distracting him from prayer, alongside Job's patience in suffering and Iblis's refusal to bow to Adam.
ar.quran.ta_ha: Ta Ha (135 verses, Meccan), opening with two of the Quran's mysterious disconnected letters, and centrally retelling Moses's call at the burning bush, his confrontation with Pharaoh and the magicians, the Exodus, and the Israelites' worship of the golden calf in his absence.
ar.quran.ya_sin: Ya Sin (83 verses, Meccan), opening with two disconnected letters and often called "the heart of the Quran" in Islamic tradition for its widespread recitation, especially for the dying and the dead; it tells a parable of messengers rejected by a town and argues for resurrection from the signs of nature.
ar.quran.yunus: Jonah (109 verses, Meccan), named for a brief mention of Jonah's people, who alone among those warned by a prophet repented in time and were spared. The sura's main concern is defending the Quran's authenticity and warning of resurrection and judgment.
ar.quran.yusuf: Joseph (111 verses, Meccan), a single sustained narrative -- the Quran's only sura devoted entirely to one story -- retelling Joseph's betrayal by his brothers, his time in Egypt including Potiphar's wife's attempted seduction, his rise to power, and his eventual reunion with his family.
ar.shabbi.diwan_wikisource: The poems of Abu al-Qasim al-Shabbi (died 1934), the Tunisian romantic whose Will to Live became the anthem of Arab nationalism and whose verse marks the point where the classical qasida gives way to modern Arabic poetry. 107 poems and 2,564 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.shanfara.lamiyyat_al_arab: The Lamiyyat al-Arab of al-Shanfara (died c. 525), the outlaw poet's declaration of solitary life in the desert among wolves, the classic of the pre-Islamic brigand poets and a school text for a thousand years. 69 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.shawqi.diwan_wikisource: Poems of Ahmad Shawqi (died 1932), the Prince of Poets of the Egyptian revival, apart from his Nahj al-Burda, which the corpus holds separately: his Andalusian exile poems, occasional odes and the Siniyya that answers al-Buhturi. 17 poems and 1,086 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.
ar.shawqi.nahj_al_burda: Ahmad Shawqi's Nahj al-Burda ("On the Path of the Burda"), a 190-verse panegyric to the Prophet Muhammad composed in the same meter and rhyme as al-Busiri's 13th-century Qasidat al-Burda, making it a deliberate mu'arada (formal answer-poem) to that model. Shawqi, the leading Arabic poet of the early 20th century and often called "Prince of Poets," wrote it in 1910, updating the Burda tradition's devotional panegyric for a modern audience while keeping its meter, rhyme, and much of its thematic structure.
ar.tarafa.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Tarafa ibn al-Abd (died c. 564 CE), one of the seven (or ten) pre-Islamic "Suspended Odes." It is especially celebrated for its extended opening description of the poet's she-camel, rendered in closely observed physical detail, before turning to reflections on youth, pleasure, and mortality, and a defense of the poet's own hedonism against his critics -- Tarafa was reportedly executed as a young man for a satire against a Bahraini ruler.
ar.zuhayr.muallaqa: The Mu'allaqa of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma (died c. 609), the ode of the peacemaker, praising the two chiefs who ended the war of Dahis and al-Ghabra and closing with the gnomic verses on age and wisdom that Arabic tradition quotes most. 62 verses from Arabic Wikisource, one verse per line.

fa.anvari.diwan: The collected poems of Anvari (died c. 1189), a court poet of the Seljuk sultans of Khorasan renowned above all for panegyric qasidas praising his patrons, alongside satirical and philosophical pieces. Later critics ranked him among the three or four greatest qasida poets in Persian for his dense, allusive style and mastery of scientific and astrological imagery.
fa.attar.diwan: The lyric divan of Farid ad-Din Attar (died c. 1221), a Sufi mystic of Nishapur better known for his narrative poem The Conference of the Birds. These ghazals and shorter poems work the same mystical territory in miniature: the soul's longing for annihilation in the divine, expressed through the standard imagery of wine, the beloved, and the moth and the flame.
fa.bidel.diwan: The divan of Mirza Abdul-Qader Bidel (died 1720), a Central Asian/Indian poet writing in the ornate "Indian style" (sabk-e hendi) prized for its dense metaphor and philosophical difficulty. Bidel is the single most influential Persian poet in the literary traditions of Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and the Indian subcontinent, though relatively little read in Iran itself.
fa.farrokhi.diwan: The divan of Farrokhi Sistani (died 1037), one of the earliest and most celebrated panegyrists of the Ghaznavid court under Sultan Mahmud. His poems typically open with a nature or wine scene before turning to praise of the sultan and his campaigns, in the plain, musical style characteristic of early classical Persian poetry.
fa.ferdowsi.diwan: The Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), Ferdowsi's roughly 50,000-verse epic completed around 1010 and dedicated to the Ghaznavid Sultan Mahmud. It narrates the mythical and legendary history of Iran from creation through the Arab conquest, including the tragedy of Rostam and Sohrab and the tyranny of Zahhak, and stands as the foundational epic and the single most important text in the Persian literary and national tradition. (Filed under the "diwan" title in this corpus; the content is the Shahnameh.)
fa.hafez.diwan: The divan of Hafez of Shiraz (died c. 1390), the most beloved lyric poet in the Persian language: several hundred ghazals of wine, love, and mystical longing, prized for their ambiguity between literal and Sufi readings and their technical perfection. Copies of Hafez's divan are still used in Iran for bibliomancy (fal-e Hafez), consulted for guidance the way others might consult an oracle.
fa.iqbal.armaghan_e_hijaz_persian: The Persian portion of Armaghan-e Hijaz ("Gift of the Hijaz"), Muhammad Iqbal's final poetry collection, published posthumously in 1938 and mixing Persian and Urdu verse. Composed as Iqbal was dying, it returns to his central themes of Islamic renewal and the awakened self in a valedictory, often elegiac register.
fa.iqbal.asrar_e_khudi: Asrar-e Khudi ("Secrets of the Self"), Muhammad Iqbal's 1915 Persian masnavi and his first major philosophical poem. It argues for khudi, the cultivation and strengthening of individual selfhood, against the Sufi ideal of self-annihilation (fana), presenting a this-worldly, dynamic ethic aimed at reviving Muslim civilization.
fa.iqbal.diwan: A Persian-language divan by Muhammad Iqbal (died 1938), the philosopher-poet of British India and Pakistan's national poet, who wrote a substantial part of his major work in Persian rather than Urdu to reach the wider Persianate world. Its themes are characteristically Iqbalian: the awakening of the self (khudi), the revival of Islamic civilization, and a reworking of classical Sufi imagery toward an ethic of dynamic self-assertion rather than self-annihilation.
fa.iqbal.javid_nama: Javid Nama ("Book of Javid"), Iqbal's 1932 Persian masnavi and generally considered his masterpiece, named for his son Javid. Modeled loosely on Dante's Divine Comedy, it takes the poet on a journey through the celestial spheres guided by Rumi, encountering historical and legendary figures who debate the fate of Islamic civilization and the nature of selfhood.
fa.iqbal.pas_cheh_bayad_kard: Pas Cheh Bayad Kard, ay Aqvam-e Sharq ("What Then Is to Be Done, O Peoples of the East"), a 1936 Persian masnavi by Iqbal that is explicitly political: a call to the peoples of Asia and the Islamic world to resist Western imperialism and materialism and to recover a self-directed, spiritually grounded civilization.
fa.iqbal.payam_e_mashriq: Payam-e Mashriq ("Message of the East"), Iqbal's 1923 collection composed explicitly as a reply to Goethe's West-Ostlicher Divan, offering an Eastern, Islamic counter-voice to Goethe's engagement with Persian poetry. It ranges across quatrains, ghazals, and philosophical fragments on selfhood, love, and the relationship between East and West.
fa.iqbal.rumuz_e_bekhudi: Rumuz-e Bekhudi ("Mysteries of Selflessness"), Iqbal's 1918 Persian masnavi and sequel to Asrar-e Khudi. Where the earlier poem argued for the cultivation of the individual self, this one turns to the self's relationship to the community (millat), arguing that individual selfhood is completed and given purpose within the collective life of the Muslim community.
fa.iqbal.zabur_e_ajam: Zabur-e Ajam ("Persian Psalms"), Iqbal's 1927 collection of ghazals and quatrains, its title deliberately echoing the Psalms of David to cast the poems as devotional utterance. It includes the long philosophical poem Gulshan-e Raz-e Jadid ("The New Garden of Mystery"), written as a modern reply to a classical Sufi text of the same name.
fa.jami.diwan: The divan of Abd al-Rahman Jami (died 1492), the last major poet of classical Persian literature's golden age, active at the Timurid court of Herat. A prolific Sufi of the Naqshbandi order, Jami is often described as summing up and closing the classical ghazal tradition that runs from Rudaki through Hafez.
fa.khaghani.diwan: The divan of Khaqani Shirvani (died c. 1190), a poet of the Caucasian Shirvanshah court famous for a difficult, densely allusive qasida style packed with technical, scientific, and Christian imagery (he traveled to Byzantine territory and wrote of its churches). His Tuhfat al-Iraqayn, an account of his pilgrimage to Mecca, and his prison poems (habsiyat) are especially celebrated.
fa.khayyam.diwan: The quatrains (rubaiyat) attributed to Omar Khayyam (died 1131), the Seljuk-era mathematician and astronomer of Nishapur who reformed the Persian calendar. The roughly small core of authentic verses, expanded over centuries by imitators, meditate skeptically on mortality, wine, and the unknowability of the universe -- famous in the West chiefly through Edward FitzGerald's 1859 free translation.
fa.manuchehri.diwan: The divan of Manuchehri Damghani (died c. 1040), an early Ghaznavid court poet known for vivid nature description, wine poems modeled on pre-Islamic Arabic ode conventions, and an unusually wide range of meters and rhyme forms. His qasidas are prized for their concrete, sensuous imagery of gardens, seasons, and the natural world.
fa.naser_khosrow.diwan: The divan of Naser Khosrow (died c. 1088), an Ismaili Shia philosopher-poet and missionary (da'i) who, after a spiritual crisis and pilgrimage recorded in his prose Safarnama, spent his exile in Badakhshan composing philosophically and religiously argumentative poetry. His verse is unusual in classical Persian for its didactic, polemical directness in defending Ismaili doctrine and denouncing the powerful.
fa.nizami.diwan: A lyric collection attributed to Nizami Ganjavi (died c. 1209), best known for the five narrative romances of his Khamsa (Layla and Majnun, Khosrow and Shirin, and others) that became the model for centuries of Persianate romance poetry. This diwan represents his shorter lyric output alongside that larger narrative achievement.
fa.parvin.diwan: The divan of Parvin Etesami (died 1941), one of the first major women poets of modern Persian literature. Her poetry is distinctively didactic and socially engaged, often cast as debate-dialogues (monazereh) between animals, objects, or abstractions that argue out a moral point in the manner of a fable.
fa.rudaki.diwan: The surviving fragments of Rudaki (died 941), traditionally honored as the father of classical Persian poetry and the first great poet of the Samanid court at Bukhara. Only a small fraction of his reputed output survives, in isolated verses and fragments quoted by later anthologists, but his plain, confident style set patterns later poets built on.
fa.rumi.diwan: The Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, Jalal ad-Din Rumi's vast collection of lyric ghazals and quatrains (distinct from his narrative Masnavi), composed after his transformative encounter with the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi around 1244. Many poems are addressed to or written in the voice of Shams, and the collection is considered one of the great outpourings of ecstatic mystical love poetry in any language.
fa.rumi.masnavi: The opening of Rumi's Masnavi-ye Ma'navi ("Spiritual Couplets"), the roughly 25,000-couplet mystical-didactic poem in six books that is, after the Quran, the single most influential text in the Persian Sufi tradition. It opens with the celebrated "Song of the Reed," the reed flute's lament of separation from the reed bed, read as an allegory of the soul's exile from God, before unfolding into hundreds of interwoven parables, anecdotes, and Quranic commentary.
fa.saadi.bustan: The opening of Saadi's Bustan ("The Orchard"), a didactic masnavi completed in 1257 and organized into ten chapters on justice, generosity, love, humility, contentment, and other ethical themes, each illustrated with short anecdotes and exemplary stories. Along with its prose-and-verse companion the Gulistan, it is one of the two works that made Saadi the classical Persian tradition's foremost poet of practical ethics.
fa.saadi.diwan: The lyric divan of Saadi of Shiraz (died c. 1292), collecting his ghazals and qasidas apart from his two most famous didactic works, the Bustan and the prose-and-verse Gulistan. Saadi's ghazals are prized for a clarity and emotional directness that later critics contrasted with the denser, more paradoxical style of Hafez.
fa.saeb.diwan: The enormous divan of Saeb Tabrizi (died 1676), the most celebrated master of the "Indian style" (sabk-e hendi) at the Safavid and Mughal courts, reputed to be one of the most prolific poets in the Persian language with well over 100,000 surviving verses. His ghazals are dense with fresh, often startlingly concrete metaphor (mazmun-e taza), the hallmark of the style.
fa.sanai.diwan: The divan of Hakim Sanai of Ghazna (died c. 1131), whose Hadiqat al-Haqiqa ("The Walled Garden of Truth") is generally credited as the first major mystical-didactic masnavi in Persian, establishing the form Attar and Rumi would later use. This divan collects his shorter lyric and qasida output alongside that pioneering achievement.

ur.akbar.kulliyat_wikisource: The poems of Akbar Allahabadi (died 1921), the satirist of colonial modernity, who turned the ghazal and the short nazm on the new English-educated class, the railway, the newspaper and the reformers, and whose couplets are still quoted as jokes. 146 poems from Urdu Wikisource, one line of verse per line.
ur.anis.marsiye_wikisource: The marsiyas of Mir Babar Ali Anis (died 1874), the Lucknow master of the Urdu elegy on the martyrdom of Husain at Karbala. Each marsiya runs to hundreds of six-line stanzas and moves through battle narrative, lament and moral reflection in a grand style that Urdu critics rank with epic. 90 marsiyas and shorter elegies from Urdu Wikisource, one line of verse per line, the largest Urdu text in the corpus.
ur.atish.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Khwaja Haidar Ali Atish (died 1847), the leading poet of the Lucknow school in its prime and the great rival of Nasikh. Atish kept the ghazal close to feeling and plain speech while Lucknow around him grew ornate, and his divan is the usual counterweight when the Delhi and Lucknow manners are compared. 104 ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line.
ur.dagh.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Dagh Dehlvi (died 1905), the last great master of the Delhi school and the most imitated ghazal poet of the late nineteenth century. Raised in the Red Fort household of Bahadur Shah Zafar, Dagh wrote in a clear, idiomatic Urdu that made his verse proverbial. 179 ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line. A natural pair with Ghalib and Zauq, the Delhi poets of the generation before him, and with Iqbal, who studied with him.
ur.dard.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Khwaja Mir Dard (died 1785), the Sufi poet of Delhi whose small divan is prized above many larger ones for its mystical concentration. A contemporary of Mir and Sauda, Dard was a Naqshbandi shaikh and wrote most of his work in Persian. 28 Urdu ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line.
ur.ghalib.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu divan of Mirza Ghalib (died 1869) in the Urdu Wikisource edition, with the ghazals numbered as they stand in the standard printed divan and arranged, as tradition requires, by the final letter of the rhyme. 272 ghazals. Use this edition when you want to cite a result by ghazal number; the older ghalib.diwan text carries the same poems in four refrain blocks without numbering.
ur.hali.kulliyat_wikisource: The poems of Altaf Husain Hali (died 1914), Ghalib's pupil and biographer, whose reforming Musaddas on the rise and fall of Islam (1879) turned Urdu poetry toward public and moral subjects. This selection from Urdu Wikisource holds 60 poems, ghazals and nazms alike, one line of verse per line; his prose essays on the same site are not included.
ur.insha.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu poems of Insha Allah Khan Insha (died 1817), the virtuoso of the Lucknow court of Saadat Ali Khan: ghazals, satires and experiments in every register, alongside his prose grammar of Urdu and the tale Rani Ketki. 80 poems from Urdu Wikisource, one line of verse per line.
ur.iqbal.armaghan_e_hijaz_urdu: The Urdu portion of Armaghan-e Hijaz ("Gift of the Hijaz"), Muhammad Iqbal's final, posthumously published 1938 collection, which mixes Urdu and Persian verse. Composed while Iqbal was dying, its Urdu poems return in a valedictory register to his lifelong themes of Islamic renewal, the awakened self, and the relationship between the individual and the community.
ur.iqbal.bal_e_jibril: Bal-e Jibril ("Gabriel's Wing"), Muhammad Iqbal's 1935 Urdu collection and, by common critical judgment, his greatest achievement in that language. It gathers ghazals, quatrains, and the long poem "Masjid-e Qurtaba" (on the Great Mosque of Cordoba), fusing classical ghazal form with Iqbal's philosophy of dynamic selfhood (khudi) and his call for Islamic civilizational revival.
ur.iqbal.bang_e_dra: Bang-e Dra ("The Call of the Marching Bell"), Iqbal's first Urdu poetry collection, published in 1924 and gathering work written from the 1900s onward. It spans an early patriotic phase, including the widely sung "Saare Jahan Se Achcha" ("Better Than the Entire World"), through the poems that mark his turn toward pan-Islamic and philosophical concerns in the collection's later sections.
ur.iqbal.zarb_e_kaleem: Zarb-e Kaleem ("The Rod of Moses"), Iqbal's 1936 Urdu collection, subtitled by the poet himself "A Declaration of War Against the Present Age." Its poems are pointed and polemical rather than lyrically ambiguous, attacking Western materialism, capitalism, and what Iqbal saw as the political passivity of contemporary Muslims, organized into thematic sections on religion and philosophy, education, politics, and more.
ur.mir.kulliyat_wikisource: The divan of Mir Taqi Mir (died 1810), generally ranked with Ghalib as one of the two greatest classical Urdu poets and, for many critics, the greater master of the ghazal's plain, direct pathos. Mir wrote in Delhi during a period of Mughal political collapse, and his poetry's characteristic melancholy (his own term for his manner was "soz," burning) is often read against that backdrop; Ghalib himself acknowledged Mir as his superior in the ghazal.
ur.nazeer.kulliyat_wikisource: The poems of Nazeer Akbarabadi (died 1830), the Agra poet who wrote about markets, festivals, animals, beggars and the seasons in a popular Urdu that no court poet would touch. His long stanzaic poems on Holi, Diwali, the kite season and the human condition (the Admi Nama) are the chief monument of Urdu poetry outside the ghazal. 277 poems from Urdu Wikisource, one line of verse per line.
ur.sauda.kulliyat_wikisource: The Urdu poems of Mirza Muhammad Rafi Sauda (died 1781), the great qasida writer and satirist of eighteenth-century Delhi and Lucknow and, with Mir, one of the two founders of the classical Urdu ghazal. 61 poems from Urdu Wikisource, one line of verse per line.
ur.wali.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Wali Muhammad Wali, called Wali Dakhani (died 1707), whose divan, when it reached Delhi around 1720, showed the northern poets that the Persian ghazal could be written in the vernacular and set off the classical Urdu tradition. The Deccani spelling of his text is kept. 34 ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line, the earliest Urdu in the corpus.
ur.zafar.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Bahadur Shah Zafar (died 1862), the last Mughal emperor, a pupil of Zauq and patron of Ghalib, exiled to Rangoon after 1857. His melancholy divan is read against the fall of Delhi, and the couplets most often quoted under his name include some that belong to other poets, which a search across this corpus can show. 52 ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line.
ur.zauq.diwan_wikisource: The Urdu ghazals of Muhammad Ibrahim Zauq (died 1854), poet laureate of the last Mughal court and Ghalib's rival for the favour of Bahadur Shah Zafar. Zauq stood for the plain classical manner against Ghalib's difficulty, and their two divans read as a running argument about what a ghazal should be. 66 ghazals from Urdu Wikisource, one hemistich per line.
